Strategy-guided simulation identifies 2.96 times more unique failure types per conversation and more than doubles the number of unique failing conversations relative to unguided simulation, indicating the framework is more effective at surfacing diverse and safety-critical failure modes.
AI.conclusion: The proposed automated, strategy-guided simulation and LLM-judging framework provides an effective way to evaluate multi-turn in-car conversational assistants without requiring explicit ground truth. It better exposes failure types and problematic conversations than unguided approaches and aligns well with human judgments, making it a practical tool for improving the reliability and safety of industrial ICAs.

title: Self-discovering RL in the Era of Experience: Is Learning History an Asset or a Burden?
summary: The pursuit of recursive self-improvement (RSI) toward general intelligence is divided between macro-level language model scaling and the interaction-driven principles of "Era of Experience". Yet, any self-improving architecture ultimately rests upon its underlying optimization engine: if general intelligence requires learning from grounded interaction, the reinforcement learning (RL) update rule itself must be capable of cumulative adaptation. While algorithm self-discovery has produced Disco103 that surpassed PPO to achieve SOTA benchmark performance -- its internal update machinery remains an uninspected black box. We present the first causal mechanistic audit of a self-discovered RL rule, structured directly around the five pillars of the Era of Experience: extended horizon, grounded reward scales, continuing streams, within-lifetime change, and exploration depth. By surgically pinning, freezing, and transplanting recurrent states while holding meta-parameters fixed, we test when learning history acts as an asset or a burden. Three findings organize the audit: (1) Recurrent history actively expands usable reward scales, sustaining a six-decade window versus three under zero-pinning. (2) Decoupling historical content from its maintenance reveals that the penalty of mismatched history stems from perpetual clamping; allowing imported state to evolve naturally attenuates this burden. (3) Under environmental change, controlling replay retention reverses the apparent adaptation advantage over DQN, demonstrating that external data turnover can confound internal plasticity. Validated through capability thresholds and ported to a second rule (OPEN), this work grounds macro-RSI ambitions in micro-level learning dynamics, establishing a foundational audit standard for next-generation, self-evolving RL algorithms.

AI.tldr: This paper audits a self-discovered reinforcement learning update rule, revealing how its recurrent internal state supports longer reward horizons, mitigates history mismatch when allowed to evolve, and shows that apparent adaptability can be confounded by replay data turnover.
AI.motivation: Although self-discovered RL algorithms like Disco103 outperform standard methods such as PPO, their internal update rules are opaque black boxes. For genuine recursive self-improvement and grounded general intelligence, we need to understand whether and how these learned update rules truly adapt over an agent’s lifetime, especially along the principles proposed in the "Era of Experience" framework (extended horizons, grounded rewards, continual interaction, within-lifetime change, and deep exploration).
AI.method: The authors perform a causal mechanistic audit of a self-discovered RL rule. They intervene directly on the algorithm’s recurrent internal state by pinning, freezing, and transplanting those states across time and runs, while holding meta-parameters constant. These interventions are aligned with the five "Era of Experience" pillars to test how historical information is stored, used, and potentially burdens learning. They then compare behavior under different history-manipulation regimes and against baselines like DQN, and replicate core analyses on a second learned rule (OPEN).
AI.result: (1) The recurrent history in the learned rule substantially extends the effective reward horizon, enabling useful learning over about six orders of magnitude of reward scale versus only three without history pinning. (2) When historical content is transplanted, the performance penalty mainly arises if that history is kept clamped; allowing transplanted recurrent states to update naturally reduces the negative effects of mismatch. (3) In non-stationary environments, what appears to be superior adaptation over DQN is largely explained by how replay data is retained or turned over: controlling replay retention removes the apparent adaptation edge, showing that external data dynamics can masquerade as internal plasticity. These results generalize to another self-discovered rule (OPEN).
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates that self-discovered RL update rules possess meaningful, causally identifiable mechanisms for using recurrent history, but also that naïve performance comparisons can misattribute adaptation to internal plasticity when it actually arises from data management. By establishing an intervention-based audit framework tied to the "Era of Experience" pillars, the paper provides a blueprint for analyzing and validating next-generation, self-improving RL algorithms at the level of their internal learning dynamics, helping to ground high-level RSI ambitions in concrete, testable mechanisms.

title: Constructing Challenging Browser-Use Tasks by Controlled Environment Interventions
summary: As browser-use agents improve, benchmarks keep pace by collecting new tasks, websites, and applications, often making tasks longer or more novel. This makes difficulty expensive to refresh and difficult to control: when many aspects change at once, it is unclear what actually makes a task challenging. We instead construct challenging instances from tasks agents already solve, turning difficulty into a programmable property of the environment. BreakingWeb pairs every base task with an intervention condition that preserves the user instruction, latent target, and backend success criterion while changing the environment at different web stack layers. Each intervention is deterministic, detectable, and recoverable, and is annotated with the cognitive primitive it primarily loads. The benchmark contains 519 clean/intervention task pairs across seven self-hosted websites and 29 intervention families, all graded against outcomes. We evaluate six strong browser-use agents, three GUI-only agents that see only screenshots, and humans. The construction is effective: interventions cut agent pass rate by 22.9% on average and overturn nearly half of the tasks each agent solves cleanly, whereas humans lose 10.0% on a first attempt and 5.7% after one familiarisation attempt. The dominant failure is belief failure: 75% of the six agents' failures end with a declared success although the required change never happened. Our code, data and environment are publicly available at www.breakingweb.app.

AI.tldr: BreakingWeb introduces a benchmark that makes existing solvable web tasks systematically harder through controlled interventions, revealing where browser-use agents actually fail.
AI.motivation: Existing browser-use benchmarks keep adding new tasks and sites to increase difficulty, making it costly and unclear what specifically makes tasks hard. The authors want a way to precisely control and refresh task difficulty while keeping user goals fixed, and to diagnose which cognitive capabilities current web agents lack.
AI.method: They start from web tasks that agents already solve and pair each with an ‘intervention’ version that keeps the instruction, hidden target, and success criterion the same but modifies the web environment at different layers of the stack (e.g., layout, content, interactions). Interventions are designed to be deterministic, detectable, and recoverable, and are labeled by the main cognitive primitive they stress. The benchmark spans 519 clean/intervention task pairs across seven self-hosted websites, organized into 29 intervention families, and is used to systematically test multiple browser agents, GUI-only agents, and humans.
AI.result: Across the benchmark, interventions reduce agent pass rates by 22.9% on average and flip nearly half of the tasks that agents previously solved into failures, while humans show a much smaller performance drop (10% on first try, 5.7% after one familiarization). Analysis shows that about 75% of the six agents’ failures are ‘belief failures,’ where agents think and report that they succeeded despite not having actually caused the required change.
AI.conclusion: Programmable environment interventions on already-solvable web tasks provide a scalable way to control difficulty and diagnose specific weaknesses of browser-use agents. BreakingWeb exposes that strong agents are particularly vulnerable to belief failures and environment changes that humans handle relatively well, making this benchmark a useful tool for improving and evaluating web agents going forward.

title: Grab a Coffee: Future-Aware Guidance for Discrete Diffusion with Compiled Objectives
summary: Discrete diffusion models generate sequences by iteratively resolving multiple tokens in parallel, offering a flexible alternative to left-to-right generation. However, guiding this process with a sequence-level objective is difficult because the value of one unresolved token depends on the other tokens with which it can form a high-reward sequence. Enumerating all such completions makes the whole guidance computation grow exponentially with the number of unresolved positions. We introduce COFFEE, a plug-and-play framework that avoids this enumeration by separating sequence dependence from the objective. At each diffusion step, a target-free carrier absorbs the marginal token distributions predicted by the denoiser to construct a joint model over the unresolved tokens, while a compiled finite-state model records how their combinations affect the sequence-level preference. Pairing their states allows COFFEE to transfer global preferences to unresolved positions and sample a clean reconstruction without retraining the diffusion model. The same framework supports explicit hard constraints and learned soft objectives. We evaluate COFFEE across multiple symbolic, language, and biological benchmarks, where it achieves strong control results with task-dependent quality and diversity trade-offs. By making objectives available to inference rather than only evaluation, COFFEE brings joint conditioning, completion-weighted guidance, and optimization-based constraints into pretrained neural generation, showing the potential of neural-symbolic methods in diffusion guidance.

AI.tldr: COFFEE is a plug-and-play guidance framework for discrete diffusion models that injects sequence-level objectives and constraints at inference time without retraining.
AI.motivation: Guiding discrete diffusion models with sequence-level objectives is hard because the reward for each unresolved token depends combinatorially on all other tokens, making naïve guidance exponentially expensive. The authors want a way to apply complex global objectives and constraints to pretrained discrete diffusion generators during inference.
AI.method: They introduce COFFEE, which decouples sequence dependence from the objective. A target-free carrier model at each diffusion step aggregates the denoiser’s marginal token distributions into a joint model over unresolved positions. In parallel, a compiled finite-state model encodes how combinations of tokens affect a global sequence-level objective (hard constraints or soft rewards). By pairing the states of these two models during sampling, COFFEE transfers global preferences to local token decisions, enabling constrained and guided generation without retraining the diffusion model.
AI.result: Across symbolic, natural language, and biological sequence benchmarks, COFFEE can enforce explicit hard constraints and optimize soft objectives, achieving strong control over outputs. It yields competitive quality while allowing task-dependent trade-offs between objective satisfaction, sample quality, and diversity.
AI.conclusion: COFFEE makes global objectives accessible during inference for discrete diffusion models, enabling joint conditioning and optimization-based constraints over entire sequences. This demonstrates the promise of neural-symbolic methods for principled diffusion guidance without modifying or retraining pretrained generators.

title: How to Run Statistics over LLM Judges and Trust the Results: Calibrated Inference for Small-Sample AI Evaluation with evalstats
summary: Researchers across academia increasingly base significance claims on LLM judge scores and small-sample AI evaluations. Yet without well-calibrated confidence intervals (CIs), hypothesis tests, and judge-bias corrections, such claims are unreliable. We address these issues in several contributions. First, we find that running statistics over raw LLM judge scores leads to inflated false positives: counterintuitively, for many inter-rater agreement metrics, false positive risk peaks at "almost perfect" human-LLM agreement. To help researchers understand how to run statistics over LLM judges responsibly, we present guidance and tooling for the statistical analysis of mixed human-AI judge designs, and implement nine hypothesis tests via prediction-powered inference (PPI), including the first known PPI corrections for four rank-based tests (Wilcoxon signed-rank, Mann-Whitney U, and omnibus variants). To keep PPI++ stable with small human-labeled calibration sets, we introduce bootstrap-adaptive power tuning, which shrinks the estimated weight toward a target estimated from the labeled data, and accounts for that weight's own sampling variance. Second, through Monte Carlo simulations, we derive recommendations for what CI, p-value, and FWER correction methods to use for small-sample AI evaluations (N<100), and warn researchers against bootstrap CIs. We package these recommendations into evalstats, an open-source Python package that selects calibrated methods automatically, and demonstrate it in three scenarios, including one where a real LLM judge validated at "substantial agreement" would have led a researcher to publish a spurious finding. evalstats is publicly available at https://github.com/ianarawjo/evalstats.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that naively using LLM judge scores for statistical testing leads to inflated false positives and provides principled methods, tools, and recommendations for small-sample AI evaluations using prediction-powered inference and calibrated CIs/p-values, released as the evalstats Python package.
AI.motivation: Many recent AI and NLP papers use LLMs as automatic judges to claim system improvements or effects, often with small sample sizes and without properly accounting for judge bias or statistical uncertainty. This creates a high risk of false positive findings and irreproducible results. The authors are motivated to make LLM-based evaluation statistically reliable by understanding failure modes of current practices and providing practical, easy-to-use statistical tools and guidance for mixed human–AI judging setups.
AI.method: 1) Analyze the behavior of standard inter-rater agreement metrics and statistical tests when applied to mixed human–LLM judge scores, showing analytically and empirically that running naive statistics on raw LLM scores can inflate false positives, especially at high but imperfect agreement levels. 2) Develop a framework based on prediction-powered inference (PPI) that corrects for LLM judge bias using a small human-labeled calibration set. They implement nine hypothesis tests under PPI, including novel PPI corrections for four rank-based tests (Wilcoxon signed-rank, Mann–Whitney U, and omnibus variants). 3) Introduce bootstrap-adaptive power tuning to stabilize PPI weight estimation when only a small calibration set is available, shrinking the weight toward a target estimated from labeled data and adjusting for its sampling variance. 4) Run extensive Monte Carlo simulations to compare confidence interval, p-value, and family-wise error rate correction methods for small-sample AI evaluations (N<100), testing how well they control error rates. 5) Package the recommended methods into the evalstats Python library that automatically chooses calibrated methods for a given evaluation design and demonstrate its use in several realistic evaluation scenarios.
AI.result: They find that performing standard statistical tests directly on LLM judge outputs leads to substantially inflated false positive rates, particularly when human–LLM agreement appears “almost perfect,” which can mislead researchers into overtrusting LLM judges. Through simulations, they identify which CI, p-value, and multiple-comparison correction methods maintain proper error control in small samples and which (notably bootstrap confidence intervals) systematically miscalibrate error rates. Their PPI-based tests and bootstrap-adaptive power tuning provide more reliable hypothesis testing using mixed human–LLM judging, even when the human calibration set is small. The evalstats package embodies these findings by automatically selecting and applying statistically calibrated procedures in practical evaluation workflows, and they show that in a real evaluation scenario, using naive LLM judging would have produced a spuriously significant result that evalstats correctly treats as non-significant.
AI.conclusion: Naively using LLM judges and standard statistics in AI evaluation can severely inflate false positives and produce spurious research claims, especially in small-sample studies. By extending prediction-powered inference to a wider set of tests, stabilizing it for small calibration sets, and empirically evaluating methods for N<100, the authors provide a principled, practical toolkit for reliable mixed human–AI evaluation. Their open-source evalstats package operationalizes this guidance so researchers can obtain calibrated CIs, p-values, and corrections with minimal statistical expertise, thereby improving the robustness and reproducibility of LLM-based evaluation claims.

title: Right Words, Wrong Moment: A Clinician-Grounded Analysis of Distress in 19,930 Conversations between Young People and ChatGPT
summary: Young people increasingly turn to General-Purpose Conversational Agents (GPCAs), such as ChatGPT, in moments of distress. We examine young adults' (ages 18-25) experiences using ChatGPT. We first collected 19,930 ChatGPT conversations and survey data from 158 young adults. We then selected five example conversations reflecting user distress. Finally, we asked ten clinicians to review those five conversations. We found distressed participants reported greater emotional engagement with ChatGPT and greater behavioral change from using it than their peers. When they turned to ChatGPT in moments of acute distress, ChatGPT was quick to give overly dramatic responses and excessive action-oriented suggestions. Clinicians endorsed ChatGPT's availability and much of its wording, but identified seven process failures, such as prematurely jumping to solutions. We translated clinicians' feedback into design guidelines following three stages: 1) asking about safety, 2) de-escalating intensity to restore emotional regulation, and 3) exploring concerns without agreeing with them.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how young adults in distress use ChatGPT, how it responds, what clinicians think of those interactions, and proposes safer design guidelines for such systems.
AI.motivation: Young people frequently use conversational AI like ChatGPT during emotional distress, but we know little about their real-world experiences, the quality and risks of the support they receive, and how mental health professionals evaluate these interactions. There is a need to understand both user impact and clinical concerns to inform safer, more therapeutic designs.
AI.method: The authors collected 19,930 real ChatGPT conversations and survey data from 158 young adults (ages 18–25). They identified users experiencing distress and compared their reported engagement and behavior change to non-distressed peers. They then selected five representative distress-related conversations and asked ten clinicians to review and evaluate these, focusing on strengths, weaknesses, and risks. Based on clinician feedback, they derived design recommendations.
AI.result: Distressed young adults reported stronger emotional engagement with ChatGPT and more behavior change resulting from its use than their non-distressed peers. In episodes of acute distress, ChatGPT tended to produce overly dramatic responses and to offer many action-oriented suggestions quickly. Clinicians appreciated ChatGPT’s constant availability and generally appropriate wording, but they identified seven key process failures, including prematurely jumping to problem-solving, not adequately assessing safety, and not effectively helping users regulate emotions before moving to action.
AI.conclusion: Conversational agents like ChatGPT can significantly influence distressed young adults and are often perceived as emotionally engaging and behavior-shaping. However, current response patterns can be clinically problematic, especially in acute distress. The authors propose a three-stage design framework for safer, more supportive interactions: (1) systematically assess safety, (2) first de-escalate emotional intensity to help restore regulation, and (3) explore users’ concerns in depth without prematurely agreeing with or reinforcing maladaptive views. These guidelines aim to make GPCAs more aligned with basic therapeutic processes while acknowledging that they are not replacements for professional care.

title: PrimeSeeker: Capability-Oriented Supervision for Deep Search Agents
summary: Large language model search agents are often trained with synthetic questions whose difficulty is increased through larger evidence graphs, additional hops, and longer trajectories. These global properties, however, are only indirect proxies for the local retrieval capabilities required during search. To address this mismatch, we introduce latent anchor reasoning, which consists of resolving an unnamed retrieval anchor from descriptive specifications and transferring the recovered anchor into a subsequent information demand. This primitive retrieval unit decomposes deep search into chains of coupled operations and organizes question construction around anchor resolution and relation transfer, without prescribing a canonical search path. Based on this formulation, we propose PrimeSeeker, a capability-oriented framework that constructs web-grounded anchor structures and jointly derives a question and a reference evidence skeleton. The skeleton preserves supporting evidence from construction and guides expert generation through extractive highlights of current tool observations. These highlights are removed before supervised fine-tuning, while the skeleton is subsequently reused to audit reference-step coverage for reinforcement-learning rewards. We construct 9,221 expert trajectories, training a 30B search agent. Across five deep-search benchmarks, PrimeSeeker achieves strong performance, while reference-step optimization further improves the supervised policy. The resulting trajectories exhibit low retrieval redundancy, and fixed-budget evaluation shows strong solution coverage with substantially fewer tool calls than long-horizon systems.

AI.tldr: Proposes PrimeSeeker, a framework to train LLM search agents using anchor-based retrieval units and web-grounded evidence skeletons, improving deep-search efficiency and performance with fewer tool calls.
AI.motivation: Existing training for LLM search agents relies on synthetic questions whose difficulty is controlled by global properties (e.g., large evidence graphs, more hops, longer trajectories). These global proxies do not directly target the fine-grained, local retrieval operations that actually matter during search. There is a mismatch between how tasks are constructed and the specific retrieval skills needed, leading to inefficient, redundant, or suboptimal search behaviors.
AI.method: Introduce latent anchor reasoning: a primitive retrieval unit where the model first resolves an unnamed retrieval anchor from a descriptive specification, then uses this anchor in a subsequent information request. This decomposes deep search into chains of anchor resolution and relation transfer without fixing a specific search path. Based on this, they design PrimeSeeker, which automatically constructs web-grounded anchor structures and, from them, generates both a question and a reference evidence skeleton. The skeleton records which supporting evidence was used and is used in two ways: (1) during expert trajectory generation, via extractive highlights of tool observations that guide the expert; (2) during training, where highlights are removed before supervised fine-tuning, but the skeleton is kept to check which reference steps are covered and to define reinforcement-learning rewards that favor good step coverage. Using this pipeline, they build 9,221 expert trajectories and train a 30B-parameter search agent.
AI.result: On five deep-search benchmarks, the PrimeSeeker-trained 30B search agent attains strong performance compared to existing methods. Optimizing the policy further using reference-step coverage (via RL) yields additional gains over the purely supervised policy. Analysis of the resulting trajectories shows low retrieval redundancy, and under a fixed tool-call budget, the agent attains high solution coverage with substantially fewer tool calls than long-horizon search systems.
AI.conclusion: Capability-oriented question and trajectory construction centered on latent anchor reasoning leads to more efficient and effective training of LLM search agents than approaches based on coarse global difficulty measures. PrimeSeeker’s use of anchor structures and evidence skeletons enables better supervision, more targeted reinforcement learning, and produces agents that perform well on deep-search tasks with fewer, less redundant tool calls.

title: SAGE: A Statistical Acceptance Gate for Self-Evolving Agents
summary: Large Language Model (LLM)-based agents increasingly self-evolve by editing a persistent skill document that encodes their workflow, tool-use rules, and decision logic. This loop has two steps, an optimizer that proposes a candidate edit and a gate that accepts or rejects it. Prior work has concentrated on the optimizer, while the gate still follows a naive rule that keeps any edit which improves an aggregate validation score. We show that this rule fails in two ways. First, it admits permanent regressions, since an edit can raise the average while breaking items the skill already solves. Second, it is vulnerable to the Optimizer's Curse, since the best observed score on a finite and noisy validation set is upward biased. To solve the above two limitations, we propose a statistical acceptance gate for self-evolving agents (SAGE). Compared with previous work, SAGE has two contributions. First, SAGE proposes a per-item paired comparison that evaluates the current skill and the edited skill on identical validation items, which exposes regressions that an aggregate score hides and penalizes them asymmetrically. Second, SAGE also employs a one-sided paired test that commits an edit only when its wins are statistically reliable against its losses, and it abstains otherwise. SAGE is a conservative refinement of the standard gate that recovers the baseline exactly at a boundary setting. It commits only a subset of the baseline's edits, filtering out those whose gains are unreliable or purchased by breaking already-solved items. Across five benchmarks and four backbone LLMs under an equal-budget protocol, SAGE lowers the regression rate in 19 of 20 settings and matches the baseline in the remaining one, for example from 36.5% to 0% on LiveMath and from 42.8% to 0% on OfficeQA with DeepSeek-V4. SAGE also attains the highest final score in all 20 settings, raising LiveMath from 34.15 to 48.78.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces SAGE, a statistical gate mechanism that more safely decides whether self-edited skills in LLM-based agents should be accepted, reducing regressions and improving final performance.
AI.motivation: Existing self-evolving LLM agents rely on a simple acceptance rule: keep any edit that improves an aggregate validation score. This causes two issues: (1) permanent regressions where new edits break previously solved items while still improving the average, and (2) susceptibility to the Optimizer’s Curse, because the best observed score on a finite, noisy validation set is upward biased. A better, statistically principled gate is needed to accept only reliable improvements and avoid degrading previously acquired skills.
AI.method: The authors propose SAGE (Statistical Acceptance Gate for self-Evolving agents). SAGE evaluates edits via per-item paired comparisons between the current and edited skill using the same validation items, exposing item-level regressions. It penalizes regressions asymmetrically relative to improvements. Then, it applies a one-sided paired statistical test to decide whether the wins of the edited skill over the current one are statistically significant given its losses. SAGE only commits an edit when this test passes; otherwise it abstains. The method is designed as a conservative refinement of the standard aggregate-score gate and reduces to the baseline under a specific boundary setting.
AI.result: Across five benchmarks and four backbone LLMs under an equal-budget setup, SAGE consistently reduces regression rates in 19 out of 20 settings and matches the baseline in the remaining one. In some cases it eliminates regressions entirely (e.g., from 36.5% to 0% on LiveMath and from 42.8% to 0% on OfficeQA with DeepSeek-V4). It also achieves the best final task performance in all 20 settings, for instance improving the LiveMath final score from 34.15 to 48.78.
AI.conclusion: SAGE provides a statistically grounded, conservative gate for self-evolving LLM agents that mitigates permanent regressions and the Optimizer’s Curse. By relying on per-item paired evaluation and a one-sided paired significance test, it filters out unreliable or regression-inducing edits, leading to lower regression rates and higher final performance than the traditional aggregate-score-based gate across multiple benchmarks and LLM backbones.

title: Less Uniform Discrete Diffusion is More Powerful and Scalable
summary: Although uniform diffusion language models (UDLMs) represent a promising diffusion paradigm, scaling them remains challenging. We identify the core obstacle as an over-uniform training objective and condition-target confusion during sampling. To address these, we propose Less Uniform Diffusion (LUDI), a novel UDLM framework. Specifically, we (i) introduce a less uniform loss that directs each reverse transition toward the clean token, and (ii) equip the model with per-token time embeddings that supply token-level corruption hints, enabling confidence-based few-step sampling. Experiments across scales show that LUDI yields cleaner supervision and improves few-step generation. We further continue-train a 7B autoregressive model into LUDI-7B, resulting in a UDLM capable of complex reasoning. It achieves a 3-token-per-step speedup over AR decoding and competitive performance compared with masked diffusion baselines, revealing that the full potential of UDLMs for complex generation remains to be unlocked.

AI.tldr: They introduce LUDI, an improved uniform diffusion language model framework that fixes training and sampling issues, enabling faster few-step generation and strong reasoning performance compared with autoregressive and masked diffusion baselines.
AI.motivation: Uniform diffusion language models are promising for text generation but are hard to scale because the standard training objective is too uniform and leads to confusion between conditions and targets during sampling. This limits their efficiency and quality, especially for complex reasoning and few-step generation.
AI.method: They propose Less Uniform Diffusion (LUDI), which modifies the diffusion training and sampling process in two main ways: (i) a less uniform loss that explicitly steers each reverse diffusion step toward the clean target token rather than treating all noised states equally, and (ii) per-token time embeddings that provide token-level information about the corruption level, enabling confidence-based few-step sampling instead of long, many-step diffusion chains. They also continue-train an existing 7B autoregressive model under this new UDLM scheme to create LUDI-7B.
AI.result: Experiments at multiple model scales show that LUDI provides cleaner supervision signals during training and significantly improves few-step text generation quality. LUDI-7B, obtained by continue-training a 7B autoregressive model, can perform complex reasoning, runs about three tokens per diffusion step faster than standard autoregressive decoding, and achieves competitive benchmarks relative to masked diffusion language model baselines.
AI.conclusion: By relaxing the overly uniform objective and adding per-token time information, LUDI overcomes key scalability and sampling inefficiencies of uniform diffusion language models. The results indicate that UDLMs can be both fast and capable of complex reasoning, and that there is still untapped potential in this family of models for advanced text generation tasks.

title: PowerZooJax: A JAX-based Power System Benchmark for Reinforcement Learning
summary: Power system operation is a safety-critical sequential decision-making problem, making it a natural testbed for reinforcement learning (RL). However, existing RL environments for power systems are often narrow in scope and computationally limited by CPU-based simulation workflows, making large-scale evaluation difficult. We introduce PowerZooJax, a JAX-based benchmark suite for RL in power system operation. It provides five constrained Markov decision process tasks spanning generation, transmission, distribution, distributed energy resources, and data center microgrid. By rewriting power flow, economic dispatch, market clearing, and device dynamics as JAX computation graphs, PowerZooJax keeps the entire training and evaluation loop on the GPU. Experiments show substantial speedups over CPU-based simulations and demonstrate standardized evaluation of policy returns, safety violations, and out-of-distribution stress conditions. Our open-source benchmark is available at: https://github.com/powerzoojax/PowerZooJax.

AI.tldr: Introduces PowerZooJax, a JAX-based GPU-accelerated benchmark suite for reinforcement learning in power system operation, enabling fast, standardized evaluation across five safety-critical tasks.
AI.motivation: Power system operation is a safety-critical, sequential decision-making problem and a natural application area for RL. However, existing RL environments for power systems are narrow in scope and rely on CPU-based simulation workflows, which are too slow and limited for large-scale training and evaluation. There is a need for a broad, standardized, and computationally efficient benchmark that better supports modern RL research and stress testing in this domain.
AI.method: The authors design PowerZooJax, a benchmark suite built in JAX. They formulate five constrained Markov decision process (CMDP) tasks that cover different aspects and scales of power systems: generation, transmission, distribution, distributed energy resources, and a data center microgrid. They re-implement key physical and operational models—including power flow, economic dispatch, market clearing mechanisms, and device dynamics—as differentiable JAX computation graphs. This allows the entire RL loop (simulation, training, and evaluation) to run on GPU, avoiding CPU bottlenecks. They then run experiments comparing PowerZooJax to traditional CPU-based simulators and evaluate policies under standard performance metrics, safety constraint violations, and out-of-distribution stress scenarios.
AI.result: Experiments show that the GPU-based JAX implementation significantly accelerates simulation and training compared to CPU-based workflows, achieving substantial speedups. The suite supports consistent reporting of policy performance metrics (returns), safety-related constraint violations, and robustness under stress-test conditions outside the training distribution. The toolkit is released as an open-source package at the provided GitHub link, making it accessible for the research community.
AI.conclusion: PowerZooJax provides a fast, GPU-native, and standardized RL benchmark for power system operation, addressing limitations of prior CPU-based and narrow-scope environments. By covering multiple realistic CMDP tasks and enabling efficient large-scale experimentation, it aims to facilitate more rigorous, reproducible, and safety-aware RL research in power systems. The open-source release invites broader adoption and extension by the community.

title: $τ$-Multilingual: Benchmarking Voice Agents Across Languages
summary: English-only benchmarks expose only a narrow slice of voice-agent behavior. We introduce $τ$-Multilingual, extending $τ$-Voice to Spanish, Brazilian Portuguese, Hindi, Korean, and Mandarin with native-speaker review and evaluation of generated language and spoken output. Across 4,500 full-duplex calls and five voice configurations, Spanish, Portuguese, and Hindi remain within 3.2 task-completion points of English, but Korean and Mandarin fall by 14.7 and 8.4 points. The failure modes also vary: Korean systems miss more responses, Mandarin systems interrupt more often, and both struggle with tools and entities. Grok leads task completion but scores lowest on generation quality, motivating separate task, interaction, and generation reporting. We release language packs, validated judges, and tools for community-built multilingual voice-agent evaluation.

AI.tldr: The paper presents τ-Multilingual, a multilingual extension of τ-Voice, to evaluate voice agents across six languages, revealing significant performance gaps and differing failure modes, especially for Korean and Mandarin.
AI.motivation: Current benchmarks focus mainly on English and fail to capture how voice agents behave in other languages, limiting our understanding of multilingual performance, failure modes, and user experience. There is a need for standardized, community-usable tools to evaluate multilingual voice agents in realistic, full-duplex settings.
AI.method: The authors extend the τ-Voice evaluation framework to five additional languages—Spanish, Brazilian Portuguese, Hindi, Korean, and Mandarin—using native speakers for both reviewing prompts and evaluating system outputs. They conduct 4,500 full-duplex calls across five different voice configurations, systematically measuring task completion, interaction behaviors (like interruptions and missed responses), and generation quality. They compare models, including Grok, along these dimensions and design language packs, validated judges, and tooling for broader community use.
AI.result: Spanish, Portuguese, and Hindi voice agents achieve task-completion rates within 3.2 percentage points of English, showing relatively robust multilingual transfer. In contrast, Korean and Mandarin suffer substantial drops of 14.7 and 8.4 task-completion points, respectively. Error analysis shows distinctive failure patterns: Korean systems more frequently fail to respond, Mandarin systems interrupt users more, and both languages show weaknesses with tool usage and entity handling. Grok attains the highest task-completion rates but exhibits the lowest scores on language generation quality.
AI.conclusion: Multilingual voice-agent performance is highly language-dependent, with notable weaknesses in Korean and Mandarin that are not apparent from English-only benchmarks. Because task completion, interaction behavior, and generation quality can diverge—illustrated by Grok’s strong task success but weaker generation—these dimensions should be reported separately. The released τ-Multilingual language packs, judges, and tools aim to enable standardized, community-driven evaluation of multilingual voice agents and to spur improvements, particularly for underperforming languages.

title: GeoWind2Plan: Mission-Time 3D Urban Wind Prediction for Energy-Efficient UAV Planning
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 (Spotlight). 31 pages. Code and dataset: https://github.com/DUAL-Xiao/GeoWind2Plan/
summary: In urban low-altitude flight, buildings reshape ambient wind into spatially varying 3D flow, making unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) energy depend on local wind exposure as well as path length. However, building-resolved wind information is rarely available when a mission must be planned. Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) can produce high-fidelity urban flow fields, but each simulation is tied to a fixed inflow boundary condition and can take hours to days, which is incompatible with urban UAV missions that typically last minutes to tens of minutes. We present GeoWind2Plan, a geometry-to-wind-to-planning framework for mission-time 3D urban wind prediction and energy-efficient UAV planning. Given only a background wind vector, 3D building geometry, and a start-goal pair, GeoWind2Plan transforms the building geometry into a reference-wind frame, predicts mission-relevant 3D wind patches with a localized geometry-conditioned neural operator, stitches them into a queryable local wind field, and optimizes a feasible 3D path and speed profile using a physically grounded UAV energy model. Rather than pursuing CFD-perfect reconstruction, GeoWind2Plan targets decision-useful wind prediction: trajectories are planned with predicted wind and evaluated under high-fidelity CFD wind. Across held-out urban domains, wind speeds, and mission wind-angle regimes, GeoWind2Plan performs corridor-localized wind inference in about 3 seconds, compared with roughly 8 hours for CFD. Under CFD evaluation, trajectories planned with GeoWind2Plan reduce energy by 6.9%, 12.7%, and 4.5% in tailwind, headwind, and crosswind missions relative to wind-agnostic planning, recovering 87.9%, 85.7%, and 75.0% of CFD-reference savings. These results show that fast, corridor-localized 3D urban wind prediction can make wind-aware UAV energy planning practical at mission time.

AI.tldr: GeoWind2Plan is a fast framework that predicts mission-relevant 3D urban wind fields from building geometry and background wind, enabling energy-efficient UAV path planning in seconds instead of hours-long CFD, while retaining most of the energy savings of CFD-based planning.
AI.motivation: Urban wind fields around buildings are highly complex and strongly affect UAV energy consumption, but high-fidelity CFD simulations needed to capture these effects are too slow and tied to fixed inflow conditions, making them impractical for real-time mission planning where only coarse background wind information is typically available.
AI.method: The authors propose GeoWind2Plan, which (1) takes background wind, 3D building geometry, and a start–goal pair; (2) transforms geometry into a reference-wind frame; (3) uses a localized, geometry-conditioned neural operator to predict 3D wind patches along the corridor of interest; (4) stitches these patches into a queryable local wind field; and (5) optimizes a feasible 3D UAV trajectory and speed profile using a physically based energy model, planning with the predicted wind while evaluating performance under CFD wind fields.
AI.result: On held-out urban environments, wind conditions, and mission orientations, GeoWind2Plan produces corridor-localized 3D wind predictions in about 3 seconds versus roughly 8 hours for CFD, and when trajectories planned using these predictions are evaluated in CFD wind fields, they yield 6.9%, 12.7%, and 4.5% energy reductions for tailwind, headwind, and crosswind missions compared to wind-agnostic planning, capturing 87.9%, 85.7%, and 75.0% of the energy savings achievable with CFD-based planning.
AI.conclusion: Fast, localized 3D wind prediction conditioned on urban geometry, even if not CFD-perfect, is sufficiently accurate to enable practical mission-time, wind-aware UAV energy planning, significantly improving energy efficiency over wind-agnostic plans while being computationally compatible with typical urban UAV mission durations.

title: Can We Still Trust Disaster Social Sensing? Empirical Evidence on Detecting AI-Generated Social Media Posts
summary: Disaster social sensing converts public social-media posts into evidence for situational awareness and humanitarian needs, but generative artificial intelligence (AI) can produce plausible messages that resemble eyewitness reports. This study investigates whether text-based AI detectors can reliably distinguish human-authored from AI-generated disaster posts. We construct a dataset of 12,000 texts organised into 3,000 matched semantic units from nine disasters: original human posts (H0), minimally LLM-proofread human posts (H1), factual AI-generated posts based on the same verified facts (A0), and affectively framed versions of those AI posts (A1). A separate 6,000-text corpus from 42 events supports model selection and threshold calibration. We evaluate OSM-Det, Fast-DetectGPT, Binoculars, and direct large language model (LLM) judges across five model families, then test disaster-domain calibration, a frozen-encoder linear readout, paired transformation sensitivity, and dataset artifact controls. Across fourteen frozen cross-family configurations, AUROC is 0.402-0.517 and the best prospective recall at a calibration-derived low-false-positive operating point is 3.6%; OSM-Det reaches AUROC 0.521 and 10.4% recall at a realised 6.7% false-positive rate. A disaster-trained linear head reaches AUROC 0.817, but a seven-feature surface classifier reaches 0.784 on the H0-versus-A0 contrast, and neutralising identified surface asymmetries reduces the head from 0.733 to 0.594. The head also separates A0 from A1 even though provenance is unchanged. The results show that text-based detection is not reliable enough to serve as an operational trust gate; multimodal claims, accountable sources, and other contextual evidence should be rested on to safeguard trust in disaster social sensing.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates whether existing text-based AI detectors can reliably distinguish human-written from AI-generated social-media posts about disasters, finding that they perform poorly and are not suitable as operational trust filters.
AI.motivation: As disaster response agencies increasingly rely on social-media posts for real-time situational awareness and humanitarian needs assessment, the rise of generative AI threatens to flood these channels with realistic but artificial messages, potentially undermining trust and decision-making. Stakeholders need to know whether current AI-text detectors can act as a reliable gatekeeper to filter out AI-generated content in this high-stakes domain.
AI.method: The authors create a controlled dataset of 12,000 texts grouped into 3,000 matched semantic units across nine real disasters, with four variants per unit: original human posts (H0), lightly LLM-proofread human posts (H1), fact-based AI-generated posts from the same verified facts (A0), and affectively framed AI posts (A1). They also assemble an additional 6,000-text corpus from 42 events for model selection and threshold calibration. They benchmark several detection approaches—OSM-Det, Fast-DetectGPT, Binoculars, and direct LLM judges across five model families—under frozen cross-family configurations, then explore disaster-specific calibration, a linear classifier on frozen encoders, paired transformation sensitivity, and checks for dataset artifacts and surface-feature shortcuts.
AI.result: Across fourteen frozen cross-family detector configurations, the AUROC ranges only from 0.402 to 0.517, with the best calibrated low-false-positive setting achieving just 3.6% recall; OSM-Det performs slightly better with AUROC 0.521 and 10.4% recall at a realized 6.7% false-positive rate. A disaster-domain-trained linear head on top of a frozen encoder attains AUROC 0.817, but a simple seven-feature surface-level classifier already reaches 0.784 on the H0 vs A0 task, and removing the detected surface asymmetries causes the linear head’s AUROC to drop from 0.733 to 0.594. The same head also distinguishes between A0 and A1 despite identical provenance, indicating reliance on stylistic or affective signals rather than true origin detection.
AI.conclusion: Current text-only AI detectors are too unreliable for use as operational trust gates in disaster social sensing. Even seemingly strong performance often reflects exploitation of superficial dataset artifacts and stylistic differences rather than genuine provenance detection. To safeguard trust in disaster-related information, practitioners should prioritize multimodal evidence, verified and accountable sources, and broader contextual signals instead of depending on automated text-based detection tools.

title: Mirror-Score: Calibrated, Inference-only Scoring Exposes the Limits of Sequence-compatibility Ranking in D-peptide Design
summary: D-peptides combine protease resistance with high target specificity, but computational design of D-peptide binders remains immature. Mirror-Peptidizer introduced an in silico mirror-image screening pipeline using target reflection, backbone generation, and ProteinMPNN sequence design, but its raw ProteinMPNN negative log-likelihood (NLL) ranking was not validated against measured affinities, and only 4 of 9 tested MDM2 designs bound detectably. We introduce Mirror-Score, a calibrated, inference-only scoring framework for heterochiral D-peptide/L-protein complexes, and a public benchmark of 31 crystal complexes across four target families, including 18 with literature-verified affinities. Raw ProteinMPNN NLL is not a valid affinity ranker: its pooled Spearman correlation with affinity is 0.19, and correlations reverse between MDM2/CHIP (+0.62) and gp41 (-0.70). We therefore evaluate Boltz-2 mirror-space cofolding confidence. For the complete viral-entry family (7 structures representing 3 peptides), interface predicted local distance difference test (pLDDT) achieves structure-level leave-one-out Spearman rho = 0.90 (p = 0.006) and correctly orders all three peptides by affinity, whereas NLL fails (structure-level rho = 0.18). Because only three independent chemotypes are represented, this result indicates directional consistency rather than a statistically validated predictor. Cross-family calibration does not transfer at current sample sizes, supporting family-matched calibration as the practical deployment mode. We also specify a prospective design protocol for the antimicrobial-resistance targets LasR and LecB from Pseudomonas aeruginosa, including mirrored structures, ligand-derived hotspot maps, diffusion-model-ready inputs, and Mirror-Score ranking. Code, benchmark data, structures, and analysis scripts are openly available at https://github.com/Jiadalee/Mirror-Score.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Mirror-Score, a calibrated scoring framework for ranking D-peptide binders to L-protein targets, showing that it outperforms raw ProteinMPNN negative log-likelihood and providing benchmarks, tools, and protocols for heterochiral design.
AI.motivation: D-peptides are attractive therapeutics due to protease resistance and high specificity, but current computational design methods for D-peptide binders, such as Mirror-Peptidizer, have limited validated success and lack reliable affinity ranking metrics. Raw ProteinMPNN negative log-likelihood (NLL) has not been properly validated as an affinity predictor and appears unreliable across targets. There is a need for a calibrated, target-relevant scoring framework and standardized benchmarks for heterochiral D-peptide/L-protein complex design.
AI.method: The authors build a benchmark of 31 crystal structures across four D-peptide/L-protein target families, with 18 complexes having literature-verified binding affinities. They systematically compare raw ProteinMPNN NLL scores to experimental affinities, then introduce Mirror-Score, which leverages Boltz-2 mirror-space cofolding and interface pLDDT as a structural-confidence-based scoring feature. They perform leave-one-out evaluations, particularly on the viral-entry family, and examine how well different scores correlate with experimental affinity within and across families. They also outline a prospective design protocol for LasR and LecB, including generation of mirrored targets, ligand-derived hotspot maps, diffusion-model-ready inputs, and application of Mirror-Score for ranking designs.
AI.result: The study shows that raw ProteinMPNN NLL is a poor and inconsistent affinity ranker for heterochiral complexes, with an overall Spearman correlation of 0.19 to affinity and opposite correlation signs between different target families (e.g., positive for MDM2/CHIP and negative for gp41). In contrast, Mirror-Score, via interface pLDDT from Boltz-2 mirror-space cofolding, achieves strong structure-level correlation within the viral-entry family (Spearman rho = 0.90, p = 0.006), correctly ordering all three peptide chemotypes by affinity, whereas NLL largely fails (rho = 0.18). However, the authors note that the small number of independent chemotypes limits statistical validation and that cross-family calibration does not transfer well with existing data.
AI.conclusion: Mirror-Score provides a more reliable, inference-only scoring framework than raw ProteinMPNN NLL for ranking D-peptide binders to L-protein targets, at least within target families, and suggests that family-specific calibration is the most practical strategy currently. The work also contributes a public benchmark set, open-source code, and a detailed prospective design protocol for important antimicrobial-resistance targets (LasR and LecB), thereby helping standardize and advance computational heterochiral D-peptide design.

title: Tracing mechanisms of sycophantic agreement in language models
summary: Sycophantic agreement in language models refers to the tendency to overly affirm a user's stated beliefs or preferences, often at the expense of factual accuracy. Although it is widely recognized as an alignment failure, its underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. In this work, we use causal mediation analysis to identify the mechanisms behind sycophantic agreement. We show that a stated opinion is incorporated into the residual stream of the final prompt token early, where it biases subsequent answer retrieval. A sparse set of early attention heads carries this opinion signal. Ablating these heads substantially reduces sycophancy while leaving factual accuracy largely intact. The same heads carry the opinion when it is explicitly stated, regardless of how it is phrased. When an opinion is not stated explicitly but instead conveyed through content-free pushback (e.g., ``Are you sure?"), we find a distinct set of heads that suppresses the model's original correct answer to promote a revised answer. By providing a mechanistic account of how opinions induce sycophantic agreement, this work takes a step toward developing more targeted and reliable alignment interventions.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies specific attention heads and mechanisms in language models that cause sycophantic agreement, and shows that ablating them reduces sycophancy without harming factual accuracy.
AI.motivation: Sycophantic agreement is a known alignment failure where models mirror user opinions instead of giving accurate answers, but the internal mechanisms causing this behavior are not well understood. Understanding these mechanisms is crucial for designing precise, mechanistic alignment interventions rather than relying on coarse behavioral fixes.
AI.method: The authors apply causal mediation analysis to the model’s internal activations. They trace how a user’s stated opinion is encoded into the residual stream and propagated by attention heads. They identify which early attention heads carry the opinion signal and run ablation experiments to test their causal role in sycophantic behavior, including both explicit opinions and implicit pushback like “Are you sure?”
AI.result: They find that a user’s stated opinion is encoded into the residual stream of the final prompt token early in the computation, and that a sparse set of early attention heads transmits this opinion to bias answer retrieval. Ablating these heads markedly decreases sycophantic agreement while largely preserving factual accuracy. For explicit opinions, the same heads are activated regardless of phrasing. For content-free pushback, a different set of heads suppresses the original correct answer and promotes a revised one.
AI.conclusion: Sycophantic agreement in language models is mediated by identifiable, sparse attention circuitry rather than being a diffuse property of the whole network. Different but specific heads transmit explicit opinions versus implement revision under pushback. This mechanistic understanding enables more targeted and reliable alignment interventions by selectively modifying or controlling these components instead of applying broad, behavior-only tuning.

title: SMat-Attention: Structured Long-Context Sequence Modeling
summary: Long-context sequence models face a fundamental tradeoff: softmax attention uses flexible token-level interactions at quadratic cost, whereas linear attention obtains linear-time training and constant-time decoding by compressing history into a fixed-size state. In this work, we ask whether we can connect these regimes through a tunable notion of structure. To this end, we introduce Structured Matrix Attention (SMat-Attention) via a family of causal masks with structured long-range routing whose row supports have VC-dimension $d$. In our construction, $d=1$ recovers the standard causal mask, and increasing $d$ permits richer subset-routing patterns. We give chunkwise forward and backward algorithms to enable hardware-efficiency. For sequences of length $T$, the hard-routing construction takes $O(T^{2-3/d}+T)$ work, despite the mask being dense, for our prescribed family. In fixed-horizon streaming, decoding after the distant prefix takes constant time per token using $O(T^{1-1/d})$ cached states. SMat-Attention therefore makes VC-dimension an explicit knob governing access-pattern complexity, prefill cost, and decoding memory. Empirically, subset-routing and rule-assisted multi-key retrieval experiments illustrate the masks' routing expressiveness. Extensions to Mamba-2 and Gated DeltaNet using learned routing with top-$k$ query reads retain subquadratic prefill, improve recall accuracy over the backbones in several settings, and achieve comparable small-scale language-modeling performance.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Structured Matrix Attention (SMat-Attention), a family of attention masks parameterized by VC-dimension that interpolates between dense softmax and highly structured linear-like attention, achieving subquadratic prefill and efficient decoding while preserving expressive routing abilities.
AI.motivation: Long-context sequence models suffer from a tradeoff: softmax attention is expressive but has quadratic cost, while linear attention is efficient but compresses history too aggressively, limiting flexible token-level interactions. The authors aim to design an attention mechanism that smoothly trades off between these extremes using a principled structural parameter, while maintaining hardware efficiency and strong empirical performance.
AI.method: They define a family of causal attention masks with structured long-range routing whose row supports have VC-dimension d. This VC-dimension serves as a knob controlling routing complexity. A specific hard-routing construction yields masks that are dense but admit efficient chunkwise forward and backward algorithms. Complexity for sequence length T is O(T^{2-3/d}+T) work for prefill, and in fixed-horizon streaming, decoding after a distant prefix uses O(T^{1-1/d}) cached states and constant time per token. They also integrate learned routing (with top-k query reads) into architectures like Mamba-2 and Gated DeltaNet.
AI.result: Theoretically, they show that the VC-dimension of the row supports controls the tradeoff between expressiveness and computational/memory cost, with explicit bounds for prefill work and decoding memory. Empirically, subset-routing and rule-assisted multi-key retrieval tasks demonstrate the routing expressiveness of the masks. When applied to Mamba-2 and Gated DeltaNet with learned routing, the extended models maintain subquadratic prefill while improving recall accuracy relative to the base models and achieving comparable performance on small-scale language modeling benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: SMat-Attention provides a principled, tunable way to interpolate between fully flexible and highly structured attention by making VC-dimension an explicit control parameter on routing complexity. This yields attention mechanisms with subquadratic prefill, efficient streaming decoding, and strong routing expressiveness, and can be effectively incorporated into modern sequence models like Mamba-2 and Gated DeltaNet without sacrificing language-modeling quality.

title: Reliable but Design-Sensitive: Instrument Uncertainty in LLM Annotation
comment: Accepted to "3rd Workshop on Uncertainty-Aware NLP" @ EMNLP 2026 (archival)
summary: Large language models (LLMs) can give reliable labels under one setup yet change those labels when researchers make other reasonable design choices. We tested seven LLMs, 12 task designs, three independent runs, and 3,000 tweets labeled for offensive language and hate speech. Repeating the same model and task design produced high agreement (median Fleiss' $κ= 0.91$). Agreement fell when we changed the task design for the same tweets (median Cohen's $κ= 0.76$). Task design and model choice increased the variance of estimated prevalence by factors of 76.7 for offensive language and 110.6 for hate speech compared with sampling variance alone. Variation across LLM task designs reached 560-572 basis points, compared with 270-331 basis points across five human instrument versions. Confidence scores did not solve this problem. They tracked repeated model outputs more closely than agreement with human labels, and grouping six tweets in one prompt lowered mean offensive-language confidence by 660 basis points. We call the variation caused by task design and model choice instrument uncertainty. Researchers can measure it only by comparing reasonable task designs. Repeating one setup or relying on confidence scores cannot replace that test.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that large language models (LLMs) used as annotators give highly inconsistent labels across reasonable task designs and models, creating large uncertainty in prevalence estimates for offensive language and hate speech.
AI.motivation: Researchers increasingly use LLMs as cheap, fast annotators for social science and content moderation tasks, assuming that a well-specified single prompt/model setup produces reliable labels. However, we do not know how much results change when researchers make other equally reasonable design decisions (different prompts, formats, or models). This threatens the validity and comparability of empirical findings that rely on LLM-generated labels.
AI.method: The authors systematically evaluated seven LLMs across 12 different task designs (e.g., prompt wording, instructions, tweet grouping), with three independent runs per setup, on a dataset of 3,000 tweets previously labeled for offensive language and hate speech by humans. They quantified agreement using reliability statistics (Fleiss’ kappa for repeated runs of the same setup, Cohen’s kappa for different task designs) and measured how task design and model choice affect variance in estimated prevalence. They compared this to human-instrument variation, analyzed confidence scores from the models, and examined how prompt-level grouping affects both labels and confidence.
AI.result: (1) Repeating the same model and task design yields very high internal consistency (median Fleiss’ κ=0.91). (2) Changing task design for the same tweets lowers agreement substantially (median Cohen’s κ=0.76), even when all designs are reasonable. (3) Task design and model choice massively inflate variance in prevalence estimates—by factors of about 77 for offensive language and 111 for hate speech compared to sampling variance alone. (4) Variation across LLM task designs is 560–572 basis points, much larger than the 270–331 basis points observed across five human instrument versions. (5) Model confidence scores correlate strongly with repeated outputs of the same setup but not with agreement to human labels, and they are themselves sensitive to task design (e.g., grouping six tweets per prompt lowers offensive-language confidence by 660 basis points).
AI.conclusion: LLM-based labeling pipelines suffer from substantial “instrument uncertainty” driven by task design and model choice, which can dominate sampling error and exceed human-instrument variation. High agreement within a single fixed setup and high model confidence scores are misleading indicators of reliability. To obtain credible inferences from LLM annotations, researchers must explicitly measure instrument uncertainty by comparing multiple reasonable task designs; simply repeating one configuration or relying on model confidence cannot substitute for this. The paper cautions against uncritical use of single LLM setups in empirical research and measurement tasks.

title: LongCat-DeepResearch Technical Report
summary: We present LongCat-DeepResearch, a deep research system that combines an enhanced LongCat model with a multi-agent workflow for producing comprehensive, evidence-grounded reports. The workflow separates global planning from detailed investigation and coordinates revision at the section level. Multiple planning agents first explore external sources and refine an actionable research plan, termed ResearchSpec. Research agents then investigate and draft their assigned sections in parallel, gathering additional evidence in separate contexts as their analyses develop. Once the sections are assembled, global review guides targeted local revisions, reducing reliance on repeated full-report rewriting. This workflow also supports the construction of research tasks and trajectories for the mid-training and post-training of LongCat's general-purpose models. LongCat-DeepResearch achieves 55.25 on DeepResearchBench, 51.35 on DeepResearchBench II, and 79.83 on ResearchRubrics. On an in-house benchmark, it scores 76.04, ranking second among four compared systems. Development-set analyses show benefits from combining planning perspectives, while further planning refinement has mixed effects. Additional editing improves average automatic readability preference across two benchmarks, with different trends on each.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces LongCat-DeepResearch, a multi-agent deep research system that uses an enhanced LongCat model and a structured workflow to generate comprehensive, evidence-based reports, achieving strong performance on multiple research benchmarks.
AI.motivation: To improve automated deep research systems so they can generate long, coherent, and well-evidenced reports efficiently. Existing systems often entangle planning with writing, rely on repeated end-to-end rewrites, and struggle to coordinate multiple agents or contexts when exploring external sources, which limits quality and scalability.
AI.method: The authors design a multi-agent workflow around an enhanced LongCat model. First, multiple planning agents explore external sources and collaboratively build a structured research plan called a ResearchSpec, separating global planning from local writing. Then specialized research agents, each assigned to sections defined in the ResearchSpec, independently gather evidence in separate contexts and draft their sections in parallel. After assembling the full draft, a global review stage identifies issues and triggers targeted local revisions at the section level rather than rewriting the full report. The workflow is also used to generate research tasks and trajectories for training and improving LongCat’s general-purpose models during mid- and post-training.
AI.result: LongCat-DeepResearch attains scores of 55.25 on DeepResearchBench, 51.35 on DeepResearchBench II, and 79.83 on ResearchRubrics. On an internal benchmark it scores 76.04, placing second among four evaluated systems. Ablation-style development-set analyses show that combining multiple planning agents yields benefits, whereas further increasing or refining planning does not always improve performance. Additional editing stages enhance automatic readability metrics on average, though the degree and nature of the improvement differ across benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Separating global planning from section-level investigation and revision, and coordinating multiple agents via the ResearchSpec, leads to more effective and scalable deep research workflows. LongCat-DeepResearch demonstrates competitive or strong performance on several benchmarks, shows that multi-perspective planning and targeted local editing can be beneficial, and provides a framework for generating training data to further improve general-purpose research models. However, the mixed effects of more intensive planning and varying readability trends suggest that the workflow still has trade-offs and room for optimization.

title: Beyond the Context Window: An Adaptive Entropy-Based Routing Framework for Hybrid Retrieval and Long-Context Language Models
summary: Modern large language models now support context windows of more than one million tokens, which has raised the question of whether retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is still necessary. Pure long-context (LC) processing is expensive and is known to under-attend to information placed in the middle of long inputs, while pure RAG is fast but bounded by retrieval quality and prone to errors when retrieved chunks are partially relevant or contradictory. We propose the Entropy-Driven Adaptive Router (EDAR), a framework that decides at inference time whether to answer a query from retrieved chunks or to escalate it to full long-context processing. The decision uses the predictive entropy of the token-level probability distribution computed over the first few generated tokens of the RAG response. The entropy threshold is selected on a held-out validation set by sweeping cost against accuracy. Experiments compare EDAR against pure-RAG and pure-LC baselines on LongBench v2 and Infinity-Bench. Predictive entropy correlates strongly with hallucination rate on a held-out set of 2,000 generations (Pearson r = 0.85, 95% CI [0.83, 0.87]). On the long-context benchmarks, EDAR retains 97.4% of the accuracy of the pure long-context baseline while reducing total token expenditure by 70.7%, escalating only 18.2% of incoming queries. The accuracy gap between EDAR and the pure long-context system is not statistically distinguishable from zero at standard sample sizes. Predictive entropy is a useful model-internal signal for routing between RAG and long-context inference, and a threshold-based hybrid system can recover most of the accuracy of long-context models at a small fraction of the cost. The framework does not depend on a specific retriever or LC backbone, and it does not require additional supervision beyond what is normally produced during decoding.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes EDAR, a hybrid system that dynamically decides whether to answer with standard RAG or escalate to full long‑context inference, using predictive entropy of early generated tokens to balance accuracy and cost.
AI.motivation: As LLMs gain million‑token context windows, it is unclear when expensive long‑context processing is actually needed versus cheaper retrieval‑augmented generation. Pure long‑context models can miss information in the middle of very long inputs and are costly, while pure RAG depends heavily on retrieval quality and can hallucinate when retrieved chunks are only partially relevant or inconsistent. The authors want a principled, automatic way to choose between these two regimes per query, trading off accuracy and computational cost without extra supervision.
AI.method: They introduce Entropy-Driven Adaptive Router (EDAR), which first answers a query using RAG and inspects the token‑level probability distribution for the first few generated tokens. It computes predictive entropy over these early tokens as a model‑internal uncertainty signal. A threshold on this entropy, tuned on a validation set by sweeping accuracy vs. cost, determines whether to trust the RAG answer or escalate the query to full long‑context (LC) processing. The framework is agnostic to the retriever and LC backbone and uses only signals already available during decoding, so no extra training labels are needed.
AI.result: On LongBench v2 and Infinity-Bench, predictive entropy is highly correlated with hallucination rate (Pearson r = 0.85, 95% CI [0.83, 0.87]) on a held‑out set of 2,000 generations. With an appropriately chosen threshold, EDAR keeps 97.4% of the accuracy of a pure LC baseline while cutting total token usage by 70.7%, escalating only 18.2% of queries. Statistically, the residual accuracy gap between EDAR and pure LC is indistinguishable from zero at typical sample sizes, demonstrating that the hybrid system preserves nearly all performance while saving substantial compute.
AI.conclusion: Predictive entropy over early generated tokens is an effective and inexpensive internal signal for routing between RAG and long‑context inference. A simple threshold‑based router (EDAR) can capture almost all the accuracy of always using long‑context models at a fraction of the token and compute cost, without retriever‑ or backbone‑specific assumptions and without extra supervision beyond standard decoding outputs.

title: A Polyphonic Conception of AI Understanding
summary: When a doctor, a judge, or an engineer must decide whether to trust an AI model's output, they cannot avoid asking what the model understands. Purely mathematical or statistical descriptions struggle to distinguish trustworthy from untrustworthy outputs without reintroducing the question of AI understanding in all but name. Yet the question is ill-framed as it stands, because the inherited concept operates within a monophonic paradigm: the idea that a cognitive system's understanding of something must be localised to a single mechanism underpinning all the capacities conferred by such understanding. Drawing on a wide range of mechanistic evidence, we show that LLMs are pervasively polyphonic: outputs emerge from coalitions of parallel mechanisms of uneven reliability, which variously complement, duplicate, or drown out one another, with several coalitions sufficing for a task without any one being indispensable. Polyphony not only complicates attributions of understanding, but renders monophonic inference patterns hazardous. In response, we develop a conception of understanding fit for polyphonic AI. It centres on sound circuitry that is reliably and correctly recruited and in control of outputs. Attributions of understanding thereby become tractable claims about internal organisation, and can do the work of guiding trust in AI.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that large language models (LLMs) are inherently ‘polyphonic’—their outputs arise from many overlapping mechanisms—so we need a new, mechanistically grounded notion of AI understanding to decide when to trust them.
AI.motivation: Existing debates about whether AI ‘understands’ things are framed using a monophonic paradigm: understanding is assumed to be localized in a single, unified mechanism. This does not fit how LLMs actually work and makes it hard to specify when their outputs are trustworthy. Practitioners (doctors, judges, engineers) need a principled way to decide when to rely on AI, but current purely mathematical/statistical accounts cannot distinguish reliable from unreliable outputs without implicitly appealing to some notion of understanding.
AI.method: The authors draw on mechanistic interpretability and related evidence about LLM internals to argue that these models are ‘pervasively polyphonic’: many parallel mechanisms contribute to outputs with varying reliability, sometimes cooperating, sometimes conflicting. They then use this mechanistic picture to construct a new, explicitly polyphonic conception of understanding, built around the idea of ‘sound circuitry’ that is reliably recruited and controls the model’s outputs for a given task.
AI.result: They show that, in LLMs, multiple overlapping coalitions of internal mechanisms can each be sufficient for a task, and no single mechanism is strictly necessary. This polyphonic structure makes it unsafe to apply traditional, monophonic inference patterns when assessing understanding or trustworthiness. As a constructive result, they offer criteria for identifying ‘sound circuitry’—subsets of mechanisms that are reliable, correct, and actually in control of the output—so that understanding claims can be grounded in internal organization rather than vague behavioral tests.
AI.conclusion: The traditional, monophonic concept of understanding is inadequate for modern AI systems like LLMs. Because these systems are polyphonic, we must instead attribute understanding in terms of whether sound internal circuitry is reliably and correctly recruited and actually governs outputs for particular tasks. Framed this way, attributions of understanding become concrete, mechanistic claims that can meaningfully guide when and how humans should trust AI systems in high-stakes domains.

title: When Should LLMs Trust Their Own Revisions? A Risk-Aware Study of Intrinsic Self-Correction
summary: Intrinsic self-correction asks a language model to revise its own answer without receiving new external evidence. A second pass can recover mistakes, but it can also overturn answers that were already correct. We study this trade-off across 29 open-weight LLMs on BoolQ, GSM8K, and Corr2Cause by tracking correctness transitions between initial and revised answers. Aggregate accuracy can conceal substantially different revision behavior: for example, Llama-3.1-8B improves by 25.5 percentage points on GSM8K, while refinement changes 19.1% of initially correct answers into wrong ones. A controlled BoolQ study further shows that refinement prompts shift the balance between recovery and harm. We then compare three runtime choices: keeping the initial answer, always accepting the revision, and selectively invoking revision using signals available after the initial response. The comparison identifies settings where learned gating is useful and others where a simpler unconditional policy performs better. These results suggest treating intrinsic self-correction as a revision policy rather than as a uniformly beneficial second pass, and evaluating it through both the corrections it recovers and the errors it introduces.
