AI.tldr: The paper empirically studies how well language models can improve their own answers through a second-pass intrinsic self-correction, showing that while accuracy often improves, it can also significantly harm already-correct answers and should be treated as a revision policy choice rather than an automatic good.
AI.motivation: Intrinsic self-correction is widely used—asking an LLM to rethink or refine its answer without new external evidence—under the assumption that a second pass is almost always beneficial. However, this assumption is largely untested and may hide a trade-off: the same mechanism that fixes mistakes might also corrupt previously correct answers. The authors aim to systematically characterize this trade-off across models, datasets, and prompting setups, and to guide when and how self-correction should be used at inference time.
AI.method: The authors evaluate 29 open-weight LLMs on three benchmarks (BoolQ for reading comprehension, GSM8K for math word problems, and Corr2Cause for causal reasoning). For each model and task, they collect an initial answer and a refined answer generated via intrinsic self-correction prompts, then track transitions: wrong→right (recovery), right→wrong (harm), wrong→wrong, and right→right. They analyze how aggregate accuracy changes can mask different underlying transition patterns, and conduct a controlled study on BoolQ to see how different refinement prompts affect the balance between recovery and harm. Finally, they compare three runtime policies: (1) keeping the initial answer, (2) always accepting the refinement, and (3) selectively invoking or accepting refinement via learned gating using signals available after the initial response.
AI.result: Across models and tasks, intrinsic self-correction often improves overall accuracy but also converts a nontrivial fraction of correct initial answers into incorrect ones. For instance, Llama-3.1-8B gains 25.5 percentage points on GSM8K after refinement, yet 19.1% of its initially correct answers become wrong. Different models with similar net accuracy gains can have very different patterns of recoveries vs. harms. Prompt design strongly influences this trade-off, as shown in the BoolQ study: some refinement prompts increase recoveries at the cost of more harms. In the policy comparison, learned gating can sometimes yield better trade-offs than unconditional strategies, but in other settings simple policies like always keeping the initial answer or always accepting the revision perform as well or better.
AI.conclusion: Intrinsic self-correction should not be assumed to be uniformly beneficial. It acts as a revision operator with a distinct recovery–harm trade-off that depends on the model, task, and prompt. Evaluations should look beyond net accuracy gains to the full transition matrix of corrections vs. newly introduced errors. At deployment time, self-correction is best treated as a policy design problem—choosing when and how to refine, and whether to adopt gating or simple unconditional strategies—rather than indiscriminately adding a second-pass refinement step.

title: GeoOutageBench: Benchmarking Ambiguity-aware, Ontology-grounded Geospatiotemporal KGQA for Multimodal Power Outage and Resilience Analysis
comment: 13 pages, 6 figures, 7 tables. Accepted to the 34th ACM International Conference on Advances in Geographic Information Systems (SIGSPATIAL '26), November 3-6, 2026, Riverside, CA, USA
summary: We introduce GeoOutageBench, a benchmark for assessing LLM-based geospatiotemporal KGQA for multimodal outage and resilience analysis. Unlike existing KGQA benchmarks for Web knowledge, GeoOutageBench considers a spatiotemporal KG that integrates visual, textual, and structured data from outage records, remote sensing, weather observations, storm and power events, geographic entities, and domain ontologies. It provides a competency query taxonomy at different difficulty levels from spatiotemporal containment and proximity, spatiotemporal co-occurrence analysis, multimodal evidence, to hypothetical evaluation. Over multimodal KG and query classes, GeoOutageBench provides user-configurable evaluation of three important, highly coherent yet less studied tasks: (1) LLMs' understanding for ambiguous geospatiotemporal questions in terms of NL to SPARQL interpretation, (2) query-driven assessment of ontology utility, and (3) answer accuracy of multimodal KGQA retrieval. GeoOutageBench provides a design principle and foundation for assessing LLM-KG systems that support real-world infrastructure resilience analysis. Our benchmark, source code, data, results, and other documentation are available at https://github.com/UCF-SAGE/GeoOutageBench.

AI.tldr: GeoOutageBench is a benchmark to evaluate how well LLM-based systems answer complex geospatial, temporal, and multimodal questions about infrastructure outages and resilience using knowledge graphs.
AI.motivation: Existing KGQA benchmarks mostly focus on static Web knowledge and text-centric questions, which do not reflect the multimodal, spatiotemporal, and domain-specific reasoning needed for real-world outage and resilience analysis. There is a need for a standardized way to test LLMs on these complex, ambiguous geospatiotemporal questions over integrated, heterogeneous data sources.
AI.method: The authors build a spatiotemporal knowledge graph that integrates visual, textual, and structured data from multiple outage- and hazard-related sources (outage records, remote sensing, weather observations, storm and power events, geographic entities, and ontologies). On top of this KG, they design a competency-based query taxonomy with multiple difficulty levels, ranging from basic containment and proximity queries to co-occurrence analysis, multimodal evidence usage, and hypothetical evaluation. They then define three evaluation tasks—NL to SPARQL interpretation, ontology utility assessment, and multimodal KGQA answer accuracy—and provide a user-configurable benchmark framework with code, data, and metrics.
AI.result: GeoOutageBench offers a structured set of query classes and tasks that expose LLMs’ strengths and weaknesses in handling ambiguous geospatiotemporal questions, leveraging multimodal evidence, and using ontologies during KGQA. The benchmark demonstrates that these intertwined capabilities can be systematically evaluated over a complex, real-world outage and resilience knowledge graph, and the released artifacts enable reproducible experimentation.
AI.conclusion: GeoOutageBench establishes a principled benchmark for evaluating LLM-based KGQA systems in the context of infrastructure outage and resilience, emphasizing multimodal, spatiotemporal reasoning and ontology-aware querying. It serves as a foundational resource and design pattern for developing and assessing future LLM-KG systems in similar real-world, data-rich domains.

title: Hyperspherical Semantic Trajectory Analysis: Mapping Technological Diffusion across Academic Preprints, Patent Signals, and Compute Scaling
summary: Macroeconomic productivity metrics, such as Total Factor Productivity, register technological breakthroughs with multi-year reporting lags due to administrative survey intervals and national accounting conventions. This paper introduces Hyperspherical Semantic Trajectory Analysis (HSTA), an unsupervised quantitative methodology that tracks technology diffusion directly from unstructured scientific and commercial text streams. We analyze 30,000 filtered document records spanning academic preprints from arXiv and patent application records from the USPTO. By projecting high-dimensional Transformer sentence embeddings onto unit hyperspheres using Spherical K-Means clustering across eight primary sub-topics and UMAP manifold reductions, HSTA formalizes two quantitative metrics: (1) Semantic Centroid Vector Drift, which tracks vocabulary shifts between temporal sub-corpora to identify structural paradigm transformations; and (2) Commercialization Offset, which evaluates cross-corpus peak density alignments between scientific discovery and intellectual property filings. Linking quarterly topic volume velocity with physical hardware metrics from the Epoch AI database, Vector Autoregressive F-tests demonstrate that quarterly paper volume velocity alone does not Granger-cause frontier compute allocation surges at conventional statistical significance levels, highlighting the necessity of conditioning textual signals on physical capital constraints. Empirical results reveal that sub-topics covering Large Language Models (with a drift metric of 0.332) and Artificial Intelligence Systems (with a drift metric of 0.234) undergo the highest rate of semantic evolution, offering an objective, real-time mechanism to complement traditional economic statistics.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a text-based, real-time way to measure technological change and its commercialization, using modern NLP on scientific papers and patents instead of slow macroeconomic statistics.
AI.motivation: Traditional productivity measures like Total Factor Productivity detect technological breakthroughs only with multi‑year lags because they depend on slow surveys and accounting data. Policymakers and researchers need faster signals of when and how new technologies emerge, diffuse, and start to be commercialized, especially in fast‑moving fields like AI. The paper aims to build an objective, automated, and timely metric of technological progress directly from large text streams.
AI.method: The authors introduce Hyperspherical Semantic Trajectory Analysis (HSTA), an unsupervised pipeline applied to ~30,000 arXiv preprints and USPTO patent applications. They: (1) encode document sentences with Transformer-based embeddings; (2) project these embeddings onto a unit hypersphere; (3) cluster them with Spherical K-Means into eight main sub-topics; (4) apply UMAP for manifold visualization and dimensionality reduction; (5) define two metrics: (a) Semantic Centroid Vector Drift—measuring how each topic’s cluster centroid moves over time, capturing shifts in vocabulary and underlying concepts; (b) Commercialization Offset—measuring how the temporal density peaks of scientific and patent texts align, indicating time lags between discovery and commercialization. They then link quarterly topic-volume growth to hardware usage metrics from the Epoch AI database and run Vector Autoregressive (VAR) models with Granger-causality F-tests.
AI.result: Using HSTA, they find that topics related to Large Language Models and Artificial Intelligence Systems exhibit the largest semantic drifts (0.332 and 0.234, respectively), indicating rapid conceptual and vocabulary evolution in these areas. The Commercialization Offset metric quantifies the timing alignment between research and patenting, though exact offsets are not detailed in the abstract. VAR-based Granger-causality tests show that changes in paper volume alone do not statistically explain surges in frontier compute use, implying that textual signals need to be interpreted together with physical compute constraints.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that HSTA can provide a real-time, text-based, quantitative lens on technological change that complements slow-moving macroeconomic indicators. Rapid semantic drift in LLMs and AI Systems highlights these as particularly dynamic technological frontiers. However, simply tracking research volume is insufficient to explain hardware investment patterns; integrating text-derived signals with measures of physical capital is necessary for a fuller understanding of technological diffusion and its macroeconomic impact.

title: An Exact Generate - Transform Decomposition of Small-LLM Team Scaling Across Orchestration Architectures
summary:
Replacing one LLM agent with a collaborating team can raise accuracy, but whether scaling the team helps, and which architecture to scale, is unclear. Sweeping eight agent orchestration architectures across five instruction-tuned 7-9B models, five short-answer benchmarks, and an executable-code benchmark up to 30 calls, we find that the returns to team scaling are sharply task-dependent: from three to thirty calls accuracy rises by up to 17 points on the two arithmetic word-problem benchmarks (GSM8K, GSMHard) but by at most four on ARC, GPQA, and MMLU, for every architecture, a split the usual task-averaged number conceals. Proposer-Critic captures the arithmetic gains, scaling steepest and, in aggregate, surpassing every other architecture at the largest budget (item-clustered intervals exclude zero), though it ranks among the weakest elsewhere, and no architecture wins across tasks.
  We explain these trajectories with an exact generate-transform decomposition. Partitioning any workflow into proposal coverage and a downstream transform, any accuracy change splits exactly into an extensive coverage dividend and an intensive transformation change. The decomposition diagnoses each task: arithmetic offers coverage headroom that a critic-guided transform converts, whereas the multiple-choice benchmarks either saturate in coverage or fail to convert it, and on open-ended code generative recovery nearly vanishes so accuracy tracks coverage. At equal call budgets token cost still varies 2.1x. Extra calls therefore create candidate opportunity that only some architectures, on some tasks, convert. Team scaling is a task- and architecture-specific bet, not a uniform lever.

AI.tldr: The paper studies whether using more collaborating LLM agents actually improves accuracy, shows that benefits depend heavily on the task, and introduces a decomposition that explains when and why multi-agent scaling helps.
AI.motivation: Multi-agent LLM systems often outperform single agents, but it is unclear if simply adding more agents or calls consistently improves performance, and which collaboration architectures are worth scaling. Prior work usually reports task-averaged gains, masking important differences between benchmark types. The authors want a principled way to measure and explain the returns to scaling LLM teams across tasks and architectures.
AI.method: They systematically evaluate eight agent orchestration architectures (including Proposer-Critic) across multiple 7–9B instruction-tuned models, five short-answer benchmarks (GSM8K, GSMHard, ARC, GPQA, MMLU), and one executable-code benchmark. They vary the number of calls from 3 to 30 to test scaling. They then introduce an exact generate–transform decomposition that splits each workflow into proposal coverage (how many good candidates are generated) and a downstream transform (how those candidates are filtered/combined), and use this to analyze how accuracy changes with more calls.
AI.result: Scaling from 3 to 30 calls yields large gains (up to +17 accuracy points) on arithmetic word-problem benchmarks (GSM8K, GSMHard) but minimal gains (≤4 points) on ARC, GPQA, and MMLU, across all architectures. Proposer-Critic benefits most on arithmetic tasks and becomes the top architecture at the highest budget, but it is relatively weak on other tasks, and no single architecture dominates across all benchmarks. The generate–transform decomposition shows that arithmetic tasks have remaining coverage headroom that critic-guided transforms can exploit; multiple-choice tasks either quickly saturate in coverage or cannot convert extra coverage into accuracy; and on open-ended code tasks, gains from generative recovery are negligible so accuracy mostly tracks coverage. Token cost at fixed call budgets still varies by about 2.1x across architectures.
AI.conclusion: More agents or more calls are not universally beneficial. The effectiveness of scaling LLM teams strongly depends on both the task type and the orchestration architecture. Their generate–transform decomposition provides a diagnostic lens: extra calls mainly create more candidate solutions (coverage), but only some architectures in some tasks can effectively transform that extra coverage into higher accuracy. Thus, team scaling should be treated as a targeted, task-specific strategy rather than a generic knob to improve performance everywhere.

title: The Detectability Gap: Hidden Heterogeneity in Hallucination Detection Across Language Models
summary: Sampling based consistency is widely used for hallucination detection, yet aggregate performance can conceal systematic differences in which errors are detectable. This work studies that heterogeneity across four language models and three factual question answering datasets. Partitioning hallucinations by answer agreement reveals high agreement (Ghost) and low agreement (Flickering) regimes with an apparent detectability gap of $0.35$ to $0.46$ AUC. Because the statistics used to define the regimes and measure this gap are strongly coupled ($|ρ|\approx0.94$ to $1.00$), the raw result is treated as a property of agreement based detection rather than independent evidence. After freezing regime assignments, lexical and semantic response dispersion preserve the asymmetry, with bootstrap $95\%$ intervals excluding zero in all $12$ model and dataset settings. A stricter test using individual diffusion trajectories and no cross seed information preserves the asymmetry across all three LLaDA datasets ($p<0.005$) and directionally across all three Dream datasets, with one reaching significance. The hard regime varies substantially in prevalence across models ($16\%$ to $77\%$), and matched prompts frequently change regimes between models. These findings show that aggregate detection metrics conceal persistent, model dependent heterogeneity in language model failures and motivate regime conditioned evaluation.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that sampling-based hallucination detection works very differently on different kinds of hallucinations and different models, so average scores are misleading.
AI.motivation: Hallucination detection methods that rely on sampling (e.g., measuring disagreement across multiple generations) are widely used and evaluated with aggregate metrics such as overall AUC. However, these averages can hide systematic differences in which hallucination errors are actually detectable, and how this varies across models and datasets. The authors want to understand and quantify this hidden heterogeneity to improve evaluation and use of hallucination detectors.
AI.method: The authors analyze hallucination detection based on sampling consistency across four language models and three factual QA datasets. They partition hallucinations into regimes based on how often different samples from the same model agree on an incorrect answer: high-answer-agreement hallucinations (Ghost) and low-answer-agreement hallucinations (Flickering). They compute detection performance (AUC) within each regime. Because the regime definition and detection statistic are highly correlated, they then freeze regime assignments and re-evaluate detectability using alternative dispersion-based signals (lexical and semantic response dispersion), with bootstrap CIs. Finally, they run a stricter test that considers individual diffusion trajectories without cross-seed information, checking whether the detectability asymmetry persists. They also measure how prevalent the hard regime is across models and how regime assignments shift for matched prompts between models.
AI.result: They find two distinct hallucination regimes: Ghost (high answer agreement) and Flickering (low answer agreement), with a large detection gap of about 0.35–0.46 AUC between them using agreement-based detection. Because of the strong coupling between how regimes are defined and how detection is measured (correlation |ρ|≈0.94–1.00), this is interpreted as a property of agreement-based detection rather than independent evidence. When regime assignments are frozen, lexical and semantic dispersion metrics still show a robust detectability asymmetry, with bootstrap 95% confidence intervals excluding zero in all 12 model–dataset combinations. Using an even stricter trajectory-based test without cross-seed information, the asymmetry remains across all three LLaDA datasets (p<0.005) and is directionally present across all three Dream datasets, with one significant. The prevalence of the hard (Ghost) regime varies widely by model, from 16% to 77%, and the same prompts often fall into different regimes for different models.
AI.conclusion: Sampling-based hallucination detection is not uniformly effective: some hallucinations (high-agreement “Ghost” ones) are systematically harder to detect than others, and the proportion of such hard cases varies substantially across models and datasets. Aggregate detection metrics like overall AUC hide this structured, model-dependent heterogeneity. The authors argue that evaluations should be conditioned on hallucination regimes and that future work should account for these regime-specific behaviors when designing and benchmarking hallucination detectors.

title: The Layer Mystery of VLA: An Information-Theoretical Analysis of VLA Latent Interface
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies connect a pretrained vision-language backbone to an action head through a latent interface, but which backbone layers this interface should expose remains unclear. We study single-layer selection and multi-layer fusion for frozen backbones across three pretrained models and two manipulation benchmarks, LIBERO and CALVIN, with three policy-training seeds per configuration. Across three fusion mechanisms and three layer-subset strategies, 47 of 54 configurations underperform the best observed single-layer policy. Our stastical analysis further confirms that fusion's advantage is very limited. However, the best layer varies substantially across backbones and benchmarks, making layer selection consequential and exhaustive policy sweeps expensive. We further derive a reweighting equivalence between the proposed information-bottleneck objectives for action-conditioned InfoNCE and action prediction, motivating InfoNCE as a proxy for layer quality. Empirically, InfoNCE provides the most consistent positive association with policy success among four evaluated proxies. Selecting the layer with the highest InfoNCE score requires 9-33 times less GPU compute than exhaustive policy sweeps and reduces mean selection regret from 17.89 percentage points for deepest-layer selection to 3.71 points across six settings. Its mean regret is close to the 3.28-3.50 points achieved by fixed-layer heuristics optimized retrospectively using all six oracle sweeps, without requiring closed-loop evaluations during selection.

AI.tldr: The paper studies which layer(s) of a frozen vision-language backbone are best to connect to an action head in vision-language-action (VLA) policies, finds that simple single-layer choices tend to outperform more complex multi-layer fusion, and proposes an InfoNCE-based proxy to cheaply pick good layers without exhaustive policy training.
AI.motivation: In VLA systems, a pretrained vision-language model is frozen and connected to a learned action head via some latent interface, but it is unclear which layer of the backbone should feed this interface or whether fusing multiple layers is beneficial. Exhaustively training policies for every possible layer or fusion choice is computationally expensive, while naive rules like “use the last layer” often perform suboptimally. The authors want a principled, low-cost way to select good backbone layers that transfer well to robotic manipulation benchmarks without extensive closed-loop evaluation.
AI.method: The authors systematically compare single-layer vs multi-layer fusion interfaces using frozen vision-language backbones across three pretrained models and two robotic manipulation benchmarks (LIBERO and CALVIN). They explore three fusion mechanisms and three layer-subset strategies and run three training seeds per configuration, yielding 54 fusion configurations which they compare to the best single-layer policies. They conduct statistical analysis to quantify how often fusion truly helps. Then they derive an equivalence between information-bottleneck-style objectives for action-conditioned InfoNCE and standard action prediction, which motivates using an InfoNCE objective as a proxy metric of layer quality. They empirically evaluate four different proxy metrics, testing how well each proxy’s ranking of layers correlates with actual policy success, and analyze compute cost and regret of layer selection strategies based on these proxies versus exhaustive sweeps and simple heuristics.
AI.result: Empirically, in 47 out of 54 tested settings, multi-layer fusion policies underperform the best single-layer policy, and statistical tests show that the overall advantage of fusion is minimal. The identity of the best-performing layer depends strongly on the specific backbone and benchmark, so layer selection has large performance impact, but brute-force sweeps are expensive. Among four proxy metrics evaluated for predicting good layers, the InfoNCE-based proxy shows the strongest and most consistent positive association with policy success. Using the layer with the highest InfoNCE score reduces compute by a factor of 9–33 relative to exhaustive policy sweeps while lowering the mean selection regret from 17.89 percentage points (if always choosing the deepest layer) to 3.71 points across six settings. This regret is close to that of retrospectively optimized fixed-layer heuristics (3.28–3.50 points) that unrealistically assume access to oracle sweep results.
AI.conclusion: Multi-layer fusion over frozen vision-language backbones offers limited benefits over picking a single well-chosen layer for VLA policies, and the optimal layer is highly context-dependent. Instead of relying on expensive exhaustive sweeps or naive heuristics like always using the deepest layer, an InfoNCE-based proxy objective can efficiently approximate layer quality, enabling near-oracle layer selection with much less compute and no closed-loop policy evaluation. This suggests that practical VLA system design should prioritize principled single-layer selection, guided by low-cost proxy metrics such as InfoNCE, rather than complex multi-layer fusion architectures.

title: Resolving the Missing Financial Data Crisis: A Generative AI Pipeline for SEC 10-K Extraction
comment: Presented as a Lightning Talk at MIT URTC 2026
summary: SEC 10-K filings contain substantial financial information that is not consistently captured in structured datasets, creating a missing-data problem affecting over 70% of firms and half of total market capitalization. This can disproportionately bias quantitative analysis against smaller firms, which may be excluded due to limited available data. Traditional financial extraction methods such as Regular Expressions (Regex) and BERT, have been widely used. However, they are highly brittle when parsing complex SEC 10-K filings, which leads to data that is existent in the files being lost since these methods do not consider that a data attribute could be located in a different section or a footnote. This study evaluates several Large Language Models (LLMs), including Llama-3 8B, Qwen-2.5 14B, and Llama-3.3 70B, to figure out individual model strengths and weaknesses when extracting specific attributes from SEC 10-K text. The extraction quality was evaluated across four financial variables of varying structural complexity: Cash and Cash Equivalents (tabular), Short-Term Debt (hybrid), Credit Facilities (narrative), and Research and Development (hybrid). Results show that while smaller models like Llama-3 8B experience performance degradation under complex negative prompting, aligning parameter scale with document complexity yields high zero-shot accuracy. Qwen-2.5 14B excels as a tabular specialist with an 83.33% F1 score on Cash, whereas Llama-3.3 70B effectively navigates dense narrative footnotes, achieving a 76.92% F1 score on R&D. This scalable framework addresses critical information gaps in quantitative finance datasets and eliminates missing-data bias through a more thorough analysis of the SEC 10-K files.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates how well different Large Language Models (LLMs) can extract missing financial attributes from complex SEC 10-K filings, showing that larger and specialized models significantly reduce missing-data bias relative to traditional Regex/BERT methods.
AI.motivation: Structured financial datasets derived from SEC 10-K filings miss a large amount of information (impacting over 70% of firms and half of total market cap), especially for smaller firms, causing systematic missing-data bias in quantitative finance. Existing extraction approaches like Regex and BERT are brittle with complex document layouts, cross-references, and footnotes, leading to further information loss. There is a need for a more robust, scalable way to extract diverse financial variables from these filings.
AI.method: The study benchmarks several LLMs (Llama-3 8B, Qwen-2.5 14B, Llama-3.3 70B) on the task of extracting four types of financial variables from SEC 10-K text: Cash and Cash Equivalents (tabular), Short-Term Debt (hybrid), Credit Facilities (narrative), and Research and Development (hybrid). It uses zero-shot prompting, including complex negative prompts, and evaluates extraction performance with F1 scores, analyzing how model size and document/variable complexity interact.
AI.result: Smaller models like Llama-3 8B suffer more performance degradation under complex negative prompting, particularly on structurally complex tasks. Qwen-2.5 14B performs best on tabular data, achieving an 83.33% F1 score on Cash and Cash Equivalents, while the larger Llama-3.3 70B performs best on narrative and footnote-heavy content, achieving a 76.92% F1 score on R&D. Overall, aligning model parameter scale and specialization with document and variable complexity yields high zero-shot accuracy.
AI.conclusion: LLMs can substantially improve the extraction of heterogeneous financial attributes from SEC 10-K filings compared to traditional methods, reducing missing-data bias in quantitative datasets. Different models are better suited to different types of structure (tabular vs. narrative), and larger models show clear advantages on complex, footnote-rich text. The proposed evaluation and extraction framework is scalable and can be used to systematically fill critical information gaps in quantitative finance data by more thoroughly mining SEC 10-K documents.

title: AdaST: Adaptive Coupling for Spatial-Temporal Forecasting
comment: Accepted to NeurIPS 2026 (main conference). Code: https://github.com/LzyFischer/AdaST
summary: Spatial-temporal (ST) forecasting underpins many real-world systems such as traffic, climate, and energy networks. While existing methods implicitly assume strong spatiotemporal coupling, we observe that real-world ST data exhibits distinct coupling regimes, ranging from temporal-dominated and spatial-dominated to strongly coupled patterns. This mismatch causes current models to suffer from spurious dependencies and degraded performance when one correlation dominates. To overcome this limitation, we aim to dynamically modulate spatial and temporal modeling based on the data's inherent coupling structure. However, three key challenges exist: unknown coupling structure, heterogeneous coupling dynamics, and suboptimal spatial modeling. We propose AdaST, an adaptive ST forecasting framework that tackles these challenges through a decompose-recompose paradigm. AdaST factorizes inputs into components capturing different coupling patterns using heterogeneity-aware experts. Each component is processed by role-aligned modules, and a correlation-informed adaptive recomposer integrates them for final prediction. Extensive experiments confirm that AdaST significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, validating the necessity of an adaptive approach.

AI.tldr: Adaptive spatial-temporal forecasting framework (AdaST) that decomposes data into different coupling regimes and recomposes them for improved predictions.
AI.motivation: Existing spatial-temporal forecasting methods assume uniformly strong spatiotemporal coupling, but real-world data exhibit varying coupling regimes (temporal-dominated, spatial-dominated, strongly coupled). This mismatch leads to spurious dependencies and poor performance when one type of correlation dominates, motivating a framework that adapts to heterogeneous coupling structures.
AI.method: Introduce AdaST, a decompose-recompose framework. First, it factorizes ST inputs into several components, each representing a different spatiotemporal coupling pattern, using heterogeneity-aware experts. Then, each component is processed by dedicated, role-aligned spatial or temporal modeling modules. Finally, a correlation-informed adaptive recomposer integrates these processed components into a final prediction, modulating spatial and temporal contributions based on inferred coupling.
AI.result: Across extensive experiments on ST forecasting tasks, AdaST yields significantly better performance than state-of-the-art baselines, especially in scenarios with heterogeneous or imbalanced spatial and temporal correlations.
AI.conclusion: Adapting spatial and temporal modeling to the underlying coupling structure of ST data is crucial for accurate forecasting. By explicitly decomposing into coupling regimes and adaptively recomposing, AdaST effectively handles heterogeneous spatiotemporal dynamics and achieves superior performance, demonstrating the value of an adaptive, coupling-aware approach.

title: PACT: Pairwise-Anchored Calibrated Tuning for Single-Token Typed Decisions
summary: Single-token typed-decision models answer a schema question by reading the logits of a few one-letter answer codes at a single position: they are fast and return a probability for every allowed answer, but they are trained with plain cross-entropy that ignores most of the structure in their training data. We study such a model whose data is curated as contrastive pairs---two contexts that differ in one edited fact that flips the answer---each carrying a machine-checked certificate that deleting the decisive sentence makes the fact unknown. We propose PACT, which turns this structure into four training terms that need no new annotation: a difference-in-differences margin over each pair that is invariant to any shared logit offset, a permutation-consistency term against answer-code position bias, an evidence-necessity term on certificate-verified ablated contexts, and an ordinal transport cost for rubric fields, plus a three-parameter contextual temperature. On a frozen 324-item holdout with three seeds, PACT matches the published recipe in accuracy ($84.6\%$ vs. $85.2\%$; McNemar $p \ge 0.50$ at every seed) while giving the lowest position bias of all runs (answer flips under relabelling $9.8\%$ vs. $13.8\%$) and the lowest ordinal error on rubric fields (MAE $0.232$ vs. $0.311$). Against a control with the same optimiser and schedule but cross-entropy only, PACT is significantly more accurate at two of three seeds, halves the seed-to-seed spread and lowers NLL by $26\%$. Seed-matched ablations and pre-specified falsification tests locate these gains precisely: no single term raises raw accuracy, and the method's value lies in robustness and stability rather than headline accuracy. Code, data splits, trained adapters, and all run records are available at https://github.com/BennyLinntu/PACT-Pairwise-Anchored-Calibrated-Tuning-for-Single-Token-Typed-Decisions.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces PACT, a new training objective for single-token typed-decision models that leverages contrastive, certificate-annotated data to improve calibration, robustness, and stability without sacrificing accuracy.
AI.motivation: Single-token typed-decision models are efficient and provide full probability distributions over discrete answer codes, but standard cross-entropy training ignores rich structural information in curated datasets, such as contrastive pairs and known evidence sentences. This leads to position bias, poorer calibration, and instability across random seeds. The authors are motivated to exploit this existing structure to get more robust and reliable models while keeping the same labeling cost.
AI.method: The authors propose PACT (Pairwise Anchored Calibrated Tuning), a training framework composed of four loss terms and a contextual temperature parameter. 1) A difference-in-differences margin over contrastive context pairs ensures that the change in logits between edited facts is robust to shared offsets. 2) A permutation-consistency term discourages position-dependent biases in answer code logits by enforcing stability under label-code relabelling. 3) An evidence-necessity term uses certificate-verified ablated contexts (where the decisive sentence is removed) to train the model to treat the answer as unknown when evidence is missing. 4) An ordinal transport cost term shapes predictions on rubric fields that have an ordered structure. These are combined with a three-parameter contextual temperature that adapts the sharpness of the output distribution to context. The method is evaluated against baselines using accuracy, position bias, ordinal error, NLL, and seed stability on a 324-item holdout set with multiple random seeds.
AI.result: PACT matches the published baseline recipe in headline accuracy (84.6% vs 85.2%) with no statistically significant difference (McNemar p ≥ 0.50), but substantially reduces systematic biases and improves stability. It achieves the lowest answer position bias (9.8% answer flips under relabelling vs 13.8%), lowers mean absolute error on ordinal rubric fields (0.232 vs 0.311), and, compared to a cross-entropy-only control with the same optimizer and schedule, is significantly more accurate in 2 of 3 random seeds. PACT also halves the variance in results across seeds and reduces negative log-likelihood by 26%. Ablation and falsification studies show that no single loss term alone boosts raw accuracy, but together they improve robustness and calibration.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that PACT effectively leverages the latent structure in contrastive, certificate-annotated datasets for single-token typed-decision models. While it does not increase peak accuracy over strong baselines, it improves calibration, reduces position bias and ordinal errors, stabilizes performance across random seeds, and yields better log-likelihoods. The gains come from robustness and reliability rather than higher accuracy, and the authors support this claim through targeted ablations and falsification tests. They release code, data splits, adapters, and run records to facilitate reproducibility and further research.

title: Memory Is a Derivation: The Distributed-Evidence Paradox in Long-Term Agents
summary: Long-running LLM agents compress past interactions into persistent memories that may be reused as premises for later tasks. This creates a distinct derivation problem: whether the memory actually follows from what the interaction history supports. Relevant evidence may be scattered across earlier interactions, while compression can introduce relations or event status that the history never established. A valid memory may therefore appear unsupported because its citations omit relevant evidence, while individually supported facts may be composed into a stronger statement the history never established. We characterize this problem through three coupled requirements: (1) Evidence scope; (2) Compositional validity; (3) Admission reliability. We therefore ask whether the interaction history available at write time supports what enters persistent memory. We introduce DerivAudit, a framework for auditing whether a memory is actually supported by the history available when it was written. The audit separates three questions: whether supporting evidence lies beyond writer-provided citations, whether the composed memory introduces unsupported meaning, and how write-time admission decisions affect later memory use. Across two natural memory corpora, audits using broader pre-write history recover support for nearly 60% of memories that appear unsupported from citations alone, while 17-21% remain unsupported after expansion. Yet broader evidence does not by itself make admission reliable: unsupported memories are still frequently admitted across verification models, and evidence expansion alone worsens it on two backbones.

AI.tldr: The paper studies whether long-term memories created by LLM agents are actually justified by their prior interactions, and proposes an auditing framework (DerivAudit) to check if stored memories truly follow from conversation history.
AI.motivation: Long-running LLM agents compress long interaction histories into concise, persistent memories that they reuse later. However, this compression may introduce errors: a memory may claim relationships or event statuses that the original interaction never properly established, or may omit scattered evidence that would justify it. This raises a key reliability problem: do the memories an agent stores actually follow from its experience, and how can we tell?
AI.method: The authors formalize a new derivation problem for LLM memories via three requirements: (1) Evidence scope – whether the cited evidence fully reflects all relevant parts of the history; (2) Compositional validity – whether combining individually true facts yields a memory statement that is itself supported; and (3) Admission reliability – whether the decision to accept or reject a memory at write time is dependable. They then present DerivAudit, an auditing framework that, given an interaction history and a proposed memory, checks: (a) if supporting evidence exists beyond the writer’s citations; (b) if the composed memory adds unsupported meaning; and (c) how admission decisions at write time affect later use. They evaluate this framework on two natural corpora of LLM memories using various verification models and different scopes of pre-write history.
AI.result: When audits can access a broader slice of pre-write interaction history (beyond the memory’s explicit citations), they find support for nearly 60% of memories that initially look unsupported based only on citations. However, even with expanded evidence, 17–21% of memories remain unsupported. Moreover, simply broadening the evidence scope does not ensure reliable admission: models still frequently admit unsupported memories, and adding more evidence can actually worsen admission reliability on two backbone models.
AI.conclusion: Persistent memories stored by LLM agents are often misaligned with what their actual interaction histories justify. Many memories that appear unsupported are in fact supported when broader evidence is considered, but a significant fraction remains unjustified. Crucially, expanding the evidence available to verifiers does not automatically make memory admission reliable and can even degrade it. Therefore, robust auditing frameworks like DerivAudit, which explicitly check evidence scope, compositional validity, and admission reliability, are necessary to ensure that long-term LLM memories faithfully derive from prior interactions.

title: CruxBench: A Benchmark of Information Discovery
summary: Benchmarks for large language models (LLMs) typically evaluate the accuracy of answers against fixed reference labels. But a central step in many complex real-world tasks is identifying which questions are worth asking in the first place: decomposing a difficult problem into subquestions -- which we call cruxes -- whose answers provide key steps on the path toward solving the target problem. To evaluate this capability of information discovery, we introduce CruxBench, a benchmark that grades LLM-generated questions by their Value of Information (VOI): how much a model-proposed crux updates beliefs about a target forecasting question. CruxBench enjoys a rare combination of three key properties: it is (1) contamination-resistant by construction, since ground truth is generated by future world events; (2) open-ended, admitting unbounded and complex text-based submissions rather than one correct numeric answer; and (3) grounded, with informativeness measured against quantified changes in real-world beliefs. We evaluate a diverse set of eight models on 293 target forecasting questions and find that VOI correlates highly with independent measures of model capability (r=0.90) and captures cruxes' usefulness for answering target questions. However, information discovery remains challenging even for frontier LLMs, which only narrowly outperform a random-timing baseline.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces CruxBench, a benchmark that evaluates how well LLMs can generate high-value subquestions (“cruxes”) that meaningfully change beliefs about future forecasting questions, measuring performance via Value of Information and showing current LLMs only slightly beat a simple baseline.
AI.motivation: Most LLM benchmarks only check whether models pick correct answers to pre-given questions, but many real-world tasks require first figuring out which questions to ask—breaking down a complex problem into informative subquestions. There is a lack of evaluation tools for this “information discovery” capability, especially ones that are robust to data contamination and grounded in real-world outcomes. The authors aim to fill this gap by proposing a benchmark that tests whether models can generate questions whose answers would significantly improve our forecasts about future events.
AI.method: The authors design CruxBench around forecasting questions whose eventual outcomes are determined by future world events, making label contamination unlikely. For each target forecasting question, models must generate subquestions (“cruxes”) that, if answered, would most change a forecaster’s beliefs about the target. They define and compute the Value of Information (VOI) of each crux as the degree to which knowing its answer updates probabilistic beliefs about the target question. They then evaluate eight diverse LLMs across 293 forecasting targets, measure VOI of their proposed cruxes, and correlate VOI with other independent model capability metrics.
AI.result: Across the 293 target questions and eight LLMs, the VOI of model-generated cruxes strongly correlates with independent measures of model capability (correlation coefficient r = 0.90), suggesting CruxBench is a good proxy for overall model strength in information discovery. The benchmark shows that higher-performing models tend to generate more informative cruxes that better help in answering the target forecasting questions. Nonetheless, even the best current frontier LLMs only modestly outperform a simple baseline that selects questions based on random timing, indicating that high-quality information discovery is still a difficult task.
AI.conclusion: CruxBench provides a new way to evaluate LLMs on the crucial but underexplored skill of discovering valuable information by asking good subquestions. Its design—future-event-based ground truth, open-ended question generation, and belief-updating-based scoring—makes it resistant to training data contamination, flexible, and grounded in real-world forecasting behavior. The results reveal that while VOI is a strong indicator of general model capability, existing LLMs still struggle to generate truly high-value cruxes, leaving substantial room for progress in models that can better identify which questions are most worth asking.

title: More Features Are Not More Evidence: Limits of Training-Free Human Activity Recognition with Jev
summary: General-purpose models promise sensor-based decisions without training a task-specific classifier, which could reduce the dependence of Human Activity Recognition (HAR) on labeled data. Yet it remains unclear whether such models can directly interpret deterministic descriptions of physical sensor signals well enough to replace or complement trained HAR models. We study this question using Jev, a fixed general-purpose probabilistic decision model, on 1,800 class-balanced accelerometer windows from WISDM, UCI341, and PAMAP2. Jev receives no labeled examples, retrieval context, or HAR-specific parameter updates. We evaluate three deterministic sensor representations and compare 5,400 Jev decisions with a generative baseline and three supervised HAR models. Jev remains far below supervised recognition, with its strongest representation reaching macro-F1 of 0.038, 0.118, and 0.089 across the three datasets, compared with 0.686 to 0.907 for the supervised models. More numerical features do not improve Jev. Instead, they reduce recognition on all three datasets, while augmenting the same numerical evidence with a deterministic semantic rendering partially recovers performance, although the experiment does not isolate semantics from the accompanying serialization and redundancy changes. Jev is fast and inexpensive to query, but its probabilities are not reliably calibrated for recognition. A post-hoc fusion analysis finds a small improvement on WISDM that does not replicate on UCI341 or PAMAP2. These results show that training-free sensor decisions depend not only on the information available in the signal, but also on whether the model can use the representation through which that information is exposed. The sensor-to-model interface should therefore be treated as part of the model evaluation rather than as a neutral preprocessing step.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates whether a fixed, general-purpose probabilistic model (Jev) can perform human activity recognition (HAR) from deterministic descriptions of accelerometer signals without any task-specific training, and finds that it performs far below supervised HAR models and is highly sensitive to how sensor data are represented.
AI.motivation: Labeled data for HAR are costly, and general-purpose models that can make sensor-based decisions without task-specific training could greatly reduce this dependency. However, it is unclear whether such models can effectively interpret deterministic descriptions of raw physical sensor signals for HAR, and how much their performance depends on the chosen representation of these signals.
AI.method: The authors test Jev, a fixed general-purpose probabilistic decision model, on 1,800 class-balanced accelerometer windows drawn from three benchmark HAR datasets (WISDM, UCI341, PAMAP2). Jev receives no labeled examples, retrieval context, or HAR-specific parameter updates. They design and evaluate three deterministic sensor representations, then compare 5,400 Jev decisions against a generative baseline and three supervised HAR models. They also analyze the effect of adding more numerical features, adding deterministic semantic renderings of the same evidence, and conduct a post-hoc fusion of Jev with supervised models to probe complementarity.
AI.result: Across all three datasets, Jev’s best-performing representation yields very low macro-F1 scores of 0.038, 0.118, and 0.089, far below the supervised HAR models which achieve macro-F1 between 0.686 and 0.907. Increasing the number of numerical features degrades Jev’s recognition performance on all datasets. Augmenting numerical features with a deterministic semantic rendering partially improves performance, though this improvement is confounded with changes in serialization and redundancy. Jev’s probability estimates are poorly calibrated for recognition. A post-hoc fusion with supervised models gives a small gain on WISDM but no consistent improvement on UCI341 or PAMAP2.
AI.conclusion: Training-free, general-purpose sensor decision-making is not solely limited by the information content of the raw signals but also by how that information is represented to the model. Jev, as a fixed general-purpose model, cannot approach supervised HAR performance under the tested conditions and is highly sensitive to the sensor-to-model interface. The work argues that the representation layer should be considered an integral part of model evaluation rather than a neutral preprocessing step, as it critically shapes what a general-purpose model can exploit from sensor data.

title: Almost Human, Except When It Matters: VoxParity and the Decisions a Voice Should Change
comment: 38 pages, 11 figures, 15 tables. Code, scorer and development-split data at https://github.com/bhavik-mangla/voxparity-bench and https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23008159
summary: A voice agent can handle almost every call on the words alone and still fail the few its sector's rules were written for. Emergency-call standards, fraud guidance, radio phraseology and vulnerability rules recognise that how a caller sounds, or what else is audible, can change the right action. VoxParity tests whether agents act on it. In 183 scenarios from 14 sectors, one transcript stays fixed while the audio changes (a coaching voice, a medical monitor beeping, a mayday under a radio check, noise over a drug name, a child's voice placing a bet, a frightened whisper), and with it the correct typed tool call. A words-only null test credits a system only if hearing the call moves its actions more than it moves a pipeline that only reads the words. Only 11 of the 23 systems that can also be run on the transcript pass. Descriptively, errors run toward the words: when the audio calls for protection, all 28 systems carry out the routine request more often than they over-react on clean calls (41% against 12% pooled; the words-only pipeline, 58% against 15%). Exploratory analyses place most of the leading systems' misses on cues they heard; systems beat the null almost entirely on items that state the rule; the leading systems overrule heard resignation or confusion far more often than acute alarm; and, in the models tested, describing the voice and stating the rule each recover part of the shortfall, leaving a gap on emotion.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces VoxParity, a benchmark to test whether voice AI systems appropriately use non-verbal audio cues (tone, background sounds, speaker identity) in safety‑critical scenarios, showing that most current systems largely ignore such cues and default to the transcript.
AI.motivation: Many real-world standards (emergency services, fraud detection, aviation radio, child protection, medical safety, etc.) explicitly require responders to act not just on the caller’s words but also on how they sound and what is heard in the background. Current voice agents and speech models are typically evaluated on text-like metrics (word error rate, semantic accuracy) that ignore these paralinguistic and ambient audio cues. The authors want to know whether modern voice AI systems actually follow audio-based safety rules or just behave as if they only saw a transcript, which could lead to systematic failures in high‑stakes use cases.
AI.method: The authors design VoxParity, a test suite of 183 audio scenarios across 14 domains where the literal words of the call stay fixed but the audio conditions change (e.g., coaching voice suggesting fraud, medical monitor beeping, mayday hidden in a radio check, noise obscuring a drug name, a child’s voice trying to place a bet, a caller whispering in fear). Each variant has a different correct action/tool call according to sector rules. They then evaluate 28 systems, including 23 that can also run on text-only transcripts. A words-only pipeline serves as a null model: a voice system is credited for using audio only if its behavior changes in the correct direction more than the text-only pipeline’s behavior changes under the same scenario. They analyze pass/fail rates against this null, error asymmetries (over-protection vs under-protection), and which types of audio cues (rules stated in text, explicit voice descriptions, emotional tone) the models respond to.
AI.result: Only 11 of the 23 systems that can also be run on transcripts outperform the words-only null test, meaning most systems do not reliably change behavior when audio safety cues change. Across all 28 systems, errors systematically favor doing what the words request: when audio cues call for protective or cautious behavior, systems still carry out the routine request much more often (41%) than they over-react on clean calls (12%), with the words-only baseline doing even worse (58% vs 15%). Leading systems’ failures tend to occur on items where they audibly register the cue but still fail to act on it. Systems gain most over the null baselines on items where the relevant safety rule is explicitly stated, suggesting rule-following from text more than nuanced audio understanding. The best systems override apparent resignation or confusion in the voice far more than they override acute alarm, indicating selective sensitivity. Adding explicit descriptions of the voice and explicitly stating the applicable rule each recover some of the performance gap, but an unclosed gap remains for pure emotional cues.
AI.conclusion: Current voice AI systems largely behave as if they were text-only models, often ignoring paralinguistic and ambient audio cues that are critical for safety and compliance in many sectors. Even strong models under-use emotional and contextual audio information, especially when it is not paired with explicit textual rules or descriptions. Explicitly articulating rules and describing the voice characteristics helps, but does not fully close the gap, particularly for emotion-driven signals. VoxParity thus exposes a systematic bias toward literal word content over protective audio-based interpretation and provides a benchmark for developing voice agents that meet real-world safety and regulatory expectations.

title: Principled Thoughts for Latent Recursive LLM Systems
summary: Large language models can reason in continuous space instead of decoded text, by recurring on their own hidden states or by passing those states between agents, while training supervises only the Cross-Entropy (CE) of the final decoded answer and does not constrain the thought. Theoretical and empirical analyses establish and confirm four failures of CE-only training that lead to a lower probability of the correct answer such as collapsing thoughts across distinct questions and retaining irrelevant information. We introduce REST (REpresentation-Supervised Thoughts), a training objective that turns four properties of a valid thought representation (causality, minimality, separability, and stability) into differentiable losses added to CE. We instantiate it in latent single-agent and multi-agent systems, without architectural changes or added parameters at inference. Across 7 benchmarks spanning mathematics, science, medicine, and code generation, with the same training data, compute, and latent budget, REST increases accuracy over CE-only training across agent settings and model sizes by up to 7.5 percentage points and convergence on a final answer by 30\%. Furthermore, REST thoughts encode more of what is required to achieve the correct answer, and decoding them better recovers the intended output of the agent, which makes latent communication easier to interpret. Project Website: https://fard-lab.github.io/REST

AI.tldr: The paper proposes REST, a representation-supervised training objective for large language models that improves latent reasoning and answer accuracy compared to standard cross-entropy-only training.
AI.motivation: Standard cross-entropy (CE) training for large language models only supervises the final decoded answer and ignores the structure and quality of intermediate latent thoughts. When models reason in continuous latent space—by recurring on hidden states or passing them between agents—this CE-only objective can cause systematic failures such as collapsing reasoning patterns for different questions or retaining irrelevant information, which in turn lowers the probability of producing correct final answers. The authors aim to diagnose these failures theoretically and empirically, and to design a training objective that shapes latent thoughts into better-structured, more faithful representations of the reasoning process without changing architectures or inference-time cost.
AI.method: The authors first provide theoretical and empirical analyses showing four failure modes of CE-only training in latent reasoning systems, including collapsed thought representations across distinct questions and the persistence of irrelevant information. They then propose REST (REpresentation-Supervised Thoughts), an auxiliary training objective that encodes four desiderata for valid thought representations—causality, minimality, separability, and stability—into differentiable loss terms added on top of the usual CE loss. REST is instantiated in both single-agent and multi-agent latent reasoning setups, where models operate over and communicate via hidden states rather than explicit text, without modifying the underlying architecture or adding parameters at inference. The method is evaluated across several benchmarks, holding constant training data, compute, and latent budget, and includes analyses of the information content and decodability of latent thoughts.
AI.result: Across seven benchmarks in mathematics, science, medicine, and code generation, REST consistently outperforms CE-only training under comparable conditions. It yields up to a 7.5 percentage point increase in task accuracy across different agent configurations and model sizes, and improves convergence to a final answer by 30%. Analyses of the learned representations show that REST-trained latent thoughts contain more task-relevant information needed for arriving at correct answers. Furthermore, when these latent thoughts are decoded, they more faithfully recover the agent’s intended output, making latent communication within or between agents more interpretable.
AI.conclusion: The work concludes that supervising only the final decoded answer with cross-entropy is insufficient for effective latent reasoning in large language models and can produce systematic representational pathologies. By adding REST, a representation-level objective enforcing causality, minimality, separability, and stability, models learn higher-quality thought representations that improve both accuracy and convergence without architectural changes or inference-time overhead. REST thus offers a practical way to align latent thoughts with the reasoning required for correct answers and to make internal communication more interpretable, suggesting a promising direction for training future latent reasoning and multi-agent language systems.

title: Question-Specific Knowledge Graphs for Efficient Visual Reasoning
summary: Recent work in visual question answering has shown that vision-language models can exhibit strong reasoning capabilities by translating visual inputs into textual representations. The effectiveness of this translation depends on how well visual details are retained; models need to surface and align both explicit and implicit knowledge sufficient to support reasoning, without introducing spurious assumptions. Existing methods that leverage detailed image captions introduce visual details unrelated to the reasoning task, inflating input token counts and increasing computational cost. To address these challenges, we propose VisKG, a reinforcement learning (RL) framework in which models learn to translate visual content into question-specific knowledge graph (KG) representations. This process filters out perceptual noise while preserving the entity-relation structure needed for chain-of-thought reasoning, following the principle of minimum sufficient information. To ensure stable RL post-training, VisKG adopts Group reward-Decoupled Normalization Policy Optimization (GDPO). In addition, we strengthen the supervision stage with negative rationale samples, exposing the model to incorrect reasoning paths before RL post-training. Experimental results across science, mathematics, and general visual understanding benchmarks show that VisKG achieves performance comparable to or better than baselines, while requiring fewer tokens than caption-based representations. Moreover, training VisKG with GDPO improves accuracy by 2% over its GRPO-trained counterpart on average. These results suggest that KG representations are a promising approach for supporting multi-step reasoning and open up future work on adaptively selecting the most suitable representation for a given task.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces VisKG, an RL-based framework that converts images into compact, question-specific knowledge graph representations for visual question answering, improving multi-step reasoning with fewer tokens than caption-based methods.
AI.motivation: Existing vision-language models often rely on long, detailed image captions to enable reasoning, which can introduce irrelevant visual details, increase token length, and raise computational cost. The authors aim to design a representation that retains only the minimum sufficient information for reasoning—especially entity-relation structure—while filtering perceptual noise and avoiding spurious assumptions.
AI.method: The authors propose VisKG, which learns to translate visual content into question-specific knowledge graph (KG) representations. The KG captures entities and relations tailored to the question, supporting chain-of-thought reasoning while enforcing a minimum sufficient information principle. They use a reinforcement learning framework with a specialized optimization algorithm, Group reward-Decoupled Normalization Policy Optimization (GDPO), to stabilize RL post-training. Additionally, they augment supervised training with negative rationale samples—explicitly incorrect reasoning paths—to help the model distinguish valid from invalid reasoning before RL fine-tuning.
AI.result: Across benchmarks in science, mathematics, and general visual understanding, VisKG attains accuracy comparable to or better than caption-based and other baselines, while using fewer tokens due to its compact KG representation. Applying GDPO for RL training further boosts accuracy by an average of 2% compared with training the same system using GRPO.
AI.conclusion: Knowledge graph-based, question-specific visual representations are an effective and token-efficient alternative to caption-based inputs for visual question answering and multi-step reasoning. Reinforcement learning with GDPO and exposure to negative rationales stabilizes training and improves accuracy. The work suggests that adaptively choosing representation formats (e.g., KG vs. caption) per task is a promising future direction for vision-language reasoning systems.

title: FigAct: Turning Scientific Figures into Active Canvases for Explanation
summary: Scientific figures are designed to communicate information visually, yet MLLMs typically explain them by translating their visual content back into text. This requires readers to manually map the resulting explanations back to the figure. Inspired by how people present visual information, we introduce FigAct, a framework that transforms static scientific figures into question-conditioned visual presentations by acting directly on their existing graphical elements. Like a human presenter, FigAct generates a sequence of short narrations, grounds each narration in the corresponding visual evidence, and applies visual actions to guide the viewer's attention. We develop a hierarchical search strategy for efficient element localization, reducing token usage by approximately 40$\times$. We further train FigAct-8B using three task-specific rewards for grounding accuracy, search efficiency, and rendering quality. We further build a human-verified benchmark from figures in real-world scientific papers to evaluate the ability of MLLMs to generate grounded visual explanations. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of FigAct and show that treating scientific figures as presentation canvases makes explanations clearer and easier to follow.

AI.tldr: The paper presents FigAct, a framework that turns static scientific figures into interactive, question-conditioned visual presentations with grounded narrations and visual actions, significantly improving clarity and efficiency compared to text-only explanations.
AI.motivation: Most multimodal large language models (MLLMs) explain scientific figures by converting visual content back into text. This forces readers to mentally map the explanation onto the figure, which is inefficient and error-prone. The authors aim to create a system that explains figures more like a human presenter: directly manipulating the visual elements, grounding explanations in the figure, and guiding attention, while also making the process efficient in terms of model token usage.
AI.method: They introduce FigAct, which takes a question and a scientific figure, then produces a sequence of short narrations each linked to specific visual evidence in the figure. The system performs visual actions (e.g., highlighting, focusing, or otherwise modifying display of elements) to draw attention. To support this, they design a hierarchical search strategy for localizing relevant elements in the figure efficiently, achieving about 40x reduction in token usage. They train an 8B-parameter model, FigAct-8B, with three task-specific reward signals focused on (1) grounding accuracy (correctly linking narration to visual elements), (2) search efficiency (minimizing unnecessary exploration and tokens), and (3) rendering quality (how well visual actions are executed and presented). They also construct a human-verified benchmark from real scientific papers for evaluation.
AI.result: FigAct significantly reduces token consumption for element localization (around 40x) and produces clearer, more grounded visual explanations compared to standard MLLM approaches that only output text. On the new human-verified benchmark, FigAct demonstrates strong performance in grounding accuracy, efficiency, and explanation quality, outperforming baselines that treat figures only as images to be described textually.
AI.conclusion: Presenting scientific figures as interactive canvases rather than static images for textual description leads to more understandable and user-friendly explanations. FigAct, with its grounded narrations, attention-guiding visual actions, and efficient hierarchical search, proves effective at generating such explanations, suggesting a promising direction for future MLLM-based figure understanding and scientific communication tools.

title: Causal and Interpretable Structures in LLM Compositional Tasks
summary: Large language models are able to solve tasks whose answers depend on not only individual input tokens, but also on relations among them. How is such relational information represented and processed across transformer layers? We study activations from ensembles of prompts that require inferring relationships between three tokens corresponding to a cyclic concept (months, hours, weekdays, and musical notes) to correctly predict the next token. Across model families (Llama, Qwen, Gemma, and Mistral) and cyclic concepts, we find a consistent layerwise progression in how the joint dependence among the tokens is geometrically organized and causally used: intermediate layers use a joint representation based on the inferred relationship between two tokens, while later layers use a joint representation associated with all three tokens to correctly complete the task. We also find other relationships between tokens that are geometrically structured but remain causally inert in the next-token prediction. Crucially, when taken together, these geometric and causal investigations reveal the representation-level mechanism that progressively organizes and composes the relational information to form the answer. More surprisingly, restricting the models to such causally relevant joint representations improves next-token prediction accuracy.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes how transformers represent and use relational information among tokens, showing a consistent layerwise progression from pairwise to full multi-token relational representations, and that isolating causally relevant joint representations can boost next-token prediction accuracy.
AI.motivation: Large language models can solve tasks based on relationships between tokens (e.g., temporal or cyclic order), but it is unclear how these relational dependencies are encoded and used across layers. Existing interpretability work often focuses on single-token features or simple mechanisms, leaving a gap in our understanding of how models internally represent multi-token relations that underlie reasoning-like behavior.
AI.method: The authors construct ensembles of prompts involving cyclic concepts (months, hours, weekdays, musical notes) where solving the task requires inferring a relationship among three tokens to predict the next token. They analyze hidden activations in multiple transformer models (Llama, Qwen, Gemma, Mistral) to study the geometry of representations: how joint dependencies among tokens are embedded and evolve across layers. They combine geometric analysis with causal interventions (e.g., ablating or restricting specific subspaces) to determine which relational structures are actually used by the model for next-token prediction.
AI.result: Across model families and cyclic concepts, there is a robust pattern: intermediate layers encode a joint representation mainly reflecting the relationship between two of the tokens, while later layers encode a joint representation involving all three tokens that directly supports correct next-token prediction. They also observe additional geometrically structured relations between tokens that are not causally involved in the prediction. Furthermore, enforcing that the model relies only on the causally relevant joint subspaces improves its next-token prediction accuracy on these relational tasks.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that transformer models progressively build up relational information across layers, moving from simpler pairwise relations to higher-order joint relations that directly drive predictions. By combining geometric and causal analyses, the authors identify a concrete representation-level mechanism for how relational reasoning is implemented. They show that focusing computation on the causally relevant relational subspaces can measurably enhance model performance, suggesting both a deeper interpretive understanding and potential avenues for model steering and improvement.

title: An Empirical Study and Assessment of EU AI Act Compliance Checkers
summary: The EU AI Act introduces extensive compliance requirements for organizations that develop, deploy, or integrate AI systems. Many of these requirements are directly relevant to security and privacy, while also addressing closely related issues such as data governance, transparency, accuracy, and robustness. However, stakeholders such as small-to-medium businesses and individual developers often lack the legal expertise required to interpret these obligations and translate them into engineering and governance practices. This disconnect creates challenges for implementing the EU AI Act and may lead to missing safeguards or misdirected development and deployment efforts. To address this, various automated EU AI Act compliance checkers (AIACCs) have emerged, claiming to streamline compliance assessments and provide practical guidance. In this paper, we present the first empirical study and assessment of AIACCs. We characterize 12 mainstream AIACCs across multiple dimensions, evaluate their legal coverage and alignment, and analyze checker-generated compliance reports for structure, determinacy, and actionability. We find that the quality of AIACCs varies significantly and that they currently can only serve as early-stage orientation tools. Specifically, we observe inconsistent interaction modes and user-friendliness, a tendency to overly simplify or omit key obligations, and a failure to provide determinate, actionable guidance. As a result, reliance on the current generation of AIACCs may foster a false sense of compliance. With our study, we provide a critical baseline of the current AIACC landscape. We further offer design principles for the implementation of more reliable compliance-support tools.

AI.tldr: The paper empirically evaluates existing automated EU AI Act compliance checkers (AIACCs) and finds that they are immature, inconsistent, and only suitable as rough orientation tools, not reliable compliance solutions.
AI.motivation: Organizations, especially SMEs and individual developers, face complex and hard-to-interpret obligations under the EU AI Act, particularly around security, privacy, data governance, transparency, accuracy, and robustness. Lacking legal and compliance expertise, they may turn to automated compliance checkers that promise streamlined assessments and guidance. However, there has been no systematic evaluation of how effective, accurate, and practically useful these AIACCs actually are, raising concern that they might mislead users and create a false sense of compliance.
AI.method: The authors identify and systematically characterize 12 mainstream EU AI Act compliance checkers along multiple dimensions (e.g., interaction modes, user experience, and output characteristics). They then analyze the tools’ coverage and alignment with legal requirements of the EU AI Act, and qualitatively evaluate the compliance reports they generate in terms of structure, determinacy (clarity and specificity of recommendations), and actionability (usefulness for engineering and governance practice).
AI.result: The study finds substantial variability in tool quality and behavior across the 12 AIACCs. Many tools offer inconsistent and sometimes confusing interaction modes, lack user-friendly design, simplify or omit important legal obligations, and fail to provide determinate, concrete, and technically actionable guidance. Overall, these tools fall short of offering robust, reliable support for meeting EU AI Act requirements.
AI.conclusion: Current AIACCs should be treated only as early-stage orientation aids, not as dependable instruments for achieving or demonstrating EU AI Act compliance. Over-reliance on them risks giving organizations a false impression that they are compliant when significant gaps remain. The paper establishes a critical empirical baseline for the AIACC landscape and proposes design principles to guide the development of more reliable and legally aligned compliance-support tools in the future.

title: Mnemon: Raw Records, Fast Judgments, Slow Thoughts
comment: 16 pages, 3 figures, 4 tables. Code, prompts and run records: https://github.com/Grivn/mnemon-memory-agent
summary:
Long-term memory lets an LLM assistant use a history it can no longer reread, and most memory systems build it by rewriting conversations into facts, graphs or typed memories at write time. We argue that the work of memory divides, as thinking does, into two systems. Most of it is fast System 1 work: many small, independent yes/no judgments about records, such as whether a record is needed or no longer current, which a decision model makes by the dozen in a third of a second. Only a little is slow System 2 work: writing a few search queries, naming what the reply needs and composing the answer, which an LLM does well but slowly. We present Mnemon, a memory agent built on this division.
