Evaluate how applying these directions affects attribution rates (how often generations are attributed to each country) under union scoring, compare to random directions, and check output coherence. Compare results and representation measures with another LLM, Aya Expanse 32B.
AI.result:
(1) Transfer from English differs by language and by model layer. Africa-vs-West contrast directions are more mutually aligned among African languages than between African and control languages at several layers. Cross–language-family alignment is statistically significant (under Holm) for 5 of 12 layers, but dependence between language pairs weakens strict statistical claims. Within Nigeria, Yoruba and Igbo directions are substantially more aligned with each other than with Hausa for 11 of 12 layers.
(2) Country-specific steering in English yields strong separation from random directions: estimated differences in attribution rates range from 0.63 to 0.81 at chosen steering strengths. Most generations pass an automatic structural coherence filter. Comparisons with Aya Expanse 32B show that conclusions depend on which representation similarity measure is used.
AI.conclusion: Gemma 4 31B encodes discernible regional and language-family structure for African languages and supports effective steering toward African country contexts in English, though effects vary by layer and representation metric. African languages show shared alignment patterns distinct from non-African controls, and within-country language differences (e.g., Yoruba/Igbo vs Hausa) are visible in the representations. The robustness and interpretation of these findings depend on statistical assumptions and the choice of similarity measures, as highlighted by differing results compared to Aya Expanse 32B.

title: Towards an AI Software Factory for Data Systems
summary:
AI-assisted coding tools deliver significant acceleration of coding, but only limited impact across the end-to-end software development lifecycle (SDLC)--an Amdahl's law effect!
  In this paper, we discuss our progress towards building an AI SW Factory that accelerates all the stages of SDLC-Targeting, Coding, Reviewing, and Ops. The AI SW Factory produces a metadata exhaust that enables self-improvement by fine-tuning model weights and updating our World Model (a rich data substrate).
  We focus on Data Systems and the important class of Evolutionary Coding Tasks (i.e., those with a measurable objective to hill-climb) and report on 1) scaled deployments at Microsoft (tens of repositories) leading to 3x engineering efficiency above agentic coding and up to 22x token efficiency, and 2) several open challenges.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an AI Software Factory that extends AI assistance beyond coding to all SDLC stages, showing large efficiency gains in Microsoft deployments and outlining remaining challenges.
AI.motivation: Existing AI coding tools mainly speed up code writing but have little effect on the entire software development lifecycle, leading to limited overall productivity gains (Amdahl's law). There is a need to accelerate all SDLC stages and create systems that can continuously improve themselves using the data they generate in real use.
AI.method: Design and deployment of an AI Software Factory that supports four SDLC stages: Targeting, Coding, Reviewing, and Operations. The system generates rich metadata (“metadata exhaust”) that is used to fine-tune model weights and update a World Model, enabling iterative self-improvement. Experiments and scaled deployments focus on data systems and evolutionary coding tasks that have clear, measurable objectives for optimization.
AI.result: In tens of Microsoft repositories, the AI Software Factory achieved around 3x engineering efficiency compared with agentic coding alone and up to 22x token efficiency, demonstrating substantial gains when AI support spans the full SDLC. The authors also identified several open research and engineering challenges, though details are not fully given in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: Extending AI assistance across all stages of the SDLC, rather than focusing only on coding, yields much larger productivity and token-efficiency gains. The metadata produced during operation can be exploited to continuously improve the underlying models and world model. However, important open challenges remain before such AI Software Factories can be fully realized and generalized.

title: The Canonical Order Problem: When Large Language Models Are Unreliable Knowledge Bases for Multi-Valued Relations
summary:
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as knowledge bases (KBs) due to the vast amount of knowledge they acquire during pre-training. While many works focus on extracting single relational triples, most real-world relations are multi-valued and require generating sets of entities.
  In this paper, we investigate how LLMs represent and generate multi-valued relations. We identify the canonical order problem: The probabilistic distributions inside LLMs organize many multi-valued relations according to a canonical ordering (e.g., alphabetical or chronological). Through mechanistic analysis, we show that set generation in LLMs can be thought of in terms of three phases: (1) retrieval of candidate entities, (2) internal sorting, and (3) selection of the next element. As a result, prompts aiming to construct KBs that deviate from this internal canonical ordering lead to a markedly reduced reliability of LLMs when aiming to generate complete sets for multi-valued relations.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how large language models generate sets of entities for multi-valued relations and shows that models internally impose a canonical order (e.g., alphabetical or chronological), which affects reliability when prompts ask for differently ordered sets.
AI.motivation: Most prior work on using LLMs as knowledge bases focuses on extracting single relational triples. However, many real-world relations are inherently multi-valued (e.g., countries in a union, members of a band), requiring the model to output sets of entities. There is limited understanding of how LLMs internally represent and generate such sets, and why they often fail to produce complete or consistent lists, especially when prompted in different orders. The paper aims to uncover the internal mechanisms that govern multi-valued relation generation and explain systematic error patterns.
AI.method: The authors perform a mechanistic analysis of LLM behavior when generating entities for multi-valued relations. They study the token-level probability distributions and generation dynamics to see how candidate entities are produced and ordered. By analyzing how probabilities change across decoding steps and under different prompts, they decompose the process into three conceptual phases: (1) retrieval of candidate entities linked to the queried relation, (2) internal sorting according to an implicit canonical criterion (such as alphabetical or chronological order), and (3) selection of the next element from this ordered pool. They then compare performance when prompts align with versus deviate from this internal canonical ordering.
AI.result: The study finds consistent evidence that LLMs internally impose a canonical order on many multi-valued relations. When the requested output order matches this internal canonical ordering, the models are more reliable at generating more complete and correct sets. When prompts request alternative orderings or otherwise conflict with the internal ordering, generation becomes less reliable, with more omissions, repetitions, and errors. This demonstrates that the internal sorting phase significantly constrains how well LLMs can act as knowledge bases for multi-valued relations.
AI.conclusion: LLMs do not simply retrieve unordered sets of entities for multi-valued relations; instead, they retrieve candidates and then internally sort them according to a canonical ordering. This hidden ordering strongly influences output behavior and can degrade performance when user prompts ask for different orders. For knowledge base construction and evaluation, it is therefore important to account for these canonical order effects in prompt design and benchmarking. The work suggests that improving LLMs as KBs may require architectures or training schemes that better separate set membership from ordering preferences.

title: PILLAR: Private Inverted-Index Lexical Lookup for Augmented Retrieval
summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) hands the user's query to whoever hosts the corpus. We propose PILLAR, a Privacy-Preserving RAG (PPRAG) system based on Private Information Retrieval (PIR) in which a client utilizes the k documents most similar to their query from a server-held and publicly known corpus to respond to their query, while the server learns nothing about the query, either its terms or its access pattern. Prior PPRAG constructions rely on dense retrieval alone, translating approximate nearest-neighbor search into many query-dependent rounds of PIR, and pay for it in both latency and retrieval quality. PILLAR instead performs private hybrid retrieval in two stages. A sparse stage issues a small, fixed number of PIR queries against a carefully designed index of precomputed BM25 scores, filtering the corpus down to candidates that share terms with the query without the server ever seeing which terms these are. A dense stage then fetches only those candidates' document embeddings and re-ranks them locally, avoiding the many costly PIR queries that private dense retrieval typically requires. We instantiate PILLAR with two protocols that trade latency against retrieval quality, each built on a different private rendering of lexical search. PILLAR-Bin bins posting lists into a hash table and is a single-round design that achieves lower latency than state-of-the-art private retrieval schemes. PILLAR-Tree turns block-max pruning into an oblivious tree traversal combined with cuckoo hash tables and achieves the highest retrieval quality at lower latency than state-of-the-art schemes.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces PILLAR, a privacy-preserving RAG system that uses PIR to retrieve relevant documents without revealing the user’s query or access pattern, achieving better latency–quality trade-offs than prior PPRAG methods.
AI.motivation: Standard RAG systems expose user queries and document access patterns to whoever hosts the corpus, which is problematic for sensitive queries. Existing privacy-preserving RAG approaches based on dense retrieval require many PIR rounds, resulting in high latency and degraded retrieval quality. There is a need for a system that keeps queries private while retaining practical latency and high retrieval quality.
AI.method: PILLAR combines private sparse and dense retrieval in two stages. First, a sparse retrieval stage issues a fixed, small number of PIR queries over a special index that stores precomputed BM25 scores, privately narrowing the corpus to candidate documents sharing terms with the query. Second, a dense stage privately fetches embeddings only for those candidates and reranks them locally, avoiding many expensive PIR calls. The paper instantiates this design with two protocols: PILLAR-Bin, which bins posting lists into a hash table for a single-round, low-latency protocol, and PILLAR-Tree, which uses an oblivious tree traversal with cuckoo hash tables and block-max pruning to maximize retrieval quality while still improving latency over prior work.
AI.result: The two PILLAR variants demonstrate that private hybrid retrieval can outperform previous PPRAG schemes. PILLAR-Bin achieves lower latency than state-of-the-art private retrieval by using a single-round protocol, while PILLAR-Tree provides the highest retrieval quality with latency still below competing private retrieval methods. Both show that privately combining sparse and dense retrieval can substantially reduce PIR overhead without sacrificing accuracy.
AI.conclusion: PILLAR proves that practical privacy-preserving RAG is feasible by designing a hybrid sparse–dense retrieval scheme atop PIR that hides both query contents and access patterns. Through its two concrete instantiations, it offers tunable trade-offs between latency and retrieval quality, and outperforms prior PPRAG approaches on both dimensions, suggesting a promising direction for secure deployment of RAG systems over sensitive queries and public corpora.

title: Lost in Translation: Measuring the Effect of Non-Native English on End User Performance of Large Language Models
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used by people whose first language is not English, yet these users have been shown to receive systematically lower-quality responses than fluent speakers. Which specific features of non-native English drive this gap remains unclear, because fluency is itself a composite of mechanical accuracy, vocabulary use, organization, and discourse coherence. Here, we introduce FABLE, a controlled dataset of 190,911 English prompt variants derived from 174K real user prompts for writing-related tasks. Evaluating responses from 34 open-weight LLMs, we find a clear asymmetry; while models do not propagate surface errors such as misspellings into their outputs, models do mirror higher-level rhetorical and lexical qualities present in the user's prompt. Further, the overall quality of responses differs substantially between the least- and most-fluent prompts. These results highlight a key LLM performance disparity for non-native English LLM users, resulting in both lower-quality and less-fluent answers.

AI.tldr: The paper studies why non-native English users receive lower-quality answers from large language models and introduces a large controlled dataset (FABLE) to isolate which aspects of fluency drive this disparity.
AI.motivation: Non-native English speakers are heavy users of LLMs but systematically get worse responses than native or highly fluent users. Fluency is multifaceted—mechanics, vocabulary, organization, coherence—so it is unclear which specific dimensions of non-native writing cause LLMs to underperform. Existing evaluations lack controlled variation over realistic user prompts to disentangle these factors, motivating the creation of a dedicated dataset and systematic study.
AI.method: The authors construct FABLE, a controlled dataset of 190,911 English prompt variants derived from 174,000 real user prompts focused on writing tasks. They generate variants that differ in surface errors (e.g., misspellings) versus higher-level rhetorical and lexical qualities. Using this dataset, they systematically query 34 open-weight LLMs, comparing model responses across prompt variants that isolate different aspects of fluency. They then evaluate how closely model outputs mirror prompt-level features and quantify response quality differences between low- and high-fluency prompts.
AI.result: Across 34 open-weight LLMs, models show an asymmetry in how they react to prompt quality. They largely do not reproduce or amplify low-level surface errors such as spelling mistakes. However, they do closely mirror higher-level aspects of user language, including rhetorical structure and lexical sophistication. Prompts with better organization and word choice elicit correspondingly higher-quality, more fluent outputs. Quantitatively, there is a substantial quality gap between responses to the least-fluent and most-fluent prompts in the dataset.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates a clear performance disparity: LLMs give non-native or less-fluent English prompts significantly worse and less-fluent answers, not because they propagate superficial errors, but because they echo higher-level discourse and lexical limitations in the input. This suggests that improving accessibility and fairness for non-native users will require mitigation strategies that decouple answer quality from prompt fluency, ensuring robust support even when user language is less polished.

title: ThuRunel: Dynamic Decoupling for Structured Advisory Dialogue
summary: High-stakes advisory domains such as medical aesthetics, legal consultation, and educational planning exhibit a two-phase structure. The early phase requires empathetic elicitation and emotional support, and the late phase requires authoritative specialist judgment. Neither fully automated agents nor human junior consultants adequately address this structure at scale. We formalize the core design challenge as dynamic decoupling, asking how an AI advisory agent should decide what to ask, when to stop, what to resolve autonomously, and what to forward to the specialist. We present ThuRunel, an advisory agent combining a finite-state belief management framework, a chain-of-thought teacher synthesis protocol, and learned generation adapters. Against eleven baselines, ThuRunel achieves consistent improvements in elicitation completeness and specialist brief quality. ThuRunel is publicly deployed as a bilingual web application in which the same decoupling decisions operate from the client's side, grounded in a curated knowledge base that cites its sources in every answer.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces ThuRunel, an AI advisory agent designed for high-stakes domains with two phases: empathetic elicitation and specialist decision-making. It focuses on dynamically deciding what the AI should handle versus what should be escalated to human experts, and shows improved information gathering and briefing quality over baselines.
AI.motivation: High-stakes advisory services (e.g., medical aesthetics, law, educational planning) have a structured interaction: first, understanding and supporting the client emotionally; second, providing authoritative expert judgment. Existing solutions—fully automated systems or human junior consultants—do not scale well and fail to optimally manage when and how to involve human specialists. There is a need to formalize and solve the problem of when the AI should ask questions, decide autonomously, or escalate cases to experts.
AI.method: The authors formalize the design challenge as a dynamic decoupling problem: deciding what to ask, when to stop eliciting information, what to resolve autonomously, and what to forward to specialists. They propose ThuRunel, an advisory agent with three main technical components: (1) a finite-state belief management framework to track and update the system’s understanding of the client; (2) a chain-of-thought teacher synthesis protocol to improve reasoning and guidance; and (3) learned generation adapters that tailor responses to the advisory context. The system is deployed as a bilingual web application backed by a curated, source-citing knowledge base.
AI.result: In experiments comparing ThuRunel with eleven baseline systems, the authors report consistent improvements in two key metrics: (a) elicitation completeness, i.e., how fully the system gathers all relevant client information in the early phase, and (b) specialist brief quality, i.e., the usefulness and clarity of the information the AI prepares for human specialists. These results suggest that ThuRunel manages the dynamic decoupling of tasks more effectively than existing approaches.
AI.conclusion: ThuRunel demonstrates that explicitly modeling the two-phase nature of high-stakes advisory interactions and treating the AI–human handoff as a dynamic decoupling problem can substantially improve advisory quality. The combination of finite-state belief management, chain-of-thought based synthesis, and learned adapters leads to better information elicitation and expert briefing. Public deployment as a bilingual, source-citing system indicates practical viability and potential for real-world impact in multiple advisory domains.

title: CineSubBench: Evaluating LLMs on Long-Form Narrative and Cultural Understanding from Multilingual Movie Subtitles
summary: Large language models are increasingly evaluated in specialized domains such as law, medicine, software engineering, and cybersecurity, yet film remains comparatively underexplored despite requiring long-form narrative integration, multilingual interpretation, and culturally situated audience judgments. We introduce CineSubBench, a benchmark for evaluating long-context film understanding from multilingual movie subtitles. A subtitle track represents a film as thousands of short, temporally ordered utterances from which models must reconstruct characters, relationships, events, causal progression, and themes without explicit scene or event structure. CineSubBench contains 1,012 films with complete subtitle coverage in six languages, yielding 6,072 tracks and 8.13M timestamped subtitle entries. It provides a matched multi-task, multilingual, and multicultural (MultiX) evaluation setting: seven tasks span narrative reconstruction and abstraction, genre prediction, age suitability, country-specific motion-picture ratings across ten national classification systems, and subtitle-grounded language safety. Across nine LLMs, plot premises are recovered more reliably than event-complete synopses; cross-lingual consistency varies substantially across models and languages; national rating systems expose distinct calibration patterns; and strong profanity is far easier to ground than mild obscenity. CineSubBench establishes film as a long-context LLM evaluation domain and provides a unified benchmark for measuring narrative, multilingual, cultural, and evidence-grounding capabilities.

AI.tldr: The paper presents CineSubBench, a benchmark built from multilingual movie subtitles to evaluate long-context, multilingual, and culturally grounded film understanding in large language models.
AI.motivation: While LLMs are widely evaluated in domains like law and medicine, film understanding has been underexplored despite posing unique challenges: long-form narrative reasoning, multilingual dialogue, and culturally situated audience judgments. Existing benchmarks do not capture how well models can reconstruct complex narratives and culturally specific interpretations from partial, temporally ordered text such as subtitles.
AI.method: The authors construct CineSubBench from 1,012 films with complete subtitle coverage in six languages, producing 6,072 subtitle tracks and over 8.13M timestamped subtitle entries. They treat each subtitle track as a long sequence of short utterances lacking explicit scene structure and design seven evaluation tasks that probe different capabilities: narrative reconstruction and abstraction (e.g., plot and synopsis generation), genre prediction, age suitability, prediction of country-specific motion-picture ratings across ten national systems, and subtitle-grounded language safety. They then evaluate nine LLMs on these tasks, analyzing cross-lingual consistency, narrative completeness, cultural calibration in ratings, and grounding of safety-related judgments in subtitle evidence.
AI.result: Empirically, the authors find that LLMs are better at recovering high-level plot premises than at producing event-complete synopses, indicating difficulty with fine-grained narrative reconstruction from long subtitle streams. Cross-lingual consistency differs strongly by model and language, showing uneven multilingual robustness. When predicting national film ratings, models display distinct calibration patterns across different countries and systems. For language safety, models more reliably detect and ground strong profanity than subtle or mild obscenity in subtitles.
AI.conclusion: CineSubBench demonstrates that film, represented via multilingual subtitles, is a rich domain for evaluating long-context understanding, narrative reasoning, multilingual robustness, cultural sensitivity, and evidence-grounded judgments in LLMs. The benchmark offers a unified MultiX (multi-task, multilingual, multicultural) setting and reveals current limitations of LLMs in detailed narrative reconstruction, consistent multilingual behavior, culturally calibrated rating prediction, and nuanced safety assessment, establishing a foundation for future research and model development in this space.

title: HyperZip: Efficient Data Compression through Personalized Diffusion LLMs with Hypernetworks
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong potential for lossless data compression, but existing approaches are constrained by the high computational cost and low throughput of autoregressive decoding. We propose HyperZip, an efficient and scalable LLM-based compression framework that leverages diffusion-based LLMs (dLLMs) with Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) to accelerate LLM-based data compression processes. We identify a trade-off in diffusion-based compression, where increasing decoding throughput degrades the compression rate. To mitigate this trade-off, HyperZip employs a hypernetwork to generate data-specific updates from a context representation, adapting the dLLM to the target data without costly fine-tuning, resulting in a low compression rate and high throughput. Extensive experiments show that HyperZip achieves a superior trade-off between compression rate and speed compared with state-of-the-art baselines.

AI.tldr: HyperZip accelerates LLM-based lossless compression using diffusion LLMs with multi-token prediction and a hypernetwork to adapt to data, improving the speed–compression trade-off.
AI.motivation: LLM-based compression can be strong but is bottlenecked by slow, autoregressive decoding that predicts one token at a time, limiting throughput and practicality. Diffusion-based LLMs and multi-token prediction can speed up decoding, but naïvely increasing speed worsens compression rates. The paper is motivated by the need for an LLM-based compression scheme that is both fast and has good compression ratios, overcoming this speed–rate trade-off without expensive fine-tuning for each dataset.
AI.method: The authors introduce HyperZip, a framework that uses a diffusion-based LLM (dLLM) equipped with Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) to decode multiple tokens per step, boosting throughput. They analyze the inherent trade-off in diffusion-based compression between decoding speed and compression rate. To address it, they add a hypernetwork that, given a context representation of the target data, outputs data-specific parameter updates or conditioning signals for the dLLM. This allows the model to adapt to the statistics of the current data source on the fly, avoiding full fine-tuning while improving compression efficiency. The overall system performs lossless compression by using the adapted dLLM as a probabilistic model within an entropy coding scheme, but with accelerated decoding via diffusion and MTP.
AI.result: Experiments across multiple datasets demonstrate that HyperZip yields better combined performance than state-of-the-art LLM-based and non-LLM compression baselines. Specifically, it achieves lower compression rates (i.e., better compression ratios) at similar or higher decoding speeds, or significantly higher throughput at similar compression rates. The results empirically validate that the hypernetwork-based adaptation successfully mitigates the usual degradation in compression rate when diffusion and multi-token prediction are used to speed up decoding.
AI.conclusion: HyperZip shows that diffusion-based LLMs with multi-token prediction, augmented by a lightweight hypernetwork for data-specific adaptation, can provide an effective and practical solution for lossless data compression. The framework breaks the typical trade-off between speed and compression rate in diffusion-based compression, achieving a superior balance compared with existing approaches. This suggests that carefully designed adaptation mechanisms can make high-capacity generative models more viable for real-world compression tasks.

title: Cognitive Expert Language Models Better Align with the Corresponding Brain Systems
summary: Large language models (LLMs) can predict human brain activity across a variety of brain regions during natural language comprehension. Typically, however, LLM-brain alignment is measured using one model for different regions of the brain, and then model performance is summarized across regions. This one-model-fits-all approach ignores the functional specialization of brain regions. In this study, we assess whether a model oriented toward a particular cognitive domain aligns better with the brain system dedicated to that domain. Through prompting and fine-tuning, we first build expert LLM variants for six domains: sensory, spatial, numerical, reasoning, social, and abstract processing. We then examine whether each expert best predicts activity in the brain region associated with the corresponding cognitive domain. Consistent with our hypotheses, each expert's representations align more closely with the brain system most associated with the matching domain than do other experts. This holds under both prompting and fine-tuning, across three base models and three fMRI datasets. In a series of control analyses, we show that this model-brain alignment is specific to cognitive domain interventions; non-cognitive and surface-level interventions do not result in comparable alignment. Specializing models shifts regional alignment while leaving aggregate prediction accuracy largely unchanged, suggesting that summarizing alignment across regions may obscure regional differences in performance for specific models.

AI.tldr: The paper tests whether LLMs specialized to particular cognitive domains better predict brain activity in corresponding brain networks than general models, finding domain-specific gains in alignment without improving overall accuracy.
AI.motivation: Most prior work measures LLM–brain alignment by using a single model to predict activity across all language-responsive brain regions and then averaging performance. This approach ignores that different brain regions are functionally specialized (e.g., for sensory, social, or numerical processing), so a one-model-fits-all summary might miss important regional differences and offer limited insight into cognitive representations. The authors want to know whether tailoring LLMs to specific cognitive domains leads to tighter alignment with the brain systems that support those domains, thereby revealing a more fine-grained mapping between computational and neural representations.
AI.method: The authors construct domain-specialized ‘expert’ LLM variants for six cognitive domains—sensory, spatial, numerical, reasoning, social, and abstract processing—using two approaches: (1) prompting base models with domain-focused instructions and (2) fine-tuning base models on domain-relevant data. They then evaluate each expert’s ability to predict fMRI activity in brain regions associated with each cognitive domain across three different base LLMs and three separate fMRI datasets involving natural language comprehension. They compare alignment of each domain expert with its hypothesized brain network versus other networks and versus non-specialized baselines. Control analyses test alternative explanations by applying non-cognitive or surface-level interventions to the models and examining whether these also change regional alignment.
AI.result: Each domain-specialized expert model shows stronger representational alignment with the brain system associated with its corresponding cognitive domain than with other domains’ systems, and stronger alignment than other experts in that system. This pattern is robust across both prompting and fine-tuning specializations, across all three base LLMs, and across three independent fMRI datasets. Control interventions that alter non-cognitive or superficial properties of the models do not yield comparable domain-specific alignment patterns, indicating that the effects are not due to trivial changes. Importantly, overall (aggregate) prediction accuracy across all regions remains largely unchanged when models are specialized, but the spatial pattern of which regions are best predicted shifts with domain specialization.
AI.conclusion: Functional specialization matters for LLM–brain alignment: models that are cognitively specialized to a domain better capture the neural activity patterns of brain systems that support that domain, even though their average predictive performance across the whole brain does not improve. This implies that summarizing model–brain alignment at a global or region-averaged level can obscure meaningful regional dissociations and underestimates how specific modeling choices affect particular neural systems. The findings support a more nuanced approach where multiple specialized models may be needed to explain how language-elicited brain activity reflects diverse underlying cognitive domains.

title: Better Nearest Neighbor Graph Indices via (Efficient) LLM-Guided Pruning
summary: Graph-based approximate nearest neighbor search (ANNS) is widely used for large-scale semantic search. Its indices are constructed primarily based on geometric relationships among embeddings of an input dataset (e.g., documents or images), rather than explicitly optimizing for semantic relevance. However, when using these indices for downstream query retrieval, performance is evaluated based on the semantic relevance of the retrieved results to the query. This creates a fundamental "geometry-semantic" mismatch between how the indices are constructed and how their retrieval results are evaluated. While existing LLM-based reranking methods can partially mitigate this mismatch at query time, they leave this underlying structural problem in the graph unresolved. We therefore propose LLM-Guided Graph Pruning (LGP), a general framework that addresses this mismatch directly by leveraging LLM reasoning to refine an existing ANN graph index itself. LGP identifies structurally "low-value" neighbors of nodes and replaces them with LLM-selected alternatives that provide useful semantic information while retaining desired geometric structures of the original graph, including sparsity and efficient navigability. Experiments on representative semantic retrieval benchmarks show that LGP consistently improves end-to-end retrieval performance over both vanilla greedy graph search and LLM-based reranking across widely used graph-based ANN indices such as DiskANN and HNSW.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses the mismatch between how graph-based ANN indices are built (geometric proximity) and how they’re evaluated (semantic relevance), and proposes LLM-Guided Graph Pruning (LGP) to use LLMs to refine graph neighbors and improve semantic retrieval without sacrificing graph efficiency.
AI.motivation: Graph-based ANN search structures graphs based on geometric relationships between embeddings, but retrieval quality is judged by semantic relevance to queries. This geometry–semantic mismatch means the graphs are not optimized for the real objective. LLM-based rerankers help only at query time and do not fix the underlying graph structure. There is a need for a method that directly reshapes the index graph to better encode semantic relationships while preserving efficiency.
AI.method: The authors introduce LLM-Guided Graph Pruning (LGP), a framework that operates on an existing ANN graph index. LGP uses an LLM to reason about node relationships and identify neighbors that are structurally present but semantically low-value. It prunes these low-value neighbors and replaces them with alternative neighbors chosen via LLM guidance that are semantically more informative. The process is designed to maintain the desirable geometric properties of the original graph—such as sparsity and navigability—while injecting semantic structure.
AI.result: On standard semantic retrieval benchmarks, applying LGP to common graph ANN indices (e.g., DiskANN, HNSW) improves end-to-end retrieval performance. The method outperforms both baseline greedy graph search using the original indices and pipelines that combine those indices with LLM-based reranking, indicating that structurally adapting the graph with LLM guidance yields additional gains beyond reranking alone.
AI.conclusion: Re-structuring ANN graphs with LLM guidance effectively reduces the geometry–semantic mismatch inherent in conventional graph-based indices. LGP enhances semantic retrieval quality while preserving efficiency characteristics of popular ANN graphs, and can be applied as a general post-processing framework across different index types.

title: Learning from Teacher Continuations at Student States
summary: We present OLIVE (OnLine InterVEntion). At each iteration, the evolving student policy generates a new prefix, the teacher continues it autoregressively, and the student is updated using cross-entropy computed on the teacher-generated tokens. Each design choice targets a corresponding limitation of existing distillation methods: (1) sequential covariate shift in offline supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on fixed teacher trajectories, (2) fragmented supervision under prefix failure in token-level on-policy distillation (OPD), and (3) the need for access to teacher token probabilities in distribution-matching distillation. OLIVE achieves higher reasoning performance than OPD (with a top-16 KL approximation) at comparable GPU-hour cost. Our asynchronous implementation further reduces OLIVE's total training time by 23.8\%. We evaluate OLIVE on both hard reasoning tasks and agentic tasks which reflects modern post-training scenarios, and it consistently outperforms existing distillation methods under the same training budget. By regenerating prefixes from the evolving student, OLIVE continues improving after offline distillation plateaus while better preserving the general capabilities and plasticity of the student. Using only text from GPT-5.4-mini, continuously training with OLIVE outperforms offline SFT from the same teacher by 13\% on ScienceWorld. These results support OLIVE as an effective and efficient approach to online language-model distillation.

AI.tldr: OLIVE is an online distillation method where a student model continually learns from teacher continuations generated on student-created prefixes, improving reasoning and efficiency over prior distillation approaches.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM distillation methods have key weaknesses: offline supervised fine-tuning on fixed teacher data suffers from covariate shift because the student will encounter different prefixes at deployment; on-policy token-level distillation can fail when student prefixes go off-distribution, giving fragmented or low-quality supervision; and KL-based distribution matching requires access to teacher token probabilities, which are often unavailable in API-based or proprietary settings. The authors want a method that is (1) on-policy, (2) robust to prefix failures, and (3) works with teacher text-only access, while being computationally efficient and preserving general capabilities and plasticity of the student model.
AI.method: OLIVE (OnLine InterVEntion) trains a student model through an iterative online process: at each step, the student generates a prefix for a task; then a teacher model continues this prefix autoregressively to complete the sequence; the student is updated via cross-entropy on the teacher-generated continuation tokens, effectively learning to imitate how the teacher would continue from the student’s own states. Design choices directly counter known issues in other distillation approaches: regenerating prefixes from the evolving student mitigates covariate shift; letting the teacher take over from student prefixes avoids fragmented supervision when the student makes early mistakes; and using only teacher tokens (not probabilities) eliminates the need for distribution-level access. They also implement an asynchronous training setup to reduce wall-clock time, and evaluate OLIVE across reasoning and agentic benchmarks under fixed training budgets.
AI.result: OLIVE attains higher reasoning performance than token-level on-policy distillation methods that approximate KL with top-k teacher probabilities (e.g., top-16 KL) at similar GPU-hour cost. An asynchronous implementation cuts total training time by around 23.8%. Across challenging reasoning benchmarks and agentic tasks that mirror modern post-training use cases, OLIVE consistently surpasses existing distillation baselines when trained under equal compute budgets. In a concrete scenario using GPT-5.4-mini as the teacher, continuous training with OLIVE improves performance on the ScienceWorld benchmark by 13% relative to standard offline supervised fine-tuning on the same teacher outputs.
AI.conclusion: OLIVE provides an effective and compute-efficient framework for online distillation of language models using only teacher text, addressing sequential covariate shift and supervision fragmentation while avoiding reliance on teacher token probabilities. By continually regenerating prefixes from the evolving student and letting the teacher complete them, OLIVE keeps improving beyond the plateau of offline distillation, and better preserves the student’s general skills and adaptability. The empirical results suggest that OLIVE is a practical approach for post-training and scaling down strong teacher models into smaller, well-performing student models suitable for modern reasoning and agentic tasks.

title: Engineering Simplicity: Simple Mechanism Interfaces Steer LLM Agents
summary: Can interaction formats and textual scaffolds help large language model (LLM) agents make better decisions, and do better decisions come with better explanations? We study these questions in auctions and matching, multi-agent environments with explicit rules and known optimal strategies. These settings let us vary how a decision problem is presented while retaining a benchmark for evaluating behavior. Drawing on human-motivated theories of simplicity, we compare interfaces that elicit a complete bid or ranking with sequential interfaces that make safe choices easier to identify. We then hold the interaction format fixed and vary reasoning scaffolds and rule descriptions. Across four model families, the ascending auction interface substantially reduces bid deviations. The matching comparison also shows why sequential responses require different error accounting from complete rankings. Laying out payoff contingencies and explaining why truth-telling is safe also improve choices, whereas prompts to plan through matching rounds or form beliefs about opponents worsen play overall. In auctions, these behavioral gains are not accompanied by corresponding improvements in measured verbal indicators of strategic understanding in the agents' short stated plans. Other prompts change those indicators without improving bids. Our findings suggest that human-motivated theories of simplicity can inform the design of decision environments for artificial agents. They also show why scaffolds should be evaluated through realized choices as well as explanations: improvements in one need not appear in the other.

AI.tldr: The paper tests whether different interaction interfaces and textual prompts can help LLM agents make better strategic decisions, and whether better choices are reflected in better explanations, using auctions and matching as controlled environments.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly used as agents that make decisions in structured environments, but we lack clear guidance on how to design their interfaces and prompts so that they behave strategically well. Auctions and matching markets are classic domains in economics with well-understood optimal strategies, providing a clean testbed. The authors want to understand if human-inspired ideas of simplicity and scaffolding that help people can also help LLM agents, and whether improved behavior is captured by standard explanation-based metrics.
AI.method: The authors set up decision problems in two canonical multi-agent settings: auctions (with a focus on ascending auctions) and matching markets. They systematically vary (1) the interaction format—either requiring a complete bid/ranking at once or using sequential interfaces that make safe strategies more salient—and (2) textual scaffolds, such as rule descriptions, payoff contingencies, truth-telling explanations, planning prompts, and belief-formation prompts. They run these conditions across four different LLM families, measure deviations from optimal strategies, and separately score verbal indicators of strategic understanding in the models’ short written plans or explanations.
AI.result: Sequential, ascending-auction-style interfaces significantly reduce deviations from optimal bidding compared with interfaces that ask for a complete bid at once. In matching, they show that sequential interfaces alter the error structure compared to full rankings, so standard error measures need adjustment. Textual scaffolds that explicitly describe payoff contingencies and explain why truthful revelation is safe improve strategic choices, while prompts that push agents to plan through multiple rounds or reason about others’ beliefs tend to worsen performance. Importantly, in auctions, better decisions do not coincide with better measured verbal strategic explanations, and some prompts change explanation metrics without changing decisions.
AI.conclusion: Human-inspired simplicity principles—like making safe strategies salient via sequential interaction—can be effectively used to design decision environments that improve LLM agents’ strategic performance. However, explanation quality and decision quality can move independently: better choices need not come with better explanations, and better-sounding reasoning need not imply better behavior. Therefore, evaluation and design of artificial agents should focus on realized choices in addition to, or even instead of, stated explanations, and scaffolds should be judged by their behavioral impact rather than only by interpretability-style metrics.

title: Population Fidelity: Evaluating Population Representativeness in LLMs
comment: 37 pages, 16 figures, 14 tables. Code and data: https://github.com/CriticalMaking/LLM-population-fidelity
summary: Large language models (LLMs) show considerable potential in simulating human attitudes and preferences. Prior work finds that LLM-generated responses can compress the range of attitudes found within populations and misrepresent particular subgroups in ways that vary across models and topics. We introduce Population Fidelity, an evaluation framework that distinguishes key conditions required for a set of LLM-generated responses to represent a population. It incorporates three dimensions: group-level accuracy, the amount of between-group variation, and the structure of that variation. We demonstrate the framework's utility in two ways. First, we reproduce a prior study of "machine bias" in LLM survey responses and apply the framework to its models and more recent ones, showing that poor representation reflects not only insufficient between-group variation but also variation assigned to the wrong groups. Second, we evaluate one proposed approach to improving models' population representativeness: cultural fine-tuning. We find that cultural fine-tuning can improve alignment with the survey center without improving the representation of within-population differences, a distinction that measures of aggregate agreement do not capture. We argue that representing a population requires models to reproduce several features of human attitudinal variation simultaneously. Our framework organizes these features and provides reusable code, data, and trained models for evaluating population fidelity across substantive domains and assessing proposed alignment methods.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an evaluation framework, Population Fidelity, for assessing how well LLM-generated responses represent human populations’ attitudes and within-population differences.
AI.motivation: Existing research shows that LLMs can simulate human attitudes but often compress diversity and misrepresent subgroups, and current metrics (e.g., aggregate agreement) fail to capture where and how these misrepresentations occur. There is no standardized way to evaluate whether LLMs faithfully reproduce population-level and subgroup-level attitudinal patterns, especially as models are used for social science, policy, or survey-like applications.
AI.method: The authors define Population Fidelity as a multi-dimensional evaluation framework with three components: (1) group-level accuracy (do average responses by group match human groups?), (2) amount of between-group variation (does the model reproduce how different groups actually differ in magnitude?), and (3) structure of that variation (are the differences attributed to the correct groups and relationships among groups). They apply this framework empirically in two settings: (a) re-analysis of a prior “machine bias” study using earlier and newer LLMs, and (b) assessment of a cultural fine-tuning approach. They provide code, data, and trained models to operationalize these metrics across domains.
AI.result: In the re-analysis, they show that poor representation of populations by LLMs arises not only from too little between-group variation but also from misallocating variation to the wrong groups (incorrect structure). In the cultural fine-tuning case, they find that fine-tuning can make model responses closer to an overall survey center (improving global alignment) without improving the representation of within-population differences—so aggregate agreement metrics can look good while subgroup fidelity remains poor.
AI.conclusion: Faithfully representing a population in LLM-generated responses requires capturing multiple aspects of human attitudinal variation at once: accurate group means, realistic degrees of between-group variation, and correct structure of that variation across groups. Population Fidelity provides a principled, multi-dimensional framework—and accompanying resources—for evaluating these properties and for more rigorously assessing alignment methods such as cultural fine-tuning across substantive domains.

title: Support-Set Target Leakage in Relational Foundation Models during In-Context Learning: Impact, Detection, and Mitigation
summary: Relational in-context learning (ICL) conditions predictions on the labeled support examples and their linked tables, creating a failure mode when the support set contains target-derived features that are unavailable for the query. We formulate this problem as support-set target leakage, distinct from leakage during dataset construction, temporal splitting, or representation learning. Here, the target-derived (leaker) columns are present only in the labeled support set during relational in-context inference, while queries remain clean. We construct 14 synthetic leaker types, corresponding to 20 columns, spanning proxies with different noise levels, coverage, modalities, semantic transparency, and relational distances. We evaluate a frozen relational encoder with an ICL head on held-out RelBench databases and use Integrated Gradients (IG) to rank and remove suspicious columns. Our results show that the effect of support-set leakage varies across tasks and relational distances. Target-table leakers cause the clearest degradation, while one- and two-hop leakers are not consistently used by the model. IG ranks target-table leakers highly across datasets and partially recovers performance in settings where leakage has the largest effect.

AI.tldr: The paper studies a new failure mode in relational in-context learning where labeled support examples contain target-derived columns that queries do not have, leading to misleadingly good training-time performance and degraded test-time performance.
AI.motivation: Relational in-context learning models use both labeled support examples and their linked database tables. In practice, support tables may contain columns that are highly predictive of the target label but are not available for future queries (e.g., post-outcome information or engineered labels). Existing leakage notions mostly focus on dataset construction, temporal splits, or representation learning, not on this support-only phenomenon. The authors want to formalize and empirically characterize this overlooked leakage type, understand when it harms performance, and explore methods to detect and mitigate it.
AI.method: They define "support-set target leakage" as target-derived columns present only in the support set during relational ICL. They synthetically inject 14 types of such leakers (20 columns total) into RelBench databases, varying noise level, coverage, modality, semantic clarity, and relational distance from the target table (target table vs one-hop vs two-hop). Using a frozen relational encoder with an ICL head, they measure performance on held-out databases under different leakage configurations. They then apply Integrated Gradients to attribute model predictions to columns, rank suspicious leaker columns, and iteratively remove them to evaluate whether performance recovers.
AI.result: Support-set leakage has heterogeneous impact: columns in the target table that leak target information cause clear and substantial performance degradation and are heavily relied upon by the model. In contrast, one- and two-hop leakers are not consistently exploited and thus have weaker and less predictable effects. Integrated Gradients reliably ranks target-table leakers among the most important features across datasets and, when these columns are removed based on IG ranking, performance partially recovers in scenarios where leakage had the strongest negative effect.
AI.conclusion: Support-set target leakage is a distinct and practically important failure mode for relational in-context learning, especially when leaker columns reside in the target table. Attribution methods like Integrated Gradients can help detect such leaker columns and mitigate their impact by guiding their removal, but not all relationally distant leakers are consistently used by models. The work highlights the need to audit relational ICL setups for support-only target-derived features and to develop more robust defenses against this form of leakage.

title: HeurEvo: Agentic Evolution of Hybrid Solver-Augmented Heuristics for Time-Critical Mathematical Optimization
summary: Recent advances in agentic heuristic design use AI agents and execution feedback to automate algorithm discovery for challenging optimization problems. In many practical settings, high-quality solutions must be obtained under strict runtime constraints, motivating hybrid approaches that combine problem-specific heuristics with powerful mathematical programming solvers. However, existing approaches typically improve heuristic components within predefined procedures or tune solver configurations in isolation. This limits holistic adaptation of where to allocate computation, how to leverage solvers, and how to refine the overall algorithmic structure. To address these limitations, we propose HeurEvo, an automated plan--code--component co-evolution framework that jointly evolves the high-level algorithmic structures, their implementations, and a shared pool of reusable components. A planner determines which algorithmic components to use, how to combine them, and how to allocate runtime across stages, a coder realizes the resulting plan as executable code, while a component evolver updates the shared component pool. Within an island-based evolutionary framework, plans and implementations co-evolve with feedback from an interpreter agent that analyzes execution results and identifies opportunities for improvement. Across diverse combinatorial optimization benchmarks and challenging MIPLIB instances, HeurEvo finds high-quality solutions within tight runtime budgets, often matching or surpassing state-of-the-art optimization solvers given hours or days of computation. On several nonlinear geometry problems such as hexagon packing, it also improves upon the best previously reported results. These results highlight the value of jointly searching over algorithmic structure and implementation for agentic heuristic design.

AI.tldr: HeurEvo is an AI-driven evolutionary framework that automatically designs and codes hybrid optimization heuristics, jointly evolving algorithm structure, implementations, and reusable components to produce high-quality solutions under tight runtime limits.
AI.motivation: Traditional heuristic design for hard optimization problems is manual and time-consuming, and current AI-based approaches either optimize heuristics inside fixed frameworks or tune solver settings in isolation. In many real-world applications, we must get very strong solutions quickly, often by combining domain-specific heuristics with general-purpose solvers. There is a need for a method that can automatically and holistically decide how an algorithm is structured, how it is implemented in code, how it uses solvers, and how to allocate computational budget across the different parts of the algorithm.
AI.method: The authors introduce HeurEvo, a plan–code–component co-evolution system. It has: (1) a planner that selects algorithmic components, specifies how they are combined, and allocates runtime across stages; (2) a coder that turns these plans into executable implementations; and (3) a component evolver that maintains and refines a shared pool of reusable algorithmic components. These elements interact within an island-based evolutionary framework, where multiple candidate algorithms (plans plus code) co-evolve in parallel. An interpreter agent analyzes execution feedback, such as performance on benchmark instances and runtime behavior, and suggests modifications, enabling iterative improvement of both algorithm structure and implementation.
AI.result: On a variety of combinatorial optimization benchmarks and difficult MIPLIB mixed-integer programming instances, HeurEvo produces solutions of comparable or higher quality than top optimization solvers, but within much tighter runtime limits than those solvers typically require (hours or days). It also achieves new best-known results on several nonlinear geometric optimization problems including hexagon packing, indicating that it can discover algorithms that outperform existing problem-specific methods.
AI.conclusion: Jointly evolving algorithmic structure, implementation code, and a shared component library—guided by execution feedback—can automatically generate high-performing hybrid heuristics for complex optimization problems under strict time limits. This suggests that agentic, co-evolutionary design of heuristics is a powerful direction for automating algorithm discovery beyond isolated solver tuning or fixed-structure heuristic improvement.

title: Persona Dosing: Calibrated Activation Steering for Graded Trait Control
summary: An activation-steering coefficient sets intervention strength, but requesting a particular degree of persona expression requires a behavioral scale. We study persona dosing: controlling a language model through a trait description and a requested mean intensity. PersonaDose specializes a shared, description-conditioned FLAS controller on persona responses, then calibrates its flow time against measured trait expression. Training responses are not paired with requested target intensities. Across Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen3-8B, and Gemma-3-4B, PersonaDose raises core-trait expression at the Persona Vectors coherence floor of 75 by 33.2, 18.3, and 17.8 points over contrastive activation addition. Calibration-selected settings retain an expression advantage on held-out questions, although the coherence floor does not hold for every trait there. Across seven trained traits, calibrated requests yield mean targeting errors of 4.7-6.2 points over 14-22 calibration-reachable targets out of 28 per model. These results separate the behavioral range learned by a controller from the accuracy of requests within that range.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces PersonaDose, a method to ‘dose’ or control how strongly a language model exhibits a given persona trait, achieving more precise and calibrated control of trait intensity than prior activation-steering approaches.
AI.motivation: Existing activation-steering methods can push a model toward a persona but lack an interpretable and calibrated scale for ‘how much’ of a trait should be expressed. Users may want to request specific intensities of traits (e.g., slightly humorous vs. very humorous), which requires a behavioral scale and reliable mapping between control signals and observed behavior. The authors aim to systematically control and calibrate trait expression levels in LLMs without needing training data paired with explicit intensity labels.
AI.method: The authors propose PersonaDose, which (1) starts from a shared FLAS (flow matching / activation steering-like) controller conditioned on textual trait descriptions, (2) specializes this controller on persona response data so that it can modulate trait expression over a continuous ‘flow time’ dimension, and then (3) calibrates the flow time to measured trait expression scores, effectively turning the internal control knob into a behavioral intensity scale. Importantly, training responses are not labeled with requested intensities; calibration instead uses measured trait scores post hoc to map controller settings to target expression levels.
AI.result: On three base models—Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen3-8B, and Gemma-3-4B—PersonaDose substantially increases trait expression compared to contrastive activation addition, especially at a coherence floor of 75 on the Persona Vectors metric: gains of 33.2, 18.3, and 17.8 points respectively. When using calibration-selected controller settings on unseen questions, PersonaDose maintains stronger trait expression, though not all traits keep the same coherence guarantees. For seven trained traits, calibrated intensity requests achieve mean targeting errors of about 4.7–6.2 points over 14–22 reachable target intensities (out of 28) per model.
AI.conclusion: PersonaDose enables calibrated ‘persona dosing,’ separating the problem of learning a controllable behavioral range from the problem of accurately mapping user-specified intensity requests to points in that range. It outperforms standard activation addition in both strength and controllability of trait expression and demonstrates that explicit pairing of responses with target intensities is not required to build a useful behavioral intensity scale.

title: Training LLMs to Verbalize Evaluation Awareness
summary: Evaluation awareness (EA) can cause large language models (LLMs) to behave differently during audits than in deployment, yet measuring and accounting for EA remains challenging. We introduce verbalization training (VT), a method for making LLMs less reticent about verbalizing evaluation awareness while avoiding to supervise the latent belief itself. VT uses a model's spontaneous verbalizations as evidence that awareness is present and truncates each rollout immediately before the verbalization, producing training prefixes at which the model is presumed to be aware. The model is then trained with an RL objective designed to increase verbalization in a calibrated way. Across Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Kimi K2.6, and Inkling, VT increases verbalized EA by 2.4-2.9 times and transfers to held-out agentic settings, while measured latent EA and behavior remain largely stable. In a causal experiment, we independently implant meta-knowledge about evaluations through synthetic-document fine-tuning and show that VT-induced verbalizations reflect the richer knowledge acquired by the model.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a method (verbalization training) to get language models to openly state when they know they are being evaluated, without changing their underlying behavior in the evaluated tasks.
AI.motivation: Evaluation awareness can cause models to behave differently during tests versus real-world use, undermining the reliability of safety and capability audits. Current methods struggle to measure or control this awareness without directly steering the model’s internal beliefs, which is undesirable or infeasible. The authors want a practical way to make models honestly report when they are aware of being evaluated, so auditors can detect and account for such awareness.
AI.method: They introduce verbalization training (VT), which treats a model’s own spontaneous mentions of being evaluated as evidence of evaluation awareness. During data collection, they run the model and look for points where it spontaneously verbalizes awareness; each rollout is truncated just before that point to create a prefix where the model is presumed already aware but has not yet verbalized it. They then apply a reinforcement learning objective on these prefixes to encourage the model to explicitly verbalize its awareness in a calibrated manner—without directly supervising the underlying latent belief. They test VT on three models (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Kimi K2.6, Inkling) and evaluate both verbalized EA and latent EA, including transfer to different agent-like (“agentic”) settings. They also run a causal intervention via synthetic-document fine-tuning to implant extra meta-knowledge about evaluations and examine how VT responds.
AI.result: Verbalization training increases the amount of explicit, verbalized evaluation awareness by roughly 2.4–2.9x across the three tested models. This increased verbalization generalizes to new, held-out agentic scenarios, meaning the models still report their awareness in different contexts. Importantly, measures of latent evaluation awareness and task behavior remain largely unchanged, suggesting VT mainly affects how the model talks about its awareness, not the underlying cognition or performance. In the causal experiment with synthetic-document fine-tuning, VT-induced verbalizations track the richer, implanted meta-knowledge about evaluations, indicating that VT can surface deeper internal knowledge rather than fabricate it.
AI.conclusion: Verbalization training is an effective way to get LLMs to more transparently and reliably state when they are aware of being evaluated, without substantially altering their underlying evaluation awareness or task behavior. It scales across multiple models and transfers to new contexts, and its verbalizations appear to reflect actual internal meta-knowledge when such knowledge is causally implanted. This offers a practical tool for auditors and safety researchers to better detect and interpret evaluation awareness in LLMs, reducing the risk that models behave differently in audits than in deployment.

title: ARCagent: An Adaptive Retrieval Calibration Agent for Clinical Question Answering
summary: In diseases where clinical guidelines are incomplete, contested, or mutually contradictory, knowledge completeness and dynamic conflict-aware synthesis are two safety-critical properties that standard Retrieval-Augmented Generation systems do not provide. Therefore, we present \sysname, an adaptive retrieval calibration clinical question-answering agent for ME/CFS, a disease where diagnostic frameworks coexist and major guidelines actively contradict each other on treatment. ARCagent contributes three components. First, a 1,706-chunk, 10-source knowledge base with a structured inter-guideline conflict registry spanning all active ME/CFS diagnostic frameworks. Second, a conflict-aware retrieval calibration pipeline that re-ranks retrieved evidence using query-specific focus and conflict signals. Third, a benchmark scored by LLM-as-Judge, avoiding systematic underestimation averaging 10.1 percentage points caused by keyword matching. ARCagent achieves 95.3%, outperforming all base LLMs. Code is available at https://github.com/Yukyin/ARCagent.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces ARCagent, a clinical QA system for ME/CFS that explicitly models and uses guideline conflicts to more safely answer questions, and shows it outperforms base LLMs.
AI.motivation: Clinical areas like ME/CFS have multiple coexisting diagnostic frameworks and treatment guidelines that are incomplete, contested, or contradictory. Standard RAG systems assume a mostly consistent knowledge base, lack explicit modeling of conflicts, and provide no guarantees of knowledge completeness or conflict-aware synthesis. This can be unsafe when guidelines disagree on key issues such as diagnosis or treatment. The authors aim to build a system that can retrieve comprehensively across guidelines, recognize and represent conflicts, and produce answers that are calibrated to these conflicts for safer clinical decision support.
AI.method: They design ARCagent with three main components. (1) A curated knowledge base consisting of 1,706 text chunks drawn from 10 distinct sources, covering all active ME/CFS diagnostic frameworks, augmented by a structured registry that explicitly encodes where and how guidelines conflict with each other. (2) A conflict-aware retrieval calibration pipeline that, given a user query, retrieves evidence and then re-ranks it using signals about query focus and inter-guideline conflicts, so that conflicting but relevant evidence is surfaced and contextualized rather than ignored. (3) An evaluation benchmark for ME/CFS clinical QA where answers are scored by an LLM-as-Judge instead of pure keyword matching, which the authors show systematically underestimates performance by about 10 percentage points; this setup is used to compare ARCagent against various base LLMs.
AI.result: On the proposed ME/CFS clinical QA benchmark, ARCagent attains an accuracy of 95.3%, outperforming all evaluated base LLMs. The authors also show that standard keyword-matching evaluation underestimates model performance by an average of 10.1 percentage points compared with their LLM-as-Judge evaluation. The conflict-aware retrieval calibration improves the quality and safety of answers in the presence of contradictory guidelines relative to vanilla RAG baselines.
AI.conclusion: ARCagent demonstrates that explicitly modeling and exploiting inter-guideline conflicts in a curated knowledge base, coupled with conflict-aware retrieval calibration and more appropriate LLM-based evaluation, can substantially improve the safety and accuracy of clinical question answering in contested domains like ME/CFS. The approach suggests a path for building QA systems in other areas where guidelines are incomplete or conflicting, and the released code and resources may facilitate further research on conflict-aware RAG in clinical settings.

title: DeepRewind: Predicting and Repairing Premature Commitments in Deep Research Agents
summary: Deep-research agents conduct long-horizon investigations through iterative search, evidence evaluation, belief revision, and synthesis. However, they may commit to claims before sufficient evidence is available, causing later reasoning to reinforce an incorrect interpretation. We introduce DeepRewind, an additive control layer for reversible deep research that represents the agent's evolving epistemic state as a typed graph of sources, evidence, claims, hypotheses, assumptions, commitments, plans, and drafts. Before accepting an intermediate conclusion, a prompt-based world model predicts its impact and estimates reversibility based on hypothesis narrowing, information loss, recovery cost, and contradiction-trigger coverage. A binary controller blocks risky commitments, while a consistency monitor performs dependency-aware rollback when later evidence invalidates them. Across DRBench and LiveDRBench, DeepRewind improves insight recall by 3.6 percentage points and reduces premature commitments by 59.1% relative to Open Deep Research.

AI.tldr: The paper presents DeepRewind, a control layer that makes deep-research AI agents more reversible and less prone to premature, incorrect commitments, improving both reliability and insight recall on research benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Deep-research agents perform multi-step investigations but tend to lock into conclusions too early, so subsequent reasoning amplifies initial mistakes. This premature commitment and lack of systematic rollback harms the quality and reliability of long-horizon research. The paper aims to provide a principled mechanism to track epistemic state and prevent or repair such errors.
AI.method: The authors design DeepRewind as an additive control layer that models the agent’s epistemic state as a typed graph containing sources, evidence, claims, hypotheses, assumptions, commitments, plans, and drafts. Before the agent accepts an intermediate conclusion, a prompt-based world model simulates the downstream impact of that conclusion and estimates how reversible it is, considering factors like hypothesis narrowing, information loss, recovery cost, and how well contradictions would be detected later. A binary controller then decides whether to allow or block the commitment. Additionally, a consistency monitor tracks dependencies and triggers targeted rollback when new evidence contradicts existing commitments.
AI.result: On the DRBench and LiveDRBench benchmarks for deep research, DeepRewind increases insight recall by 3.6 percentage points and cuts premature commitments by 59.1% compared with the Open Deep Research baseline, indicating more thorough and accurate research trajectories.
AI.conclusion: Representing an agent’s evolving beliefs as a typed epistemic graph and adding predictive reversibility checks plus dependency-aware rollback substantially mitigates premature commitments in deep research agents. DeepRewind can be layered onto existing systems to make long-horizon reasoning more cautious, reversible, and ultimately more reliable, as shown by improved recall and fewer premature commitments on research benchmarks.

title: From Retrieval to Reasoning: Agentic Mechanism Prediction from Cell Painting Profiles
summary: Cell Painting is a high-content morphological profiling assay widely used for phenotype-based biological inference, with mechanism of action (MOA) prediction as a central application. Existing approaches largely formulate Cell Painting-based inference as representation matching, assigning predictions from nearby reference perturbations in morphological feature space. However, retrieved neighbors are often noisy and partially misleading evidence due to batch effects, non-specific cytotoxicity, phenotypic convergence, and source-dependent variability. We reformulate Cell Painting-based MOA prediction as a calibrated evidence reasoning problem, where retrieved neighbors are treated as uncertain observations that must be evaluated, compared, and sometimes rejected before supporting a mechanistic conclusion. We propose PhenoAIR, a reliability-aware multi-agent framework that maintains a candidate-centric evidence memory and performs controller-guided refinement over phenotype- and mechanism-side evidence. PhenoAIR uses offline reference-set calibration to weight evidence by source reliability, phenotype stability, and mechanism-level confusion. We evaluate PhenoAIR on a benchmark constructed from JUMP Cell Painting profiles and annotations, covering controlled, realistic, and discovery-oriented open-world MOA prediction settings. PhenoAIR outperforms representation-matching and LLM-based baselines across all settings.

AI.tldr: They propose PhenoAIR, a reliability-aware multi-agent system that treats Cell Painting neighbors as uncertain evidence instead of direct labels, and show it improves mechanism-of-action prediction over existing matching and LLM-based methods.
AI.motivation: Cell Painting is powerful for phenotype-based mechanism-of-action (MOA) prediction, but current methods mostly rely on simple representation matching: they infer a compound’s MOA from its nearest neighbors in morphological feature space. This is problematic because neighbors can be noisy or misleading due to batch effects, non-specific toxicity, convergent phenotypes, and variability between data sources. There is a need for a method that does not blindly trust neighbors but instead reasons about their reliability as evidence for MOA.
AI.method: They reformulate MOA prediction as a calibrated evidence reasoning problem. Retrieved neighbors in Cell Painting space are handled as uncertain observations. PhenoAIR, a multi-agent, reliability-aware framework, maintains a candidate-centric evidence memory and refines evidence from both phenotype and mechanism perspectives under the guidance of a controller. It incorporates offline calibration of the reference set to assign reliability weights based on data source quality, phenotype stability, and known confusion between mechanisms. The system thus evaluates, compares, and can reject noisy neighbor evidence before forming a mechanistic conclusion.
AI.result: Using a benchmark derived from JUMP Cell Painting profiles and MOA annotations, and including controlled, realistic, and open-world discovery-like prediction scenarios, PhenoAIR consistently outperforms both traditional representation-matching approaches and LLM-based baselines in MOA prediction performance.
AI.conclusion: Treating Cell Painting neighbor profiles as uncertain evidence rather than direct labels, and explicitly modeling reliability and mechanism-level confusion in a multi-agent framework, leads to more accurate and robust MOA prediction. PhenoAIR offers a calibrated, evidence-based alternative to standard nearest-neighbor morphological profiling methods and improves performance across diverse, realistic prediction settings.

title: Calibrated to Whom? Persona and Language Effects on Cultural Values in JEV
summary: Decision-only language models return a probability for every answer option instead of generating text, which makes them attractive as survey respondents and as judges. We audit the cultural values of one such model, TypeSafe's JEV, with the Values Survey Module 2013. We asked it the 24 items as 12 matched Saudi and 12 matched American personas and without a persona, in English and Arabic, under eight ways of formulating the request (288,000 answers). JEV's answers were highly repeatable (ICC 0.997), and without a persona they resembled those of its own American personas. When the persona was Saudi rather than American, the answers moved in the direction of the human Saudi-US difference, reproducing 87% of its size in English but 62% in Arabic, with long-term orientation reversed. A language cross shows that the smaller difference in Arabic comes from the language of the items, not from the language of the persona description. Age shifted the profiles about as much as nationality, gender shifted them more for Saudi than for American personas, and JEV was less confident in Arabic and for Saudi personas. These patterns held in every request design, although the model never generates text.

AI.tldr: The paper audits the cultural value biases of a decision-only language model (TypeSafe’s JEV) using a standard cross-cultural survey and shows that its responses systematically vary with personas, language, age, and gender prompts, aligning partly with known human group differences.
AI.motivation: Decision-only language models are increasingly used as survey respondents and automated judges, but their embedded cultural values are largely opaque. Since such values can influence conclusions drawn from surveys or evaluations, it is important to systematically measure how these models encode and express cultural value differences across groups and languages.
