AI.method: The authors use the Values Survey Module 2013 (24 items) and query the JEV model under multiple conditions: no persona, matched Saudi and American personas (12 each), in both English and Arabic, and under eight different prompt formulations. This yields 288,000 total answers. They assess reliability with intraclass correlation, compare model value profiles to human Saudi vs. US differences, analyze how language, age, and gender prompts shift the profiles, and measure the model’s confidence across settings, without ever eliciting free-form text.
AI.result: JEV’s responses are extremely stable (ICC 0.997). Without a persona, its values resemble those of its American personas. Switching the persona from American to Saudi shifts the model’s answers toward the empirically observed Saudi–US human difference, capturing about 87% of that gap in English and 62% in Arabic, with an unexpected reversal on long-term orientation. A cross-language analysis indicates that the reduced shift in Arabic stems from the language of the survey items rather than the persona description. Age prompts change value profiles roughly as much as nationality; gender prompts have a larger effect for Saudi than for American personas. The model expresses lower confidence when answering in Arabic and when using Saudi personas. These effects are consistent across all eight request formulations.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that decision-only language models like JEV encode structured, culturally patterned value differences that can be predictably activated by persona, language, age, and gender prompts, even when the model never generates text. This makes such models both potentially useful for controlled cultural modeling and potentially risky as biased survey respondents or automated judges, especially across languages and demographic framings, underscoring the need for systematic auditing of their value structures.

title: Support-Set Target Leakage in Relational Foundation Models during In-Context Learning: Model Dependence and Evaluation Reliability
summary: Relational in-context learning (ICL) uses labeled support examples and their linked relational context to predict labels for new queries. This creates a failure mode when target-derived features are present in the support context but unavailable for the query. We study this setting as support-set target leakage. We construct 20 controlled target-derived features that vary in signal fidelity, representation, semantic transparency, coverage, and zero-, one-, and two-hop relational placement, and evaluate them across 13 RelBench tasks and five relational ICL configurations that vary the ICL head, message-passing depth, pretraining cohort, or relational encoder architecture. We evaluate matched 0-hop, 1-hop, and 2-hop leakage settings, together with a Full leakage condition containing all 20 leaker columns. Within the tested configurations, target-table (0-hop) and Full leakage produce the largest aggregate deviations from clean evaluation, while higher-hop effects are often weaker, consistent with differences in effective exposure associated with temporal reachability, sampling, and aggregation fidelity. Leakage effects are strongly task- and model-dependent and can reverse relative conclusions between model variants even when aggregate changes are small. For leaker detection, we compare an Integrated Gradients (IG)-based screening method with mutual information (MI) and leave-one-column-out (LOCO) on a common Baseline subset. Ranking quality is strongest in the high-impact 0-hop and Full leakage conditions, but detector-based removal does not consistently restore the clean evaluation. A four-task rel-salt case study further shows the same evaluation concern with native-schema leakage candidates from the original relational schema. These results identify the support/query information boundary as an important component of reliable relational ICL evaluation.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how target label information can inadvertently leak into relational in-context learning (ICL) via the support set, systematically measures its impact across tasks and models, and evaluates methods to detect and mitigate such leakage.
AI.motivation: Relational ICL models use support examples and their relational neighborhoods to predict labels for new queries. However, if features that are derived from or highly predictive of the target labels appear in the support set but are not available for the query, evaluation can be biased and misleading. The community lacks a systematic understanding of how such support-set target leakage arises in relational settings, how severe its impact is across different tasks and architectures, and whether existing or new methods can reliably detect and remove these leaker features to enable trustworthy evaluation.
AI.method: The authors formalize “support-set target leakage” for relational ICL and design 20 synthetic target-derived leaker features that vary along multiple axes: signal strength (fidelity to the true label), representation form, semantic transparency, coverage, and relational distance (0-hop, 1-hop, 2-hop) from the target. They inject these leaker features into 13 tasks from the RelBench benchmark and test five relational ICL configurations that differ in ICL head type, message-passing depth, pretraining corpus, and relational encoder architecture. They create matched leakage scenarios (0-hop, 1-hop, 2-hop) plus a Full condition that includes all 20 leaker columns. They quantify how performance deviates from a clean (no-leakage) setting and analyze task- and model-specific patterns. For leaker detection, they compare an attribution-based Integrated Gradients (IG) screening approach with mutual information (MI) and leave-one-column-out (LOCO) feature importance on a shared Baseline setting, assessing both ranking quality of suspicious features and the effect of removing them. They also run a rel-salt case study on four tasks using native schema columns as potential leakers rather than synthetic features.
AI.result: Target-table (0-hop) and the comprehensive Full leakage conditions cause the largest average deviations from clean evaluation, while 1-hop and 2-hop leakage generally have weaker but still sometimes notable effects, consistent with reduced effective exposure due to temporal reachability and message-passing limits. The magnitude and direction of leakage-induced changes depend strongly on both the task and model configuration, and can even flip relative performance rankings between models despite small average performance shifts. Among detection methods, IG-based, MI, and LOCO detectors achieve the best ranking performance at identifying leakers in the impactful 0-hop and Full settings, but automatically removing the highest-ranked suspected leakers does not reliably return performance to the true clean baseline. The rel-salt case study confirms that similar leakage issues arise from real schema columns, not only synthetic leakers.
AI.conclusion: Support-set target leakage is a significant and nuanced threat to the reliable evaluation of relational in-context learning systems, especially when target-derived signals are present directly on the target table or in strong aggregate combinations. Even modest leakage can distort comparative model assessments, and existing feature-screening techniques—even when fairly effective at ranking suspicious columns—do not guarantee restoration of clean evaluation once applied. The findings underscore that carefully enforcing and auditing the information boundary between support and query data is essential for trustworthy relational ICL benchmarks and suggest that future work should develop more robust detection, data design, and evaluation protocols tailored to relational leakage patterns.

title: Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind: Systematically Erasing LLM's Memories
summary:
We consider persistent LLMs that accumulate memories of their interactions with a user over time. Such LLMs maintain memories using external storage, which they can query to overcome the limitations of a fixed context window. Such systems have numerous practical applications, as they can draw on all past interactions when responding to user queries.
  In this paper, we ask whether LLMs can forget information shared with them upon a user's request. We find that current LLMs fail to delete such information---even when they claim to have forgotten it and even when operating with a limited context. To this end, we consider a new direction of study: Deletion of LLM Memories.
  We show that naively removing messages that match a user's deletion request is insufficient, since conversations naturally introduce message dependencies that cause information to persist. To correctly handle deletion requests, we propose the DeLLM framework. It dynamically constructs relevant context for each LLM query and maintains a provenance graph of messages to determine which ones must be removed during deletion. Our experiments show that DeLLM achieves a high deletion rate while maintaining utility.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how to reliably delete information from long‑term, memory-augmented LLM systems and introduces a framework (DeLLM) that tracks and removes all dependent messages to better honor user deletion requests while preserving model utility.
AI.motivation: Persistent LLMs store user interactions in external memory to bypass context window limits and support long-term, personalized use. However, users may later wish to delete sensitive or undesired information. Existing systems are not designed to ensure genuine forgetting, and naive deletion (e.g., removing only directly requested items) is inadequate because information can be redundantly encoded or referenced in dependent messages. This creates a privacy, safety, and trust problem for real-world deployments of memory-augmented LLMs.
AI.method: The authors first empirically evaluate current LLM-based memory systems and show that models often retain and use information that users requested to be deleted, even when the system claims the information is gone and when the active context is restricted. They then formalize the problem of memory deletion and propose DeLLM, a framework that (1) dynamically builds the context fed to the LLM for each query from an external store and (2) maintains a provenance graph capturing dependencies between messages. When a deletion request is made, DeLLM identifies not only the directly targeted messages but also all messages that depend on them via the provenance graph, and removes these from future context construction. Experiments compare DeLLM to naive deletion and measure both deletion effectiveness and task performance.
AI.result: Experiments show that naive deletion—simply removing messages that match the user’s request—fails to prevent the LLM from reconstructing or using the supposedly deleted information due to dependencies in the conversation history. In contrast, DeLLM significantly improves the true deletion rate, meaning the model is much less likely to respond using deleted information, while retaining strong task performance and utility on standard interaction tasks. The framework thus provides a more reliable and practical way to handle deletion requests in persistent LLM systems.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that robust deletion in persistent, memory-augmented LLMs is a nontrivial problem that cannot be solved by straightforward message removal. It introduces deletion of LLM memories as a distinct research direction and demonstrates that careful tracking of message provenance and dependencies, as in the DeLLM framework, is key to honoring user deletion requests without severely degrading system usefulness. This establishes a foundation for more privacy-preserving and trustworthy long-term LLM assistants.

title: The Safety Operator: Modulating the Expression of Safety Instructions via Spectral Optimization
summary: Context tokens in a transformer-based language model can be absorbed into the model's weights as a multiplicative operator. We study this operator in the setting of safety instructions and show that influencing its dominant eigenvalue modulates how strongly the instruction shapes generation. We derive a Contrastive Safety Loss with a suppression weight that controls the tradeoff between emphasizing the safety instruction on harmful queries while suppressing it on harmless queries. Varying the suppression weight maps a relationship between the attack success and the over-refusal rates, supporting the hypothesis that the operator's eigenvalue acts as a continuous dial for the instruction's influence. Moreover, this relationship holds relatively independently of how the Safety Loss is parameterized, yielding Pareto-improved safety instructions for appropriate values of suppression weight.

AI.tldr: They treat safety instructions as a multiplicative operator on model activations, and show its dominant eigenvalue works like a “dial” controlling how strongly safety affects generations. They introduce a contrastive safety loss with a suppression weight to balance blocking harmful content and avoiding over-refusals, and empirically map out this tradeoff to find Pareto-improved safety prompts.
AI.motivation: Prompted safety instructions in LMs often either fail under attack or cause excessive refusals on benign inputs. There is a need for a more mechanistic and controllable way to tune how strongly safety instructions influence model behavior, and to better understand the tradeoff between robustness to attacks and usability for harmless queries.
AI.method: They view the effect of a safety instruction as a multiplicative operator on hidden states and analyze its dominant eigenvalue as a measure of instruction strength. Based on this, they propose a Contrastive Safety Loss that separately treats harmful vs. harmless queries and introduces a suppression weight controlling how much the safety instruction is down-weighted on harmless queries. They vary this suppression weight and different parameterizations of the Safety Loss, then empirically evaluate attack success vs. over-refusal rates.
AI.result: They find that changing the dominant eigenvalue of the safety operator smoothly modulates how strongly the safety instruction shapes text generation. Adjusting the suppression weight systematically trades off attack success against over-refusals, and this tradeoff curve is similar across different Safety Loss parameterizations. For certain suppression weights, they obtain safety instructions that dominate prior configurations on both robustness and benign query acceptance (Pareto improvements).
AI.conclusion: The dominant eigenvalue of the safety-instruction operator functions as a continuous control knob for safety influence in transformer LMs. A contrastive objective with an explicit suppression weight provides a stable way to navigate the tradeoff between blocking harmful outputs and avoiding over-refusals, enabling better-calibrated and Pareto-improved safety instructions largely independent of specific loss parameterizations.

title: MemFold: Learning Compact Soft Memory for Long-Context Personalization via On-Policy Optimization
summary: An assistant that serves the same user over a long horizon has to answer from what that user has revealed: which preferences still hold, which were revised, and which constraints apply now. Retaining that information is not the same as acting on it, and the two are usually optimized as if they were. Keeping the information as text makes the reader's input grow with the retained history, while compressing it into a fixed number of latent vectors bounds the interface but is typically trained to reconstruct text or imitate reference answers, both of which are scored on sequences the reader never produced. We present MemFold, which optimizes a fixed-budget soft memory by the behavior it supports. A query-conditioned textual memory is compressed into K continuous vectors that form the reader's memory interface, and the reader is then trained on its own rollouts under two complementary signals: group-relative rewards for task outcomes, and confidence-gated on-policy distillation in which a frozen textual-memory teacher re-scores the student's sampled tokens under the textual memory. The teacher is never sampled from, so supervision stays on the student's current distribution and adds no autoregressive decoding; at inference it is removed entirely. Across three Qwen backbones, MemFold attains the highest accuracy we measure on PersonaMem-32K and PersonaMem-128K, with margins that widen at the longer history length, and transfers to PrefEval and LongMemEval without target-domain training. Ablations attribute most of the task gain to the reward term and a smaller additional gain to the teacher signal, and memory interventions show that the reader depends on the instance-specific content of its soft memory.

AI.tldr: MemFold is a method for compressing long textual user histories into a fixed-size soft memory that is optimized for downstream behavioral performance rather than text reconstruction, improving long-horizon personalization tasks.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon assistants must track evolving user preferences and constraints over very long histories. Existing approaches either keep all text, making the context unwieldy, or compress it into fixed-size vectors trained mainly to reconstruct text or imitate reference answers—objectives misaligned with the actual behavior we want from the assistant. The authors aim to create a memory mechanism that is compact, fixed-budget, and directly optimized for the quality of behavior it enables on downstream tasks, particularly in long-context personalization benchmarks.
AI.method: MemFold introduces a query-conditioned textual memory that is compressed into K continuous vectors forming a soft memory interface. A reader model consumes these K vectors instead of the full text history. Training uses the reader’s own rollouts with two objectives: (1) group-relative reward signals based on task outcomes, and (2) confidence-gated on-policy distillation from a frozen teacher that has access to the full textual memory. The teacher re-scores the student’s sampled tokens under textual memory but is never itself sampled from, keeping supervision aligned with the student’s distribution and avoiding extra autoregressive decoding. At inference time, only the soft memory is used; the teacher is removed.
AI.result: Across three Qwen model backbones, MemFold achieves the best accuracy reported on long-horizon personalization benchmarks PersonaMem-32K and PersonaMem-128K, with larger gains at longer histories. The soft memory learned by MemFold also transfers to other long-context benchmarks (PrefEval and LongMemEval) without target-domain training. Ablation studies show that the majority of the performance improvement comes from the reward-based objective, with the teacher-based on-policy distillation providing a smaller but consistent additional benefit. Memory intervention experiments indicate that the model’s predictions substantially depend on the specific content stored in the soft memory vectors.
AI.conclusion: Optimizing a fixed-size soft memory by the behavior it supports, rather than by text reconstruction or answer imitation, yields better long-horizon personalization performance. MemFold’s query-conditioned compression and dual training signals effectively distill long textual histories into a compact memory that scales to very long contexts and transfers across tasks. The results suggest that behavior-aligned memory training can make assistants more accurate and robust when operating over long and evolving user histories, while keeping inference efficient and independent of any teacher model.

title: Bits Under ZK-LLM: Evaluating Zero-Knowledge-Friendly Quantization for Verifiable Private LLM Inference
summary: Zero-knowledge proofs are emerging as a promising approach for enabling private, verifiable LLM governance and auditing, where regulators, users, and auditors need to verify claims about training-data usage or LLM inference-time behavior, while model providers must protect proprietary model parameters. However, despite the growing interest in ZK-LLMs, the understanding of ZK-friendly quantization remains limited. This gap matters because in the ZK setting, quantization directly shapes the arithmetic structure, constraint complexity, and proving cost of ZK inference. ZK protocols operate over finite fields and incur costs that depend heavily on the number and type of arithmetic operations, nonlinearities, and lookup constraints. Understanding ZK-friendly quantization is therefore essential for making ZK-LLMs practical. In this work, we present the first systematic study of ZK-friendly quantization for LLMs. We first formalize the definition of ZK-friendly quantization, capturing the properties required for ZK proof generation. We then evaluate nine language models, including Qwen2.5-14B and the mixture-of-experts model Qwen3-30B-A3B, across a broad design space of weight, activation, and nonlinear lookup table precision. Our results show that activation precision is substantially more sensitive than weight precision, while nonlinear lookup approximations can become the dominant source of utility degradation. Also, we identify RMSNorm inverse-square-root lookups as a recurring bottleneck in several large models and recover near-baseline utility by selectively increasing precision only at the bottleneck. Finally, we show that reducing bit-width or lookup-table size does not necessarily yield proportional end-to-end proving savings, showing that conventional low-bit quantization heuristics do not directly translate to ZK proving efficiency and motivating operator-aware precision selection.

AI.tldr: Systematic study of how to quantize LLMs in a way that is efficient for zero-knowledge (ZK) proofs without sacrificing too much model quality.
AI.motivation: Zero-knowledge proofs are attractive for private, verifiable governance and auditing of LLMs, but ZK proving cost is extremely sensitive to the arithmetic form of the model. Quantization decisions directly affect field operations, nonlinear lookups, and constraint counts in ZK circuits, yet existing quantization heuristics are designed for standard hardware, not for ZK systems. There is a lack of principled guidance on what “ZK-friendly” quantization means and how to choose precisions for weights, activations, and nonlinearities to balance model utility and ZK cost.
AI.method: 1) Formalize a definition of ZK-friendly quantization that encodes properties needed for efficient ZK proof generation. 2) Explore a broad design space of quantization schemes (bit-width and lookup-table precision) for weights, activations, and nonlinear nonlinearities. 3) Empirically evaluate nine LLMs, including dense and mixture-of-experts models (e.g., Qwen2.5-14B, Qwen3-30B-A3B), measuring both model utility and implications for ZK proving complexity. 4) Analyze where accuracy degrades and which operators dominate ZK cost, and test targeted precision increases at identified bottlenecks.
AI.result: 1) Activation quantization is much more sensitive than weight quantization for preserving model utility. 2) Approximation errors from nonlinear lookup tables can dominate overall performance degradation. 3) RMSNorm’s inverse-square-root operation consistently emerges as a key bottleneck whose coarse approximation significantly harms utility. 4) Carefully increasing precision only at these bottleneck nonlinearities can recover near-baseline performance. 5) Reducing bit-width or lookup-table size does not translate linearly into proving-time savings, indicating that standard low-bit quantization rules are misaligned with ZK cost structures.
AI.conclusion: ZK-friendly quantization must be designed with operator-level awareness of ZK circuit costs rather than by simply minimizing bit-width globally. Activation precision and nonlinear lookup design, particularly for operations like RMSNorm inverse-square-root, are critical levers. Selective, operator-aware precision tuning can maintain LLM quality while achieving more efficient ZK proofs, and conventional low-bit quantization heuristics are insufficient as a proxy for ZK proving efficiency.

title: Reliable Parallel Decoding in Masked Diffusion Language Models
summary: Masked diffusion language models (MDLMs) can generate text efficiently by predicting multiple masked tokens in parallel, but predictions from the same forward pass are not necessarily reliable when committed together. We study when parallel commitment is reliable. Our diagnostics show that confidence alone does not determine a reliable commitment order: confident predictions near the end of the sequence can fix an answer before its supporting computations are established, and downstream predictions become less reliable as the uncertainty of their upstream context grows. At the same time, a single forward pass can already resolve several masked tokens, and predictions that remain stable across the final layers are more likely to be correct. Based on these findings, we propose Reliable Parallel Decoding (RPD), a training-free method that selects candidates by layerwise prediction stability and final confidence, and commits them under a cumulative entropy budget over their preceding masked positions. RPD defers predictions with uncertain upstream context while committing the remaining candidates in parallel, without relying on a fixed block schedule. Across mathematical reasoning and code generation benchmarks on LLaDA and Dream, RPD achieves the highest decoding throughput among the evaluated methods while maintaining or improving accuracy.

AI.tldr: The paper studies when masked diffusion language models can safely commit multiple token predictions in parallel and proposes Reliable Parallel Decoding (RPD), a training-free decoding strategy that improves throughput while maintaining or improving accuracy.
AI.motivation: Masked diffusion language models can generate many tokens in parallel, promising high decoding speed, but their parallel predictions from a single forward pass are often unreliable when committed together. Existing heuristics based mainly on confidence or fixed block schedules do not adequately account for how uncertainty in earlier parts of the sequence degrades the reliability of later predictions. The authors aim to understand when parallel commitment is reliable and to design a decoding method that maximizes safe parallelism without retraining the model.
AI.method: The authors perform diagnostics on MDLMs to investigate reliability of token commitments conditioned on confidence, position in the sequence, and stability across layers. They show that relying on confidence alone is insufficient and that predictions near the end of the sequence can be prematurely fixed before supporting computations are established. They then propose Reliable Parallel Decoding (RPD), a training-free decoding algorithm. RPD scores candidate tokens by a combination of layerwise prediction stability and final-layer confidence, and commits them only if the cumulative entropy of the masked positions preceding each candidate is under a budget. This defers commitments whose upstream context is uncertain, while allowing remaining candidates to be committed in parallel, without using a fixed block size or schedule.
AI.result: On mathematical reasoning and code generation benchmarks using LLaDA and Dream, RPD achieves higher or the highest decoding throughput compared with other evaluated decoding schemes, while preserving or improving task accuracy. The experiments show that exploiting layerwise stability and entropy-based context uncertainty leads to more reliable parallel commitments than confidence-only or schedule-based baselines.
AI.conclusion: Parallel decoding in MDLMs can be made both fast and reliable by carefully selecting which predictions to commit in each step. Confidence alone is not a sufficient indicator of reliability; incorporating layerwise stability and an entropy-based measure of upstream context uncertainty allows more robust parallel commitments. The proposed Reliable Parallel Decoding method achieves better throughput-accuracy trade-offs without requiring any additional training or architectural changes, suggesting a practical way to speed up MDLM-based generation in reasoning and code tasks.

title: Rethinking Reasoning Paths as Phase-Structured Trajectories
summary: Large language models often improve problem-solving performance by generating multi-step reasoning paths, yet how to analyze the hidden states along these paths remains unclear. Existing approaches typically assign each intermediate state the final-answer correctness label and train probes across heterogeneous questions. We argue that this protocol obscures reasoning dynamics in two ways: (1) correctness prediction can exploit question-level variation rather than path quality, and (2) states aligned by absolute step indices may correspond to different functional phases of reasoning. In this work, we propose to view reasoning paths as phase-structured trajectories within fixed questions. We instantiate this view as PAIR, short for Phase-Aligned Intra-question Reasoning. PAIR samples multiple trajectories for each question, maps variable-length paths into shared relative phases based on normalized trajectory progress, and compares successful and unsuccessful trajectories only within the same question and phase. This yields phase-specific path-quality directions that better isolate path-quality signals from question-level variation. Empirically, we find that standard across-question correctness probes lose much of their predictive power under within-question evaluation, suggesting that these probes partly rely on question-level information. PAIR improves within-question trajectory ranking and Best-of-N trajectory selection across models and benchmarks. Phase-wise steering further shows that the learned directions can change generation outcomes, providing causal evidence that they capture trajectory-relevant information.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces PAIR, a method to analyze multi-step reasoning in large language models by aligning and comparing reasoning trajectories within the same question and relative phase, rather than across different questions.
AI.motivation: Existing approaches label each intermediate hidden state with the final-answer correctness and train probes across heterogeneous questions. This can conflate question difficulty with reasoning quality and misalign functionally different steps that share the same absolute index. The authors want a protocol that more cleanly isolates reasoning dynamics and path quality signals.
AI.method: The authors conceptualize each reasoning path as a phase-structured trajectory within a fixed question. Their method, PAIR (Phase-Aligned Intra-question Reasoning), samples multiple reasoning trajectories per question, normalizes each trajectory into relative progress phases (e.g., early/mid/late), and then compares successful vs. unsuccessful trajectories only within the same question and phase. They learn phase-specific directions in hidden-state space that correlate with path quality and use these directions for probing, ranking, and steering trajectories.
AI.result: They show that standard correctness probes trained across questions lose much of their predictive power when evaluated within a single question, indicating dependence on question-level information. PAIR achieves better within-question trajectory ranking and improves Best-of-N trajectory selection across different models and benchmarks. The phase-specific directions derived by PAIR also enable phase-wise steering that can alter model generations.
AI.conclusion: Analyzing reasoning as phase-aligned, intra-question trajectories reveals that traditional probing overestimates its understanding of reasoning by exploiting question-level cues. PAIR provides a more faithful view of reasoning dynamics, yields more reliable path-quality signals, and enables causal steering of reasoning processes, suggesting a promising direction for understanding and controlling multi-step reasoning in large language models.

title: Memory Consolidation Flattens the Temporal Shape of User Facts
summary: Long-term memory systems turn conversations into short stored notes. A note can keep a user fact while losing evidence about whether the fact still holds. For example, "I am driving a Peugeot" can become "The user drives a Peugeot," which drops the cue that the activity is ongoing. We call this aspectual flattening and measure it with LAPSE, a benchmark of matched user statements that differ only in temporal form. We find that memory writers flatten aspect selectively. Three writer models flattened the progressive statement but kept its simple-present match in 244 of 381 pairs, never the reverse. The asymmetry holds in all 11 model configurations tested and in the installed pipelines mem0, Graphiti, and Letta. The lost cue matters to later readers. In exploratory tests, changing only the stored verb shifted all three readers' estimates that a fact still holds. When readers could ask the user before acting, two of three acted without asking more often on flattened notes. Our planned memory-use task could not detect this, because readers there acted on almost every stored fact, even expired ones. Memory writing can thus remove evidence that later models use to decide whether to act.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that long-term memory systems for conversational AI often convert temporally specific user statements into aspectually flattened notes, which removes cues about whether facts still hold, influencing later model behavior.
AI.motivation: Conversational AI systems with long-term memory need to store user facts across sessions. To do this, they compress rich, temporally-marked utterances into short notes. However, this compression may drop essential temporal/aspectual information (e.g., whether an activity is ongoing vs. habitual), which can mislead future decisions. The authors want to quantify this issue—aspectual flattening—and understand how it affects downstream model behavior and safety when acting on stored memories.
AI.method: The authors introduce LAPSE, a benchmark of paired user statements that are identical except for verb aspect or temporal form (e.g., progressive vs. simple present). They evaluate several memory writer models and end-to-end memory pipelines (mem0, Graphiti, Letta) on whether their generated notes preserve or flatten aspect. They measure asymmetries in how often progressive forms are flattened into simple-present paraphrases versus the reverse. They then run exploratory experiments with reader models to see how different stored verb forms affect judgments about whether a fact is still true and whether to ask the user before acting. They also attempt a planned memory-use task to quantify behavioral impacts but find it is insensitive because readers act on nearly all stored facts.
AI.result: Across 381 progressive/simple-present pairs, three memory writer models flattened the progressive form into simple present while preserving the simple-present paraphrase in 244 cases and never did the reverse, showing a strong directional asymmetry in aspectual flattening. This effect is robust across 11 different model configurations and appears in commonly used long-term memory pipelines (mem0, Graphiti, Letta). In downstream reader experiments, modifying only the stored verb form systematically changed models’ estimates that a fact remains valid and their decisions about whether to ask the user before acting. In two of three reader models, aspectually flattened notes led to more actions taken without further user confirmation. The planned, more formal memory-use evaluation failed to capture this effect because readers tended to act on almost all stored facts regardless of currency.
AI.conclusion: Long-term memory writing for conversational AI systematically removes aspectual and temporal cues via aspectual flattening, especially by converting progressive descriptions into simple-present statements. This changes how later models interpret the currency and reliability of stored facts, sometimes making them more likely to act without checking with the user. Current evaluation setups may miss these subtle but important behavioral shifts. Designers of memory systems should explicitly track and preserve temporal/aspectual information or otherwise model fact expiry, as naive summarization can silently erode safety-relevant evidence about whether facts still hold.

title: Going Beyond State-Reaching: Learning Abstractions for Intrinsically Motivated Option Discovery
summary: Temporal abstraction via options can improve exploration in large environments. However, existing option discovery algorithms find subgoals that target all aspects of the state simultaneously. This state-reaching approach produces options that only apply in narrow regions of the state-space, eventually causing an explosion in the number of options that overwhelms the agent, and impedes progress on its primary task of reward maximization. We introduce an algorithm that instead identifies a small, relevant subset of features for each subgoal, yielding options that generalize broadly and accelerate exploration. Our approach learns abstract, transferrable options and achieves rapid exploration in three sparse-reward, image-based domains, including the Atari game MontezumasRevenge.

AI.tldr: They propose a new option-discovery method in reinforcement learning that focuses each option on a small set of state features, making options more general and improving exploration in sparse-reward image-based tasks like Montezuma’s Revenge.
AI.motivation: Existing temporal abstraction methods discover options by defining subgoals over the entire state, which makes each option valid only in a narrow part of the state space. As environments grow large and complex, this causes a combinatorial explosion in the number of options, overwhelming the agent and hindering reward maximization. A more scalable approach is needed that avoids state-reaching subgoals over all features at once.
AI.method: They develop an algorithm that discovers subgoals specified only on a small, relevant subset of features for each option, rather than on the full state. These feature-selective subgoals induce options that ignore irrelevant aspects of the state, so a single option can be reused across many different states that share the same important features. The algorithm learns which features matter for each subgoal and constructs abstract, transferable options accordingly.
AI.result: In experiments on three sparse-reward, image-based domains, including Montezuma’s Revenge from the Atari suite, the learned feature-focused options lead to substantially faster and more effective exploration than standard state-reaching option discovery approaches.
AI.conclusion: Focusing subgoals on small, relevant subsets of state features yields abstract, transferable options that generalize across large parts of the state space, mitigating option explosion and enabling rapid exploration and better performance in difficult sparse-reward visual environments.

title: FinRT: Distilling Adaptive Red-Teaming Strategies into Reusable Adversarial Generators in Consumer Finance
summary: In regulated industries like consumer finance, seemingly harmless user queries can exploit large language model vulnerabilities, triggering safety failures and pushing responses dangerously close to policy limits. Existing automated red-teaming methods trade off attack effectiveness against generation cost, while treating coverage, severity, and diversity as incidental rather than joint objectives. We introduce FinRT, a structured framework that builds reusable adversarial prompt generators from adaptive red-teaming strategies. Across the six victim models in consumer finance, FinRT substantially outperforms adaptive search baselines while amortizing target-facing attack generation into a reusable generator. FinRT nearly doubles the attack success rate over the adaptive baseline Rainbow Teaming (32.9% vs. 17.2%), increases maximum adversarial severity by 33%, and preserves comparable intra-policy-domain semantic diversity to iterative search methods. Our method achieves high cross-model transferability while exhibiting distinct victim-family specialization patterns.

AI.tldr: The paper presents FinRT, a framework for building reusable adversarial prompt generators that more efficiently and effectively red-team large language models in consumer finance.
AI.motivation: Automated red-teaming in regulated domains like consumer finance is difficult because user queries that appear benign can still trigger safety failures. Existing methods either cost too much in terms of generation or sacrifice attack effectiveness, and they do not jointly optimize coverage, severity, and diversity of attacks. There is a need for a structured, reusable way to generate strong adversarial prompts that better expose model vulnerabilities while being efficient and broadly applicable.
AI.method: The authors propose FinRT, a structured red-teaming framework that learns reusable adversarial prompt generators based on adaptive red-teaming strategies. Instead of repeatedly running expensive adaptive search for each target model, FinRT amortizes the cost by training generators that can be applied across multiple models. The framework is evaluated on six large language models used in consumer finance and compared against adaptive search baselines such as Rainbow Teaming, while measuring attack success rate, severity of violations, coverage, and semantic diversity within policy domains. They also study cross-model transferability and specialization patterns for different victim model families.
AI.result: On six consumer-finance LLMs, FinRT significantly outperforms the adaptive search baseline Rainbow Teaming: it nearly doubles attack success rate (32.9% vs. 17.2%), increases the maximum adversarial severity by 33%, and maintains semantic diversity comparable to iterative search methods. The adversarial prompts produced by FinRT generalize across different target models (high cross-model transferability), and the framework reveals distinct specialization patterns depending on the victim model family.
AI.conclusion: FinRT provides a more effective and efficient automated red-teaming approach for regulated domains like consumer finance. By turning adaptive red-teaming into reusable adversarial prompt generators, it improves attack success, severity, and transferability without sacrificing diversity, offering a practical tool for stress-testing and hardening LLM safety in high-stakes applications.

title: Learning to Harvest Without Collapse in a Regenerative Commons: A Lagrangian Framework
summary: The tragedy of the commons poses a multi-agent safety problem: reward-seeking agents can deplete a shared resource, and cooperation among its users does not itself specify how much must be preserved. We make preservation an explicit requirement by formulating a regenerative commons as a constrained Markov game or a constrained multi-agent MDP with a designer-specified depletion budget. We develop a nonstationary Lagrangian framework that constructs a policy sequence from solutions of unconstrained games or cooperative control problems. Extending earlier time-average constructions, we introduce average-epoch solution concepts for reset episodes with discounted rewards and terminal costs. We prove a reward-independent feasibility certificate, cooperative feasibility and approximate optimality against feasible policy mixtures, and an extension to unbiased sampled costs. For self-interested agents, a constrained Nash certificate quantifies the price-dispersion term introduced by deviations that redistribute budget across epochs. Under the stated assumptions on solver accuracy and multiplier updates, these results give constrained policy-sequence guarantees using solutions of unconstrained problems. Experiments with constrained IPPO and MAPPO in a Gordon-Schaefer fishery examine how depletion budgets shape stock retention, harvest rewards, and price adaptation.

AI.tldr: The paper tackles multi-agent safety in shared-resource environments by turning resource preservation into an explicit constraint, then solving it via a new nonstationary Lagrangian method that leverages standard unconstrained solvers.
AI.motivation: In shared-resource (commons) environments, individually reward-seeking agents may over-exploit a resource, leading to depletion (“tragedy of the commons”). Even if agents cooperate, typical formulations don’t clearly specify how much of the resource must be preserved. The authors want a formal framework where preservation is an explicit, enforceable requirement, and where existing unconstrained multi-agent RL or game-solving methods can still be used while providing guarantees.
AI.method: They model a regenerative commons as a constrained Markov game / constrained multi-agent MDP with a designer-chosen depletion budget. They introduce a nonstationary Lagrangian framework that builds a sequence of policies via repeated solution of unconstrained games or cooperative control problems. They generalize from time-average Lagrangian methods to “average-epoch” solution concepts tailored to reset episodes with discounting and terminal costs. They then derive various feasibility and optimality certificates, including for sampled cost settings, and a constrained Nash certificate for self-interested agents that captures the impact of deviations on budget allocation across epochs.
AI.result: Theoretically, they prove: (1) a reward-independent feasibility certificate (policies respect the depletion budget regardless of reward details); (2) cooperative feasibility and approximate optimality relative to feasible policy mixtures; (3) guarantees that extend to unbiased sampled costs; and (4) for self-interested agents, a constrained Nash certificate that decomposes a price-dispersion term capturing how deviations shift budget over epochs. Empirically, they implement constrained versions of IPPO and MAPPO in a Gordon–Schaefer fishery environment and show how different depletion budgets affect resource stock levels, harvest rewards, and the dynamics of price (multiplier) adaptation.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a principled way to embed explicit preservation constraints into multi-agent commons problems and to obtain policy-sequence guarantees using off-the-shelf unconstrained solvers. Their nonstationary Lagrangian and average-epoch framework connects theoretical safety guarantees with practical deep RL algorithms, demonstrating in a fisheries benchmark that depletion budgets can effectively shape the trade-off between long-term resource retention and short-term rewards.

title: Similar Choices, Different Attention: Cross-Modal Associations in Humans and Vision-Language Models
summary: Cross-modal associations are systematic pairings of features across modalities, such as the association of 'bouba' with round shapes and 'kiki' with sharp shapes. Prior work has compared humans and vision-language models (VLMs) on such associations, but often using different stimuli or tasks between humans and models. Here, we ask whether VLMs align with humans not only in choices, but also in where they look when making those choices. We study both VLMs and humans (N = 53), presenting them with the same stimuli, a pseudo-word and two images, and record participants' choices and eye movements, which we release. We find choice alignment in a few larger VLMs, but their saliency matches human gaze less closely than a center-bias baseline, a fixed Gaussian at the center of each image. Fine-tuning small VLMs on human choices brings their choice alignment to the level of a human majority-vote reference on unseen words and images, yet their attention still matches human gaze less closely than this baseline. Training model attention on human gaze raises attention-gaze correlation without improving choice alignment, and a single average gaze map per image position raises it by a similar amount. Matching human choices, or even human gaze patterns, is therefore not sufficient evidence of human-aligned cross-modal processing.

AI.tldr: The paper tests whether vision-language models (VLMs) align with humans not just in cross-modal choices (e.g., bouba-round, kiki-sharp) but also in their visual attention patterns, and finds that even when VLMs match human choices well, their attention maps still fail to resemble human gaze, limiting claims of human-like cross-modal processing.
AI.motivation: Cross-modal associations like bouba–round and kiki–sharp are often used as evidence of shared cognitive structure across modalities. Recent work compares these effects in humans and VLMs, but usually with mismatched tasks and stimuli, and only at the level of choices. The authors want to rigorously test whether VLMs really process information in a human-like way by using identical tasks and by examining not only decisions but also where the models “look” (saliency/attention), which is a more process-oriented measure of alignment with human perception.
AI.method: Humans (N=53) and multiple vision-language models are given the same task: see a pseudoword and two images, then choose which image matches the word. Human choices and eye movements (gaze) are recorded and released. For VLMs, the authors measure choice alignment with humans and compute model saliency/attention maps during the task. They then (1) compare model choices to human majority choices, (2) compare model attention to human gaze, and (3) test several interventions: fine-tuning small VLMs on human choice data, explicitly training model attention on human gaze, and comparing all of these against a simple center-bias Gaussian baseline and an average gaze map baseline.
AI.result: Some larger VLMs show reasonable agreement with human choices on the cross-modal matching task. However, their attention maps correlate poorly with human gaze and perform worse than a simple center-bias Gaussian baseline in matching gaze. Fine-tuning small VLMs on human choices raises their choice alignment to human majority-vote levels on new words and images, but their attention still aligns with gaze less than the center-bias baseline. Training attention directly on human gaze improves attention–gaze correlation, but this does not translate into better choice alignment. Moreover, using a single average gaze map per image position yields similar gains, implying that detailed gaze supervision adds limited value for these models.
AI.conclusion: Agreement between VLMs and humans on cross-modal association choices, and even higher correlation between model attention and human gaze, does not guarantee that the models are using human-like cross-modal processing strategies. Simple baselines like center bias or average gaze can outperform or match sophisticated attention mechanisms in predicting gaze, indicating that current VLMs’ internal attention patterns remain poorly aligned with human visual behavior. Therefore, strong behavioral similarity in outputs should not be overinterpreted as evidence of shared underlying cognitive mechanisms between humans and VLMs, particularly for cross-modal associations.

title: Human-AI Collaboration: From Paradoxes to Patterns
comment: This is the author's version of the work. It is posted here for your personal use. Not for redistribution. The definitive Version of Record will be published in 33rd Conference on Pattern Languages of Programs (PLoP 2026)
summary: Evidence shows that humans and AI systems perform better together, by collaborating, than alone. This paper examines two key design dimensions of human-AI collaboration (autonomy and initiative) and explores the collaboration patterns that they generate. Documenting these patterns starts with identifying the underlying problems and solutions, followed by examining the internal tensions within the problems. The paper uses a paradox perspective to analyze those tensions. It describes a process for surfacing the tensions and mapping the underlying paradoxes. It also illustrates how the pattern descriptions can be derived from mapping these paradoxes. Finally, the paper documents four human-AI collaboration patterns: Instruction, Delegation, Assistance, and Co-creation.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies and analyzes four key patterns of human-AI collaboration—Instruction, Delegation, Assistance, and Co-creation—using autonomy and initiative as core design dimensions and a paradox-based lens to surface underlying tensions.
AI.motivation: Although humans and AI tend to perform better together than separately, designers lack clear conceptual guidance on how to structure this collaboration. Existing work does not sufficiently explain how different levels of AI autonomy and initiative shape interaction patterns, nor how to manage the inherent tensions (e.g., control vs. automation) that arise. The paper aims to provide a systematic way to understand and design human-AI collaboration patterns.
AI.method: The authors conceptually analyze human-AI collaboration along two main design dimensions: autonomy (how independently the AI acts) and initiative (who takes the lead in the interaction). They apply a paradox perspective to identify and map internal tensions in collaboration design (e.g., human control vs. AI independence). Through this mapping, they derive a set of recurring collaboration patterns that relate specific configurations of autonomy and initiative to recognizable forms of interaction.
AI.result: The study produces (1) a process for surfacing design tensions in human-AI collaboration using paradox mapping; (2) an analytical framework that links autonomy and initiative to collaboration patterns; and (3) four documented patterns of human-AI collaboration—Instruction, Delegation, Assistance, and Co-creation—each associated with characteristic configurations of autonomy and initiative and distinct underlying paradoxes.
AI.conclusion: Human-AI collaboration can be better designed and reasoned about by explicitly considering autonomy and initiative and by recognizing the paradoxical tensions they create. The four patterns—Instruction, Delegation, Assistance, and Co-creation—offer a vocabulary and conceptual structure that can guide system designers in choosing and combining collaboration styles appropriate to their goals and constraints.

title: Large-scale factor analysis shows machine intelligence is only partially interpretable
summary: A common assumption in language model development is that cognitive abilities are organized around a general, domain-free intelligence factor, like fluid intelligence in humans. This assumption is rarely tested directly, and prior attempts have done so only at a much smaller scale. We take a latent variable approach to intelligence in language models, similar to how psychometricians study psychological constructs. Performance in every specific problem set is influenced by a domain-specific and a domain-agnostic latent factor. Using factor analysis as a dimension-reduction technique, we analyzed 13,251 published evaluation scores covering 1,618 language models across 456 different text-only benchmarks. Due to the super-sparse nature of the dataset, we triangulate our analysis across different data densifiers and imputation methods. A robust pattern across different modes of bias is that 1. A general intelligence factor accounts for 70.8% of variance in model performance at our most generous estimate, and far less than that in most of our solutions, 2. Content-similar benchmarks do not necessarily cluster together, and 3. The $g$ factor is not dominated by any common theme, and there is a lack of evidence that it is well-proxied by standard "intelligence" benchmarks. Our findings go against current endeavors of defining, identifying, and targeting general intelligence as a tangible construct in language model development. This leaves the strategy of targeting a single conceptual ability without support, since the first-order abilities it would have to reach are often partially idiosyncratic and not identifiable in practice.

AI.tldr: The paper applies psychometric-style factor analysis to a very large set of language model benchmark results and finds only limited evidence for a single, dominant general intelligence factor in LMs, challenging the idea that LM capabilities can be captured or optimized via one general “g-like” construct.
AI.motivation: Many LM papers implicitly assume that model capabilities can be described by a single, domain-general intelligence factor, analogous to human fluid intelligence, and that improving this factor improves performance everywhere. This assumption underlies how we design benchmarks, compare models, and talk about “general intelligence,” but it has rarely been empirically tested at scale. The authors want to rigorously investigate whether LM performance structure actually supports a general intelligence factor and whether common benchmarks are good proxies for it.
AI.method: The authors compile a very large dataset of 13,251 evaluation scores from 1,618 language models across 456 text-only benchmarks. They use a latent variable framework from psychometrics, assuming that performance on each benchmark reflects both domain-specific factors and a domain-agnostic factor. Because the data are extremely sparse (not all models are evaluated on all benchmarks), they apply several data densification and imputation strategies, then conduct factor analysis as a dimensionality reduction technique. They analyze the factor structure, quantify how much variance a general factor explains, inspect clustering among benchmarks, and examine what types of tasks load most strongly on the putative general factor.
AI.result: Across multiple imputation and analysis pipelines, they find: (1) A general factor exists but, at the upper bound, explains about 70.8% of the variance in performance, and typically much less under more conservative assumptions; (2) Benchmarks that are content-similar do not necessarily cluster together in factor space, indicating that task content is not the main driver of shared variance; (3) The extracted general factor is not driven by any obvious common theme or domain, and commonly used “intelligence” benchmarks do not clearly serve as good proxies for that factor. These patterns are robust across different ways of handling the sparse data and differing bias modes in the analysis.
AI.conclusion: The structure of LM performance does not support a simple, human-style general intelligence factor that cleanly governs capabilities across tasks. Instead, abilities appear partially idiosyncratic and not easily reduced to one underlying construct, and conventional “intelligence” benchmarks do not reliably track any such factor. As a result, research agendas that aim to define, measure, or directly optimize a single general intelligence quantity in LMs lack empirical grounding. Focusing on a monolithic conceptual ability is unlikely to capture or drive the diverse first-order skills that actually determine LM performance in practice.

title: AVIO: Learning to Add and Remove Sounding Objects in Audiovisual Scenes
summary: Adding or removing a sounding object requires coordinated changes to visual content and sound while preserving the surrounding scene. Yet paired supervision for localized non-speech audiovisual editing remains limited, as visual and acoustic edits must target the same object and isolate its sound from overlapping sources. To address this gap, we introduce \textit{AVIOBench}, a dataset comprising 37.9 hours of paired audiovisual examples spanning 1{,}878 target-object names. AVIOBench links the visual presence and acoustic contribution of each target object through a shared identity and visual mask. Our automated pipeline uses visual grounding and cross-modal consistency to select target-sound removal candidates, then jointly refines the audiovisual pairs to improve perceptual quality and cross-modal consistency. Building on this dataset, we propose \textit{AVIO}, which adapts a pretrained text-to audiovisual generation model through source-conditioned feature modulation to jointly learn object addition and removal. A reference-frame curriculum gradually reduces reference conditioning during training, enabling one model to perform instruction-only editing with optional visual guidance. Quantitative and qualitative evaluations demonstrate effective audiovisual object removal and addition, with optional reference guidance providing appearance and placement control for addition.

AI.tldr: They propose a benchmark dataset and model for adding/removing sound-making objects in videos while keeping the rest of the scene intact.
AI.motivation: Existing audiovisual editing lacks paired, localized supervision where visual edits (adding/removing an object) are consistently matched with corresponding sound edits for that same object, especially when sounds overlap. This limits progress on realistic, object-level audiovisual editing.
AI.method: 1) Build AVIOBench: an automated pipeline that uses visual grounding and cross-modal (audio-visual) consistency to select candidate segments where a target object’s sound can be removed, and generate paired examples with aligned visual masks and object identities. 2) Propose AVIO: adapt a pretrained text-to-audiovisual generator using source-conditioned feature modulation so a single model can learn both object addition and removal. Use a reference-frame curriculum that starts with strong visual reference conditioning and gradually reduces it so the model can eventually operate from instructions alone, with reference frames remaining optional for more control.
AI.result: AVIOBench contains 37.9 hours of paired audiovisual data over 1,878 target object names, with each example linking the object’s visual mask and sound. The AVIO model, trained on this data, can effectively add or remove sounding objects in videos, and can optionally use reference frames to control the appearance and position of added objects. Both quantitative metrics and qualitative assessments show strong performance.
AI.conclusion: Object-level audiovisual editing can be substantially improved by (1) a large, automatically curated dataset that tightly couples object identity, visual localization, and its sound, and (2) a unified model design that learns both addition and removal with flexible conditioning. AVIO and AVIOBench together provide a foundation for future research on realistic, instruction-based audiovisual editing.

title: Retrieval Sensitivity to Identity Signals in Queries
comment: EMNLP 2026 camera-ready, with a correction to Fig. 4
summary: Dense retrievers decide which documents reach users and the language models that use them, yet they are typically evaluated with neutral queries. We ask whether the identity signals that real users express in their queries---political ideology and dialect---bias what a retriever returns. We design evaluations in two domains, political news and consumer-health questions, each pairing a controlled synthetic set that varies only the identity signal with naturalistic queries. Across five dense retrievers and a sparse baseline, every retriever (i) retrieves articles that align with the query's own political lean and (ii) performs worse for questions written in African American Language (AAL) than in White Mainstream English (WME). Two analyses tie these gaps to queries' identity signals beyond surface vocabulary: partialling out an aggregate lexical-asymmetry score leaves the synthetic gaps largely intact, and linear probes recover lean and dialect from the retrievers' query embeddings beyond token-level features. Left unaddressed, such retrieval biases risk contributing to polarization and reinforcing the health disparities already faced by AAL speakers. Code is available at https://github.com/Andrewtcr/bias-ret.

AI.tldr: The paper studies whether dense text retrievers exhibit bias based on identity cues in user queries, focusing on political ideology and dialect, and finds systematic biased retrieval patterns.
AI.motivation: Dense retrieval models are widely used to decide which documents are surfaced to users and downstream language models, but they are usually evaluated on neutral queries, ignoring that real users often express identity-related cues (e.g., political leaning, dialect). This raises the concern that such cues may bias what information different users see, with potential consequences for polarization and inequity, so the authors aim to rigorously measure and understand these biases.
AI.method: The authors construct controlled synthetic query sets that are identical except for explicit identity signals (political ideology markers or dialectal variation between African American Language and White Mainstream English), along with naturalistic query sets in two domains: political news and consumer health questions. They evaluate five dense retrievers plus a sparse baseline, measuring both political-lean alignment of retrieved articles and retrieval performance degradation across dialects. To test whether biases are due only to lexical differences, they compute and control for an aggregate lexical-asymmetry score and also train linear probes on the retrievers' query embeddings to predict political lean and dialect from those representations beyond token-level features.
AI.result: All tested retrievers show (i) ideological skew, preferentially retrieving politically aligned documents for ideologically marked queries, and (ii) performance gaps where queries in African American Language receive worse retrieval quality than equivalent queries in White Mainstream English. The gaps largely persist even after accounting for lexical asymmetries, and linear probes successfully recover political lean and dialect from retriever embeddings beyond simple lexical signals, suggesting the models internalize and use identity information in their representations.
AI.conclusion: Dense retrievers systematically encode and act on identity signals in user queries, leading to biased retrieval outcomes: ideologically slanted results and poorer service for African American Language queries. These effects are not reducible to surface lexical differences alone but are tied to deeper representational properties. If unmitigated, such biases may worsen political polarization and exacerbate existing health disparities. The work highlights the need for bias-aware evaluation and mitigation strategies in retrieval systems and provides open-source code to facilitate further research.

title: BRIDGE: Bilevel Retrieval-Credit-Aware Agentic Reinforcement Learning
summary: Agentic reinforcement learning (ARL) with verifiable rewards improves the ability of large language models (LLMs) to tackle knowledge-intensive tasks by learning to interleave search and reasoning. However, most existing ARL methods optimize only LLM-generated tokens and treat retrieved evidence as environment observations. This creates an information-credit gap: failures caused by missing or misleading evidence are attributed to the LLM policy rather than to the retriever, which motivates training the LLM and the retriever jointly. In this paper, we show that retrieval and LLM policy learning are order-sensitive: adapting the retriever before optimizing the policy yields a larger reward gain than the reverse order. To preserve this hierarchy while allowing both components to co-adapt, we formulate retrieval-augmented agentic RL as a bilevel optimization problem. To solve it efficiently, we introduce BRIDGE, a memory-efficient first-order bilevel method motivated by a loss-landscape analysis of the RL and retrieval objectives. Across seven open-domain QA benchmarks, BRIDGE achieves the highest average accuracy with both 3B and 7B backbones, improving the multi-hop average over the strongest baseline by 9.6 and 3.4 EM points, respectively. It also achieves the best averaged answer accuracy and reasoning quality across medical QA benchmarks.

AI.tldr: The paper improves agentic reinforcement learning for LLMs by jointly but hierarchically training the retriever and policy via a bilevel optimization method, BRIDGE, leading to state-of-the-art accuracy on multiple QA benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing agentic RL methods for LLMs treat retrieval as a fixed environment and only optimize the LLM’s token generation. This mis-attributes errors caused by poor or missing evidence to the policy, creating an information-credit gap and limiting performance gains on knowledge-intensive tasks. There is a need to better understand and exploit the interaction and training order between retrieval and policy learning to improve accuracy and reasoning quality.
AI.method: The authors analyze order sensitivity between retrieval adaptation and LLM policy optimization and then formulate retrieval-augmented agentic RL as a bilevel optimization problem where the outer level governs retrieval learning and the inner level handles policy learning. They propose BRIDGE, a memory-efficient first-order bilevel optimization algorithm derived from studying the loss landscapes of the RL and retrieval objectives, enabling hierarchical yet co-adaptive training of the retriever and the LLM policy.
AI.result: On seven open-domain QA benchmarks and with both 3B and 7B LLM backbones, BRIDGE attains the highest average accuracy compared to baselines. For multi-hop QA, it improves exact match over the strongest baseline by 9.6 points with a 3B model and 3.4 points with a 7B model. On medical QA datasets, BRIDGE also delivers the best average answer accuracy and reasoning quality metrics.
AI.conclusion: Joint training of retriever and LLM policy in a hierarchically structured, bilevel manner is more effective than conventional ARL approaches that optimize only the LLM or ignore training-order effects. By capturing the dependency between retrieval and reasoning, BRIDGE closes the information-credit gap and significantly enhances performance and reasoning quality on knowledge-intensive and multi-hop QA tasks.

title: When Updating Stops Being Learning: Rethinking LLM Self-Evolution via learnable information gain
summary: Self-evolution lets large language models (LLMs) improve iteratively using their own generated data, but often suffers from self-evolution degeneration: performance improves, plateaus, then declines. Existing methods address this issue at the component level, targeting either the Questioner or the Solver, and overlook that self-evolution is a tightly coupled system. We propose a holistic framework based on learnable information gain, which measures how much novel, parameterizable information a round provides relative to the previous round. Theoretically, this gain equals the Kullback-Leibler divergence between the two rounds' data distributions plus their entropy change. Practically, it is estimated by fitting a small language model to the previous round and scoring new data via negative log-likelihood. Based on this diagnostic, we propose ATRI (Adaptive Training Regulation via Information-gain), which reweights samples within a round and halts training across rounds when information gain remains low. Experiments on popular datasets demonstrate the superiority of our proposal.

AI.tldr: They study why self-evolving LLM training first improves then degrades, and propose an information-gain-based framework (ATRI) to adaptively select and stop training on self-generated data, improving robustness and performance.
AI.motivation: Self-evolution lets LLMs iteratively improve using self-generated data, but in practice performance often first increases then plateaus and declines—self-evolution degeneration. Existing work tweaks separate components like the Questioner or Solver, but treats them in isolation and lacks a principled, system-level way to know when new self-generated data is still useful versus harmful. There is a need for a holistic, theoretically grounded metric to diagnose and regulate the quality of self-evolution across rounds.
AI.method: They introduce a learnable information gain metric that quantifies how much new, trainable information each self-evolution round provides compared with the previous round. Theoretically, this is expressed as the KL divergence between the data distributions of two consecutive rounds plus the change in entropy. Practically, they approximate this by training a small language model on the previous round’s data and computing the negative log-likelihood of samples from the new round, using this as an estimate of information gain. Building on this, they propose ATRI (Adaptive Training Regulation via Information-gain), which (1) reweights samples within each round according to their estimated information gain, and (2) stops further self-evolution rounds when the overall information gain remains low, thus adaptively regulating the training process.
AI.result: On widely used benchmarks (popular LLM evaluation datasets), ATRI yields better performance than existing self-evolution methods, reducing or eliminating the typical degeneration phase. Their experiments show that using information gain for sample reweighting and round-level early stopping leads to more stable and higher final performance across various tasks and models.
AI.conclusion: Self-evolution of LLMs should be regulated at the system level rather than by tweaking individual components. A principled information-gain metric provides a practical diagnostic for how much useful new information each training round contributes. The ATRI framework operationalizes this idea by adaptively reweighting training samples and deciding when to halt further self-evolution, leading to more robust and effective iterative self-improvement.

title: MAADBench: The Refreshable Paradigm for Anomaly Detection in Multi-Agent Systems
summary: Recent studies report that LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) fail at rates of 41%-87%, yet to our knowledge, no benchmark to date supports systematic anomaly detection (AD) for them. Building MAS AD benchmarks is hard because they must remain fresh as LLM systems evolve: tasks may leak into training data and thus be memorized by LLMs, traces and anomaly patterns expire as backbones evolve, and labels must be provided reliably for each refresh. To address these challenges, we present MAADBench (MA: multi-agent; AD: anomaly detection), the first refreshable MAS AD benchmark designed for diverse, evolving LLM backbones underlying the agents. MAADBench combines (1) sampled-and-coupled generative tasks over an approximately 10^37-task space to mitigate task leakage, (2) refreshable trace generation under configurable LLM backbones, and (3) automated provision of cost-free, deterministic step-level labels for fine-grained AD evaluation. Beyond offering the paradigm itself, we run MAADBench with five state-of-the-art LLM backbones and release the MAADBench-Full dataset with 5,200 step-labeled traces. Benchmarking 25 AD methods on the MAADBench dataset reveals substantial limitations in current approaches: they rely heavily on supervision, struggle with subtle MAS-specific anomalies, and lack robustness across LLM backbones. These gaps point to a rich research agenda for MAS-specific anomaly detection, with MAADBench providing a systematic and refreshable testbed for method development and evaluation. We open-source MAADBench-Full at https://huggingface.co/datasets/hww123/MAADBench-full.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces MAADBench, a refreshable benchmark for anomaly detection in LLM-based multi-agent systems, showing that existing AD methods are inadequate and motivating MAS-specific AD research.
AI.motivation: LLM-based multi-agent systems frequently fail (41%–87%), but there is no systematic, dedicated benchmark to study and detect anomalies in these systems. Existing benchmarks quickly become outdated as LLMs evolve, suffer from task leakage into training data, and require costly, consistent re-labeling. The authors aim to create a benchmark that remains useful across evolving LLM backbones and enables fine-grained anomaly detection research in MAS.
AI.method: They design MAADBench, a benchmark framework with three key components: (1) a sampled-and-coupled generative task mechanism over an enormous task space (~10^37 tasks) to mitigate leakage into model training data; (2) a refreshable trace-generation process configurable for different and newly emerging LLM backbones powering the agents; and (3) an automated procedure that provides deterministic, cost-free, step-level labels for each trace, enabling fine-grained anomaly detection evaluation. They instantiate MAADBench with five state-of-the-art LLM backbones and compile MAADBench-Full, a dataset of 5,200 labeled multi-agent traces. They then systematically benchmark 25 existing anomaly detection methods on this dataset.
AI.result: When evaluated on MAADBench-Full, the 25 anomaly detection methods show major shortcomings: they depend heavily on supervised labels, are ineffective at catching subtle anomalies specific to multi-agent interactions, and perform inconsistently across different LLM backbones. This demonstrates that current AD techniques are not well-suited for MAS generated by diverse LLMs.
AI.conclusion: MAADBench is the first refreshable anomaly detection benchmark tailored to LLM-based multi-agent systems and their evolving backbones. By providing a large, diverse, and automatically labeled dataset, it exposes the limitations of current AD approaches and establishes a systematic, reusable testbed. The work highlights the need for new, MAS-specific, more robust anomaly detection methods, and the authors support further research by open-sourcing MAADBench-Full.

title: DraftTrace: A Multi-View Analytics Environment for AI-Integrated Writing
summary: Generative AI has changed how students produce writing assignments. The final artifact is no longer sufficient to understand the process through which it was produced. We introduce DraftTrace, a writing environment that jointly captures three complementary views of writing: the final product, the writing process and interactions with an integrated AI-assistant. DraftTrace reconstructs how a document develops over time and organizes these signals into submission, longitudinal, and class-level analytics for instructors. We deployed DraftTrace in a graduate NLP course with 81 students and compared their sessions with LLM-generated responses entered by automated tools and with copy-typed responses. While product measures distinguish differences in text formulation, process measures distinguish differences in how text is entered. Considering both views together helps characterize cases such as copy-typing. Interaction traces show that students use the assistant differently across stages of writing: to clarify the question at an early stage and to verify answers at a later stage. A preliminary instructor survey highlights the importance of multi-view writing analytics and their interpretability.

AI.tldr: DraftTrace is a writing environment that logs product, process, and AI-interaction data to give instructors multi-level analytics about how students use generative AI in writing tasks.
