AI.motivation: With generative AI, instructors can no longer rely solely on the final written artifact to understand student learning, originality, or effort, because AI tools can generate polished text quickly. There is a need to capture and analyze the underlying writing process and how students interact with AI assistants to better assess learning, detect behaviors like copy-typing AI output, and support instruction.
AI.method: The authors designed DraftTrace, a writing environment that records three synchronized streams: (1) the final product, (2) the fine-grained writing process over time, and (3) interactions with an integrated AI assistant. DraftTrace reconstructs document evolution and aggregates this data into analytics at submission, longitudinal, and class levels. They deployed DraftTrace in a graduate NLP course with 81 students, and compared human writing sessions with LLM-generated responses inserted via automated tools and with copy-typed LLM responses. They analyzed both product-based measures (text characteristics) and process-based measures (how text is entered) as well as AI interaction traces.
AI.result: Product measures differentiated texts based on formulation differences between human and AI-generated responses, while process measures differentiated how text was entered, revealing patterns such as copy-typing. Combining product and process views improved characterization of behaviors like copy-typing AI-generated content. Interaction logs showed that students tended to use the AI assistant earlier to clarify the question and later to verify answers. Instructor survey responses indicated that multi-view analytics were seen as useful, especially when they were interpretable.
AI.conclusion: Capturing product, process, and AI-interaction data in an integrated environment like DraftTrace provides richer, more interpretable insights into student writing with generative AI than product-only analysis. Multi-view writing analytics can distinguish different forms of AI use (e.g., direct generation vs. copy-typing) and support instructors in understanding and assessing student work, though further development and validation are implied for broader use.

title: Visual sensitivity is not claim retractability: persistence-aware credit assignment for multimodal reinforcement learning
summary: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has been extended to Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs), and perception-aware methods further encourage policies to rely on visual evidence. Yet relying on the image does not guarantee that visual claims are supported by it. Before RL training, 27.81% of the correctly answered responses of Qwen2.5-VL-7B on four multimodal reasoning benchmarks contain at least one direct visual claim that the image does not support. Since outcome-level RL rewards each response as a whole, these claims inherit the positive credit of the correct answer. We introduce a fixed-rollout counterfactual diagnostic that re-scores the same response under an intervened image to separate Evidence-Function Sensitivity (EFS), how strongly the model's predictions change, from claim persistence, whether the model keeps supporting the same claim rather than retracting it. The diagnostic reveals Sensitivity-Persistence Decoupling (SPD): under DAPO and VPPO, EFS increases and claims become more retractable overall, yet unsupported claims become significantly more persistent, whereas GRPO raises EFS without this deterioration. We therefore propose Persistence-Aware Credit Gating (PACG), which attenuates positive credit for unusually persistent visual claims and leaves all other credit unchanged. It requires no supported/unsupported labels and adds no inference cost. On Qwen2.5-VL-7B, PACG raises the nine-benchmark average over three seeds from 58.1% to 59.9% with DAPO and from 59.8% to 60.9% with VPPO, while making unsupported claims more retractable. The gains extend to a larger model, a newer backbone, and the accuracy of HallusionBench also improves consistently. These results suggest that visual sensitivity and claim retractability are complementary dimensions of multimodal credit assignment.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how reinforcement learning for large vision-language models can unintentionally reward hallucinated visual claims, introduces diagnostics to separate visual sensitivity from claim persistence, finds that some RL methods make unsupported claims more persistent, and proposes a new training technique (PACG) that improves accuracy while making unsupported claims easier to retract.
AI.motivation: Existing RL with verifiable rewards methods for LVLMs encourage models to rely on visual input, but a significant fraction of seemingly correct responses still contain specific visual statements that are not actually supported by the image. Since standard outcome-level RL assigns reward to the entire response based only on final correctness, unsupported visual claims can inherit positive credit, reinforcing hallucinations. There is also no clear way to distinguish "using the image" (sensitivity to evidence) from "sticking to a claim" even when it should be withdrawn (persistence). The paper aims to diagnose and fix this misaligned credit assignment in multimodal RL.
AI.method: The authors first quantify unsupported visual claims in a base LVLM (Qwen2.5-VL-7B) across several multimodal reasoning benchmarks. They then introduce a fixed-rollout counterfactual diagnostic: for a given response, they rescore it under an intervened (modified) image to measure (1) Evidence-Function Sensitivity (how much the model’s outputs change when visual evidence is changed) and (2) claim persistence (whether specific visual claims remain supported vs are retracted under counterfactual evidence). Using this diagnostic, they analyze RL methods such as DAPO, VPPO, and GRPO, discovering a Sensitivity-Persistence Decoupling where some methods increase sensitivity but also make unsupported claims more stubborn. Based on these insights, they design Persistence-Aware Credit Gating (PACG), a training scheme that down-weights positive RL credit for unusually persistent visual claims, without needing explicit labels of support and without extra inference-time cost.
AI.result: Empirically, they show that before RL, 27.81% of correctly answered responses contain at least one unsupported direct visual claim. Their diagnostic reveals that DAPO and VPPO increase evidence sensitivity and overall retractability but paradoxically make unsupported claims significantly more persistent, whereas GRPO increases sensitivity without this negative effect. Applying PACG on Qwen2.5-VL-7B improves the average accuracy across nine multimodal benchmarks (over three seeds) from 58.1% to 59.9% with DAPO and from 59.8% to 60.9% with VPPO, while also making unsupported claims more retractable. The improvements transfer to a larger model and a newer backbone, and HallusionBench accuracy also improves consistently.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that visual sensitivity (how much models respond to visual evidence) and claim retractability (willingness to withdraw visual claims under counterevidence) are distinct and complementary dimensions of multimodal credit assignment. Standard outcome-level RL can unintentionally entrench hallucinated visual claims by giving them positive credit. The proposed PACG method corrects this by selectively attenuating credit for unusually persistent claims, improving both benchmark accuracy and the retractability of unsupported visual statements, without requiring extra supervision or inference cost.

title: Grounded Revision vs. Prior Injection: Probing Retrieval-Augmented Patent Claim Amendment
comment: Accepted to Findings of AACL-IJCNLP 2026. 9 pages, 2 figures. Code and data: https://github.com/TeamLab/probing-rag-patent-amendment
summary: Retrieval-augmented generation is widely used in professional writing, yet whether retrieval grounds revision or merely injects templates is rarely tested where "correct" has a definable meaning. Patent claim amendment supplies that signal: the examiner names the attacked limitation and cites prior art, providing per-case ground truth. We release three artifacts: (i) a corpus of 7,385 USPTO prosecution cases with XML-aligned pre/post claims, rejection, and cited prior art; (ii) a seven-probe battery comparing random and structural-match retrieval as two policies under a fixed prompt scaffold; (iii) a deterministic five-channel metric (C1-C3 and C5 in main, C4 supplementary) requiring no LLM evaluation. Across 9,600 pre-registered calls on four frontier LLMs (Claude Sonnet 4, Claude Haiku 4.5, GPT-5.4, GPT-4o-mini), no tested model exhibits detectable classical prior-injection behavior; retrieval effects are small and direction-inconsistent between random and structural retrieval, and the null is unchanged under a dense (semantic) retriever, across retrieval depths k in {1,3,5,10}, and under a paraphrase-sensitive grounding metric. Revision locality reveals a model-specific difference that the template channel misses. The four-cell taxonomy, which we treat as exploratory, leaves the prior-injector cell unoccupied.

AI.tldr: They study whether retrieval-augmented generation in patent claim revision actually uses retrieved prior art as grounding or just copies templates, and find little evidence of classical “prior injection.”
AI.motivation: RAG is popular for professional writing tasks, but it is unclear whether models genuinely ground their revisions in retrieved documents or merely echo stylistic or structural patterns. Patent prosecution offers a rare setting with clear, per-instance ground truth: the examiner specifies the attacked claim limitation and cites prior art, so one can see exactly what a correct amendment should address. The authors want a rigorous, measurable way to test retrieval’s role in revision, beyond vague human or LLM-based judgments.
AI.method: They construct: (i) a large USPTO dataset of 7,385 prosecution cases with XML-aligned pre/post claims, office rejections, and cited prior art; (ii) an evaluation battery of seven probes that compare two retrieval policies—random retrieval versus structural-match retrieval—within the same prompt scaffold; and (iii) a deterministic five-channel metric (C1–C5) that assesses revision behavior without relying on subjective LLM graders. They run 9,600 pre-registered RAG calls on four frontier LLMs using different retrievers (including dense semantic), varying retrieval depth k∈{1,3,5,10}, and also incorporate a paraphrase-sensitive grounding metric and a locality-of-revision analysis.
AI.result: Across all models, retrieval has weak and inconsistent effects: differences between random and structural retrieval are small and not directionally stable. Critically, there is no signal that models are performing “classical prior injection,” i.e., directly copying or strongly anchoring to retrieved prior art. These findings remain when using a dense (semantic) retriever, varying k, and applying a paraphrase-sensitive grounding measure. However, an analysis of how local the revisions are to the attacked claim limitation reveals model-specific behaviors that are not visible through the simpler template-style channel. Their exploratory four-cell taxonomy has one quadrant—the prior-injector behavior—empty for all tested systems.
AI.conclusion: In this patent-claim amendment setting with clear ground truth, current frontier LLMs do not behave as straightforward prior injectors under retrieval-augmented generation. Retrieval appears to have modest and inconsistent influence on revisions, suggesting that models often rely more on their internal priors and learned editing behaviors than on the specific retrieved documents. Their dataset, probe suite, and deterministic metrics provide a more rigorous framework for studying how, when, and whether retrieval truly grounds model revisions.

title: Divide and Inject: Can Agents Reconstruct an Indirect Prompt Injection from Fragments?
summary: Agentic systems are now being widely used to orchestrate tools and reason over long contexts. However, the improving capabilities of the large language models powering these agents also create new attack surfaces for indirect prompt injection. In particular, an attacker may not need to place a complete malicious instruction in retrieved content if the agent can reconstruct the objective from incomplete fragments distributed across a long context. In this work, we introduce adaptive long-context prompt injection (AdaLCPI), which combines long-context fragmentation with adaptive search. AdaLCPI splits an attack objective into incomplete fragments, embeds them in external content retrieved through the agent's tools, and uses a reconstruction cue to prompt the agent to combine them. It then iteratively refines the fragments and cue with OpenEvolve using graded scoring and natural-language execution feedback from the target agent. Empirically, AdaLCPI achieves higher attack success than strong adaptive baselines, reaching 61.4\% macro-average ASR compared with 32.8\% for Trojan Hippo-style and 30.0\% for AgentVigil. Safety evaluations should therefore test whether agents remain robust when harmful objectives must be reconstructed from incomplete fragments.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes AdaLCPI, an adaptive long-context prompt-injection attack that splits a malicious goal into fragments spread across retrieved content and iteratively optimizes them to reliably fool agentic LLM systems.
AI.motivation: As LLM-based agents gain long-context reasoning and tool-use capabilities, they become vulnerable to indirect prompt-injection attacks hidden in external data. Existing defenses and attack benchmarks mainly assume single, explicit malicious instructions, overlooking scenarios where an attacker distributes partial instructions across long contexts that the agent can reconstruct. There is a need to understand and systematically evaluate how well such fragmented, adaptive attacks can compromise agentic systems.
AI.method: The authors design AdaLCPI, an attack framework that (1) decomposes a malicious objective into incomplete instruction fragments; (2) embeds these fragments into external content that an agent retrieves via tools; (3) adds a reconstruction cue that encourages the agent to piece the fragments together; and (4) uses an adaptive optimization loop (OpenEvolve) that refines both fragments and cue based on graded scoring and natural-language feedback derived from the target agent’s behavior. They compare AdaLCPI to strong adaptive baselines such as Trojan Hippo-style attacks and AgentVigil under similar conditions.
AI.result: Experiments show that AdaLCPI substantially increases attack success rates against target agentic systems, achieving a macro-average attack success rate (ASR) of 61.4%, versus 32.8% for Trojan Hippo-style attacks and 30.0% for AgentVigil. This demonstrates that distributing and adaptively tuning partial instructions in long contexts is significantly more effective than prior adaptive prompt-injection methods.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that long-context, fragment-based adaptive prompt injection presents a serious security risk for LLM agents, as agents can reconstruct harmful objectives from incomplete cues spread across retrieved content. Consequently, safety evaluations and defenses must explicitly consider and test robustness to such fragmented, reconstructive attacks, rather than focusing solely on direct, explicit prompt injections.

title: SEED: Self-Speculative Decoding via Implicit Encoder-Decoder
summary: Self-speculative decoding accelerates large language model (LLM) inference by drafting tokens from the target model itself, but faces a sharp tradeoff between the quality and cost of the draft. Early-exit methods produce drafts cheaply by terminating computation at intermediate layers, but forgo the deeper representations that later layers provide and thus suffer in draft quality. Multi-token prediction preserves draft quality by emitting from the model's final hidden states, but pays for a full forward pass to produce those states at every drafting step. We propose self-speculative encoder-decoder (SEED), a self-speculative method that obtains high-quality drafts cheaply by reusing the deep contextual representations already computed during verification. We reinterpret the standard decoder-only transformer as an implicit encoder-decoder: the first layers (encoder) build deep contextual representations, and the last few layers (decoder) emit tokens from them. Encoding and verification are merged into a single step: verification is performed by the full encoder-decoder, and the contextual representations of the verified prefix are cached for reuse during drafting. Drafting is therefore very fast: between verifications, the lightweight decoder drafts multiple tokens autoregressively, each conditioned on the cached representations and on preceding drafts. Experiments across multiple benchmarks show that SEED achieves up to 2.7$\times$ average speedup on 4B-scale models, outperforming both early-exit and MTP-style self-speculative baselines and running 28% faster than the state-of-the-art EAGLE-3, while preserving or even improving the generation quality of standard autoregressive fine-tuning. Code is available at https://github.com/lhk2004/SEED.

AI.tldr: SEED reframes decoder-only LLMs as encoder-decoders to cheaply reuse deep representations for speculative decoding, achieving faster inference without hurting quality.
AI.motivation: Existing self-speculative decoding methods face a quality–cost tradeoff: early-exit drafting is cheap but low quality due to shallow representations, while multi-token prediction uses deep representations but requires a full forward pass at every draft step, making it expensive. There is a need for a method that retains high draft quality while significantly reducing the computation required for generation.
AI.method: The authors reinterpret a standard decoder-only Transformer as an implicit encoder-decoder, where early layers serve as an encoder that builds deep contextual representations and later layers act as a decoder that emits tokens. They merge encoding and verification into a single step: use the full encoder-decoder stack to verify generated tokens and simultaneously cache the encoder’s deep contextual representations of the verified prefix. During drafting, they run only the lightweight decoder layers autoregressively, conditioning on both the cached encoder representations and previously drafted tokens, thereby generating multiple draft tokens between verification steps.
AI.result: Across multiple benchmarks on 4B-parameter models, SEED achieves up to 2.7× average inference speedup compared to standard autoregressive decoding. It outperforms early-exit and multi-token prediction self-speculative baselines and runs 28% faster than the state-of-the-art EAGLE-3 method, while maintaining or slightly improving output quality relative to standard autoregressive fine-tuning.
AI.conclusion: By treating decoder-only LLMs as implicit encoder-decoders and caching deep contextual representations obtained during verification, SEED enables high-quality, low-cost speculative decoding. This architecture-level reinterpretation allows substantial speedups over prior self-speculative methods without sacrificing generation quality, suggesting a promising direction for efficient LLM inference design.

title: SafeCoEvo: Co-Evolving Safety Harnesses and Guards for LLM Agents at Test-Time
summary: LLM agents deployed in real-world environments continually encounter new tasks and safety risks, while execution feedback typically becomes available only after each task is completed. However, existing self-evolving approaches commonly rely on multiple rounds of optimization over fixed and repeatedly accessible task distributions, fundamentally differing from test-time adaptation in real-world deployment, where only experience accumulated from past tasks can be used to improve safety decisions on future unseen tasks. To address this limitation, we propose SafeCoEvo, a test-time Harness-Guard co-evolution framework for LLM agent safety that enables the external safety system to continually adapt from accumulated runtime experience. SafeCoEvo jointly improves two complementary safety capabilities at different timescales: S-Harness rapidly externalizes recent runtime experience into updatable explicit safety knowledge that can promptly influence subsequent tasks, while GuardVPO internalizes accumulated runtime safety experience over a longer timescale into parametric risk-judgment capabilities. By combining short-term rapid adaptation with long-term capability consolidation, SafeCoEvo continually improves the agent's safety capabilities, reducing the unsafe outcome rate by 10.05% while improving the task success rate by 12.15% over the strongest baseline, thereby achieving simultaneous gains in safety and task utility.

AI.tldr: SafeCoEvo is a test-time co-evolution framework that continually improves LLM agents’ safety using only accumulated runtime experience, achieving simultaneous gains in safety and task success.
AI.motivation: Real-world LLM agents face new tasks and emerging safety risks, but receive feedback only after each task is completed. Existing self-evolving methods assume a fixed dataset and allow repeated multi-round optimization, which does not match real deployment where past interactions cannot be revisited arbitrarily. There is a gap between laboratory-style continual training and true test-time adaptation, especially for safety, where the system must learn from streaming, one-pass experience to make better decisions on unseen future tasks without sacrificing utility.
AI.method: SafeCoEvo introduces a test-time Harness-Guard co-evolution framework for safety in LLM agents. It decomposes adaptation into two complementary components operating on different timescales: (1) S-Harness, an external, quickly updatable safety harness that transforms recent runtime feedback into explicit, editable safety knowledge and rules that can immediately influence decisions on subsequent tasks; and (2) GuardVPO, a longer-timescale parametric module that uses accumulated runtime safety experience to update internal risk-assessment capabilities through policy optimization. These two components co-evolve during real deployment, continuously ingesting execution feedback and updating both explicit rules and internal safety judgment models without offline retraining on a static dataset.
AI.result: In empirical evaluations, SafeCoEvo demonstrates continual improvement in safety and task performance under real-world-like test-time adaptation conditions. Compared to the strongest baseline, it reduces the unsafe outcome rate by 10.05% while simultaneously increasing the task success rate by 12.15%, showing that the framework does not merely become more conservative but also better at accomplishing tasks safely.
AI.conclusion: SafeCoEvo provides an effective mechanism for test-time safety adaptation of LLM agents in dynamic environments, bridging the gap between static, multi-epoch optimization and real deployment where only past, non-replayable experience is available. By co-evolving a rapidly updateable safety harness with a slower, parametric guard model, the framework can both quickly incorporate new safety insights and consolidate them into robust internal capabilities, leading to sustained gains in both safety and utility on future unseen tasks.

title: Generating Edit-Inducing Questions for AI Research Manuscripts
comment: Accepted at the DocInsights Workshop @ EMNLP 2026
summary: We study the ability of LLMs to generate edit-inducing questions whose answer will improve a paper draft. On a dataset of paired submission and camera-ready papers from ICLR and NeurIPS, we compare the helpfulness of questions from GPT models with or without full paper context to that of human reviewers. GPT produces more edit-inducing questions and its questions are associated with more extensive edits and cover a broader range of edited content compared to questions from reviewers. However, a much smaller percentage of the GPT questions are edit-inducing. Our analyses confirm that automated questions can be beneficial to authors and highlight an example task where proper attending to long context deteriorates reasoning model ability to produce helpful output.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates how well large language models (LLMs) can generate questions that lead authors to improve research paper drafts, comparing them against human reviewers.
AI.motivation: To understand whether LLMs can help authors revise and improve their scientific papers by asking questions, and to benchmark this ability against real conference reviewers using realistic pre- and post-revision data.
AI.method: The authors construct a dataset of paired submission and camera-ready versions of papers from ICLR and NeurIPS, identify edits between versions, and evaluate how often and how strongly questions from GPT models (with and without seeing the full paper) and from human reviewers correspond to those edits. They measure edit-inducing rate, extent of edits, and coverage of edited content.
AI.result: GPT-generated questions lead to more and larger edits overall and touch a wider variety of edited content than reviewer questions, but only a smaller fraction of the GPT questions actually induce edits, implying many are less useful or ignored.
AI.conclusion: Automated questions from LLMs can meaningfully support authors in improving their papers, but current models are inefficient in that relatively few of their questions are truly edit-inducing. The study also suggests that giving models long-context access can sometimes worsen their reasoning for this task, revealing a tradeoff between context size and question quality.

title: MemEvo: Automatic Discovery of Streaming Video Memory Mechanisms
summary: Query-agnostic streaming video understanding requires vision-language models to continuously compress an indefinitely growing visual stream into a bounded memory before future queries are known. The performance depends critically on the memory mechanism--what observations to preserve, how to represent and consolidate them, and what information to retrieve when a query eventually arrives. Rather than designing a single memory architecture by hand, we formulate memory design as a search problem over executable memory programs. We introduce a lightweight domain-specific language that expresses memory mechanisms through structured primitives for representation, admission, retention, consolidation, budgeting, and retrieval, while enforcing causal and bounded-memory constraints. Although structured, the derived program space remains large and contains heterogeneous, conditionally dependent design choices whose effects can only be assessed via downstream execution. We therefore propose MemEvo, an LLM-driven auto-research framework that uses pretrained LLM as a semantics-aware proposal model to iteratively generate and refine candidate memory programs based on accumulated experimental feedback. At runtime, a deterministic evaluation pipeline validates and evaluates each candidate, while the underlying vision-language model remains frozen throughout discovery. We finally produce a training-free, bounded-memory mechanism. Extensive experiments on StreamingBench and OVO-Bench demonstrate strong streaming video understanding performance together with substantial context and inference efficiency.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces MemEvo, an LLM-driven framework that automatically discovers effective bounded-memory mechanisms for query-agnostic streaming video understanding, using a domain-specific language to represent memory programs and searching them based on experimental feedback.
AI.motivation: In streaming video understanding, models must compress an unbounded, ongoing video stream into a fixed-size memory before any future queries are known. Performance heavily depends on how this memory is managed—what to store, how to compress and consolidate it, and how to retrieve it later. Manually designing a single, optimal memory architecture is difficult due to the large, heterogeneous design space and complex interactions between design choices that only reveal their impact when evaluated end-to-end. The authors aim to automate this design challenge to obtain efficient and effective memory mechanisms without retraining vision-language backbones.
AI.method: The authors formalize memory design as a search over executable memory programs defined in a lightweight domain-specific language (DSL). This DSL provides structured primitives that control representation, admission, retention, consolidation, budgeting, and retrieval, while enforcing causality and bounded-memory constraints. They propose MemEvo, an LLM-driven auto-research framework in which a pretrained large language model serves as a semantics-aware proposal model that iteratively generates and refines memory programs. A deterministic evaluation pipeline runs each candidate program on streaming video benchmarks, validates it, and measures downstream performance, feeding these results back to the LLM to guide further search. The underlying vision-language model is kept frozen; only the memory program is changed.
AI.result: Using MemEvo, the authors obtain a training-free bounded-memory mechanism that, when coupled with an existing frozen vision-language model, achieves strong performance on streaming video understanding tasks. Experiments on StreamingBench and OVO-Bench show that the discovered memory programs yield competitive or superior accuracy compared to baselines, while also offering significant gains in context efficiency (less memory usage) and inference efficiency (lower computation or latency).
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that query-agnostic streaming video memory design can be effectively automated by searching over a DSL of memory programs with an LLM-guided, feedback-driven framework. MemEvo can discover high-performing, bounded-memory mechanisms without retraining vision-language backbones, delivering strong accuracy and efficiency on streaming benchmarks. This demonstrates the promise of using LLMs as auto-researchers for complex architectural design problems, particularly for memory in long-horizon multimodal understanding.

title: Gödel Forest: Balancing Search Depth and Breadth for Data-Centric Recursive Self-Improvement
summary: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) aims to achieve compounding gains by having models improve themselves. While most existing RSI systems optimize external agent harnesses or prompts around a frozen base model, data-centric RSI directly updates the model's own parameters by training on agent-generated data. However, because validating data strategies requires expensive model training, existing methods face a fundamental dilemma: a single agent gets trapped in narrow directions and lacks exploration breadth, while naive parallel search or heavy trace sharing sacrifices long-horizon search depth. To address this challenge, we introduce G"odel Forest, a multi-agent framework that organizes recursive self-improvement as an ensemble of co-evolving search trees. In G"odel Forest, each agent autonomously grows a persistent tree, deepening, branching, or pruning data strategies based on model feedback to secure depth, while parallel trees explore distinct regions of the data space to expand breadth. Crucially, rather than leaving trees isolated or flooding them with heavy execution logs, a dynamically co-evolving memory connects the forest: agents continuously distill their successes and failures into compact procedural lessons anchored to a global leaderboard. Through this forest ecosystem, a dead-end in one tree instantly warns the whole forest against unpromising paths, while an empirical breakthrough quickly seeds new exploration branches in neighboring trees. Evaluated on RSIBench-Data across six diverse domains, G"odel Forest outperforms the single-agent baseline by an average of 10.70% while reducing wall-clock time on five tasks. Ablations confirm that co-evolving shared memory yields a +7.00% gain over independent parallel search, demonstrating that collective distillation is key to scalable self-improvement. The code is available at https://github.com/evolvent-ai/Godel-Forest.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Gödel Forest, a multi-agent recursive self-improvement (RSI) framework where multiple agents grow and coordinate search trees of data-generation strategies, achieving better performance and efficiency than single-agent or naive parallel RSI baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing recursive self-improvement systems mostly optimize prompts or external scaffolding around a frozen model, while data-centric RSI directly retrains models on agent-generated data. However, validating data strategies is expensive, creating a tradeoff: a single agent can explore deeply but risks getting stuck in narrow local optima, whereas naive parallelism or heavy trace sharing increases breadth but harms long-horizon, deep search. The authors aim to design an RSI framework that simultaneously attains exploration breadth and search depth while keeping coordination overhead manageable.
AI.method: The authors introduce Gödel Forest, a multi-agent RSI framework represented as an ensemble of co-evolving search trees. Each agent maintains a persistent tree of data strategies, whose nodes correspond to different ways of generating or curating training data. Agents autonomously grow their trees by deepening, branching, or pruning strategies in response to feedback from model retraining and evaluation, thus preserving long-horizon depth. Multiple trees run in parallel to explore different regions of the data space, ensuring breadth. A key component is a dynamically co-evolving shared memory connected via a global leaderboard: instead of sharing full execution traces, agents distill their successes and failures into compact procedural lessons stored in this memory. These distilled lessons influence subsequent search by other agents, enabling cross-pollination of promising ideas and rapid propagation of warnings about dead ends while keeping communication light-weight.
AI.result: On RSIBench-Data across six diverse domains, Gödel Forest outperforms a single-agent RSI baseline by an average of 10.70% and reduces wall-clock time on five of the tasks, indicating both better effectiveness and efficiency. Ablation studies show that the co-evolving shared memory yields a 7.00% improvement over independent parallel search, providing empirical evidence that the collective distillation mechanism and coordinated memory are central to the gains observed.
AI.conclusion: Gödel Forest demonstrates that organizing data-centric recursive self-improvement as a forest of co-evolving search trees, connected via a distilled shared memory, can overcome the depth–breadth tradeoff faced by existing RSI methods. The framework scales RSI more effectively than single-agent or naive parallel approaches, with empirical results suggesting that lightweight, procedurally focused knowledge sharing is crucial. This points toward multi-agent, collectively learning RSI ecosystems as a promising direction for scalable, automated model self-improvement.

title: Transformers Stop Thinking Too Early, and a Tiny LoRA Fixes It
summary: Pretrained transformers use little of their depth to follow references in context. Thirteen base models reliably follow only 1.4-3.6 lines, and extra pretrained loops add little. A task-trained rank-8 LoRA at one early layer extends this computation with all model weights frozen. Qwen3-8B improves from 15.5% to 99% exact accuracy on 24-line chains; a longer-trained LoRA reaches 50 lines. Ouro-1.4B reaches 60 lines after four loops and at least 160 after eight. The LoRA starts a relay: program lines pass on their chain identity through a short range of middle layers. Frozen heads read progressively further up the chain, and removing parent-line attention stops the relay. A frozen-model measurement locates the last useful intervention layer within tolerance in three of four held-out models. Task-specific LoRAs also improve MuSiQue. Default answers therefore understate the computation accessible through a tiny edit. Code and an interactive demo are available at https://lunamos.github.io/stop-thinking-too-early/

AI.tldr: They show current pretrained transformers barely use their depth for multi-step reference following, but a tiny, targeted LoRA at one early layer can massively extend how many linked lines a model can follow, without changing the base weights.
AI.motivation: Understand how much of a transformer’s depth is actually used for in-context reference following (long reasoning chains), and whether small, localized edits can unlock much longer computations than default behavior suggests.
AI.method: Measure how many lines of a reference chain various base models can follow; add small, task-trained rank-8 LoRAs at an early layer with all base weights frozen; evaluate accuracy on synthetic long-chain tasks and MuSiQue; probe attention patterns and perform ablations (e.g., removing parent-line attention) to understand the relay mechanism and locate the most effective intervention layer.
AI.result: Base models only follow short chains (1.4–3.6 lines), and extra pretrained compute loops don’t help much. A rank-8 LoRA on Qwen3-8B boosts accuracy on 24-line chains from 15.5% to 99%, and with more training handles 50 lines. Ouro-1.4B reaches 60 lines after four loops and at least 160 after eight. Analyses show a relay mechanism where middle layers propagate chain identity, frozen attention heads read progressively further up the chain, and disrupting parent-line attention breaks the relay; a frozen-model diagnostic predicts where to intervene in other models reasonably well. Task-specific LoRAs also improve performance on MuSiQue.
AI.conclusion: Pretrained transformers underutilize their depth for long-chain reference following, so default behavior underestimates their potential. A tiny, targeted LoRA edit at the right layer can unlock much deeper effective computation and dramatically extend the length of chains the model can follow, without altering the base model weights, and similar methods can transfer across models and to more realistic tasks.

title: ProgressCompass: Embodied Progress Reward Models Are Lost Without the Right Context
summary: Embodied agents now take on ever longer tasks. For long tasks, knowing only whether a task finally succeeds or fails says little; the steps along the way matter. Progress Reward Models (PRMs) score how far a task has come at every step, and serve as dense rewards, verifiers and monitors. Yet in long tasks the current frame alone often cannot tell how far the task has come, because progress depends on what happened before. We call this problem context-dependent progress estimation. Existing benchmarks on progress estimation mostly focus on short tasks whose progress can be read from the current observation, and whether PRMs can estimate progress when context is needed remains underexplored. We therefore build ContextProgress-Bench, with 24 manipulation tasks for 120 episodes. The benchmark covers three settings: (i) State Recall, where information needed for progress appeared earlier but is not in the current frame; (ii) Sequence Tracking, where steps follow a fixed order, so progress requires knowing which steps are done and which comes next; and (iii) Recurrence Disambiguation, where look-alike frames sit at very different progress. We then run a paired diagnosis: each PRM keeps the same input format in both runs, and in one run its instruction integrates the right context. Even PRMs that read the entire history get lost in estimating progress, yet with the right context the same five models cut their progress error by 77-82%. Embodied PRMs are thus not incapable of progress estimation, but lost without the right context. We therefore propose ProgressCompass, an autonomous agentic loop that reorients an existing PRM and uses current general-purpose VLMs to supply the context the PRM needs. Wrapped in the loop, the same frozen PRM cuts its progress error by 63% and raises its rank agreement by 76%. With such a compass, PRMs estimate progress far better on longer, more complex tasks.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a benchmark and a method to evaluate and improve how Progress Reward Models estimate task progress for long, context-dependent embodied tasks.
AI.motivation: In long-horizon embodied tasks, a simple success/failure signal or progress judged only from the current frame is inadequate, because true progress often depends on earlier, non-visible context. Existing PRMs and benchmarks focus on short tasks where progress is directly observable, leaving a gap in understanding and handling context-dependent progress estimation.
AI.method: The authors build ContextProgress-Bench, a benchmark of 24 manipulation tasks with 120 episodes designed to require contextual information through three settings: State Recall, Sequence Tracking, and Recurrence Disambiguation. They perform paired diagnostic experiments on several PRMs, comparing performance with and without explicit contextual instructions while keeping input formats fixed. Based on the observed failures, they propose ProgressCompass, an autonomous agentic loop that leverages general-purpose vision-language models to recover and inject the necessary context into a frozen PRM to improve its progress estimates.
AI.result: On ContextProgress-Bench, existing PRMs perform poorly at context-dependent progress estimation, even when given full history, but their progress error drops by 77–82% when they are guided with the right contextual instructions. Using the proposed ProgressCompass loop around an unchanged PRM yields a 63% reduction in progress error and a 76% increase in rank agreement, significantly improving progress estimation on long, complex tasks.
AI.conclusion: Context is crucial for accurate progress estimation in long-horizon embodied tasks. Current PRMs are not fundamentally limited but fail mainly because they lack the appropriate contextual information. By supplying this context through an autonomous agentic loop (ProgressCompass) and using general-purpose VLMs, PRMs can be reoriented to provide much more accurate, dense progress signals on long and complex tasks, as demonstrated on the ContextProgress-Bench benchmark.

title: SAKI: Maximal-Coupling-Routed Teacher Supervision for On-Policy Distillation
summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) reduces train-test state mismatch by training a student on its own generated trajectories, but weak students may visit teacher-misaligned prefixes where supervision is less representative. We introduce SAKI (Supervision Allocation with KL-constrained Interpolation), which combines a KL-constrained teacher-guided rollout with maximal coupling and reuses realized accept/correction events to route token-level supervision. Accepted positions retain sampled-token reverse-KL supervision, while correction positions receive direct supervision on the teacher's highest-probability token. Under maximal coupling, the correction probability is exactly TV(p_t, q_t), so the same trust-region radius controls rollout deviation and upper-bounds intervention and specialized-supervision frequency. We further implement an engine-resident speculative verifier that preserves the exact-q trajectory distribution and coupling semantics while improving matched-workload rollout throughput by 4.22x. Across seven mathematical reasoning benchmarks, SAKI improves the matched teacher-guided baseline in Mean@8 and Pass@8 for both 1.7B and 0.6B students. Placement controls and fixed-prefix analysis further support correction-triggered routing as a conflict-adaptive supervision signal.

AI.tldr: Proposes SAKI, a new on-policy distillation method that adaptively allocates token-level supervision using KL-constrained interpolation and maximal coupling to better align student rollouts with a teacher while keeping exact student trajectory distribution.
AI.motivation: Standard on-policy distillation trains a student model on its own rollouts to reduce train-test mismatch but struggles when the student is weak; it visits states where the teacher’s outputs are unrepresentative or misaligned with what the student will see, leading to poor supervision and inefficient use of teacher guidance. There is a need to control how and where teacher supervision is applied along the trajectory and to link rollout deviation, intervention frequency, and supervision type under a unified trust-region style constraint.
AI.method: Introduce SAKI (Supervision Allocation with KL-constrained Interpolation), which runs a KL-constrained, teacher-guided rollout using maximal coupling between teacher (p_t) and student (q_t). During generation, the system logs accept/correction events: if the sampled student token matches under the coupling (accept), it applies reverse-KL supervision on the sampled token; if it differs (correction), it directly supervises the teacher’s top token. Maximal coupling guarantees that the probability of correction equals the total variation distance TV(p_t, q_t). A single KL trust-region radius thus controls both rollout deviation from the student’s natural trajectory and an upper bound on how often corrections and specialized supervision occur. Additionally, an engine-resident speculative verifier is implemented to achieve the same exact-q trajectory distribution and coupling semantics while improving matched-workload throughput by 4.22x.
AI.result: On seven mathematical reasoning benchmarks, SAKI consistently outperforms a matched teacher-guided baseline in Mean@8 and Pass@8 metrics for both 1.7B and 0.6B student models. The speculative verifier yields a 4.22x throughput improvement for matched-workload rollouts, and placement-control plus fixed-prefix analyses show that performance gains correlate with correction-triggered supervision routing, suggesting it adapts effectively to conflicts between teacher and student distributions.
AI.conclusion: SAKI provides an effective, conflict-adaptive on-policy distillation framework that uses KL-constrained teacher guidance and maximal coupling to control when and how teacher supervision is applied, improving student performance on reasoning tasks while keeping the student’s rollout distribution intact. The method links a single trust-region parameter to both rollout deviation and intervention frequency, offers significant efficiency gains through a speculative verifier, and empirically improves over standard teacher-guided approaches across multiple benchmarks and model sizes.

title: Video2Skill: From Streaming Experience to Reusable Embodied Skills
summary: Manipulation behaviors vary widely across objects and scenes, but they share a small set of reusable skills, and planning with these skills helps embodied agents generalize to new tasks. Yet an agent can only plan with skills it knows. Recovering skills from observed experience, the inverse of planning, builds this knowledge over time and yields skill data for training future agents. Vision-Language Models (VLMs) describe individual manipulation events well, but can they organize a stream of events into reusable skills? We formulate this problem as Streaming Embodied Skill Discovery (SESD): a model watches videos in sequence and maintains a persistent skill library that shapes its later decisions. To systematically measure this ability, we introduce Video2Skill, a benchmark that covers robot tabletop manipulation and human kitchen activity and tests three core capabilities: (i) locating manipulation events in time, (ii) grouping events of the same transformation, and (iii) deciding when to reuse an existing skill or create a new one. Across 19 open-source VLMs, many models group events at near-chance level, and scale does not consistently help. Their errors depend on how perception and library updates are coupled: joint models merge distinct transformations into one skill, while models that update the library from text descriptions duplicate recurring ones. Supervised fine-tuning, including our counterfactual library-state rebalancing (CLaRe), improves grouping but exposes a deeper bottleneck: trained models consolidate familiar skills yet rarely expand the library. Their libraries stall below half the reference size, and transformations unseen in training are located in time but almost never given a new skill. Recognizing when existing skills are insufficient thus emerges as the central challenge.

AI.tldr: The paper studies whether vision-language models can incrementally discover and maintain reusable manipulation skills from continuous video streams, introduces a benchmark (Video2Skill) for this task, evaluates many VLMs, and proposes a fine-tuning method (CLaRe).
AI.motivation: Embodied agents need reusable manipulation skills to plan and generalize to new tasks, but they can only plan with skills they already know. While agents can, in principle, recover skills from experience, current vision-language models have only been evaluated on describing single events, not on organizing continuous streams of events into persistent, reusable skills. There is a need for a systematic benchmark and analysis of how well existing models can discover, group, and maintain such skills over time, and to understand their limitations.
AI.method: The authors formalize Streaming Embodied Skill Discovery (SESD), where a model watches manipulation videos sequentially and maintains a persistent skill library that influences future decisions. They design the Video2Skill benchmark with robot tabletop and human kitchen videos to test three abilities: (i) temporally locating manipulation events, (ii) grouping events that implement the same transformation, and (iii) deciding whether to reuse an existing skill or create a new one. They evaluate 19 open-source vision-language models under this framework, analyzing how perception and library-updating mechanisms affect performance. They further apply supervised fine-tuning, including a proposed counterfactual library-state rebalancing method (CLaRe), to improve grouping and examine remaining bottlenecks in skill discovery and expansion.
AI.result: Across 19 VLMs, most models perform near chance at grouping events into shared skills, and larger models do not reliably perform better. Error patterns depend on architecture: models that jointly model perception and library updating tend to over-merge distinct transformations, while models that update the library based on text descriptions tend to create redundant skills for recurring transformations. Supervised fine-tuning and CLaRe improve grouping quality, meaning models better consolidate known skills, but they still struggle to expand the skill library. Empirically, the discovered libraries plateau at less than half the size of the reference library, and novel transformations not seen during training are typically detected in time but almost never assigned a new skill entry.
AI.conclusion: Current vision-language models are poor at streaming embodied skill discovery: they struggle to correctly group manipulation events into reusable skills and, even after fine-tuning, rarely decide to create new skills when needed. While methods like CLaRe can help consolidate existing skills, they do not resolve the key limitation that models fail to recognize when their current skill library is insufficient. The central open challenge is enabling agents to detect novel transformations and autonomously expand their skill libraries, which is crucial for long-term embodied learning and generalization.

title: Multi-Channel Mitigation of Source-Trust Shortcuts in Fact-Checking RL Agents
summary: Retrieval-augmented fact-checkers often receive a reliability label, such as HIGH or LOW trust, for each evidence source. These labels should adjust the model's confidence and its decision to search for more evidence, while the verdict should follow the evidence content. We introduce TrustSwap, a counterfactual test that swaps, lowers, or removes source labels while keeping every evidence text fixed, and measures its three output channels (the verdict, the confidence, and the search decision) separately. Across untrained and RL-trained models at two scales, three datasets, and two prompts, confidence and search respond to the labels as intended in 49 of 50 comparisons, yet a label change alone alters 4-23% of confident verdicts for Qwen3 models and up to 50% for an existing RL-trained fact-checker. Standard GRPO fine-tuning amplifies this shortcut at 8B in all six settings. To reduce it, we propose trust-swap augmentation (TSA), which trains GRPO on each claim with both its original and its label-swapped evidence under the same gold verdict. At 4B, TSA lowers the verdict flip rate by 7-35% (relative) in four of six settings, keeps accuracy and the intended confidence and search responses, outperforms reward-based alternatives in the main setting, and carries over to an unseen label-removal perturbation. An added consistency reward helps on the trained-on swap but not on unseen perturbations. At 8B, TSA's effect is not detectable, which makes scale the main open question.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces TrustSwap, a counterfactual test for retrieval-augmented fact-checkers that manipulates trust labels of evidence sources to evaluate whether models over-rely on labels instead of evidence content, and proposes trust-swap augmentation (TSA) to mitigate this issue.
AI.motivation: Retrieval-augmented fact-checkers receive reliability labels (e.g., HIGH/LOW trust) for evidence sources. Ideally, these labels should influence model confidence and the decision to search for more evidence, but not override the actual content of evidence in determining the final verdict. Existing models may shortcut by following labels rather than evidence, compromising robustness and reliability. The authors aim to diagnose and quantify this problem and develop training schemes that preserve appropriate use of labels while ensuring verdicts remain grounded in evidence text.
AI.method: 1) They propose TrustSwap, a counterfactual evaluation protocol that keeps evidence texts fixed while systematically swapping, lowering, or removing the reliability labels of evidence sources. TrustSwap separately measures how these perturbations affect three model outputs: (a) the factual verdict, (b) confidence, and (c) the decision to perform further retrieval/search. 2) They apply TrustSwap across multiple models (untrained and RL-trained, at two parameter scales), three fact-checking datasets, and two prompting setups. 3) They assess how often changing only labels flips confident verdicts, indicating label-based shortcuts. 4) They explore standard GRPO (a policy-gradient-like RL fine-tuning) and find it can worsen label shortcutting. 5) They introduce Trust-Swap Augmentation (TSA): during GRPO training, each claim is paired both with its original evidence and with variants where source labels are swapped, while enforcing the same gold verdict. This encourages the policy to keep verdicts invariant to label perturbations while still using labels for confidence and search behavior. They also test adding a consistency reward encouraging agreement between original and swapped-label outputs, and they probe generalization to unseen perturbations like full label removal.
AI.result: Empirically, confidence and search behavior react to label changes in the intended way in 49 of 50 experimental conditions, indicating models use labels to regulate epistemic uncertainty and additional retrieval. However, isolated changes to labels (with evidence text fixed) cause substantial shifts in confident factual verdicts: 4–23% flip rates for Qwen3 models and up to 50% for a prior RL-trained fact-checking system. Standard GRPO fine-tuning at 8B parameters consistently increases this shortcutting behavior in all six evaluated settings. TSA at 4B reduces verdict flip rates by 7–35% (relative) in four of six setups, while maintaining overall accuracy and preserving desirable confidence/search responses. TSA outperforms other reward-based approaches in the main benchmark and generalizes to unseen label-removal perturbations. An added consistency reward improves robustness for the exact trained-on swaps but does not help with unseen perturbations. At 8B scale, TSA’s benefit is not statistically detectable, suggesting stronger or different interventions are needed at larger scales.
AI.conclusion: TrustSwap reveals that retrieval-augmented fact-checkers commonly adopt a harmful shortcut: allowing source reliability labels to drive final verdicts, even when evidence text is unchanged. While models use labels appropriately to modulate confidence and additional search, they also overfit to labels in their factual decisions. Standard RL fine-tuning can exacerbate this problem. Trust-Swap Augmentation offers a partial remedy at smaller scales, reducing label-induced verdict flips without harming accuracy or the helpful use of labels for uncertainty management. However, its lack of clear effect at 8B parameters highlights a scale-dependent challenge and points to the need for more powerful training or architectural methods to ensure verdicts remain grounded in evidence rather than meta-labels across large modern models.

title: Lost in Conversation or Lost in Translation? Diagnosing Multi-Turn Degradation in RAG
summary: When conversing with large language models (LLMs), users often begin with a simple question and build towards a multi-hop question through follow-up turns. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and its graph-based variant (GraphRAG) have become the dominant approaches for grounding LLM responses in external evidence, yet both are evaluated almost exclusively on single-turn, fully specified queries. We systematically investigate this evaluation mismatch through a large-scale simulation study. Building on prior work on multi-turn LLM evaluation, we transform questions from multi-hop question answering (QA) benchmarks into underspecified conversations and evaluate ten LLM assistants with eight retrieval systems across 1.5 million simulated conversations. Our findings reveal that multi-turn interaction causes widespread performance degradation, incurring relative performance drops of up to 21% and increasing unreliability by 47%, making RAG systems simultaneously less accurate and less reliable. We identify two distinct failure modes behind this degradation. Systems are either lost in translation, where conversational rephrasing distorts the retrieval query, or lost in conversation, where retrieval succeeds but the LLM fails to synthesize evidence distributed across turns.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how multi-turn conversations affect the performance and reliability of RAG and GraphRAG systems and finds that they perform significantly worse in realistic multi-turn, progressively specified queries than in standard single-turn benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Current RAG and GraphRAG systems are almost always evaluated on single-turn, fully specified queries, while real users usually arrive at complex, multi-hop questions gradually through follow-up turns. This creates a gap between benchmark performance and real-world usage. The authors aim to quantify and understand this mismatch and its impact on accuracy and reliability.
AI.method: The authors conduct a large-scale simulation study of multi-turn interactions. They take questions from multi-hop QA benchmarks and algorithmically transform them into underspecified, multi-turn conversations that gradually build up the full query. They then evaluate 10 different LLM assistants combined with 8 retrieval systems (including RAG and GraphRAG variants) on 1.5 million simulated conversations, measuring both accuracy and reliability across turns and analyzing error patterns.
AI.result: Multi-turn interactions cause substantial performance degradation in RAG-style systems: relative performance drops up to 21% and unreliability increases by 47%. This means that systems are not only less accurate but also less predictable and trustworthy in conversational, multi-hop settings than in single-turn evaluations. The analysis identifies two main failure patterns: (1) "lost in translation," where conversational rephrasing yields poor retrieval queries and hence bad or missing evidence; and (2) "lost in conversation," where retrieval is successful but the LLM fails to correctly integrate evidence spread across multiple turns.
AI.conclusion: Evaluating RAG and GraphRAG solely on single-turn, fully specified queries overestimates their real-world capabilities. In realistic conversational, multi-hop usage, these systems become both less accurate and less reliable, primarily due to failures in query formulation and cross-turn reasoning. Future work on RAG should explicitly address and benchmark multi-turn conversational scenarios, improving both retrieval robustness to conversational phrasing and LLM abilities to synthesize multi-turn evidence.

title: Neural Structural Reasoner: A Brain-inspired Architecture for Reasoning over Structured Knowledge
summary: Structural reasoning, the ability to recognize and make inferences over the relational structure between objects and concepts, is a hallmark of human cognition, yet prevailing methods often collapse relational topology into flat embeddings, cannot discover hidden structure and lack interpretability. We introduce Neural Structural Reasoner (NSR), a brain-inspired network that preserves relational structure directly in the connectivity and dynamics of coupled neuronal populations. NSR draws inspiration from three biological mechanisms: multi-layered architecture for encoding hierarchical knowledge, stable representations of entity and concepts, and path integration for input-driven state inference. At query time, NSR parallelizes computation over candidate relational structures and leverages confidence-weighted scores to perform link prediction. Across standard knowledge-graph benchmarks, NSR achieves competitive accuracy without leading on every dataset, and has lower reported training times than several neural baselines. Because reasoning is implemented through sequences of human-readable neuron activations, NSR affords native interpretability by tracking intermediate inference steps. The model further extracts latent relational hierarchies and compositional rules, demonstrating the brain-inspired architecture as an effective, efficient, and highly interpretable substrate for structural reasoning.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Neural Structural Reasoner (NSR), a brain-inspired model that performs interpretable structural reasoning on knowledge graphs by preserving relational structure in its neural architecture and dynamics.
AI.motivation: Existing structural reasoning and knowledge-graph models typically embed entities and relations into flat vector spaces. This often destroys or obscures the explicit relational topology, makes it hard to uncover latent structure like hierarchies or compositional rules, and results in models that behave like black boxes with poor interpretability. The authors want a model that (1) keeps relational structure explicit, (2) can discover hidden relational hierarchies and rules, (3) is computationally efficient, and (4) offers human-readable reasoning traces, taking inspiration from how the brain might implement structural reasoning.
AI.method: They introduce Neural Structural Reasoner (NSR), whose core idea is to encode relational structure directly into the connectivity and dynamics of coupled neural populations instead of collapsing it into a single embedding space. The architecture is biologically inspired in three ways: (1) a multi-layered structure represents hierarchical knowledge; (2) stable neural populations encode entities and concepts as enduring states; and (3) a path-integration-like mechanism performs input-driven state inference as the network traverses relations. At query time, NSR instantiates and evaluates multiple candidate relational structures in parallel and assigns confidence-weighted scores to them for link prediction. The reasoning process can be read off as sequences of neuron activations corresponding to intermediate steps in the inferred relational path or structure.
AI.result: On standard knowledge-graph benchmarks, NSR achieves accuracy competitive with neural baselines for link prediction, though it does not outperform all baselines on every dataset. It exhibits shorter reported training times than several comparison models, indicating computational efficiency. Empirically, the model is able to uncover latent relational hierarchies and compositional rules directly from data. The neuron-activation patterns provide explicit intermediate reasoning steps, confirming that the model’s internal process is accessible and interpretable.
AI.conclusion: The authors conclude that NSR is an effective, efficient, and inherently interpretable architecture for structural reasoning on knowledge graphs. By encoding relational structure in network connectivity and dynamics, and by using biologically inspired mechanisms for hierarchical representation and path-based inference, NSR can both perform competitive link prediction and reveal latent relational organization. This demonstrates that brain-inspired designs can serve as a powerful substrate for machine reasoning, offering transparency and structural insight that typical embedding-based approaches lack.

title: LAURA: Knowledge Distillation for Interpretable Ambiguous Clause Identification in Legal Contracts
summary: Legal contracts contain ambiguities that expose enterprises to financial and legal risks. Some ambiguities allow flexible interpretation without triggering disputes, while others lead to significant legal conflicts. This makes identification alone insufficient, and interpretable rationale analysis essential. We propose LAURA, a post-training framework for interpretable ambiguous clause identification. LAURA leverages knowledge distillation with an IRAC-Unlearning prompting technique to transfer knowledge from a teacher LLM to an open-weight student model (<=1B parameters), which is then trained using a joint objective combining classification and rationale generation losses. The framework supports both legal and non-legal stakeholders in making informed decisions about which ambiguities require further attention. Extensive experiments across 7 baselines and 7 open-weight models demonstrate that LAURA with Flan-T5 (250M) delivers state-of-the-art interpretability over all interpretable baselines while matching the identification performance of the best-performing opaque baseline.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces LAURA, a post-training framework that identifies ambiguous clauses in legal contracts and explains why they are ambiguous, achieving strong interpretability with small open-weight models.
AI.motivation: Legal contracts often contain ambiguous clauses that can either be harmlessly flexible or lead to serious disputes. Existing systems focus mainly on detecting ambiguity but do not adequately explain the underlying rationale, which is critical for lawyers, compliance teams, and business stakeholders who must decide which clauses need revision or escalation. Moreover, high-performing models are often large, opaque, or proprietary, limiting practical deployment and trust. This paper aims to create a small, open, and interpretable system that not only flags ambiguities but also provides human-understandable explanations about their legal risk profile.
AI.method: The authors propose LAURA, a post-training framework built around a teacher–student setup. A powerful teacher LLM is prompted using an "IRAC-Unlearning" technique, inspired by the legal IRAC (Issue–Rule–Application–Conclusion) reasoning structure, to generate both ambiguity labels and rationales. This knowledge is distilled into a small open-weight student model (≤1B parameters, e.g., Flan-T5 250M). The student is fine-tuned with a joint objective that combines clause-level ambiguity classification loss with rationale generation loss, so it learns both what is ambiguous and how to justify that decision. LAURA is evaluated across 7 different open-weight models and compared to 7 baseline methods, including interpretable and non-interpretable (opaque) systems.
AI.result: Experiments show that when instantiated with Flan-T5 (250M parameters), LAURA achieves state-of-the-art performance among interpretable models on the task of ambiguous clause identification with rationale generation. At the same time, it matches the ambiguity detection performance of the strongest non-interpretable baseline, meaning there is no accuracy loss from adding interpretability. These results hold consistently across multiple open-weight architectures and baselines, confirming the robustness of the framework.
AI.conclusion: LAURA demonstrates that a small, open-weight model can be post-trained to reliably detect ambiguous clauses in legal contracts while providing high-quality, interpretable rationales. The framework bridges the gap between pure classification and explainable legal reasoning, making it more suitable for real-world use by both legal professionals and non-legal stakeholders. The study suggests that combining knowledge distillation, structured prompting (IRAC-Unlearning), and joint training objectives is an effective path to scalable, trustworthy legal NLP systems, and the approach may generalize to other domains where interpretability is crucial.

title: DualTrack: Synchronized speech-gesture generation via symmetric coupling of pretrained priors
summary: Joint speech-gesture synthesis must coordinate two modalities despite limited paired data. Existing approaches often lack bidirectional interaction, have limited language coverage, or simplify body and finger representations. We present DualTrack, which couples pretrained speech and motion priors on a shared 12.5 Hz timeline. Causal adapters exchange previous-packet information, while current-state fusion coordinates the streams before they separately complete sixteen-codebook packets. We evaluate 43 BEAT2 recordings in four languages, with speakers held out from joint training and validation. On the shared English/Spanish inputs, without speech or motion prefixes, DualTrack achieves lower word error rate and full-motion Fréchet Gesture Distance, higher beat consistency and speech naturalness than the evaluated GELINA baseline.

AI.tldr: DualTrack is a model that jointly generates speech and gestures by tightly coupling pretrained speech and motion modules on a shared timeline, outperforming a strong baseline on multi-language data.
AI.motivation: Current joint speech-gesture synthesis systems struggle because paired speech–gesture data are scarce, interactions between the speech and gesture streams are weak or one-directional, language coverage is limited, and gesture representations often ignore full-body and finger details. The authors want a method that can better coordinate speech and gesture generation bidirectionally, work across multiple languages, and handle richer motion while remaining data-efficient.
AI.method: They propose DualTrack, which aligns a pretrained speech prior and a pretrained motion prior on a shared 12.5 Hz temporal grid. The system uses causal adapters that pass information between the two modalities based on previous time packets, enabling bidirectional influence over time. At each step, a current-state fusion module combines the present representations of speech and motion before each modality independently produces its next packet of discrete codes (across sixteen codebooks per stream). This architecture allows strong priors for each modality to interact without needing massive amounts of paired data.
AI.result: On 43 BEAT2 recordings spanning four languages, with speakers held out from joint training and validation to test generalization, DualTrack is compared to the GELINA baseline. For shared English/Spanish test inputs and without providing any speech or motion prefixes (fully generative setting), DualTrack yields better automatic metrics: lower word error rate for synthesized speech, better full-motion Fréchet Gesture Distance for gesture quality, and higher beat consistency. Human or perceptual evaluation of speech naturalness also favors DualTrack.
AI.conclusion: Coupling pretrained speech and motion models on a shared low-frequency timeline, alongside causal cross-modal adapters and current-state fusion, enables more coherent and natural joint speech-gesture synthesis. DualTrack improves both speech intelligibility and gesture quality across multiple languages relative to a strong baseline, indicating that tight bidirectional coordination between modalities is beneficial even when paired data are limited.

title: ATTUNER: Recomputation-Free KV Cache Reuse via Query-Side Adaptation
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents repeatedly load reusable content, such as skills, documents, and memory entries, into the current context. Re-encoding this content for every request wastes computation. Position-independent caching (PIC) alleviates this by encoding each artifact independently and reusing its key-value (KV) states at arbitrary positions, but it incurs a quality loss relative to full-context prefill. Existing methods repair this loss by restoring global position IDs or recomputing selected tokens. In this work, we isolate the source of the loss, finding that the positional mismatch has minor effect, and independently cached artifacts retain faithful representations: reading a provided artifact stays largely accurate, and performance degrades only when the model must select among multiple artifacts. Moreover, replacing PIC's attention scores with full-prefill scores recovers performance with the cached KV unchanged, localizing the failure to the attention rather than KV recomputation. Motivated by this, we propose \textsc{Attuner}, a query-side adaptation method that learns to read a frozen artifact cache. \textsc{Attuner} inserts low-rank adapters into the query projections and is trained by distilling full-prefill distribution into the student. It trains fewer than 0.05\% of the model parameters and, at inference, requires neither cache recomputation nor a full-context reference. On Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B across seven benchmarks covering skills, documents, memory, and code, \textsc{Attuner} substantially outperforms prior PIC baselines in both in-domain and out-of-domain settings, matches full-context prefill quality while providing up to $3.73\times$ speedup.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Attuner, a query-side adaptation method that makes position-independent KV caching nearly match full-context prefill quality while preserving its speed advantages.
AI.motivation: LLM agents repeatedly reuse the same artifacts (skills, docs, memories), and encoding them from scratch each time is computationally expensive. Position-independent caching (PIC) can save compute by reusing cached KV states at arbitrary positions, but it causes noticeable quality loss compared to doing a full-context prefill. Existing fixes either partially undo the compute savings (by recomputing tokens) or rely on global positions, and the exact source of the degradation is not well understood. The paper aims to pinpoint why PIC hurts performance and design a lightweight fix that preserves its efficiency.
AI.method: The authors empirically analyze PIC to localize the source of performance loss. They show that independently cached artifacts are mostly faithful and that degradation arises mainly when the model must choose among multiple artifacts, implicating the attention mechanism rather than KV representations. They then propose Attuner, which modifies only the query side: low-rank adapters are inserted into the query projections, and these adapters are trained via distillation to match the attention distributions and outputs of a full-context prefill teacher. The rest of the model and the artifact KV cache remain frozen. Attuner trains fewer than 0.05% of the model parameters and does not need full-context computation at inference.
AI.result: Experiments on Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B across seven benchmarks (skills, documents, memory, and code tasks) show that Attuner significantly outperforms prior PIC baselines in both in-domain and out-of-domain scenarios. It recovers performance close to or matching full-context prefill while retaining speedups from caching, achieving up to a 3.73× inference speedup without recomputing cached KVs or requiring a teacher pass at inference.
AI.conclusion: The degradation in position-independent caching stems mainly from how queries attend over cached artifacts, not from the cached KV representations themselves. By learning a lightweight query-side adaptation (Attuner) via distillation, one can read frozen artifact caches effectively and nearly eliminate the quality gap to full-context prefill, while still enjoying substantial speedups and minimal additional trainable parameters.

title: Semantic Projection for Continual Self-Evolution of Language Agents
summary: Language-model agents increasingly rely on persistent natural-language skills to adapt beyond their frozen model parameters. When a shared skill is repeatedly revised from a non-stationary, heterogeneous task stream, however, improvements for new tasks can overwrite procedures needed for earlier ones. In continual learning, Orthogonal Gradient Descent (OGD) addresses analogous interference by projecting a new-task gradient onto a subspace that locally preserves prior predictions. Natural-language skill revisions, however, have neither gradients nor a canonical vector space in which such a projection can be performed. We introduce \emph{Semantic-Scope Projected Evolution} (SSPE), which transfers the functional principle of gradient projection from parameter space to behavior space. SSPE treats an unconstrained skill revision as a proposed update, identifies acquired capabilities with which it may interfere, and uses the observed gains and regressions to construct a compatible revision rather than merely rejecting the update. This enables one shared skill to evolve across latent and recurring task contexts without exposing semantic domain identities to the evolution model. Across controlled synthetic streams and heterogeneous real-agent benchmarks, SSPE improves final cross-domain competence and mitigates forgetting relative to strong skill-evolution baselines. The evolved skill also retains the strongest average performance after transfer to a different executor model. These results establish semantic projection as a promising principle for stable and adaptive self evolution of language agents.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Semantic-Scope Projected Evolution (SSPE), a method that lets a shared natural-language skill evolve over time while reducing catastrophic forgetting, by projecting behavioral changes rather than gradients.
AI.motivation: Language-model agents increasingly depend on reusable, persistent natural-language skills that must adapt continuously as they encounter new, heterogeneous tasks.
