Standard continual learning methods like Orthogonal Gradient Descent (OGD) work in parameter space using gradients and representations that are not directly available when the evolving object is a natural-language skill (e.g., a prompt, tool description, or policy script). When these skills are repeatedly revised on non-stationary task streams, improvements on new tasks often interfere with and overwrite behaviors needed for earlier tasks, causing forgetting. There is a need for a mechanism that enables stable, continual evolution of such skills in behavior space, without requiring explicit task labels or exposing semantic domain identities.
AI.method: The authors introduce Semantic-Scope Projected Evolution (SSPE). SSPE considers each unconstrained revision to a shared natural-language skill as a proposed update. It then: (1) detects which existing capabilities (latent tasks) this proposal might affect; (2) evaluates how the proposal changes performance on these capabilities, identifying both gains and regressions; and (3) constructs a revised update that preserves helpful prior behavior while incorporating beneficial new behavior, analogous to gradient projection in continual learning but performed in behavior/semantic space rather than parameter space. Instead of rejecting conflicting updates outright, SSPE projects the proposed behavioral change onto a subspace that is more compatible with prior competencies. The process does not require explicit domain labels and operates on observable behavioral outcomes of the agent across a stream of tasks.
AI.result: Through experiments on both controlled synthetic task streams and heterogeneous real-agent benchmarks, SSPE achieves higher final cross-domain competence and substantially reduces forgetting compared to strong baselines for skill evolution. Moreover, the natural-language skill evolved with SSPE transfers better: when moved to a different executor model, it retains the highest average performance relative to skills evolved by competing methods. These empirical results show that SSPE is robust across task distributions and model backends.
AI.conclusion: Semantic-Scope Projected Evolution (SSPE) successfully adapts the idea of gradient projection from parameter space to behavior space, enabling stable and adaptive continual evolution of natural-language skills for language agents. By selectively integrating proposed revisions based on their semantic impact on previously acquired capabilities, SSPE mitigates catastrophic forgetting, improves cross-domain performance, and yields skills that generalize better across executor models. The work positions semantic projection as a promising general principle for self-evolving language agents operating in non-stationary, heterogeneous environments.

title: Distilling What Matters: Confidence-Aware Selective Distillation for Large Language Models
summary: Knowledge Distillation (KD) trains a smaller-capacity student model to imitate a larger-capacity teacher model by matching output distributions, implicitly assuming the teacher to be a reliable oracle. In large language models (LLMs), this assumption often fails: teacher predictions can exhibit high entropy and hallucinations, causing standard KD to degrade well-calibrated student priors. We propose CaRE-KD, a confidence-gated distillation framework that replaces static objectives with uncertainty-adaptive optimization. CaRE-KD has two components: a token-level loss (CaRE-Divergence) that adaptively switches between Forward and Reverse KL divergence based on teacher--student confidence, and a batch-level epistemic rejection mechanism (Revival) that suppresses updates when the teacher is more uncertain than the student. We provide a gradient-level analysis showing how this dual-granularity design induces a conditional calibration mechanism that prior static divergences cannot reproduce. Empirically, across eight teacher--student pairs and eleven benchmarks spanning instruction following, chat alignment, code generation, and mathematical reasoning, CaRE-KD delivers consistent gains over strong baselines (Skewed-KL, $α$--$β$ divergence). Highlights include up to $+3.2$ average ROUGE-L on instruction-following tasks, $+2.1$ pass@1 on MBPP, $+1.7$ accuracy on GSM8k, and $+1.8$ accuracy on CollegeMath over the strongest baseline, with consistent gains in LLM-as-a-judge factuality (up to $+2.5$ per task over Skewed-RKL). Revival further acts as a principled, loss-agnostic plug-in that systematically strengthens existing distillation objectives by filtering epistemically unreliable teacher supervision.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes CaRE-KD, a confidence-aware knowledge distillation framework for LLMs that adapts the training objective based on teacher and student uncertainty to avoid copying unreliable teacher outputs, yielding consistent performance and calibration gains across diverse tasks.
AI.motivation: Standard knowledge distillation assumes the teacher is a reliable oracle, which breaks down for large language models whose outputs can be high-entropy, hallucinated, or poorly calibrated. This can make students worse than their own priors and limit the benefits of distillation for real-world LLM deployment. The authors want a distillation method that leverages teacher knowledge when it is trustworthy while protecting the student from being misled when the teacher is uncertain or wrong.
AI.method: They introduce CaRE-KD, a confidence-gated distillation framework with two levels of adaptivity. At the token level, a new loss called CaRE-Divergence dynamically switches between Forward KL and Reverse KL divergences depending on the relative confidence of teacher and student; this tailors the learning signal to whether the teacher is sharper or more diffuse than the student. At the batch level, a mechanism called Revival estimates epistemic uncertainty and rejects or suppresses gradient updates when the teacher is judged more uncertain than the student, acting as a gating filter on supervision. They provide a gradient-level theoretical analysis to show that this design yields conditional calibration behavior not obtainable with static divergence choices.
AI.result: In experiments covering eight teacher–student LLM pairs and eleven benchmarks across instruction following, dialogue alignment, code generation, and math reasoning, CaRE-KD consistently outperforms strong distillation baselines such as Skewed-KL and alpha–beta divergence. Reported gains include up to +3.2 ROUGE-L on instruction tasks, +2.1 pass@1 on MBPP coding, +1.7 accuracy on GSM8K math word problems, and +1.8 accuracy on CollegeMath, as well as up to +2.5 improvements in factuality judged by an LLM-as-a-judge setup. Adding Revival on top of existing losses also systematically improves them by filtering out epistemically unreliable teacher updates.
AI.conclusion: Confidence-agnostic KD is suboptimal for LLMs because teachers are not always reliable; distillation must be uncertainty-aware. CaRE-KD’s combination of token-level adaptive divergence and batch-level epistemic rejection provides a general framework for conditionally trusting the teacher, leading to better-calibrated and more capable students. The Revival component is a modular, loss-agnostic plug-in that can strengthen a wide range of existing KD objectives by gating supervision based on teacher–student uncertainty comparisons.

title: Distilling Agentic Systems: A Roadmap across Models, Artifacts, and Harnesses
summary: Modern agents increasingly rely on memories, tools, and execution logic, so their competence extends beyond model parameters. This shift exposes a limitation of conventional knowledge distillation, which asks how a student model imitates a teacher model. We define Agent Distillation as the persistent transfer of task-solving knowledge from a teacher agent to a student agent. Our study organizes the field by where transferred knowledge is retained: within the model, as artifacts, through the execution harness, or across substrates. This perspective separates transfer evidence from its outcome and clarifies how knowledge moves between agent components. We develop an evaluation framework that relates retention to causal contribution and deployed utility. Together, these contributions establish a foundation for the reliable, maintainable, and safe development of increasingly complex agentic systems.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces and formalizes Agent Distillation, focusing on how task-solving knowledge is transferred and retained in modern AI agents that use memories, tools, and execution logic.
AI.motivation: Traditional knowledge distillation focuses only on transferring knowledge between model parameters, which is insufficient for modern agents whose capabilities also come from external memories, tools, and execution frameworks. There is a need to systematically understand and evaluate how knowledge is transferred and retained across all components of such agents.
AI.method: The authors define Agent Distillation as persistent transfer of task-solving knowledge between agents and propose a taxonomy based on where the transferred knowledge is stored: inside the model, as external artifacts, in the execution harness, or across different substrates. They build a conceptual and evaluation framework that separates evidence of transfer from its outcomes and links different forms of retention to their causal role and practical utility in deployed systems.
AI.result: They produce a structured categorization of knowledge transfer mechanisms for agents and an evaluation framework that shows how to measure retention, causal impact, and deployed usefulness across different agent components. The results primarily clarify concepts and relationships rather than presenting numerical benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: The work provides foundational concepts and an evaluation framework for Agent Distillation, enabling more reliable, maintainable, and safe development of complex agentic systems that go beyond static model parameters. It reframes knowledge distillation for modern agents and highlights where and how knowledge can be persistently stored and assessed.

title: VAA-CSEC: Vote-guided Advantage Allocation for Chinese Semantic Error Correction
summary: Chinese Semantic Error Correction (CSEC) targets semantic errors in Chinese text, which are typically more subtle and complex than spelling and grammatical errors but remain relatively underexplored. Existing LLM-based approaches face two recurring obstacles in this task: over-correction, and unclear interaction between Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning and self-consistency decoding, such that the benefits brought by CoT cannot be reliably transferred to final corrections. We propose Vote-guided Advantage Allocation for CSEC (VAA-CSEC), a multi-stage framework that combines CoT distillation, Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), Reinforcement Learning (RL) and self-consistency decoding. During RL, we design a task-specific reward function that directly aligned with the minimal-editing principle of CSEC. We further introduce Group-Level Relative Policy Optimization (GLPO), which reallocates GRPO advantages according to the margin between individual rollout rewards and the vote-aggregated group reward, aligning the RL training objective with the self-consistency objective used at inference time. Experiments on CSED-C and NaSGEC-Exam show that VAA-CSEC outperforms all LLM-based baselines on CSED-C with an F0.5 of 47.72%, achieves the highest recall of 42.15% among all methods, and establishes a new state of the art of 41.55% F0.5 on NaSGEC-Exam.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes VAA-CSEC, a reinforcement learning and self-consistency based framework that improves Chinese semantic error correction while reducing over-corrections, achieving new state-of-the-art results on two benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Chinese Semantic Error Correction is harder and less explored than spelling or grammar correction, and current LLM-based methods suffer from over-correction and ineffective use of Chain-of-Thought with self-consistency, limiting performance and reliability.
AI.method: The authors design VAA-CSEC, a multi-stage framework combining CoT distillation, supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, and self-consistency decoding. They define a CSEC-specific reward that enforces minimal necessary edits and propose Group-Level Relative Policy Optimization, which reallocates advantages within rollouts based on the gap between each rollout’s reward and a vote-aggregated group reward, so that training aligns with the self-consistency decoding strategy used at inference.
AI.result: On CSED-C, VAA-CSEC surpasses all LLM-based baselines with an F0.5 of 47.72% and achieves the best recall of 42.15%; on NaSGEC-Exam, it sets a new state of the art with 41.55% F0.5.
AI.conclusion: Aligning RL training objectives with minimal-editing rewards and the self-consistency voting mechanism yields more precise and reliable Chinese semantic error correction, effectively mitigating over-correction and pushing state-of-the-art performance on standard benchmarks.

title: RankBuffer: Efficient Ranking-Based Rewards for Open-Ended Generation
summary: Open-ended generation lacks canonical answers, making pointwise rewards difficult to calibrate for group-based reinforcement learning. Directly ranking same-query rollouts provides a more suitable relative reward signal, but existing ranking-based reward methods can incur substantial judging cost. We introduce RankBuffer, which maintains an ordered, query-specific buffer of previously judged responses as a reusable quality scale. Each rollout is first inserted into an anchor interval through an independent coarse judgment, after which only rollouts assigned to the same interval undergo local fine ranking. The resulting complete order is converted into bounded rank rewards, while boundary expansion, local refinement, and inactive-anchor pruning adapt the buffer as the policy evolves. Across four open-ended benchmarks, RankBuffer consistently outperforms all pointwise baselines. It also achieves nearly on-par performance with the strongest ranking-based reward baseline while substantially reducing judging cost. Ablations demonstrate the importance of both local fine ranking and anchor response content, while buffer analyses show that rollout-derived anchors progressively extend and refine the covered quality scale. These results establish response reuse as an effective approach to efficient relative reward construction.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes RankBuffer, a method to efficiently construct relative rewards for open-ended text generation by reusing previously judged responses as a dynamic ranking reference, achieving strong performance with lower judging cost.
AI.motivation: In open-ended generation tasks, there is no single correct answer, so traditional pointwise reward models are hard to calibrate and may provide unreliable signals. Ranking-based rewards are more suitable because they compare multiple outputs for the same prompt, but they require many pairwise or listwise human judgments, which are expensive. The motivation is to design a more cost-efficient way to obtain reliable relative rewards for reinforcement learning while still leveraging the strengths of ranking-based feedback.
AI.method: The authors introduce RankBuffer, an ordered buffer of responses maintained separately for each query. For a new rollout, an initial coarse judgment assigns it to an anchor interval within this buffer. Only responses in that same interval are then locally fine-ranked via more detailed comparison. This two-stage process yields a complete order over all responses in the buffer. The ranks are transformed into bounded scalar rewards for RL. The buffer is dynamically updated with procedures like expanding boundaries when higher- or lower-quality responses appear, refining local rankings, and pruning anchors that are no longer useful, so that the quality scale evolves with the policy.
AI.result: On four open-ended generation benchmarks, RankBuffer consistently surpasses all pointwise reward baselines and comes close to the best existing ranking-based reward method, while significantly cutting down the number of human or model judging operations required. Ablation studies show that removing local fine ranking or ignoring the content of anchor responses degrades performance, and buffer diagnostics indicate that as training progresses, rollout-derived anchors broaden and sharpen the represented quality spectrum.
AI.conclusion: RankBuffer demonstrates that reusing and incrementally refining a buffer of previously judged responses is an effective and efficient way to construct relative rewards for open-ended generation. By combining coarse interval placement with targeted local ranking and adaptive buffer maintenance, it preserves the performance benefits of ranking-based rewards while reducing judgment cost, suggesting a practical path for scalable group-based RL in open-ended settings.

title: Rethinking Multimodal Fake News Detection in the Generative AI Era
summary: Generative content is increasingly entering the production and dissemination of news, transforming fake news from manually fabricated or simply manipulated material into complex forms in which native and generated content jointly participate. Existing multimodal fake news detection research primarily focuses on veracity assessment and rarely characterizes how generativity differences affect the reliability of evidence. In contrast, AIGC detection primarily determines whether content is generated or modified by generative models, but it does not by itself establish whether the underlying news event is true. To bridge the separation between these tasks in data and evaluation, we construct Weibo26, a multimodal fake news detection dataset for generative-content scenarios. On this basis, we propose the Generativity-Aware Hierarchical Reasoning (GAHR) framework, which combines global judgment with local correction so that generativity information participates in news-veracity reasoning. Experiments on multiple existing fake news detection benchmarks and Weibo26 show that GAHR achieves competitive veracity-detection performance while effectively identifying generative content.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a new multimodal fake news dataset tailored to generative-content scenarios and a generativity-aware reasoning framework that jointly detects fake news and AI-generated content.
AI.motivation: Existing multimodal fake news detection focuses on deciding if news is true or false, without modeling how AI-generated vs. human-written content patterns affect the reliability of evidence. Meanwhile, AIGC (AI-generated content) detection only decides if content is generated or modified by models, without telling whether the news event itself is real. There is a gap between veracity detection and generative-content detection: they use different data and evaluation settings and ignore each other’s signals. The motivation is to bridge this gap so that knowledge about generativity can help fake news detection, and veracity reasoning can be done in realistic generative-content scenarios.
AI.method: The authors first build Weibo26, a multimodal dataset based on Weibo that explicitly captures generative-content scenarios for fake news detection (including both native and generated text/image content). Then they propose GAHR (Generativity-Aware Hierarchical Reasoning), a framework that integrates generativity signals into the veracity reasoning process. GAHR performs hierarchical reasoning that combines global judgment about the news item with local correction steps at the content-component level, using generativity-aware features so that the system can jointly reason about whether parts are AI-generated and whether the overall claim is true or false.
AI.result: On the newly proposed Weibo26 dataset and several existing multimodal fake news detection benchmarks, GAHR reaches competitive or superior performance in fake news (veracity) detection compared with prior methods. At the same time, it effectively detects AI-generated or AI-modified content, demonstrating that incorporating generativity into the reasoning process does not harm and can enhance veracity detection, while also providing AIGC detection capability.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating generativity information into multimodal fake news detection is both feasible and beneficial. By creating a dataset tailored to generative-content scenarios and proposing the GAHR framework that hierarchically reasons with generativity signals, the authors show that one can jointly address veracity assessment and AI-generated content detection. This helps align data, evaluation, and modeling for more realistic news environments where human and AI-generated content are intertwined.

title: FineSID: Scalable and Efficient Semantic Identifier Learning for Generative Recommendation
summary: A critical prerequisite of generative recommendation is designing semantic identifiers (SIDs) that are both scalable to large item sets and efficiently learnable. Existing SID learning methods fundamentally rely on Top-1 hard assignment during vector quantization. While heuristic strategies -- such as clustering-based initialization or forced post-hoc collision resolution -- can artificially inflate codebook coverage, they often disrupt end-to-end semantic alignment and fail to address the underlying optimization bottleneck: sparse gradient propagation. In standard Top-1 assignment, gradients concentrate on a narrow subset of frequently selected codewords, leaving the majority inherently under-trained and causing severe SID collisions. To overcome this limitation natively without relying on complex initialization priors, we propose FineSID, a unified quantization framework that moves beyond Top-1 assignment by enabling fine-grained gradient propagation across the entire codebook. Instead of updating only a single selected codeword, FineSID distributes learning signals to all codewords in a soft, differentiable manner. This design promotes globally balanced codebook optimization while strictly preserving semantic consistency, effectively alleviating SID collisions and stabilizing training in large, high-dimensional codebooks. Extensive experiments on multiple public benchmarks demonstrate that FineSID is robust to initialization configurations and consistently improves both codebook utilization and recommendation accuracy. Our work provides a principled, initialization-agnostic solution for semantic identifier learning, advancing the practicality of generative recommendation.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes FineSID, a new quantization framework to learn semantic identifiers (SIDs) for generative recommendation that improves codebook utilization and recommendation accuracy.
AI.motivation: Generative recommenders need semantic IDs for items that both scale to very large catalogs and are easy to train. Existing methods rely on Top-1 hard assignment in vector quantization, where each item only updates its single closest codeword. This causes sparse gradients: frequently selected codewords are over-trained while most codewords are under-trained, leading to collisions (different items sharing the same SID), poor codebook coverage, and instability. Heuristic fixes like special initialization or post-hoc collision handling break end-to-end semantic alignment and do not solve the core optimization problem.
AI.method: The authors introduce FineSID, a unified quantization framework that replaces Top-1 hard assignment with a soft, differentiable assignment scheme. Instead of updating only the single selected codeword per item, FineSID propagates gradient signals to all codewords in a fine-grained way. The framework is designed to: (1) maintain semantic consistency between continuous representations and discrete SIDs, (2) promote globally balanced training across the entire codebook, and (3) integrate seamlessly into end-to-end generative recommendation models. This soft, global update mechanism natively addresses gradient sparsity without relying on clustering-based initialization or ad-hoc collision resolution.
AI.result: On multiple public recommendation benchmarks, FineSID yields higher codebook utilization (more codewords are meaningfully used and trained) and better recommendation accuracy than prior SID learning methods. The method is shown to be robust across different initialization schemes, indicating that it does not depend on carefully engineered codebook starting points. Training is more stable, and SID collisions are significantly reduced in large, high-dimensional codebooks.
AI.conclusion: FineSID offers a principled alternative to Top-1 hard vector quantization for semantic identifier learning in generative recommendation. By enabling soft, fine-grained gradient propagation to the entire codebook, it mitigates gradient sparsity, reduces SID collisions, and improves both utilization and accuracy, while remaining robust to initialization. This enhances the scalability and practicality of generative recommendation systems for large item catalogs.

title: Momentum-Coupled Rubric Adaptation for Detailed Image Captioning
comment: 28 pages, natural language processing, computer vision
summary: Detailed image captioning requires accurate and comprehensive descriptions of fine-grained visual content, yet caption quality spans factual accuracy, information coverage, and clarity. Compared with conventional methods that rely mainly on high-quality supervision or holistic rewards, rubric-based reinforcement learning decomposes these requirements into explicit criteria and provides targeted, structured feedback. However, existing methods often use separate models for caption generation, rubric construction, and judging, which may lead to inconsistent interpretations across roles. Some dynamic rubric methods alternate updates between the caption policy and rubric generator while keeping the judge fixed, but staged optimization may still leave rubric construction and judging out of step with policy optimization. We propose MoCo Rubric, a two-stage framework that coordinates these roles. First, role-conditioned, shared-parameter multi-task supervised fine-tuning equips a single vision--language model to serve as the Caption Policy, Rubric Generator, and Rubric Judge. Then, the Generator constructs rubrics online from captions sampled by the current Policy, reference captions, and image evidence. The Judge provides rubric-based rewards, and only the Policy receives GRPO updates. As Policy updates change the candidates being evaluated, we use an exponential moving average of the Policy parameters to update one momentum model shared by the Generator and Judge. This gradual transfer lets both rubric roles track Policy updates without separate RL optimization while smoothing parameter changes that could disrupt their rubric capabilities under direct synchronization. Across five captioning benchmarks, MoCo Rubric achieves an average pairwise win rate of 72.83\%, the best mean rank in blind ranking, and the highest average score in caption-based question answering.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes MoCo Rubric, a coordinated rubric-based reinforcement learning framework that uses a single shared vision-language model to generate, evaluate, and reward fine-grained image captions, improving caption quality across multiple benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Detailed image captioning must be factually accurate, comprehensive, and clear. Traditional approaches rely on high-quality labeled data or holistic rewards, which do not explicitly address these distinct quality dimensions. Existing rubric-based RL systems decompose quality into criteria but typically use separate models for captioning, rubric generation, and judging, causing inconsistencies between roles. Dynamic rubric methods partly adapt but still decouple rubric construction and judging from the evolving caption policy, leading to misalignment over training. The motivation is to create a more coordinated, stable, and effective rubric-based RL framework where caption policy, rubric generator, and judge remain consistent and adapt together.
AI.method: The authors introduce MoCo Rubric, a two-stage framework. Stage 1: They perform multi-task supervised fine-tuning of a single vision-language model with role conditioning so that the same backbone model can act as Caption Policy, Rubric Generator, and Rubric Judge while sharing parameters. Stage 2: In RL, the current Policy samples captions for images. The Rubric Generator, using the same backbone, constructs rubrics online based on the sampled captions, reference captions, and image content. The Rubric Judge then scores candidate captions according to these rubrics to produce rubric-based rewards. Only the Policy is updated with GRPO (a policy optimization algorithm). To keep the Rubric Generator and Judge aligned with the evolving Policy without destabilizing them, the method maintains an exponential moving average (EMA, momentum model) of the Policy parameters, and this momentum model is used for both Generator and Judge, allowing them to smoothly track Policy updates without separate RL training.
AI.result: On five image captioning benchmarks, MoCo Rubric outperforms baselines. It achieves an average pairwise win rate of 72.83%, obtains the best mean rank in blind human (or judge) rankings, and records the highest average score in caption-based question answering evaluations, indicating stronger factual accuracy, coverage, and clarity in generated captions.
AI.conclusion: MoCo Rubric effectively coordinates caption generation, rubric generation, and rubric-based judging within a single shared vision-language model and a momentum-update mechanism. This unified, role-conditioned framework reduces inconsistencies between roles and enables more stable rubric-based reinforcement learning. The approach yields substantial gains in detailed image captioning across multiple benchmarks, demonstrating that jointly aligning policy and rubric roles via shared parameters and EMA tracking improves multi-criterion caption quality compared to previous methods using disjoint or statically optimized components.

title: FairDiff: Mitigating the Self-Reinforcing Matthew Effect in Diffusion Recommender Models
summary: While the "Matthew Effect" and filter bubbles are widely recognized outcome-level biases in recommender systems, we reveal that Diffusion Recommender Models (DRMs) uniquely compound this issue through their generative dynamics. Rather than merely inheriting data imbalances, DRMs trigger a self-reinforcing amplification of popularity bias. We identify that this phenomenon is driven by two compounding mechanisms. First, while optimization loss is universally dominated by high-frequency items across recommenders, DRMs suffer from a unique structural prior mismatch during generation. Because the forward terminal distribution of long-tailed data deviates significantly from the standard Gaussian prior, reverse sampling trajectories inherently collapse toward high-density popular items, fundamentally suppressing niche item generation. To dismantle this self-reinforcing loop, we propose FairDiff, a plug-and-play fairness-aware diffusion framework. To overcome the popularity-dominated loss, we introduce Popularity Condition Guidance (PCG). Rather than altering the training objective, PCG acts as an inference-time distributional reweighting mechanism, mathematically reshaping the score-based gradient field to penalize high-popularity regions and guide trajectories toward niche semantics. Furthermore, we design a Semantic Calibration (SC) Module to bridge the prior mismatch, aligning the forward and reverse distributions via one-step optimal transport. Comprehensive evaluations demonstrate that FairDiff achieves state-of-the-art performance while effectively mitigating the self-reinforcing Matthew Effect, highlighting its value as a general framework for DRMs.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that diffusion-based recommender models amplify popularity bias (Matthew Effect) more than other recommenders, and proposes FairDiff, a plug-and-play framework that reweights generation toward niche items while aligning priors, achieving better fairness without sacrificing accuracy.
AI.motivation: Recommender systems already suffer from popularity bias and filter bubbles, and newer diffusion recommender models appear to worsen this by generatively favoring already popular items. The authors aim to understand why DRMs structurally amplify the Matthew Effect and to design a method that reduces this self-reinforcing bias without degrading recommendation quality, providing a fairer generation process especially for long-tail (niche) items.
AI.method: They first analyze DRMs to identify two mechanisms behind amplified popularity bias: (1) optimization loss being dominated by high-frequency (popular) items, and (2) a mismatch between the Gaussian prior assumed in diffusion and the true forward terminal distribution on long-tailed data, which pushes reverse sampling toward high-density popular regions. Based on this, they propose FairDiff, a plug-and-play framework with two main components: (a) Popularity Condition Guidance (PCG), an inference-time distributional reweighting that reshapes the score-based gradient field to penalize high-popularity regions and guide samples toward niche items; and (b) a Semantic Calibration (SC) module that uses one-step optimal transport to better align the prior and data distributions, thus reducing the structural collapse toward popular items in generation.
AI.result: Experiments on standard benchmarks for recommender systems show that FairDiff mitigates the self-reinforcing Matthew Effect in DRMs by increasing exposure and recommendation of long-tail items, while maintaining or even improving overall accuracy and quality metrics. The method outperforms prior state-of-the-art approaches in balancing fairness (reduced popularity bias) and performance.
AI.conclusion: Diffusion-based recommender models are intrinsically prone to stronger popularity amplification because of loss domination by popular items and a prior mismatch that biases reverse diffusion toward popular regions. By introducing FairDiff with PCG and SC, the authors provide a general, plug-and-play framework that can be applied at inference to significantly reduce this bias while preserving state-of-the-art recommendation quality, suggesting a practical path to fairer generative recommenders.

title: RAEGNet: Relation-Aware Evidence Graph Network for Harm-Aware Multimodal Fake News Detection
summary: Existing multimodal fake news detection methods often introduce external information to assist detection. However, most of them rely on entity-level retrieval and are therefore prone to introducing event-irrelevant noise. Meanwhile, existing methods mainly focus on improving overall performance and do not account for differences in the degree of harm posed by different instances of fake news. To address these limitations, we design an Event-Level Evidence Retrieval Framework (ELERF) and propose a Relation-Aware Evidence Graph Network (RAEGNet). ELERF retrieves external evidence based on the complete event semantics of a news item. RAEGNet constructs a directed graph that incorporates news-evidence stance relations and evidence-evidence interaction relations, and introduces a conditional-harm branch to jointly model authenticity and potential harm. Experimental results demonstrate that RAEGNet outperforms multiple baseline methods across all evaluated metrics on Weibo-21, Fakeddit, and our self-constructed SSS dataset.

AI.tldr: They propose an event-level evidence retrieval and graph-based reasoning framework that considers both truthfulness and potential harm of news, reducing noise from irrelevant evidence and improving multimodal fake news detection.
AI.motivation: Current multimodal fake news detectors rely heavily on entity-level retrieval of external information, which often brings in evidence unrelated to the actual event, creating noise. Moreover, they treat all fake news instances equally, ignoring that some pieces are more harmful than others. There is a need for a detection approach that (1) retrieves evidence at the event level to better match news semantics and (2) explicitly models the potential harm posed by a news item alongside its authenticity.
AI.method: They design an Event-Level Evidence Retrieval Framework (ELERF) that retrieves external evidence using complete event semantics instead of only entity mentions. On top of that, they propose a Relation-Aware Evidence Graph Network (RAEGNet), which builds a directed graph where nodes represent news and evidence, and edges encode stance relations between news and evidence as well as interactions among evidence pieces. RAEGNet includes a conditional-harm branch that models the potential harm conditioned on authenticity, enabling joint learning of truthfulness and harm level.
AI.result: Experiments on three datasets—Weibo-21, Fakeddit, and a new self-constructed SSS dataset—show that RAEGNet achieves better performance than multiple strong baselines across all evaluated metrics, indicating more accurate and robust multimodal fake news detection and harm estimation.
AI.conclusion: Event-level evidence retrieval combined with relation-aware graph reasoning and explicit harm modeling leads to more effective multimodal fake news detection. By reducing event-irrelevant noise and jointly capturing authenticity and harm, ELERF+RAEGNet provides a more practical and fine-grained approach to assessing online news, outperforming existing methods on several benchmarks.

title: MLToolBench: Learning Tool-Augmented Agents for Machine Learning Development
summary: Machine learning engineering (MLE) agents have made substantial progress, but learning through ML experimentation remains costly in time and computation. Synthetic environments reduce these costs while introducing variations in data and experimental settings that require task-specific diagnosis. Access to diagnostic tools alone does not ensure that agents learn when to use them or how to act on their findings. We introduce ToolMLBench, a suite of executable tools for data inspection, code verification, and experiment diagnosis, together with an SFT and RL pipeline for learning their use. Diagnostic calls acquire evidence whose value depends on subsequent decisions, so final outcomes provide limited guidance on which calls to reinforce. We address this challenge with SPICE, which measures how privileged context changes the likelihood of a sampled tool action and uses this difference as a turn-level reward alongside the final outcome. We train on 80 synthetic tasks and evaluate on 25 in-domain and 10 out-of-domain tasks. Providing tool interfaces and descriptions alone yields inconsistent gains across unadapted models. With the same diagnostic interface, our training pipeline raises in-domain success from 24.8% to 52.4% for Qwen3-8B and from 35.6% to 69.2% for Qwen3.5-35B-A3B. The latter also improves from 31% to 48% out-of-domain, supporting learned diagnostic tool use on held-out sources and targets.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces ToolMLBench and a training pipeline to teach ML engineering agents how to effectively use diagnostic tools, significantly improving performance on synthetic ML tasks.
AI.motivation: Running ML experiments is expensive in time and compute, and synthetic environments, while cheaper, introduce diverse data and setup variations that require careful, task-specific diagnosis. Merely giving agents access to diagnostic tools for data inspection, code checking, and experiment analysis does not guarantee they will know when to invoke these tools or how to interpret and act on their outputs. There is a need for a principled way to train agents to use such tools efficiently and strategically so that they can improve ML experimentation autonomously.
AI.method: The authors create ToolMLBench, a suite of executable diagnostic tools for data inspection, code verification, and experiment diagnosis, embedded in synthetic ML experimentation tasks. They design a supervised fine-tuning (SFT) plus reinforcement learning (RL) pipeline that trains models to use these tools. A central component is SPICE, a reinforcement learning signal that quantifies how adding privileged diagnostic context changes the probability of a sampled tool action; this change is used as a turn-level reward, combined with the final task outcome. Training is done on 80 synthetic tasks, and evaluation is conducted on 25 in-domain and 10 out-of-domain tasks, with models given the same diagnostic tool interfaces and descriptions.
AI.result: Unadapted models that only receive tool interfaces and descriptions show inconsistent and often limited gains from the tools. With the proposed SFT+RL training pipeline and SPICE-based rewards, the Qwen3-8B model’s in-domain success rate increases from 24.8% to 52.4%, while the larger Qwen3.5-35B-A3B model’s in-domain performance improves from 35.6% to 69.2%. On out-of-domain tasks, Qwen3.5-35B-A3B’s success rises from 31% to 48%, indicating that the learned diagnostic behavior generalizes to held-out task sources and targets.
AI.conclusion: ToolMLBench and the associated SFT+RL pipeline effectively teach ML agents to use diagnostic tools for ML experimentation. Simply exposing models to tool APIs is insufficient; targeted training with SPICE-based turn-level rewards leads to much better and more consistent performance. The improvements in both in-domain and out-of-domain tasks suggest that the learned strategies for diagnostic tool use are robust and transferable, offering a promising direction for scalable, tool-augmented ML engineering agents.

title: MultiTalk: Scaling Full-Duplex Speech Models to Long, Multi-Party, Bilingual Conversation
summary: End-to-end full-duplex speech models have brought open-source machine conversation closer to human-like interaction, yet existing systems remain limited in two intertwined dimensions: long-context robustness and multi-party interaction. Real-world scenarios such as meetings, group lessons, and social-robot reception require a single model to track, contextualize, and respond to multiple speakers over extended durations. Progress is constrained by both data and evaluation: open multi-party speech corpora remain small and are not designed for codec-frame-level full-duplex modeling, while existing long-audio benchmarks focus on passive listening and speech-to-speech benchmarks are mostly short and dyadic. We extend the Moshi paradigm jointly along the long-horizon and multi-party axes in English and Chinese. First, we release 57.6k hours of synthetic training data ($\href{https://huggingface.co/datasets/MultiTalk/MultiTalkPT}{MultiTalkPT}$ and $\href{https://huggingface.co/datasets/MultiTalk/MultiTalkFT}{MultiTalkFT}$) for long-form, multi-party, English-Chinese full-duplex dialogue, with controllable length, participant count, turn-taking, overlap, backchannels, interruptions, addressee shifts, and long-range coreference. Second, we introduce $\href{https://huggingface.co/datasets/MultiTalk/MultiTalkBench}{MultiTalkBench}$, built from real human recordings, for evaluating long-form, multi-party, bilingual full-duplex dialogue. Conversations average 32.6 minutes and include probes for long-range entity tracking, topic coherence, and addressee selection. Third, we train a bilingual Moshi-style model that sustains coherent multi-party English-Chinese conversations over extended durations and substantially outperforms open-source baselines including Moshi, MiniCPM-o-4.5, and Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B-Instruct on MultiTalkBench.

AI.tldr: They propose and evaluate a bilingual, long-context, multi-party, full-duplex speech dialogue system, enabled by new large synthetic datasets and a real-audio benchmark, achieving strong performance over baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing end-to-end full-duplex speech models are typically limited to short, two-party (dyadic) interactions and struggle with long-context understanding and realistic multi-speaker scenarios such as meetings or group lessons. There is also a lack of suitable large-scale training data and challenging benchmarks specifically designed for codec-frame-level, long-horizon, multi-party, bilingual speech dialogue, which hinders progress.
AI.method: 1) Construct 57.6k hours of synthetic English-Chinese multi-party full-duplex dialogue data (MultiTalkPT and MultiTalkFT) with fine-grained control over conversation parameters such as length, number of participants, overlap, backchannels, interruptions, addressee shifts, and long-range coreference; 2) Build MultiTalkBench from real human recordings, containing ~32.6-minute bilingual multi-party conversations with targeted probes for entity tracking, topic coherence, and addressee selection; 3) Train a bilingual Moshi-style end-to-end model on these datasets for long-form, multi-party, full-duplex English-Chinese speech dialogue; and 4) Evaluate this model on MultiTalkBench against open-source baselines.
AI.result: The trained bilingual Moshi-style model can sustain coherent, long-duration, multi-party English-Chinese conversations and achieves substantially better performance on MultiTalkBench compared to strong open-source full-duplex baselines, including Moshi, MiniCPM-o-4.5, and Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B-Instruct.
AI.conclusion: Rich synthetic training data plus a realistic benchmark tailored to long-horizon, multi-party, bilingual full-duplex speech enables building models that significantly improve coherence and interaction quality in complex conversational settings. Their approach successfully scales the Moshi paradigm to multi-party, long-context English-Chinese dialogue and sets a stronger open baseline for future research in multi-party spoken interaction.

title: JudgeProfile: Understanding and Steering Subjectivity in LLM Judges
summary: LLM judges are inherently subjective, often favoring different responses in pairwise comparison when neither option is objectively wrong. To study this subjectivity, we introduce JudgeProfile, a framework that dissects LLM evaluation into perception (how a judge compares two responses across specific attributes like clarity, correctness, and detail) and prioritization (how much each attribute influences the final choice). We curate SubjectiveSet, a dataset of 50,013 response pairs from 17 public data sources, evaluated by 21 LLM judges across 87 attributes. We find a hidden consensus in perception: judges frequently agree on attribute judgments even when their overall choices diverge. Building on this separation, we first characterize each judge's prioritization using attribute weights estimated from its own overall choices. These weights differ across judges even when estimated from the same attribute judgments. We then learn new weights from reference labels to adapt their decisions to a target evaluation standard. Reweighting perceived attributes improves average held-out agreement with reference labels from 66.48% to 71.97%, outperforming fine-tuning and rubric prompting. Our findings show that understanding and steering the subjectivity of LLM judges requires attention not only to what they perceive, but also to how they prioritize it.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes why large language model (LLM) judges disagree on pairwise evaluation and proposes a framework that separates what they perceive in responses from how they prioritize different evaluation attributes, enabling better alignment to a target standard by reweighting attributes.
AI.motivation: LLM judges are widely used to automatically evaluate other models’ outputs, but they can be inconsistent and subjective, especially when multiple reasonable answers exist. Existing methods often treat a judge’s decision as a black box or focus only on prompting or fine-tuning, without disentangling why judges disagree. The authors aim to understand whether disagreements stem from differences in what judges notice in responses (perception) or from how they value different aspects (prioritization), and to see if this structure can be exploited to make judgments more consistent and better aligned with human or reference standards.
AI.method: The authors propose JudgeProfile, which decomposes LLM judging into two components: (1) perception, where each judge assesses pairwise responses along many explicit attributes (e.g., clarity, correctness, detail); and (2) prioritization, where a set of learned weights over these attributes is used to predict the final preference. They build SubjectiveSet, a large dataset of 50,013 response pairs collected from 17 public benchmarks. Each pair is evaluated by 21 LLM judges along 87 attributes, plus an overall preference. They first analyze agreement in attribute-level perceptions versus final choices. Then they estimate each judge’s attribute weights from its own overall choices, and separately learn new weights from external reference labels to adapt a judge’s decisions to a desired evaluation standard. They compare reweighting-based adaptation to fine-tuning and rubric-style prompting for improving agreement with reference labels.
AI.result: Empirically, the authors find that LLM judges often agree on attribute-level perceptions (e.g., which answer is more detailed or clearer) even when their final pairwise preferences differ, revealing a substantial shared perception. However, the inferred attribute weights—i.e., prioritization—vary notably across judges, including when they share the same perceived attributes. By reweighting the perceived attributes using weights learned from reference labels, they increase held-out agreement with reference decisions from 66.48% to 71.97%. This reweighting method outperforms both fine-tuning the judge models and using rubric prompting, indicating that explicitly modeling and adjusting prioritization is an effective way to steer judge behavior.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that much of the subjectivity in LLM judges comes less from what they perceive in candidate responses and more from how they prioritize different evaluation attributes. By separating perception from prioritization and learning attribute weights aligned to a target standard, one can systematically adjust judges’ preferences without retraining their perception abilities. This structured approach yields more consistent and aligned evaluations than common alternatives like fine-tuning or rubric prompts, and suggests that future work on LLM-based evaluation should explicitly model and control prioritization to manage subjectivity.

title: BaLEEN: Biasing with Latent Encoded Entities for Context-Aware ASR
summary: Transcribing domain-specific entities and rare proper nouns remains a major challenge in automatic speech recognition (ASR). In this paper, we propose BaLEEN (Biasing with Latent Encoded Entities), a lightweight, hypernetwork-based framework for dynamic contextual adaptation without fine-tuning the underlying ASR model. BaLEEN encodes variable-length contextual keywords using a pretrained language model, compresses them into a fixed sequence of latent vectors via a Perceiver bottleneck, and injects context-dependent bias vectors directly into the intermediate encoder representations of the ASR model. Because both the language model and the backbone ASR model remain entirely frozen during training, BaLEEN operates as a plug-and-play adapter that incurs zero computational overhead at inference time when context biases are precomputed. We evaluate our method on a CTC-based ASR model using a Wikipedia-derived corpus with annotated named entities and synthetic speech. Experimental results demonstrate that BaLEEN reduces keyword miss rate by 8.7% on the test set relative to the unbiased baseline while simultaneously improving overall word error rate by 21% and character error rate by 28%.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces BaLEEN, a plug-and-play hypernetwork that uses contextual keywords to improve recognition of rare and domain-specific entities in ASR without retraining the base model.
AI.motivation: Standard ASR systems struggle with domain-specific terms and rare proper nouns, especially when they are not well represented in training data. Existing contextual biasing methods often require modifying or fine-tuning the ASR model, add inference-time overhead, or do not generalize well to variable-length context lists. The authors aim to design a lightweight, dynamic contextual adaptation mechanism that can improve recognition of such entities without retraining or slowing down the ASR model.
AI.method: BaLEEN uses a pretrained language model to encode variable-length contextual keyword lists, then compresses these encodings into a fixed sequence of latent vectors via a Perceiver-style bottleneck. A hypernetwork then produces context-dependent bias vectors that are injected into intermediate encoder representations of a CTC-based ASR model. Both the ASR backbone and the language model are kept frozen; only the BaLEEN adapter is trained. Context biases can be precomputed so that, at inference time, the ASR model runs with essentially no additional computational cost.
AI.result: On a Wikipedia-derived corpus with annotated named entities and synthetic speech, BaLEEN reduces keyword miss rate by 8.7% compared to an unbiased baseline and also improves overall recognition quality, achieving a 21% relative reduction in word error rate and a 28% relative reduction in character error rate.
AI.conclusion: The proposed BaLEEN framework enables effective, dynamic contextual biasing for ASR as a plug-and-play module that does not require fine-tuning the underlying ASR system and adds no runtime cost when biases are precomputed. The gains in keyword detection and global WER/CER demonstrate that contextual adapters can improve both entity recognition and overall transcription quality in CTC-based ASR.

title: Can AI Scientists Change Their Minds? Prior-Evidence Conflict in Synthetic Universes
summary: Can a scientific agent distinguish a law it inferred from evidence from one it merely recognizes? We introduce Synthetic Universes, a controlled benchmark that pairs canonical famous worlds with matched twisted twins governed by nearby noncanonical mechanisms. We evaluate each reported law twice: by executing it on held-out continuations and transfer settings, and by independently checking whether it recovers the generating mechanism. In the current checkpoint of a pre-specified 60-cell study, 22 trials were graded and one additional run ended in infrastructure failure. Among 20 twin trials, 8 pass predictive verification while 5 recover the generator. The dissociation is bidirectional: six parsable outputs predict successfully while missing the mechanism, whereas three recover the mechanism but fail predictive rollout. Drag exhibits the first pattern (5/5 predictive pass, 1/5 mechanism recovery); Gravity exhibits the second (1/5 predictive pass, 4/5 mechanism recovery). Because matched famous controls, the corrected identifiability sweep, and the Evidence Ladder remain incomplete, we do not claim a confirmatory causal prior-conflict effect. Instead, the completed runs establish a narrower verification result: predictive adequacy and mechanism recovery are distinct scientific claims and require distinct tests.

AI.tldr: The paper studies whether a scientific AI can tell apart genuinely inferred laws from merely recognized ones, using controlled synthetic environments with paired canonical and slightly altered ‘twin’ worlds.
AI.motivation: To understand if a scientific agent that discovers laws from data is actually inferring the underlying mechanisms or just pattern-matching to familiar laws, and to design a benchmark that can separate these abilities.
AI.method: The authors create ‘Synthetic Universes’: paired canonical famous physical worlds and closely related ‘twisted twin’ worlds with modified governing rules. For each hypothesized law the agent produces, they evaluate it twice: (1) predictive performance on held‑out continuations and transfer scenarios, and (2) whether the inferred law correctly recovers the true generative mechanism. They run a multi‑cell study (60 planned), reporting interim results from 22 graded trials and one failed run.
AI.result: Out of 20 ‘twin’ world trials, 8 pass the predictive evaluation and 5 correctly identify the generator. There is a bidirectional dissociation: some laws predict well but miss the mechanism, while others recover the mechanism but do not predict well. For drag, all 5 runs pass prediction but only 1/5 recovers the mechanism; for gravity, 4/5 recover the mechanism but only 1/5 passes predictive tests.
AI.conclusion: Predictive adequacy and correct mechanism recovery are distinct capabilities in scientific inference and must be evaluated with different tests. Current data are insufficient to make strong claims about causal effects of prior conflicts, but they establish that being able to predict does not guarantee having inferred the true underlying law, and vice versa.

title: Can Language Models Learn to Forecast Stock Prices
summary: Post-training has been shown to significantly improve language models' performance on tasks with verifiable outcomes, including mathematical reasoning, software engineering, and computer use. However, whether the same approach can improve forecasting in financial markets is much less clear. Compared with tasks with verifiable outcomes, not only are realized returns noisy, but even what constitutes a relevant information set for making effective predictions is not obvious a priori: the model must decide which observations to gather and then commit to a numerical judgment before the outcome is known. We study this question in a chronological stock-price sandbox, where a language model gathers price, volume, relative-performance, and market-context evidence and predicts a future return. We post-train Qwen3-4B with supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on tool-use demonstrations, then proximal policy optimization (PPO) with a terminal reward given by the forecast score against the realized return. The resulting AURA-4B more than doubles the starting direction--magnitude score, from 20.94 to 43.31, and is comparable to frontier language models on this benchmark. Conditional magnitude agreement rises from 33.3 to 66.2, while directional accuracy changes from 62.9 to 65.4. SFT expands tool use, and PPO further increases the share of ranking and market-context queries. These results show that post-training can substantially improve financial forecasting performance, together with changes in how the model investigates the market, on this outcome-selected benchmark.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates whether post-training methods that improve language models in verifiable domains (like math or coding) can also enhance financial market forecasting, showing substantial gains on a chronological stock-price benchmark.
AI.motivation: While post-training (SFT, RL) has greatly improved language models on tasks with clear, verifiable outcomes, it is unclear if similar gains are possible for financial forecasting, where outcomes are noisy and relevant information is not obvious. The authors want to understand if and how post-training can improve a model’s ability to gather market data via tools and make better stock return predictions over time.
AI.method: The authors use a chronological stock-price sandbox in which a language model can call tools to gather information such as price, volume, relative performance, and broader market context, then output a numerical prediction of future returns. They start from Qwen3-4B and apply supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on tool-use demonstrations to teach effective querying, followed by reinforcement learning with proximal policy optimization (PPO), where the reward is based on how well the forecast matches the realized return. They then measure forecast quality and analyze the pattern of tool use before and after post-training.
AI.result: The post-trained model, AURA-4B, more than doubles the direction–magnitude forecast score from 20.94 to 43.31, reaching performance comparable to much larger frontier language models on the benchmark. Conditional magnitude agreement increases markedly from 33.3 to 66.2, and directional accuracy improves modestly from 62.9 to 65.4. Tool usage becomes richer: SFT increases tool calling overall, and PPO further raises the proportion of ranking and market-context queries used in forming predictions.
AI.conclusion: Post-training with SFT plus PPO meaningfully improves a 4B-parameter model’s financial forecasting performance in a controlled chronological stock sandbox, both in terms of accuracy metrics and the sophistication of its information-gathering behavior. This suggests that reinforcement learning on outcome-based rewards can train language models to conduct more effective tool-driven market investigations and produce better forecasts, even in noisy, partially defined tasks like stock return prediction.

title: Can Agents Design Libraries for Agents?
comment: 26 pages, 6 figures, 11 tables. Code and data: https://github.com/SprocketLab/librarydesignbench
summary: Agents increasingly build on code written by other agents, and they reimplement rather than reuse, growing the codebases later agents must work in. To measure how well agents design libraries for other agents, we introduce LibraryDesignBench, a two-phase benchmark in which an agent implements a full-featured library from a specification that defines required capabilities and potential use cases without prescribing the design. We evaluate the library through the correctness and simplicity of programs written by three user agents from different model families. The benchmark spans 242 expert-validated programming problems across 15 library-design tasks in four languages. On eleven of the fifteen tasks, agent designers reproduce the abstractions of the human-written production library. Downstream agents adopt agent- and human-written libraries alike but underuse them, reimplementing capabilities the library already provides. Our failure analysis finds that downstream agents write extra code mainly because agent-written libraries are rigid or hard to use, not because capabilities are missing. We also experiment with giving designers more prescriptive, agent-first guidance and having them test their library with subagents; this improves downstream scores and yields simpler programs. LibraryDesignBench provides both a testbed for evaluating library-design practices for agent users and an initial design baseline that improves downstream reuse.

AI.tldr: Introduces LibraryDesignBench, a benchmark to evaluate how well AI agents design reusable code libraries for other agents, finding that current agents often create rigid, hard-to-use libraries that lead to unnecessary reimplementation, and showing that agent-first guidance and subagent testing improves reuse.
AI.motivation: As multi-agent coding systems grow, agents frequently build on code produced by previous agents. However, instead of reusing existing functionality, they tend to reimplement capabilities, causing codebases to expand unnecessarily and become harder to manage. There is a lack of systematic evaluation of how effectively agents design libraries intended to be used by other agents. The paper aims to diagnose and improve library design practices for AI agents so that downstream agents can better reuse abstractions, leading to more maintainable and efficient collaborative codebases.
AI.method: The authors propose LibraryDesignBench, a two-phase benchmark. In phase one, a designer agent implements a full-featured library based on a specification that lists required capabilities and potential use cases but does not prescribe an API or design. In phase two, three downstream user agents from different model families are tasked with solving programming problems using the designed library. The benchmark covers 242 expert-validated problems across 15 library-design tasks in four programming languages. Library quality is evaluated by: (1) whether agents independently rediscover abstractions found in human-written production libraries, and (2) how correct and simple the downstream agent solutions are, including the extent of code reuse versus reimplementation. The authors also run variants where designers receive more prescriptive, agent-first guidance and/or test their libraries with subagents before finalizing them.
AI.result: On 11 out of 15 tasks, designer agents produce libraries whose abstractions are similar to those found in human-written production libraries, indicating some capacity for good API design. Downstream user agents are generally willing to adopt both agent- and human-designed libraries; however, they frequently underuse them, writing extra code to reimplement capabilities that the library already provides. The analysis reveals that this is largely due to agent-written libraries being overly rigid or hard to use, as opposed to lacking necessary functionality. When designer agents are given more prescriptive, agent-first design guidance and allowed to test their libraries with subagents, downstream agent solutions achieve higher correctness scores and become simpler, with better reuse of library functionality.
AI.conclusion: LibraryDesignBench offers a structured benchmark to study and improve how agents design code libraries for other agents. The findings show that while agents can replicate human-level abstractions in many cases, usability and flexibility issues lead downstream agents to reimplement rather than reuse existing functionality. Providing agent-first design instructions and enabling iterative testing with subagents measurably improves downstream performance and code simplicity. The benchmark thus serves both as an evaluation framework for multi-agent library design and as an initial baseline that promotes better reuse and more effective agent-to-agent collaboration in codebases.

title: Benchmarking Automatic Speech Recognition Tools for Iberian Languages
summary: Comprehensive evaluations of automatic speech recognition (ASR) for Iberian languages remain limited, and low-resource languages, biases, and efficiency trade-offs are underexplored. We benchmark eleven systems, ten open-weight models and one commercial API, across five Iberian languages (Basque, Catalan, Galician, Portuguese, Spanish), with German and Turkish as controls. Evaluation uses an 85-hour dataset covering read speech, broadcast media, and audiobooks, assessing accuracy and efficiency via word error rate (WER) and real-time factors (RTF/RTFx). Results show no single model dominates: accuracy, efficiency, and language coverage present clear trade-offs. Low-resource languages, especially Basque, degrade significantly, highlighting the role of training coverage. We observe consistent sex disparities across most systems, highlighting fairness challenges in multilingual ASR. Overall, the benchmark provides practical guidance for real-world model selection.

AI.tldr: The paper benchmarks 11 ASR systems on 5 Iberian languages (plus 2 control languages), showing trade-offs between accuracy, efficiency, and language coverage, with notable weaknesses for low-resource languages and fairness issues across sexes.
AI.motivation: There is a lack of comprehensive, comparative evaluations of ASR systems for Iberian languages, particularly regarding low-resource languages, potential biases, and computational efficiency. Practitioners lack guidance on which models work best in realistic, multilingual scenarios and under different resource constraints.
AI.method: The authors evaluate 11 ASR systems (10 open-weight, 1 commercial API) on an 85-hour multilingual dataset spanning Basque, Catalan, Galician, Portuguese, and Spanish, with German and Turkish as controls. Speech styles include read speech, broadcast media, and audiobooks. They compute word error rate (WER) for accuracy and real-time factors (RTF/RTFx) for efficiency, and analyze performance by language and speaker sex to investigate trade-offs and fairness issues.
AI.result: No single ASR model is best across all metrics: systems differ in accuracy, speed, and language coverage. Performance drops markedly for low-resource Iberian languages—especially Basque—implicating limited training data and coverage. The analysis reveals consistent sex-related performance disparities across most models, indicating fairness concerns.
AI.conclusion: ASR model choice for Iberian languages must be application-specific, balancing accuracy, efficiency, and language support rather than relying on a single dominant model. Training coverage is crucial for low-resource languages, and sex-based performance gaps show that fairness needs to be addressed in multilingual ASR. The benchmark serves as a practical reference to guide model selection in real-world deployments.

title: BiFE: Search-Efficient Discovery of CPU-Only Branching Policies via LLM-based Bi-Fidelity Evolution
summary: In branch-and-bound (B&B) for mixed-integer linear programming (MILP), branching variable selection critically impacts efficiency. Existing neural branching policies often require GPU inference, while CPU-efficient symbolic expressions lack the representational capacity for complex logic. Large Language Model (LLM)-generated code provides a flexible search space for designing lightweight branching rules with diverse algorithmic logic. To discover effective rules within LLM-based evolutionary frameworks, a core challenge arises: full B&B evaluation on real instances is prohibitively expensive, whereas offline imitation learning suffers from distribution shift. To address this, we introduce a Bi-Fidelity Evolutionary framework (BiFE). It employs low-fidelity imitation scores as a rapid pre-screener and selectively applies high-fidelity on-instance evaluation only to elite candidates, effectively balancing search efficiency with performance reliability. Experiments validate both the search efficiency of BiFE and the competitiveness of its discovered rules, which outperform the SCIP solver and other baselines on CPUs, and even surpass certain GPU-based neural policies.

AI.tldr: They design an efficient evolutionary search framework (BiFE) that uses LLM-generated branching rules and combined low-/high-fidelity evaluation to find CPU-efficient branching strategies for MILP that beat standard solvers and some GPU-based neural methods.
AI.motivation: Branching decisions in branch-and-bound for MILP strongly affect performance. Powerful neural branching policies often need GPUs at inference time, which is impractical in many real deployments, while hand-crafted or symbolic rules that run efficiently on CPUs lack the expressiveness to encode rich algorithmic logic. Using LLMs to generate code for branching rules creates a large, flexible search space of lightweight, CPU-friendly strategies, but systematically finding strong rules is hard: evaluating each candidate by running full B&B on real problem instances is extremely expensive, and purely offline imitation learning from expert data generalizes poorly due to distribution shift between training and search-time policies.
AI.method: They propose BiFE (Bi-Fidelity Evolutionary framework). First, they use large language models to generate candidate branching rules as code, providing a rich, flexible policy space. Then they run an evolutionary search where each candidate is evaluated in two stages: (1) a low-fidelity imitation score that quickly estimates quality by how well the candidate mimics strong reference behavior, serving as a cheap pre-screening filter; (2) a high-fidelity evaluation via actual on-instance B&B runs applied only to the top-ranked (elite) candidates from stage (1). This bi-fidelity evaluation balances computational cost and reliability, enabling efficient exploration and refinement of candidate branching rules over evolutionary iterations.
AI.result: BiFE efficiently searches the space of LLM-generated branching rules and discovers policies that, when run on CPUs, outperform the SCIP solver’s default branching and other baseline methods. The learned rules also exceed the performance of some existing GPU-based neural branching policies, showing that carefully searched, LLM-generated symbolic rules can be both computationally cheap and highly effective.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates that LLM-generated code, combined with a bi-fidelity evolutionary search strategy, can yield high-quality, CPU-efficient branching rules for MILP. BiFE mitigates the cost and distribution-shift issues of standard evaluation or imitation-learning approaches, and the resulting rules achieve state-of-the-art or competitive performance without requiring GPU-based neural inference, suggesting a promising direction for integrating LLMs and evolutionary search in combinatorial optimization algorithms.

title: Dating the Model: Hidden Dates in System Prompts Affect LLM Evaluation
summary: Reproducibility is essential for scientific research, yet prior work shows that LLM outputs vary with hardware and batching. We identify an overlooked factor: the hidden injection of the current date into system prompts, which users cannot control and which changes every day. Across 9 recent LLMs and 6 datasets spanning multiple-choice QA (MCQA), math reasoning, code generation, and machine translation, performance varies solely with the current date, with deltas of up to 6% on MCQA, 14% on math reasoning, 7% on code generation, and 2.84 BLEU on machine translation. Model rankings also shift, affecting leaderboards. This date effect exceeds other sources of non-determinism, such as batch size and numerical precision. Standard prompting techniques -- chain-of-thought and few-shot prompting -- do not reduce the sensitivity; chain-of-thought even amplifies it. Our findings underscore the need for careful evaluation protocols to ensure reproducibility and fair comparisons in LLM research.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that hidden, automatically injected dates in LLM system prompts cause sizable, day-to-day performance fluctuations and ranking changes across models and tasks, threatening reproducibility and fairness in evaluation.
AI.motivation: Reproducible evaluation is central to scientific progress, but existing studies have mainly focused on hardware, batching, and numerical issues as sources of nondeterminism in LLM outputs. The authors are motivated by the observation that many LLM deployments silently inject the current date into system prompts, something users neither see nor control. They aim to test whether this subtle design choice alone can systematically alter performance and model rankings, which would undermine the reliability of benchmarks and leaderboards.
AI.method: The authors empirically evaluate 9 recent LLMs on 6 datasets covering multiple-choice QA, math reasoning, code generation, and machine translation. They hold everything constant except for the injected current date in the system prompt, varying only the date across runs. They compare performance across dates, measure the magnitude of performance deltas on each task, and observe how model rankings change. They also test whether standard prompting strategies such as chain-of-thought and few-shot prompting mitigate or exacerbate date sensitivity, and compare the date effect with known nondeterminism sources like batch size and numerical precision.
AI.result: They find that model performance changes solely as a function of the current date string injected into the system prompt, even when all other conditions are fixed. The observed differences are substantial: up to 6% in MCQA accuracy, 14% in math reasoning, 7% in code generation, and 2.84 BLEU in machine translation. These variations are large enough to reorder model rankings, directly impacting leaderboards. Furthermore, the date effect is larger than other known nondeterminism factors such as batching and numerical precision, and chain-of-thought prompting actually amplifies the sensitivity rather than reducing it.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that hidden date injection into system prompts is a major, previously underappreciated source of evaluation instability for LLMs. Because this factor can significantly affect absolute performance and relative model rankings, the authors argue that current benchmarking and leaderboard practices may yield misleading comparisons unless they control for or report date conditions. They call for stricter, more transparent evaluation protocols that either remove or standardize such hidden prompt components to ensure reproducible and fair LLM research.

title: Distinguish or Homogenize: Last-Chance Policy Identification and Risk-Budgeted Recovery under Irreversible Resource Depletion
summary: Under irreversible resource depletion, an agent can spend resources to distinguish among latent fault models, or to change the system state so that the remaining models admit a common acceptable continuation--at which point further diagnosis becomes unnecessary. This distinguish-or-homogenize principle identifies a path that existing frameworks for identification, planning, and diagnosis do not make explicit: prior formulations treat the mapping from fault models to acceptable policies as a given, whereas LCPI makes it a function of the agent's own actions. We formalize this principle through Last-Chance Policy Identification (LCPI), where correctness is evaluated at the state the agent reaches rather than at the initial state. The Last Identifiable Margin (LIM) marks the feasibility boundary between distinguishing and homogenizing. For deterministic diagnostic graphs we provide the Exact-LIM recursion; for noisy finite-horizon recovery we propose Risk-Budgeted Compatibility Planning (RBCP), which searches a compatibility-aware frontier under a hard worst-case failure constraint. Across incident recovery on abstract microservice topologies and latent-damage navigation in MiniGrid, RBCP improves risk-feasible recovery while satisfying the failure budget. A sham control--cost-matched actions that preserve model incompatibility--eliminates the gain entirely, confirming that the benefit comes from changing which policies are acceptable for which models, not from extra search or additional budget.

AI.tldr: Paper introduces Last-Chance Policy Identification (LCPI), where an agent either uses resources to distinguish fault models or to drive the system into states where all remaining models share at least one acceptable policy, making further diagnosis unnecessary.
AI.motivation: Existing planning/diagnosis frameworks assume a fixed mapping from fault models to acceptable policies, thus focusing only on better identification or planning under a given model set. However, in irreversible or resource-limited settings, the agent’s own actions can change which policies are acceptable under which models by moving the system to states where the remaining models become behaviorally compatible. The authors want a framework that explicitly optimizes over this distinguish-or-homogenize tradeoff, especially under risk/failure constraints.
AI.method: They formalize the distinguish-or-homogenize principle as Last-Chance Policy Identification (LCPI), where policy correctness is evaluated at the state ultimately reached, not only at the initial state.
