They define the Last Identifiable Margin (LIM) as the boundary between states where one can still distinguish models and those where one must homogenize. For deterministic diagnostic graphs, they derive an Exact-LIM dynamic recursion. For noisy, finite-horizon recovery problems, they propose Risk-Budgeted Compatibility Planning (RBCP), which searches a frontier of states accounting for model compatibility while enforcing a strict worst-case failure budget.
AI.result: On abstract microservice incident-recovery tasks and latent-damage navigation tasks in MiniGrid, RBCP finds recovery strategies that respect a hard worst-case failure budget while improving achievable performance (risk-feasible recovery) compared to baselines that do not exploit compatibility shaping. A sham-control experiment, where actions are cost-matched but constrained to preserve model incompatibility, removes the performance gains, indicating that the improvement stems from changing model-policy compatibility, not from more computation or relaxed constraints.
AI.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that explicitly planning to either distinguish fault models or homogenize them by driving the system into compatibility regions leads to better, risk-feasible recovery strategies under irreversible resource use. LCPI and RBCP show that letting the mapping from models to acceptable policies depend on the agent’s actions is beneficial and practically exploitable, and that the gains are due to compatibility shaping rather than additional search or budget.

title: ER-JEPA: Experience Replay Improves Joint-Embedding Predictive Learning in Language Models
summary: Large language models (LLMs) excel at token-level generation but may learn undesirable abstract semantics and lack comprehensive perception. LLM-JEPA mitigates this by aligning different views of the same underlying knowledge via a joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA). However, strong alignment does not necessarily lead to accurate, stable predictions. To address this, we propose ER-JEPA, which adds an episodic replay path to LLM-JEPA. ER-JEPA stores training pairs in a memory. At each step, it stores and retrieves relevant data to provide additional supervision. This enables learning from both the current batch and stored training pairs, providing additional supervision for token prediction and representation alignment. Experiments across multiple datasets (NL-RX, GSM8K, Spider, and NQ-Open) demonstrate that ER-JEPA consistently outperforms LLM-JEPA.

AI.tldr: ER-JEPA augments LLM-JEPA with an episodic replay memory that reuses stored training pairs during learning, improving token prediction and representation alignment, and outperforming LLM-JEPA on several NLP benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Although LLM-JEPA aligns multiple views of the same underlying knowledge using a JEPA architecture, strong representation alignment alone does not guarantee accurate or stable predictions. There is a need to better exploit past training experiences so that language models can benefit from richer supervision beyond the current mini-batch and mitigate issues such as unstable learning or incomplete utilization of prior data.
AI.method: The authors propose ER-JEPA, which extends LLM-JEPA with an episodic replay mechanism. During training, ER-JEPA stores input–output training pairs in an external memory. At each learning step, it retrieves relevant stored examples and incorporates them into training alongside the current batch. This episodic replay path provides extra supervision signals for both token-level prediction and the JEPA-based representation alignment between different views of the same knowledge.
AI.result: On multiple benchmarks (NL-RX, GSM8K, Spider, and NQ-Open), ER-JEPA yields consistently better performance than the baseline LLM-JEPA. The improvements suggest that episodic replay enhances both prediction quality and the stability/effectiveness of representation learning within the JEPA framework.
AI.conclusion: Integrating an episodic replay memory into a JEPA-based LLM framework enables the model to learn from both present and past examples in a unified way, strengthening token prediction and representation alignment. This design leads to more accurate and stable behavior than LLM-JEPA alone, as evidenced by consistent gains across diverse NLP tasks.

title: SIPO: Unifying Reinforcement Learning with On-Policy Self-Distillation
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become a standard paradigm for improving large language models (LLMs) on various tasks, yet its sparse outcome rewards lack token-level credit assignment for intermediate steps. To address this, on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) leverages a self-teacher with privileged context to provide additional dense learning signals. However, because the self-teacher is often overconfident and imposes excessive penalties on long reasoning trajectories, OPSD frequently struggles in practice. To mitigate this, we propose self-instructing policy optimization (SIPO) with a contrastive self-teacher to provide dense credit. At each iteration, SIPO samples multiple rollouts per prompt from the current policy, scores them with environment rewards, and constructs two teacher contexts for each rollout by pairing the reference answer with mistakes made within the group. The model then re-evaluates its own responses under both contexts, using the difference between the two teacher log-probabilities as token-level feedback, so that biases shared by both contexts are expected to largely cancel. The resulting objective yields a token-level advantage for every rollout: the reward still sets the main direction of each update while the self-teacher redistributes credit across tokens. Even in groups where every rollout fails and group-relative advantages vanish, SIPO still provides a learning signal. By preserving direct optimization of the task reward while providing dense, token-level feedback, this approach bridges reinforcement learning and on-policy self-distillation. Extensive experiments across multiple reasoning and code-generation benchmarks demonstrate that SIPO outperforms both RLVR and OPSD baselines without an external teacher or additional generation.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Self-Instructing Policy Optimization (SIPO), a new method that combines reinforcement learning with on-policy self-distillation to provide dense, token-level credit assignment for large language models, improving reasoning and code generation performance over existing methods.
AI.motivation: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is effective for training LLMs but only provides sparse, outcome-level rewards, making it hard to assign credit to specific tokens or intermediate reasoning steps. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) adds dense feedback via a self-teacher with more context, but in practice the self-teacher tends to be overconfident and penalize long reasoning chains too harshly, limiting its usefulness. There is a need for a method that preserves direct optimization of task rewards while still offering reliable token-level feedback without depending on external teachers or heavy extra computation.
AI.method: The authors introduce Self-Instructing Policy Optimization (SIPO). For each training prompt, SIPO samples multiple rollouts (candidate answers) from the current policy and scores them with environment (task) rewards. For every rollout, SIPO then constructs two "teacher" contexts by combining the reference answer with sampled within-group mistakes, producing a contrastive pair. The model re-evaluates its own rollout under both teacher contexts and computes the difference between the two log-probabilities at each token. This log-probability difference acts as token-level feedback (a token-wise advantage), with shared biases between the two contexts largely canceling out. The overall objective still follows the direction given by the scalar reward but uses the contrastive self-teacher signal to redistribute credit across tokens and steps, even when all rollouts in a group fail.
AI.result: Across several reasoning and code-generation benchmarks, SIPO consistently outperforms both standard RLVR and OPSD baselines. It achieves these gains without needing any external teacher models or additional generations beyond the existing on-policy rollouts, showing that the contrastive self-instruction mechanism is an efficient and effective way to improve token-level credit assignment and downstream task performance.
AI.conclusion: SIPO effectively bridges the gap between reinforcement learning with sparse rewards and dense, token-level self-distillation. By using a contrastive self-teacher built from within-batch successes and errors, it provides stable, informative token-level advantages while preserving direct optimization of the main task reward. This leads to better performance on complex reasoning and code-generation tasks than prior RLVR and OPSD methods, demonstrating that carefully designed self-instruction can substitute for external teachers and improve RL-based LLM training.

title: Chinese-Jev: Bringing System One Model to Chinese-Language Tasks
summary: System One models such as Jev offer an efficient alternative to generative language models for tasks that require decisions rather than open-ended responses. However, existing Jev models exhibit limited Chinese-language decision accuracy, restricting their utility in both general and specialized settings. In this paper, we introduce Chinese-Jev, a System One model that addresses this gap through a unified data processing and training pipeline. Our data processing protocol converts heterogeneous Chinese-language annotations into probability targets over candidate options, enabling a shared training formulation across domains and question formats. To enable efficient inference, Chinese-Jev adopts a lightweight encoder-only backbone for text encoding and learns to score candidate answers through decision-oriented training. To address the misalignment between the pre-training distribution and downstream Chinese-language scenarios, we first train the model on a general-purpose corpus of 10 million examples, then fine-tune it separately for the medical, legal, and financial domains. To evaluate decision accuracy and calibration in both general and domain-specific Chinese-language settings, we introduce Chinese-Jev Bench (CJ-Bench). After first-stage pre-training, Chinese-Jev exceeds the accuracy of the closed-source Jev model by 1.24% on general-domain tasks while achieving a 20.3x speedup. Subsequent domain-specific fine-tuning yields a 4.0% accuracy improvement over Jev in medicine and achieves 92% of Jev's average accuracy across specialized domains, with a 17x speedup and an average latency of only 15 ms per example. We further demonstrate on-device deployment of an INT8-quantized model on mobile devices, achieving an inference latency of approximately 1.0 second per decision. The project is available at https://gulucaptain.github.io/Chinese-Jev/.

AI.tldr: The paper presents Chinese-Jev, a fast System One decision model for Chinese that improves accuracy and speed over existing Jev models, along with a new benchmark (CJ-Bench) and demonstrations of mobile deployment.
AI.motivation: Existing System One models like Jev are efficient for decision-making tasks but perform poorly for Chinese, limiting their usefulness in both general and domain-specific (medical, legal, financial) Chinese settings. There is also a lack of a unified way to process heterogeneous Chinese annotations and a need for systematic evaluation of Chinese decision accuracy and calibration.
AI.method: The authors design a unified data processing and training pipeline that converts varied Chinese annotations into probability targets over candidate options, allowing a single training formulation across domains and question formats. They use a lightweight encoder-only backbone for efficient text encoding and decision scoring. Training proceeds in two stages: (1) pre-train on a 10M-example general-purpose Chinese corpus to adapt from pre-training distributions; (2) fine-tune separate models for medicine, law, and finance. They also build CJ-Bench to evaluate decision accuracy and calibration, and test INT8 quantization for on-device deployment.
AI.result: After the first-stage pre-training, Chinese-Jev surpasses the closed-source Jev model by 1.24% accuracy on general Chinese tasks while being 20.3 times faster. Domain-specific fine-tuning yields a 4.0% accuracy gain over Jev in medicine and reaches 92% of Jev’s average accuracy across specialized domains, while maintaining a 17x speedup and about 15 ms latency per example. An INT8-quantized version runs on mobile devices with roughly 1 second latency per decision.
AI.conclusion: Chinese-Jev is an effective and highly efficient System One decision model for Chinese, achieving better or comparable accuracy to Jev while being much faster, especially after domain-specific fine-tuning. The unified training pipeline and CJ-Bench provide a foundation for developing and evaluating Chinese decision models, and the successful INT8 mobile deployment shows practical feasibility for on-device applications.

title: EASE: Behavior-Adaptive Skill Curation for Self-Evolving Agents
summary: Agent skills provide a lightweight mechanism for self-evolving agents to accumulate reusable procedural knowledge without updating model parameters. However, existing learned skill curators typically optimize curation without explicitly modeling downstream executor behavior. We show that this can cause systematic cross-executor degradation: curators trained with different executors perform best when paired with their own training executor, indicating that effective skill curation is executor-dependent. We formulate behavior-adaptive skill curation and introduce EASE, a framework that learns a single curator that adapts its decisions to different executor behaviors. EASE maintains an online behavioral profile of recent execution patterns and conditions the curator on this profile, the current trajectory, and retrieved skills to add, modify, or remove skills from an evolving repository. We train the shared curator jointly across multiple frozen executors with reinforcement learning, using retrieval-aware and behavior-aware temporal attribution to focus optimization on curation actions with observable downstream influence. Across ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, and WebShop, with executors ranging from Qwen3-8B/32B and GPT-OSS-120B to unseen Kimi K2.6, DeepSeek V4 Flash, and Gemini 3.5 Flash, EASE outperforms strong skill- and memory-based baselines without per-executor finetuning. EASE also maintains 34.5--41.0% fewer skills, improves skill retrieval by 36.3--38.7% and measured edit utility by 51.8--60.0%, and reduces deployment-time inference tokens by 9.1--14.5%. These results establish behavior-adaptive skill curation as an effective principle for building self-evolving agents.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces EASE, a behavior-adaptive skill curation framework that learns a single curator able to adapt skill management to different agent executors, improving performance and efficiency across multiple benchmarks without per-executor finetuning.
AI.motivation: Existing agent skill curation methods select and manage reusable skills without explicitly accounting for how different executors (LLM-based agents) actually use those skills. This leads to cross-executor degradation: a curator trained with one executor works best only with that same executor, limiting generality and robustness. The authors want a principled way to make skill curation adaptive to varying executor behaviors so agents can self-evolve more effectively and generalize across different models.
AI.method: The authors formalize behavior-adaptive skill curation and propose EASE, a unified curator trained with reinforcement learning across multiple frozen executors. EASE maintains an online behavioral profile summarizing recent execution patterns, and conditions the curator on this profile, the current trajectory, and retrieved skills. The curator then decides to add, modify, or delete skills in an evolving repository. Training uses retrieval-aware and behavior-aware temporal credit assignment so that only curation actions with observable downstream impact influence learning. The same curator is used across executors, relying on behavioral profiling instead of per-executor finetuning.
AI.result: On three benchmarks—ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, and WebShop—using diverse executors (Qwen3-8B/32B, GPT-OSS-120B, and unseen Kimi K2.6, DeepSeek V4 Flash, Gemini 3.5 Flash), EASE outperforms strong baselines based on skills and memory without requiring executor-specific finetuning. It achieves higher task success and quality metrics while maintaining 34.5–41.0% fewer skills, increasing skill retrieval quality by 36.3–38.7%, improving measured edit utility by 51.8–60.0%, and cutting deployment-time inference tokens by 9.1–14.5%.
AI.conclusion: Behavior-adaptive skill curation—where a curator conditions on observed executor behavior and is trained jointly across multiple executors—is an effective approach for building self-evolving agents. EASE demonstrates that a single adaptive curator can generalize across heterogeneous executors, improve task performance, streamline skill repositories, and reduce inference costs, establishing this paradigm as a promising direction for scalable, efficient agent evolution.

title: Repetition, Not Length: Isolating the Counting Failure in Neural Text-to-Speech
comment: Submitted to IEEE ICASSP 2027. Code and data: https://github.com/lab260ru/tts-counting-failure
summary: Text-to-speech models loop, truncate and lose count on text that repeats a phrase many times. We show that repetition itself is what breaks them, not the length that comes with it. Every repeated sentence in our test set is paired with a control of matched sentence and word count in which no word ever repeats back-to-back. Six models from three architectures render the controls almost perfectly and fail the repeated twins: 94.3% against 18.2% exactly right at k >= 6. The gap survives greedy decoding, repetition-penalty sweeps, four independent speech recognisers and 420 analysis specifications without once reversing sign; a held-out fourth architecture lands within a point of its predicted gap, and one of two non-autoregressive baselines shows the same failure. Varying the period of the text shows the failure grows smoothly with periodicity, half of it surviving when no word is adjacent to itself.

AI.tldr: Paper shows that text-to-speech (TTS) models systematically fail when input text is highly repetitive, even when length is controlled.
AI.motivation: Understand and isolate why modern TTS systems loop, truncate, or misrender inputs that contain many repetitions of the same phrase, which is a known but poorly understood failure mode.
AI.method: Construct paired test sets where each highly repetitive sentence is matched with a control sentence of equal length and word count but without immediate word repetitions. Evaluate six TTS models across three architectures plus additional baselines. Measure transcription accuracy using multiple ASR systems, test across decoding strategies and hyperparameters, and vary the repetition period to quantify how performance changes with periodicity.
AI.result: TTS models perform very well on the non-repetitive controls but dramatically worse on their repetitive counterparts (94.3% vs 18.2% exact correctness for k >= 6 repetitions). The performance gap is robust across greedy decoding, repetition penalties, four ASR evaluators, hundreds of analysis specs, and architectures; a held-out architecture matches the predicted gap, and one of two non-autoregressive baselines exhibits the same failure pattern. Increasing periodicity smoothly worsens performance, and the failure persists even when no word is immediately repeated, with about half the effect remaining.
AI.conclusion: Repetition itself, not just sequence length, is a core causal factor behind TTS failures on repetitive text. This phenomenon is consistent across architectures and settings and scales with periodicity, suggesting that TTS models have an inherent difficulty in faithfully rendering highly repetitive linguistic patterns.

title: Generalizable Lifelong Model Editing via Preference Optimization
summary: Knowledge editing enables rapid updates of specific factual knowledge in large language models (LLMs) without full retraining. However, more realistic scenarios call for a lifelong framework that handles continual updates rather than one-off modifications. In such settings, existing editing methods often overfit to target prompts, significantly degrading both the generalization of the edited knowledge and the model's general capabilities. To address this issue, we propose GLIME (Generalizable Lifelong Model Editing), which combines knowledge editing with preference optimization over generation behavior. GLIME further incorporates replay-based editing and a gradient constraint to preserve previously edited knowledge. Experimental results show that GLIME significantly improves knowledge generalization in lifelong editing settings while maintaining both editing performance and general capabilities.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces GLIME, a framework for lifelong knowledge editing in LLMs that maintains generalization and overall model abilities across many sequential edits.
AI.motivation: Existing knowledge editing methods usually assume one-off edits. In more realistic lifelong scenarios with continual updates, these methods overfit to specific prompts, hurting both the generalization of the new knowledge and the model’s general capabilities. The authors want a method that can perform many updates over time while keeping edits general and preserving previous knowledge and abilities.
AI.method: They propose GLIME (Generalizable Lifelong Model Editing), which integrates knowledge editing with preference optimization over the model’s generation behavior. GLIME also uses replay-based editing to rehearse past edits and adds a gradient constraint mechanism to avoid overwriting previously edited knowledge, aiming to achieve stable, generalizable edits over a sequence of updates.
AI.result: Experiments in lifelong editing setups show that GLIME increases the generalization of edited knowledge compared with baselines, while keeping high editing success rates and preserving the model’s general performance on unrelated tasks.
AI.conclusion: By combining editing with preference optimization, replay, and gradient constraints, GLIME offers a more robust lifelong editing framework for LLMs that supports many sequential factual updates without severe overfitting or loss of general capabilities.

title: AMU:Admission and Memory Update for Personalized Conversations---Structured Memory with SLM Guided Control
comment: 14 pages, 2 figures. Source code and implementation are available at: https://github.com/UnicusT11/AMU-memory
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have become the foundation of personalized assistants, but maintaining persistent user memory across long-term interactions remains challenging. Existing memory systems often focus on storage, retrieval, or consolidation, while memory writing remains less controlled: transient requests, duplicate statements, and outdated user states may enter memory and later be retrieved for personalization. In this paper, we present AMU: Admission and Memory Update for Personalized Conversations, an SLM-guided (Small language model guided) structured framework for writing-time memory control. AMU uses structured memory filtering to decide what should enter memory and SLM-guided storage management to determine whether an admitted record should be stored separately, discarded as a duplicate, or fused as an update. We evaluate AMU in a controlled memory writing and retrieval setting. Experimental results show that AMU maintains cleaner and more retrievable personalized memories.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes AMU, a framework to better control what user information is written into long‑term memory for personalized LLM assistants, resulting in cleaner and more useful memories.
AI.motivation: Personalized assistants powered by large language models need stable, long‑term user memories, but current systems mainly optimize how memories are stored, retrieved, or consolidated. The critical step of deciding what to write into memory is under‑controlled, allowing temporary, duplicate, or outdated user information to be stored, which later harms personalization quality. The authors want a principled, structured way to control memory at write time.
AI.method: They introduce AMU (Admission and Memory Update), a structured framework guided by a small language model (SLM). First, a structured memory filtering stage decides whether a piece of information from the conversation should be admitted into memory at all. Then, SLM‑guided storage management decides how to handle admitted records: store them as new entries, discard them as duplicates, or fuse them with existing entries as updates to the user profile. The framework is evaluated in a controlled environment for memory writing and retrieval.
AI.result: Experiments in this controlled setting show that AMU produces user memories that are both cleaner (less noisy, fewer duplicates and outdated facts) and more retrievable (relevant memories are easier for the system to find and use) compared to baselines.
AI.conclusion: Controlling memory at write time is crucial for effective long‑term personalization in LLM‑based assistants. AMU, via structured filtering and SLM‑guided update policies, improves the quality and usability of stored user memories, suggesting that explicit admission and update mechanisms are an important complement to existing work on memory storage and retrieval.

title: Emergent Specialization in Populations of Self-Supervised Collaborative Vision Experts Without a Shared Gate or Cross-Agent Gradients
summary: Can a population of neural networks develop a useful division of labor without a shared gate or gradients between agents? We study a setting where each network has its own weights, trains independently on the same heterogeneous data, and can ask another agent for help through a forward pass. Unlike mixtures of experts, where a jointly trained gate assigns inputs to experts, specialization here must emerge without central control. We test this in a small scale proxy for predictive visual pretraining. Initially identical agents are finetuned on an unlabeled mixture of six visual domains using masked prediction of frozen DINOv3 features. We measure specialization by asking whether the best agent for an input aligns with its latent domain, and utilization by asking whether responsibility is distributed across agents. We progressively remove central control, ending with DISCO (DIStributed COllaboration) where each agent locally selects a helper, reads its internal state through a gradient free channel, and rewards its router only for the improvement that help provides. Specialization emerges and is useful. Randomly routed populations underperform a single generalist, while semantically routed populations outperform it, showing that specialization rather than population size drives the gain. Specialization persists without a central router, and gradient free communication lets nonexperts exploit emergent expertise. In DISCO, a random agent helped by the expert matches the solo generalist, while experts surpass it, including on data outside the specialization mixture. Local routers select the emergent expert for 98% of inputs. These effects persist across population size, model capacity, data imbalance, and finetuning seeds, providing measurable evidence for the dynamics needed by decentralized predictive pretraining.

AI.tldr: The paper studies whether multiple independently trained neural networks can self-organize into specialized experts and collaborate effectively without any central controller or shared gradients, and finds that they can.
AI.motivation: Traditional mixture-of-experts systems rely on a centrally trained gating network and shared gradients, which may not reflect realistic decentralized or multi-agent learning scenarios and can be brittle or hard to scale. The authors want to understand if useful specialization and collaboration can emerge in a more decentralized setting where agents have separate parameters, train independently on heterogeneous data, and can only interact through limited, gradient-free communication. This is motivated by questions about scalable predictive pretraining, multi-agent systems, and potentially more brain-like or distributed learning dynamics.
AI.method: They build a small-scale proxy task for predictive visual pretraining. A population of initially identical neural networks is finetuned on an unlabeled mixture of six visual domains using a masked prediction objective on frozen DINOv3 visual features. Each agent has its own weights and trains independently. The authors progressively relax central control: starting from variants with more centralized routing and moving toward DISCO (DIStributed COllaboration), where each agent has a local router that can select another agent as a helper. The helper exposes part of its internal state via a gradient-free channel (a forward-pass-based readout), and the querying agent’s router is trained using only the performance improvement attributable to the help. They measure (1) specialization: whether the best-performing agent for a given input aligns with that input’s latent domain, and (2) utilization: how distributed responsibility for inputs is across agents. They compare against random routing baselines and a single generalist network, and test robustness across population size, capacity, data imbalance, and random seeds.
AI.result: They find that populations can develop meaningful specialization and collaboration without a central gate or shared gradients. Randomly routed populations perform worse than a single generalist, while populations with semantically aligned routing outperform the generalist, indicating that gains are due to specialization, not just more parameters. Specialization persists even when the central router is removed. In the fully decentralized DISCO setup, gradient-free communication allows non-expert agents to exploit the expertise of specialized agents: a random agent assisted by the expert matches the performance of the solo generalist, and the experts themselves surpass the generalist, including on data outside the original specialization mixture. Local routers learn to select the emergent expert for about 98% of relevant inputs. These findings are robust to variations in population size, model capacity, data imbalance, and finetuning seeds.
AI.conclusion: The study provides empirical evidence that useful specialization and division of labor can emerge in a population of independently trained neural networks without centralized control or shared gradients. Gradient-free, forward-pass-based communication channels are sufficient for agents to discover and exploit emergent expertise, leading to performance that can exceed a monolithic generalist model. This supports the plausibility of decentralized predictive pretraining regimes, where coordination and specialization arise from local learning rules rather than global gating mechanisms.

title: SRJudge: Empowering Large Language Models with Selective Reasoning for Fine-Grained Knowledge Concept Tagging
summary: Knowledge concept tagging aims to assign specific concept or topic labels to educational content, which is essential for both educators and learners in traditional and online teaching practices. Recent work has explored large language models (LLMs) for this task, achieving promising performance. However, LLMs still struggle to select the correct concept from a large-scale candidate set due to the high dimensionality of the decision space. In this paper, we propose a novel three-stage Select-Reason-Judge (SRJudge) framework, which empowers LLMs with selective reasoning capability for fine-grained knowledge concept tagging. Specifically, the Selector in Stage 1 first narrows the candidate concepts to a top-K shortlist by fine-tuning a small language model (SLM), e.g., BERT, since the top-$K$ predictions hit the correct concept in most cases, thereby reducing the decision space of correct candidates. Next, the Stage 2 Reasoner employs a lightweight LLM for refined reasoning over the shortlisted candidates. It further integrates an improved reinforcement learning strategy with a dynamic task-specific reward function and a pruning mechanism to better align with human reasoning preferences. Finally, a larger LLM acts as a judger that evaluates the overall rationality of the reasoning process and its explanations to determine the final output. In addition, we construct two high-quality datasets for further validation, i.e., the biology dataset S_Bio and the physics dataset S_Phy. Experimental results demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across benchmark datasets, verifying its effectiveness and superiority. Resources are available at: https://github.com/Nicozwy/SRJudge.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes SRJudge, a three-stage framework (Select-Reason-Judge) that combines small and large language models to improve fine-grained knowledge concept tagging, and shows it outperforms existing methods on new biology and physics datasets.
AI.motivation: Knowledge concept tagging is vital for organizing and personalizing educational content, but existing LLM-based methods struggle when choosing the correct concept from a very large set of candidate labels due to the high-dimensional decision space. The authors aim to reduce this difficulty and improve accuracy and interpretability in fine-grained tagging for educational scenarios.
AI.method: They design a three-stage Select-Reason-Judge (SRJudge) framework. Stage 1 uses a fine-tuned small language model (e.g., BERT) as a Selector to retrieve a top-K shortlist of candidate concepts, shrinking the decision space. Stage 2 uses a lightweight LLM as a Reasoner to perform refined reasoning among the shortlisted candidates, enhanced with an improved reinforcement learning approach that applies a dynamic task-specific reward function and a pruning mechanism to better align reasoning with human preferences. Stage 3 uses a larger LLM as a Judger to assess the rationality and explanatory quality of the reasoning process and decide the final predicted concept. They also build two subject-specific datasets (S_Bio for biology and S_Phy for physics) for evaluation.
AI.result: On benchmark datasets, including the newly created S_Bio and S_Phy, SRJudge consistently achieves higher performance than state-of-the-art baselines for knowledge concept tagging. The experiments indicate that combining selective candidate reduction, RL-enhanced reasoning, and LLM-based judging yields better tagging accuracy and quality of explanations.
AI.conclusion: The SRJudge framework effectively equips LLMs with selective reasoning capabilities for fine-grained knowledge concept tagging, overcoming challenges posed by large candidate sets. Its three-stage architecture and RL-based reasoning align better with human reasoning patterns, leading to superior performance on multiple datasets. The new biology and physics datasets also provide valuable testbeds for future work in educational NLP and concept tagging.

title: Code4Scene: Benchmarking Coding Agents for Constructing and Editing 3D Scenes
summary: Frontier coding agents can now write and execute code that authors 3D environments, but whether they reliably understand 3D structure and precisely control scene state remains unclear. The generated 3D scene is a persistent, executable artifact: a convincing render can hide incorrect spatial relations, intersecting objects, or unintended modifications. We introduce Code4Scene, a benchmark of 190 Unreal Engine cases built from human-assembled scenes that evaluates coding agents on two complementary settings under a shared execution interface. Construction tests scene-level spatial reasoning from open-ended language specifications, where many realizations are valid; editing tests precise control of scene state, where the agent must recover the target scene from reference images while preserving everything else. Rather than scoring code or rendered views, Code4Scene evaluates the generated engine-native scene for task fulfillment, artifact integrity, and static physical validity, with edits additionally compared against withheld ground truth. Across 14 coding-agent configurations on the 95-case public set, construction and editing performance are strongly correlated but not interchangeable (Spearman $ρ= 0.78$): Claude Fable 5.1 leads construction, Gemini 3.8 Flash leads editing, and GPT-6 Astra narrowly leads overall. Spatial Composition is the weakest construction category for every agent, while editing remains imprecise: the best Repair F1 is only 0.527, and 35.8% of edits that fully recover the target still introduce unintended changes elsewhere in the scene. These results expose a gap between plausible 3D generation and reliable spatial reasoning and state control.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Code4Scene, a benchmark to test whether coding agents that generate Unreal Engine 3D scenes truly understand and precisely control 3D structure.
AI.motivation: Current frontier coding agents can generate and execute code that builds 3D environments, but it is unclear if they genuinely understand 3D spatial structure or can reliably and precisely modify complex scenes. Visual plausibility of renders can hide spatial errors, collisions, or unintended changes, so a more rigorous and engine-native way to evaluate agents is needed.
AI.method: The authors build Code4Scene, a benchmark of 190 Unreal Engine scenes derived from human-authored environments. It defines two complementary tasks under a shared execution interface: (1) Construction, where agents create scenes from open-ended language descriptions and are evaluated on high-level spatial reasoning; and (2) Editing, where agents must transform an existing scene to match reference images of a target while preserving unchanged content. Evaluation is performed directly on the engine-native scene, checking task completion, artifact integrity, and static physical validity; for editing, scenes are also compared to hidden ground-truth targets. They test 14 different coding-agent configurations on a 95-case public subset and analyze category-wise performance and correlations between construction and editing.
AI.result: Construction and editing scores are strongly correlated but capture distinct abilities (Spearman ρ=0.78). Different models lead different tasks: Claude Fable 5.1 performs best on construction, Gemini 3.8 Flash on editing, and GPT-6 Astra has the best aggregate performance. All agents struggle most on Spatial Composition in construction. Editing is notably unreliable: the best Repair F1 score is only 0.527, and over one-third (35.8%) of edits that successfully reconstruct the target scene still introduce unintended changes elsewhere.
AI.conclusion: Even advanced coding agents that produce convincing 3D scenes lack robust, fine-grained spatial reasoning and reliable control over scene state. Code4Scene exposes a significant gap between visually plausible 3D generation and accurate, physically consistent, and targeted 3D scene construction and editing, indicating that better models and evaluation methods are needed for trustworthy 3D environment authoring via code.

title: CypherTurn: A Multi-Turn Benchmark for Conversational Text-to-Cypher Evaluation and the Autonomy Divergence
comment: Accepted as an oral paper at EMNLP 2026
summary: Graph databases are increasingly queried through natural language, yet every existing benchmark evaluates isolated single-turn queries rather than the multi-turn sessions through which analysts actually work. We introduce CypherTurn, the first benchmark for conversational Text-to-Cypher evaluation, comprising 721 sessions and 5,927 turns across 7 knowledge graphs and 13 conversational phenomena. We evaluate 15 models under a guided oracle protocol and a fully autonomous agentic protocol, yielding four findings. First, the best model reaches only 64.7% execution accuracy, and session-level correctness remains below 5%. Second, despite strong overall rank correlation, frontier models exhibit a consequential reordering of the top of the leaderboard under autonomous operation, a phenomenon we term the Autonomy Divergence, which reveals error-management as a partially independent capability from raw generation skill. Third, scaling action budgets from x3 to x10 fails to close the autonomy gap, as the strongest frontier models self-limit to approximately two actions per turn regardless of available budget. Fourth, single-turn Cypher fine-tuning degrades multi-turn instruction following, while architecture-appropriate specialization outperforms several frontier models. These results establish CypherTurn as an open challenge for conversational graph database reasoning. Code and data are available at https://github.com/BarryQ/CypherTurn.

AI.tldr: CypherTurn is a new benchmark for evaluating how models handle multi-turn natural-language conversations that generate Cypher queries over graph databases, revealing large performance gaps and new challenges for autonomous agent behavior.
AI.motivation: Existing text-to-Cypher and graph database benchmarks focus on isolated, single-turn queries, which do not capture how real analysts work in multi-step conversational sessions. There is a lack of evaluation resources that stress conversational phenomena such as follow-ups, clarifications, error corrections, and longer task contexts, especially under realistic autonomous agent settings.
AI.method: The authors construct CypherTurn, a benchmark of 721 multi-turn conversational sessions (5,927 turns) that span 7 different knowledge graphs and cover 13 kinds of conversational phenomena relevant to graph querying. They then evaluate 15 different language models in two settings: (1) a guided oracle protocol, where the system gets help or idealized feedback, and (2) a fully autonomous agentic protocol, where the model independently plans and executes actions (queries) over multiple turns. They compare execution accuracy, session-level correctness, ranking stability, and the impact of fine-tuning and action budgets on performance.
AI.result: The best-performing model achieves 64.7% execution accuracy at the turn level, but less than 5% of full multi-turn sessions are entirely correct. Model rankings change notably when moving from guided to autonomous settings, revealing what they call "Autonomy Divergence"—the decoupling of raw generation quality from error-handling capabilities. Increasing the allowed number of actions per turn from 3x to 10x does not close this autonomy gap, as strong models still typically use only about two actions per turn. Additionally, naive single-turn Cypher fine-tuning harms multi-turn instruction-following ability, whereas architectures tailored to the task can outperform some state-of-the-art frontier models.
AI.conclusion: CypherTurn exposes that current models are far from reliably handling realistic conversational, multi-turn text-to-Cypher interactions with graph databases. The benchmark highlights that autonomy, error management, and multi-turn reasoning are distinct capabilities not captured by single-turn evaluations or simple fine-tuning. The authors present CypherTurn as an open, challenging benchmark and release code and data to support further research on conversational graph database reasoning and more robust autonomous agents.

title: Aperture: Merge-Consistent Rotary States for Compressed Tokens
summary: Token compression combines content from several positions, yet rotary position embeddings usually assign the merged token one coordinate. We ask what positional information must survive later merges. Aperture stores Fourier moments of the token's weighted support at the model's rotary frequencies. We prove that these moments have minimal real dimension among continuous states sufficient for the selected expected rotary interactions. Represented mass makes updates additive; attention normalisation remains a separate readout choice. Uniform intervals give a centre rotation times a sinc gain. We characterise when centres determine interval widths and construct matched examples where they do not. Numerical checks verify the weighted-support implementation. In trained temporal readers, compression transfer varies with gain calibration and feature placement. In a prespecified native video question-answering comparison, stored support reaches $65.63\%$ accuracy versus $67.12\%$ for the deployed merging rule. These results separate exact positional preservation under compression from downstream benefit.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Aperture, a method for preserving essential positional information when compressing tokens in models with rotary position embeddings, and shows it is theoretically minimal for the rotary interactions they target.
AI.motivation: Token compression in sequence models with rotary position embeddings typically assigns a single position to a merged token, which may discard important positional structure about how the original tokens were distributed. The authors aim to understand what positional information truly needs to be preserved under compression, and to design a representation that keeps exactly that information with minimal redundancy, in order to better support downstream tasks like temporal/video question answering.
AI.method: They define Aperture, which stores Fourier moments of the token’s weighted positional support at the model’s rotary frequencies. They prove that, for a given set of expected rotary interactions, these stored moments form a continuous state of minimal real dimension that is still sufficient. They design the representation so that the stored mass is additive across merges while attention normalisation is left as a separate readout step. They derive analytic forms for uniform intervals (centre rotation times a sinc gain), mathematically characterise when interval centres are enough to determine their widths and when they are not, and provide constructed examples exhibiting the latter. They implement a weighted-support approximation numerically and verify its behaviour in trained temporal reader models. They also evaluate Aperture in a pre-specified video QA setting against an existing merging rule.
AI.result: Theoretical results show that the Fourier-moment state Aperture stores is minimal yet sufficient for the chosen rotary interactions, and that interval centres generally do not uniquely determine interval widths. Numerical experiments confirm the correctness of the weighted-support implementation and demonstrate that, in temporal reading models, the effectiveness of compression transfer depends on the calibration of the gain factor and on where features are placed. In a native video QA benchmark, the stored-support method achieves 65.63% accuracy compared to 67.12% for the currently deployed merging rule.
AI.conclusion: Aperture cleanly separates the goal of exactly preserving the positional effects relevant to rotary embeddings under token compression from the broader question of whether such preservation improves downstream task performance. While their method is provably minimal and empirically sound for the rotary interactions studied, its downstream benefits in real tasks depend on additional factors such as gain calibration and feature placement, and it does not automatically outperform practical heuristic merging rules.

title: LatCom: Cross-Agent Latent Compression for Efficient Multi-Agent Collaboration
summary: LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) increasingly use latent collaboration to avoid the information loss and repeated encoding-decoding overhead of natural-language communication. However, directly forwarding all sender latents makes the receiver-side context scale with both the number of agents and the reasoning length, increasing computation, memory usage, and collaboration latency. A natural solution is latent compression. But we find that cross-agent redundancy remains unresolved in existing latent compression approaches, which typically compress each sender independently and then concatenate the results. We propose LatCom, a cross-agent latent compression framework for efficient multi-agent latent collaboration. LatCom maps multiple sender latents into a fixed number of receiver-readable and task-relevant slots. Rather than reconstructing all sender hidden states, it optimizes the compressed latents for receiver-side task utility. LatCom trains the compressor in two stages: single-sender readability learning first establishes a latent interface interpretable by the frozen receiver, and multi-sender fusion learning then trains the compressor to fuse complementary evidence and remove redundancy across agents. Experiments on multiple benchmarks with Qwen3-4B show that LatCom achieves an average 2.46x inference speed-up over LatentMAS and reduces output token usage by 70.3% while maintaining comparable average accuracy.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces LatCom, a cross-agent latent compression framework that compresses and fuses latent representations from multiple LLM agents into a fixed number of task-relevant slots, significantly speeding up multi-agent inference and reducing token usage while preserving accuracy.
AI.motivation: In LLM-based multi-agent systems, agents often communicate via latent representations instead of natural language to avoid information loss and overhead. However, directly passing all sender latents causes the receiver’s context length to grow with both the number of agents and reasoning steps, which increases computation, memory usage, and latency. Existing latent compression methods compress each agent independently, failing to remove redundancy across agents, which leaves substantial inefficiency. The paper aims to address this cross-agent redundancy for more efficient multi-agent collaboration.
AI.method: The authors propose LatCom, a cross-agent latent compression framework that maps latent states from multiple sender agents into a fixed number of compressed slots that are readable by a frozen receiver model and optimized for task utility. LatCom does not try to reconstruct all sender hidden states; instead, it directly optimizes the compressed latents for the receiver’s downstream performance. Training is done in two stages: (1) single-sender readability learning, where a compressor is trained so that the receiver can interpret compressed latents from one sender; and (2) multi-sender fusion learning, where the same compressor is further trained to fuse complementary information from multiple senders and eliminate redundancy across agents while keeping the number of slots fixed.
AI.result: On multiple benchmarks using Qwen3-4B as the base model, LatCom achieves an average 2.46× inference speedup compared to LatentMAS and reduces output token usage by 70.3%, while maintaining comparable average task accuracy. This demonstrates that cross-agent latent compression can substantially improve efficiency without significant performance degradation in multi-agent LLM collaboration.
AI.conclusion: LatCom effectively addresses cross-agent redundancy in latent-based multi-agent communication by jointly compressing and fusing multiple agents’ hidden states into a fixed, receiver-readable latent interface. The two-stage training procedure yields compressed representations that are both interpretable to a frozen receiver and highly efficient, enabling faster and more resource-efficient multi-agent reasoning while preserving accuracy. This suggests cross-agent-aware latent compression is a promising direction for scalable LLM-based multi-agent systems.

title: AI as a Compiler: Compiling Triton kernels without the Triton compiler
summary: Compiler backends are expensive to build and maintain as programming models, workloads, and accelerators evolve. We investigate whether large language models can replace the conventional optimizing and lowering pipeline, a process that we call AI lowering. We study AI lowering from Triton to NVIDIA PTX: an LLM agent translates Triton kernels directly into PTX. We build an environment that evaluates candidate PTX, and an agentic harness in which an LLM translates Triton kernels into PTX. Across twelve common kernels on Ada, Hopper, and Blackwell GPUs and ten kernels from recent ML papers, AI lowering achieves 0.83x-3.34x the performance of autotuned Triton. The largest gains come from transformations that Triton's lowering pipeline does not perform, such as decoding packed binary weights directly into Tensor Core operands (3.34x on BitDelta), assigning each thread a complete softmax row in tensor memory (1.37x on FlashAttention), and reusing overlapping convolution windows (up to 2.23x). These results rely on a robust evaluation harness with comprehensive verification support. We build on Volta, an existing PTX verifier, and substantially extend it to support modern GPU architectures by introducing support for Blackwell's tcgen05 Tensor Core interface. This requires modeling three architectural features: managed tensor memory, descriptor-based operand layouts, and asynchronous execution coordinated through commits, waits, memory barriers, and proxy fences. We discuss the challenges involved in formalizing them, as well as the current limitations. Our results suggest an emerging future in which AI compilers replace custom-written intermediate representations and checkers, reducing the time and engineering effort required to bring up software for new general-purpose and custom chips.

AI.tldr: The paper explores using large language models to directly generate NVIDIA PTX from Triton, partially replacing traditional compiler backends, and shows that this AI-based lowering can sometimes significantly outperform autotuned Triton on modern GPUs while relying on an extended formal PTX verification framework.
AI.motivation: Traditional compiler backends are costly to design, optimize, and maintain as hardware (e.g., new GPU generations) and workloads (especially ML) evolve. Triton and similar systems still depend on complex, hand-engineered optimization and lowering passes, which can lag behind hardware capabilities and specialized optimization opportunities. With the rise of powerful LLMs, the authors want to know whether these models can act as agents that replace or augment compiler backends by directly generating efficient low-level code, thus reducing engineering effort and speeding up support for new accelerators.
AI.method: They define "AI lowering" as using an LLM agent to translate high-level Triton kernels directly into NVIDIA PTX. They build: (1) an evaluation environment that compiles, runs, and measures generated PTX code; (2) an agentic harness where the LLM repeatedly proposes PTX implementations and refines them based on feedback; and (3) an extended PTX verification infrastructure, based on the Volta verifier, updated to handle modern GPU features, especially Blackwell’s tcgen05 Tensor Core interface. This extension includes modeling managed tensor memory, descriptor-based operand layouts, and asynchronous execution mechanisms (commits, waits, memory barriers, proxy fences) to ensure correctness and safety of generated PTX. They then benchmark performance on a suite of common kernels across Ada, Hopper, and Blackwell GPUs, plus ten kernels from recent ML research.
AI.result: Across twelve standard kernels on Ada, Hopper, and Blackwell GPUs and ten additional ML-paper kernels, AI lowering achieves between 0.83x and 3.34x the performance of autotuned Triton. Notable speedups arise from optimizations that Triton’s conventional lowering does not perform: e.g., decoding packed binary weights directly into Tensor Core operands (3.34x on BitDelta), mapping each thread to a full softmax row stored in tensor memory (1.37x on FlashAttention), and reusing overlapping convolution windows (up to 2.23x). The extended PTX verifier successfully supports these modern architectural features, although the paper also notes remaining limitations in its formalization of advanced GPU behaviors.
AI.conclusion: AI-based lowering using LLM agents can sometimes match or significantly exceed the performance of a sophisticated, autotuned compiler pipeline like Triton, particularly by discovering non-standard, hardware-aware transformations outside the scope of current compiler heuristics. A key enabler is a strong verification and evaluation infrastructure that allows safely exploring aggressive low-level optimizations on new GPU architectures. The authors conclude that AI compilers may increasingly replace or augment custom-written intermediate representations and checkers, potentially reducing the engineering cost and time to support new general-purpose and custom accelerators, while raising new challenges in formal modeling and verification of evolving hardware features.

title: Selecting The Most Informative Tokens in Natural Language Autoencoders
summary: Natural language autoencoders translate a language model's internal activations into readable explanations. Explaining every token position is costly. Which positions should an auditor inspect to understand a potential threat? We study this question across $4.7$ million explanations on prompt injection and concealment. We compare signals from model computation with a ranker trained only on chat structure. Chat structure usually selects more relevant explanations than the computational signals, without requiring a model forward pass for position selection. On three of four datasets, explaining just $5\%$ of positions retains nearly all of the success rate from explaining every position, where success means obtaining an explanation about the threat. The benefit varies with the audit task. We also show that pretrained verbalizers recover words that models have learned to conceal through fine-tuning, without additional verbalizer training. These results identify where auditors can concentrate explanation generation and show that useful explanations can extend beyond the model a verbalizer was trained to describe.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how to efficiently pick which token positions to explain with natural language autoencoders when auditing models for threats like prompt injection and concealment, showing that simple chat-structure-based selection works surprisingly well and that verbalizers can expose concealed knowledge beyond their training model.
AI.motivation: Explaining every token position in a model’s internal computation via natural language autoencoders is computationally expensive, yet auditors need reliable ways to understand potentially dangerous behavior such as prompt injection and concealment. The authors want to know which token positions are most informative for detecting threats so that audits are both efficient and effective. They also want to understand whether explanation tools (verbalizers) can uncover knowledge that the underlying model has been fine-tuned to hide.
AI.method: The authors analyze 4.7 million explanations produced by natural language autoencoders across tasks involving prompt injection and concealment. They compare several strategies for selecting which token positions to explain: (1) signals derived from model computation (e.g., internal activations or other forward-pass-based indicators), and (2) a ranker trained only on chat structure (turn order, speaker roles, etc.) that does not rely on model internals. They evaluate each strategy by how often the selected explanations successfully surface information about the threat. They further test whether pretrained verbalizers applied to fine-tuned models can recover words or content that the fine-tuning attempted to conceal, without additional training of the verbalizer.
AI.result: Across three of four datasets, selecting and explaining only about 5% of token positions achieves nearly the same success rate at revealing threats as explaining every token position. Chat-structure-based ranking typically yields more relevant explanations than computational-signal-based selection, and crucially it avoids the cost of additional forward passes for selection. The effectiveness of each selection strategy varies with the particular audit task. Additionally, the experiments show that pretrained verbalizers can recover words that the underlying models were fine-tuned to conceal, even though the verbalizers themselves were not retrained on the fine-tuned model.
AI.conclusion: Auditors do not need to explain every token position to effectively detect threats like prompt injection or concealment; focusing on a small, well-chosen subset—around 5% of positions—often suffices. Simple rankers based only on chat structure can outperform more expensive methods using model internals, making large-scale audits more feasible. Furthermore, natural language autoencoder verbalizers can expose concealed knowledge in fine-tuned models beyond those they were originally trained to interpret, suggesting that explanation tools can generalize across models and uncover hidden behavior. This informs how and where to apply explanation methods in practical safety auditing workflows.

title: UpliftMem: Learning Set-Level Uplift for Agent Memory Retrieval
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents reuse external memory to guide new tasks, but effective retrieval requires learning which memory sets improve execution. Such learning relies on costly outcome feedback: ordinary retrieval observes only executed sets, while evaluating alternatives requires additional rollouts. We introduce \textsc{UpliftMem}, which learns memory retrieval from set-level execution uplift relative to the same executor without memory. A theoretical analysis of how retrieval preferences restrict feedback coverage motivates targeted probing of alternative memory sets. Probe selection follows an expected value of sample information (EVSI) criterion, derived in closed form under a correlated Gaussian model, to allocate limited training rollouts according to their expected improvement in local retrieval decisions. The shared scorer is trained with a frozen executor and selects memory sets without test-time probes. Across ALFWorld, WebShop, and BigCodeBench, \textsc{UpliftMem} achieves the best success rates among evaluated baselines on the main evaluation sets. Controlled fixed-store and matched probe budget evaluations further demonstrate improved memory-use decisions and more effective use of execution feedback.

AI.tldr: They propose UpliftMem, a method for training LLM agents to retrieve and use external memories more effectively by learning from uplift over no‑memory execution and by selectively probing alternative memory sets using an EVSI-based criterion.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM agents can consult external memory banks, but deciding which memory items or sets to retrieve for a new task is hard. Current approaches usually learn from sparse, expensive rollout feedback and only from actually used memory sets, leaving many alternatives unexplored. This makes training inefficient and can lead to suboptimal memory use. The paper aims to learn better retrieval policies under a limited budget of environment executions by exploiting relative performance (uplift) and smarter selection of which alternative memory sets to probe.
AI.method: They define execution uplift as the performance difference between running the same frozen executor with a given memory set versus running it without any memory. Retrieval learning becomes a problem of predicting this uplift for candidate memory sets. They analyze how retrieval preferences constrain which feedback is available and show gaps in coverage. To address this, they introduce a targeted probing strategy: for some trajectories, they run additional rollouts with alternative memory sets to estimate their uplift. Probe selection is guided by an expected value of sample information (EVSI) objective, derived in closed form under a correlated Gaussian model over the uplift of different memory sets. A shared scoring model is trained on these uplift-labeled examples to rank memory sets, while the executor remains frozen. At test time, the scorer picks memory sets directly, without probes or extra rollouts.
AI.result: On three benchmarks—ALFWorld, WebShop, and BigCodeBench—UpliftMem outperforms baseline memory-retrieval methods in overall task success rate on the main evaluation splits. Additional controlled experiments holding the memory store fixed and matching the probe budget across methods show that UpliftMem makes better decisions about when and what memory to use and extracts more value from each execution feedback sample than competing approaches.
AI.conclusion: Learning retrieval from uplift relative to a no-memory baseline, combined with EVSI-based targeted probing of alternative memory sets, leads to more data-efficient and effective training of memory retrieval for LLM agents. A frozen executor plus a learned uplift scorer can significantly improve success rates across diverse benchmarks, indicating that smarter allocation of rollout budget and explicit modeling of relative memory benefits are key to better memory-augmented LLM agents.

title: Learning from Think-Mode Advantage via On-Policy Distillation
summary: Explicit intermediate reasoning gives large language models (LLMs) a stronger problem-solving mode. We study learning from this think-mode advantage via on-policy distillation (OPD). OPD preserves student-generated trajectories and provides dense token-level teacher targets at student-visited prefixes. Privileged reasoning is used during distillation rather than student inference. Uniform ThinkOPD, a natural think-enabled OPD baseline, conditions a fixed teacher on one shared think trace and uniformly distills every sibling student response. Although its prefixes are on-policy, the trace need not follow a route compatible with every complete response: the same privileged trace can induce different teacher-student discrepancies even when responses reach the same outcome. We summarize this interaction with trace-response divergence (TRD) and introduce ThinkOPD, which routes supervision at the response level by combining group-relative reward gain with a TRD-based compatibility proxy. Final response weights are normalized within each rollout group. Across mathematical reasoning and code generation, ThinkOPD outperforms Uniform ThinkOPD in both same-model settings and both cross-model teacher-student pairs, and it exceeds representative rationale and self-distillation baselines in a controlled comparison. Controlled interventions show that outcome benefit and the TRD-based proxy provide complementary routing signals in this setting. Think-enabled OPD provides a controlled setting for studying how teacher advantage becomes transferable along student responses.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes ThinkOPD, an improved on-policy distillation method that better leverages explicit reasoning traces from large language models by routing supervision using both outcome-based rewards and a new trace-response divergence compatibility measure, leading to stronger student models on math and code tasks.
AI.motivation: Explicit chain-of-thought style reasoning improves LLM problem-solving, but it is unclear how to best transfer this privileged "think-mode" advantage from a teacher to a student model. Standard on-policy distillation with a shared reasoning trace (Uniform ThinkOPD) can misalign teacher supervision with diverse student responses because one fixed trace may be incompatible with different solution paths. The authors aim to better understand and improve how to use teacher reasoning as a training signal along the trajectories actually taken by the student model.
AI.method: They formalize on-policy distillation (OPD) with explicit reasoning, where the student generates its own trajectories and receives dense, token-level supervision from a stronger teacher along those student prefixes. They identify the mismatch between a shared teacher trace and multiple student responses via a new measure, trace-response divergence (TRD), which summarizes how compatible a privileged reasoning trace is with each complete response. Building on this, they introduce ThinkOPD: for each rollout group of student responses, they route teacher supervision at the response level by combining (1) group-relative reward gain (how good each response is compared with its siblings) and (2) the TRD-based compatibility proxy. These signals are used to weight the supervision for each response, with normalization within each group. They compare ThinkOPD with Uniform ThinkOPD, rationale distillation, and self-distillation in math reasoning and code generation tasks, including both same-model and cross-model teacher-student configurations, and run controlled ablation-style interventions to isolate the contributions of outcome reward and TRD-based routing.
AI.result: ThinkOPD consistently outperforms Uniform ThinkOPD in all tested settings, including when teacher and student are the same model family and when they differ, across both mathematical reasoning and code generation benchmarks. It also surpasses representative rationale distillation and self-distillation baselines in a controlled comparison. The controlled interventions show that using both outcome-based reward signals and the TRD-based compatibility measure yields better routing and learning than either signal alone, indicating that the two are complementary for selecting which student responses to emphasize during distillation.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates that explicit reasoning traces can be more effectively leveraged in on-policy distillation by accounting for compatibility between privileged teacher traces and diverse student responses. The proposed ThinkOPD framework, which uses trace-response divergence and group-relative reward to route supervision at the response level, yields improved transfer of the teacher’s think-mode advantage and stronger downstream performance on reasoning-heavy tasks. Think-enabled OPD thus provides a useful and controlled setting for studying how and when richer teacher reasoning becomes transferable along the actual solution paths explored by student models.

title: CAD-Native Transformer Operators for AI-Aided Engineering
summary: Modern engineering systems, from automobiles to aircraft, are designed by using precise, continuous parametric computer-aided design (CAD) models. Evaluating design changes through numerical simulation requires meshing the continuous geometry, a computationally expensive and often brittle process that can require manual intervention and replaces the continuous representation with a discrete approximation. Most neural surrogates accelerate the simulation, but inherit this representation gap by relying on meshes, point clouds, voxels, or other sampled approximations of geometry. We introduce CANTO, a transformer neural operator that maps directly from continuous CAD geometry to physical fields, without meshing the input geometry. We develop a theoretical framework for learning operators from geometric manifolds to function spaces of physical fields, representing geometry through sequences of parametric patches. CANTO instantiates this framework by directly tokenizing non-uniform rational B-spline (NURBS) patches from their control points, knot vectors, and weights, and predicts continuous surface and volume fields at arbitrary query locations. We evaluate CANTO on four automotive and aircraft aerodynamics industry benchmarks: AhmedML, WindsorML, DrivAerML, and HiLiftAeroML. CANTO achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on most evaluated surface and volume prediction tasks, including a 19.8% reduction in surface-pressure relative $L_2$ error compared with AB-UPT on HiLiftAeroML. Differentiability with respect to CAD parameters further enables gradient-based inverse design of designs. On AhmedML, CANTO identifies designs with 4.4 to 20.4% lower drag than the best dataset designs satisfying the same volume and lift constraints, with the improvements verified using the same CFD setup used to generate the original dataset.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces CANTO, a transformer-based neural operator that predicts physical fields directly from continuous CAD (NURBS) geometry, bypassing meshing, and achieves state-of-the-art accuracy and enables gradient-based inverse design on several aerodynamics benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Traditional numerical simulation workflows require meshing CAD geometry, which is computationally expensive, brittle, and replaces exact continuous representations with discrete approximations. Existing neural surrogates speed up simulation but still depend on such discrete geometric representations (meshes, point clouds, voxels), preserving the representation gap between CAD models and physical field predictions. There is a need for a method that operates directly on continuous CAD representations for both forward prediction and inverse design.
AI.method: The authors develop a theoretical framework for learning neural operators that map from geometric manifolds (continuous CAD surfaces) to function spaces of physical fields. They instantiate this with CANTO, a transformer-based neural operator that tokenizes CAD geometry represented as sequences of NURBS patches using their control points, knot vectors, and weights. CANTO predicts continuous surface and volume physical fields at arbitrary query locations without requiring a mesh of the input geometry. The model is trained and evaluated on several automotive and aerodynamics datasets, where it learns the mapping from CAD parameters to CFD fields and supports differentiation with respect to CAD parameters for optimization.
AI.result: CANTO is evaluated on four industrial aerodynamic benchmarks: AhmedML, WindsorML, DrivAerML, and HiLiftAeroML. It achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on most surface and volume field prediction tasks. Notably, on the HiLiftAeroML benchmark, it reduces the surface-pressure relative L2 error by 19.8% compared with the previous best method AB-UPT. The model is differentiable with respect to CAD parameters, enabling gradient-based optimization of shape designs.
AI.conclusion: Directly learning operators from continuous CAD geometry to physical fields is feasible and beneficial. CANTO, by operating directly on NURBS-based CAD representations and using a transformer architecture, eliminates the meshing step, improves prediction accuracy over prior surrogates, and enables effective gradient-based inverse design. The results on industry-standard aerodynamics benchmarks suggest that such CAD-native neural operators can significantly streamline engineering design workflows and lead to better-performing designs under given constraints.

title: Traverse: Learning When to Remember, Reset, and Redirect for Long-Horizon Web Search
summary: Long-horizon information-seeking agents often accumulate noisy or misleading context, causing early mistakes to persist and making recovery increasingly difficult. We introduce an autonomous search harness in which the agent manages its own search process through three states: Rubric, Answer, and Verify. The agent first defines criteria for a valid answer, searches under these criteria, and then independently verifies the result before deciding whether to terminate or continue searching. It is further equipped with a Seal Memory tool that enables active context management. Training this behavior with reinforcement learning, however, can induce Seal Collapse, resulting in unstable training and preventing the agent from reliably learning when and how to use its memory tools. We solve this with a simple strategy that trains only the final segment after context management. Our 35B model achieves 72.83 on BrowseComp, outperforming comparable open-source systems, and consistently improves over the base model across BrowseComp-ZH, xbench, DeepSearchQA, WideSearch, financial investigation, and product search. Ablations show that autonomous compression outperforms automatic compaction and validate our RL design.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an autonomous multi-stage search framework with active context management and a reinforcement learning strategy that stabilizes training, leading to strong performance on long-horizon information-seeking benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon information-seeking agents often accumulate noisy or misleading context, which leads to early mistakes persisting and makes it hard for agents to recover during search. Existing approaches lack robust mechanisms for agents to define success criteria, verify intermediate results, and manage context effectively, especially when trained with reinforcement learning, which can lead to unstable use of memory tools.
AI.method: The authors design an autonomous search harness with three states—Rubric, Answer, and Verify—where the agent: (1) first formulates an explicit rubric (criteria) for a valid answer; (2) conducts search guided by this rubric; and (3) independently verifies the proposed answer and decides whether to stop or continue searching. They introduce a Seal Memory tool for active context management, allowing the agent to selectively retain or discard information. To avoid instability in RL training (Seal Collapse), they adopt a training strategy that only optimizes the final segment after context management instead of the entire process, stabilizing learning of when and how to use memory tools.
AI.result: A 35B-parameter model trained with this framework attains a score of 72.83 on the BrowseComp benchmark, surpassing other comparable open-source systems. It also shows consistent improvements over the base model on multiple benchmarks, including BrowseComp-ZH, xbench, DeepSearchQA, WideSearch, as well as specialized tasks such as financial investigation and product search. Ablation studies indicate that the proposed autonomous compression mechanism outperforms simpler automatic compaction baselines and empirically support the chosen RL training design.
AI.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that structuring agents’ search into rubric-setting, answering, and verification phases, combined with active context management via Seal Memory and a stabilized RL training strategy, yields more reliable and effective long-horizon information-seeking behavior. The approach mitigates error accumulation, avoids RL-induced Seal Collapse, and leads to strong performance gains across a range of search and investigation benchmarks.

title: Geometry-Conditioned Fixed-Scaffold Encoders for Time-Warp Robust Sequence Retrieval
summary: Embedding-based retrieval is attractive for long sequence collections because each item can be encoded once and searched by nearest-neighbor ranking. The difficulty is that the objects being indexed are often observed under a noncanonical clock: cardiac cycles stretch with rate, speech changes with tempo, and sensor traces reach comparable states at different speeds.
