This paper studies a specific source of instability in patch-based encoders for this regime. If patch boundaries are chosen from signal geometry, then the tokenization can change under the same temporal deformation that the representation is expected to tolerate. We propose GeoPatch, a fixed-scaffold patch encoder that keeps token support independent of geometry and uses slope, curvature, acceleration, affine-residual, and confidence descriptors only as continuous conditioning variables. The design turns boundary variation into feature modulation: geometry can change the embedding through a controlled pathway, but it cannot change the number, order, or support of local tokens. We formalize this distinction through a mechanism-level stability analysis that separates boundary drift, affine timing variation, confidence-weighted geometry perturbation, and retrieval-margin effects. The same local tokens support global embedding retrieval and late-interaction scoring, so the scoring rule can be matched to the evaluation protocol. Across ECG, speech, and multivariate time-series retrieval tasks, GeoPatch improves early-rank retrieval under timing variation while exposing a clear trade-off between local surface matching and strict non-overlap retrieval.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces GeoPatch, a new way to tokenize long time-series so that retrieval with embeddings is stable under timing changes (e.g., speed/tempo).
AI.motivation: Standard embedding-based retrieval of long time-series is unstable when the same pattern occurs at different speeds. Patch-based encoders often define patch boundaries from signal geometry (like peaks and valleys), so temporal deformations that should be tolerated by the representation also shift those boundaries, changing the tokenization and harming retrieval robustness.
AI.method: The authors propose GeoPatch, a patch encoder with a fixed temporal scaffold: patches are defined on fixed supports independent of signal geometry. Geometric properties—slope, curvature, acceleration, affine-residual, and confidence—are used only as continuous conditioning variables rather than for defining patch boundaries. This design ensures the number, order, and temporal support of tokens are invariant to geometry. They provide a mechanism-level stability analysis that decomposes instability into boundary drift, affine timing variation, confidence-weighted geometry perturbation, and retrieval-margin effects. The same local tokens can be used both for global embedding retrieval and for late-interaction scoring.
AI.result: On ECG, speech, and multivariate time-series retrieval benchmarks with timing variation, GeoPatch improves early-rank retrieval performance compared to baselines. It also makes explicit a trade-off between matching local surface details and enforcing strict non-overlap in retrieval.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling token boundaries from signal geometry and using geometry only as conditioning features yields more stable, timing-robust embeddings for long time-series retrieval. GeoPatch provides a mechanism to control how temporal deformations affect embeddings and supports both global and late-interaction retrieval scoring within a unified tokenization framework.

title: What Does Post-Training Change in Multilingual Reasoning?
comment: 20 pages, 9 figures, 21 tables. Main paper and supplementary material in one document
summary: Open-source reasoning models provide unequal access to reasoning capability across languages. When a model can solve a problem but cannot deliver a complete solution in the user's language, language becomes an access barrier rather than merely a source of performance variation. We audit Qwen3 checkpoints on competition-mathematics tasks in eleven languages. Across the ten non-English languages, only 15.4-17.9% of problems receive a correct, terminating solution with visible reasoning in the requested language in any of 16 samples, compared with 92.9% in English. To identify the source of this disparity, we evaluate thirteen endpoints from one model family, spanning released checkpoints, multilingual supervised fine-tuning (SFT) at two scales, controlled SFT ablations, and three reinforcement-learning (RL) reward formulations. We jointly track correctness, language adherence, termination, and delivery efficiency. The dominant bottleneck shifts across post-training stages. Released models often reason in English. Multilingual SFT restores target-language reasoning, but accuracy declines across multilingual, English-only, and single-language SFT runs, showing that this cost is not specific to multilingual mixing; non-English reasoning traces additionally become prone to non-terminating loops. RL restores termination in both arms at no cost in accuracy, but only the arm whose reward includes a language term delivers: rewarding correctness alone returns the model to English. Together, these stages establish a constructive post-training path from English-pivoted capability to multilingual reasoning that is reliably delivered.

AI.tldr: The paper audits and improves multilingual reasoning in open-source Qwen3 models, showing a large gap between English and other languages and proposing a post-training recipe (multilingual SFT + language-aware RL) that recovers accurate, terminating reasoning in target languages.
AI.motivation: Open-source reasoning models, though powerful in English, often fail to provide complete, correct reasoning traces in users' non-English languages. This creates an access barrier: a user whose language is not English cannot reliably benefit from the model’s reasoning ability, even if the model is capable in principle. The authors want to rigorously measure this disparity, understand its causes across post-training stages, and design a concrete post-training procedure that turns English-centric capability into truly multilingual, user-language-aligned reasoning.
AI.method:
1) Audit: Evaluate Qwen3 checkpoints on competition-math benchmarks across 11 languages. Use multi-sampling (16 samples per problem) and track four dimensions: (a) correctness, (b) language adherence of the reasoning trace, (c) termination vs. infinite/non-terminating loops, and (d) delivery efficiency (how often the user actually receives a usable solution in the requested language).
2) Ablation of post-training: Compare 13 endpoints from the same model family, including: (i) base/released checkpoints, (ii) multilingual SFT at two scales, (iii) English-only and single-language SFT, and (iv) several RL configurations.
3) RL variants: Train reinforcement-learning policies with different reward formulations—some reward only correctness, others reward correctness plus language adherence and termination—to isolate how each component affects final behavior.
4) Analyze bottlenecks: For each training stage, identify whether the key failure is English pivoting, loss of accuracy, non-termination, or failure to follow the requested language.
AI.result:
1) Massive language disparity: In English, 92.9% of problems receive at least one correct, terminating solution with visible reasoning among 16 samples. For the ten non-English languages, the analogous rate is only 15.4–17.9%, revealing a large inequality in accessible reasoning.
2) English pivot in released models: Pretrained/released models often carry out reasoning in English even when another language is requested.
3) SFT trade-offs: Multilingual SFT successfully pushes reasoning into the target languages, but it reduces mathematical accuracy and introduces non-terminating loops in non-English chains of thought. These accuracy and stability costs are also seen in English-only and single-language SFT, indicating they stem from SFT itself rather than from multilingual data mixing.
4) RL effects: RL post-training recovers stable termination behavior without hurting accuracy. However, if the RL reward only incentivizes correctness, the model reverts to reasoning in English. Only when the reward explicitly includes a language term does the model consistently deliver solutions in the requested language.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates that current open-source reasoning models exhibit strong English bias that severely limits effective access for non-English users. By tracing how different post-training stages affect correctness, language use, and termination, the authors show that: (1) SFT can localize reasoning into target languages but at a cost in accuracy and stability; (2) RL can repair termination issues; and (3) explicit language-aware reward is necessary to avoid reversion to English. Collectively, these findings yield a constructive recipe for turning English-pivoted reasoning capability into robust, multilingual, user-language-aligned reasoning, thereby reducing language as a barrier to AI-assisted problem solving.

title: Calibrate the Decisions That Change the Future: On-Policy Post-Training Quantization for Multimodal Large Language Models
summary: Post-training quantization (PTQ) lowers deployment cost for multimodal large language models, but calibration typically reconstructs fixed sequences with local objectives. This overlooks autoregressive feedback: a quantization-induced token change redirects the prefix and changes future states. Yet on-policy coverage alone is insufficient because many decision mismatches barely affect future generation. We propose OnPTQ, an on-policy framework that calibrates on trajectories visited by the current quantized policy. On shared prefixes, OnPTQ identifies quantization-eroded boundaries, evaluates competing tokens through short counterfactual rollouts, and combines current discrepancy with branch consequence into a Decision--Consequence risk. The risk prioritizes critical states, while context anchoring and trajectory refresh preserve multimodal behavior and keep calibration aligned with the updated policy. We further derive a Decision--Consequence bound linking behavioral deviation to current policy discrepancy and action-conditioned future-value span. Across vision--language and omni-modal Qwen models under multiple low-bit settings, OnPTQ improves downstream performance and yields fewer correctness flips against the corresponding Dense/FP16 references, without changing the deployed inference graph.

AI.tldr: A new on-policy post-training quantization (OnPTQ) method that accounts for autoregressive feedback to better preserve behavior of multimodal LLMs under low-bit quantization.
AI.motivation: Existing PTQ methods for multimodal large language models usually calibrate using fixed sequences and local reconstruction objectives, ignoring that quantization errors can change generated tokens, alter prefixes, and propagate through future states in autoregressive generation. Moreover, simply matching on-policy trajectories is not enough, since many token-level mismatches have negligible impact on downstream behavior. There is a need for a quantization calibration method that both respects on-policy trajectories of the quantized model and focuses effort on decisions whose changes have high future impact.
AI.method: They propose OnPTQ, an on-policy PTQ framework. It calibrates using trajectories actually visited by the current quantized policy instead of fixed reference sequences. For shared prefixes between dense and quantized models, it: (1) detects boundaries where quantization has eroded the decision margin between candidate tokens; (2) evaluates alternative token choices via short counterfactual rollouts; and (3) defines a Decision--Consequence risk that combines immediate policy discrepancy at a state with the estimated impact (consequence) of choosing different tokens. This risk is used to prioritize calibration on critical states. Additional mechanisms include context anchoring to preserve multimodal behavior and trajectory refresh to realign calibration with the evolving quantized policy. They also derive a theoretical Decision--Consequence bound relating overall behavioral deviation to immediate policy discrepancies and the span of future values conditioned on actions.
AI.result: On multiple Qwen-based vision-language and omni-modal models and across several low-bit quantization settings, OnPTQ shows improved downstream task performance compared to baselines. It reduces the number of cases where model correctness flips relative to dense/FP16 reference models, indicating better behavioral preservation, and it achieves this without modifying the deployed inference graph.
AI.conclusion: OnPTQ demonstrates that explicitly modeling autoregressive feedback and prioritizing high-impact decision points during PTQ leads to better quantized multimodal LLMs. By calibrating on on-policy trajectories, using Decision--Consequence risk to target critical states, and maintaining alignment through context anchoring and trajectory refresh, it can significantly mitigate behavior degradation under low-bit quantization while keeping deployment-time inference unchanged.

title: Cross-Linguistic Effects in Bilingual Phoneme BabyLMs
comment: 13 pages, 8 figures, 3 tables; Accepted at the 2nd BabyLM Workshop at EMNLP 2026
summary: Cross-linguistic effects are a central topic in bilingual first-language acquisition. Artificial learners can help investigate L1-L2 interactions by enabling controlled comparisons across language combinations and learning conditions. Recent work explores this direction by training bilingual language models under developmentally plausible constraints. However, human and model learners still diverge in fundamental ways, with one major difference being input modality: children learn primarily from spoken input, whereas language models are typically trained on orthographic text. To reduce this gap, researchers have trained models on phonemic representations of speech. In this work, we combine these research directions to train bilingual BabyLMs with phonemic input. We keep English fixed as the L2 and vary the L1 across German, Swedish, Persian, and Basque, selected to represent contrasting combinations of syntactic and phoneme-inventory distance from English. Our results show stronger L1-related variation in grammatical learning trajectories under phonemic than orthographic input, while early lexical differences align with phoneme-inventory similarity.

AI.tldr: The paper trains small bilingual language models on phonemic input to study how a learner’s first language (L1) affects learning English (L2), finding that phonemic input amplifies L1-driven grammatical differences and that early vocabulary effects track phoneme-inventory similarity.
AI.motivation: Bilingual children’s two languages influence each other, but it is hard to control all variables in human studies. Artificial learners let researchers systematically vary language combinations and learning conditions to probe cross-linguistic effects. Prior work uses bilingual language models under child-like constraints, yet a key mismatch remains: children mostly hear spoken language, whereas models are trained on written text. Some recent work closes this gap by training on phonemic representations. This paper aims to merge these strands—bilingual learning and phonemic input—to better approximate bilingual child language acquisition and clarify how L1 properties shape L2 development.
AI.method: The authors train “BabyLM”-style small language models in bilingual settings where English is always the L2, and the L1 is one of German, Swedish, Persian, or Basque. These L1s are chosen to span different syntactic profiles and different phoneme-inventory distances from English. Models are trained not on orthographic text but on phonemic transcriptions of the input languages, under developmentally plausible constraints on data and model size. They then compare learning trajectories, focusing on grammatical development and lexical (vocabulary) acquisition, across the different L1–English pairings and across phonemic vs orthographic training conditions.
AI.result: When trained on phonemic input, bilingual BabyLMs show stronger variation in how their grammar learning unfolds depending on which L1 they are paired with, compared with models trained on orthographic text. In contrast, early lexical learning differences across language pairs primarily reflect how similar each L1’s phoneme inventory is to English: languages that sound more like English at the phonemic level support faster or easier early word learning in English.
AI.conclusion: Using phonemic instead of orthographic input brings artificial learners closer to spoken-language conditions and reveals more pronounced L1-driven differences in grammatical development. At the same time, vocabulary learning effects correlate with phonological similarity between languages. This suggests that input modality and phonological structure critically shape cross-linguistic influence in bilingual acquisition, and that phonemic BabyLMs are a promising tool for modeling bilingual child language learning.

title: The Default Trap: Rethinking Plan Evaluation in Tool-Using LLM Agents
summary: An executor can respond strongly to a change in a supplied plan's priority while showing a small change in the same information-selection probability when a default-aligned whole plan is removed. We call the risk of interpreting the latter as weak responsiveness to alternative priorities the default trap. We compare paired plans that prioritize different information targets with a shared no-plan reference. An accounting identity relates these distinct behavioral contrasts. Across 3,200 decision windows on 160 selected Retail, Airline, and AgentDojo tasks, switching priorities strongly redirects two models' choices, while the two plan-versus-default contrasts differ. In 2,160 additional windows, reversing account-list order shifts default target selection by 63.3-98.3 percentage points; priority-switching effects remain 96.7-100.0 points in either order. A separate 3,240-window component study finds strong control under single priority sentences, with effects of additional text varying by group and direction. Finally, 1,080 full-task episodes yield observed success differences of -19.4 to +8.3 points relative to no plan. All Retail and Airline success intervals include zero; AgentDojo results describe four fixed application worlds. These findings support joint reporting of priority responsiveness, presentation-dependent defaults, and task success and cost.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how AI executors respond to priority changes in plans versus default behaviors, identifying a “default trap” where weak-looking responses to plan removal can be misread as low priority sensitivity.
AI.motivation: To understand and correctly measure how decision-making systems (executors) respond to changes in task priorities, and to show that common evaluation based only on plan-vs-default comparisons can be misleading because of default-aligned behaviors.
AI.method: The authors define the “default trap” and an accounting identity linking different behavioral contrasts. They then run large-scale experiments (thousands of decision windows and over a thousand full-task episodes) on Retail, Airline, and AgentDojo tasks. They compare paired plans that emphasize different information targets against a shared no-plan baseline, manipulate priority sentences and text length, and reverse account-list order to study default effects and plan responsiveness.
AI.result: Switching stated priorities strongly redirects model choices, indicating high sensitivity to priority changes. However, the behavioral differences between plan-vs-default conditions are smaller and sensitive to presentation (e.g., list order), showing strong default effects. Priority-switching effects remain very large regardless of order, while success rates relative to no-plan vary from moderately worse to slightly better, with many confidence intervals including zero (no clear effect).
AI.conclusion: Evaluating executors only by comparing plan conditions to a default can misdiagnose their responsiveness to priorities because of strong presentation-dependent defaults. Reliable assessment should jointly report (1) responsiveness to explicit priority changes, (2) how defaults shift with presentation, and (3) task-level success and cost outcomes.

title: LLM unbranding: Erasing Commercial Identity while Preserving Generic Utility
summary:
Establishing unbranding as a critical practice to prevent visual logos from acquiring negative connotations is standard in image generation. Large Language Models (LLMs) now face a parallel and emerging challenge. These models frequently generate brand descriptions within diverse contexts. This frequency introduces significant risks, such as trademark dilution, false attribution, and brand defamation. In response, we formally define the novel task of LLM Unbranding. We specifically address the complex challenge of managing trade dress within textual outputs. This involves neutralizing characteristic language, slogans, and stylistic markers that define brand identity. Crucially, these elements are less evident than explicit visual logos. To benchmark this task, we introduce a comprehensive evaluation dataset incorporating prominent brands from multiple commercial domains. We rigorously evaluate existing state-of-the-art machine unlearning models using this benchmark. This evaluation identifies their limitations in selective textual unbranding. Finally, we propose MUTE, a novel inference-time method that effectively neutralizes textual trade dress while preserving the LLM's general capabilities and utility. By leveraging an iterative refinement loop, MUTE systematically optimizes system instructions to safely eliminate brand leakage without requiring fragile parameter updates.
  Code and dataset: The evaluation dataset and code for LLM Unbranding are available at https://github.com/KajetanOzog/LLM_unbranding. The implementation of MUTE is available at https://github.com/KajetanOzog/MUTE.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces and formalizes “LLM Unbranding,” the task of preventing language models from leaking or mimicking brand-specific textual identity, and proposes MUTE, an inference-time method that neutralizes brand trade dress while preserving general model performance.
AI.motivation: As LLMs increasingly generate text involving brands, they risk trademark dilution, false attribution, and defamation by reproducing or inventing brand-like language, slogans, and styles. Existing unbranding practices focus on images and logos, leaving a gap for textual brand identity (trade dress), which is more subtle yet legally and ethically important to control.
AI.method: The authors (1) formally define the LLM Unbranding task focused on textual trade dress, (2) build an evaluation dataset covering many well-known brands across domains, (3) benchmark state-of-the-art machine unlearning approaches on this dataset to assess their ability to selectively suppress brand-related content, and (4) introduce MUTE, an inference-time, iterative refinement loop that automatically optimizes system instructions to reduce brand leakage without modifying model parameters.
AI.result: Experiments on the new benchmark show that existing machine unlearning methods perform poorly at selective textual unbranding, either failing to fully remove brand-specific expressions or harming general model abilities. MUTE, in contrast, more effectively neutralizes textual trade dress while maintaining the LLM’s overall utility, demonstrating better trade-offs between safety and performance.
AI.conclusion: Textual brand identity poses a novel and underexplored risk for LLMs that is not adequately handled by current unlearning techniques. The proposed LLM Unbranding framework and dataset make this challenge measurable, and the MUTE method offers a practical, parameter-free way to suppress brand trade dress at inference time, mitigating legal and reputational risks while preserving the usefulness of the model.

title: Where Does Staleness Accumulate? Pool Aware Effective Staleness Control for Asynchronous RL in LLM Post-Training
summary: Fully asynchronous reinforcement learning (RL) improves resource utilization in large language model post-training by overlapping rollout generation with policy optimization, but it also introduces policy lag as trajectories are generated and queued while the trainer continues to update. We study how this lag accumulates over a trajectory's lifetime and how it can be controlled without sacrificing the wall-clock benefits of asynchronous execution. We decompose trajectory staleness into Generation Staleness, accumulated before rollout completion, and Waiting Staleness, accumulated after a completed trajectory enters the pool. Motivated by this decomposition, we introduce PACE (Pool-Aware Control of Effective Staleness). PACE converts excess pool occupancy into an adaptive rejection budget and ranks completed trajectories using an effective-staleness score that combines Waiting Staleness with prefix-aware Generation Staleness. This avoids penalizing long or interrupted rollouts solely because they span multiple policy versions. In single-turn mathematical reasoning, PACE improves the six-benchmark average validation accuracy by 18.7\% over unfiltered asynchronous RL at the same wall-clock budget and matches synchronous RL performance with 47.1\% less GPU time. PACE also improves validation performance in multi-turn tool-integrated reasoning, outperforming both synchronous and unfiltered asynchronous RL. Further experiments with the mixture-of-experts model and an alternative RL algorithm support its applicability across model architectures and training algorithms.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses policy lag in fully asynchronous reinforcement learning for large language model post-training and proposes PACE, a pool-aware trajectory filtering method that controls effective staleness to retain wall-clock speedups while improving performance.
AI.motivation: Fully asynchronous RL boosts hardware utilization by overlapping data collection and training, but this causes policy lag because trajectories are generated using older policies while the trainer keeps updating. This staleness can hurt learning, especially for complex LLM reasoning tasks. Existing approaches either accept this degradation or revert to more synchronous schemes that lose wall-clock efficiency. The authors aim to understand how lag accumulates and design a mechanism that mitigates its negative effects without giving up the efficiency gains of asynchrony.
AI.method: They analytically decompose trajectory staleness into two components: Generation Staleness (policy lag accumulated during trajectory rollout) and Waiting Staleness (additional lag while completed trajectories wait in a pool before training). Based on this, they propose PACE (Pool-Aware Control of Effective Staleness), which: (1) tracks pool occupancy and converts excess occupancy into an adaptive rejection budget; (2) defines an effective-staleness score for each completed trajectory that combines Waiting Staleness with a prefix-aware treatment of Generation Staleness so that long or interrupted rollouts are not over-penalized just because they span multiple policy versions; and (3) ranks and selectively filters trajectories using this score, discarding the stalest ones while keeping throughput high.
AI.result: On single-turn mathematical reasoning benchmarks, PACE improves average validation accuracy by 18.7% compared with unfiltered asynchronous RL under the same wall-clock budget and achieves parity with synchronous RL while using 47.1% less GPU time. In multi-turn tool-augmented reasoning tasks, PACE also yields better validation performance than both synchronous and unfiltered asynchronous RL. Additional experiments on mixture-of-experts models and with a different RL algorithm show that the benefits of PACE generalize across architectures and RL training setups.
AI.conclusion: By explicitly modeling and controlling trajectory staleness in fully asynchronous RL, PACE recovers or surpasses synchronous performance without sacrificing, and often improving, hardware efficiency. Its pool-aware rejection mechanism and effective-staleness metric allow practitioners to enjoy the throughput advantages of asynchronous training while mitigating the harmful effects of policy lag across a range of LLM architectures and RL algorithms.

title: Bridging Semantic Gaps in RAG through Generated Context Knowledge Fusion
comment: This paper is accepted by NLPCC 2026
summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation has established itself as a fundamental framework in natural language processing, seamlessly integrating information retrieval with the generative capabilities of large language models. However, this process is fundamentally constrained by a critical challenge: semantic space mismatch between queries and retrieved contexts. We propose Knowledge-Aware Semantic Bridging (KASB), a novel framework that improves passage selection quality through semantic space alignment between queries and retrieved documents through intelligent knowledge fusion. Our approach leverages the complementary strengths of generative and retrieval-based knowledge through a multistage process that enhances both relevance and accuracy. We evaluate KASB on three popular open-domain Question Answering datasets to demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Knowledge-Aware Semantic Bridging (KASB), a framework to reduce semantic mismatch between queries and retrieved passages in Retrieval-Augmented Generation, improving passage selection and QA accuracy.
AI.motivation: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems often suffer because the semantic representations of user queries and retrieved documents are misaligned, leading to suboptimal passage selection and weaker QA performance. The authors aim to address this semantic space mismatch so that retrieved contexts better match what generative models need for accurate answers.
AI.method: They propose KASB, which performs semantic space alignment between queries and retrieved passages via knowledge-aware, multistage knowledge fusion. The framework combines generative model knowledge and retrieval-based knowledge, refining query and/or document representations in several stages to better match each other and improve ranking/selection of passages.
AI.result: KASB is evaluated on three standard open-domain QA benchmarks, where it yields better passage selection quality and improved relevance and accuracy of answers compared to baseline RAG systems.
AI.conclusion: Aligning the semantic spaces of queries and retrieved contexts with a knowledge-aware framework like KASB can significantly improve RAG performance, suggesting that intelligent fusion of generative and retrieval-based knowledge is a promising direction for open-domain QA systems.

title: ARC-KV: Amortizing Anchor Search for Reconstruction-Based KV Cache Compaction
summary: Long-context large language model inference is bottlenecked by KV caches that grow linearly with sequence length. This burden is especially severe for long, reusable context prefixes, whose cache must serve many downstream queries. Reconstruction-based methods such as Attention Matching achieve strong downstream task performance with compact KV caches. However, iterative anchor search dominates the compaction cost of OMP-based Attention Matching. This motivates our selective amortization principle of learning a reusable anchor-selection policy across contexts while retaining context-specific reconstruction. In this work, we propose ARC-KV, a novel reconstruction-based KV cache compaction method that follows this principle. To this end, we first train a value-aware indexer to select real-key anchors in a single scoring pass. ARC-KV then applies convex-hull-constrained key merging and fits an attention-mass bias and compact values against the full cache. At inference time, ARC-KV builds the compact cache once per context using the frozen indexer and reuses it for all subsequent queries. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ARC-KV outperforms reported compaction methods in most settings across QuALITY, RULER, and LongBench on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. In particular, at 10% KV retention on QuALITY, ARC-KV improves accuracy from 0.6409 to 0.6474 over Attention Matching while reducing compaction time by a factor of 25.73, from 959.8 s to 37.3 s.

AI.tldr: ARC-KV is a KV-cache compaction method for long-context LLMs that learns a reusable anchor-selection policy to greatly speed up reconstruction-based compression while preserving accuracy.
AI.motivation: Long-context LLM inference is expensive because KV cache memory and computation grow linearly with sequence length, especially for long shared prefixes that must be reused across many queries. Existing reconstruction-based compaction methods like Attention Matching achieve good accuracy with smaller caches, but their iterative anchor search (e.g., OMP) makes compaction very slow. There is a need for a method that keeps the reconstruction quality of these approaches while making cache compaction fast and reusable across contexts.
AI.method: The paper introduces ARC-KV, which follows a selective amortization principle: it learns a reusable anchor-selection policy across contexts while keeping reconstruction steps context-specific. First, a value-aware indexer is trained to select key anchors (real-key positions) in a single scoring pass, avoiding iterative OMP-style search. Then, given these anchors, ARC-KV performs convex-hull-constrained key merging and learns an attention-mass bias plus compact value vectors to approximate the full KV cache. At inference, for each long context, ARC-KV uses the frozen indexer to build a compact KV cache once, then reuses this compact cache for all subsequent queries that share the context prefix.
AI.result: On Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct evaluated over long-context benchmarks QuALITY, RULER, and LongBench, ARC-KV generally outperforms previous cache compaction methods. On QuALITY at 10% KV retention, ARC-KV increases accuracy from 0.6409 (Attention Matching) to 0.6474 while cutting compaction time by 25.73x, from 959.8 seconds to 37.3 seconds. Similar improvements are reported in most other tested settings, showing ARC-KV maintains or improves task performance while drastically reducing compaction cost.
AI.conclusion: ARC-KV demonstrates that learning a reusable, value-aware anchor-selection policy plus efficient reconstruction (via convex-hull-constrained key merging and attention-mass bias fitting) can significantly accelerate KV cache compaction without sacrificing downstream performance. This validates the selective amortization principle for long-context LLMs and suggests that reconstruction-based compaction can be made practical for real-world deployments with frequent reuse of long context prefixes.

title: VLM Fine-Tuning for End-to-End Combinatorial Optimization
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have provided a unified interface for end-to-end combinatorial optimization (CO), but textual serialization alone may obscure spatial and relational structures that are important for generating effective CO solutions. This paper presents a general-purpose vision-language solver that augments textual instance descriptions with input-derived visual representations. A single vision-language model (VLM) is applied across different CO tasks and trained using supervised fine-tuning followed by verifier-guided reinforcement learning. While the visual inputs contain no gold solutions or solution-derived information, our experiments show that the VLM generally improves solution quality over its text-only counterpart, with particularly clear gains on more complex CO problems such as CVRP and JSSP. The advantage of visual information is more pronounced at large problem scales.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a vision-language model (VLM) for combinatorial optimization that augments text with visual representations, improving solution quality over text-only LLMs, especially on complex and large-scale problems.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based combinatorial optimization solvers rely solely on textual serialization of problem instances, which can obscure essential spatial and relational structures. This limitation becomes more severe in complex and large-scale CO tasks, motivating a method that can better capture and exploit structural information beyond text.
AI.method: The authors propose a general-purpose vision-language solver that uses both textual descriptions and automatically derived visual representations of problem instances. They train a single VLM across multiple CO tasks using supervised fine-tuning to learn basic solving behavior, followed by verifier-guided reinforcement learning to further improve solution quality. Visual inputs are constructed without using ground-truth solutions or solution-related labels, ensuring they only encode instance structure.
AI.result: Experiments across various CO benchmarks show that the proposed VLM consistently outperforms a comparable text-only model. The performance gains are most evident in more complex CO problems such as Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem (CVRP) and Job Shop Scheduling Problem (JSSP), and the margin of improvement grows with problem scale.
AI.conclusion: Augmenting LLM-based CO solvers with input-derived visual representations yields a more effective, general-purpose vision-language framework for combinatorial optimization. Visual information, even when not containing any solution labels, helps the model better exploit structural properties of large and complex instances, leading to higher-quality solutions than text-only approaches.

title: Automated Screw Planning for Reduced Pelvic Fractures Based on Statistical Shape Models and Deep Learning
summary: Percutaneous iliosacral screw fixation is an important minimally invasive treatment for unstable pelvic fractures. Because the sacroiliac region has complex anatomy and narrow screw corridors, the accuracy and safety of screw placement directly affect surgical outcomes. Accurate and reliable preoperative screw planning is therefore essential to improve surgical success and reduce intraoperative risks. Conventional preoperative planning typically requires surgeons to determine screw trajectories through manual measurements, a labor-intensive process that depends on subjective clinical experience. To address these challenges, we propose a fully automated pipeline for preoperative iliosacral screw planning in patients with pelvic fractures. Using patient-specific three-dimensional anatomy, the pipeline automatically identifies safe screw corridors and generates individualized insertion trajectories to support clinical preoperative planning. We evaluated the proposed pipeline on 200 clinical cases of pelvic fractures. Compared with conventional manual measurements, the safety margin of the safe insertion corridors increased by 2% across the four screw types, the mean planning time decreased by more than 90%, and the clinical acceptance rate reached 95%.

AI.tldr: An automated preoperative planning pipeline for iliosacral screw fixation that increases safety margin, drastically shortens planning time, and achieves high clinical acceptance.
AI.motivation: Manual preoperative planning for iliosacral screw fixation is labor-intensive, highly dependent on surgeon experience, and challenged by complex sacroiliac anatomy and narrow screw corridors. This creates variability and potential safety risks in screw placement for unstable pelvic fractures. There is a need for an accurate, efficient, and objective planning method that can reliably identify safe screw paths tailored to each patient.
AI.method: The authors develop a fully automated computational pipeline that uses patient-specific 3D pelvic anatomy (likely from CT) to automatically detect safe iliosacral screw corridors and generate individualized insertion trajectories. The system replaces manual measurements with algorithmic assessment of bone corridors and safety margins for four common screw types, enabling automated preoperative planning without direct manual input for each case.
AI.result: On 200 clinical pelvic fracture cases, the automated planning increased the safety margin of safe screw insertion corridors by about 2% for four screw types, reduced mean planning time by over 90% compared to manual planning, and achieved a 95% clinical acceptance rate among surgeons.
AI.conclusion: A fully automated, patient-specific preoperative planning pipeline for iliosacral screw fixation can improve safety margins, greatly reduce planning time, and is highly acceptable to clinicians. This approach can standardize and streamline planning for pelvic fracture surgery, potentially improving outcomes and reducing intraoperative risk.

title: CredWise: A Controlled Agentic Decision-Intelligence Framework for Explainable and Auditable Credit-Risk Assessment
summary: Credit-risk prediction is important in banking, but a prediction alone does not explain why an applicant is risky or how it should be combined with other evidence. This paper presents CredWise, a decision-support framework that integrates credit-risk prediction, probability calibration, explainable artificial intelligence, policy retrieval, SQL analytics, and controlled agent-based workflows. An XGBoost model is trained on Lending Club data (1,345,310 loans, 18 features) using a temporal split: 2007--2016 for training, 2017 for validation, and 2018 for testing. On the 2018 test set, the calibrated model achieved a ROC-AUC of 0.7109, PR-AUC of 0.2993, F1-score of 0.3714, and accuracy of 65.44\%. Calibration reduced the Brier score from 0.2157 to 0.1273 and the expected calibration error from 0.2862 to 0.0585. SHAP explanations were temporally stable, with a Spearman correlation of 0.9959 between 2017 and 2018 feature rankings. On 28 labeled queries covering nine policy sections, FAISS achieved the best Hit@1 (0.929) and MRR (0.964), while all three retrieval methods reached Hit@5 = 1.0. Agent routing achieved 95.6\% accuracy (43 of 45 cases), and the SQL benchmark scored 1.0 on exact-match, execution-success, and result-match across six cases. These results show that CredWise can combine predictions, explanations, policy evidence, and structured analytics in one controlled workflow. It is an academic research prototype, and final decisions remain with a human reviewer.

AI.tldr: CredWise is a research prototype framework that integrates calibrated credit-risk prediction, explainability, policy retrieval, SQL analytics, and agent-based workflows to support human credit decisions.
AI.motivation: In banking, standard credit-risk prediction models output risk scores but do not explain why an applicant is risky, how reliable the probabilities are, or how to systematically combine model outputs with institutional policies and other structured evidence. There is a need for a comprehensive decision-support framework that not only predicts risk but also calibrates probabilities, provides stable explanations, retrieves relevant policy guidance, and orchestrates these components in a controlled, auditable workflow so that human reviewers can make better-informed credit decisions.
AI.method: The authors build CredWise, a modular framework that integrates: (1) an XGBoost credit-risk model trained on Lending Club data with a temporal train/validation/test split; (2) probability calibration to improve reliability of predicted default probabilities (evaluated with Brier score and expected calibration error); (3) SHAP-based explainable AI to interpret model predictions and assess temporal stability of feature importance; (4) policy retrieval using several methods, including FAISS, evaluated on labeled queries and policy sections using Hit@k and MRR; (5) SQL analytics for structured data queries, evaluated via an exact-match and execution-success benchmark; and (6) controlled agent-based workflows for routing tasks to appropriate agents, evaluated by routing accuracy across labeled cases.
AI.result: On the 2018 test set, the calibrated XGBoost model achieved ROC-AUC 0.7109, PR-AUC 0.2993, F1-score 0.3714, and accuracy 65.44%. Calibration substantially improved probability quality, reducing the Brier score from 0.2157 to 0.1273 and expected calibration error from 0.2862 to 0.0585. SHAP-based explanations were highly temporally stable, with Spearman correlation 0.9959 between 2017 and 2018 feature rankings. For policy retrieval on 28 labeled queries over nine policy sections, the FAISS-based method achieved Hit@1 of 0.929 and MRR of 0.964, while all retrieval methods reached Hit@5 = 1.0. Agent routing within workflows reached 95.6% accuracy (43/45 cases), and the SQL benchmark scored 1.0 on exact-match, execution success, and result match across six test cases.
AI.conclusion: CredWise successfully demonstrates that calibrated credit-risk prediction, explainability, policy retrieval, SQL analytics, and agent-based task routing can be integrated into a single, controlled decision-support workflow. The system delivers reasonably accurate and well-calibrated predictions, stable explanations, effective policy retrieval, and reliable workflow orchestration. However, it is presented as an academic prototype, with the explicit stance that final lending decisions should remain with human reviewers, positioning CredWise as a tool to augment rather than replace human judgment in credit-risk evaluation.

title: When Upstream Messages Override Correct Answers: A Controlled Study of Multi-Agent LLM Collaboration
summary: Multi-agent LLM systems rely on message passing among specialized agents to accomplish complex tasks. However, an upstream agent may provide useful information or an incorrect answer that causes a downstream agent to override a correct answer supported by its own evidence. Prior work has not clearly separated the benefits of communication from the damage caused by incorrect messages. We study this problem with controlled experiments across five benchmarks and five receivers, keeping the downstream task and evidence fixed while comparing answers under three conditions: no message, the upstream agent's original message, or a message with the opposite conclusion. Our experiments reveal three key findings. First, messages often help when the downstream agent would otherwise answer incorrectly. Second, messages can also hurt: when the downstream agent would answer correctly without a message, an incorrect upstream message changes the answer in up to 32% of cases. Third, in 94% of audited harmful cases, the downstream agent copies the upstream's specific wrong answer--a pattern we term answer substitution. Removing unreliable messages recovers part of the lost accuracy, suggesting that communication should be selective based on upstream reliability and the evidence already available to the downstream agent.

AI.tldr: The paper empirically studies when and how communication between specialized LLM agents helps or harms performance, isolating the effect of upstream messages on downstream answers.
AI.motivation: In multi-agent LLM systems, agents pass messages to each other to solve complex tasks. While this communication can provide useful hints, it can also propagate and amplify errors: a wrong upstream answer can override a correct downstream answer even when the downstream agent has sufficient evidence. Prior work hasn’t cleanly distinguished the genuine benefits of communication from the harms caused specifically by incorrect messages, so it’s unclear how often and in what ways communication is actually beneficial versus risky.
AI.method: The authors run controlled experiments across five benchmarks and five types of downstream receiver models. For each task, they keep the downstream task and evidence fixed and systematically compare the downstream agent’s answers under three conditions: (1) no upstream message, (2) the real upstream agent’s message, and (3) a counterfactual message with the opposite conclusion. This design isolates the causal impact of the content and correctness of upstream messages. They then analyze performance differences and qualitatively audit error cases.
AI.result: They find: (1) upstream messages frequently improve performance when the downstream agent would otherwise answer incorrectly; (2) misleading upstream messages can significantly harm performance—when the downstream would be correct unaided, an incorrect upstream message flips the answer in up to 32% of cases; and (3) in 94% of such harmful cases, the downstream agent repeats the upstream’s specific wrong answer, a behavior they term “answer substitution.” They also show that filtering out unreliable messages can partially recover lost accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Communication between LLM agents is a double-edged sword: messages can rescue wrong answers but also induce incorrect “answer substitution,” where a downstream agent abandons its own supported answer in favor of an upstream’s wrong one. Because the downstream agent is highly suggestible, multi-agent systems must incorporate selective or reliability-aware communication, taking into account both upstream trustworthiness and the downstream agent’s existing evidence, to realize the benefits of cooperation while mitigating error propagation.

title: Follow the Entities: A Corpus Map for Agentic Search
summary: Answering questions and completing tasks over large document collections often requires connecting evidence spread across multiple documents, such as a project's approval recorded in one, its requirements in another, and its latest status in a third. Recent LLM agents approach this by iteratively searching the full corpus rather than reading only a fixed set of top-ranked documents. However, when the corpus is exposed only as a flat collection of files, a relevant document gives no indication of how it relates to others, so the agent must rediscover these relationships for every query, often missing complementary evidence while simultaneously consuming substantial additional tokens. To address this, we introduce CorpusMap, a navigation layer that organizes the corpus around its recurring entities, which are identifiable from the documents themselves and can link a single document to many others across sources. Specifically, CorpusMap represents each recurring entity as an Entity Page that aggregates information about it and links to every document that refers to it, forming a graph between entities and documents that the agent can traverse to gather otherwise disconnected evidence. Moreover, since CorpusMap is constructed offline by resolving mentions of the same entity across documents, its links are shared across queries rather than rediscovered repeatedly at inference time. Using 7 different models with 3 benchmark datasets, we show that CorpusMap improves both evidence discovery and answer quality over raw-corpus agentic search while using fewer tokens on average, and further outperforms 4 alternative navigation layers, suggesting that entities serve as effective anchors for navigating large document collections.

AI.tldr: CorpusMap is a navigation layer for large text corpora that organizes documents around entities to help LLM agents find and connect evidence more accurately and efficiently.
AI.motivation: LLM agents answering questions over large document collections must often combine evidence scattered across multiple files. Current agents repeatedly search flat corpora, lacking persistent structure that reveals how documents relate via shared entities. This leads to missed complementary evidence and high token costs. A better way to expose relationships in the corpus is needed so that agents can navigate more intelligently and reuse this structure across queries.
AI.method: The authors build CorpusMap, an offline navigation layer that identifies recurring entities across the corpus and resolves mentions of the same entity to a single node. For each entity, they create an Entity Page that aggregates information about it and links to all documents mentioning it. This yields a bipartite graph of entities and documents that LLM agents traverse at inference time: starting from initial hits, they move through entity pages to discover connected documents and gather evidence. The system is evaluated with 7 different LLMs on 3 multi-document QA/task benchmarks and compared against raw-corpus agentic search and four alternative navigation layers.
AI.result: Across 3 benchmark datasets and 7 LLMs, CorpusMap leads to better evidence discovery and higher answer quality than standard agentic search over an unstructured corpus, while reducing average token usage. It also outperforms four other navigation-layer baselines, demonstrating that entity-centric organization is particularly effective for guiding retrieval and reasoning over large collections.
AI.conclusion: Organizing a corpus around recurring entities and exposing it as a graph of entity pages and documents provides an effective, reusable navigation layer for LLM agents. CorpusMap enables agents to connect otherwise disconnected evidence more reliably and cheaply than flat search and outperforms alternative navigation schemes, indicating that entities are strong anchors for navigating large document collections.

title: IronLLM: Forging Compact Edge-Native Language Models for Real-Time Embodied Intelligence
summary: We present IronLLM-0.6B, a 654M-parameter language model designed for efficient on-device inference. IronLLM-0.6B combines a hybrid attention architecture with X-MTP, a lightweight shared-KV multi-token prediction design that eliminates per-depth KV-cache replay and employs a lightweight verification head for rollback-free drafting, achieving a 1.48x decoding speedup. The model is pretrained on approximately 6.2 trillion tokens using a quality-oriented data pipeline and is further post-trained with Multi-Domain On-Policy Distillation to integrate capabilities from domain-specialized teachers. To better meet the low-latency requirements of on-device scenarios, IronLLM-0.6B adopts an Instruct-Only design. Evaluations show that IronLLM-0.6B achieves competitive performance relative to larger models such as Qwen3.5-0.8B and MiniCPM5-1B, while producing more concise responses on many tasks. We further present IronLLM-0.6B-Light, which replaces RMSNorm with Dynamic Tanh and simplifies several computationally expensive components to improve inference and quantization efficiency. Together, the IronLLM models provide an effective performance-efficiency trade-off for resource-constrained deployment.

AI.tldr: IronLLM-0.6B is a 654M-parameter, on-device-optimized language model with a hybrid attention and X-MTP multi-token prediction design, trained on 6.2T tokens and post-trained via multi-domain distillation, offering competitive performance vs slightly larger models and a lighter variant for even better efficiency.
AI.motivation: There is growing demand for capable language models that can run efficiently on resource-constrained, on-device hardware with low latency and strong performance. Existing small models often either underperform or rely on architectures that are not optimized for fast decoding and quantization on edge devices. The authors aim to design a small, instruction-tuned model that achieves a better performance–efficiency trade-off and practical on-device usability, including concise responses and support for efficient deployment.
AI.method: The authors build a 654M-parameter language model, IronLLM-0.6B, using a hybrid attention architecture and X-MTP, a shared-KV multi-token prediction mechanism. X-MTP eliminates per-layer KV-cache replay and uses a lightweight verification head for rollback-free drafting, improving decoding speed. The model is pretrained on about 6.2T tokens with a quality-focused data pipeline, then post-trained via Multi-Domain On-Policy Distillation from specialized teacher models to integrate various domain skills. To meet on-device latency needs, they adopt an Instruct-Only design. They also propose a variant, IronLLM-0.6B-Light, which swaps RMSNorm for Dynamic Tanh and simplifies costly components to boost inference and quantization efficiency.
AI.result: IronLLM-0.6B achieves a 1.48x decoding speedup due to the X-MTP design. Benchmarks indicate that it performs competitively with larger models such as Qwen3.5-0.8B and MiniCPM5-1B, while generating more concise responses across many tasks. The IronLLM-0.6B-Light variant further improves inference and quantization efficiency, though likely with some trade-offs in accuracy (not detailed in the abstract).
AI.conclusion: IronLLM-0.6B and its lightweight variant provide an effective balance between performance and efficiency for resource-constrained, on-device deployment. The combination of hybrid attention, X-MTP multi-token prediction, extensive pretraining, and multi-domain distillation yields a small yet capable instruction-tuned model that rivals slightly larger baselines, offers faster decoding, and supports efficient quantized inference on edge hardware.

title: SemOPT: Fixing Semantic Errors in LLM-based Optimization Modeling via Reward-Guided Search
summary: Operations research supports decision-making in domains such as energy, economics, and healthcare. Solving operations research problems typically begins with optimization modeling, which translates a natural-language problem description into executable solver code. LLMs offer a promising way to automate this process, but they remain prone to errors. In practice, these errors can be divided into two categories: syntactic errors refer to solver code that fails to run successfully or is judged infeasible by the solver; semantic errors refer to solver code that successfully returns an objective value but violates the intent of the original problem. Since semantic errors do not trigger runtime failures, they are difficult to detect and rectify. To address this problem, we introduce SemOPT, a semantic-guided framework for correcting LLM-based optimization models. SemOPT combines a semantic reward model that distinguishes faithful math models from plausible but incorrect ones with an adaptive correction system that applies hierarchical reward-guided search over the modeling space. Experiments on seven optimization modeling benchmarks show that SemOPT establishes a new state of the art and achieves an average 7.6% accuracy improvement over the strongest baseline on complex datasets.

AI.tldr: The paper presents SemOPT, a framework that uses semantic feedback to automatically correct optimization models generated by large language models, significantly improving their accuracy on operations research benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Large language models can translate natural-language descriptions of operations research problems into optimization models, but they often make mistakes. Syntactic errors are easy to catch because the solver fails, but semantic errors are harder since the model runs and returns a value while still misrepresenting the original problem. Detecting and fixing these semantic errors is crucial for safely automating optimization modeling in practical domains like energy, economics, and healthcare.
AI.method: The authors propose SemOPT, which consists of two key components: (1) a semantic reward model trained to distinguish correct, faithful optimization models from plausible but incorrect ones, and (2) an adaptive correction mechanism that performs a hierarchical, reward-guided search over the modeling space to iteratively refine and correct LLM-generated solver code. The framework uses feedback from the reward model to steer modifications of the optimization model toward semantically faithful formulations.
AI.result: On seven optimization modeling benchmarks, including difficult, complex datasets, SemOPT outperforms existing methods. It sets a new state of the art and yields, on average, a 7.6% absolute improvement in accuracy compared with the strongest baseline approach for correcting LLM-generated optimization models.
AI.conclusion: SemOPT demonstrates that incorporating semantic guidance and reward-based search can substantially reduce semantic errors in LLM-generated optimization models. This enables more reliable automation of optimization modeling in operations research, suggesting that semantic reward models and structured search are a promising direction for improving LLM reliability in applied mathematical modeling tasks.

title: State Trace Rationale As Auxiliary Task in Reinforcement Learning
comment: Under review as a conference paper at ICLR 2027
summary: We propose STRAT, an auxiliary task that trains deep reinforcement learning (RL) agents to predict a short textual trace of their own state. Inspired by human spatial navigation, the description combines landmark, route, and survey knowledge, tracking the agent's position, inventory, goals, and immediate progress. Environment rules generate this text online without human labelling. Our method adds a single auxiliary head to a standard policy. Across 60 sparse-reward XLand-MiniGrid tasks, STRAT solves complex environments where standard RL fails outright, while compacting state representations and preventing rank collapse. Beyond performance gains, the predicted trace provides a readable account of agent beliefs at every step for no extra cost.

AI.tldr: They add an auxiliary text-prediction task (STRAT) to RL agents so they learn to describe their own state in words, which improves performance in sparse-reward navigation tasks and yields interpretable internal beliefs.
AI.motivation: Sparse-reward, partially observable environments make it hard for deep RL agents to learn compact, structured state representations and to remain stable (avoiding representation rank collapse). Humans, however, use rich internal narratives about landmarks, routes, and goals when navigating. The authors want to leverage a similar structured, language-like representation to help RL agents learn better and provide interpretability, without relying on costly human annotations.
AI.method: Introduce STRAT, an auxiliary head attached to a standard RL policy network. Alongside maximizing reward, the agent is trained to predict a short textual ":trace" that describes its current state (position, inventory, goals, local progress) using automatically generated environment text. The environment provides rule-based textual labels online, so no human labelling is needed. The auxiliary head learns to map internal representations to these text descriptions, encouraging the encoder to organize information about landmarks, routes, and survey-like knowledge. They evaluate across 60 sparse-reward XLand-MiniGrid tasks and compare against standard deep RL baselines without STRAT.
AI.result: With STRAT, RL agents successfully solve complex sparse-reward navigation tasks in XLand-MiniGrid that standard RL agents fail to solve at all. The learned representations are more compact, and the method prevents representation rank collapse, indicating healthier internal feature structure. At inference time, the model produces a textual trace that matches the agent’s beliefs and progress, at negligible additional computational cost.
AI.conclusion: Training RL agents with STRAT, an auxiliary state-trace text prediction task, substantially improves learning in sparse-reward environments, leading to better performance, more compact and stable representations, and built-in interpretability. Automatically generated textual traces allow the approach to scale without human labeling, and the readable state descriptions offer an ongoing window into the agent’s internal state while it acts.

title: Compiling Learning Problems into Adaptation Programs for Language Models
summary: Model adaptation is typically governed by a fixed recipe, even though different update programs can produce substantially different behavioral outcomes. We introduce adaptation compilation, which reframes where, how, and to what extent a model should adapt as a joint prediction and decision problem. Rather than searching over candidate programs anew for each learning episode, a compiler learns from prior adaptations to predict a vector-valued counterfactual response surface over candidate programs---their expected effects on acquisition, transfer, boundedness, and preservation---and selects a program before adaptation begins. Because this predicted geometry captures multiple behavioral consequences rather than a single winner or scalar score, it can be reused under different downstream priorities without retraining. Across five learning types, preferred programs vary meaningfully across episodes, and this variation is predictable from pre-adaptation information. On Llama-3.1-8B, compiler-selected programs approach exhaustive search while outperforming global and objective-specific defaults. Replication on Gemma-2-9B preserves program heterogeneity and selection headroom, but shows that exploiting this headroom requires accounting for uncertainty when departing from strong defaults. Together, these results show that adaptation search can be amortized across related learning problems, turning prior adaptation experience into a basis for deciding how future learning should occur.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes 'adaptation compilation', a learned system that predicts and selects the best model adaptation program for new learning tasks, amortizing adaptation search across tasks.
AI.motivation: Different adaptation update programs (e.g., fine-tuning strategies, parameter-efficient methods, or training recipes) lead to substantially different behaviors, yet practitioners usually fix a single recipe. Exhaustive search over adaptation programs per task is expensive and task-specific, and existing approaches tend to optimize a single objective. The authors aim to automatically decide how a model should adapt (where, how, and how much) using prior experience, and to capture multiple behavioral trade-offs relevant for downstream use.
AI.method: They frame adaptation selection as a joint prediction-and-decision problem. A 'compiler' is trained on past adaptation episodes to predict a vector-valued counterfactual response surface over candidate adaptation programs. Each program is characterized by expected effects on several behavioral dimensions (acquisition, transfer, boundedness, preservation). For a new episode, the compiler uses pre-adaptation information to estimate this response geometry and then selects an adaptation program before training begins. Because predictions are vector-valued, the same learned geometry can be re-used under different priority weightings without retraining. They evaluate this on multiple learning types and models (Llama-3.1-8B and Gemma-2-9B).
AI.result: Across five learning types, the paper finds substantial variation in which adaptation programs are preferred on a per-episode basis, and that this variation is predictable from pre-adaptation signals. On Llama-3.1-8B, the compiler’s program choices nearly match the performance of exhaustive search while outperforming both global default programs and defaults tuned for specific objectives. On Gemma-2-9B, they observe similar heterogeneity and remaining headroom for program selection, but also find that realizing this headroom safely requires incorporating uncertainty when deviating from strong baseline defaults.
AI.conclusion: Adaptation strategies need not be fixed or re-searched from scratch for every task. By learning a predictor over the behavioral consequences of many candidate adaptation programs, adaptation search can be amortized across related tasks. This enables automated, task-specific selection of adaptation recipes that are competitive with exhaustive search and more flexible with respect to multi-objective trade-offs, effectively turning prior adaptation experience into a policy for how future learning should proceed.

title: WEFT: Scaling Tool-Use Post-Training for General-Purpose Agents
summary: Recent efforts to scale tool-use post-training have largely centered on the synthesis of executable environments, which constitute only one component of a broader agentic interaction system comprising the environment, task, agent harness, and evaluator. Scaling environments in isolation, however, does not guarantee commensurate gains in model performance, because reliable learning signals depend on coherent interactions among all components of the agentic interaction system. To address this problem, we introduce WEFT (Whole-system Evolution For Tool-use Post-training), which couples scalable agentic interaction system construction, execution-driven self-evolution, and stable post-training. WEFT scales agentic interaction system construction across environment breadth, task complexity, and interaction diversity. Execution-driven self-evolution iteratively uses execution traces and state evidence to attribute failures and revise the responsible components, with fresh rollouts evaluating the changes and providing evidence for subsequent evolution rounds. For stable post-training at scale, WEFT addresses both optimization and execution reliability: prefix-preserving sampling retains verified progress and atomic-turn credit assignment localizes learning signals, while MegaMCP maintains isolated, recoverable state across concurrent rollouts over shared tool services. Extensive experiments across various models and benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of WEFT for tool-use post-training. WEFT-8B and WEFT-14B outperform all evaluated matched-size environment-scaling baselines on BFCL V4, $τ^2$-Bench, and Claw-Eval. In particular, WEFT-14B improves over Agent-World-14B by 6.41, 2.23, and 12.27 percentage points. WEFT-35B-A3B further extends these gains to more challenging long-horizon workflow benchmarks, including Toolathlon-Verified and AutomationBench.

AI.tldr: WEFT is a framework for whole-system evolution in tool-use post-training that jointly scales environments, tasks, agent harnesses, and evaluators, using execution-driven self-evolution and stable post-training techniques to reliably improve tool-using LLMs.
AI.motivation: Existing approaches to scaling tool-use post-training mostly focus on synthesizing and enlarging executable environments alone. However, tool-use performance depends on an entire agentic interaction system including environment, tasks, harness, and evaluation. Scaling just the environment can give poor or noisy learning signals if the other components are not aligned or sufficiently robust. The authors are motivated to build a method that scales all components coherently and turns real execution feedback into reliable training signals, so that larger, more diverse tool-use setups actually translate into better model performance.
AI.method: The paper proposes WEFT (Whole-system Evolution For Tool-use Post-training). WEFT has three key elements: (1) scalable construction of agentic interaction systems, expanding along three axes: environment breadth (more tools/services), task complexity (harder, longer-horizon tasks), and interaction diversity (richer multi-step interactions); (2) execution-driven self-evolution, where execution traces and state evidence from rollouts are used to diagnose where failures occur (environment, task spec, harness, evaluator, or model) and to revise the responsible components; changes are then validated by new rollouts, and this process iterates; (3) stable post-training mechanisms, including prefix-preserving sampling to keep validated partial solutions while exploring continuations, atomic-turn credit assignment that localizes gradients/rewards to specific turns in the interaction, and MegaMCP, an infrastructure layer that keeps rollout states isolated and recoverable while sharing tool services across many concurrent runs.
AI.result: In experiments over multiple models and benchmarks, WEFT-based post-training improves tool-use performance compared to strong baselines that only scale environments. Specifically, WEFT-8B and WEFT-14B consistently surpass all matched-size environment-scaling baselines on BFCL V4, τ^2-Bench, and Claw-Eval. WEFT-14B outperforms Agent-World-14B by 6.41, 2.23, and 12.27 percentage points on these benchmarks, respectively. A larger configuration, WEFT-35B-A3B, further improves results on harder long-horizon workflow benchmarks such as Toolathlon-Verified and AutomationBench, demonstrating scalability to complex, multi-step tool-use tasks.
AI.conclusion: Treating tool-use post-training as a whole-system problem—jointly evolving environments, tasks, harnesses, and evaluators—yields more reliable learning signals and better-performing agents than approaches that scale only the environment. WEFT’s execution-driven self-evolution and stable post-training techniques enable robust scaling across breadth, complexity, and interaction diversity, leading to substantial performance gains on diverse tool-use and long-horizon workflow benchmarks.

title: Look What You Made Us Cluster: Hate Narrative Extraction from Reddit Discourse
summary: Narrative extraction allows us to identify online hate narratives, supporting the construction of rigorous detection systems. Existing computational approaches, however, are limited in precision as they rely on semantic representations, which tend to capture only surface-level meaning. To detect more precise and interpretable narratives, we present an extraction pipeline that represents narratives as entity-evaluation pairs. Narratives are extracted using a Large Language Model (LLM) reasoning process that extends Aspect-Based Sentiment Analysis, identifying the aspect, classifying its judgement type as the basis for evaluation, and deriving the evaluation accordingly. Extracted narratives are then clustered using Leiden, following which clusters are resolved to an intended level of granularity through an LLM-guided refinement process. We illustrate this narrative pipeline with English Reddit comments from 2024 that criticize Taylor Swift, analyzing a representative cluster that exhibits hate speech patterns to demonstrate its interpretive value.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a narrative-extraction pipeline that uses LLM reasoning and clustering to detect precise, interpretable hate narratives online, illustrated on Reddit comments criticizing Taylor Swift.
AI.motivation: Existing computational methods for detecting hate narratives online rely heavily on semantic representations, which mainly capture surface-level meanings and result in low precision and limited interpretability. There is a need for approaches that can represent and extract narratives in a more structured, fine-grained, and explainable way to improve hate speech detection systems.
AI.method: The authors model narratives as entity–evaluation pairs. They design an extraction pipeline where a Large Language Model performs a reasoning process similar to and extending Aspect-Based Sentiment Analysis: (1) it identifies the relevant aspect (entity), (2) classifies the type of judgement used as the basis for an evaluation, and (3) derives the specific evaluation. These extracted narratives are then clustered using the Leiden community detection algorithm. Finally, an LLM-guided refinement step adjusts and resolves clusters to achieve a desired level of narrative granularity.
AI.result: The pipeline is applied to English Reddit comments from 2024 criticizing Taylor Swift. The system successfully extracts and clusters narratives into coherent groups. A representative cluster that clearly shows hate speech patterns is analyzed qualitatively to demonstrate that the extracted entity–evaluation narratives are precise and interpretable, revealing structured hate narratives rather than only surface-level sentiment.
AI.conclusion: Representing narratives as entity–evaluation pairs and extracting them via an LLM-based, ABSA-inspired reasoning process, followed by Leiden clustering and LLM-guided refinement, yields more precise and interpretable hate narrative detection than standard semantic methods. The illustrative case study on Reddit comments about Taylor Swift suggests that this approach can support more rigorous and explainable hate speech detection systems and can be adapted to other domains and targets.

title: Beyond Sub-Gaussian Detector Scores: Robust Weighted Profile-Loss Change Point Detection for Human-LLM Text Segmentation
summary: Mixed human-LLM documents require locating authorship transitions from detector scores whose reliability varies across text units. Existing weighted mean contrasts are vulnerable to extreme scores, while directly replacing means with robust centers obscures how a misplaced boundary changes the population objective. We propose Robust Weighted Profile-Loss Change Point Detection (RWCP), which combines capped reliability weights, Huber profile gains, and narrowest-over-threshold search in reliability coordinates. Our key analysis expresses the population gap between a true and a displaced split as a merge cost, avoiding a closed-form solution for the nonlinear center of a mixed segment. Under explicit curvature, spacing, and dependence conditions, core RWCP recovers the number of changes and localizes their boundaries; its quadratic-loss limit recovers squared weighted CUSUM. We also study RWCP-R, a separately evaluated decoder that shares source centers across nonadjacent passages. Across five retrospective cached-score benchmark families, core RWCP reduces family-macro WindowDiff by 17.6\% relative to weighted change-point detection, and RWCP-R lowers it further. Boundary recovery improves most clearly for isolated changes, while both fixed configurations miss changes in collaborative and densely alternating text.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces RWCP, a robust change-point detection method tailored to mixed human-LLM documents, improving boundary detection between human and LLM-authored segments by handling unreliable detector scores and outliers.
AI.motivation: In mixed human-LLM documents, we need to find where authorship switches occur, but we only observe noisy, reliability-varying detector scores. Existing weighted mean contrast methods are sensitive to extreme scores, and straightforward robustification (e.g., replacing means with robust centers) breaks the interpretability of how boundary misplacement affects the objective. There is thus a need for a principled, robust, and interpretable change-point detection method that uses reliability information effectively.
AI.method: The authors propose Robust Weighted Profile-Loss Change Point Detection (RWCP). RWCP uses capped reliability weights to limit the influence of highly uncertain scores, employs Huber profile gains to robustly measure changes while retaining some sensitivity, and conducts a narrowest-over-threshold search in a transformed space defined by reliability coordinates. Analytically, they characterize the population objective by expressing the gap between the true and a displaced split as a merge cost, avoiding the need for closed-form solutions of nonlinear robust centers in mixed segments. They provide theoretical guarantees under curvature, spacing, and dependence conditions, showing that RWCP recovers both the number and locations of change points and that, in the quadratic-loss limit, RWCP reduces to squared weighted CUSUM. They also introduce RWCP-R, a decoder variant that reuses estimated source centers across nonadjacent passages, evaluated separately from core RWCP.
