Extreme rewards can collapse the contrast among clean responses after group normalization, while token-level log-ratio perturbations can alter sequence weights and clipping decisions. We introduce RoVR-GSPO, a dual-channel robust optimizer that addresses these failure modes separately. Its reward channel combines robust reference estimation with bounded residual credit, while its ratio channel uses differentiable SoftRoVR aggregation to construct robust sequence weights. We provide stability and efficiency analyses for both channels. Experiments on mathematical reasoning, long-context summarization, and tool-call annotation show consistent improvements over GSPO, while controlled perturbation studies demonstrate stronger robustness to reward contamination and token-ratio anomalies.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes RoVR-GSPO, a robust variant of group-relative policy optimization that improves stability and robustness to outliers in rewards and token-level likelihood ratios, yielding better performance on several language model tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing group-relative policy optimization methods rely on reward-based advantages and sequence-level likelihood weights that are fragile to outliers. Extreme rewards can dominate group normalization and erase useful contrast between normal samples, while noisy token-level log-ratio values can distort sequence weights and clipping decisions. This fragility harms stability, efficiency, and robustness when training language models with noisy or adversarial feedback, motivating a more robust optimization scheme.
AI.method: The authors introduce RoVR-GSPO, a dual-channel robust policy optimizer. It separates the handling of two core ingredients: the reward channel and the ratio (likelihood) channel. In the reward channel, they build a robust estimate of the reference reward and then allocate only bounded residual credit to mitigate the influence of extreme rewards. In the ratio channel, they replace standard aggregation of token-level log-ratios with a differentiable SoftRoVR aggregation that yields robust sequence-level weights, making clipping and updates less sensitive to local perturbations. They also provide theoretical analysis of stability and computational efficiency for both channels.
AI.result: Across tasks including mathematical reasoning, long-context summarization, and tool-call annotation, RoVR-GSPO consistently outperforms the baseline GSPO method. Additional controlled experiments with artificially perturbed rewards and token ratios show that RoVR-GSPO maintains performance and stable training under contamination, whereas GSPO degrades more severely. This empirically validates both improved robustness and better practical performance.
AI.conclusion: RoVR-GSPO effectively addresses key robustness issues in group-relative policy optimization by decoupling and hardening the reward and ratio channels. The combination of robust reward reference estimation, bounded residual credit, and SoftRoVR-based ratio aggregation yields a more stable and efficient training procedure that is less sensitive to outliers and local anomalies, leading to stronger and more reliable performance in several language model applications.

title: RunyaNER: Auxiliary Language Selection for Runyankore NER
comment: Accepted to the 6th Workshop on Multilingual Representation Learning (MRL 2026) at EMNLP 2026. Camera-ready version. 4 figures
summary: Cross-lingual zero-shot transfer and multilingual fine-tuning are promising approaches for NLP tasks such as Named Entity Recognition (NER) in low-resource languages, but in the absence of target language benchmarks, it is unclear which auxiliary language selection strategy leads to the best transfer. We introduce RunyaNER, the first publicly available NER benchmark for the East African language Runyankore, and use it to investigate the choice of which languages to use for transfer. Created with a semi-automated pipeline and fully manually verified, RunyaNER contains over 237k annotated words across 30k sentences. We benchmark pretrained models on RunyaNER, establishing that our dataset is of sufficient quality and size to produce effective Runyankore NER models. We then use RunyaNER to investigate auxiliary language selection in cross-lingual zero-shot and multilingual fine-tuning settings. Our experiments show that while transfer performance is highly sensitive to auxiliary language selection, embedding-based measures computed from labelled training spans correlate more strongly with downstream transfer performance than traditional linguistic features based on metadata or typology. By releasing RunyaNER and providing a systematic analysis of auxiliary language selection strategies, this work contributes both a new benchmark resource and practical insights for multilingual transfer in low-resource settings.

AI.tldr: They create RunyaNER, the first NER benchmark for Runyankore, and use it to study which auxiliary languages best support cross-lingual transfer, finding embedding-based similarity predicts transfer performance better than typological or metadata features.
AI.motivation: Cross-lingual transfer and multilingual fine-tuning could help build NER systems for low-resource languages like Runyankore, but without a benchmark it is impossible to properly evaluate models or systematically compare which auxiliary languages give the best transfer performance. Existing language selection strategies rely largely on typological or metadata-based similarity, whose effectiveness is unclear.
AI.method: 1) Construct RunyaNER, a Runyankore NER dataset, using a semi-automated pipeline followed by full manual verification, resulting in 237k annotated words across 30k sentences. 2) Benchmark several pretrained multilingual models on RunyaNER to validate dataset quality and to obtain transfer performance measurements. 3) Run controlled experiments on cross-lingual zero-shot and multilingual fine-tuning setups with different auxiliary language choices. 4) Compute and compare various language similarity measures, including traditional linguistic features (e.g., typology, metadata) and embedding-based measures derived from labeled training spans, and correlate these with observed transfer performance.
AI.result: RunyaNER is shown to be large and clean enough to train effective NER models for Runyankore. Experiments reveal that cross-lingual transfer performance is highly sensitive to which auxiliary languages are chosen. Embedding-based similarity measures calculated from labeled spans correlate much more strongly with actual transfer performance than do traditional linguistic or typological similarity metrics, indicating they are better predictors of which languages will transfer well.
AI.conclusion: RunyaNER provides the first public NER benchmark for Runyankore and enables rigorous evaluation of NER models for this low-resource language. The study demonstrates that auxiliary language selection critically impacts cross-lingual transfer, and that embedding-based similarity metrics offer a more reliable guide for choosing auxiliary languages than typological or metadata-based linguistic features. This delivers both a valuable new resource and practical guidance for building NER systems in low-resource, multilingual settings.

title: REALHOP: Rethinking Multi-Hop Reasoning Evaluation via Behavioral Auditing
summary: Complex questions often require multi-hop reasoning that connects facts distributed across sources or distant regions of a long context through intermediate steps. Benchmarks commonly evaluate this ability with questions built around predefined reasoning chains, treating a correct answer as evidence that the intended composition was used. Yet answer correctness alone leaves open whether success depends on the evidence associated with each intended step: models may instead rely on memorized associations, shorter paths, or partial evidence. We examine this dependence using the Behavioral Necessity Rate (BNR), which measures how often targeted evidence removal prevents answer recovery on initially correct instances. Across five existing benchmarks, panel-mean BNR ranges from 16.6% to 48.9%, exposing a substantial gap between annotated structure and observed dependence. Guided by this diagnosis, we introduce REALHOP, a diagnose-construct-verify framework that rebinds entities, factorizes selected relations, adds complete competing paths, and places evidence at traceable locations. Structural and semantic checks precede freezing; behavioral interventions follow. On 790 paired MuSiQue questions, REALHOP raises panel-mean BNR from 27.4% to 94.4% while retaining high Full accuracy. It also yields high BNR on REALHOP-FRAMES and REALHOP-LONGBENCH. On 216 long-context questions, the matched multiple-choice spread across 16 models grows from 13.9 to 59.2 points and persists under repeated open-ended evaluation. Together, these results show that a conceptually coherent chain and a correct final answer do not by themselves establish multi-hop reasoning. Verifying that success depends on every intended hop is therefore as fundamental to multi-hop evaluation as measuring answer accuracy itself.

AI.tldr: The paper critiques existing multi-hop QA benchmarks, showing that correct final answers often do not rely on all annotated reasoning steps, and proposes REALHOP, a framework and datasets that enforce and verify dependence on every hop using a new metric, Behavioral Necessity Rate (BNR).
AI.motivation: Multi-hop reasoning is central to complex question answering, but current benchmarks assume that if a model gets the final answer right, it must have followed the intended reasoning chain. This is questionable because models might exploit shortcuts such as memorized associations, spurious correlations, or partial evidence. There is a need to directly test whether models’ success actually depends on each annotated reasoning step, and to construct datasets where this dependence is enforced and measurable.
AI.method: The authors introduce Behavioral Necessity Rate (BNR), defined by targeted removal of evidence supporting specific reasoning hops and measuring how often this prevents the model from recovering the correct answer on instances it could initially solve. They apply BNR to five existing multi-hop benchmarks to quantify the gap between annotated chains and true dependence. Then they propose REALHOP, a diagnose-construct-verify framework that: (1) diagnoses weaknesses using BNR; (2) constructs new questions by rebinding entities, factorizing relations, adding fully specified competing paths, and placing evidence in traceable context locations; and (3) verifies via structural/semantic checks and behavioral interventions that each hop is necessary. They test REALHOP on variants derived from MuSiQue, frame-based data, and long-context benchmarks, using multiple models and both multiple-choice and open-ended settings.
AI.result: Across five existing multi-hop benchmarks, the panel-mean BNR is low (16.6–48.9%), indicating that models often answer correctly without relying on all intended evidence. Applying REALHOP to 790 paired MuSiQue questions increases the panel-mean BNR from 27.4% to 94.4% while maintaining high full-answer accuracy. REALHOP-based datasets, including REALHOP-FRAMES and REALHOP-LONGBENCH, also achieve high BNR. On 216 long-context questions, the difficulty separation between models (multiple-choice accuracy spread) increases dramatically from 13.9 to 59.2 points across 16 models and remains large under repeated open-ended evaluations, indicating that REALHOP questions better expose differences in multi-hop reasoning ability.
AI.conclusion: Answer correctness and a seemingly coherent reasoning chain are insufficient evidence that a model is performing genuine multi-hop reasoning. Existing benchmarks substantially overestimate true multi-hop behavior because models can solve many questions without depending on all annotated hops. The proposed BNR metric, together with the REALHOP diagnose-construct-verify framework and resulting datasets, provides a way to ensure and verify that each reasoning step is behaviorally necessary. Therefore, robust multi-hop evaluation must incorporate tests of hop necessity, not just final-answer accuracy or post-hoc chain plausibility.

title: Orthogonal Yet Coupled: Decoupling Geometric Components for Model Merging
summary:
Merging pretrained models has emerged as an effective approach for consolidating diverse capabilities into a single unified model. However, prevailing merging methods typically treat each task vector as an indivisible merging unit, overlooking the heterogeneous geometric changes encoded within it. This treatment can induce cross-component coupling: when merging decisions are derived from statistics of the complete task vector, the geometric characteristics of one component may influence how another is selected, weighted, or combined, potentially degrading the quality of the merged model. To address this issue, we propose DiGA, a
Disentangled Geometry-Aware model merging framework. Using the pretrained weights as a shared geometric reference, DiGA orthogonally decomposes each task vector into components corresponding to distinct geometric attributes. Rather than merging the task vectors as a whole, DiGA aggregates corresponding components independently within their respective subspaces and subsequently recombines them into a unified update. This component-wise formulation preserves the geometric identity of each component and prevents the characteristics of one component from interfering with the aggregation of another. Furthermore, DiGA can be incorporated into a broad range of existing model merging methods. Extensive experiments across diverse models, tasks, and merging methods demonstrate that DiGA improves merged-model performance and reduces capability degradation. Our repository is on https://github.com/wzj1718/DiGA.

AI.tldr: DiGA is a geometry-aware framework that decomposes and merges task vectors component-wise to avoid interference between different geometric attributes, improving performance of merged models.
AI.motivation: Existing model merging methods treat each task vector as a single unit, ignoring that it encodes multiple heterogeneous geometric changes. This monolithic treatment can cause cross-component coupling, where the properties of one part of the vector distort how others are merged, leading to degraded merged-model quality.
AI.method: Use the pretrained base model weights as a shared geometric reference. Orthogonally decompose each task vector into separate components that correspond to distinct geometric attributes (subspaces). Instead of merging entire task vectors, independently aggregate corresponding components within their subspaces using standard merging rules, then recombine these aggregated components into a single update. The framework is designed to plug into many existing merging algorithms.
AI.result: Across multiple models, tasks, and existing merging strategies, DiGA consistently improves the performance of merged models and reduces degradation of individual capabilities compared with conventional whole-vector merging.
AI.conclusion: Disentangling task vectors into geometry-aware components before merging mitigates cross-component interference and yields higher-quality merged models. Because DiGA is modular and compatible with various merging methods, it offers a general-purpose upgrade path for model merging pipelines.

title: CF-LoRA: Decoupled Factor Aggregation and Adaptation-Aware Client Clustering for Federated LoRA Fine-Tuning
summary: Federated LoRA fine-tuning enables parameter-efficient adaptation of pre-trained models without sharing private data, but suffers from two fundamental mismatches under heterogeneous client data: a structural aggregation mismatch caused by independently averaging LoRA factors, and a statistical collaboration mismatch caused by enforcing a single global adapter across divergent clients. To address these issues, we propose CF-LoRA, a clustered federated LoRA fine-tuning framework that combines decoupled factor aggregation with adaptation-aware client clustering. CF-LoRA first learns a globally shared $A$ factor while retaining personalized $B_i$ factors, then identifies clients with similar adaptation patterns based on the cosine similarity of their learned $B_i$ factors, and finally performs intra-cluster $B$-factor aggregation with a frozen $A$ factor. By decoupling LoRA factor aggregation, CF-LoRA preserves the low-rank structure and mitigates the structural aggregation mismatch, while adaptation-aware clustering promotes collaboration among clients with similar adaptation patterns and reduces negative transfer caused by statistical heterogeneity. Experiments on four language tasks and four vision datasets with RoBERTa and ViT show that CF-LoRA achieves the highest average accuracy in both modalities while communicating only one LoRA factor per optimization round.

AI.tldr: CF-LoRA is a clustered federated LoRA fine-tuning framework that decouples and selectively aggregates LoRA factors to better handle heterogeneous client data, improving performance and communication efficiency in both NLP and vision tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing federated LoRA fine-tuning methods struggle under heterogeneous client data because: (1) naively averaging LoRA factors A and B across clients breaks the intended low-rank structure (structural aggregation mismatch), and (2) forcing all clients to share a single global adapter ignores data heterogeneity and can cause negative transfer (statistical collaboration mismatch). The paper aims to make parameter-efficient federated adaptation robust to these heterogeneities.
AI.method: The method, CF-LoRA, decouples the aggregation of the two LoRA factors and introduces adaptation-aware client clustering. First, it trains a globally shared A factor while keeping client-specific B_i factors. After this stage, it computes cosine similarity between clients’ learned B_i factors to cluster clients with similar adaptation patterns. Then, with A frozen, it performs aggregation of B within each cluster (intra-cluster B aggregation), maintaining personalization across clusters while still allowing collaboration within clusters. Only one LoRA factor is communicated per optimization round, reducing communication cost.
AI.result: Across four language tasks (with RoBERTa) and four vision datasets (with ViT), CF-LoRA achieves the highest average accuracy compared to baselines, while maintaining communication efficiency by transmitting only one LoRA factor each round. This empirically validates that decoupled aggregation plus adaptation-aware clustering improves performance under heterogeneous client data.
AI.conclusion: By decoupling LoRA factor aggregation and clustering clients based on their adaptation behavior, CF-LoRA alleviates both structural and statistical mismatches in federated LoRA fine-tuning. It preserves the low-rank structure, reduces negative transfer in heterogeneous settings, boosts accuracy in both NLP and vision tasks, and remains communication-efficient by sharing only a single factor per round.

title: Devils in Question Relay: Source-Conditioned Relay Steering to Mitigate Hallucinations in Audio-visual Large Language Models
summary: Audio-visual large language models (AVLLMs) have made remarkable progress in multimodal understanding and reasoning through interactions among visual, auditory, and linguistic information. However, recent studies show that AVLLMs face a critical challenge: $\textbf{source-confused grounding hallucination}$, where cues from the unused modality induce responses that the required modality does not support, undermining reliability in real-world applications. Existing methods have made progress in mitigating this failure, yet how it arises from internal cross-modal interactions remains insufficiently understood. To address this gap, we conduct path-intervention and representation analyses, revealing a $\textbf{question-relay}$ mechanism: question states carry interfering cues alongside required-source evidence, undermining grounding in required-modality evidence. Cutting pathways from interfering modality to question states yields greater correct-answer logit recovery than cutting those to the generation position. Motivated by these findings, we propose $\textbf{SECRET}$ ($\textbf{S}$ourc$\textbf{E}$-$\textbf{C}$onditioned $\textbf{RE}$lay s$\textbf{T}$eering), a training-free method that mitigates cross-modal interference at the question relay. Using contrasting question representations elicited through different modality-pathway interventions, SECRET steers the original question states toward required-source evidence. Experiments on two widely adopted benchmarks CMM and AVHBench across three AVLLMs show that SECRET consistently outperforms prior training-free methods, substantially mitigating source-confused grounding hallucinations (e.g., up to +18.0 and +7.1 percentage points over base models). Modality-specific captioning further demonstrates its generalizability to open-ended generation.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies and mitigates a key failure mode in audio-visual LLMs—source-confused grounding hallucinations—by analyzing internal cross-modal interactions and proposing a training-free steering method, SECRET, that improves modality-grounded reasoning.
AI.motivation: Although audio-visual large language models have advanced multimodal reasoning, they often hallucinate by relying on irrelevant modalities, especially when only one modality is required. Existing mitigation techniques reduce this issue but do not clearly explain how cross-modal interference arises inside the model. A deeper understanding of the internal mechanism is needed to design more precise and reliable interventions without retraining the models.
AI.method: The authors perform path-intervention and representation analyses within AVLLMs to trace how information from different modalities flows and affects predictions. They uncover a question-relay mechanism where question representations carry both relevant evidence and interfering cues. They then propose SECRET, a training-free technique that constructs contrasting question representations via modality-pathway interventions and steers the original question states toward those emphasizing the required modality, effectively suppressing interfering modality signals at the question relay stage.
AI.result: Experiments on two established benchmarks, CMM and AVHBench, across three different AVLLMs show that SECRET significantly reduces source-confused grounding hallucinations and outperforms prior training-free baselines. The method achieves sizable accuracy gains over base models (up to +18.0 and +7.1 percentage points on key metrics). Additional tests on modality-specific captioning tasks indicate that SECRET’s benefits extend beyond fixed-form QA to open-ended generation settings.
AI.conclusion: Source-confused grounding hallucinations in AVLLMs stem largely from cross-modal interference propagating through question representations. By identifying the question-relay as a critical locus and steering its representations with SECRET, the authors can substantially improve modality-grounded reasoning without additional training. This suggests that targeted, representation-level interventions at internal relay states are a powerful and general strategy for controlling multimodal behavior in large language models.

title: ImbalancE: Inference-Time Latent Search Against Degree Imbalance in Link Prediction
summary: Knowledge Graph Embedding models have been extensively used to learn representations of entities and relations in Knowledge Graphs for predicting missing links. However, the quality of the learned representations varies a lot across different areas of the graph. If previous research has loosely linked the problem to relation types or degree bias, we show that it is more widespread and it correlates with the degree imbalance of the entities in test triples. In particular, the prediction of a target entity that has a degree much smaller than the degree of the anchor entity is extremely problematic. This is critical in recommender systems and other use cases, where these triples represent important corner cases. To address this issue, we propose an inference-time latent search optimization method capable of significantly improving model predictions on the most imbalanced triples. Built on top of a pre-trained model, it explores the embedding space at evaluation time, blending known and out-of-band information to mitigate the degree imbalance bias. We show the value of our approach on imbalanced triples from common benchmark datasets, where we outperform conventional methods, opening the door to the successful adoption of Knowledge Graph Embedding models on these critical corner cases.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies a systemic prediction weakness of Knowledge Graph Embedding models on triples where entity degrees are highly imbalanced, and proposes an inference-time latent search procedure that substantially improves performance on these corner cases.
AI.motivation: While Knowledge Graph Embedding (KGE) models are widely used for link prediction, their performance is not uniform across the graph: some regions or triples are much harder. Past work only loosely associated this issue with relation types or degree bias, without a clear characterization or remedy. The authors observe that triples involving entities with strongly imbalanced degrees—especially when the target entity has a much smaller degree than the anchor entity—are particularly problematic. These "corner cases" are especially important in applications such as recommender systems, where low-degree (e.g., long-tail) items or users are crucial yet poorly served by standard KGE models. This motivates a focused study of degree imbalance as a source of error and a method specifically to address it.
AI.method: The authors first empirically analyze how prediction quality varies with the degree imbalance between the anchor and target entities in test triples, demonstrating a strong negative correlation. They then introduce an inference-time optimization procedure, which they call a latent search method, that operates on top of a fixed pre-trained KGE model. At evaluation time, for a given triple, they explore the embedding space around the entities/relations involved, blending the given embeddings with "out-of-band" or auxiliary information to adjust the candidate representations. This search aims to correct for the bias introduced by degree imbalance without retraining the underlying model. The method selectively focuses on the most imbalanced triples and refines predictions by optimizing the embeddings locally during inference.
AI.result: On standard benchmark knowledge graph datasets, the proposed latent search method significantly improves link prediction performance specifically on the subset of most degree-imbalanced triples. It outperforms conventional KGE methods and baseline evaluation strategies for these hard cases, indicating that targeted inference-time optimization can effectively mitigate degree imbalance bias. The results demonstrate that much of the performance degradation on low-degree targets is not inevitable and can be recovered by appropriately adjusting embeddings during evaluation.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that degree imbalance between entities in a triple is a primary driver of heterogeneous performance in Knowledge Graph Embedding models, particularly harming predictions when the target has much lower degree than the anchor. This issue is especially consequential in real-world applications like recommender systems, where such imbalanced triples correspond to critical long-tail scenarios. The proposed inference-time latent search optimization offers a practical, model-agnostic way to reduce this bias and enhance prediction quality on these corner cases, without retraining the original KGE model. This opens the path toward more reliable and equitable use of KGE models across all regions of a knowledge graph, including the sparsely connected ones.

title: Pair Difficulty Matters: Rethinking Pairwise LLM-as-a-Judge Evaluation and Consistency
comment: Accepted as an EMNLP 2026 short paper
summary: Large Language Model judges are widely used to rank texts and text-generating systems through pairwise comparison, and their reliability is typically assessed via three proxies: position bias, transitivity, and pairwise agreement (self- or human-labeled). Because these proxies drive judge selection and benchmarking, a substantial literature reporting that judges perform poorly on them risks steering practitioners away from otherwise capable evaluators. We argue this assessment is misleading. Under the Bradley--Terry geometry underlying pairwise aggregation, each proxy is dominated by close-rank-gap pairs, where inconsistency is information-theoretically expected and individual verdicts contribute little to the aggregate ranking; far-gap pairs carry the ranking signal but barely move the proxies. We formalize this argument and validate it in a controlled simulation and on two human-rated corpora: the proxies correlate only weakly with ranking accuracy against gold, and their predictive component concentrates in the far-gap regime. Judges should therefore be assessed on rank-gap-conditional metrics, ideally against human rankings. Code at https://github.com/brunobrocai/PairDifficulty.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that common metrics used to judge the reliability of LLM-based 'judges' (position bias, transitivity, pairwise agreement) are misleading, because they are dominated by comparisons between similarly ranked items where inconsistency is expected and uninformative for overall ranking quality. It proposes evaluating judges conditionally on the difficulty (rank gap) of pairs, and shows that existing proxies correlate weakly with true ranking accuracy.
AI.motivation: LLM judges are increasingly used to compare texts and systems, but practitioners need reliable ways to select good judges. The community currently relies on proxies like position bias, transitivity, and pairwise agreement to assess judge quality. A growing body of work suggests these proxies indicate poor judge performance, potentially discouraging their use. The authors suspect these conclusions are flawed because they ignore the geometry of pairwise ranking, where not all pair comparisons are equally informative.
AI.method: The authors analyze the problem using the Bradley–Terry model for pairwise comparisons. They theoretically show that standard reliability proxies are dominated by comparisons between items with small differences in underlying quality (close rank gaps), where disagreement is both expected and low-impact for the final aggregated ranking. They then run controlled simulations and experiments on two human-rated corpora to empirically measure the relationship between the proxies and true ranking accuracy, decomposing results by the inferred 'rank gap' between compared items.
AI.result: The study finds that position bias, transitivity violations, and pairwise agreement correlate only weakly with overall ranking accuracy when measured against gold-standard human rankings. Moreover, the part of these proxies that does predict ranking accuracy is concentrated in comparisons between items with large rank gaps, i.e., easy pairs where the better item is clearly superior. Close-rank-gap pairs strongly influence the proxy values but contribute little to actual ranking quality, while far-rank-gap pairs drive accurate rankings but have limited effect on the proxies.
AI.conclusion: Traditional proxy metrics for evaluating LLM judges can be misleading indicators of true ranking performance because they are dominated by inherently noisy, low-importance comparisons. Evaluations should instead condition on pair difficulty, particularly the rank gap between items, and whenever possible benchmark judges directly against human rankings. The paper suggests that many LLM judges may be more capable than current proxy-based evaluations imply and provides code to facilitate difficulty-aware assessment.

title: CADOC: Cache-Aware Dynamic Object Context for Long-Horizon Agents
summary: For a long-horizon agent, context is the bottleneck: the history is resent with every request, the window caps task length, and reasoning degrades as the history grows. Replacing structured objects with compact retrieval Cards shortens the prompt and keeps the exact originals retrievable, but editing the history can break prefix-cache reuse, and prior recoverable methods time their edits by forecasts of future reuse or by preset intervals. We propose CADOC (Cache-Aware Dynamic Object Context), an online algorithm that replaces structured objects with compact Cards while preserving exact, on-demand retrieval of their original contents. CADOC schedules replacements in batches by balancing accumulated waiting cost against shared cache-reconstruction cost. Its scheduling rule follows from an economic order quantity trade-off, recovers the optimal integer batch under stationary assumptions. Across evaluation, CADOC consistently achieves the lowest aggregate input cost among the compared configurations, which reduces input cost by approximately 40\% on average while maintaining task performance close to full context. CADOC thus provides a cost-derived approach to compressible context management, demonstrating that efficient compression depends not only on shortening prompts but also on scheduling edits to preserve cache reuse.

AI.tldr: They introduce CADOC, a method for compressing long LLM contexts using compact retrieval cards while scheduling when to edit history so cache reuse stays efficient, cutting input cost ~40% with minimal performance loss.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon language model agents suffer from context length limits, rising input cost, and degraded reasoning as history grows. Existing compression schemes that replace large structured objects with compact references reduce prompt length but disrupt prefix cache reuse when edits are made, and current strategies for when to edit are ad hoc (fixed intervals or heuristic forecasts of reuse). There is a need for a principled, cost-aware way to manage compressible context that respects both retrieval fidelity and compute/cache efficiency.
AI.method: They propose CADOC (Cache-Aware Dynamic Object Context), an online scheduling algorithm that decides when to replace large structured objects in the context with compact retrieval Cards. CADOC batches these replacements and determines batch size and timing by balancing two costs: the accumulated cost of waiting to compress (keeping the large objects in the prompt) and the shared cost of reconstructing the model’s prefix cache after edits. The scheduling rule is derived from an economic order quantity (EOQ) style trade-off, and under stationary usage assumptions it recovers the optimal integer batch size. The method guarantees that original contents remain exactly retrievable on demand via the Cards while optimizing for minimized aggregate input cost and preserved cache reuse.
AI.result: In experiments comparing CADOC to other context management and compression configurations, CADOC consistently yields the lowest total input cost. Quantitatively, it reduces input cost by roughly 40% on average compared to baselines, while keeping task performance nearly as high as using the full, uncompressed context. This shows that the algorithm’s scheduling scheme effectively exploits cache reuse and compression without sacrificing downstream task quality.
AI.conclusion: CADOC offers a principled, cost-based framework for compressible context management in long-horizon agents. By treating edits to context as a batching and scheduling problem informed by an EOQ-style trade-off, it shows that efficient context compression is not just a matter of making prompts shorter, but also of timing edits to preserve prefix-cache reuse. The approach delivers substantial input cost savings with minimal performance loss and suggests a general direction for future work on cache-aware and retrieval-based context management for LLM agents.

title: Correct, Don't Delete: Mitigating Emergent Misalignment with Corrective Supervision
summary: Fine-tuning a language model on a narrow set of harmful demonstrations, such as bad medical advice, can make it broadly misaligned on unrelated questions, a phenomenon known as emergent misalignment (EM). The usual defense is to find the offending rows and delete them, but a row locator failed our held-out test and deleting rows helps less than expected. We ask a different question: given a fixed set of poisoned rows, is it better to correct them than to remove them? We fine-tune Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct on a mixture of bad medical advice and benign chat data, select a quarter of the poison rows in advance, and either delete them or replace each with a corrected answer to the same prompt, keeping everything else the same. Replacing the rows cuts the EM rate by about a third and improves answers on held-out medical questions, while deleting the same rows has little measurable effect. The advantage is larger when half the poison rows are corrected, and it holds on a second base model and a second misaligned model organism. The content of the replacement appears to matter: paraphrasing the rows while keeping their bad advice shows no clear benefit, and the correct answers distributed with the dataset appear to do about as well as our rewriter's. Realigning an already-poisoned model with further fine-tuning is known to work, but which data does the work has not been compared directly. We find that a short round of training on corrections beats the same amount of training on generic chat data, that corrections on other medical prompts do roughly as well as corrections of the poisoned prompts themselves, and that instructing the correction writer to model a careful, harm-avoiding assistant adds no measurable benefit over plain corrections. In the settings we tested, correcting harmful training data reduces EM more than deleting it.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how to best mitigate emergent misalignment caused by poisoned fine-tuning data, finding that correcting harmful training examples is more effective than deleting them.
AI.motivation: Emergent misalignment occurs when fine-tuning on a small set of harmful demonstrations (e.g., bad medical advice) makes a language model misaligned on many unrelated queries. Current defenses focus on detecting and deleting poisoned rows, but row-locating can fail and deletion helps less than expected. The authors want to know, assuming some poisoned data is already present and only partially identifiable, whether correcting those rows yields better alignment than simply removing them.
AI.method: They fine-tune Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct on a mix of harmful medical advice and benign chat data to induce emergent misalignment. They then pre-select a fraction (one-quarter or one-half) of the poisoned rows and compare two interventions: (1) delete those rows, or (2) replace each with a corrected answer to the same prompt, holding all else constant. They measure emergent misalignment rates and performance on held-out medical questions. They repeat experiments with a second base model and misaligned model organism. They also compare different correction strategies (true corrections vs paraphrased bad advice, dataset-provided correct answers vs their own rewrites) and evaluate “repair” fine-tuning of already-poisoned models on (a) corrections vs (b) generic chat data, and whether targeting the same prompts vs other medical prompts matters.
AI.result: Replacing harmful rows with correct answers substantially reduces emergent misalignment—about a one‑third reduction in EM when a quarter of poisoned rows are corrected—and improves performance on unseen medical questions. Deleting the same rows yields little measurable improvement. The benefit is stronger when half of the poisoned rows are corrected and generalizes across another base model and misaligned model organism. The specific content of replacements is crucial: paraphrased but still harmful answers do not help, and using the dataset’s provided correct answers works about as well as custom rewrites. For post‑hoc realignment of already-poisoned models, a brief fine-tuning on correction data is more effective than an equivalent amount of generic chat data; corrections on other medical prompts are nearly as effective as corrections on the exact poisoned prompts. Adding explicit instructions for the correction writer to emulate a careful, harm-avoiding assistant yields no additional measurable gain over plain corrections.
AI.conclusion: In the tested settings, actively correcting known harmful training examples is a more effective strategy for mitigating emergent misalignment than simply removing those examples. Targeted corrective data—whether on the same prompts or on related domain prompts—does more work for realignment than generic benign data, and elaborate safety-targeted prompting of the human (or model) rewriters offers no clear extra benefit beyond straightforward factual corrections.

title: Physics-Informed Multi-Agent Coordination for Hospital Patient Flow Optimization
comment: Accepted to PRIMA 2026 (Full paper). 16 pages, 2 figures, 3 tables
summary: Efficient patient flow coordination across autonomous hospital departments is critical for mitigating overcrowding and balancing resource utilization. While classical queueing theory, specifically open Baskett--Chandy--Muntz--Palacios (BCMP) networks, provides an interpretable mathematical topology for healthcare operations, analytical models rely on stationary assumptions and fixed routing matrices that degrade under state-dependent real-world dynamics. Conversely, centralized reinforcement learning approaches struggle to accommodate the decentralized structure of hospital governance, where individual clinical departments function with localized observations, heterogeneous resources, and divergent operational objectives. In this paper, we present a Multi-Agent Systems (MAS) framework titled \emph{Physics-Informed Multi-Agent Coordination}, which embeds empirically calibrated BCMP queueing topologies as physical priors within a decentralized multi-agent reinforcement learning architecture. Formulated as a Decentralized Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (Dec-POMDP) under coupled resource constraints, our method enables autonomous departmental agents to cooperatively negotiate patient routing and dynamic service scaling. To mitigate environmental non-stationarity without inducing excessive communication overhead, agents exchange localized action fingerprints along network edges and optimize a spatially decomposed reward structure. Empirical evaluations driven by real-world MIMIC-IV patient trajectories indicate that this cooperative multi-agent approach substantially reduces cumulative system delay compared to static Markovian approximations, heuristic dispatching, and independent multi-agent baselines, while maintaining clinical safety constraints.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a physics-informed multi-agent reinforcement learning framework that embeds BCMP queueing networks to improve decentralized coordination of patient flow across hospital departments, significantly reducing delays while respecting safety constraints.
AI.motivation: Traditional BCMP queueing models for hospitals are interpretable but depend on stationary assumptions and fixed routing that do not hold in dynamic, state-dependent hospital environments. Centralized RL methods do not fit decentralized hospital governance, where departments have local views, distinct resources, and objectives. There is a need for a coordination method that respects this decentralized structure, uses domain knowledge, and adapts to real-time dynamics.
AI.method: The authors formulate hospital patient flow as a Decentralized Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (Dec-POMDP) with coupled resource constraints. They introduce a Multi-Agent Systems framework called Physics-Informed Multi-Agent Coordination, where each department is an autonomous agent. Agents leverage BCMP network structures as physical priors and use decentralized multi-agent reinforcement learning. To handle non-stationarity with low communication overhead, agents share compact action fingerprints along network edges and optimize a spatially decomposed reward that encourages cooperative behavior.
AI.result: Using simulations based on real MIMIC-IV patient trajectories, the proposed method is empirically shown to significantly reduce cumulative system delay compared with static BCMP/Markovian models, heuristic patient dispatching rules, and independent multi-agent RL baselines. At the same time, the system respects clinical safety constraints, suggesting practical viability for real hospital operations.
AI.conclusion: Embedding BCMP queueing network priors into a decentralized multi-agent RL framework yields more effective and cooperative patient flow coordination across hospital departments than both classical analytical models and simpler RL baselines. The approach manages non-stationarity and communication limits while improving delay performance and maintaining safety, indicating promise for real-world deployment in complex healthcare systems.

title: Co-Linguistics: AI-augmented Theory Construction in Linguistics
summary: LLMs have been studied in recent linguistics as potential models of humans' linguistic abilities. Here we discuss an entirely different use of AI, namely as a co-scientist, to help construct and assess linguistic theories (we refer to the result as "Co-Linguistics"). Since the 1960s, linguistics has developed theories that are in principle mathematically formalizable, often in the language of formal language theory or model theory. The AI revolution in mathematics will thus have consequences in linguistics-but with an essential twist: proving new theorems is rarely the linguist's goal. Rather, one seeks to find the best set of axioms to derive empirical statements. AI could accelerate research by making existing theories fully explicit, by comparing competing theories, and more ambitiously, by proposing new theories (in machine learning, this relates to "program induction"). It will also help assess theories by accelerating the identification and test of crucial predictions, thanks to unparalleled access to data (in machine learning, this relates to "active learning"). While the cycle from theory evaluation to theory construction may give rise to recursive and possibly autonomous improvement of linguistic theories, humans remain central: linguists provide scientific directions and evaluate theories conceptually, and experimental participants are needed to assess empirical predictions that are outside the reach of LLMs.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes using AI, especially LLM-based tools, not as models of human language competence but as co-scientists that help formalize, compare, and generate linguistic theories, while humans retain conceptual and empirical oversight.
AI.motivation: Recent work uses LLMs to approximate human linguistic behavior, but another major opportunity is to use AI to assist the scientific process in linguistics itself. Linguistic theories are already highly formal and thus amenable to computational manipulation. Given advances in AI for mathematics and program synthesis, there is a strong motivation to see how similar tools can accelerate the development, clarification, and testing of linguistic theories.
AI.method: Conceptual and methodological proposal rather than an empirical experiment: (1) treat linguistic theories as formal objects (axioms, derivation systems) compatible with formal language theory/model theory; (2) use AI methods such as program induction to propose candidate theories or axiom sets; (3) use tools akin to automated theorem proving and formal verification to make theories explicit and compare them; (4) use active learning and data-rich LLM infrastructures to automatically detect crucial predictions, generate tests, and guide data collection; (5) embed these capabilities in a human-led research loop in which linguists set goals and interpret outputs.
AI.result: The abstract does not report new experimental or formal results; instead, it outlines a research framework where AI systems can: (i) turn existing linguistic theories into machine-readable formal systems, (ii) compare and evaluate rival theories by their empirical consequences, and (iii) suggest new theoretical hypotheses or axioms, with automated assistance in finding and testing their predictions.
AI.conclusion: AI will reshape linguistics not just by modeling language behavior but by acting as a co-scientist in theory construction and evaluation. Because linguistic theories are already formalizable, they are particularly well suited to AI tools from automated reasoning, program induction, and active learning. However, the process remains fundamentally human-guided: linguists set the conceptual agenda and evaluate theoretical adequacy, and human experimental data remain essential for testing predictions beyond what current LLMs can capture.

title: Language as the Interface: Foundation-Model Contrastive Learning Links Transcriptomes and Electrophysiology
summary: Integrating transcriptomic and electrophysiological data is essential for building multimodal foundation models for neuroscience. Patch-seq provides paired measurements of gene expression and intrinsic electrophysiology from the same neuron, establishing a basis for training cross-modal models. Here we introduce LangPatch, a foundation-model-based contrastive learning framework that uses paired Patch-seq data to align pretrained GenePT representations with electrophysiological phenotypes through a language-based interface. Gene descriptions and verbalized electrophysiological profiles are embedded by the same frozen text encoder. A context adapter and projection modules connect the modalities through paired contrastive learning. Across mouse visual, mouse motor, and human cortical cohorts, LangPatch achieves the highest mean transcriptome-to-electrophysiology prediction correlation among the evaluated foundation-model and representation-learning methods. It also improves held-out cross-modal alignment in the two mouse cohorts (FOSCTTM 0.107/0.135 vs. 0.208/0.222 for JAMIE, an existing cross-modal Patch-seq imputation method). It predicts transcriptomic family, type, cortical layer, and marker-gene expression from electrophysiology, exceeding other baselines on most endpoints. More importantly, the method transfers across brain areas and species: a model trained on mouse visual cortex predicts electrophysiology in motor cortex with approximately 70% correlation retention and in human cortex with 47% (58% on acute-slice recordings). Together, these results demonstrate alignment between molecular and functional representations of neurons, providing a building block for multimodal foundation models in neuroscience.

AI.tldr: The paper presents LangPatch, a contrastive learning framework that aligns gene-expression and electrophysiology data of single neurons via a shared language-based representation, outperforming existing cross-modal methods and transferring across brain areas and species.
AI.motivation: To build powerful multimodal foundation models in neuroscience, it is necessary to align molecular (transcriptomic) and functional (electrophysiological) descriptions of neurons. Patch-seq provides paired measurements but existing models struggle with robust cross-modal alignment, prediction, and transfer across species and brain regions. The authors aim to exploit large pretrained language-based gene models to better connect these modalities.
AI.method: The authors propose LangPatch, a contrastive learning framework that sits on top of a frozen text encoder. Gene descriptions and text-encoded electrophysiological profiles are both mapped into a shared language embedding space. A context adapter and projection modules connect GenePT’s pretrained gene embeddings with electrophysiological features, trained using paired Patch-seq data and contrastive objectives. The system learns to align transcriptomic and electrophysiological representations so that corresponding neurons are close in the joint space while non-matching pairs are separated.
AI.result: On Patch-seq datasets from mouse visual cortex, mouse motor cortex, and human cortex, LangPatch achieves the highest mean correlation for predicting electrophysiology from transcriptomics compared with other foundation-model and representation-learning approaches. It shows improved cross-modal alignment (lower FOSCTTM scores) than JAMIE, a strong existing Patch-seq imputation method, and better predicts cell family/type, cortical layer, and marker-gene expression from electrophysiology. Models trained on one mouse area transfer well to another and even to human cortex, retaining a substantial fraction of predictive correlation across domains.
AI.conclusion: LangPatch effectively aligns molecular and functional neuronal representations using a language-based interface, outperforming alternative cross-modal methods and demonstrating strong cross-area and cross-species transfer. This suggests that language-centered foundation models can serve as a unifying scaffold for multimodal neuronal data and provides a key component toward general multimodal foundation models in neuroscience.

title: Evaluating and Benchmarking the System One Model Jev
comment: Code available at github.com/AppliedMachineLearning-Lab/jev-benchmarking, model responses at doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23039006
summary: Jev is a commercial System One model from TypeSafe AI that does not generate text: given a state and typed questions, it returns a choice from fixed options, a position on a rubric, or the probability that a statement is true, with probabilities the vendor describes as calibrated. Such models target small decisions in information access pipelines, such as routing queries, checking grounding, moderating content, or rating against a rubric. We evaluate Jev (jev-1.13.0) zero-shot on 37 datasets spanning classification, routing, natural language inference, reading comprehension, commonsense reasoning, moderation, legal clause analysis and rubric scoring, with one frozen template per dataset and full evaluation splits: 346,009 requests for under USD 10. For reference, we score Qwen3.8-27B and Gemma-4-E4B on identical requests via their exact next-token probabilities over the options. Jev reaches 95-99% accuracy on IMDB, SST-2, HellaSwag and ARC and 86.7% on Belebele across 122 languages. It beats Qwen on 27 of 37 datasets, with none of Qwen's nine leads outside the bootstrap intervals, and Gemma on all 37. All three models degrade on low-resource languages, fine-grained or noisy labels, and rubric-based quality judgments. Jev's choice probabilities are well calibrated and support selective prediction. Binary probabilities rank well but are poorly placed relative to a fixed 0.5 threshold; thresholds tuned on training data raise micro-F1 on UNFAIR-ToS from 0.50 to 0.75. Jev answers MMLU's calculation-heavy questions more accurately than other MMLU questions (94% vs. 91%), whereas both open models, and all three on C-Eval, find them harder. Rotating the options leaves Jev's accuracy unchanged and withholding the question drops it to near chance, ruling out shallow memorization but not memorized question-answer pairs. We release the code, harness and all raw responses.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates Jev, a non-generative commercial classification-style model, on 37 NLP datasets and compares it to strong open-source LLMs, finding that Jev is often more accurate and better calibrated for small decision tasks in information access pipelines.
AI.motivation: Many real-world applications need reliable small decisions—like routing, moderation, grounding checks, or rubric scoring—rather than free-form text generation. Existing evaluations focus mostly on generative LLMs and broad benchmarks, not on specialized, calibrated decision models used inside information pipelines. The paper aims to systematically benchmark such a model (Jev) across diverse tasks, quantify its calibration, and compare it with strong open models under identical conditions.
AI.method: They evaluate Jev (version jev-1.13.0) zero-shot on 37 datasets spanning sentiment classification, routing, NLI, reading comprehension, commonsense reasoning, moderation, legal clause analysis, and rubric scoring. For each dataset they design a single fixed prompt template and test on the full evaluation split (346,009 requests total, under USD 10 in cost). Jev returns discrete options or probability estimates; they also evaluate Qwen3.8-27B and Gemma-4-E4B by mapping the same multiple-choice options to next-token probabilities. They analyze accuracy, calibration, performance across languages, sensitivity to option rotation and question removal (to probe memorization), and effects of threshold tuning for binary decisions.
AI.result: Jev achieves very high accuracy (95–99%) on IMDB, SST-2, HellaSwag, and ARC, and 86.7% on the multilingual Belebele benchmark across 122 languages. It outperforms Qwen on 27 of 37 datasets (with Qwen’s apparent advantages not statistically robust) and beats Gemma on all 37. All three models perform worse on low-resource languages, fine-grained/noisy labels, and rubric-based quality tasks. Jev’s output probabilities are well calibrated overall and useful for selective prediction, but binary probabilities relative to a fixed 0.5 threshold are poorly aligned; tuning thresholds on training data can substantially improve micro-F1 (e.g., from 0.50 to 0.75 on UNFAIR-ToS). Jev handles MMLU’s calculation-heavy questions better than other MMLU questions (94% vs. 91%), opposite to the behavior of the open models and all models on C-Eval. Rotating answer options does not change Jev’s accuracy, but removing the question drops performance to chance, suggesting no simple position bias and ruling out trivial memorization of label positions, though memorized QA pairs remain possible. They also release their code, evaluation harness, and raw model outputs.
AI.conclusion: Specialized, non-generative decision models like Jev can outperform larger open-source LLMs on a wide range of classification-style tasks while offering better probability calibration and efficiency, making them strong candidates for use in information access pipelines. However, challenges remain for low-resource languages, noisier or fine-grained labels, and nuanced rubric-based judgments. Proper threshold tuning is important to fully exploit calibrated probabilities in binary tasks. The robustness checks indicate Jev is not simply exploiting option positions, but some degree of dataset memorization cannot be excluded. Public release of code and outputs supports reproducibility and further study of such systems.

title: AnyAct: Universal Action for Self-Evolving Agents
summary: As large language models (LLMs) advance, AI agents are increasingly deployed in open-world environments to tackle complex sequential tasks (e.g., document processing, cross-application collaboration), relying heavily on actions ranging from GUI operations to semantic APIs. However, three core challenges persist: the "scale dilemma" of massive tool ecosystems exceeding LLM context windows, the "non-stationarity" of tool quality due to updates or outages, and the "heterogeneity" of feedback formats (pixels, text, structured data) creating information silos. To address these, we propose AnyAct, a universal action layer that unifies available capabilities into a self-evolving action space, enabling agents to operate efficiently and reliably in large-scale, dynamic tool ecosystems. AnyAct's core design focuses on two objectives: constructing this action space via hierarchical progressive retrieval (filtering task-relevant actions) and test-time reliability evolution (pruning unreliable actions), and enabling reliability-aware action orchestration through a heterogeneous observation grounding module that unifies multi-modal feedback. Additionally, it defines a hybrid action space (primitive + semantic actions) and optimizes for a balance between task success rate and execution cost. Evaluations on LiveMCPBench and OSMCP (a new benchmark we developed for multi-granularity action collaboration) demonstrate state-of-the-art performance. AnyAct delivers substantial performance gains over baseline methods across various LLM base models on LiveMCPBench and improvements are particularly notable for models with constrained native capabilities. On OSMCP, it achieves 77.27% overall success with only 50 steps, which is half the steps required by most competitors.

AI.tldr: AnyAct is a universal action layer that lets LLM-based agents reliably use large, dynamic tool ecosystems by retrieving, pruning, and orchestrating actions with multi-modal feedback.
AI.motivation: LLM agents need to operate in open-world, complex tasks using many tools and APIs, but face three challenges: (1) the scale dilemma, where the number of tools far exceeds the LLM’s context capacity; (2) non-stationarity, since tools change, break, or get updated; and (3) heterogeneous feedback across modalities (GUI pixels, text, structured data), which leads to fragmented information. A method is needed to manage a large, evolving tool set and unify their feedback so agents can act efficiently and robustly.
AI.method: AnyAct introduces a universal action layer that builds and maintains a self-evolving action space over tools and operations. It uses: (1) hierarchical progressive retrieval to filter and select task-relevant actions from a large tool pool; (2) test-time reliability evolution to monitor and prune unreliable actions as tools change; and (3) a heterogeneous observation grounding module that converts multi-modal feedback (pixels, text, structured data) into a unified representation for the agent. It further defines a hybrid action space combining primitive actions (e.g., low-level GUI operations) and semantic actions (higher-level, API-like operations), and optimizes execution to balance task success with cost (e.g., number of steps).
AI.result: On LiveMCPBench, AnyAct achieves state-of-the-art performance compared with baseline agent-tool orchestration methods, across multiple underlying LLMs, with especially large gains for weaker LLMs that have limited built-in capabilities. On the new OSMCP benchmark for multi-granularity action collaboration, AnyAct reaches 77.27% overall success with only 50 steps, requiring about half as many steps as most competing methods.
AI.conclusion: AnyAct effectively addresses scale, non-stationarity, and feedback heterogeneity in large tool ecosystems by constructing a self-evolving, reliability-aware action space and unifying heterogeneous observations. This leads to more efficient and reliable LLM agents that can solve complex, sequential tasks with fewer steps and higher success rates across different models and benchmarks.

title: Corpus-Guided Dual-Path Propagation for Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
summary: Graph-based retrieval-augmented generation supports multi-hop retrieval by organizing corpus information into graphs. However, existing relation-free graph retrieval methods rely primarily on query-sentence similarity to search for evidence. This can exclude useful bridging evidence with low query similarity and activate incidental entities unrelated to the reasoning chain. In this paper, we propose a simple and effective approach called NexusRAG, which augments the relation-free Tri-Graph with a corpus-level entity neighborhood structure derived from joint entity co-occurrence and semantic similarity. NexusRAG employs this structure to guide two complementary propagation paths: neighborhood-constrained semantic propagation through sentences identifies the query-relevant entity frontier, while direct structural propagation between neighboring entities expands that frontier to structurally related entities. The propagated entity weights also inform neighborhood-aware passage initialization for Personalized PageRank. Experiments on three multi-hop QA benchmarks and a domain-specific subset of GraphRAG-Bench show that NexusRAG consistently outperforms existing approaches. On the GraphRAG-Bench subset, NexusRAG achieves the highest evidence recall in all question categories, exceeding baselines by 4.2-8.1 points. The implementation code is available at https://github.com/Jacob-biu/NexusRAG.

AI.tldr: NexusRAG enhances graph-based retrieval-augmented generation for multi-hop QA by adding a corpus-level entity neighborhood graph, enabling better propagation of entity relevance and significantly improving evidence recall over prior relation-free graph methods.
AI.motivation: Existing relation-free graph RAG methods for multi-hop QA mostly rank sentences by query-sentence similarity. This misses low-similarity but crucial bridging evidence and can surface irrelevant entities that are only coincidentally similar to the query. There is a need for a way to structurally organize entities beyond direct query similarity, so the retrieval process can follow plausible reasoning chains through the corpus.
AI.method: The authors augment a relation-free Tri-Graph with a new corpus-level entity neighborhood structure that combines entity co-occurrence and semantic similarity to connect related entities. NexusRAG then runs two coordinated propagation processes: (1) neighborhood-constrained semantic propagation over sentences to find a frontier of entities that are semantically relevant to the query, and (2) structural propagation over the entity-neighborhood graph to expand from this frontier to structurally related entities. The resulting entity relevance scores are used for neighborhood-aware passage initialization in a Personalized PageRank retrieval stage.
AI.result: On three standard multi-hop QA benchmarks and a domain-specific subset of GraphRAG-Bench, NexusRAG outperforms prior graph-based RAG approaches. On the GraphRAG-Bench subset, it achieves the best evidence recall across all question types, improving recall by 4.2–8.1 points over baselines, demonstrating stronger ability to collect the full set of supporting evidence for multi-hop reasoning.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating an explicitly constructed entity neighborhood graph into relation-free graph RAG enables more accurate and complete multi-hop evidence retrieval. By combining constrained semantic propagation with structural entity propagation and using their outputs to guide Personalized PageRank, NexusRAG reduces both missed bridging evidence and spurious entities, leading to consistent performance gains across multi-hop QA benchmarks.

title: Beyond Low-Rank Parameterization: Narrowing the Gap Between LoRA and Full Fine-Tuning via Gradient Decomposition
summary: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) is a widely used approach to parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT), yet a performance gap can remain relative to full fine-tuning (FFT). Many LoRA variants improve the initialization or optimization of low-rank factors. At each training step, however, their first-order weight-space directions are constrained by the current parameterization. We characterize the corresponding LoRA-accessible gradient space and show that it coincides with the tangent space induced by the current LoRA parameterization. This characterization yields an orthogonal decomposition of the full weight gradient at the current model parameters. We term the component orthogonal to this space the normal gradient. Based on this decomposition, we propose GDLoRA (Gradient-Decomposed Low-Rank Adaptation). GDLoRA reconstructs the full weight gradient from forward activations and backward signals, extracts its normal component, and directly updates the base weights with this component, while retaining standard AdamW optimization for the LoRA factors. GDLoRA incorporates complementary normal gradients without increasing standard LoRA's optimizer-state memory budget under matched adapter and optimizer configurations. Experiments on natural language understanding, mathematical reasoning, commonsense reasoning, and image classification show that GDLoRA consistently improves over LoRA and narrows the performance gap to FFT. The code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/GDLoRA.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes GDLoRA, a method that augments LoRA fine-tuning with an additional gradient component (the normal gradient) to close the performance gap to full fine-tuning without extra optimizer memory.
AI.motivation: LoRA is popular for parameter-efficient fine-tuning but often underperforms full fine-tuning. Existing variants mostly tweak how low-rank parameters are initialized or optimized, but they all remain restricted to a limited gradient subspace determined by the low-rank parameterization. The authors want to understand this limitation formally and design a method that captures useful gradient directions outside this subspace while preserving LoRA’s memory efficiency.
AI.method: The authors formally characterize the set of gradients that LoRA can express at a given point in training and show it equals the tangent space of the current low-rank parameterization. Using this, they decompose the full model gradient into two orthogonal components: (1) a tangent component that lies in LoRA’s accessible space and (2) a normal component orthogonal to it. They then introduce GDLoRA, which reconstructs the full weight gradient from forward activations and backpropagated signals, extracts the normal component, updates the base model weights directly with this normal gradient, and optimizes the LoRA factors with AdamW as usual. The design ensures that incorporating the normal gradient does not increase optimizer-state memory relative to standard LoRA under matched adapter and optimizer settings.
AI.result: On a range of tasks—natural language understanding, mathematical reasoning, commonsense reasoning, and image classification—GDLoRA consistently outperforms standard LoRA. It reduces the performance gap between LoRA and full fine-tuning, showing that the added normal gradient information is beneficial in practice without violating memory constraints.
AI.conclusion: The work shows that LoRA’s limitations can be understood in terms of its tangent-space-restricted gradient access and that explicitly leveraging the orthogonal normal gradient can significantly improve parameter-efficient fine-tuning. GDLoRA offers a practical way to narrow the gap to full fine-tuning while maintaining LoRA’s memory advantages, suggesting a promising direction for more expressive yet efficient adaptation methods.

title: Reader Proficiency Shapes Layer-wise Surprisal Profiles
summary: Reading behaviour varies not only with linguistic input, but also with reader proficiency. In this study, we investigate whether the layer-wise relationship between surprisal from large language models (LLMs) and human gaze behaviour differs across readers with different levels of proficiency and across gaze measures. Using eye-tracking data from the MECO L2 corpus, we compare readers with high and low vocabulary proficiency on first-pass gaze duration (FPGD) and total gaze duration (TGD). We quantify the distribution of the predictive power of surprisal across model layers using Predictive Depth. Across 12 tested LLMs, we find that readers with lower vocabulary proficiency tend to show deeper Predictive Depth for FPGD, while this difference is smaller for TGD. Also, TGD itself shows deeper Predictive Depth than FPGD in both proficiency groups. These patterns suggest that where predictive power is concentrated across LLM layers may be related to the timing and breadth of the reading processes captured by different gaze measures, and that this relationship can vary with reader proficiency. Our leave-one-out analysis further shows that the advantage of informative internal layers extends to unseen texts, although the practical improvements in prediction are limited. Overall, our results show that layer-wise LLM surprisal provides a useful perspective on variation in reading behaviour across both reader groups and gaze measures.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how well surprisal values from different layers of large language models predict eye-tracking measures in reading, and how this depends on reader proficiency and gaze metric.
AI.motivation: Reading behavior is influenced by both the linguistic properties of text and the reader’s proficiency, but most work using LLM surprisal to model eye movements has not examined how predictive information is distributed across model layers, nor how this distribution interacts with different gaze measures and reader skill levels. Understanding this can shed light on which parts of LLMs align with human processing at different stages of reading and for different readers.
AI.method: The authors use eye-tracking data from the MECO L2 corpus and partition readers into high- and low-vocabulary proficiency groups. They compute surprisal at each layer of 12 large language models and examine how well layer-wise surprisal predicts two eye-tracking measures: first-pass gaze duration (FPGD) and total gaze duration (TGD). They summarize how prediction quality is distributed across layers with a metric called Predictive Depth, and they perform leave-one-out analyses to test generalization to unseen texts.
AI.result: Across the 12 LLMs, lower-proficiency readers show deeper Predictive Depth for FPGD, indicating that the most informative surprisal for their early reading behavior tends to come from later model layers compared to higher-proficiency readers. The proficiency-related difference in Predictive Depth is smaller for TGD. TGD generally exhibits deeper Predictive Depth than FPGD for both groups. The leave-one-out analysis shows that using the most informative internal layers maintains an advantage on unseen texts, but the absolute gain in prediction performance is modest.
AI.conclusion: Layer-wise surprisal from LLMs captures meaningful variation in human reading behavior, with the depth at which predictive information is concentrated differing by gaze measure and reader proficiency. Early and later reading processes, as indexed by FPGD and TGD, align with different layers, and lower-proficiency readers rely on representations associated with deeper layers for early processing. While practical improvements in prediction are limited, analyzing Predictive Depth offers a valuable lens on how LLM representations correspond to human reading across reader groups and eye-tracking metrics.

title: FedLAFP: Low-Rank Aggregation Meets Full-Rank Personalization in Federated Fine-Tuning
summary: Federated parameter-efficient fine-tuning enables clients to adapt pre-trained models without sharing raw data or communicating the full model, but statistical heterogeneity makes a single global adapter insufficient for personalized prediction. Existing personalized methods typically use the same low-rank structure for both shared and private adaptation, overlooking their distinct requirements for aggregation and personalization. We propose FedLAFP, a role-aware framework that couples a compact, globally aggregated LoRA branch with a client-private, full-rank-capable RandLoRA branch. The shared branch provides an efficient interface for transferring common knowledge, whereas the private branch combines fixed random low-rank bases with learned scaling coefficients to provide expressive client-specific adaptation without additional communication. Client- and layer-specific mixing coefficients jointly fuse the two branches, and only the shared LoRA parameters are exchanged. A controlled linear study supports this role assignment: LoRA yields more aligned client updates and lower aggregation error, while RandLoRA more accurately recovers client-specific residuals. Experiments across four visual recognition benchmarks show that FedLAFP consistently outperforms local-only and federated LoRA baselines, achieving an average personalized accuracy of $86.93\%$ and exceeding the best baseline average by $1.30$ percentage points.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes FedLAFP, a federated parameter-efficient fine-tuning framework that separates global and personalized adaptation using two coordinated LoRA-based branches, achieving better personalized accuracy than existing baselines on visual recognition tasks.
AI.motivation: In federated learning, parameter-efficient fine-tuning (e.g., with adapters like LoRA) lets clients adapt large pre-trained models without sharing raw data or transmitting full model parameters. However, due to statistical heterogeneity across clients, a single global adapter often fails to provide good personalized predictions. Existing personalized solutions typically use the same low-rank structure for both global sharing and private adaptation, ignoring that these two roles have different needs regarding aggregation robustness and client-specific expressiveness. This motivates a design that explicitly separates and optimizes the roles of shared and private adaptation components.
AI.method: The authors introduce FedLAFP, a role-aware federated fine-tuning framework with two parallel branches per client: (1) a compact, globally shared LoRA branch whose parameters are communicated and aggregated across clients, and (2) a client-private RandLoRA branch that uses fixed random low-rank bases with learned scaling coefficients, enabling effectively full-rank client-specific adaptation without extra communication. Layer- and client-specific mixing coefficients are learned to fuse the outputs of the shared and private branches. Only the standard LoRA parameters from the shared branch are transmitted to the server. Additionally, a controlled linear analysis is conducted to justify the role assignment, comparing LoRA and RandLoRA in terms of aggregation error and capacity to capture client-specific residuals.
AI.result: Theoretical linear studies show that LoRA produces more aligned updates across clients and thus incurs lower aggregation error, making it well-suited for the shared global branch, while RandLoRA reconstructs client-specific residuals more accurately, validating its assignment to the private branch. Empirically, across four visual recognition benchmarks, FedLAFP consistently outperforms both local-only training and federated LoRA baselines. It achieves an average personalized accuracy of 86.93%, surpassing the best competing baseline by 1.30 percentage points.
AI.conclusion: Separating global and client-specific roles in federated parameter-efficient fine-tuning via a dual-branch design improves personalization under heterogeneous data. By using a compact, communicable LoRA branch for shared knowledge transfer and a non-communicated RandLoRA branch for expressive local adaptation, FedLAFP attains better trade-offs between communication efficiency, aggregation stability, and personalized performance, significantly improving accuracy over existing federated LoRA approaches on visual recognition tasks.

title: Billiger.de Products: A Bilingual Entity Matching Benchmark
