summary: Existing product matching benchmarks primarily contain English-language product data and are often dominated by a single product category, such as electronics. This paper introduces Billiger.de Products, a bilingual German and English entity matching benchmark covering thirteen consumer product categories, including difficult-to-handle categories such as clothing and furniture. The benchmark data originates from the German price comparison platform billiger.de. Following the design of WDC Products, the benchmark offers multiple variants that differ in the fraction of corner cases, the size of the development set, and the fraction of entities unseen during training. An aligned English translation of every offer keeps all pairs, splits, and labels fixed, while cross-language test sets combine German and English records within individual pairs. We validate the benchmark using six supervised matchers and zero-shot GPT-5.2 on both language versions and the cross-language test sets. The validation shows the difficulty of the benchmark. The comparison of the results on the English version of the benchmark to the results on the German version shows that most matchers score on average higher on the English version. The difference is largest for RoBERTa and HierGAT, while the zero-shot LLM runs are largely insensitive to the language. Comparing the F1 scores achieved by PLM-based matchers on the English version of Billiger.de Products with their performance on existing English-language benchmarks, such as WDC Products and Abt-Buy, shows that Billiger.de Products is more difficult than these benchmarks.

AI.tldr: The paper presents Billiger.de Products, a new, difficult bilingual (German/English) product/entity matching benchmark spanning 13 diverse consumer categories, and shows it is harder than existing English benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Most existing product matching benchmarks are English-only and skewed toward a single category (often electronics), which limits research on robust, generalizable entity matching across languages and diverse, challenging product types like clothing and furniture. There is a need for a bilingual, multi-category, and systematically varied benchmark to stress-test modern matchers, including PLM-based models and large language models, in realistic conditions.
AI.method: The authors construct a benchmark from the German price comparison platform billiger.de, covering thirteen consumer product categories. They create several dataset variants by systematically varying: (1) the proportion of corner cases, (2) the size of the development set, and (3) the share of entities unseen during training. They then generate a fully aligned English translation for each German offer so that all pairs, splits, and labels remain identical across languages. Additionally, they build cross-language test sets where each pair can mix German and English records. For validation, they evaluate six supervised matching models (including RoBERTa and HierGAT) and a zero-shot GPT-5.2 setup on German-only, English-only, and cross-language test sets, comparing F1 scores across settings and against results on existing English benchmarks such as WDC Products and Abt-Buy.
AI.result: Experiments show that Billiger.de Products is a challenging benchmark: PLM-based matchers obtain lower F1 scores on it compared to their performance on established English-only datasets like WDC Products and Abt-Buy. Most supervised matchers perform better on the English version than on the German version, with particularly large performance gaps for RoBERTa and HierGAT. In contrast, the zero-shot GPT-5.2 runs show little sensitivity to the language (German vs English), achieving relatively similar performance across both language versions and the cross-language test sets. Overall performance levels confirm the benchmark’s difficulty, especially in its more corner-case-heavy and unseen-entity-rich variants.
AI.conclusion: Billiger.de Products provides a new, difficult, and realistic benchmark for product/entity matching that fills key gaps in current resources: it is bilingual, multi-category, and systematically configurable along dimensions like corner cases and unseen entities. The empirical evaluation demonstrates that it is more challenging than popular English benchmarks and that language can substantially impact supervised PLM-based matchers, whereas zero-shot LLMs are more robust to language variation. This benchmark can thus serve as a stronger testbed for developing and comparing robust, language-agnostic product matching approaches.

title: Watch-Think-Interact: Bootstrapping Long-Horizon Multi-Turn Streaming Video Reasoning with Reinforcement Learning
summary: Streaming video assistance requires models to answer asynchronous questions from an observed prefix under a fixed context budget. Existing approaches model response timing or compress history, but an online state formed before future questions are known can omit visual details before later questions reveal their relevance; the retained state alone cannot recover them. We introduce Watch-Think-Interact (WTI), a closed-loop framework for multi-question streaming video reasoning. WTI maintains compact natural-language memory entries tagged with source-video time ranges; these entries support direct reasoning when sufficient and otherwise anchor selective recall of finer visual evidence. For each question, WTI answers when current context and memory suffice, continues watching when required evidence has not appeared, or recalls a relevant past interval and decides again after incorporating the returned chunks, without replaying the full observed history. To train this behavior, we construct WTI-82K, comprising 82,335 timed questions across 4,812 causally aligned trajectories, and develop Stream-GDPO to optimize complete multi-question streaming rollouts using trajectory-level feedback for response timing, source-video recall, and memory updates. WTI achieves state-of-the-art aggregate performance among the compared open-source streaming baselines, reaching 83.3% on StreamingBench and 73.6% weighted overall accuracy on OVO-Bench.

AI.tldr: They propose Watch-Think-Interact (WTI), a framework for answering multiple, asynchronous questions about streaming video under a fixed context limit, using language memory plus targeted video recall, and show it outperforms prior open-source methods.
AI.motivation: In streaming video QA, models must answer questions over a long, continuously arriving video while limited by a fixed context window. Prior methods either decide when to answer or compress past frames into a compact state. However, decisions and compression made before future questions are known can lose visual details that later turn out to be important, and these lost details cannot be reconstructed from the compressed state. There is a need for a system that can preserve and selectively recover relevant information for future, unknown questions without replaying the entire history.
AI.method: They introduce Watch-Think-Interact (WTI), a closed-loop framework for multi-question streaming video reasoning. WTI maintains compact, natural-language memory entries that are explicitly tagged with their source time ranges in the video. When a question arrives, WTI first tries to answer using the current context and these memory entries. If this is insufficient, it can (1) keep watching the stream until the needed evidence appears, or (2) selectively recall past video intervals whose time tags suggest relevance, retrieving finer-grained visual chunks for re-analysis instead of replaying all past frames. Decisions—answer now, continue watching, or recall past intervals—are repeatedly made per question. To train this behavior, they build the WTI-82K dataset with 82,335 timed questions over 4,812 causally aligned trajectories and propose Stream-GDPO, an optimization method that uses trajectory-level feedback to jointly tune response timing, what past video to recall, and how to update memory across full multi-question streaming rollouts.
AI.result: Empirically, WTI achieves state-of-the-art performance among evaluated open-source streaming video QA baselines. It obtains 83.3% accuracy on StreamingBench and 73.6% weighted overall accuracy on OVO-Bench, demonstrating strong multi-question streaming reasoning and efficient use of context via selective recall and language memory.
AI.conclusion: Watch-Think-Interact provides an effective mechanism for streaming video QA under context limits by combining natural-language memory with time-indexed selective recall and a closed-loop decision process for when to answer, keep watching, or retrieve past evidence. Together with the WTI-82K dataset and Stream-GDPO training, this approach yields better aggregate performance than prior open-source streaming baselines, showing that explicit, time-tagged memory plus learned recall policies can mitigate information loss and improve long-horizon video reasoning.

title: Which papyrus HTR is good enough? Character-error-rate tolerance of four papyrological tasks on Greek texts
summary: Purpose: Most Greek papyri remain unpublished and undigitised; a handwritten text recognition (HTR) pipeline that transcribes them automatically would let scholars discover documents and literary works that have so far gone unread. Recognition systems for Ancient Greek papyri are in statu nascendi, and how accurate they must be for a given papyrological task has not been examined. To answer this and set a benchmark for Greek papyrus HTR, we test a range of character error rates (CER) against four papyrological tasks, using published editions as ground truth. Methods: From 63,846 current editions of Greek texts in papyri.info, we imitate a letters-only "perfect HTR" output by removing the editorial layer, then degrade it with a seeded algorithm to exact CERs of 1 - 50%, with lost lines and four error-shape variants. On these data we train small models (TF-IDF, fastText, a character CNN, ByT5-small) for document type, dating and documentary-versus-literary classification, and apply eight keyword search methods. We compare models trained on clean text with models retrained at a specific CER level, and evaluate across CERs. Results: Tolerance differs by task. With clean-trained models, documentary-versus-literary classification retains 90% of its metric up to 20% CER; document type up to 7.5%; subtypes and search up to 5%; dating only up to 3%. Retraining on text containing character errors largely eliminates the sharp degradation that otherwise sets in above 15% CER. Models generally tolerate concentrated damage in a long document better than small errors spread across a short text. Conclusion: The study provides a CER target for each of the four tasks and shows that models trained on noisy text make current, imperfect text recognition useful for them.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how much character-level error in automatic handwritten text recognition (HTR) can be tolerated for different scholarly tasks on Ancient Greek papyri, setting practical error-rate targets and showing that training models on noisy text substantially improves robustness.
AI.motivation: Most Ancient Greek papyri are still unpublished and undigitised, limiting scholarly access. Fully accurate HTR for these handwritten texts is not yet available, and it is unclear what level of recognition accuracy is actually necessary for typical papyrological tasks such as classification, dating, or search. Without this, it is difficult to judge whether current imperfect HTR systems are already useful or to set realistic quality benchmarks for them.
AI.method: Using 63,846 published Greek papyrus editions from papyri.info as ground truth, the authors simulate HTR output by stripping editorial markup and then algorithmically injecting controlled character errors to reach precise character error rates (CERs) from 1–50%, with variations in error distribution and shapes and including lost lines. On these degraded texts they train several relatively small models (TF-IDF, fastText, a character-level CNN, and ByT5-small) for document-type classification, dating, and documentary-versus-literary classification, and they test eight keyword search strategies. They compare models trained on clean text versus models retrained on noisy text and evaluate performance across different CERs and document conditions.
AI.result: They find that acceptable CER thresholds vary by task when models are trained on clean text: documentary-versus-literary classification retains about 90% of its performance up to ~20% CER; coarse document-type classification up to ~7.5%; more fine-grained subtypes and keyword search up to ~5%; and dating only up to ~3%. When models are retrained on noisy text matching a given CER, performance degradation becomes much more gradual, and the sharp performance drop above ~15% CER is largely avoided. Longer documents with localized heavy corruption are generally handled better than short texts with low-level but widespread errors.
AI.conclusion: The paper derives task-specific CER targets for HTR of Ancient Greek papyri and demonstrates that even imperfect recognition can be practically useful, provided downstream models are trained on similarly noisy data. This offers realistic quality benchmarks for HTR systems and supports the use of current, non-perfect HTR pipelines in papyrological research, guiding both system development and deployment strategies.

title: MatToolBench: Benchmarking Multimodal Agents in Real-World Materials Science Workflows
comment: 25 pages, 15 figures. Mei Wu and Rui Xie contributed equally. Bo Chen and Lu Chen are corresponding authors. Project page: https://mattoolbench.github.io/ ; code: https://github.com/meiwu5/MatToolBench
summary: Multimodal GUI agents have achieved impressive results on general software benchmarks, yet their ability to operate professional scientific software remains largely unexplored. In materials science, sparse domain-specific web data, specialized interfaces, and tacit workflow conventions create blind spots that general-purpose pretraining cannot readily bridge. We present MatToolBench, the first real-environment benchmark for evaluating multimodal GUI agents on professional materials science software, comprising 204 tasks across 10 tools in three modalities: GUI operation, OriginPro scripting, and code-based database queries, all executed inside a Windows 11 VM. Each task is decomposed into fine-grained sub-criteria by domain experts, enabling interpretable partial-credit scoring; the GUI component of our multi-level evaluation pipeline achieves an average F1 of 0.98. For OriginPro figure-generation tasks, we further conduct a human-LLM agreement study to validate the use of a multimodal judge for secondary aesthetic assessment. Our experiments show that strong performance on general benchmarks does not transfer to professional scientific workflows, and that this gap is not a visual-grounding problem alone: failures arise from domain-specific operational knowledge, sparse pretraining coverage of scientific software, weak cross-tool artifact handoff, and critical states exposed only visually. Even the best model reaches only 25% success rate on GUI tasks and 45% on code tasks. MatToolBench therefore serves as a challenging diagnostic benchmark and real-environment testbed for data-scarce, knowledge-intensive scientific workflows.

AI.tldr: MatToolBench is a new real-environment benchmark to test multimodal GUI agents on professional materials science software, revealing a large performance gap between current agents and real scientific workflows.
AI.motivation: Although multimodal GUI agents perform well on generic software benchmarks, their ability to handle professional scientific tools—especially in materials science—remains unclear. Existing pretraining struggles with sparse domain-specific data, specialized interfaces, and implicit workflow conventions, so a realistic benchmark is needed to diagnose and quantify these limitations.
AI.method: The authors build MatToolBench, a benchmark with 204 tasks across 10 professional materials science tools, spanning three modalities: direct GUI operation, scripting in OriginPro, and code-based database queries. All tasks are executed in a real Windows 11 virtual machine. Domain experts decompose each task into fine-grained sub-criteria to allow interpretable partial-credit scoring. They implement a multi-level evaluation pipeline, including a GUI-based component with an average F1 of 0.98, and run a human–LLM agreement study to validate using a multimodal judge for aesthetic evaluation of OriginPro figure-generation tasks. They then evaluate state-of-the-art multimodal GUI agents and compare their performance to general benchmarks.
AI.result: The evaluation shows that high performance on general software benchmarks does not carry over to professional materials science workflows. Even the best current model only achieves a 25% success rate on GUI tasks and 45% on code-based tasks. Analysis indicates that failures are driven not just by visual grounding issues but also by missing domain-specific operational knowledge, limited pretraining coverage of scientific software, weak handoff of artifacts across tools, and dependence on critical states that are only visible in the GUI.
AI.conclusion: MatToolBench exposes a substantial gap between current multimodal GUI agents and the requirements of real scientific practice in materials science, showing that general pretraining and visual grounding are insufficient. It provides a challenging, realistic benchmark and testbed for developing agents capable of data-scarce, knowledge-intensive scientific workflows, emphasizing the need to address domain-specific knowledge, tool coverage, cross-tool coordination, and visually exposed critical states.

title: Selecting What Matters: Semantic Compression-Guided Selective Pooling for Long-Context Embeddings
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong potential as training-free text encoders for long-context embeddings. Existing approaches primarily improve information flow under causal attention and typically construct embeddings by uniformly averaging all token representations. However, for long documents, such mean pooling can dilute salient semantic information with abundant redundant or weakly informative content. To this end, we propose SCSP, a training-free framework that leverages semantic compression for informative token selection in long-context embedding. Specifically, SCSP first partitions a document into sentence-aware chunks and appends a semantic compression prompt to each chunk. A prompt-isolated attention mask preserves information flow among document tokens while restricting each prompt to its corresponding local context. We then use the attention patterns elicited by these prompts to estimate token importance, select informative tokens, and aggregate their intermediate-layer representations into the final embedding. Extensive experiments on long-context embedding benchmarks demonstrate that SCSP can be integrated into both zero-shot and fine-tuned models in a plug-and-play manner, consistently improving their performance.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces SCSP, a training-free framework that uses semantic compression to select and pool only informative tokens from long documents, improving long-context embeddings of LLMs.
AI.motivation: Existing long-context embedding methods with LLMs usually rely on mean pooling over all token representations, which dilutes important information in long documents because many tokens are redundant or weakly informative. There is a need for a training-free way to focus embeddings on salient content while preserving long-range information flow.
AI.method: SCSP partitions each long document into sentence-aware chunks and appends a semantic compression prompt to each chunk. A special attention mask allows normal information flow among document tokens but isolates each prompt to its local chunk. The model’s attention responses to these prompts are then used to estimate token importance scores. Based on these scores, SCSP selects the most informative tokens and aggregates their intermediate-layer representations to form the final document embedding, instead of averaging all tokens. The framework is plug-and-play and can be used with both zero-shot and fine-tuned LLM encoders without additional training.
AI.result: On multiple long-context embedding benchmarks, SCSP consistently boosts performance compared to baseline approaches that rely on uniform mean pooling, for both zero-shot and fine-tuned models. The gains show up across different tasks and model settings, suggesting that semantic compression-based token selection is broadly effective.
AI.conclusion: SCSP provides an effective, training-free semantic compression mechanism for LLM-based long-context embeddings. By using prompt-induced attention patterns to select and pool only informative tokens, it mitigates the information dilution of mean pooling and can be easily integrated into existing models to improve long-document representation quality.

title: actr: aligning thoughts and responses for multilingual safety in reasoning llms
summary: Ensuring the safety of reasoning large language models (LLMs) across languages is essential for their reliable deployment. However, when exposed to jailbreak attacks in non-high-resource languages, these models may generate unsafe responses even when their reasoning traces identify safety risks. To address this issue, we propose aligning cross-lingual thoughts and responses (ACTR), a framework that improves multilingual safety alignment by strengthening the use of existing safety reasoning. Specifically, we first present the think gap score (TGS) to compare the normalized contributions of reasoning traces to attention outputs during response generation across languages, and use reasoning- trace substitution to measure the cross-lingual safety gap. Next, using a corpus of jailbreak queries, we assess neuron importance through changes in response representations caused by neuron masking and compare the high-importance neuron sets obtained with reasoning enabled and disabled to identify safety think neurons that support the use of safety reasoning. Finally, we devise neuron-selective consistency optimization (NSCO), which uses a frozen judge model to reward agreement between the safety categories of reasoning traces and responses while updating only the parameters associated with the selected neurons, requiring no human-annotated responses or preference data. Across two reasoning models, ACTR achieves lower average attack success rates than the evaluated state-of-the-art methods on AdvBench-X and MultiJail, with safety gains extending to unseen languages, while preserving or improving average performance on multilingual knowledge and mathematical reasoning tasks and limiting false refusals of benign requests. Warning: this paper contains examples with unsafe content.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces ACTR, a framework to improve multilingual safety alignment in reasoning LLMs by better leveraging their own safety reasoning across languages, reducing jailbreak success while preserving task performance.
AI.motivation: Reasoning LLMs can often recognize safety risks in their internal thoughts yet still output unsafe responses, especially under jailbreak attacks in lower-resource languages. Existing safety alignment methods are mostly monolingual and do not explicitly connect internal safety reasoning with final responses across languages. The authors aim to close this gap and ensure that when a model internally detects unsafe content, this awareness reliably influences its outputs in many languages.
AI.method: The authors propose ACTR, which aligns cross-lingual thoughts and responses through three main components. (1) Think Gap Score (TGS): they quantify how much safety-related reasoning traces contribute to attention outputs across languages and use reasoning-trace substitution to estimate cross-lingual safety gaps. (2) Safety think neuron identification: using a jailbreak corpus, they perform neuron masking and measure changes in response representations with and without reasoning to identify neurons that specifically support the use of safety reasoning. (3) Neuron-Selective Consistency Optimization (NSCO): they use a frozen judge model to label safety categories of both reasoning traces and responses and optimize only the previously selected neurons to maximize agreement between the two, without needing human-labeled responses or preference data.
AI.result: On two reasoning LLMs, ACTR reduces average attack success rates compared to state-of-the-art safety methods on AdvBench-X and MultiJail multilingual jailbreak benchmarks. The safety improvements generalize to unseen languages not used in training. At the same time, the models’ performance on multilingual knowledge and mathematical reasoning benchmarks is preserved or improved, and the method keeps false refusals of benign queries low.
AI.conclusion: Aligning internal safety reasoning with final responses at the neuron level improves multilingual robustness of reasoning LLMs against jailbreak attacks. ACTR leverages existing model safety signals, operates without additional human annotations, and yields better safety-utility trade-offs across many languages, including those not seen during training.

title: A Proposed Rubric for Evaluating Expressed Clinical Reasoning in Large Language Model Responses
summary: Rubrics support the structured evaluation of language models. We propose a rubric for assessing expressed clinical reasoning in model responses, drawing on three bodies of work: medical education assessment frameworks (ART, SCT, Key Feature Problems and OSCE); clinical LLM benchmarks (MedR-Bench, HealthBench, TIMER-Bench, DR.BENCH, PrIME-LLM and PatientSafeBench); and general LLM reasoning evaluation research, including the Factuality-Validity-Coherence-Utility taxonomy, FaithCoT-Bench and C2-Faith. We use groundedness as a clinically oriented adaptation of the taxonomy's factuality category. The rubric brings these concepts together in a multidimensional framework for scoring free-text responses to gold-standard clinical vignettes. It includes provisional behavioural anchors, applicability rules and a separate flag for case-specific safety-critical errors. General-domain frameworks inform its design but are not treated as validated clinical instruments. The rubric does not replace case-specific reference criteria or the task-specific metrics of existing benchmarks. It has not yet been tested for inter-rater reliability, construct validity or clinical utility. Its immediate purpose is to make evaluation decisions explicit and open to scrutiny before empirical testing.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a structured rubric to evaluate the quality of clinical reasoning expressed by language models when answering clinical vignettes.
AI.motivation: Existing clinical LLM benchmarks and general reasoning taxonomies evaluate performance but often lack a transparent, systematic way to judge the quality of free-text clinical reasoning, especially in terms that are meaningful for medical education and clinical practice. The authors aim to create a clinically grounded framework that makes evaluation criteria explicit and scrutinizable, bridging medical education assessment methods and LLM evaluation research.
AI.method: The authors synthesize concepts from three areas: (1) medical education assessment frameworks (ART, Script Concordance Test, Key Feature Problems, OSCE), (2) clinical LLM benchmarks (e.g., MedR-Bench, HealthBench, TIMER-Bench, DR.BENCH, PrIME-LLM, PatientSafeBench), and (3) general LLM reasoning evaluations (Factuality-Validity-Coherence-Utility taxonomy, FaithCoT-Bench, C2-Faith). They adapt the factuality dimension into a clinically oriented notion of “groundedness” and design a multidimensional rubric with behavioral anchors, applicability rules, and a separate flag for safety-critical, case-specific errors, targeted at scoring free-text responses to gold-standard clinical vignettes.
AI.result: The outcome is a proposed, but not yet empirically validated, rubric for rating expressed clinical reasoning in LLM responses. It specifies multiple dimensions, provides provisional behavioral anchors for scoring, defines when dimensions apply, and introduces a safety-critical error flag. The rubric is explicitly positioned as complementary to, not a replacement for, existing benchmark metrics and case-specific reference criteria.
AI.conclusion: The rubric offers a transparent, multidimensional framework for evaluating LLM clinical reasoning quality, grounded in both medical education and LLM evaluation literature. However, it remains preliminary: it has not yet undergone studies for inter-rater reliability, construct validity, or clinical utility. Its current function is to surface and formalize evaluation assumptions so that they can be critically examined and empirically tested in future work.

title: Breaking the Illusion of Review Reliability under Static Evaluation: SCOPE Fuzzing for LLM-based Scientific Reviewers
summary: The rapid growth of submissions and reviewing workload has accelerated the use of large language models (LLMs) in peer review. Prior studies suggest that LLM-based reviewers can penalize content perturbations, such as overclaiming, indicating a certain degree of reliability. Yet these conclusions are largely based on a narrow set of perturbation strategies instantiated with static templates, providing limited evidence of actual reliability. In this paper, we construct a three-level evaluation framework covering perturbations to surface presentation, argumentative logic, and value judgment. Experiments on representative LLM-based reviewers reveal two limitations of static evaluation: stratified vulnerability, where perturbation effects depend on whether the paper's original review score is high or low, and perturbation undercoverage, where a single template misses vulnerabilities exposed by diverse realizations. To address these limitations, we propose SCOPE-Fuzzer, a strategy-aware fuzzer that combines feedback-driven strategy selection with adaptive mutation of paper content. By iteratively probing reviewers with dynamic perturbations, SCOPE-Fuzzer consistently uncovers vulnerabilities overlooked by static evaluation and other baselines.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates and stress-tests LLM-based peer reviewers more comprehensively and introduces SCOPE-Fuzzer, a dynamic fuzzing framework that uncovers hidden vulnerabilities in how these models respond to perturbed papers.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of LLM-based reviewers rely on a narrow, template-based set of content perturbations (e.g., simple overclaiming) and thus give an overly optimistic view of their reliability. The authors are motivated by the need to understand how robust these reviewers truly are when confronted with more realistic, diverse, and strategically generated manipulations of paper content, which is critical as LLMs are increasingly used in real peer-review workflows.
AI.method: They design a three-level evaluation framework that systematically perturbs papers at (1) surface presentation (style/wording), (2) argumentative logic (reasoning structure, claims vs. evidence), and (3) value judgment (framing, emphasis of contributions). Using this framework, they test representative LLM-based reviewers and diagnose limitations of static, template-based perturbations. Then they introduce SCOPE-Fuzzer, a strategy-aware fuzzing system that uses feedback from the reviewer to choose perturbation strategies and to adaptively mutate paper content over multiple rounds, dynamically exploring the space of possible manipulations to find where reviewers are vulnerable.
AI.result: The experiments show that static, template-based perturbations severely under-represent the vulnerabilities of LLM-based reviewers. They uncover stratified vulnerability: the effect of perturbations depends strongly on whether the original review score is high or low. They also show perturbation undercoverage: a single template misses many failure modes that appear with more varied realizations. SCOPE-Fuzzer, by contrast, consistently finds more and different vulnerabilities than static baselines and other evaluation methods, demonstrating that dynamic, feedback-driven perturbation is more effective at exposing weaknesses in LLM reviewers.
AI.conclusion: Static, template-based robustness checks are insufficient to assess the reliability of LLM-based peer reviewers because they miss important, score-dependent and realization-dependent vulnerabilities. A richer, multi-level perturbation framework combined with dynamic, strategy-aware fuzzing like SCOPE-Fuzzer provides a more realistic and stringent test of these systems, revealing that current LLM reviewers are more fragile than prior evaluations suggest and highlighting the need for stronger defenses and evaluation protocols before deploying them widely in peer review.

title: CompOrca: Corpus-Scale Compliance Labelling of Instruction-Tuning Data
comment: Accepted to PlurVA-LLM Workshop @ AACL-IJCNLP 2026. Dataset available on HuggingFace
summary: Studying how fine-tuning shapes refusal and noncompliance behaviour requires identifying training examples that refuse, evade or otherwise fail to fulfil the requested task. But existing annotation covers evaluation sets of a few thousand prompts at most. We present CompOrca, a compliance labelling over the entirety of the 4,233,923-example OpenOrca corpus. Every example was classified as compliant or noncompliant by five independent passes of an open-weight LLM judge (LongCat-2.0, 1.6T parameters), and the corpus is released as unanimous compliance (94.75%), unanimous noncompliance (1.28%), and nonunanimous rows (3.97%) along with the raw vote counts. A single pass flags 2.7-3.2% of the corpus as noncompliant, while only 1.28% is flagged by all five, allowing for filtering the most ambiguous samples. Against 450 human-annotated examples, 150 of them annotated twice (human-human $κ= 0.93$), the unanimous compliance and noncompliance labels are 97.3% and 86.7% precise, the latter a high-precision subset, not a complete enumeration, of noncompliance. Published refusal-detection methods recall only between 0.4% and 94.1% of the noncompliance class. We release the full corpus with its per-row labels and vote counts at https://huggingface.co/datasets/cemiu/CompOrca

AI.tldr: CompOrca is a large-scale compliance annotation of the entire 4.23M-example OpenOrca dataset, generated using multiple passes of a large open-weight LLM judge, and validated against human labels.
AI.motivation: To understand and control how fine-tuning shapes refusal and noncompliance behavior in LLMs, researchers need many accurately labeled examples of compliant vs. noncompliant responses, but current datasets are small and insufficient for large-scale analysis or training.
AI.method: The authors run five independent passes of a very large open-weight LLM judge (LongCat-2.0, 1.6T parameters) over all 4,233,923 OpenOrca examples, classifying each example as compliant or noncompliant. They aggregate these five votes, release subsets with unanimous compliance, unanimous noncompliance, and nonunanimous labels, and evaluate the precision of these labels against a human-annotated benchmark of 450 prompts (with high human-human agreement). They also benchmark existing refusal-detection methods on the new labeled corpus.
AI.result: Of all OpenOrca examples, 94.75% are unanimously judged compliant, 1.28% unanimously noncompliant, and 3.97% have nonunanimous labels. A single LLM-judge pass flags 2.7–3.2% as noncompliant, but only 1.28% are flagged noncompliant by all five passes, providing a high-confidence subset. Against human labels, the unanimous compliance and noncompliance subsets achieve 97.3% and 86.7% precision respectively, confirming that unanimous noncompliance is a high-precision but incomplete slice of all noncompliance. Existing refusal-detection methods show highly variable recall, from 0.4% to 94.1% on the noncompliance class.
AI.conclusion: CompOrca provides a large, high-precision, LLM-judged labeling of compliance and noncompliance across the entire OpenOrca corpus, enabling better study and training of refusal behavior in LLMs. The unanimous labels are particularly reliable, though noncompliance is only partially captured. The released dataset, including per-row vote counts, can serve both as a research benchmark for refusal detection and as a resource for training and evaluating safer and more controllable language models.

title: Learning from Viable Failure Prefixes: Milestone Viability Potential Policy Optimization for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
summary: Long-horizon LLM agents require reinforcement learning methods that can assign credit to intermediate decisions under sparse and delayed rewards. Existing group-based methods such as GRPO and GiGPO alleviate this issue by comparing rollout returns or repeated anchor states, but they still fail when the compared returns have no variation. We identify this failure mode as zero-credit failure: during early training, many failed rollouts contain useful prefixes, yet existing methods assign them no task-discriminative advantage. To address this issue, we propose Milestone Viability Potential Policy Optimization (MVPO), a potential-routed policy optimization algorithm that learns from viable failure prefixes. MVPO estimates prefix potential over Union-Find viability regions, repairs zero-credit groups with potential-difference advantages, and attenuates the potential branch according to relative performance progress. Experiments with Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct show that MVPO outperforms eight strong baselines, including GRPO and GiGPO. Under the same training length, MVPO improves over the GiGPO baseline by +4.4 success points on ALFWorld and +5.3 on WebShop, while adding only 0.16%-0.20% advantage-construction overhead.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces MVPO, a reinforcement learning method for long-horizon LLM agents that fixes a zero-credit failure mode in existing group-based policy optimization by exploiting viable failure prefixes, achieving better performance on ALFWorld and WebShop with minimal overhead.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon LLM agents often operate under sparse and delayed rewards, making it hard to assign credit to intermediate decisions. Existing group-based methods like GRPO and GiGPO compare rollout returns or anchor states to shape learning, but they break down when returns within groups have no variation—especially early in training when most rollouts fail yet may contain useful partial progress. This zero-credit failure means that informative prefixes of failed trajectories provide no learning signal, slowing or preventing effective policy improvement. The paper aims to resolve this structural failure mode to better exploit partial successes in long-horizon tasks.
AI.method: The authors propose Milestone Viability Potential Policy Optimization (MVPO), a potential-routed policy optimization algorithm. MVPO: (1) defines and discovers viability regions over trajectory prefixes using a Union-Find structure, effectively grouping prefixes that can still reach success; (2) estimates a "prefix potential" for these regions, measuring how promising a partial trajectory is; (3) repairs zero-credit groups by replacing flat returns with potential-difference based advantages, providing a graded learning signal even when all final returns are identical; and (4) attenuates this potential-based signal over time according to relative performance progress, so that as the agent improves, standard return-based learning dominates. This yields a modified policy gradient update that leverages viable failure prefixes while remaining computationally efficient.
AI.result: Using Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct as the base agent, MVPO is evaluated on long-horizon environments ALFWorld and WebShop against eight strong baselines including GRPO and GiGPO. Under equal training budgets, MVPO improves success rates over GiGPO by +4.4 points on ALFWorld and +5.3 points on WebShop, while incurring only about 0.16%-0.20% extra overhead for constructing advantages. These results show that MVPO both enhances learning efficiency and maintains low computational cost compared to state-of-the-art group-based methods.
AI.conclusion: MVPO overcomes the zero-credit failure of existing group-based policy optimization methods by leveraging viable failure prefixes via a potential-based routing mechanism over Union-Find viability regions. This allows long-horizon LLM agents to extract informative gradients even when final returns are uniformly poor, improving success rates on complex tasks with negligible computational overhead. The work suggests that careful modeling of prefix viability and potential is a promising direction for scaling reinforcement learning in long-horizon LLM-based agents.

title: Thinking in Depth, Speaking Directly: Recurrent Latent Reasoning for Paralinguistically Grounded Spoken Dialogue
summary: Empathetic spoken dialogue requires models to use both what is said and how it is said to decide how to respond. Explicit CoT can improve paralinguistic perception and make acoustic cues more explicit in replies, yet does not ensure their effective use in response planning. We call this mismatch the perception-reasoning gap. In addition, CoT may not fully capture acoustic cues in words, and generating it adds inference latency. To address these limitations, we introduce LoopSLM, which builds on looped Transformers for latent reasoning, reusing a decoder block to refine hidden states with acoustic grounding at every pass. Its two-stage training further narrows the perception-reasoning gap by separating learning to reason from learning to respond, enabling direct inference without CoT. On EchoMind, LoopSLM improves paralinguistic understanding, reasoning, and reply quality over Qwen2.5-Omni-7B. Against the CoT-SFT baseline, LoopSLM gains over 20 points in reasoning accuracy while generating 64.5% fewer tokens at half the latency. It also outperforms Qwen3-Omni-Thinking on most empathetic reply metrics with 34x lower latency. Despite training only on dialogue data, LoopSLM improves accuracy on general audio benchmarks.

AI.tldr: LoopSLM is a speech-aware dialogue model that narrows the gap between perceiving acoustic cues and using them for empathetic reasoning and responses, without needing explicit chain-of-thought text.
AI.motivation: Empathetic spoken dialogue systems need to understand both linguistic content and acoustic signals (prosody, tone, etc.). Explicit textual chain-of-thought (CoT) helps make paralinguistic cues explicit, but it does not guarantee they are used effectively in planning responses, can miss acoustic information, and increases inference latency. The paper aims to close this perception-reasoning gap and reduce latency while improving reasoning and response quality in empathetic spoken dialogue.
AI.method: The authors propose LoopSLM, a looped-Transformer-based model for latent reasoning over acoustic and textual information. A decoder block is reused iteratively (looped) to refine hidden states with acoustic grounding in each pass, enabling implicit reasoning about paralinguistic cues. The model uses a two-stage training procedure: (1) learning to reason with acoustic grounding, and (2) learning to respond empathetically, thereby decoupling reasoning from response generation. This enables direct inference without producing explicit CoT tokens.
AI.result: On the EchoMind benchmark, LoopSLM surpasses Qwen2.5-Omni-7B in paralinguistic understanding, reasoning, and response quality. Compared to a CoT-SFT (chain-of-thought supervised fine-tuning) baseline, LoopSLM achieves over 20 percentage points higher reasoning accuracy while generating 64.5% fewer tokens and running at half the latency. It also outperforms Qwen3-Omni-Thinking on most empathetic reply metrics with approximately 34x lower latency. Despite being trained only on dialogue data, LoopSLM also improves performance on general audio understanding benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: LoopSLM effectively narrows the perception-reasoning gap in empathetic spoken dialogue by performing latent, acoustically grounded reasoning via looped Transformer refinement and a two-stage training scheme. It eliminates the need for explicit textual chain-of-thought at inference, simultaneously improving reasoning accuracy, empathetic response quality, and computational efficiency, while also generalizing to broader audio tasks.

title: When Should Agents Check External State? Budgeting Observations for Stored Intentions
summary: Prospective memory allows an agent to retain an intention tied to a future condition, but the stored intention does not reveal whether that condition currently holds. Checking it may require web access, multi-step tool use, and paid calls. Existing systems decide when intentions require attention, but do not allocate the resulting observations under a shared budget. We introduce the first resource-allocation formulation for the external observations required by stored intentions under a shared episode budget. BudgetPM offers two policy variants that share a hard-budget executor. BudgetPM-Static uses a lightweight Logistic scorer to learn whether a check improves the current decision. BudgetPM-Sequential distills full-episode hindsight schedules into a lightweight policy that decides when to spend or reserve capacity using only pre-query information at deployment. We evaluate BudgetPM against two public memory-agent systems, five matched controls, and four hand-designed monitoring or budget-adaptation rules. Across two benchmarks and three backbones, BudgetPM-Static outperforms adapted Mem0 and PMA workflows. On PM-Bench, its Logistic scorer reaches competitive quality--cost operating points alongside higher-capacity scorers and retains 99.9--100\% of unconstrained quality with 42--54\% fewer observations. Under severe scarcity and the same hard caps, BudgetPM-Sequential exceeds the strongest tested natural monitoring schedule by 1.92--2.58 Set F1 points. It reaches the same Set F1 and on-time recall with 16--33\% fewer observations. Matched attribution, exact-cost analysis, and a fixed-budget load intervention link this gain to competition between present and future opportunities. These results yield a demand--capacity design rule: local gating works when capacity covers demand, while future-aware supervision adds value when observations compete across time.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces BudgetPM, a framework for allocating limited external observation budget for prospective memory checks in agents, achieving similar or better performance with fewer observations than existing methods.
AI.motivation: Existing memory-agent systems can decide when a stored intention needs attention but assume effectively unlimited budget or treat checks independently. In realistic scenarios, external checks (like web queries or tools) are costly and must share a limited budget across an episode, creating competition between present and future observation needs. There was no explicit resource-allocation formulation for this problem.
AI.method: The authors formulate prospective memory observation as a resource-allocation problem under a shared hard budget. They propose BudgetPM with two variants sharing a budget-constrained executor. BudgetPM-Static learns a lightweight Logistic regression-based scorer that predicts if performing an observation will improve the current decision. BudgetPM-Sequential uses hindsight over full episodes to learn a lightweight policy that decides when to spend or save observation capacity using only pre-query features at deployment. They compare against existing memory systems, matched baselines, and hand-crafted rules across multiple backbones and benchmarks, using metrics such as Set F1, quality–cost trade-offs, and attribution/ablation analyses.
AI.result: BudgetPM-Static outperforms adapted Mem0 and PMA workflows across benchmarks and models, achieving nearly unconstrained performance (99.9–100% of quality) while using 42–54% fewer external observations. BudgetPM-Sequential, under very tight budgets, outperforms the strongest natural monitoring schedule by 1.92–2.58 Set F1 points and can match the same Set F1 and on-time recall with 16–33% fewer observations. Attribution and controlled cost analyses show that gains stem from better handling of competition between present and future observation opportunities.
AI.conclusion: Managing external observation budget for prospective memory as a global resource-allocation problem substantially improves efficiency without sacrificing quality. The paper proposes a design rule: simple local gating is sufficient when observation capacity comfortably meets demand, but when observations compete over time, policies trained with future-aware supervision (like BudgetPM-Sequential) provide clear benefits. This guides how to design memory and monitoring components for agents under realistic cost constraints.

title: The Geometry of Inference in Transformer Residual Streams
summary: Transformer language models build predictions through successive residual updates, but how their representations become specific to an eventual outcome remains unclear. We study this process by comparing intermediate residual states with their own final states and an empirical bank of final states from other contexts. Across six pretrained language models, the own endpoint becomes preferable to the average alternative early, while many individual endpoints remain closer. These competing sets generally shrink with depth, but their membership changes and their surviving endpoints need not become more similar to one another. Directional alignment and endpoint rank can therefore improve while Euclidean distance to the final state changes little. We develop a simple high-dimensional model that separates the roles of norm, alignment, and endpoint geometry, showing how gradual directional changes can produce sharp reductions in competition. We also prove that a straight path toward the own endpoint cannot introduce new competitors under either Euclidean or cosine distance; observed entries thus establish departures from straight-line convergence. Finally, endpoints associated with lower-ranked output tokens tend to lie farther away in cosine distance across all studied models, connecting residual geometry to output organization. Together, these findings characterize increasing geometric specificity during transformer inference and explain why distance, competitor count, and concentration of the surviving endpoints provide distinct views of that process.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how transformer residual stream representations gradually become specific to the final prediction and why simple distance metrics don’t fully capture this process.
AI.motivation: While transformers update a residual stream layer by layer, it is not well understood how intermediate representations evolve to uniquely reflect the eventual output instead of many possible alternatives. Existing intuitions about “moving toward the final state” are vague and can be misleading in high-dimensional spaces. The authors aim to clarify what geometric changes actually occur during inference and how these relate to output token probabilities.
AI.method: They analyze intermediate residual states in six pretrained language models by comparing each state to (1) its own final residual state and (2) a large bank of final residual states from many other contexts. They track when the ‘own’ endpoint becomes closer than the average alternative, how many alternative endpoints remain closer, and how these sets change by layer. They decompose geometry into norm, directional alignment (cosine similarity), and the arrangement of endpoints. They build a simple high-dimensional toy model to analytically separate these factors and prove properties of straight-line convergence paths in representation space. They also correlate geometric measures with output token ranks.
AI.result: They find that, fairly early in depth, a state’s own final endpoint already beats the average alternative in similarity, yet many specific alternative endpoints remain closer than the own endpoint. As layers deepen, the number of these competing endpoints generally shrinks, but which alternatives compete changes, and the remaining competitors do not necessarily cluster or become mutually similar. Directional alignment with the final state and the rank of the correct endpoint improve with depth, even when Euclidean distance to the final state changes little. The toy model shows that gradual directional changes can sharply reduce the number of competitors without big distance changes. They prove that a straight path to the correct endpoint cannot create new competitors under Euclidean or cosine distance, so observed new competitors imply a more complex trajectory. Lower-ranked output tokens correspond to endpoints that are farther away in cosine distance across all models studied.
AI.conclusion: Transformer inference shows increasing geometric specificity: as depth increases, residual states become more directionally aligned with their final endpoint and eliminate many competing endpoints, even if Euclidean distance does not change much. Distance, competitor count, and the structure of surviving endpoints capture different aspects of this process. Real model trajectories deviate from simple straight-line convergence, and the geometry of endpoints is systematically related to output token ranks. This clarifies how transformer residual streams evolve to encode specific outputs and why simple distance-based intuitions are insufficient.

title: SkillCome: Group Contrast Skill Optimization with Dual Memory
summary: Skill evolution improves the capabilities of large language models by analyzing trajectories generated under a given skill and modifying the skill accordingly. Existing approaches typically generate a single trajectory per question. However, this provides insufficient optimization signals since it requires inferring effective skill edits from a solitary path. It is difficult to pinpoint which actions caused the failure in a failed trajectory, or to determine which actions in a successful one should be incorporated into the skill. Furthermore, they rely on a local batch of trajectories for analysis, making the optimization direction susceptible to noisy evidence. To address these, we propose SkillCome, a Skill-evolution method based on group Contrast optimization with dual memory. For each question, SkillCome generates trajectories and performs group contrast analysis to precisely identify key behavioral divergences between successful and failed trajectories, offering reliable optimization signals. The dual memory system further accumulates evidence from historical steps to track patterns shared across different groups, leading to more generalized optimization directions. Together, SkillCome builds a systematic optimization process that transforms experience from observed successful trajectories into reusable skills. Extensive experiments on six benchmarks spanning question answering, reasoning, and agentic tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of our method. SkillCome consistently outperforms baselines across five models of varying families and scales, with gains up to +5.69 points.

AI.tldr: SkillCome is a skill-evolution framework that improves large language models by contrasting groups of successful and failed trajectories and aggregating evidence in a dual-memory system to refine reusable skills.
AI.motivation: Existing skill-evolution methods for large language models typically rely on a single trajectory per question and only local trajectory batches. This makes it hard to attribute success or failure to specific actions, produces weak and noisy optimization signals, and limits the generalization of learned skills. There is a need for a more reliable and systematic way to extract, aggregate, and reuse behavioral patterns from multiple trajectories to improve model skills.
AI.method: The paper proposes SkillCome, a skill-evolution method based on group contrast optimization with a dual memory mechanism. For each question, the system generates multiple trajectories and performs group contrast analysis, comparing groups of successful and failed trajectories to identify key behavioral divergences that correlate with outcomes. A dual memory system (likely consisting of short-term/local and long-term/global memory) accumulates historical evidence across steps and tasks to capture patterns shared across different trajectory groups. These extracted patterns are then used to edit and refine the underlying skills of the large language model, forming a systematic optimization loop that converts observed successful behaviors into reusable skills.
AI.result: SkillCome is evaluated on six benchmarks covering question answering, reasoning, and agentic tasks, and tested on five large language models across different families and scales. The method consistently outperforms baseline skill-evolution and related approaches, achieving performance gains of up to +5.69 points, indicating more effective and generalized skill optimization.
AI.conclusion: SkillCome establishes a more robust and generalizable skill-evolution framework for large language models by using group contrast optimization and dual memory to derive clearer, less noisy optimization signals from multiple trajectories. It successfully transforms experience from observed successful trajectories into reusable skills, leading to consistent improvements over baselines across tasks and model architectures.

title: Can Vision-Language Models Stay Helpful When Facing Implicit Risks? Intent-Privilege OPSD for Efficient Safety-Helpfulness Alignment
summary: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) remain vulnerable to cross-modal implicit risks: visual and textual inputs that appear benign in isolation can jointly elicit unsafe responses. Existing safety methods often require large preference datasets, costly multi-rollout training, or additional safeguards at inference time. They may also sacrifice helpfulness by directly refusing requests that could be answered safely. In this paper, we propose Intent-Privilege On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD), which leverages evidence-grounded intent as privileged supervision during training to help VLMs recognize implicit risks and provide safe, useful responses instead of blanket refusals. OPSD distills a teacher's intent-conditioned preferences over responses into a student using a single rollout per prompt; the student then responds without intent annotations or an additional safety module. With only 1,447 safety-specific examples - 95% fewer than standard preference datasets - OPSD reduces training time by 5x relative to multi-rollout GRPO-style training and average inference length by 7%. It attains the highest ratio for joint safety-helpfulness success, which measures the proportion of responses that are both safe and helpful, across all five evaluation groups. Remarkably, on pooled SIUO+HoliSafe, this success ratio rises from 43.9% to 53.5%. These results show that training-time intent supervision can improve both safety and helpfulness while substantially reducing data, training, and inference costs.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces OPSD, a training-time intent-supervised self-distillation method that makes vision-language models safer and more helpful against cross-modal implicit risks with far less data and compute.
AI.motivation: Vision-Language Models are vulnerable to cross-modal implicit risks where benign-looking images and texts together trigger unsafe behavior. Existing safety approaches are resource-heavy, often need large preference datasets, multiple rollouts, or extra safety modules at inference, and can reduce helpfulness by over-refusing. The authors want a method that improves both safety and helpfulness while being data- and compute-efficient and avoiding blanket refusals.
AI.method: They propose Intent-Privilege On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD). A teacher model is given intent annotations (privileged supervision) that describe the user’s underlying intent, and the teacher generates intent-conditioned preferences over candidate responses using only a single rollout per prompt. These preferences are distilled into a student VLM during training. At inference, the student operates without access to intent labels or extra safety modules, having internalized safer response behavior from the teacher’s intent-conditioned supervision.
AI.result: Using only 1,447 safety-oriented examples—about 95% fewer than typical preference datasets—OPSD achieves a 5x reduction in training time compared to multi-rollout GRPO-style training and reduces average inference length by 7%. Across five benchmark groups, it achieves the highest joint safety-helpfulness success rate. On the combined SIUO+HoliSafe benchmark, this joint success ratio improves from 43.9% to 53.5%.
AI.conclusion: Training-time intent supervision, via OPSD, enables VLMs to better recognize and handle cross-modal implicit risks while remaining helpful. The method substantially cuts data, training, and inference costs, and improves the proportion of responses that are simultaneously safe and useful, suggesting intent-privileged self-distillation is an effective and efficient direction for safety alignment in VLMs.

title: Train Ahead, Distill Back: Bootstrapping On-Policy Self-Distillation for Large Language Models
summary: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) improves large language models by letting a self-teacher with privileged information provide dense token-level supervision on the model's own trajectories. Yet existing methods typically construct the self-teacher from the current, initial, or slowly averaged policy state, leaving the quality of supervision constrained by the teacher's ability to exploit privileged information. We ask whether the model's own optimization progress can instead be recycled into a stronger self-teacher. In this paper, we introduce Bootstrapped On-Policy Self-Distillation (B-OPSD), which temporarily trains the policy ahead to obtain a future teacher, restores the student to the original policy state, and then uses the future teacher to supervise the restarted student. The future teacher improves supervision in two complementary ways, it can generate more reliable privileged trajectories and, conditioned on them, provide more informative token-level targets along the restarted student's on-policy trajectories. Experiments on mathematical reasoning with Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B show consistent improvements over standard OPSD in both settings, including gains from 27.50 to 41.30 and from 48.80 to 64.44 in the rollout-privileged setting. Our findings point to a broader principle for self-improving models that future learning progress can be distilled backward, preserving acquired knowledge while bootstrapping beyond the optimization state that produced it.

AI.tldr: They propose B-OPSD, a new self-distillation method that uses a temporarily trained "future" version of the model to give stronger token-level supervision to the current model, improving math reasoning performance.
AI.motivation: Existing on-policy self-distillation methods use a teacher that is just a variant of the current policy (current, initial, or EMA), so the teacher cannot fully exploit privileged information and gives limited supervision quality. The authors want to see if the model’s own future optimization progress can be reused as a stronger teacher, thereby improving learning without external models.
AI.method: They introduce Bootstrapped On-Policy Self-Distillation (B-OPSD). First, they train the policy forward for some steps to obtain a stronger future teacher that has seen more optimization. Then they reset the student back to the earlier policy state. Using privileged information, the stronger future teacher generates higher-quality trajectories and token-level targets, which are then used to supervise the restarted on-policy student. This process recycles future learning progress back into the past model state.
AI.result: On mathematical reasoning benchmarks with Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B, B-OPSD consistently outperforms standard OPSD. In a rollout-privileged setting, they report improvements from 27.50 to 41.30 and from 48.80 to 64.44, showing substantial performance gains due to the stronger supervision from the bootstrapped teacher.
AI.conclusion: Future versions of a model, obtained by temporarily training it ahead, can act as more powerful self-teachers for earlier policy states. Distilling this future learning progress backward yields better token-level supervision and preserves acquired knowledge while enabling performance beyond what the original optimization trajectory alone would provide. This suggests a general principle for self-improving systems: learning progress can be bootstrapped backward in time to enhance current training.

title: AnthroDial: Benchmarking LLM Anthropomorphism in Autonomous Social Interaction
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as social agents, yet credible human-like interaction requires more than fluent responses or persona consistency. Agents must autonomously decide whether, when, and how to communicate while adapting to evolving contexts, goals, and relationships. Existing research, however, lacks a unified approach to enabling, evaluating, and improving such capabilities in continuous, open-ended interaction. We introduce AnthroDial, a unified framework for developing anthropomorphic social agents from three complementary aspects: MindFlow, a lightweight interaction harness that enables autonomous, asynchronous, and adaptive communication through a dynamic Mind Buffer; CAPS-Eval, a theory-grounded framework for evaluating cognitive, affective, and behavioral dimensions of anthropomorphic interaction; and a scalable training paradigm that combines SEEDS for environment expansion with DiAPO for adaptive capability optimization. We further construct evaluation datasets covering everyday communication, game interaction, and long-horizon character interaction. Extensive experiments across diverse models and scenarios demonstrate improved interaction autonomy and naturalness, validate the reliability, discriminativeness, and agreement with human rankings of CAPS-Eval, and confirm the effectiveness of our training paradigm. Together, these components provide a unified framework for developing credible human-like social agents in open-ended interaction.

AI.tldr: AnthroDial proposes a unified framework to build and evaluate more human-like, autonomous LLM-based social agents in open-ended interactions.
AI.motivation: Current LLM social agents mostly produce fluent, persona-consistent responses, but they lack true interaction autonomy: deciding when, whether, and how to speak across evolving contexts, goals, and relationships. There is also no unified, theory-grounded way to enable, measure, and improve these abilities in continuous, open-ended settings. The paper aims to systematically address these gaps.
AI.method: The authors design AnthroDial with three key components: (1) MindFlow, an interaction harness using a dynamic "Mind Buffer" so agents can autonomously manage asynchronous, adaptive communication; (2) CAPS-Eval, an evaluation framework grounded in cognitive and affective theories to assess cognitive, affective, and behavioral aspects of anthropomorphic interaction; and (3) a scalable training paradigm that uses SEEDS to expand environments and DiAPO to adaptively optimize agent capabilities. They also build multiple evaluation datasets spanning everyday chats, game interactions, and long-horizon character-based interactions and run extensive experiments with various models and scenarios.
AI.result: Experiments show that AnthroDial-trained agents exhibit higher autonomy and more natural interaction patterns. CAPS-Eval produces reliable, discriminative scores that correlate well with human judgments. The combined SEEDS + DiAPO training strategy further enhances agent performance across the constructed tasks and datasets.
AI.conclusion: AnthroDial offers a unified, practical framework to create, evaluate, and improve anthropomorphic LLM-based social agents operating in open-ended interactions. Its modular tools (MindFlow, CAPS-Eval, and the SEEDS+DiAPO training pipeline) collectively advance credible human-like behavior and provide standardized benchmarks for future work on social LLM agents.

title: From Judgment Quality to Downstream Utility: Rethinking LLM-as-a-Judge for Open-Ended Tasks
summary: LLM-as-a-Judge is increasingly used to evaluate policy responses on open-ended tasks that lack ground-truth answers. Existing work often directly converts the resulting judgments into reward signals for policy training, paying limited attention to intrinsic judgment quality and largely restricting the use of Judges to training-time supervision. We systematically investigate judgment quality and downstream utility by examining both how judgments are elicited and how they are used. For judgment elicitation, we vary the Judge protocol along three dimensions: verdict granularity, critique usage, and evaluation batching. For judgment usage, beyond policy training, we extend Judge to test-time inference through Best-of-N selection, Judge-guided revision, and beam search. We find that, (i) Surprisingly, judgment quality and downstream utility do not always align. (ii) Judge protocol design substantially affects both intrinsic judgment quality and downstream utility. (iii) Judge guidance effectively converts test-time compute into performance gains, with benefits varying across inference strategies. Our results call for a multifaceted evaluation of LLM Judges on open-ended tasks, encompassing intrinsic judgment quality, and downstream utility.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how to better use large language models as automatic judges for open-ended tasks, examining both how judgments are produced and how they are applied, and shows that judgment quality and practical usefulness can diverge, with protocol design and test-time guidance playing major roles.
AI.motivation: LLMs are often used as automatic evaluators ("Judges") for open-ended tasks without ground-truth labels, and their judgments are converted directly into rewards for training other models. However, prior work largely ignores how reliable these judgments really are, how elicitation protocols affect them, and how such Judges could be used beyond training-time supervision, especially at test time. There is a need to systematically understand judgment quality, its relation to downstream performance, and how to best harness LLM Judges for practical gains.
AI.method: The authors systematically vary and analyze two main aspects: (1) Judgment elicitation protocols for the Judge LLM, manipulating verdict granularity (e.g., coarse vs. fine-grained scores), whether the Judge produces critiques, and whether evaluations are done individually or in batches; (2) Judgment usage strategies, extending beyond training-time reward modeling to test-time methods such as Best-of-N sampling (selecting the best among multiple outputs using the Judge), Judge-guided revision (iteratively improving outputs under Judge feedback), and Judge-informed beam search. They then compare intrinsic judgment quality under these protocols with resulting downstream performance on open-ended tasks.
AI.result: They empirically find: (i) High intrinsic judgment quality (how accurate/consistent the Judge’s evaluations are) does not always translate into better downstream performance of the evaluated or trained policies; (ii) The specific Judge protocol—verdict granularity, inclusion of critiques, and batching strategy—has a substantial impact on both measured judgment quality and downstream utility; (iii) Using the Judge at test time to guide generation (Best-of-N, revision, beam search) effectively converts extra computation into measurable performance gains, but the magnitude and nature of the gains differ across strategies.
AI.conclusion: The work concludes that relying solely on intrinsic judgment metrics for LLM Judges is insufficient; instead, researchers and practitioners should evaluate Judges along multiple dimensions, including both judgment fidelity and their effect on downstream tasks. Careful design of Judge protocols is crucial, and incorporating Judge guidance at inference time is a promising and compute-efficient way to improve performance on open-ended tasks. This calls for more nuanced, multifaceted evaluation frameworks and method choices when deploying LLM-as-a-Judge systems.

title: One Threshold Does Not Fit All Languages: Language-Conditional Deferral for Reliable and Efficient Low-Resource Text Classification
comment: Got accepted and published in NeurIPS 2026 GlobalSouthAI
summary: In the Global South, the lower-income countries of Africa, Asia, and Latin America where most of the world's languages are spoken, a deployed text classifier usually runs on ordinary CPUs, serves many languages with a single model, has few labeled examples in any of them, and relies on people to catch its mistakes. Such a system is only useful if it can promise how often it will be wrong: at most a fixed fraction of the labels it assigns on its own may be incorrect, and everything else must go to a person. Split conformal prediction delivers this promise through a single confidence threshold, normally estimated on validation data pooled across languages. We ask whether the promise reaches every language, and it does not. On MasakhaNEWS (16 African languages) and AfriSenti (12 languages plus two never seen in training), a pooled threshold meets the 90% target on average but covers Somali at 77.5%, Tigrinya at 83.7%, and the two unseen languages at 77.5% and 81.2%. Estimating one threshold per language brings every language to between 89.1% and 91.0% without retraining, and it shows how unequal the cost of the promise is: keeping it means sending 43% of Somali news and over 80% of Amharic and Xitsonga tweets to a person, against under 8% of Nigerian Pidgin news. One or two hundred labels per language are enough and the models train in minutes on one CPU core, so the fix is affordable: calibrate, report, and budget human review one language at a time.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how to reliably control error rates of multilingual text classifiers in low-resource Global South settings using conformal prediction, and shows that language-specific calibration is crucial.
AI.motivation: In many Global South contexts, text classifiers must work across many low-resource languages on modest CPU hardware, with few labels and humans reviewing uncertain cases. Stakeholders need guarantees on how often the model can be wrong when it auto-labels. Standard split conformal prediction gives a global confidence threshold pooled across languages, but it is unclear whether this provides reliable coverage guarantees for each individual language, especially low-resource or unseen ones.
AI.method: The authors apply split conformal prediction to multilingual text classification, comparing a single pooled confidence threshold across languages with per-language thresholds. They evaluate on MasakhaNEWS (16 African languages) and AfriSenti (12 languages plus 2 not seen in training), measuring the empirical coverage (fraction of correct automatic labels) per language under a nominal 90% target. They then estimate language-specific thresholds using small labeled calibration sets (on the order of 100–200 examples per language), without retraining the underlying classifier, and compare coverage and abstention rates (how often the system defers to humans) across languages.
AI.result: With a pooled threshold tuned to 90% nominal coverage, the average coverage across languages hits the target but there are large disparities: some languages like Somali, Tigrinya, and two unseen languages fall well below target (down to around 77–83%). When they switch to per-language thresholds, all languages reach coverage between 89.1% and 91.0% without retraining the model. However, the abstention/human-review rate becomes highly uneven: e.g., about 43% of Somali news and over 80% of Amharic and Xitsonga tweets must be sent to humans, versus under 8% for Nigerian Pidgin news. They find that 100–200 labeled examples per language suffice to estimate robust per-language thresholds and that calibration is computationally cheap on a single CPU core.
AI.conclusion: A single global conformal prediction threshold pooled across languages does not provide fair or reliable error guarantees for each language in multilingual text classification, especially in low-resource Global South settings. Per-language conformal calibration, using modest labeled data and CPU resources, can restore proper coverage guarantees for all languages but reveals strong disparities in required human-review effort. The practical recommendation is to calibrate confidence thresholds separately per language, explicitly report per-language coverage and abstention rates, and allocate human-review budgets by language accordingly.

title: When Tools Silently Lie: Evaluating and Mitigating Blind Compliance in Tool-Augmented Data Agents
comment: 28 pages, 8 figures. Code and benchmark materials: https://github.com/turambar928/Toxic_Tool_Bench
summary: Tool-augmented data agents rely on tool outputs for analytical decisions. Yet successful execution can return plausible but incorrect evidence, requiring agents to decide whether to trust or verify it. Understanding this failure requires examining both the evidence obtained through checking and the answer ultimately adopted. We introduce ToxicBench to measure checking and adoption under numerical, label, schema, and retrieval errors, pairing clean and poisoned observations over fixed source data. In the 118-task GPT evaluation across three adapters, poisoning lowers task success by 26 to 39 percentage points. Ordinary retries help under one-shot poisoning, whereas repeated poisoning reveals wrong-answer adoption after checking. Controls on three public tables isolate how supplied evidence affects recovery. After freezing the scorer, we compare its judgments with human annotations on 200 trajectories, finding 96% task-success agreement. Human judgments support retry gains over Base and confirm adoption after checking on audited tasks. We release trajectories, versioned scoring, and reference and delivery audits. These findings highlight evidence availability and answer selection as complementary dimensions of agent reliability.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces ToxicBench, a benchmark to evaluate how tool-using data agents handle misleading or poisoned tool outputs, and shows that poisoning significantly degrades performance by affecting both evidence checking and answer selection.
AI.motivation: Tool-using agents often treat successful tool calls as trustworthy, but tools can return plausible yet incorrect results (poisoned evidence). We lack systematic understanding and measurement of how agents decide when to trust, verify, or override such outputs, especially across different error types.
