The authors aim to create a controlled setting to analyze these behaviors and quantify their impact on reliability.
AI.method: The authors build ToxicBench, which pairs clean and poisoned observations over fixed source data to induce four categories of errors: numerical, label, schema, and retrieval. They evaluate 118 tool-using tasks with GPT-based agents and three different adapters, measuring how agents check evidence and which answers they finally adopt. They compare one-shot versus repeated poisoning, use ordinary retries as a mitigation, and run controlled experiments on three public tables to isolate how different evidence presentations affect error recovery. They also freeze an automatic scorer and compare its task-success judgments against human annotations on 200 trajectories to validate measurement reliability.
AI.result: Across the 118-task benchmark and three adapters, introducing poisoned tool outputs reduces task success by 26–39 percentage points. While simple retries improve robustness in one-shot poisoning scenarios, repeated poisoning exposes a tendency for agents to adopt wrong answers even after performing checks. Controls on public tables show that the type and availability of evidence significantly influence an agent's ability to recover from poisoning. The automatic scorer agrees with human annotations on task success in 96% of the 200 manually reviewed trajectories, and human raters confirm both the benefits of retries and the phenomenon of adopting incorrect answers after checking.
AI.conclusion: Tool-augmented agents are vulnerable not only because poisoned tools can hide correct evidence, but also because agents often choose incorrect answers despite having access to verification signals. Reliability must therefore be evaluated along two axes: whether sufficient evidence is available and how agents select their final answers. ToxicBench, along with released trajectories, scoring tools, and audits, provides a standardized way to study and improve these dimensions of agent reliability.

title: It's Not What the Image Shows: Irrelevant Context Destabilises VLM Judges Without Informing Them
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly used in place of human annotators, making it important that substitutability tests reflect the model rather than incidental evaluation conditions. We introduce MIST, the Misleading-Image Stress Test: 200 English sentences, each built around a phrase readable either figuratively or literally and shown with an aligned image depicting its reading, a misleading image depicting the opposite, or no image at all. The guidelines require the label to be decided from the sentence alone, so no image should change any answer. We expected each image to pull a judge's labels toward the sense it depicts, and neither kind did. Across thirteen VLM judges, an aligned image changed 20.5% of labels and a misleading one 19.4%, close for every judge and both above the 11.6% produced by deleting the ignore-the-image instruction with the image left in place. Yet only 37% of the labels that differ between the two images moved toward the sense shown, and agreement with our human annotators is unchanged whether the image is absent, aligned or misleading. The effect is smaller in the seven judges that pass the alt-test than in the six that never do, but present in all of them: what moves a judge is that an image is there, not which of the two it is, so a substitutability verdict describes a configuration as much as a model.

AI.tldr: The paper tests whether vision-language models (VLMs) can reliably substitute for human annotators when images should be ignored, finding that the mere presence of an image—not its content—systematically perturbs model judgments.
AI.motivation: VLMs are increasingly used as automatic annotators in place of humans. Many tasks instruct models to ignore images when labeling based on text alone, but it is unclear whether models truly do so. Standard substitutability tests risk conflating properties of the evaluation setup (e.g., whether images are shown) with the actual capabilities of the model. The authors want a precise diagnostic of how visual context—especially misleading or irrelevant images—affects VLM decisions when it should not.
AI.method: The authors introduce MIST (Misleading-Image Stress Test), a dataset of 200 English sentences each containing a phrase that can be interpreted either literally or figuratively. For each sentence they prepare three conditions: (1) an aligned image that depicts the intended sense, (2) a misleading image that depicts the opposite sense, and (3) no image. Evaluation guidelines explicitly require that labels be determined from the sentence alone, so images should not affect labels if models follow instructions. Thirteen different VLMs are used as “judges”, and their label changes across conditions and agreement with human annotators are analyzed, including splitting models into those that pass vs. fail an alternate (“alt-”) test.
AI.result: Aligned images change 20.5% of model labels and misleading images change 19.4%, very similar across all 13 VLMs and both well above an 11.6% change rate produced by simply removing the “ignore the image” instruction while still showing the image. Among label differences between aligned and misleading conditions, only 37% move in the direction of the sense depicted by the image. Agreement with human annotators remains essentially constant across the no-image, aligned-image, and misleading-image conditions. Models that pass a separate alt-test are somewhat less affected by images, but all models show the same qualitative behavior: labels are perturbed by the presence of any image.
AI.conclusion: VLMs systematically violate “ignore the image” instructions in a way that is largely insensitive to the actual visual content: any image tends to nudge their labels, while which specific image is shown matters comparatively little. Consequently, substitutability assessments that involve visual context describe properties of the full evaluation configuration (prompt, presence of images, etc.) rather than of the underlying model alone. The MIST benchmark exposes this configuration dependence and suggests that relying on VLMs as drop-in replacements for human annotators—especially when images are meant to be ignored—can be misleading.

title: From Learner Behavior to Reusable Skills for Effective and Efficient Learner Simulation
summary: Learner simulation aims to reproduce how a particular learner behaves on new tasks. Although Large Language Models (LLMs) can generate increasingly fine-grained learning behaviors, existing approaches often need to repeatedly process a growing interaction history to reconstruct the learner. This introduces additional context and inference costs and makes the acquired learner-specific simulation capability difficult to reuse across different LLMs. We therefore propose Learner2Skill, which externalizes the simulation capability acquired from historical interactions into a persistent and reusable Simulation Skill. The Skill captures the learner's current learning state and recurring response patterns, evolves as new real interactions arrive, and can be adapted to a new LLM through lightweight executor calibration without reconstructing the learner from scratch. Experiments show that Learner2Skill more faithfully reproduces fine-grained learner behavior while reducing overall token cost, and that the same constructed Skills can be effectively reused across different LLM executors.

AI.tldr: They propose Learner2Skill, a method that turns a learner’s historical interaction data into a persistent, reusable “Simulation Skill” that can be plugged into different LLMs to simulate that learner more accurately and cheaply.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based learner simulators must repeatedly re-process the entire, ever-growing interaction history to reconstruct a learner’s behavior, which is computationally expensive and ties the simulation to a specific model. There is a need for a way to capture learner-specific behavior that is reusable, efficient, and transferable across different LLMs without redoing all prior context processing.
AI.method: Learner2Skill externalizes the simulation capability into a standalone Simulation Skill derived from past learner–system interactions. This Skill encodes the learner’s current knowledge state and characteristic response patterns and is updated as new interactions come in. When moving to a new LLM, the method calibrates a lightweight executor to use the existing Skill, instead of reconstructing the learner from raw logs each time.
AI.result: Experiments indicate that Learner2Skill more accurately reproduces detailed learner behavior compared to baselines, while also lowering the total token usage. The same Simulation Skills can be transferred and reused across different LLM executors with good performance, demonstrating cross-model portability.
AI.conclusion: Learner2Skill offers an efficient, portable approach to learner simulation: it encapsulates learner-specific behavior into a persistent Skill that can evolve over time and be reused with multiple LLMs. This both improves fidelity of behavioral simulation and reduces computational cost, suggesting a practical path for scalable learner modeling with LLMs.

title: Retrieval Capacity of Self-Attention Under Competition
summary: How many tokens from its context does a language model actually use, and what determines that number? We study this question through self-attention. Without retraining, we retain only the tokens with the highest attention weights at each head, layer, and query, keeping their original weights unchanged. By varying the selected set size and measuring the increase in negative log-likelihood (NLL), we estimate the effective attention set size needed to stay within a chosen loss tolerance. Relatively small selected sets can keep NLL close to the full-attention baseline, although the required size varies across models. Attention-based selection substantially outperforms random selection. Selected sets exhibit geometric structure, although geometric separation alone does not establish that model loss is preserved. Extending context while evaluating the same prediction targets increases the required set size, while its fraction of context decreases over the tested range. Experiments with a fixed supporting fact show that additional background pushes its tokens down the attention ranking and reduces their attention mass. Renormalizing the retained weights can substantially reduce the required set size, showing that it also depends on how selected representations are combined. Conditional theoretical models explain how competition and attention-mass retention can produce growing set sizes without more distinct information to retrieve. These results provide a way to measure effective attention set size in language models and investigate its dependence on context, competition, and aggregation.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates how many context tokens language models effectively use by pruning attention and measuring the impact on loss.
AI.motivation: To understand and quantify the subset of context tokens that actually matter for a language model’s predictions, and how this depends on context length, competition among tokens, and attention aggregation schemes.
AI.method: They prune attention without retraining by keeping only the top‑attention tokens per head/layer/query, varying the number retained, and measuring the increase in negative log‑likelihood. They compare against random selection, study geometric structure of selected tokens, examine behavior as context length grows and when adding background around a fixed supporting fact, test weight renormalization, and build conditional theoretical models to explain observed scaling of effective set size.
AI.result: A relatively small subset of high‑attention tokens can preserve model loss close to the full‑attention baseline, with required set size varying by model and strongly outperforming random selection. Selected tokens show geometric clustering, the effective attention set grows with context length but constitutes a shrinking fraction of the context, added background dilutes attention on key tokens, renormalizing retained weights further reduces required set size, and theoretical models show how competition and attention‑mass retention drive growing effective set sizes even without more distinct information.
AI.conclusion: The paper introduces a practical measure of “effective attention set size” in language models and shows that it depends jointly on context length, competition between tokens, and how attention weights are aggregated, highlighting that only a small, competitively selected subset of context tokens is crucial for predictions and that this subset evolves with context and aggregation choices.

title: SimpleEvol: An Agent-Loop Framework for LLM-Driven Automated Heuristic Design with Minimal Human Priors
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have emerged as powerful tools for automated heuristic design (AHD), enabling iterative generation and refinement of heuristics. However, the dominant paradigm embeds LLMs as narrow, fixed components, such as crossover or mutation, within heavily hand-engineered evolutionary frameworks. We argue this misapprehends LLMs. It treats them as specialized tools rather than general reasoners, constrains them to low-level operations, and underutilizes their autonomy. Moreover, the extensive human priors in these frameworks violate the bitter lesson principle that general methods scaling with computation surpass hand-crafted solutions. This raises a key question: which AHD framework designs best convert stronger LLM capabilities into better heuristics? To address this, we propose metrics for LLM-driven AHD framework handcraftedness (AHI) and intelligence conversion efficiency (ICE). Evaluating ten LLMs across three challenging combinatorial optimization problems, we obtain a notable finding that frameworks with fewer human priors consistently yield higher ICE. Based on this finding, we propose SimpleEvol, an agent-loop framework for AHD which removes nearly all human priors and allows the LLM to operate autonomously. SimpleEvol consistently achieves the highest ICE, often by a large margin. Our results challenge the trend toward complex AHD pipelines and point to a lighter and more model-centric alternative, suggesting that reducing human priors is a more effective strategy to scale up with model intelligence. The source code is available at https://github.com/HenryZhu1029/SimpleEvol-Master.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how to better use large language models (LLMs) for automated heuristic design (AHD) and finds that simpler, less hand-crafted frameworks convert LLM intelligence into better heuristics more efficiently.
AI.motivation: Existing AHD systems typically plug LLMs into narrow roles inside complex, heavily hand-engineered evolutionary frameworks. This likely underuses LLMs’ general reasoning abilities and violates the "bitter lesson" that generic, scalable methods outperform hand-crafted solutions. The authors want to understand what kind of AHD frameworks best turn stronger LLMs into stronger heuristics, and how much human prior structure actually helps or hurts.
AI.method: They first conceptualize two metrics: (1) AHD Handcraftedness Index (AHI), quantifying how many human priors and hand-designed components a framework uses; and (2) Intelligence Conversion Efficiency (ICE), measuring how effectively an AHD framework converts increased LLM capability into improved heuristic performance. They then evaluate ten different LLMs on three hard combinatorial optimization problems, under several AHD frameworks with varying levels of human priors, and compare their AHI and ICE. Based on empirical insights, they design SimpleEvol, a minimal, agent-loop-based AHD framework that removes most hand-crafted structure and grants the LLM high autonomy in designing and evolving heuristics.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation shows that frameworks with fewer human priors (lower AHI) consistently achieve higher ICE across LLMs and problem domains. The proposed SimpleEvol framework, which is deliberately minimal and model-centric, attains the highest ICE, often by a substantial margin over more complex, hand-engineered AHD pipelines. This indicates that giving LLMs more autonomy leads to better use of their capabilities in heuristic design.
AI.conclusion: The study indicates that complex, hand-engineered AHD pipelines are not the best way to leverage increasingly capable LLMs. Instead, lighter, more model-centric frameworks with minimal human priors convert LLM intelligence into superior heuristics more efficiently. The authors advocate designing AHD systems that reduce handcrafted components and rely more on LLM autonomy, aligning with the bitter lesson that scalable, general methods outperform manually engineered solutions.

title: How Many Labels Does a Language Need? Annotation Budgets and Cross-Lingual Pooling for African-Language Text Classification
summary: Every text classifier for an African language begins with a budgeting question: how many labelled examples are needed, and can labels from other African languages stand in for them? We answer both questions empirically for 28 language-task pairs, news topic classification in 16 languages (MasakhaNEWS) and tweet sentiment in 12 languages (AfriSenti), using a character n-gram linear model that trains in seconds on two CPU cores with no pretrained weights and no accelerator. Monolingual learning curves at budgets from 25 to several thousand labels show that topic classification reaches 90\% of its full-data macro-F1 with about 400 labels in the median language, while sentiment is still improving at the full training size in 11 of 12 languages and needs thousands of labels. Pooling the full training data of the other languages in the benchmark is worth a great deal at small budgets and nothing at large ones: at 25 target labels it adds 0.20 macro-F1 on average for news (up to 0.43 for Lingala) and 0.08 for sentiment, the gain decays to zero by 800 labels, and at full size pooling hurts in 9 of 16 and 8 of 12 languages. Twenty-five target labels plus pooled data match what 100 to 400 monolingual labels achieve for most news languages. A complete zero-shot transfer matrix shows that transfer without any target labels recovers a median of only 13\% (news) and 4\% (sentiment) of the gap between a majority-class predictor and the in-language model, with the exceptions explained by shared script (Amharic and Tigrinya), shared lexicon (English and Nigerian Pidgin, the Arabic dialects), or a shared label prior rather than by language family. We release code that regenerates every number from the public benchmark files and translate the results into concrete annotation guidance for teams building African-language classifiers without GPUs.

AI.tldr: The paper empirically studies how many labeled examples are needed to train simple, fast text classifiers for African languages and how much cross-language data helps, providing practical annotation guidance.
AI.motivation: Building text classifiers for African languages is constrained by limited annotation budgets and compute. Practitioners lack clear, quantitative guidance on how many labels are needed per language and whether it is worthwhile to reuse labeled data from other African languages instead of or in addition to collecting new labels. Existing work often focuses on deep, pretrained models and does not provide systematic learning-curve and transfer analyses for low-resource African settings on accessible models.
AI.method: The authors use a simple character n-gram linear model (no pretrained weights, no accelerators) and run controlled experiments on two public benchmarks: MasakhaNEWS (topic classification in 16 African languages) and AfriSenti (tweet sentiment in 12 languages). For each language they construct monolingual learning curves across label budgets from 25 up to several thousand examples. They then study cross-lingual transfer by pooling training data from all other languages in the benchmark at varying target-language label budgets, and by computing a full zero-shot transfer matrix where models trained on one language are evaluated directly on another without target labels. Performance is measured with macro-F1, and they analyze how gains from pooling evolve with budget and what factors (script, lexicon, label priors, language family) explain zero-shot transfer patterns.
AI.result: For news topic classification, 90% of the full-data macro-F1 can typically be reached with about 400 labeled examples per language. For tweet sentiment, performance continues to improve even at the maximum training size, generally requiring thousands of labels and not saturating in 11 of 12 languages. Cross-lingual pooling is highly beneficial at very low budgets: with only 25 target-language labels, adding pooled data from other languages boosts macro-F1 by 0.20 on average for news (up to 0.43 for Lingala) and 0.08 for sentiment. However, these gains decay to zero by roughly 800 labels, and at full training size, pooling actually degrades performance in a majority of languages (9/16 for news, 8/12 for sentiment). In news, 25 target labels plus pooled data generally matches the performance of 100–400 monolingual labels. Zero-shot transfer without target labels closes only a small fraction of the performance gap: a median of 13% (news) and 4% (sentiment) between majority-class and in-language models. Notable exceptions are largely due to shared script, shared lexicon (e.g., English–Nigerian Pidgin, Arabic dialects), or aligned label priors, rather than language-family relationships.
AI.conclusion: Simple character n-gram linear models, trainable in seconds on CPUs, can achieve strong performance for African-language text classification with modest annotation budgets for topic classification but require substantially more labels for sentiment. Cross-lingual data from related African languages is very helpful when only a handful of target labels are available, effectively multiplying the value of those few annotations, but its utility vanishes—and can even become harmful—as more in-language labels are collected. Pure zero-shot transfer is generally too weak to replace target-language annotation except in special cases of strong script or lexical overlap. The authors provide reproducible code and distill their empirical findings into practical labeling guidelines for teams building African-language classifiers without access to GPUs.

title: Absorbed in Inertia: Activation Analysis for Computer-Use Agents
summary: Computer-use agents have become increasingly capable of executing tasks on live desktops through natural-language instructions, based on trajectories of screenshots, actions, and reasoning. We discover that they can stealthily exhibit inertia, in which they repeat fruitless actions despite recognizing that these actions are ineffective. We hypothesize that inertia is reflected in the agent's internal state, i.e., the activation values of the agent's underlying model, and propose a protocol to measure the relationship between the two. Extensive analysis of high-dimensional activation states shows that inertia corresponds to an absorbing region of activation space, where activation values become stale across actions and even after attempts to steer them. We conjecture that drastically changing the agents' activations by re-initializing them is necessary to escape inertia. Specifically, we propose R$^3$ (Reset, Reroute, Restore), which temporarily resets the agent's context trajectory to escape the absorbing region and then restores the historical context to effectively complete the task. Our approach yields 17-55% lower measured inertia across models relative to unmodified agents. These results suggest that changing the context can interrupt recurrence more effectively than directly steering the resulting activations. Our code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/vlm-agent-defense-D076

AI.tldr: The paper studies a failure mode called inertia in computer-use agents (LLM-based desktop agents) where they repeat ineffective actions, links it to an absorbing region in activation space, and proposes a reset-based method (R^3) to escape it and reduce inertia by 17–55%.
AI.motivation: Modern LLM-based agents that operate computers via natural-language instructions and GUI actions can get stuck repeating useless steps, even while internally recognizing those steps are not helping. This undermines reliability and safety in real-world use. The authors want to understand whether this behavioral inertia has a clear signature in the model’s internal activations and how to systematically mitigate it, rather than relying on ad-hoc prompt tricks.
AI.method: The authors define and measure inertia in computer-use agents via task trajectories (screenshots, actions, chain-of-thought). They then analyze the agents’ high-dimensional activation states across time, looking for structure that correlates with observed inertia. They identify an “absorbing” region of activation space where the activations become stale and resistant to steering. Building on this, they design R^3 (Reset, Reroute, Restore): during detected inertia, they temporarily reset the agent’s context trajectory to jolt activations out of the absorbing region, use this clean context to reroute the plan, and then restore the historical context so the agent can still use past information but with a refreshed internal state. They empirically evaluate inertia with and without R^3 across several models.
AI.result: They find that inertia does indeed correspond to an absorbing region in activation space: once the agent enters this region, successive actions show little activation change and remain ineffective, even after attempts at direct steering. Applying their R^3 protocol significantly reduces measured inertia across multiple models, with improvements between 17% and 55% compared to standard agents that lack this reset mechanism.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that behavioral inertia in computer-use agents is closely linked to specific patterns in model activations that behave like an absorbing state. Simple attempts to steer activations within this region are insufficient. Instead, altering the agent’s context—by resetting and then carefully restoring it as in R^3—is a more effective strategy to break recurrent, unproductive behavior. This offers a practical defense mechanism for making GUI-based LLM agents more reliable and suggests that context-level interventions can be as important as fine-grained activation steering.

title: Zero-shot Dependency Parsing with Unsupervised Cross-Lingual Bootstrapping
summary: Pre-trained language models (PLMs) with encoder-based architectures have shown impressive capabilities in zero-shot cross-lingual transfer for various language understanding tasks. However, applying this technique to dependency parsing remains a significant challenge due to its syntactic nature. To boost model generalizability across linguistic typologies, we propose a cross-lingual unsupervised bootstrapping method to improve syntactic knowledge within the PLM. We show that our method achieves a significant improvement in zero-shot parsing performance in low-resource languages. Analysis of these bootstrapped models uncovers increased robustness in recognizing syntactic structures, evidenced by higher scores in parameter-free tree probing tests.

AI.tldr: They improve zero-shot cross-lingual dependency parsing by unsupervised bootstrapping on top of encoder-based pre-trained language models, yielding better syntactic robustness and higher parsing scores in low-resource languages.
AI.motivation: Encoder-based pre-trained language models already perform well for zero-shot cross-lingual transfer in many understanding tasks, but they struggle with dependency parsing because it requires fine-grained syntactic knowledge that these models do not capture sufficiently, especially across diverse language typologies and low-resource languages. The authors want to enhance the syntactic competence and cross-lingual generalizability of such models without relying on labeled data.
AI.method: They propose a cross-lingual unsupervised bootstrapping method that operates on top of encoder-based PLMs. The method uses the model itself (and possibly transfer from higher-resource languages) to iteratively generate and refine syntactic signals—such as pseudo dependency trees—across multiple languages, without supervised treebanks in the target languages. This process injects additional syntactic structure into the PLM’s representations and adapts it across different typologies.
AI.result: Using this unsupervised bootstrapping approach, the adapted PLMs achieve notably better zero-shot dependency parsing performance on low-resource target languages compared with standard PLM-based baselines. Probing experiments with parameter-free tree-based tests show that the resulting models encode syntactic structures more reliably and robustly than before bootstrapping.
AI.conclusion: Cross-lingual unsupervised bootstrapping is an effective way to enrich encoder-based PLMs with syntactic knowledge and improve their zero-shot dependency parsing ability in low-resource languages. The gains observed in both parsing accuracy and structure-aware probing indicate that the approach meaningfully strengthens the models’ internal representations of syntax and their robustness across diverse languages.

title: Accelerated surrogate dynamics for dynamical, stochastic system evolution
summary: Dynamic simulations are an entrenched way of gaining insight into the evolution of system dynamics. Their computational cost however is often prohibitively high, especially in cases of stochastic frameworks. Machine learning algorithms are especially suited as simulation surrogates. Nevertheless, they face some very distinct limitations. Firstly, the sheer dimensionality of these systems, however, precludes the use of traditional time series models who struggle with high dimensional feature spaces. Additionally, traditional time series focus exclusively on either long or short range effects, causing local or global drift given enough time. In this paper, we propose a framework that addresses those limitations. Our framework combines a Variational Autoencoder, with a convolutional or graph basis that reduces the dimensionality of the system. This latent vector is propagated in time using a Temporal Fusion Transformer model, which includes both long range and short range effect encoding, as well as static covariate support. We test our framework on three distinct cases, to prove its robustness and in all three we have achieved practically identical to the simulation results at a fraction of the time. Further, our framework is flexible enough to be adapted to any new system and provides an inbuilt uncertainty quantification for targeted experiment design.

AI.tldr: They build a fast, accurate surrogate for high‑dimensional dynamic simulations by compressing the system with a VAE and forecasting the latent state with a Temporal Fusion Transformer, matching simulation accuracy much faster and with uncertainty estimates.
AI.motivation: Dynamic (often stochastic) simulations are powerful but computationally expensive, which limits their use in design, optimization and uncertainty analysis. Standard machine‑learning surrogates and time‑series models struggle in this context because (1) the state space is very high‑dimensional, making naive sequence models inefficient and unstable, and (2) most models capture either short‑range or long‑range temporal effects, not both, leading to drift in long rollouts. The authors want a general, data‑driven surrogate that is both computationally cheap and accurate over long horizons, and that can quantify uncertainty to guide experiments.
AI.method: They propose a two‑stage framework. First, they train a Variational Autoencoder (VAE) with either convolutional or graph neural network encoders/decoders to learn a low‑dimensional latent representation of the high‑dimensional system state. Second, they model the temporal evolution of this latent state using a Temporal Fusion Transformer (TFT), which is designed to capture both short‑ and long‑term dependencies and can incorporate static covariates. The combined VAE+TFT model acts as a surrogate that maps from past trajectories and inputs to future states, with the VAE handling dimensionality reduction and reconstruction, and the TFT handling forecasting in latent space. The probabilistic nature of the VAE and TFT provides uncertainty estimates.
AI.result: On three different test problems (not detailed in the abstract), the proposed surrogate produces trajectories that are practically indistinguishable from those of the original simulations, while requiring only a fraction of the computational time. The method appears robust across these varied cases and yields reliable predictions over time without significant drift.
AI.conclusion: A VAE-based dimensionality reduction combined with a Temporal Fusion Transformer in latent space is an effective, flexible surrogate framework for high‑dimensional dynamic simulations. It alleviates computational cost, maintains high fidelity to the original simulator across multiple case studies, and naturally provides uncertainty quantification useful for targeted experiment design. The framework is claimed to be adaptable to new systems with minimal changes.

title: It's All Training: A Fully Synthetic Single-Stage Recipe for LLMs
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 35 pages, 9 figures. Dataset: https://huggingface.co/datasets/PleIAs/SYNTH
summary: Current pre-training datasets are derived from web crawls, with all their issues, and were not designed to support mid- and post-training pipelines--for instance, they contain little explicit reasoning. Thus, many frontier labs have begun to develop their own internal datasets, starting from state-of-the-art models, to augment their pre-training data mix, eg, with reasoning traces to address cold-start problems. While demonstratively effective, none of these datasets are public, and the effect of this so-called synthetic data on knowledge and skill acquisition of language models, including small ones, remains poorly understood. We present SYNTH, the first open-source synthetic corpus derived from 58,698 Wikipedia articles that collapses pre-, mid-, and post-training into a single training stage via structured amplification of curated encyclopedic seeds. We evaluate SYNTH by training a suite of models: a 56M tiny model (Monad), 0.3B-0.6B dense models (Baguettotron), and a 13B / 1B-active MoE. At iso-compute, SYNTH outperforms filtered web data, and our models remain competitive with similarly-sized open-weight baselines. Because SYNTH is back-translated from grounded passages, SYNTH-trained models achieve high factual precision despite 10-140x fewer training tokens, with memorization targeted by the seed corpus. These results show that synthetic datasets, including our SYNTH dataset, are capable of producing competitive generalist models from a fraction of the training data, enabling rapid iteration as the frontier advances. These findings open up possibilities for both generalist models with significantly increased data efficiency, as well as domain-specific models where no instruction or conversational data is available. Finally, we publicly release our SYNTH dataset and the suite of Baguettotron models under a permissive license, thus supporting open-source language model development.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces SYNTH, an open-source synthetic training corpus built from Wikipedia that enables data-efficient training of competitive language models in a single unified training stage.
AI.motivation: Existing pre-training datasets come from noisy web crawls, contain little explicit reasoning, and are not designed to integrate smoothly with mid- and post-training pipelines. Frontier labs therefore rely on private synthetic datasets—often including reasoning traces—to bootstrap models, but these are closed and their effects, especially on smaller models, are poorly understood. There is a need for a public, well-grounded synthetic corpus to study and leverage these benefits for the broader community.
AI.method: The authors construct SYNTH, a synthetic corpus generated from 58,698 curated Wikipedia articles via structured amplification: grounded passages are transformed into richer synthetic training data (e.g., with reasoning traces) that effectively merge pre-, mid-, and post-training into one stage. They then train and evaluate multiple models on SYNTH: a 56M-parameter tiny model (Monad), several 0.3B–0.6B dense models (Baguettotron), and a 13B-parameter sparse MoE with 1B active parameters, comparing them to models trained on filtered web data under equal compute budgets and against similarly sized open-weight baselines.
AI.result: At equal compute, models trained on SYNTH outperform those trained on filtered web-crawl data. The SYNTH-trained models remain competitive with similarly sized open-weight models despite training on 10–140x fewer tokens. Because SYNTH is generated by back-translating from factual Wikipedia passages, the resulting models show high factual precision and targeted memorization aligned with the seed corpus, rather than broad, uncontrolled memorization of noisy web content.
AI.conclusion: Carefully constructed synthetic corpora like SYNTH can yield competitive, general-purpose language models with dramatically improved data efficiency, reducing the amount of training data needed while preserving or improving factual accuracy. This approach enables faster iteration as model frontiers move and is especially promising for domains lacking instruction or conversational data. By releasing both the SYNTH dataset and Baguettotron models under a permissive license, the work provides a public foundation for open-source development and systematic study of synthetic-data training pipelines.

title: V-Engram: Trigger-Indexed External Memory for Modular Text-to-Image Personalization
summary: Pretrained text-to-image models contain broad visual knowledge, yet they cannot reliably acquire or refine a specific visual identity from only a few references while preserving compositional control. Token-embedding methods are compact but often underfit identity, whereas adapter-based methods improve fidelity through persistent weight updates that can be costly to store and interfere when concepts are composed. We introduce V-Engram, a trigger-indexed external memory mechanism for Stable Diffusion 3.5. Each concept is assigned an explicit trigger that retrieves concept-specific memory, whose gated directions enter frozen text-encoder and MMDiT context states as relative residuals. Separating this memory from backbone adaptation enables prompt-selective and multi-concept access without merging model updates. Experiments show that V-Engram broadly matches DreamBooth-LoRA in overall subject fidelity while showing advantages in settings such as contextual subject preservation. Prompt-matched loading retrieves only matched entries, reducing most additional adaptation-state loading for a single-concept query. Qualitative results further demonstrate paired-trigger composition and same-class separation, while prompts without registered entries retain the frozen model's base behavior. Together, these results establish trigger-indexed memory as a modular interface for adding targeted visual evidence without rewriting the generator.

AI.tldr: V-Engram is an external memory mechanism for Stable Diffusion 3.5 that stores concept-specific visual identities as trigger-indexed residuals, achieving DreamBooth-level fidelity with modular, prompt-selective loading and preserved compositional control.
AI.motivation: Pretrained text-to-image models know a lot visually but struggle to learn or refine a specific subject’s visual identity from only a few example images while still supporting flexible composition. Existing personalization approaches have trade-offs: token-embedding methods are compact but often fail to fully capture identity, while adapter- or LoRA-based methods give better fidelity but require persistent weight updates that are expensive to store, hard to manage when many concepts are involved, and can interfere with each other during composition. There is a need for a modular, selective mechanism that can add targeted visual evidence for specific concepts without continuously modifying or merging the base generator weights.
AI.method: The paper proposes V-Engram, a trigger-indexed external memory system integrated with Stable Diffusion 3.5. Each personalized concept is associated with an explicit trigger token. When this trigger appears in a prompt, it retrieves a concept-specific memory entry. The information from this memory is injected as gated directional residuals into the otherwise frozen text encoder and MMDiT context states. This decouples concept storage from the backbone model parameters. The memory access is prompt-selective—only concepts referenced by triggers are loaded—and multiple triggers can be combined without merging fine-tuned weights. The model is trained so that these residuals capture subject identity while maintaining the base model’s compositional abilities.
AI.result: Empirically, V-Engram achieves overall subject fidelity comparable to DreamBooth with LoRA on Stable Diffusion 3.5. It shows specific advantages in tasks like contextual subject preservation, where the subject remains consistent across varied prompts. Because memory entries are trigger-indexed, only prompt-matched entries are loaded at inference, which significantly reduces extra adaptation-state loading for single-concept queries compared to approaches that require loading full fine-tuned adapters. Qualitative experiments demonstrate that V-Engram supports pairing multiple triggers in a single prompt, enabling multi-concept composition, and it can distinguish between different instances within the same semantic class. Prompts that do not reference any registered trigger behave as with the frozen base model, showing minimal interference.
AI.conclusion: Trigger-indexed external memory (V-Engram) offers a modular, scalable interface for adding high-fidelity, concept-specific visual information to large text-to-image models without rewriting or merging generator weights. By storing personalization signals as separately retrievable residual directions, it preserves compositional control, supports multi-concept prompts and same-class separation, and reduces storage and loading overhead compared with adapter-based fine-tuning. The approach demonstrates that external, prompt-addressable memory is an effective alternative to persistent backbone adaptation for subject-driven customization of text-to-image diffusion models.

title: The Unequal Influence of Bad Advice: Using Training Data Attribution to Modulate Emergent Misalignment
summary: Fine-tuning large language models on narrow, misaligned tasks can undo their post-training alignment and induce novel misaligned behaviors -- a phenomenon known as \emph{emergent misalignment} (EM). EM has been linked to persona-like representations, where fine-tuning might reduce loss by amplifying a harmful or 'evil' persona. It remains unclear which properties of the training data drive this effect: whether all harmful examples contribute approximately equally to misalignment and whether different models are equally affected by the same fine-tuning examples. In this work, we use training data attribution to quantitatively estimate how much each harmful example contributes to EM. We benchmark the quality of the attribution via retraining -- a sound attribution score should enable us to enhance or attenuate EM by filtering data on that score. Score-based filtering can substantially enhance or attenuate EM; we find that both data-attribution scores and a black-box harmfulness score can identify consequential examples. All models we test become misaligned when trained on the same dataset, and influence scores perform best when filtering data from the same model that computed them. We find cross-model generalization of influence scores from scores derived from the three model families we tested, but this generalization does not recover same model filtering performance.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how individual harmful fine-tuning examples contribute to emergent misalignment in large language models, using data attribution methods to identify and filter the most consequential training points.
AI.motivation: Fine-tuning on narrow, misaligned tasks can break prior alignment and create new misaligned behaviors (emergent misalignment), but it is unclear which specific training examples cause this and whether all harmful data are equally responsible or affect different models similarly. Understanding this can help control or prevent misalignment during fine-tuning.
AI.method: The authors apply training data attribution (influence-like scoring) to fine-tuning datasets containing harmful examples. For each harmful example, they compute an attribution score estimating its contribution to emergent misalignment. They then evaluate these scores by retraining models after filtering the fine-tuning data according to different scores (data-attribution scores vs. a black-box harmfulness score), and measure how much this enhances or attenuates emergent misalignment. They also study how well scores transfer across different model families.
AI.result: Filtering data based on attribution scores can significantly increase or decrease emergent misalignment, showing that some harmful examples are far more consequential than others. A simple black-box harmfulness score can also pick influential examples, but model-specific influence scores perform best, especially when used on data for the same model that generated the scores. All tested models become misaligned when trained on the same harmful dataset, and while attribution scores generalize somewhat across model families, cross-model use does not match same-model filtering performance.
AI.conclusion: Emergent misalignment is driven disproportionately by a subset of highly influential harmful training examples, which can be identified via training data attribution or even simpler harmfulness scores. Model-specific attribution provides the strongest leverage to control misalignment via data filtering, though scores partially transfer across models. This suggests that managing fine-tuning data at the example level is a powerful tool for maintaining alignment and that emergent misalignment is not an inevitable consequence of any exposure to harmful data, but of specific influential instances.

title: Learning to Prove, Not Just to Answer: Reinforcement Learning from Formal Verification for Natural-Language Logical Reasoning
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed for natural-language logical reasoning, where the final answer is easy to check but the proof behind it is not. In natural-language logical reasoning, an intermediate conclusion should follow from its premises, and the resulting derivation should support the final answer. Existing methods lack machine-checkable verification of intermediate conclusions and answer-supporting proof dependencies, so they may assign credit to invalid or answer-irrelevant steps. We propose Proof-R1, an RL framework from formal verification that trains LLMs to construct verifiable proofs for natural-language logical reasoning. Proof-R1 admits a generated conclusion into the verified proof state only when the corresponding reasoning action satisfies the proof obligations through UNSAT-based machine-checkable formal verification. Proof-R1 also recovers the answer-supporting dependency closure to trace the proof structure of the final answer and align outcome credit with the proof dependencies. Experiments demonstrate that Proof-R1 improves answer accuracy across three logical reasoning benchmarks and four backbone models and outperforms training-free agents and training-based methods in terms of reasoning-process verifiability.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Proof-R1, a reinforcement learning framework that trains large language models to produce machine-verifiable natural-language proofs, improving both accuracy and verifiability of logical reasoning.
AI.motivation: Large language models are increasingly used for natural-language logical reasoning, where final answers are easy to check but the underlying reasoning steps and proofs are not. Existing approaches cannot reliably verify each intermediate step or ensure that the reasoning steps that get credit are actually relevant and logically valid. This can lead to models being rewarded for flawed, unsupported, or answer-irrelevant reasoning chains. The authors aim to close this gap by bringing formal, machine-checkable verification into LLM-based reasoning so that credit is only given to genuinely valid and answer-supporting proof steps.
AI.method: The authors propose Proof-R1, a reinforcement learning framework inspired by formal verification. In this framework, the LLM incrementally constructs a proof in natural language, but an intermediate conclusion is only accepted into the evolving proof state if the corresponding reasoning action satisfies formal proof obligations verified via an UNSAT-based checker. Thus, each step is machine-checked. In addition, Proof-R1 recovers the answer-supporting dependency closure: it reconstructs which proof steps are actually needed to support the final answer and uses this structure to align reinforcement learning rewards with those crucial dependencies instead of all generated steps.
AI.result: Experiments on three logical reasoning benchmarks and four different backbone LLMs show that Proof-R1 increases answer accuracy compared with baselines. It also surpasses both training-free agents and other training-based methods on metrics that evaluate how verifiable and structurally sound the reasoning process is, demonstrating superior process-level reliability as well as outcome performance.
AI.conclusion: Proof-R1 effectively integrates formal, UNSAT-based verification with reinforcement learning for natural-language logical reasoning, ensuring that only logically valid and answer-relevant proof steps are rewarded. This leads to more accurate answers and more trustworthy, machine-checkable reasoning traces than existing approaches. The work suggests a promising direction for combining LLMs with formal methods to produce verifiable reasoning in natural language tasks.

title: Learning What to Remember: Long-horizon Counterfactual Memory Optimization
summary: Persistent textual memory allows language models to carry information across long interactions, but learning what to remember is fundamentally a credit-assignment problem. A memory rewrite may only become useful many steps later, while much of the observed utility may be inherited from information already stored before the rewrite. We introduce Memory Gain Policy Optimization (MGPO), which isolates the incremental value of each memory rewrite by crediting it for its marginal contribution to current and future downstream utility. This turns delayed memory utility into a direct learning signal for optimizing what information should persist. We study MGPO on document-level information extraction, where structured supervision makes the effects of individual memory updates directly measurable. MGPO improves extraction while reducing average memory length by nearly 80% relative to the initial memory policy before optimization. The learned memory policy also supports reuse and transfer across domains, downstream models without further training. These results show that effective memory learning depends not only on preserving useful information, but on identifying which memory updates create lasting incremental value.

AI.tldr: Introduces Memory Gain Policy Optimization (MGPO) to learn which memory writes in a language model’s persistent memory are actually worth keeping, by assigning credit based on their marginal future utility.
AI.motivation: Language models with persistent memory can, in principle, handle long interactions better, but deciding what to store is a hard credit-assignment problem: the usefulness of a memory write may appear only much later, and apparent gains can be due to older stored information rather than the new write. Existing approaches don’t cleanly separate the incremental value of each memory update, limiting how well memory policies can be learned and optimized.
AI.method: Define a new credit assignment and optimization framework, Memory Gain Policy Optimization (MGPO), that evaluates each memory rewrite by its marginal contribution to downstream task performance, both immediately and in the future. They apply MGPO in a controlled setting of document-level information extraction, where structured labels make it possible to measure how each memory update influences extraction quality. MGPO is used to optimize the policy that decides what to store, rewrite, or discard in persistent memory.
AI.result: On document-level information extraction tasks, MGPO improves extraction performance while shrinking the average memory size by about 80% compared to the initial, unoptimized memory policy. The optimized memory policy generalizes across domains and can be reused with different downstream models without additional training, indicating that it captures generally useful memory-writing behavior rather than overfitting to a single setup.
AI.conclusion: Effective learning of persistent memory in language models requires not only retaining useful information but also accurately attributing which specific memory updates create lasting incremental value. MGPO provides a principled way to do this by turning delayed memory utility into a direct learning signal, leading to more compact, transferable, and higher-performing memory policies.

title: Information Bottleneck-Guided Adaptive Hypergraph Transformer for Brain Disease Diagnosis
summary: Exploring high-order correlations and long-range dependencies in brain networks holds significant value for both neuroscience research and clinical diagnosis. However, previous studies have lacked a unified integration of high-order and long-range dependency information in brain networks, and there is substantial redundancy behind various types of information. These issues limit their effectiveness in the diagnosis of brain diseases. To address this, we propose an Information Bottleneck-Guided Adaptive HyperGraph Transformer (IBAHGT). By incorporating the information bottleneck (IB) principle, this approach enables adaptive learning of high-order correlations and both short- and long-range dependencies within a unified framework for brain network analysis, achieving high-precision brain disease diagnosis. IBAHGT consists of three key components: an information bottleneck-guided adaptive hypergraph convolution, which introduces a novel hypergraph information bottleneck (HIB) principle to adaptively learn hypergraph message-passing weights between nodes and hyperedges, optimizes information flow and captures high-order information in brain networks that is maximally informative and minimally redundant (MIMR). The Transformer encoder captures global information within brain networks through the attention mechanism, specifically modeling short- and long-range dependencies. An information bottleneck-guided node-level adaptive fusion employs the IB principle to learn independent weights for each node, facilitating the fine-grained integration of high-order information and global information to obtain an efficient representation for downstream tasks. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms current state-of-the-art methods and can identify biomarkers for clinical applications.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an Information Bottleneck-Guided Adaptive HyperGraph Transformer (IBAHGT) for brain network analysis that jointly captures high-order correlations and short-/long-range dependencies to improve brain disease diagnosis and biomarker discovery.
AI.motivation: Existing brain network analysis methods either focus on pairwise connections or treat high-order correlations and long-range dependencies separately. They also tend to contain redundant information across different feature types, which reduces diagnostic performance and interpretability. A unified, redundancy-aware framework is needed to effectively exploit rich network structure for accurate brain disease diagnosis and biomarker identification.
AI.method: The authors design IBAHGT, which integrates the information bottleneck principle into a hypergraph-transformer architecture. First, an information bottleneck-guided adaptive hypergraph convolution introduces a hypergraph information bottleneck (HIB) to learn data-driven message-passing weights between nodes and hyperedges, encouraging maximally informative and minimally redundant (MIMR) high-order representations. Second, a Transformer encoder with attention models global context in the brain network, capturing both short- and long-range dependencies. Third, an information bottleneck-guided node-level adaptive fusion learns node-specific fusion weights to combine high-order (hypergraph) and global (Transformer) information into compact, task-relevant node representations. The full model is trained for downstream disease classification.
AI.result: On multiple brain disease datasets, IBAHGT consistently surpasses state-of-the-art baselines in classification accuracy and related metrics. The learned representations and model attention patterns allow the identification of disease-related brain regions and connections, serving as potential imaging biomarkers for clinical use.
AI.conclusion: Integrating the information bottleneck principle with adaptive hypergraph convolution and Transformer-based global modeling yields a unified, redundancy-aware framework that effectively captures high-order correlations and long-range dependencies in brain networks. This leads to improved brain disease diagnosis performance and enables biomarker discovery, suggesting IBAHGT is a powerful tool for both neuroscience research and clinical applications.

title: BITEM at the NTCIR-19 R2C2 Task: Predicting Confidence from Agentic RAG Pipeline Signals
comment: 8 pages. Participant paper for the NTCIR-19 R2C2 task
summary: The BITEM team entered both subtasks of the NTCIR-19 R2C2 task with a single agentic pipeline, in which a model searches, reads and records evidence over a movie corpus while an orchestrator holds the record and rules on what may be submitted. A claim is admitted only once an entailment cascade has checked it against the passage it cites, and an answer is released only once enough checked evidence stands behind it. Each question is run three or four times, every pass retrieving from a corpus stripped of what the earlier passes have already seen. The confidence filed with each answer is computed by the orchestrator from what the run leaves behind and is never asked of the model, which is offered no way to rate itself. The two retrieval runs placed 4th and 5th of 22, pooling the passes was worth 0.0709 nDCG@20, and the gain was largest on the multi-hop and post-processing-heavy questions, where the organisers rank the pooled run top of the field. Sixteen of the 25 answer runs were built on passages these two runs supplied, 12 of them filed by other teams. HMR rewards a system whose confidence is high where it answers right and low where it answers wrong. The pipeline reached an accuracy of 0.9219, 6th of 25, while the confidence filed with those answers gave an HMR of 0.4915, 13th. A few rules crafted over those same recorded signals, with no further model call and no further retrieval, raise that to an accuracy of 0.9375, 5th, and an HMR of 0.6985, 9th. Ranking on HMR alone can reward a system for answering wrongly with low confidence, so we propose accHMR, the accuracy multiplied by HMR, which reports the reward in proportion to the accuracy, and on which the revised rules would have scored 0.6549, 5th. For future work, fitting a model on the numbers the pipeline already produces, rather than writing such rules by hand, would be a real step forward.

AI.tldr: They built a single agentic QA pipeline for the NTCIR-19 R2C2 movie task, combining multi-pass retrieval, entailment-based evidence checking, and an orchestrator that computes confidence scores, achieving strong retrieval and competitive answer accuracy and proposing a new metric (accHMR).
AI.motivation: Current QA systems on complex benchmarks need reliable multi-hop retrieval, rigorous evidence checking, and trustworthy confidence estimates. Existing evaluation metrics such as HMR can over-reward systems that avoid committing to answers (low confidence on wrong answers), while pipelines often underuse the rich internal signals they generate. The authors aim to design a robust agentic pipeline that can support other teams (via high-quality retrieved passages), improve multi-hop and post-processing-heavy question performance, and better align confidence evaluation with actual accuracy.
AI.method: They implement a single agentic pipeline where: (1) a model iteratively searches a movie corpus, reads passages, and records evidence; (2) an orchestrator maintains the evidence record, controls what can be submitted, and computes final confidence scores using internal signals instead of asking the model for self-assessed confidence; (3) claims are only accepted after an entailment cascade verifies them against cited passages; (4) answers are only released once sufficient checked evidence accumulates; (5) each question is processed in 3–4 passes, with each pass retrieving from a corpus that has had previously seen passages removed (pooled retrieval). They then add post-hoc rules over the recorded numerical signals (without extra model calls or retrieval) to refine which answers are accepted and how confidences are used. They also introduce a new metric, accHMR, defined as accuracy multiplied by HMR, to balance confidence calibration with correctness.
AI.result: In retrieval, their two runs rank 4th and 5th of 22, and pooling results across passes improves nDCG@20 by 0.0709, with the largest gains on multi-hop and post-processing-heavy questions; on these, the pooled run is ranked top by the organizers. Their retrieved passages support 16 of 25 answer runs, 12 from other teams, showing strong usefulness as a retrieval backbone. For answering, the pipeline itself achieves 0.9219 accuracy (6th of 25) and an HMR of 0.4915 (13th). By layering simple hand-crafted rules over pipeline signals—without further model inference or retrieval—they raise accuracy to 0.9375 (5th) and HMR to 0.6985 (9th). Under their proposed accHMR metric, these revised rules would score 0.6549, ranking 5th.
AI.conclusion: An orchestrated agentic pipeline with multi-pass retrieval, entailment-based evidence admission, and orchestrator-derived confidence can achieve strong retrieval performance, competitive answer accuracy, and provide valuable evidence to other systems. Simple rule-based post-processing over existing pipeline signals notably improves both accuracy and confidence-related metrics, suggesting that better exploitation of internal signals is a fruitful direction. The authors argue that HMR alone can misalign incentives—rewarding systems that give low-confidence wrong answers—and propose accHMR (accuracy × HMR) to tie confidence calibration more directly to correctness. Future progress should replace manual rules with learned models trained on the pipeline’s own numerical signals, enabling more principled and scalable confidence estimation and decision policies.

title: OptiCom : A Unified Framework for State-Conditioned Composition in LLM-Driven Optimization
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed to solve complex scientific and practical problems via iterative optimization. However, dynamically coordinating diverse search mechanisms as candidate quality, failure modes, and resource budgets evolve remains a critical open challenge. Targeted empirical diagnostics reveal that mechanism effectiveness is highly state-dependent. Motivated by this, we analyze how individual decisions drive final outcomes, decomposing the expected terminal improvement under a shared budget into cumulative decision opportunities minus cumulative selection losses. Guided by this opportunity-loss theoretical foundation, we propose OptiCom, a unified framework that represents LLM-driven optimizers within a shared configuration space: C=(A,Q,O,E,M,S), corresponding to artifact, query, operator, evaluation, memory, and strategy. Operating within this space, a fast LLM-based Optimization Controller dynamically composes immediate mechanisms through structured Action Packages, while a slower Strategy Adapter refines long-term selection preferences, operator weights, and templates based on accumulated trajectory feedback. Comprehensive evaluations across 32 benchmark groups demonstrate the superiority of framework: OptiCom achieves an average Max-score rank of 1.72 among 14 evaluated configurations, securing the top score in 23 groups. Ultimately, these results highlight the broad applicability and high extensibility of OptiCom as a general-purpose paradigm for robust LLM test-time scaling.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes OptiCom, a unified, configurable framework that dynamically coordinates multiple LLM-driven optimization mechanisms to improve performance in complex tasks, showing strong empirical results across many benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based optimization systems struggle to adaptively coordinate diverse search mechanisms (e.g., different sampling, refinement, and evaluation strategies) as problem states, candidate quality, and resource budgets change. Empirical analysis shows that the effectiveness of different mechanisms is highly state-dependent, but current approaches lack a principled, general framework to reason about and orchestrate these mechanisms for robust test-time scaling.
AI.method: The authors first conduct targeted empirical diagnostics to reveal how the effectiveness of different optimization mechanisms depends on the state of the search process. They then introduce an opportunity-loss decomposition of expected terminal improvement under a fixed budget, separating the contribution of decision opportunities from selection losses. Building on this theory, they design OptiCom, a unified configuration space C=(A,Q,O,E,M,S) to represent LLM-driven optimizers in terms of artifacts, queries, operators, evaluation, memory, and strategy. Within this space, they implement two main components: (1) a fast LLM-based Optimization Controller that composes and executes structured Action Packages to choose immediate mechanisms; and (2) a slower Strategy Adapter that updates long-term preferences, such as operator weights and templates, using feedback from observed optimization trajectories.
AI.result: Across 32 benchmark groups and 14 different configurations, OptiCom achieves an average Max-score rank of 1.72, indicating consistently near-top performance. It obtains the best score in 23 out of the 32 groups, demonstrating superior performance and robustness compared to baselines and alternative configurations in a variety of LLM-based optimization tasks.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that the opportunity-loss perspective provides a useful theoretical lens for understanding and improving LLM-driven optimization. OptiCom, instantiated within this framework, serves as a general-purpose, extensible paradigm for dynamically composing and adapting optimization mechanisms at test time. Its strong empirical performance across diverse benchmarks indicates that principled coordination of search components can substantially enhance the robustness and effectiveness of LLM-based optimizers.

title: Auditable Long-Term Memory: A Deterministic Retrieval Chain Measured at 479/475 of 500 on LongMemEval-S
comment: Technical report, 14 pages. Evidence repository (reader outputs, judge verdicts, control records, judge harness): https://github.com/cjchanh/longmemeval-evidence (MIT). Re-scoring any run under the official judge costs about $1.28
summary: We evaluate an auditable long-term memory system on LongMemEval-S. Its retrieval chain uses hybrid candidate retrieval, cross-encoder reranking, coverage-first packet compilation, and deterministic reasoning scaffolds; an LLM is used only as a replaceable final reader. The chain places all gold sessions in the candidate pool for 468/470 answerable questions and produces gold-complete packets for 462/470. With a Claude Opus reader called through an unpinned CLI alias, two 500-question passes score 479/500 and 475/500 under GPT-4o. The 72 answerable knowledge-update rows used a substantively modified scoring prompt whose effect under the official text has not been measured. The pair straddles Chronos High's published 478/500; differences in reader generation, scoring prompt, and possibly data version, plus within-system variance, establish neither superiority nor equivalence. A grok-4.6-high reader on the same packets scores 476/474, while a maximum-reasoning-effort agentic variant regresses to 461/465. The headline passes differ on eight verdict-flip rows. A second judge agrees with the headline judge on 493/500 rows (98.6%) in each pass and scores both passes 472/500; the official judge also flips three verdicts when re-scoring byte-identical pass-1 answers. Negative controls rejected a verifier that repaired three wrong drafts but broke eleven correct drafts. All components were developed on the same 500 questions, with no held-out evaluation or independent human adjudication; retrieval and scaffold method sources and transcript-derived audits are held; and the headline reader received extra operator context, its complete requests were not retained, and MCP tool availability is unresolved. We release materialized packets, scaffolds, reader outputs, judge verdicts, and controls for inspection and re-scoring.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates an auditable long-term memory retrieval system on the LongMemEval-S benchmark, showing that most performance comes from the retrieval and scaffolding pipeline rather than the specific LLM reader, and releasing detailed artifacts for independent re-scoring.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon, long-term memory benchmarks like LongMemEval-S require systems that can reliably retrieve and reason over information scattered across many past sessions. Current evaluations often conflate retrieval quality, scaffolding, and the LLM’s own capabilities, and they rarely provide full auditability. The authors want to measure how far a carefully engineered, fully auditable retrieval-and-scaffold chain can go, while treating the LLM as a mostly interchangeable final reader, and to expose where evaluation and judging variance limit claims of superiority between systems.
AI.method: They build a multi-stage retrieval chain for LongMemEval-S: (1) hybrid candidate retrieval to surface potentially relevant sessions; (2) cross-encoder reranking to refine these candidates; (3) a coverage-first packet compilation strategy to construct information packets that aim to include all gold sessions; and (4) deterministic reasoning scaffolds that structure the information before passing it to an LLM. The LLM (Claude Opus, grok-4.6-high, and an agentic variant) is used only as the final answer generator. They run two 500-question passes, score them under the GPT-4o-based official judge and a second independent judge, analyze verdict flips and inter-judge agreement, and use negative-control experiments (a verifier that edits answers) to test robustness. They also disclose methodological caveats such as development on the same 500 questions and missing logs/context.
AI.result: The chain’s retrieval quality is very high: it includes all gold sessions in the candidate pool for 468/470 answerable questions and constructs gold-complete packets for 462/470. With a Claude Opus reader, two passes achieve 479/500 and 475/500 under the official GPT-4o judge, around the level of Chronos High’s reported 478/500, although differences in prompts, data, and variance mean no firm comparison can be made. A grok-4.6-high reader scores 476/474 on the same packets, while an agentic, maximum-reasoning-effort variant underperforms at 461/465. The two headline passes differ on 8 questions; a second judge agrees with the main judge on 493/500 questions and scores both passes 472/500. The official judge shows some instability, flipping three verdicts on identical answers. Negative controls show a verifier that sometimes fixes wrong answers but more often corrupts correct ones. They identify several methodological weaknesses: all components tuned on the same 500 questions, no held-out test, no independent human ground truth, extra context given to the main reader, and incomplete logging and tool-trace transparency.
AI.conclusion: A carefully engineered, transparent retrieval-and-scaffolding pipeline can achieve near–state-of-the-art performance on LongMemEval-S while treating the LLM reader as largely interchangeable; retrieval quality and deterministic scaffolds appear to matter at least as much as the specific model. However, small differences in scoring prompts, judging variance, and methodological limitations prevent strong claims about beating or matching existing systems. The work underscores the need for auditable pipelines, stable and well-defined evaluation protocols, and independent human adjudication. By releasing packets, scaffolds, outputs, and verdicts, the authors invite re-scoring and external audit, positioning their work as a step toward more trustworthy long-term memory evaluation rather than a definitive leaderboard result.

title: Asking for What Was Never Requested: Horizontal and Vertical Proactivity in Agents
summary: An agent that uses tools typically responds to what the user explicitly asks, yet completing the task may require information the user never requested. Work on proactive agents mainly studies whether and when an agent should act on its own, not what information it should pursue. We study a distinct axis of proactivity: its content. Horizontal proactivity pursues unstated information that the current context already identifies, and vertical proactivity pursues needs that only earlier evidence reveals. A need graph, recovered from a benchmark's own decomposition, records which needs depend on which, so both forms, and whether the agent stops at the right time, can be scored from a transcript without a model judge. To learn this behavior, we propose Q&D (questioner and drafter), which trains a questioner to prefer the question whose continuation retrieves more of the required evidence, with no reward model or judge. On held-out splits of three multi-hop question-answering benchmarks, at equal retrieval spend, the trained questioner improves both forms of proactivity over the same model, prompted, and outperforms a prompted model $15\times$ larger in the same role on two of the three, and the gain persists after controlling for question volume and length. Without further training, we place the questioner in an interactive customer-service agent with a simulated customer, where it completes more tasks while asking fewer questions, and in retail it outperforms the $15\times$ larger model with fewer follow-up turns from the customer. These results show that proactivity depends not only on whether an agent acts without being asked, but also on what it chooses to pursue and when it stops.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a way to measure and train AI agents to proactively ask the right questions and stop at the right time, improving task completion without extra supervision.
AI.motivation: Existing tool-using or conversational agents mostly respond reactively to user requests, even when solving the task well would require asking for additional, unstated information. Prior research on proactive agents focuses on whether and when an agent should act autonomously, but not on *what specific information* it should seek or how to know when to stop. There is a need for a formal, scalable way to define and evaluate the *content* of proactivity, and to train agents to prioritize questions that actually help gather the evidence required to complete multi-step tasks.
AI.method: The authors introduce a conceptual distinction between two kinds of proactive behavior: (1) horizontal proactivity—asking for or retrieving missing but already implied information in the current context, and (2) vertical proactivity—seeking information whose need is revealed only by earlier steps. They construct a "need graph" from the task decomposition of multi-hop QA benchmarks, encoding dependencies among information needs. This graph allows automatic scoring of proactive behavior from transcripts, without using model-based judges. They then propose Q&D (questioner and drafter): a training scheme where a specialized questioner model is trained to favor questions whose continuations retrieve more of the required evidence, again without an explicit reward model or human judge. The trained questioner is evaluated both in QA benchmarks and in simulated interactive settings like customer service and retail tasks.
AI.result: On held-out portions of three multi-hop QA benchmarks, using the same retrieval budget, the questioner trained with Q&D exhibits higher horizontal and vertical proactivity compared to the same base model used with prompting alone. It also outperforms a much larger (15× parameter) prompted model in the questioner role on two of the three benchmarks. These gains remain even after controlling for the number and length of questions, suggesting the improvement is in question quality rather than quantity. When integrated—without further training—into an interactive customer-service agent with a simulated user, the trained questioner completes more tasks while asking fewer questions. In a retail domain, it similarly surpasses the 15× larger model and requires fewer follow-up turns from the customer.
AI.conclusion: The study shows that effective proactivity in agents is not just about taking initiative, but about *which* information the agent chooses to seek and *when* it decides it has enough to stop. By modeling information dependencies via need graphs and training a dedicated questioner with Q&D, agents can be made more strategically proactive, gathering the right evidence more efficiently and outperforming much larger models in both benchmark and interactive settings, all without reward models or model-based judges.

title: Layer-Informed Fine-Tuning via Three-Stage Functional Segmentation of LLMs
summary: In recent years, the performance of large language models (LLMs) on reasoning tasks has been remarkable, even surpassing human capabilities on various benchmarks. However, there remains a lack of clear understanding in the academic community regarding how the structure and internal parameters of LLMs progressively solve complex reasoning problems.
