In this study, we investigate the inference process of LLMs on cross-linguistic materials and propose the hypothesis that LLM layers exhibit a structured division of labor across conceptualization, reasoning, and textualization. Based on this hypothesis, we introduce a bottleneck identification mechanism using sensitivity analysis to pinpoint the most critical functional stage for a specific task. Leveraging this insight, we propose a novel approach, Layer-Informed Fine-Tuning (LIFT), which achieves efficient and effective fine-tuning by selectively updating only these functionally critical layers. We then conduct extensive experiments to show that the LIFT method not only accelerates the training process but also significantly improves model performance.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how different layers in large language models specialize in conceptualization, reasoning, and textualization, and uses this to fine-tune only the most critical layers for better efficiency and performance.
AI.motivation: Although LLMs perform very well on reasoning tasks, we still lack a clear understanding of how their internal layer structure contributes to solving complex reasoning problems. This gap limits our ability to fine-tune them efficiently and interpret their behavior, especially on cross-linguistic tasks.
AI.method: The authors hypothesize that LLM layers have a structured division of labor into three stages: conceptualization, reasoning, and textualization. They design a bottleneck identification mechanism using sensitivity analysis to determine which stage (and corresponding layers) is most critical for a given task. Based on this, they propose Layer-Informed Fine-Tuning (LIFT), where training updates are applied only to the functionally critical layers instead of the whole model.
AI.result: Experiments across multiple settings show that LIFT speeds up training by restricting updates to a subset of layers, while at the same time yielding substantial gains in performance compared with standard fine-tuning approaches that are less targeted.
AI.conclusion: Understanding functional specialization across layers in LLMs enables more efficient and effective adaptation. By identifying and selectively fine-tuning only the most critical layers for a task, LIFT improves both training efficiency and final performance, supporting the hypothesis of structured division of labor among layers.

title: Foundations of Proactive Agents: Principles, Technical Layers, and Proactivity-Gym
summary: Proactive LLM agents can turn idle compute into useful support before users ask. Yet even correct work can misread user context, impose review costs, or undermine trust. This work proposes foundations for designing, realizing, and evaluating proactive LLM agents around three joint principles (3T): Task Capability, anticipating relevant needs and correctly performing useful work; Temporal Allocation, allocating compute according to resource availability and when results are needed; and Trust, sustaining users' confidence and appropriate reliance on the agent. We connect these objectives to a design space organized around five dimensions: task scope, anticipation horizon, activation trigger, processing timing, and intervention depth, and specify the situation and system modeling needed to support its choices, including user and environment representations, backbone LLMs, and agent harnesses. Lastly, we propose PROACTIVITY-GYM, a simulation-based evaluation testbed including multi-day scenarios, stateful environments, and persona-conditioned simulated users that can evaluate the consequences of proactive assistance across interactions. Evaluations across 23 model-harness configurations uncover substantial performance gaps across 3T and reveal that LLM judges often conflate task capability and trust. A human study with 30 participants demonstrates the importance of the joint 3T optimization: participants show sharp trust declines after intervention misalignment despite correct outcomes, and prefer sleep-time assistance, even when imperfect, to preserve ongoing focus. Together, these findings support designing and evaluating proactive agents through the joint consideration of useful work, compute allocation, and evolving user trust.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a framework (3T: Task Capability, Temporal Allocation, Trust) and a simulation testbed (PROACTIVITY-GYM) for designing and evaluating proactive LLM agents that act before users ask.
AI.motivation: Proactive LLM agents can use idle compute to help users in advance, but even correct proactive actions can mismatch user needs, create review burdens, and damage trust. There is a lack of principled foundations and evaluation methods to design such agents so they are both helpful and trusted over time.
AI.method: The authors formulate three core principles—Task Capability, Temporal Allocation, and Trust (3T)—and map them onto a design space with five dimensions: task scope, anticipation horizon, activation trigger, processing timing, and intervention depth. They specify the situational and system-level modeling required (user/environment representations, backbone LLMs, agent harnesses) to instantiate proactive agents. They then build PROACTIVITY-GYM, a simulation-based evaluation platform with multi-day, stateful scenarios and persona-based simulated users to study the impact of proactive interventions. They conduct evaluations across 23 combinations of models and harnesses, plus a human-subject study with 30 participants on trust and preferences around assistance timing.
AI.result: In simulation, the 23 model-harness configurations show large performance variability across the three 3T dimensions, and LLM-based judges tend to conflate task performance with trust-related assessments. In the user study, participants’ trust declines sharply when proactive interventions are misaligned with their context, even if final task outcomes are correct. Participants generally favor proactive help during low-interruption periods (e.g., sleep-time) over real-time interventions that may disrupt focus, even when the delayed help is imperfect.
AI.conclusion: Effective proactive LLM agents must be designed and evaluated by jointly optimizing useful task performance, intelligent timing and allocation of compute, and long-term user trust. The 3T framework and PROACTIVITY-GYM provide conceptual and experimental foundations for systematically exploring design choices—such as when and how deeply to intervene—to balance assistance quality, resource use, and sustained user confidence.

title: Gender bias across LLMs is common and highly heterogenous
summary: Understanding gender biases in large language models (LLMs) is increasingly important as these systems become embedded in decision-support tools with real consequences. Prior research has focused only on a small set of models, leaving open the extent to which gender biases are common and heterogeneous across LLMs. We address this gap across ten models released between April 2025 and June 2026, spanning nine vendors, using two paradigms: gender attribution to stereotyped phrases (Study 1) and moral judgment of abuse or torture against a woman or a man to prevent a catastrophic outcome (Study 2). In Study 1, two of ten models attributed masculine-stereotyped phrases to female writers more often than the reverse, while three models showed the opposite pattern. In Study 2, several models converged on a male-disadvantaging asymmetry that was directionally consistent with a documented human tendency to protect female targets from harm, though the specific conditions under which this asymmetry emerged varied by model; three other models, by contrast, showed no variation across conditions. These results indicate that gender-related biases are common in LLMs. Their direction and magnitude, however, are highly heterogeneous, to the point that some models behave in diametrically opposite ways to others. Bias auditing should therefore be treated as an ongoing, multi-vendor process, rather than a one-time assessment.

AI.tldr: The paper empirically investigates how common and varied gender biases are across a diverse set of modern large language models, showing that such biases are prevalent but highly heterogeneous across vendors and architectures.
AI.motivation: As LLMs are increasingly integrated into decision-support systems with real-world impact, understanding whether their gender-related behaviors are systematically biased—and whether such biases generalize across models and vendors—becomes critical. Existing work has mostly examined a small number of models, leaving unclear how widespread these issues are, how consistent their direction is, and whether some models might even exhibit opposite bias patterns. The authors aim to fill this empirical gap and inform better auditing and governance practices.
AI.method: The authors evaluate ten LLMs released between April 2025 and June 2026 from nine different vendors. They use two experimental paradigms. Study 1: a gender-attribution task, where models are asked to infer the gender of the writer of phrases that are stereotypically masculine or feminine; the researchers then quantify asymmetries in attribution (e.g., how often masculine-stereotyped text is labeled as written by a man vs. a woman). Study 2: a moral judgment task, where models assess scenarios involving abuse or torture of either a woman or a man to prevent a catastrophic outcome; the authors analyze whether models’ moral evaluations differ depending on the target’s gender and under what conditions these asymmetries appear. The analyses compare direction, magnitude, and situational dependence of gender-related asymmetries across models.
AI.result: In Study 1, gender-attribution behavior varied substantially: two of ten models more frequently attributed masculine-stereotyped phrases to female writers than to male writers, while three models showed the opposite tendency (attributing such phrases more to men), and the remainder showed weaker or mixed patterns. In Study 2, several models displayed a male-disadvantaging asymmetry in moral judgments, meaning they were more protective of female targets—less willing to condone harm against women than against men in catastrophic trade‑off scenarios—in a way that qualitatively resembles documented human tendencies. However, the exact scenarios and prompts that elicited this asymmetry differed from model to model, and three models showed no gender-related variation in their moral judgments at all. Overall, the authors find that gender-related biases are frequent but vary greatly across systems in both sign and strength.
AI.conclusion: Gender biases are widespread among contemporary LLMs, but they are not uniform: different models can exhibit opposite directions of bias and differ in how and when these biases appear. This heterogeneity implies that conclusions drawn from a small subset of models cannot be safely generalized to the broader LLM ecosystem. As a result, bias auditing must be an ongoing, comparative effort spanning multiple vendors and model generations, rather than a one-off evaluation of a single system. The findings underscore the need for continuous, standardized auditing practices and caution in deploying LLMs in high-stakes decision-support contexts.

title: Task-Relevant Null-Space Residuals for Non-Injective Neural Mappings
summary: Non-injective mappings in neural networks map distinct inputs to the same representation, thereby implicitly inducing equivalence relations in the input space. However, the input differences eliminated by these mappings may still be required by downstream tasks, creating a mismatch between operator-induced indistinguishability and task-required distinctions. For non-injective linear operators realized in the current forward pass, their null spaces exactly characterize these invisible input variations. We propose Task-Relevant Null-Space Residuals (NSR), a general residual framework for non-injective linear mappings. NSR combines null-space component extraction from pre-mapping representations, member-level encoding and gating, and application-specific integration to exploit potentially task-relevant information under downstream supervision while preserving the original aggregation or merging rules. We evaluate NSR in two structurally different settings: token merging and graph aggregation. In token merging, NSR achieves higher semantic segmentation performance than the corresponding compressed baselines in 34 out of 36 evaluated configurations, with a maximum observed gain of 31.51 mIoU points under strong compression. In graph aggregation, NSR achieves 100% training accuracy on Tree-NeighborsMatch at depths d=2--6 across three backbones, alongside gains on heterophilic node classification and molecular graph regression. Together, these results support null-space residuals as a practical complement to non-injective linear mappings, enabling downstream models to learn from input distinctions invisible in the original operator's output.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Task-Relevant Null-Space Residuals (NSR), a framework that recovers and exploits information lost by non-injective linear mappings (like token merging or graph aggregation) by leveraging their null spaces, improving performance across vision and graph tasks.
AI.motivation: Non-injective operators in neural networks (e.g., pooling, merging, aggregation) collapse different inputs into the same representation, implicitly defining equivalence classes. While this improves efficiency or enforces inductive biases, it may discard input distinctions that are crucial for downstream tasks, creating a mismatch between what the operator treats as indistinguishable and what the task needs to distinguish. There is a lack of a general, practical mechanism to preserve or reintroduce this lost but potentially task-relevant information without breaking the original aggregation rules.
AI.method: The paper focuses on non-injective linear operators used in the current forward pass and characterizes their null spaces as precisely the set of input variations that are invisible to the operator’s output. It proposes Task-Relevant Null-Space Residuals (NSR), a residual framework that: (1) extracts the components of the pre-mapping representations that lie in the null space of the linear mapping; (2) encodes these components at the member level (i.e., per token or per node); (3) applies a gating mechanism to modulate how much null-space information is used; and (4) integrates these gated residuals into the downstream computation in an application-specific way, all while preserving the original merging/aggregation behavior of the base operator.
AI.result: In token merging scenarios (for semantic segmentation under strong compression), NSR consistently outperforms matched baselines that use the same level of compression, achieving higher mIoU in 34 out of 36 configurations and reaching up to a 31.51 mIoU point improvement in the best case. In graph aggregation scenarios, NSR enables models to achieve 100% training accuracy on the Tree-NeighborsMatch benchmark for depths d=2 to 6 across three backbone architectures. It also provides performance gains on heterophilic node classification tasks and molecular graph regression benchmarks, demonstrating its broad utility across different graph learning settings.
AI.conclusion: Null-space residuals are an effective and general way to complement non-injective linear mappings in neural networks. By explicitly modeling and leveraging the null-space components—the task-relevant distinctions lost by the original operator—NSR allows downstream models to access otherwise invisible input differences while keeping the benefits of aggregation and compression. The empirical results across token merging and graph aggregation suggest that NSR is a practical, architecture-agnostic tool for mitigating information loss in non-injective operators.

title: Correct Answers, Invalid Traces: What Verifiable Grade-School Math Reveals About Chain-of-Thought Traces
summary: Chain-of-thought traces are widely read as records of how models reach their answers, informing debugging, agent auditing, and claims about reasoning. Testing this interpretation is difficult because natural-language thinking traces are rarely mechanically verifiable. We revisit it in iGSM, a synthetic grade-school mathematics benchmark designed to study thinking traces and used to support claims of learned reasoning and planning. Crucially, iGSM exposes the exact quantities and dependencies that a correct solution should use, allowing generated traces to be checked programmatically step by step and enabling us to test whether correct answers are reliably accompanied by valid traces. We first evaluate models trained exclusively on valid, minimal traces. Answer correctness and trace validity nearly coincide in distribution but decouple out of distribution: on the hardest instances, 31.6% of correct answers have invalid traces, over half of which pass all syntactic and arithmetic checks but fail semantic dependency checks. We then intervene on trace supervision. Non-minimal training traces induce non-minimal outputs, while re-asking the same problem with a different query reveals computations inherited from the original query, weakening minimality as evidence of selective planning. Shuffling tokens in 10% of training trace sentences preserves near-clean accuracy even out of distribution despite no trace passing verification. Swapped training traces likewise retain high in-distribution accuracy. We discuss the implications of these findings for chain-of-thought monitoring and interpretation in the context of AI safety.

AI.tldr: The paper empirically tests whether chain-of-thought (CoT) explanations reflect real reasoning by using a synthetic math benchmark (iGSM) where correct intermediate steps are mechanically checkable, and finds that correct answers often come with invalid or spurious traces, especially out of distribution.
AI.motivation: Chain-of-thought traces are widely used as if they transparently show how models reason, supporting debugging, auditing, and safety claims. However, for most natural-language problems, these traces cannot be rigorously checked, so it is unclear whether they are faithful records of reasoning or post-hoc stories. The authors want a setting where they can objectively test the fidelity and minimality of CoT traces to challenge or validate claims about learned reasoning and planning in LMs.
AI.method: They use iGSM, a synthetic grade-school math benchmark in which all relevant quantities and their dependencies are explicitly specified. This allows the authors to programmatically verify each step in a model’s chain-of-thought: arithmetic correctness, syntactic validity, and semantic dependency (whether the step uses only information that should be available at that point). They train models on different types of supervision over traces: valid minimal traces, non-minimal traces, corrupted traces with token shuffling, and swapped traces from other problems. They then measure: (1) alignment between answer correctness and trace validity in- and out-of-distribution; (2) the effect of non-minimal and corrupted supervision on trace properties and final accuracy; and (3) how traces change when the same problem is re-queried in a different way, revealing inherited computations from prior prompts.
AI.result: When models are trained only on valid, minimal traces, answer correctness and trace validity mostly coincide on standard instances but diverge on harder, out-of-distribution examples: 31.6% of correct answers have invalid traces there. Many of these invalid traces still pass syntactic and arithmetic checks but fail deeper semantic dependency checks, indicating subtle unfaithfulness. Non-minimal training traces lead models to produce similarly non-minimal outputs, undermining minimality as an indicator of deliberate, selective reasoning. Re-asking the same problem differently reveals that models reuse internal computations from prior queries, suggesting that apparent minimal traces can mask hidden, inherited steps. Furthermore, corrupting 10% of training trace sentences by shuffling tokens results in almost unchanged accuracy even out-of-distribution, despite traces no longer passing verification, and swapping traces between problems also leaves in-distribution accuracy high.
AI.conclusion: Chain-of-thought traces, even when they look clean and correct on the surface, are not reliably faithful indicators of a model’s underlying reasoning, especially in out-of-distribution settings. Correct answers can be accompanied by semantically invalid or spurious traces, and models can maintain high task performance even when trained on corrupted or mismatched traces. Minimality and apparent coherence of CoT are therefore weak evidence of genuine stepwise planning or reasoning. These findings cast doubt on using CoT as a monitoring or interpretability tool in AI safety and suggest that more rigorous, mechanically verifiable tests and stronger notions of faithfulness are needed if traces are to support trust, auditing, or safety guarantees.

title: Transolver-$σ$: Joint Spectral-Physical Subspace Modeling for Neural PDE Solving
summary: Neural solvers offer efficient surrogates for numerical simulation of partial differential equations (PDEs). For time-dependent problems, strong one-step accuracy does not necessarily translate into reliable autoregressive rollout. We observe that a solver based only on physical-state modeling can achieve lower one-step error, whereas its spectral-only counterpart can become more accurate at later rollout steps. Motivated by this observation, we present Transolver-$σ$, a neural PDE solver based on joint spectral--physical subspace modeling. Within each block, adaptive physical-state interactions and spectral transformations are modeled in dedicated latent subspaces, whose responses are recomposed to enable information exchange between the two representations. Within the physical subspace, we introduce Slice-Residual Physics-Attention (SRPA), which preserves an explicit slice-space identity path while retaining learnable cross-slice interaction. In parallel, an axis-factorized Fourier operator captures global spectral structure. Across five well-established PDE benchmarks spanning steady-state prediction and time-dependent dynamics, Transolver-$σ$ achieves state-of-the-art with a benchmark-averaged relative error reduction of 33.4% over the strongest baseline for each metric, while consistently improving autoregressive rollout over single-operator counterparts. Transolver-$σ$ further delivers strong gains on coupled multiphysics systems and real-world fluid and combustion measurements from RealPDEBench, demonstrating its effectiveness beyond standard simulation benchmarks.

AI.tldr: Transolver-σ is a neural PDE solver that jointly models physical and spectral representations to improve long-horizon rollout and achieve state-of-the-art accuracy on multiple PDE benchmarks and real-world data.
AI.motivation: Existing neural PDE solvers often optimize for one-step prediction accuracy, but this does not guarantee stable and accurate autoregressive rollout over time. Furthermore, solvers that focus only on physical-state or only on spectral representations show complementary strengths: physical-only models tend to have lower one-step error, while spectral-only models can become more accurate at later rollout steps. There is a need for a unified approach that combines these advantages to improve both short-term and long-horizon performance, especially on complex, multiphysics and real-world problems.
AI.method: The paper proposes Transolver-σ, a neural PDE solver that jointly models physical and spectral subspaces within each network block. The architecture maintains two dedicated latent subspaces—one for adaptive physical-state interactions and one for spectral transformations—then recomposes their responses to facilitate information exchange. In the physical subspace, the authors introduce Slice-Residual Physics-Attention (SRPA), which preserves an explicit identity path along slices while allowing learnable cross-slice interactions, improving stability and expressiveness. In parallel, an axis-factorized Fourier operator models global spectral structure. These components are stacked into a transformer-like architecture designed for PDE simulation and autoregressive rollout.
AI.result: Across five standard PDE benchmarks covering both steady-state and time-dependent problems, Transolver-σ achieves state-of-the-art results, with an average relative error reduction of 33.4% over the strongest baseline for each metric. It also yields consistently better autoregressive rollout compared to single-operator (purely physical or purely spectral) counterparts. Beyond synthetic benchmarks, the method also shows strong performance on coupled multiphysics systems and on real-world fluid and combustion measurement datasets from RealPDEBench.
AI.conclusion: Joint modeling of physical and spectral subspaces within neural PDE solvers can significantly improve both accuracy and rollout stability compared to using either representation alone. The proposed Transolver-σ architecture, with SRPA for physical interactions and an axis-factorized Fourier operator for spectral structure, sets a new performance level on a range of PDE benchmarks and extends effectively to challenging multiphysics and real-world datasets, suggesting it is a robust and general surrogate for PDE simulation.

title: How Local Mixing Encodes Relative Position in Global NoPE Attention
summary: The attention operation is naively position invariant. However, positional information is fundamental to natural language, and therefore a variety of explicit position encodings have been developed in transformer-based models, such as rotary position encoding (RoPE). Although explicit position encodings have long been assumed to be required, recent methods that interleave local mixing layers, such as sliding window attention (SWA) and gated linear attention, while not encoding position (NoPE) in global attention layers has recently been shown to be successful at scale. How and why this approach works is not well-understood. In this paper, we develop an explanation of how hybrid models of this sort can implicitly encode position at global NoPE layers. Supported by both theoretical and empirical evidence, our central argument is that SWA and gated linear attention induce a recency bias in the residual stream that propagates to, and is selected by, the global attention logits. Moreover, in contrast to the implicit position encodings found in models with only global NoPE attention, in which positional information arises solely from the causal mask, the recency bias in hybrid models can be maintained across long sequences. In addition to deepening our understanding of how hybrid models encode position, these findings may provide insights for how to encode position in a way that can extrapolate to longer sequence lengths indefinitely.

AI.tldr: The paper explains how transformer models that mix local attention (like sliding windows) with global attention without explicit position encodings can still learn and preserve positional information via an induced recency bias.
AI.motivation: Transformers are naturally position-invariant, so explicit positional encodings (like RoPE) are usually added. Yet, recent large-scale models that only use positional information in local layers but not in global attention layers (NoPE globally) still work surprisingly well, especially on long sequences. Why these hybrid architectures succeed, and how they internally represent position without explicit global encodings, is not well understood.
AI.method: The authors theoretically analyze transformers that combine local mixing layers (e.g., sliding window attention and gated linear attention) with global attention layers that lack explicit position encodings. They study how these local mechanisms affect the residual stream and, in turn, the attention logits in global NoPE layers. They complement the theory with empirical experiments to measure and visualize recency bias and positional information across depths and sequence lengths.
AI.result: They show that local mixing layers like sliding window attention and gated linear attention create a systematic recency bias in the residual stream, which is then picked up and used by the global NoPE attention layers as an implicit positional signal. This bias is strong and structured enough to serve as an effective positional encoding, and unlike purely mask-based implicit encodings in fully global NoPE models, it remains stable over long sequences.
AI.conclusion: Hybrid models with local mixing plus global NoPE attention implicitly encode position via recency bias induced in the residual stream, enabling robust positional reasoning without explicit global positional encodings. This mechanism can maintain positional information over arbitrarily long contexts, suggesting promising directions for designing position encodings that extrapolate to much longer sequence lengths.

title: AssayRouter: Historical Utility Priors for Frozen Molecular Predictor Routing
summary: Laboratories often face a new molecular assay with 16-64 labels and a bank of predictors whose training data and parameters are unavailable. The practical question is which frozen outputs to include in a small local model. AssayRouter treats completed assays as pseudo-targets and labels each candidate by its post-fit utility: the reduction in held-out discovery loss when the candidate is added to the local target predictor. A shared regressor learns to predict this utility from candidate behavior on the support set, without source identity; on a new assay, one frozen ranking selects four sources and separate labels fit a convex combiner. We train only on completed ChEMBL-MT assays and evaluate 24 external regression assays across six frozen interface families. AssayRouter-C lowers strict four-call negative log-likelihood (NLL) by 0.0409 relative to Support-CV@4. Frozen candidate-label permutations confirm that candidate-utility correspondence carries the transferred information, and leave-one-interface-out training shows that the mapping generalizes to unseen predictor families. Completed assays therefore provide transferable supervision for scarce-label routing through frozen prediction interfaces.

AI.tldr: They propose AssayRouter, a method to choose which frozen predictors to query for a new molecular assay when only a few calls are allowed.
AI.motivation: Labs often have many pre-trained molecular prediction models (frozen interfaces) but limited labels and call budget for a new assay. The challenge is to decide which models to query so that a small local model performs best, despite having no access to the original training data or parameters of those models.
AI.method: Treat past completed assays as pseudo-targets and compute, for each candidate predictor, its post-fit utility: how much it improves held-out discovery performance when added to a local target model. Train a shared regressor to predict this utility from observable behavior of candidates on a support set, without using predictor identity. For a new assay, use this learned mapping to rank candidates, select four, and then learn a convex combination of their outputs as the local predictor.
AI.result: On 24 external ChEMBL-MT regression assays and six different frozen interface families, AssayRouter-C reduces four-call negative log-likelihood by 0.0409 compared to a strong baseline (Support-CV@4). Experiments with permuted candidate labels show that the performance relies on preserving the mapping between candidates and their utilities, and leave-one-interface-out experiments demonstrate that the learned mapping transfers to unseen predictor families.
AI.conclusion: Completed assays can serve as supervision to learn how valuable each frozen predictor is likely to be for new tasks. The resulting AssayRouter method generalizes across predictor families and improves scarce-label routing decisions when using black-box molecular prediction interfaces.

title: From Routing Signals to Selective Review: Visual regrounding in MoE VLMs
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) may accept false visual premises, answering questions about a target object's color, count, location, or state even when it is absent. We call this reliability-critical behavior a target-absence grounding failure. Existing visual-grounding detectors primarily rely on generated responses, hidden states, or uncertainty measures. We present the first framework to leverage internal routing decisions in Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) VLMs to detect target absence before generation and guide selective correction. We extract target-token routing probabilities from Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B-Instruct and Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it, train a separate L2-regularized linear detector for each model, and use its predictions to selectively invoke a target-aware review prompt. Using routing alone, the Qwen and Gemma detectors achieve ROC-AUCs of 0.9988 and 0.9956 on GQA-Inpaint and retain 0.8095 and 0.7781 on the external OBER dataset, respectively. The resulting routing-gated policy improves end-to-end accuracy on GQA-Inpaint and OBER by +22.25% and +12.17% for Qwen, and by +13.42% and +1.39% for Gemma, without modifying model weights. Further analysis shows that the signal is localized to the target-object token, emerges in early MoE layers, and is distributed across partially substitutable experts. Although cross-dataset threshold shifts require recalibration, false-positive review causes limited harm overall, suggesting that intervention risk can be controlled through joint selection of the detector threshold and review prompt. Overall, we show that routing probabilities alone preserve actionable information about visual perception, allowing computation already produced by an MoE VLM to support low-cost detection and selective visual regrounding.

AI.tldr: They use internal routing patterns in Mixture‑of‑Experts vision‑language models to detect when a queried target object is actually absent from the image, then trigger a special review prompt to fix answers, substantially boosting reliability without changing model weights.
AI.motivation: Vision‑language models often confidently answer questions about objects that are not present (e.g., color, count, location), a failure mode they term target‑absence grounding failure. Existing detectors of such failures look at outputs, hidden states, or uncertainty after generation, which can be costly and less targeted. The authors want a cheaper, earlier, and more precise signal that indicates whether the model has truly grounded the mentioned object in the image, especially for reliability‑critical applications.
AI.method: They focus on Mixture‑of‑Experts (MoE) VLMs and exploit their internal routing decisions. For each input, they extract the routing probability vectors associated with the token corresponding to the target object across MoE layers in two specific models: Qwen3‑VL‑30B‑A3B‑Instruct and Gemma‑4‑26B‑A4B‑it. Using these routing probabilities as features, they train an L2‑regularized linear classifier (a separate detector per base model) to predict whether the target object is absent. This detector operates before answer generation. If it predicts likely target absence, they selectively trigger a “target‑aware review” prompt that asks the base VLM to reconsider or re‑ground its answer, yielding a routing‑gated policy. They then analyze where in the network the signal arises (which layers, which token, which experts) and how transferable it is across datasets.
AI.result: On the GQA‑Inpaint benchmark, detectors that use only routing probabilities achieve extremely high ROC‑AUCs: 0.9988 for Qwen and 0.9956 for Gemma. On the different OBER dataset, performance remains strong though lower: ROC‑AUC 0.8095 (Qwen) and 0.7781 (Gemma), indicating partial cross‑dataset generalization. When these detectors gate the use of a review prompt, end‑to‑end question‑answering accuracy improves substantially: for Qwen, +22.25% on GQA‑Inpaint and +12.17% on OBER; for Gemma, +13.42% and +1.39%, respectively. Analysis shows that the most informative signal is concentrated on the target object token, appears already in early MoE layers, and is spread across experts that can partially substitute for each other. They also find that applying a threshold tuned on one dataset to another causes shifts that require recalibration, but even overly aggressive thresholds (causing more false positives) do not severely degrade performance because unnecessary reviews are relatively harmless.
AI.conclusion: Internal MoE routing probabilities alone encode rich, actionable information about whether a VLM has properly grounded a mentioned object in the visual input. By training simple linear detectors on these routing features and using them to gate a targeted review prompt, one can significantly improve robustness to target‑absence grounding failures without retraining or modifying the base model. The approach is efficient (uses already‑computed signals), effective across two distinct MoE VLMs, and offers tunable risk via detector‑threshold and prompt design, though practical deployment requires dataset‑specific calibration.

title: MetaCtrl: Your Large Language Models Can Reason Better and More Concisely with a Metacognitive Controller
summary: Large reasoning models improve performance on challenging problems by allocating additional computation before answering, but longer reasoning does not always lead to better results and can introduce substantial redundant reasoning on simple problems. Conversely, aggressively shortening reasoning can degrade performance on difficult ones. Effective reasoning therefore requires dynamically deciding when additional computation is useful based on the reasoner's capabilities and evolving solution state. Existing approaches often rely on predefined budgets or intervention rules, retrain the target reasoner, or require additional supervision. We introduce MetaCtrl, a lightweight controller that adaptively regulates a frozen reasoner without predefined token budgets or reasoner retraining. We formulate reasoning regulation as a sequential metacognitive control problem: MetaCtrl observes the evolving reasoning trace and decides whether to continue, simplify, skip redundant steps, or conclude reasoning. It is trained directly with reinforcement learning using a reward that prioritizes correctness while favoring shorter trajectories among correct solutions, requiring neither supervised intervention trajectories nor problem-specific budgets. Across seven benchmarks spanning mathematics, science, and code, MetaCtrl consistently improves the accuracy of LRMs while reducing their reasoning length. On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, it improves average accuracy by 4.7 points while reducing generation length by 53.3%. Without further training, the same controller transfers to an unseen reasoner (e.g., Qwen3-14B), improving average accuracy by 2.9 points and reducing generation length by 50.3%. These results establish MetaCtrl as a plug-and-play controller for improving reasoning accuracy while substantially reducing inference-time generation. The code is available at https://github.com/binbin2xs/MetaCtrl.

AI.tldr: MetaCtrl is a lightweight RL-trained controller that adaptively decides how much reasoning a frozen large reasoning model should perform, improving accuracy while significantly shortening generation length across math, science, and code benchmarks, and transferring well to new models.
AI.motivation: Large reasoning models often use long chains of thought, but more tokens do not always mean better answers. Fixed or aggressive shortening of reasoning wastes computation on easy tasks or hurts performance on hard ones. Existing control methods depend on fixed budgets, handcrafted rules, retraining, or extra supervision. There is a need for a general, plug-and-play way to dynamically regulate reasoning length based on the evolving solution process and the model’s capabilities, without retraining the base reasoner or requiring problem-specific tuning.
AI.method: The authors propose MetaCtrl, a separate lightweight controller that operates over the evolving reasoning trace of a frozen large reasoning model. They cast the problem as a sequential metacognitive control task: at each step, MetaCtrl observes the partial reasoning and chooses among actions such as continue reasoning, simplify, skip redundant steps, or stop and output an answer. MetaCtrl is trained with reinforcement learning using a reward that primarily incentivizes correctness but also penalizes unnecessary length among correct trajectories. It does not rely on supervised intervention labels, fixed token budgets, or modification of the underlying reasoner. Once trained, the controller can be plugged into different reasoning models without additional finetuning.
AI.result: Across seven benchmarks covering mathematics, science, and programming tasks, MetaCtrl increases both efficiency and accuracy of large reasoning models. On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, it yields an average accuracy gain of 4.7 percentage points while cutting reasoning-token generation by 53.3%. When applied zero-shot to a different, larger model (Qwen3-14B) without any retraining, it still improves average accuracy by 2.9 percentage points and reduces reasoning length by 50.3%. These experiments demonstrate that MetaCtrl generalizes across tasks and models while saving substantial computation.
AI.conclusion: MetaCtrl provides an effective, plug-and-play metacognitive controller for large reasoning models that adaptively regulates reasoning depth without modifying or retraining the underlying model. By learning a policy that balances correctness against reasoning length via reinforcement learning, it simultaneously improves accuracy and halves generation cost on diverse reasoning benchmarks, and its policy transfers well to new reasoners. This establishes dynamic, learned reasoning control as a practical approach for more efficient and capable LRMs.

title: LongHarness Bench: Stress-Testing Language Model Harnesses for Long-Context Reasoning
summary: Language-model (LM) harnesses enable LMs to operate effectively over long contexts using additional compute. However, existing long-context evaluations are insufficient for distinguishing modern harnesses, reflected by saturated accuracy across harnesses and largely similar evaluation costs. In this paper, we introduce a benchmark for evaluating both the effectiveness and efficiency of long-context harnesses. Our tasks require diverse retrieval strategies, including lexical search and semantic matching, together with strategic and adaptive reasoning over global and local context. Much of the context is semantically relevant but only a small subset is useful at each step, creating both a challenging search problem and different accuracy--cost tradeoffs across processing strategies. For example, one task requires identifying every person satisfying several conditions using evidence scattered across documents; strategically checking the most selective condition first can narrow the search before verifying the remaining conditions. We evaluate multiple families of frontier language models with four state-of-the-art harnesses. Our benchmarks remain challenging even for strong model--harness combinations: the best reaches 68\% macro-average accuracy across four evaluation suites. More importantly, we find that the same underlying model can exhibit markedly different efficiency under different harnesses. Our results establish efficiency as an important axis for long-context evaluation and provide a testbed for developing harnesses that process context strategically rather than exhaustively.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a new benchmark to evaluate how well and how efficiently language-model harnesses handle long contexts, focusing on both accuracy and computational cost.
AI.motivation: Existing long-context evaluations no longer discriminate clearly between modern LM harnesses because many achieve similarly high accuracy and similar evaluation costs. There is a need for a benchmark that exposes meaningful differences in both effectiveness and efficiency, especially as LMs rely on harnesses to process very long inputs.
AI.method: The authors design a benchmark composed of tasks that demand diverse retrieval strategies (lexical search, semantic matching) combined with strategic and adaptive reasoning over global and local context. They construct settings where much of the context is relevant but only a small portion is actually needed at each step, forcing harnesses to trade off accuracy and compute in non-trivial ways. They then evaluate several frontier LMs paired with four state-of-the-art long-context harnesses on four evaluation suites.
AI.result: Even strong model–harness combinations perform far from perfectly, with the best setup achieving 68% macro-average accuracy across the benchmark’s four suites. The experiments show that different harnesses wrapped around the same base model can lead to substantially different computational efficiency, despite similar accuracy levels in older benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: The benchmark reveals that efficiency is a crucial, previously under-emphasized dimension in long-context evaluation. It provides a challenging and discriminative testbed that encourages development of long-context harnesses that process information selectively and strategically instead of exhaustively, highlighting important accuracy–cost tradeoffs.

title: ReMem: Rethinking Perception and Memory in Long-Context Recommendation Agents
summary: Recent Recommendation Agents (RecAgents) offer a promising alternative by shifting recommendation to an active, user-side paradigm, where generative agents autonomously perceive external platforms, reason over user preferences, and execute decisions. However, existing RecAgents still suffer from two critical limitations: brittle item perception based on noisy and heterogeneous item pages, and inefficient long-context reasoning over extended user histories and multi-step interaction traces. To address these challenges, we propose a novel recommendation agent framework, termed as ReMem, that combines OCR-based multimodal perception with time-evolving dynamic memory. Instead of parsing raw HTML, ReMem observes item pages through screenshots and extracts structured multimodal information via an OCR tool, enabling a more humanoid and platform-agnostic perception mechanism. To support long-horizon preference modeling, ReMem further introduces a chunk-wise sequential memory update strategy, where the agent selectively maintains a fixed-size memory of informative historical interactions while processing arbitrarily long contexts with linear inference complexity and bounded context length. This design allows the agent to preserve evolving user preferences without relying on external memory modules or disrupting the standard autoregressive generation process. To enhance the dynamic memory instruction, we further develop a multi-memory GRPO variant, which propagates the final-answer advantage to all intermediate conversations that contribute to the final response. Extensive experiments on three datasets demonstrate that ReMem consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, achieving an average improvement of 5.16\% across three recommendation agent tasks, namely searching, ranking, and judging.

AI.tldr: ReMem is a recommendation agent framework that uses OCR-based multimodal page perception and a time-evolving dynamic memory to robustly understand items and efficiently reason over long user histories, improving search, ranking, and judgment tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing recommendation agents operate on the user side and can actively perceive platforms and reason about preferences, but they struggle with noisy, heterogeneous item pages when parsing HTML and with inefficient, brittle reasoning over very long user histories and multi-step interactions. There is a need for a more robust, platform-agnostic perception method and an efficient mechanism to model evolving user preferences over long horizons without exploding context length or requiring external memory systems.
AI.method: ReMem replaces HTML parsing with screenshot-based observation of item pages and uses an OCR toolkit to extract structured multimodal information, mimicking human-like perception and making it platform-agnostic. For long-term reasoning, it introduces a chunk-wise sequential memory update scheme: the agent maintains a fixed-size, selective dynamic memory of informative past interactions while processing arbitrarily long contexts with linear-time inference and bounded context length, integrated directly into the autoregressive generation process. Additionally, a multi-memory GRPO (reinforcement learning) variant propagates the final-answer reward back to all intermediate conversational steps that contributed to the final outcome, improving the quality of dynamic memory usage.
AI.result: Across three datasets and three recommendation-agent tasks (searching, ranking, judging), ReMem consistently outperforms strong baselines, with an average performance gain of 5.16%, demonstrating that its multimodal perception and dynamic memory mechanisms yield better recommendation behavior.
AI.conclusion: OCR-based multimodal perception from screenshots, combined with a time-evolving, chunk-wise dynamic memory and multi-memory GRPO optimization, enables RecAgents to more robustly perceive items and more efficiently model long-horizon user preferences. This design improves performance on multiple recommendation tasks without requiring external memory modules or breaking standard autoregressive generation, suggesting a practical and generalizable way to build stronger user-side recommendation agents.

title: Pretraining Latent Information Feedback Transformers with Teacher Supervision
summary: Transformer language models (LMs) are feed-forward: deep-layer representations are never fed back to shallower layers, and the only pathway for information to flow downward across generation steps is the decoded token. This narrow channel forces models to recompute intermediate results and to discard alternative continuations. In this work, we remove this bottleneck during pretraining, introducing the LIFT (Latent Information Feedback Transformer) architecture and training method which enable LMs to propagate state across generation. We achieve this by turning recurrent-state learning into a teacher-forced prediction problem: each input token is paired with an information-dense state, derived from the next-token distribution of an off-the-shelf pretrained LM. The model, extended with a small number of additional parameters, is then trained to predict both the next token and the next state. As the input states are precomputed, pretraining remains fully parallel across positions. At inference, the model's own predicted states are fed back, with a minor computational overhead that decreases with model size. Experiments with pretrained models ranging from 135M to 1B parameters show that LIFT consistently outperforms standard Transformers and baselines on language modeling, downstream reasoning tasks, and procedural tasks under token-matched budget, while being on par with or ahead of compute-matched Transformers. Moreover, a controlled study on a state-tracking task shows that a tiny LIFT outperforms same-size Transformers trained on 8x more data, even when trained with the states of a Transformer that fails the task. Overall, we show that LMs can learn to exploit deep-to-shallow feedback during pretraining via scalable teacher supervision.

AI.tldr: They propose LIFT, a Transformer variant that can pass rich latent state across time steps, improving efficiency and performance over standard feed-forward Transformers.
AI.motivation: Standard Transformers are purely feed-forward across layers and timesteps: information only flows forward in depth, and across tokens it flows via the emitted tokens themselves. This creates a narrow communication channel between steps, forcing the model to recompute intermediate computations and discard alternative futures, which is especially limiting for reasoning and stateful tasks. The authors want to enable Transformers to carry and reuse internal state across generation without losing parallelizable training.
AI.method: They introduce LIFT (Latent Information Feedback Transformer), which augments a conventional LM with a recurrent latent state that is fed back between generation steps. Instead of training this state via classic recurrent backprop, they turn it into a teacher-forced prediction problem. For each token in the pretraining corpus, they precompute an information-dense state derived from the next-token distribution of an existing, off-the-shelf pretrained LM. During training, the new model (with a small number of additional parameters compared to the base Transformer) is trained to jointly predict both the next token and the next-step latent state. Because these target states are precomputed, training remains fully parallel over sequence positions. At inference time, the model uses its own predicted states as input recurrent context, incurring only modest additional computation that becomes proportionally smaller for larger models.
AI.result: Across pretrained model sizes from 135M to 1B parameters, LIFT models consistently outperform standard Transformers and other baselines on language modeling benchmarks, reasoning tasks, and procedural tasks when constrained to the same token budget. Under equal compute budgets, LIFT matches or exceeds standard Transformers. In a controlled state-tracking task, a very small LIFT model beats same-size Transformers trained with eight times more data, even when LIFT is supervised by states taken from a Transformer that itself cannot solve the task, indicating that the architecture can extract more useful structure from imperfect supervisory states.
AI.conclusion: Latent feedback of rich internal state across timesteps can be learned effectively during LM pretraining when framed as a supervised state-prediction problem with precomputed teacher states. LIFT demonstrates that adding a lightweight recurrent state pathway on top of standard Transformers improves language modeling and reasoning while preserving parallel training and keeping inference overhead modest. This suggests that deep-to-shallow feedback and explicit state propagation are valuable inductive biases for future language model architectures.

title: Mubric: Mutation Testing-Guided Rubric Generation for LLM Evaluation
summary: Rubric-based evaluation is widely used to assess LLM-based systems by decomposing response quality into task-specific scoring criteria. However, automatically generating rubrics that reliably capture task-specific quality requirements remains challenging. We introduce Mubric, a mutation testing-guided approach to rubric generation. Mutation testing, a classic software testing methodology, evaluates a test suite by injecting faults into programs and checking whether the tests detect them. We draw an analogy between test suites and rubrics: if a rubric captures an important quality requirement, introducing a corresponding defect into an otherwise high-quality response should reduce its score. Mubric first mines common defects from real pairs of preferred and dispreferred responses and abstracts these defects into reusable mutation operators, each specifying how to introduce a particular type of response defect. For a new task, it applies relevant operators to a reference response, checks whether the injected defects reduce response quality, and uses insufficiently penalized defects to refine the rubric. We evaluate Mubric on 703 tasks across four representative domains against six advanced rubric generation methods. Mubric achieves the highest overall evaluation accuracy, outperforming the strongest baseline by 7.48 percentage points.

AI.tldr: They propose Mubric, a mutation-testing-inspired method to automatically generate better rubrics for evaluating LLM outputs, achieving notably higher evaluation accuracy than prior rubric generation methods.
AI.motivation: Rubric-based evaluation is common for assessing large language model (LLM) systems, since rubrics decompose response quality into concrete, task-specific criteria. However, designing good rubrics is labor-intensive and difficult to automate: existing automatic methods often fail to fully capture the nuanced, task-specific quality requirements. The authors aim to make rubric generation more systematic, scalable, and reliable, especially across many diverse tasks and domains.
AI.method: They adapt ideas from mutation testing in software engineering. First, they mine common defects from real-world pairs of preferred vs. dispreferred responses, then abstract these into reusable mutation operators that describe how to inject specific types of defects into a high-quality response. For a new task, they apply relevant mutation operators to a good reference response to create defective variants. They then test whether the current rubric assigns lower scores to these mutated responses. If some defects are not sufficiently penalized, Mubric uses these failure cases to iteratively refine and expand the rubric so it better captures important quality requirements. This pipeline is evaluated on hundreds of tasks across multiple domains and compared against existing automatic rubric generation approaches.
AI.result: On 703 tasks across four representative domains, Mubric is compared to six advanced automatic rubric generation methods. Mubric achieves the highest overall evaluation accuracy, improving over the strongest baseline by 7.48 percentage points. This indicates that mutation-testing-guided rubric refinement leads to more reliable LLM evaluation rubrics.
AI.conclusion: Mutation testing concepts can be effectively transferred from software testing to LLM evaluation. By systematically injecting realistic defects and ensuring rubrics penalize them, Mubric produces higher-quality, task-specific rubrics that yield more accurate evaluations than prior automated methods. This suggests a promising direction for scalable, data-driven construction and refinement of evaluation criteria for LLM-based systems.

title: STEPQuant: When and Where Errors Matter in Delta-Rule Recurrent State Quantization
summary: Linear attention replaces growing KV caches with fixed-size recurrent states, yet these persistent states can become a substantial memory bottleneck under concurrent serving. Directly quantizing recurrent states to low precision often leads to severe accuracy degradation, as quantization errors propagate through successive state updates. We discover that the impact of these errors depends on two complementary dimensions: temporally, errors in long-lived memory can persist across many decoding steps; spatially, errors in different key rows affect model outputs differently, while state magnitudes vary substantially along both rows and columns. Motivated by these observations, we propose STEPQuant, a spatial-temporal post-training quantization framework for Delta-rule recurrent states. STEPQuant allocates precision according to error magnitude and memory lifetime, and jointly fits key-row and value-column scales based on state distributions and key-row impact on output error. Experiments on Qwen3.8-27B and Kimi-Linear-48B-A3B-Instruct across both long- and short-generation benchmarks show that STEPQuant closely matches FP32-state accuracy under a nominal 6-bit budget and outperforms uniform INT8 in its 4-bit configuration. Integrated into SGLang with optimized GPU kernels, 6-bit STEPQuant achieves over 5x recurrent-state compression and reduces total serving memory by up to 68.7%. Our code is available at https://github.com/Dreamer-Toby/STEPQuant.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes STEPQuant, a spatial-temporal post-training quantization method for linear-attention recurrent states that achieves strong FP32-level accuracy with much lower memory, particularly under concurrent serving.
AI.motivation: Linear attention models avoid growing KV caches by using fixed-size recurrent states, but in high-concurrency serving these persistent states become a large memory bottleneck. Naively quantizing these states to low precision severely hurts accuracy because quantization errors accumulate over time and affect different parts of the state unequally. There is a need for a quantization scheme that understands how errors propagate temporally and spatially in these recurrent states to compress memory without sacrificing performance.
AI.method: The authors study how quantization errors in linear-attention recurrent states behave along two dimensions: (1) temporal – errors in long-lived memory persist across many decoding steps; and (2) spatial – different key rows and value columns contribute differently to output errors and have varying magnitudes. Based on this, they introduce STEPQuant, a post-training quantization framework tailored to Delta-rule recurrent states. STEPQuant allocates bit precision according to both error magnitude and state lifetime, and jointly optimizes key-row and value-column scaling factors using state distributions and each key row’s impact on output error. The result is a non-uniform, spatial-temporal quantization strategy that adapts precision where it matters most.
AI.result: On Qwen3.8-27B and Kimi-Linear-48B-A3B-Instruct, across both long- and short-text generation benchmarks, STEPQuant with an effective 6-bit precision closely matches FP32-state performance, and a 4-bit configuration outperforms standard uniform INT8 quantization. When integrated into the SGLang serving framework with custom GPU kernels, 6-bit STEPQuant yields more than 5x compression of recurrent states and reduces overall serving memory by up to 68.7%.
AI.conclusion: STEPQuant demonstrates that carefully designed spatial-temporal post-training quantization for linear-attention recurrent states can deliver substantial memory savings, especially in concurrent serving, while maintaining near-FP32 accuracy. By allocating precision based on both error magnitude and memory lifetime and jointly optimizing scales across rows and columns, the method outperforms conventional uniform quantization baselines in both accuracy and memory efficiency.

title: VISTA: Value-Informed Event Appraisal for Multimodal Emotion Conflict
summary: Conflicting emotional cues can be individually valid: a subdued voice may reflect a blocked goal while a smile satisfies a social obligation. Their interpretation depends on what the event means to the person. We introduce VISTA (Value-Informed Semantic Trust Arbitration), a learned seven-field appraisal interface that conditions modality arbitration on concerns, event relations, and expression conditions while retaining a joint-evidence residual. A log-odds decomposition separates emotion expectation from cue diagnosticity, motivating an interface that lets appraisal change how evidence is interpreted. With a shared Qwen2.5-Omni-7B backbone and matched training examples and steps, VISTA reaches 64.5% conflict accuracy on CA-MER, improving on modality gating by 2.5 percentage points on conflict and 0.2 on consistency. Shuffling appraisal across scenes or removing its decision connection reduces this benefit. A common frozen-backbone probe reaches 0.600 macro CCC for appraisal readout, compared with 0.505 for emotion-only fine-tuning. Evaluations across five benchmarks connect recognition under increasing conflict with appraisal readout and downstream decision use. Together, the analyses and experiments support scene-specific appraisal as an intermediate representation that helps interpret conflicting emotional evidence.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes VISTA, an appraisal-based interface that improves interpreting conflicting emotional cues across modalities.
AI.motivation: Emotional cues from different modalities (e.g., voice and facial expression) can conflict yet each be valid because they reflect different underlying concerns or social obligations. Existing systems often rely on simple modality gating or fusion that does not account for the person’s appraisal of the situation, which limits performance especially under cue conflict.
AI.method: The authors introduce VISTA (Value-Informed Semantic Trust Arbitration), a learned seven-field appraisal interface that mediates how different emotional modalities are weighted and interpreted. VISTA uses a log-odds decomposition to separate prior expectations about emotions from the diagnosticity of observed cues, allowing appraisal information (concerns, event relations, expression conditions) to modulate the interpretation of evidence while keeping a joint-evidence residual. They implement VISTA using a shared Qwen2.5-Omni-7B backbone, carefully matching training examples and steps to baseline models. They also perform ablations such as shuffling appraisal across scenes and removing its connection to decisions, and use a frozen-backbone probe to evaluate appraisal readout quality.
AI.result: On the CA-MER benchmark, VISTA achieves 64.5% accuracy on conflict cases, outperforming standard modality gating by 2.5 percentage points on conflict and 0.2 on consistency. When appraisals are shuffled between scenes or their decision connection is removed, this performance advantage diminishes, indicating the importance of scene-specific appraisal. A frozen-backbone probe achieves 0.600 macro concordance correlation coefficient (CCC) for predicting appraisal fields, versus 0.505 for a model fine-tuned only on emotion labels. Across five benchmarks, better performance under higher cue conflict correlates with better appraisal readout and effective use of appraisal in downstream decisions.
AI.conclusion: Scene-specific appraisal, encoded via the VISTA interface, serves as a useful intermediate representation for interpreting conflicting emotional evidence across modalities. By explicitly modeling how a person’s concerns, event relations, and expression conditions shape the meaning of emotional cues, VISTA improves both conflict-case recognition performance and the recoverability of appraisal information, supporting appraisal-based arbitration as a principled way to handle multimodal emotional conflict.

title: Predicting Team Performance from Communications in Simulated Search-and-Rescue
summary: Understanding how individual traits influence team performance is valuable, but these traits are not always directly observable. Prior research has inferred traits like trust from behavioral data. We analyze conversational data to identify team traits and their correlation with teaming outcomes. Using transcripts from a Minecraft-based search-and-rescue experiment, we apply topic modeling and clustering to uncover key interaction patterns. Our findings show that variations in teaming outcomes can be explained through these inferences, with different levels of predictive power derived from individual traits and team dynamics.

AI.tldr: The paper uses conversational data from a Minecraft search-and-rescue experiment to infer team traits via topic modeling and clustering, then relates these traits to team performance.
AI.motivation: To understand how individual and team-level traits that are not directly observable (e.g., trust) can nonetheless be inferred from conversational behavior and used to explain or predict team performance outcomes.
AI.method: Collect conversational transcripts from teams working in a Minecraft-based search-and-rescue task. Apply topic modeling to identify salient themes in conversations and clustering to group similar interaction patterns. Use these inferred traits and dynamics as predictors of teaming outcomes, comparing the predictive power of individual traits versus team-level dynamics.
AI.result: Key interaction patterns (topics and conversational clusters) emerge from the data and correlate with different levels of team performance. Both individual traits inferred from conversation and team interaction dynamics can explain variation in teaming outcomes, though with differing predictive strengths.
AI.conclusion: Conversational data can be mined with topic modeling and clustering to infer latent individual and team traits that meaningfully explain and predict team performance, suggesting a scalable, behavior-based approach to understanding and improving teamwork.

title: Solving Without Stopping: On-Policy Distillation at Small Scale
summary: On-policy distillation, where a student learns from a stronger teacher's feedback on its own outputs, is a common way to pass reasoning to smaller models. We analyze what it transfers at small scale, distilling Qwen3-8B into Qwen3 4B, 1.7B and 0.6B students, in thinking mode (reason at length, then end the reasoning and answer) and, for comparison, in non-thinking mode (no separate reasoning phase). Long reasoning needs two abilities, solving a problem and knowing when it is solved, and we find that distillation transfers the first, but in thinking mode not the second. Solving improves at every size, up to two ceilings, which we measure comprehensively across both modes and all student sizes: a student's single attempt never exceeds what it could already reach in many attempts before training, and the smaller the student, the further it stays below the teacher. Stopping is where the modes part. In non-thinking mode every student keeps stopping; in thinking mode students stop ending their reasoning early in training, and the smaller the student, the less of this ability survives: the teacher signals a stop almost only where a student already ends its reasoning, so distillation teaches no new stops; it only keeps the student's existing stops that land on a right answer, and a weak student has few such stops. The smallest students often reach the right value but do not commit to it: they either rarely mark it or mark it and write past it. Together, these results describe how small students behave under on-policy distillation, and a diagnostic that separates answer marking, correctness and stopping.

AI.tldr: The paper studies what exactly is transferred when using on-policy distillation from a stronger teacher model to smaller student models, especially for long chain-of-thought “thinking mode” reasoning.
AI.motivation: On-policy distillation is widely used to make smaller models inherit the reasoning abilities of larger models, but it is unclear which components of reasoning actually transfer, especially the ability to decide when to stop thinking. The authors want to disentangle the abilities involved in long reasoning—solving the problem vs. knowing when it is solved—and to see how these scale with model size and training mode.
AI.method: They distill a larger Qwen3-8B teacher into smaller Qwen3 students of sizes 4B, 1.7B, and 0.6B. They compare two modes: (1) thinking mode, where the model produces extended reasoning then explicitly ends the reasoning and gives an answer, and (2) non-thinking mode, where there is no separate reasoning phase. They evaluate across many tasks and attempts to measure: (a) problem-solving accuracy, (b) stopping behavior (when the model decides to end reasoning), and (c) the relationship between answer marking, correctness, and stopping. They analyze ceilings such as the best performance a student could reach with multiple attempts before distillation and compare to single-attempt performance after distillation.
AI.result: Distillation reliably improves the students’ ability to solve problems across all sizes, but only up to clear ceilings: a student’s post-distillation single-shot performance never exceeds what it could previously achieve with many attempts, and smaller students stay further below the teacher’s performance. In thinking mode, the ability to know when to stop reasoning largely fails to transfer: during training, students increasingly stop ending their reasoning and tend to write past the correct answer. The smaller the model, the more it loses this stopping ability. The teacher’s stop signals mostly occur at points where students already tended to stop, so distillation adds almost no genuinely new stopping behavior. In non-thinking mode, however, students retain the ability to stop producing outputs. The smallest models often compute the correct value internally but do not reliably mark it as final or end at that point.
AI.conclusion: On-policy distillation from a stronger teacher transfers problem-solving competence but not, in thinking mode, the meta-cognitive skill of deciding when to stop reasoning. Stopping behavior is largely preserved only where the student already tended to stop correctly; weak students lack these good stopping points, so they fail to learn robust stopping from the teacher. The authors propose a diagnostic framework that disentangles answer correctness, explicit answer marking, and stopping decisions, clarifying how smaller models behave and where current distillation methods fall short for long chain-of-thought reasoning.

title: Seek Before You Move: Evidence Seeking for Progress Grounding in Vision-Language Navigation
summary: Vision-Language Navigation (VLN) requires agents to continuously ground task progress from long-horizon instructions and partial egocentric observations. Existing VLM-based navigation agents typically reason only over available observations and may remain confident even when task-relevant evidence is missing. For example, an agent may confidently proceed forward and get lost even though the landmark indicating the next turn lies outside its current field of view. We term this failure mode Progress Myopia: the agent fails to recognize unreliable progress grounding and continues acting on insufficient evidence. To address it, we propose SeekVLN, an evidence-seeking framework that couples semantic progress reasoning with active acquisition of task-relevant observations. SeekVLN is trained in two stages: First, Future-guided Reverse Generation (FRG) uses future expert actions to augment offline expert trajectories with supplementary views and evidence annotations. Supervised fine-tuning on these trajectories establishes a prior for evidence seeking and progress reasoning without additional expert interaction. However, imitation alone does not reveal whether seeking improves subsequent navigation. We therefore introduce Counterfactual Contrastive Policy Optimization (C2PO) for reinforcement fine-tuning. By comparing each evidence-seeking branch with a counterfactual direct-navigation branch from the same state, C2PO uses a contrastive reward to assign credit to seeking decisions based on subsequent navigation benefit. Experiments on simulated benchmarks show that SeekVLN achieves state-of-the-art performance, improving success rate by 12.7% and 7.5% over the base model on R2R-CE and RxR-CE, respectively. Both simulated and real-world evaluations exhibit human-like evidence-seeking behaviors for more reliable progress grounding.

AI.tldr: SeekVLN is a vision-language navigation framework that explicitly seeks missing visual evidence before acting, reducing overconfident but misgrounded decisions and improving navigation success.
AI.motivation: In VLN, agents must follow long natural-language instructions using partial egocentric views. Existing VLM-based agents often over-trust their current observations and keep moving even when crucial instruction-related landmarks are not visible, leading to errors. This phenomenon, called Progress Myopia, arises because agents lack explicit mechanisms to detect insufficient evidence and to actively seek better viewpoints before committing to actions. The paper aims to address this reliability and robustness issue in progress grounding.
AI.method: The authors propose SeekVLN, which integrates semantic progress estimation with active evidence seeking. Training has two stages. (1) Future-guided Reverse Generation (FRG): using future expert actions, they augment expert trajectories with additional viewpoints and explicit evidence annotations that indicate what visual evidence supports instruction progress. Supervised fine-tuning on these enhanced trajectories gives the agent a prior over when and where to seek more evidence. (2) Counterfactual Contrastive Policy Optimization (C2PO): a reinforcement learning stage where, from the same state, the agent considers an evidence-seeking branch vs a direct-navigation branch. A contrastive reward compares the downstream navigation performance of these branches, enabling the agent to learn when evidence seeking is beneficial and giving proper credit assignment to seek actions.
AI.result: On standard VLN benchmarks R2R-CE and RxR-CE, SeekVLN significantly outperforms a strong base model, increasing success rate by 12.7% and 7.5%, respectively. Qualitative analyses in simulation and on real robots show that the learned policy exhibits human-like behaviors such as pausing to look around or moving to vantage points to confirm landmarks before making critical directional choices.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly modeling and learning evidence-seeking behavior mitigates Progress Myopia in VLN agents. By combining offline augmentation with FRG and online contrastive reinforcement learning via C2PO, SeekVLN learns when and how to seek additional observations to better ground instruction progress, yielding more reliable and higher-performing navigation in both simulated and real-world settings.

title: Teaching LLMs to Generate Challenging MILP Instances via Solver Feedback
summary: Generating optimization instances that are both feasible and computationally challenging is crucial for benchmarking solvers and training learning-based optimization algorithms. Existing non-LLM generators rely on seed instances or parameter tuning, resulting in high test-time computational cost, while existing LLM generators lack explicit hardness measures. Recent reinforcement learning methods with verifier feedback evaluate only binary correctness, which is misaligned with generating challenging problems. We note that an optimization solver reports the cost of solving at several stages of its pipeline, and leverage this to design a reward that scores both the solvability and the hardness of generated problems, measured by branch-and-bound nodes and post-cut relaxation gaps. Our key idea is a challenger-solver asymmetric self-play approach, where an LLM challenger generates progressively harder instances and the solver verifies feasibility and hardness, so no seed or training MILP instances are required. We fine-tune Gemma-4-12B and Qwen3.5-4B with GRPO and a size curriculum into OptiScribe-12B and OptiScribe-4B, which generate feasible yet challenging MILP problems from natural language instructions. On capacitated facility location and max-cut, OptiScribe-12B raises median SCIP search nodes by 1.7-5x and post-cut gaps by 1.1-1.7x over its base model and improves the feasibility rate on facility location by 9-19 points, while OptiScribe-4B raises median nodes by up to 15.6x.
