The problems cover a wider difficulty range than public benchmarks of the same size, follow instructions on density and difficulty, and can tune solver settings for families that public libraries lack. These results indicate that optimization-specific rewards, used in self-play mode, can teach LLMs to generate high-difficulty optimization benchmarks. We will release our code and models publicly on acceptance.

AI.tldr: They train LLMs to generate MILP optimization instances that are both feasible and hard, using solver-based rewards and asymmetric self-play between a generator and a solver.
AI.motivation: Benchmarking and training optimization algorithms require instances that are feasible and genuinely challenging. Traditional generators depend on seed instances or manual parameter tuning, which is expensive and inflexible, and recent LLM-based or RL-based methods either lack explicit hardness measures or only check binary correctness. The authors aim to automatically generate a broad range of difficult optimization problems, with explicit control over hardness, without relying on curated training instances.
AI.method: They design an optimization-specific reward that uses rich feedback from a MILP solver, including branch-and-bound node counts and post-cut relaxation gaps, to evaluate both solvability and hardness of generated instances. Using an asymmetric self-play setup, an LLM “challenger” generates instances from natural language instructions, while a solver “verifier” checks feasibility and scores hardness. They fine-tune base LLMs (Gemma-4-12B and Qwen3.5-4B) with GRPO and a size curriculum, producing OptiScribe-12B and OptiScribe-4B, specialized for generating challenging MILPs such as capacitated facility location and max-cut instances.
AI.result: OptiScribe-12B generates instances that are both more feasible and harder than those of the base models: median SCIP search nodes increase by 1.7–5x and post-cut relaxation gaps by 1.1–1.7x, with feasibility on facility location improving by 9–19 percentage points. OptiScribe-4B achieves up to 15.6x more median nodes. The generated instances span a wider difficulty range than public benchmarks of comparable size, respect user instructions on density and difficulty, and can be used to tune solver settings for problem families underrepresented in existing libraries.
AI.conclusion: By incorporating optimization-specific hardness and feasibility rewards into an asymmetric self-play framework, LLMs can be trained to generate high-difficulty, instruction-following MILP benchmark instances without seed problems. This approach yields richer and more challenging benchmarks than standard libraries and suggests a general path for using solver feedback to specialize LLMs as optimization instance generators. The authors plan to publicly release code and models.

title: Pretrain Once, Route Anywhere: Towards a Foundation Model for LLM Routing
summary: Large language model (LLM) routing aims to assign each query to the most suitable model from a heterogeneous candidate pool, improving the quality--efficiency trade-off of LLM inference. Existing routers are typically learned through local fitting: a router is optimized for a particular query workload and candidate pool, and often requires additional supervision or retraining as the routing environment changes. We ask whether LLM routing can instead be approached from a foundation-model perspective, learning a reusable routing capability that generalizes across tasks, candidate models, and deployment conditions. To this end, we introduce RouteFM, which learns to characterize anonymous candidate models from behavioral context and infer their target-specific capabilities, rather than binding routing decisions to fixed model identities or a single environment. Through episodic pretraining across heterogeneous routing environments, this capability can be reused by a frozen router and adapted to new environments through context alone. Experiments demonstrate transfer across changes in domains, modalities, candidate pools, and context budgets, with the largest gains when behavioral evidence is limited. On MMR-Bench, which is excluded from pretraining, RouteFM outperforms the strongest baseline by 2.23 quality points with only eight observations per candidate. These results support moving LLM routing from repeated local fitting toward a pretrain once, route anywhere paradigm. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/LAMDA-Model-Reuse/RouteFM.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes RouteFM, a foundation-model-style router that can generalize LLM routing decisions across tasks, model pools, and deployment settings by learning from behavioral context rather than fixed model identities.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM routing methods are locally trained for specific workloads and model pools, requiring retraining or extra supervision when the environment changes, which limits scalability and reusability. The authors want a general, reusable routing capability that can adapt to new routing environments without retraining, analogous to how foundation models generalize across tasks.
AI.method: They design RouteFM, a routing model that observes behavioral context from anonymous candidate models (e.g., a few example inputs and outputs) and infers their capabilities for a given target query. Instead of binding routing to fixed model IDs, RouteFM episodically pretrains across many heterogeneous routing environments—varying tasks, domains, modalities, candidate sets, and constraints—so it learns to characterize models and select the best one in context. At deployment, the router is frozen and only provided with context samples from the current environment to make routing decisions.
AI.result: In experiments, RouteFM transfers effectively to new routing settings unseen during pretraining, handling shifts in domains, modalities, candidate model pools, and context budgets. It especially improves performance when only a small number of behavioral examples per candidate model are available. On the held-out MMR-Bench benchmark, RouteFM surpasses the strongest baseline by 2.23 quality points using just eight observations per candidate model.
AI.conclusion: LLM routing can be approached as a foundation-model problem: by pretraining a router on diverse episodic routing tasks to infer model capabilities from behavior, one can obtain a frozen router that adapts to new environments via in-context information alone. This reduces the need for repeated local retraining and moves toward a "pretrain once, route anywhere" paradigm for efficient and high-quality LLM inference.

title: Beyond Prompt Count: How Data Shapes Transfer in On-Policy Distillation
summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains students using teacher feedback on their own sampled responses, yet how prompt choice shapes transfer across teacher-student pairs remains poorly understood. We systematically study prompt quantity, source, and selection across RL- and SFT-continuation pairs and cross-model settings. We find that OPD can be highly prompt-efficient: a few prompts can approach large-pool performance, with four DAPO prompts matching the observed mathematics score of 3,840 DeepMath prompts. However, prompt utility is relational rather than intrinsic: changing only the teacher can reverse the relative effectiveness of mathematics and code prompts. To characterize these transfer differences, we analyze parameter and functional changes across prompt supports and model pairs. Functional alignment with the teacher varies across supports and target tasks; in continuation pairs, teacher-aligned prediction changes can coexist with weak parameter alignment. Continued OPD on effective supports can restore performance after unfavorable transfer. Finally, targeted selection does not consistently outperform uniform random sampling, and filtering out a source that performs poorly alone yields no consistent gain across three paired support draws. Overall, our results distinguish prompt efficiency from prompt interchangeability and show that effective data choice depends on the teacher-student pair and target capability, with random sampling providing a competitive baseline in the studied settings.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how different prompt choices affect on-policy distillation (OPD) between teacher and student language models, finding OPD can be very prompt-efficient but that prompt effectiveness depends strongly on the specific teacher-student pair and task.
AI.motivation: On-policy distillation uses teacher feedback on student-generated responses, but it is unclear how the number, domain (e.g., math vs. code), and selection strategy of prompts influence knowledge transfer across different teacher-student model pairs. Understanding this can make distillation more data-efficient and reliable.
AI.method: The authors systematically vary prompt quantity, domain/source (math, code, etc.), and selection strategy (random vs. targeted) across both RL- and SFT-based continuation teacher-student pairs and cross-model OPD setups. They then analyze performance on target tasks, as well as parameter-level and functional changes, to characterize how different prompt supports affect transfer and alignment between teacher and student.
AI.result: They show that OPD can achieve near-best performance with very few prompts (e.g., four DAPO prompts matching performance from 3,840 DeepMath prompts), but the usefulness of a given prompt set is relational: changing only the teacher can reverse which prompt domain is better. They find that functional alignment with the teacher varies by prompt support and task and that strong teacher-aligned prediction changes can occur even with weak parameter alignment. Continued OPD on effective supports can recover from bad transfer. Targeted prompt selection does not reliably beat uniform random sampling, and excluding individually poor-performing sources does not yield consistent gains.
AI.conclusion: Prompt efficiency in OPD does not imply prompts are interchangeable: effective data depends on the specific teacher-student pair and target capability. Random sampling of prompts is a strong baseline, and sophisticated selection or naive filtering of prompt sources does not consistently improve transfer. Understanding relational prompt utility and alignment behavior is key for robust, efficient OPD.

title: Direct Experience World-Model Optimization: Learning the World Beyond Action Imitation
comment: World Action Model; post-deployment training; dexterous manipulation
summary: World-Action Models (WAMs) couple action generation with predictions of how physical interactions unfold. However, current post-deployment learning paradigms typically improve behavior without requiring better world predictions. Especially in dexterous manipulation, small execution errors can compound in high-dimensional action spaces, hindering policy improvement and pushing interactions beyond the world model's training distribution. Motivated by this, we propose Direct Experience World-Model Optimization (DEWO), a post-deployment learning paradigm for WAMs that, alongside action imitation, refines world representations through visual experience to better condition action generation. Specifically, it identifies interaction turning points and learns from successful and failed futures to support classifier-free guidance. An additional value head estimates task progress from video representations and activates guidance when progress stalls during inference. Across five DexJoCo tasks, DEWO improves average success across all three WAM formulations. Ablations show that visual supervision from successful and failed continuations improves both prediction and control beyond action supervision alone. On four real-world tasks across Wuji and Sharpa, 3 x 3 grid evaluations show that two rounds of deployment learning increase success from 51.0% to 71.7% in cells with at least one initial success, a gain of 20.7 percentage points. These findings support continued predictive learning for improving control through deployment experience, making world modeling an active part of WAM adaptation.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces DEWO, a post-deployment learning paradigm that jointly improves world models and action policies for dexterous manipulation by learning from both successful and failed futures in visual interaction data.
AI.motivation: Existing world-action models can generate actions and predict futures, but post-deployment learning mostly optimizes behavior without forcing better world prediction. In dexterous manipulation, small errors in high-dimensional spaces compound and push the system outside the training distribution of the world model, limiting policy improvement. The authors want a way to keep improving the world model itself from deployment experience so that control keeps getting better as the model encounters new situations.
AI.method: They propose Direct Experience World-Model Optimization (DEWO), which augments standard action imitation with targeted world-model training from deployment rollouts. DEWO: (1) detects interaction “turning points” in trajectories; (2) conditions a world-action model on these points and learns from both successful and failed continuations using classifier-free guidance; and (3) adds a value head that estimates task progress from video features. During inference, this value head monitors progress and triggers stronger guidance when progress stalls, effectively steering the policy using improved world predictions.
AI.result: In simulation on five DexJoCo dexterous manipulation tasks and across three different WAM formulations, DEWO increases average success over baselines. Ablation studies show that including visual supervision from both successful and failed futures improves predictive accuracy and control quality more than action-only supervision. On four real robot tasks using Wuji and Sharpa platforms, a 3×3 grid evaluation reveals that two rounds of deployment learning raise success rates from 51.0% to 71.7% in grid cells where there was at least one initial success, a 20.7 percentage point improvement.
AI.conclusion: DEWO demonstrates that explicitly continuing to train the world model from deployment experience—especially using visual feedback from both successes and failures—yields better control performance than optimizing actions alone. This makes the predictive component of world-action models an active participant in adaptation, supporting more robust and effective dexterous manipulation as the system encounters new conditions.

title: Routing Should Pay for Itself: Sparse Supervision for Economical LLM Routing
summary: Large language model (LLM) routing reduces serving cost by assigning each query to an appropriate model while preserving response quality. Learning such a router, however, often requires executing multiple candidate models on historical queries to collect query--model quality feedback, creating a nontrivial supervision cost before deployment. Existing work largely focuses on serving-time efficiency, overlooking whether the resulting savings are sufficient to recover this upfront expenditure. We further observe that routing quality often saturates well before all query--model feedback is collected, suggesting that dense supervision can be economically over-provisioned. We propose SaveRouter, a sparse-supervision routing framework that selectively acquires informative model feedback and shares capability information across related queries, while retaining query-level refinement for fine-grained routing. We evaluate routing by jointly accounting for supervision expenditure and subsequent serving-time savings. Across four routing benchmarks, the main setting uses only about 33--41% of available training feedback while maintaining competitive or better routing quality, and reduces the break-even deployment volume by approximately 1.9--9.5 times compared with the fastest conventional router. Further analysis shows that acquiring more supervision is not always economically preferable: the supervision level that minimizes serving cost can differ from the one that achieves the earliest payback. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/LAMDA-Model-Reuse/SaveRouter.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces SaveRouter, a cost-aware LLM routing framework that learns with sparse supervision to minimize total cost (supervision + serving), achieving similar or better routing quality with much less training feedback and earlier economic break-even.
AI.motivation: LLM routing can cut serving costs by sending queries to cheaper or more suitable models, but training a good router itself is expensive because it needs many query–model evaluations as supervision. Existing work focuses on making routing at serving time efficient, but largely ignores whether the savings during deployment actually compensate for this significant upfront supervision cost. Additionally, empirical behavior suggests that routing performance saturates before full supervision is used, hinting that dense feedback may be wasteful. This motivates a method that strategically reduces supervision while maintaining high routing quality and explicitly accounts for economic trade-offs.
AI.method: The authors propose SaveRouter, a sparse-supervision routing framework. It selectively acquires query–model feedback only where it is expected to be most informative, instead of exhaustively labeling all query–model pairs. SaveRouter shares capability information across related queries so that supervision for some queries can benefit others, yet still preserves query-level refinement to enable fine-grained routing decisions. The method is evaluated under a cost framework that combines the expense of collecting supervision with the downstream serving-time savings from improved routing, and compared with conventional routers that rely on denser supervision.
AI.result: On four LLM routing benchmarks, SaveRouter uses roughly 33–41% of the available training feedback while maintaining competitive or better routing quality than baselines. When economic metrics are considered, it substantially reduces the deployment volume needed to break even on the initial supervision investment, by about 1.9–9.5× relative to the fastest conventional router. Additional analyses show that simply increasing supervision does not always improve economic outcomes: the optimal supervision level for minimizing long-run serving cost can differ from the level that yields the earliest cost payback.
AI.conclusion: Sparse and selective supervision for training LLM routers can substantially reduce total cost without sacrificing quality. SaveRouter demonstrates that by acquiring only informative feedback and sharing capability information across related queries, routers can reach strong performance with much less supervision and achieve earlier economic break-even than conventional approaches. Moreover, optimal supervision should be determined by economic objectives (e.g., minimizing total serving cost or achieving fastest payback), not just by maximizing routing accuracy, implying that future routing methods should be evaluated under explicit cost–benefit criteria.

title: Demistifying Data and Simulator Assumptions in Supervised Causal Discovery
summary: Supervised causal discovery learns to infer causal structure for a new dataset from training datasets paired with structural labels. These training pairs are typically simulated, making the simulator both a source of supervision and a carrier of assumptions about causal graphs, mechanisms, and noise. Understanding the resulting predictions therefore requires examining how these assumptions supplement the information available in observational data, which may be compatible with multiple causal graphs. This paper examines that relationship across representative methods available through June 2026. We organize these methods by prediction target, prediction granularity, encoder, structural decoder, and training regime to relate what each method predicts to how it uses data and simulator-based supervision. Using this framework, we distinguish two questions: whether the target is identifiable under the assumed model class, and whether a trained predictor generalizes beyond its training distribution. Restrictions on mechanisms and noise can make otherwise ambiguous causal directions identifiable, but predictive accuracy under those restrictions does not establish transfer when they change. This distinction motivates evaluation that matches metrics to the identifiable graph target and tests changes in graphs, mechanisms, and noise between training and deployment. Extending such evaluation to real data also requires documenting the external causal evidence and uncertainty behind benchmark reference graphs. Together, these analyses guide method comparison and identify open questions in transfer, test-time adaptation, and uncertainty assessment.

AI.tldr: The paper surveys and systematizes supervised causal discovery methods, focusing on how simulator assumptions and observational data jointly determine what can be learned and transferred to new settings.
AI.motivation: Supervised causal discovery methods rely heavily on simulated training data, whose built‑in assumptions about graph structure, mechanisms, and noise strongly influence predictions on real observational data. Because observational data alone often underdetermines the causal graph, we need a clear framework to understand which parts of a learned predictor come from data and which from simulator assumptions, and when these predictors can be expected to generalize beyond their training distributions.
AI.method: The authors review representative supervised causal discovery approaches available up to June 2026 and categorize them along several axes: (1) prediction target (e.g., full graph, edge directions, or properties), (2) prediction granularity (local vs. global), (3) encoder architecture, (4) structural decoder that maps representations to graph predictions, and (5) training regime, including how simulators generate graph structures, mechanisms, and noise. They then analyze identifiability of the causal targets under the assumed model classes and separate this from empirical generalization behavior when deployment conditions differ from simulation assumptions.
AI.result: Their analysis clarifies that constraints on functional mechanisms and noise (e.g., additive noise models) can render certain causal directions identifiable that would otherwise be ambiguous from observational data alone. However, they show that good predictive performance under these constraints does not imply robustness when the real‑world mechanisms or noise deviate from the simulator’s assumptions. They also delineate which metrics match which identifiable targets and highlight mismatches in some current evaluations.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that meaningful evaluation of supervised causal discovery must (i) align metrics with the actually identifiable causal targets under the modeling assumptions and (ii) explicitly test robustness to distribution shifts in graphs, mechanisms, and noise between training and deployment. For real‑world benchmarks, researchers must carefully document the external evidence and uncertainty supporting reference graphs. These insights provide a basis for comparing methods and point to open problems in transfer, test‑time adaptation, and uncertainty quantification for supervised causal discovery.

title: Commitment Hierarchies under Intent Revision: A Belief-Revision Account of Salvage in Tool-Use Agents
comment: Accepted in the 27th International Conference on Principles and Practice of Multi-Agent Systems
summary: When a user changes their mind partway through a task, an agent that has already split the task into sub-goals and paid for tool calls must decide, per cached sub-result, whether to keep, patch, or discard it (salvage), restarting wastes valid work and continuing unchanged answers the old question. Our main finding is that salvage quality is a matter of role design rather than model capability: a language model asked the keep/patch/discard question one node at a time is unreliable, but asked to classify the revision once, with a deterministic layer propagating the decision, it reaches the cost-optimal oracle on all three models tested, from two vendors. Modeling the plan as a commitment hierarchy and the intent change as a belief-revision operator with AGM style postulates, we prove that no policy observing only a node's local view can be both safe and cost optimal, while the single classification design is both. Across three environments the policy recovers the full achievable savings, 43% cheaper than restart, at 100% correctness.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how AI agents can efficiently reuse partial work when user goals change mid-task, showing that the key is how the agent’s decision-making role is structured, not raw model capability.
AI.motivation: In multi-step tool-using tasks, users often change their minds after the agent has already generated sub-goals and paid for tool calls, creating a salvage problem: deciding which intermediate results to keep, modify, or discard. Naively restarting wastes money and time, while continuing unchanged solves the wrong problem. There is a need for principled, cost-optimal strategies for salvaging partial work under changing user intents.
AI.method: The authors formalize task plans as commitment hierarchies and model user intent changes using a belief-revision operator satisfying AGM-style postulates. They compare two designs for salvage decisions: (1) a local design where the language model independently decides per node whether to keep/patch/discard; and (2) a global design where the model classifies the revision once and a deterministic propagation layer induces per-node actions. They theoretically analyze safety and cost optimality of policies under limited observability and empirically evaluate policies on three environments and three language models from two vendors.
AI.result: They prove that any policy that only sees a node’s local information cannot be both safe (never producing incorrect answers) and cost-optimal. In contrast, the single global classification combined with deterministic propagation is both safe and cost-optimal under their formal model. Empirically, this design matches a cost-optimal oracle across three different environments and three tested models, recovering all achievable savings—making runs 43% cheaper than naive restart—while maintaining 100% correctness.
AI.conclusion: The work concludes that effective salvage in changing-intent tasks is primarily a design problem: by structuring the agent so that the model performs a single global revision classification and delegating per-node salvage actions to a deterministic layer, one can achieve provably safe and cost-optimal reuse of partial work. This architecture consistently realizes the full theoretical savings across models and environments, demonstrating that careful role and system design can overcome apparent limitations of LLM reliability in salvage decisions.

title: Governing the Edge: Automating Commercial Property and Casualty Insurance Underwriting via a Hybrid Local-Cloud Multi-Agent Framework
comment: Accepted at AIxB 2026. 6 pages, 2 figures, 7 tables. Data and Code in github: https://github.com/vsingh45/governing-the-edge
summary: Underwriters in commercial Property and Casualty (P&C) insurance spend 30 to 40% of their time on administrative work rather than risk judgment, and a single submission takes about 40 minutes by hand. We present Governing the Edge, a multi-agent framework for that layer, organized around a data-residency constraint: sensitive submission data must not leave the perimeter. Eleven agents and two deterministic control nodes, one a human-escalation interrupt, form a 13-node LangGraph workflow across two tiers. Agents touching raw submissions run locally on Gemma 2, each bound through a tool interface logging every invocation (synthetic stubs in the current prototype); only anonymized scores and non-identifying fields cross to Claude Sonnet in the cloud. Compliance rules are encoded as conditions on graph edges, so a non-compliant submission never reaches pricing. We walk through one full scenario end to end, a commercial auto submission whose principal driver carries serious violations, showing every agent call, every tool invocation, and the resulting routing decision. The framework processes a 40-minute manual submission in a few minutes on a single edge device, dominated by serialized on-device inference. On the hard-stop violation tier the framework enforces every rule correctly and reproducibly, since hard stops are deterministic predicates over fields extracted at temperature 0; overall compliance accuracy across the 20-scenario benchmark is 70%, with the remaining gap concentrated in softer, judgment-based tiers. It keeps a complete audit trail and respects the privacy boundary throughout. We release all code, compliance rules, tool stubs, and synthetic datasets.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a multi-agent, edge-first workflow to automate underwriting submissions in commercial P&C insurance, enforcing privacy and compliance while cutting processing time from ~40 minutes to a few minutes.
AI.motivation: Underwriters in commercial P&C insurance spend 30–40% of their time on administrative tasks, and each submission can take around 40 minutes manually. This is inefficient and diverts experts from their core task of risk judgment. At the same time, strict privacy and data-residency constraints prevent sending raw submission data to the cloud, and compliance rules must be enforced consistently and auditable. The paper is motivated by the need to automate this administrative layer while respecting privacy boundaries and regulatory compliance.
AI.method: The authors design "Governing the Edge", a 13-node LangGraph-based multi-agent framework deployed in two tiers. Eleven agents and two deterministic control nodes form the workflow. Agents that handle raw, sensitive submission data run locally on an edge device using Gemma 2 models, wrapped via tool interfaces that log every invocation. Only anonymized scores and non-identifying fields are sent to a cloud model (Claude Sonnet). Compliance rules are formalized as conditions on graph edges, ensuring non-compliant submissions never proceed to pricing. The system includes a human-escalation interrupt node and uses temperature-0 extraction for fields that feed hard-stop rules. The paper walks through an end-to-end scenario of a commercial auto submission and evaluates the system on a 20-scenario benchmark.
AI.result: The framework reduces processing time for a submission from about 40 minutes of manual work to a few minutes on a single edge device, with runtime dominated by serialized on-device inference. On the hard-stop violation tier, the system enforces all rules correctly and reproducibly because these are deterministic predicates over deterministically extracted fields. Across a 20-scenario benchmark, overall compliance accuracy is 70%, with misclassifications mainly in softer, judgment-based tiers. The system successfully maintains data-residency constraints and logs a full audit trail of every agent and tool call.
AI.conclusion: The proposed multi-agent, edge-governed framework can significantly accelerate underwriting submission processing while preserving strict privacy boundaries and improving consistency of compliance enforcement. Deterministic, rule-based hard stops are handled reliably, though softer, judgment-based tiers remain a source of error and an avenue for future improvement. By releasing code, rules, tool stubs, and synthetic datasets, the authors aim to enable further research and adaptation of similar governed edge workflows in insurance and other regulated domains.

title: VeriWeave Govern: Evidence-Gated Deterministic Runtime Governance for Enterprise AI Agents
summary: Enterprise artificial-intelligence agents increasingly call tools, modify infrastructure, and process protected data, creating a need to separate action generation from action authorization. This article presents VeriWeave Govern, a deterministic runtime governance layer that evaluates structured agent actions against versioned policies, validates typed evidence, applies fixed deny > review > allow precedence, routes consequential actions to accountable human review, and records replayable tamper-evident audit state. GovernBench evaluates the design over 30 independent seeds and 60,000 oracle-labelled cases spanning five enterprise domains, adversarial evidence, out-of-distribution actions, and temporal policy evolution. VeriWeave achieves 0.9888 mean accuracy, 0.9836 macro-F1, zero observed aggregate false allows, and zero observed Governance Attack Success Rate on the evaluated cases. Six ablations show that evidence gating, deny precedence, out-of-distribution fail-safe behavior, human review, contradiction handling, and temporal replay contribute complementary safety. The deployed API additionally passes 12/12 end-to-end scenarios and a 40,040-request concurrency matrix with zero failures. A separate 150-case EU/Austria regulation-grounded evaluation uses frozen predictions and two independent blinded human annotators, who agree on all decisions. On this set, deterministic engines remain conservative, while a Gemma 4 31B comparator aligns more closely with the human consensus. The results expose a measurable safety--utility trade-off and motivate evidence-aware, replayable governance as an independent control plane for enterprise agent execution.

AI.tldr: Introduces VeriWeave Govern, a deterministic governance layer for enterprise AI agents, plus a benchmark (GovernBench) showing high safety and accuracy with measurable safety–utility trade-offs.
AI.motivation: Enterprise AI agents increasingly perform high-impact actions—calling tools, modifying infrastructure, and handling protected data—so organizations need a robust way to separate what an AI proposes from what is actually authorized and executed. Existing approaches often rely on the same model that generates actions to also self-regulate, leading to opaque, non-deterministic, and hard-to-audit decisions. This motivates a deterministic, auditable control plane that can enforce policies, require evidence, and route risky actions to humans before they affect real systems.
AI.method: The paper designs VeriWeave Govern, a deterministic runtime governance layer that sits between AI agents and their execution environment. It evaluates structured agent actions against explicit, versioned policies; validates typed supporting evidence; enforces a strict deny > review > allow precedence; routes consequential or ambiguous actions to accountable human reviewers; and logs all decisions in a replayable, tamper-evident audit trail. To assess this, the authors build GovernBench, a benchmark of ~60,000 oracle-labelled governance decisions across 5 enterprise domains, including adversarial evidence, out-of-distribution actions, and changing policies over time. They run 30 random seeds, perform six ablations on key design features (evidence gating, deny precedence, OOD fail-safe, human review, contradiction handling, temporal replay), and compare deterministic engines to an LLM-based comparator (Gemma 4 31B) on a separate regulation-grounded evaluation set.
AI.result: On GovernBench, VeriWeave Govern attains 0.9888 mean accuracy and 0.9836 macro-F1, with zero observed aggregate false allows and zero Governance Attack Success Rate in evaluated cases. Ablation experiments show that removing any of the six core design components degrades safety, and that each contributes complementary protective value. In deployment-style tests, the system passes 12/12 end-to-end scenarios and handles a 40,040-request concurrency matrix with no failures. In a separate 150-case EU/Austria regulation-grounded study with frozen predictions and two independent blinded human annotators, the annotators fully agree with each other, deterministic engines behave conservatively relative to them, and a Gemma 4 31B comparator aligns more closely with human consensus.
AI.conclusion: VeriWeave Govern demonstrates that a deterministic, evidence-aware governance layer can reliably mediate enterprise AI agent actions with strong safety guarantees, albeit at the cost of some utility due to conservative behavior. The experiments reveal a quantifiable safety–utility trade-off and support the idea that governance should be implemented as an independent, replayable control plane—separate from the generative model—using versioned policies, evidence validation, and human-in-the-loop review for consequential decisions.

title: CRASM-Gate: Deterministic-First Constraint- and Role-Aware Semantic Mapping with Selective Model Assistance Across Heterogeneous Industrial Standards
summary: Industrial standards often encode the same engineering concept through incompatible hierarchies, identifiers, roles, and structural constraints, so the nearest lexical or embedding match can still be technically inadmissible. This article presents CRASM, a deterministic constraint- and role-aware semantic mapping method, and CRASM-Gate, its selectively model-assisted extension. The framework separates standard-specific canonicalization, bounded retrieval, deterministic rules, destination-versus-origin role interpretation, semantic and structural ranking, ambiguity refusal, and target validation. CRASM-Gate adds a confidence/disagreement gate that may invoke a candidate-constrained large language model, while final authority remains with deterministic validation. A controlled artifact covers six directed industrial-standard pairs, three difficulty levels, and ten configurations, yielding 14,400 sample-level decisions. With a fixed local model endpoint, CRASM-Gate reaches mean F1 0.9938 and an implemented structural-validity rate of 1.0000; deterministic CRASM reaches 0.9931 without generative-model calls; and the model-only baseline reaches 0.5347. Relative to the model-only baseline, CRASM reduces top-1 errors from 670 to 10 while exhibiting 0.0688 s/sample rather than 24.5263 s/sample observed latency. CRASM-Gate improves CRASM by one additional correct decision out of 1,440, with observed latency increasing to 15.7666 s/sample. The results support a deterministic-first interoperability architecture in which model assistance is optional, measurable, candidate-bounded, and unable to bypass structural validation.

AI.tldr: Proposes CRASM and CRASM-Gate, deterministic and selectively LLM-assisted methods for mapping concepts across incompatible industrial standards with near-perfect accuracy and strict structural validity.
AI.motivation: Industrial standards that represent the same engineering concepts use incompatible hierarchies, identifiers, roles, and constraints. Purely lexical or embedding-based matching (including LLMs used naively) often yields mappings that look semantically close but are structurally or technically invalid. There is a need for an interoperability approach that respects roles and constraints, gives deterministic guarantees, and uses models only in a controlled, auditable way.
AI.method: Introduce CRASM, a deterministic pipeline for semantic mapping across standards that: (1) canonicalizes each standard; (2) performs bounded retrieval of candidate targets; (3) applies deterministic rules for mapping; (4) distinguishes destination and origin roles; (5) ranks candidates using semantic and structural criteria; (6) refuses mappings when ambiguous; and (7) validates candidates against target structural constraints. Extend this with CRASM-Gate, which adds a confidence/disagreement gate to optionally query a large language model, but only within a constrained candidate set and with deterministic structural validation as the final authority. Evaluate both on a controlled artifact spanning six directed standard pairs, three difficulty levels, and ten configurations, producing 14,400 mapping decisions.
AI.result: With a fixed local model endpoint, CRASM-Gate achieves a mean F1 score of 0.9938 and 100% implemented structural-validity. Deterministic CRASM attains a similar mean F1 of 0.9931 without any generative-model calls. A model-only baseline performs substantially worse, with mean F1 0.5347. CRASM reduces top-1 errors from 670 to 10 relative to the model-only baseline and lowers latency from 24.5263 s/sample to 0.0688 s/sample. CRASM-Gate yields one additional correct decision out of 1,440 over CRASM but increases latency to 15.7666 s/sample.
AI.conclusion: Deterministic, constraint- and role-aware mapping can nearly eliminate errors and guarantee structural validity when aligning industrial standards, outperforming a model-only baseline in both accuracy and efficiency. LLM assistance is most effective when used as an optional, gated component that operates over bounded candidates and cannot override deterministic structural validation. This supports a deterministic-first architecture for standards interoperability in which generative models are auxiliary, measurable, and tightly controlled.

title: Authority Before Utility: Non-Compensatory Control for Persistent LLM Memory
summary:
Persistent memory creates a control problem that retrieval relevance alone does not solve: a memory can remain highly useful after an update, deletion, or revocation makes it inadmissible for the current answer. We formalize this as a separation between utility and authority. A fixed finite penalty applied to an unnormalized utility score cannot guarantee exclusion under arbitrary positive-affine reparameterization of that score; by contrast, rank-normalized compensation is scale-invariant and therefore forms a stronger empirical comparator.
  Our prospectively frozen TIDE/LongMemEval primary was quarantined before a valid HELDOUT comparison because the materialized TIDE adapter conflated historical age with query-relative inadmissibility and the aligned LongMemEval split left no DEV set for the predeclared penalty selection. We therefore report a post-primary replacement diagnostic on Memora Remembering, where update/delete operations provide item-level forgetting state.
  On Qwen3-8B, DEV selected lambda = 0.6 from a ten-point normalized SOFT family. Across 185 HELDOUT units in 28 dependency clusters, HARD exclusion yields 4.04% balanced construct error versus 19.66% for locked SOFT, a paired difference of 15.61 points with a 20,000-replicate cluster-bootstrap 95% interval of [13.07, 18.76].
  The effect is driven primarily by forgotten-value leakage while current-value recall is preserved. This is same-Q operator-comparison evidence, not a universal claim that scalar control fails, not an evaluation of learned authority inference, and not an independent downstream-harm endpoint.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how to reliably prevent inadmissible memories from influencing answers in long-term memory systems for language models, showing that rank-normalized, hard exclusion works better than simple scalar penalties on utility scores.
AI.motivation: In systems with persistent memory for language models, some stored items may become inadmissible for a given query (e.g., after an update, deletion, or revocation), but still remain highly useful for answering. Simple relevance-based retrieval or adding a fixed penalty to a memory’s utility score can fail to keep such items out under different scalings of the utility function. The authors want a principled, scale-invariant way to enforce authority constraints (what is allowed to be used) separately from utility (what is useful).
AI.method: They formalize the problem as a separation between utility and authority, analyze why a fixed finite penalty on an unnormalized utility score is not robust under arbitrary positive-affine transformations, and propose rank-normalized compensation as a scale-invariant alternative. Empirically, they test control strategies on a benchmark (Memora Remembering) where items can be updated or deleted, giving ground-truth forgetting state. Using Qwen3-8B and a DEV set, they select a rank-normalized SOFT-penalty parameter (lambda=0.6) from a ten-point family, and then compare this to HARD exclusion on HELDOUT units clustered by dependency structure, using cluster bootstrapping to estimate confidence intervals on balanced construct error (combining both leakage of forgotten values and loss of current values).
AI.result: On HELDOUT data (185 units, 28 dependency clusters), HARD exclusion dramatically outperforms the selected SOFT penalty: 4.04% balanced construct error versus 19.66% for locked SOFT, a paired difference of 15.61 percentage points with a bootstrapped 95% confidence interval of [13.07, 18.76]. The main source of improvement is reduced leakage of forgotten values, while preserving recall of current values.
AI.conclusion: Rank-normalized, HARD exclusion provides much stronger and more reliable control over inadmissible memories than scalar SOFT penalties on utility scores, at least in the tested setting. The findings highlight that retrieval relevance alone is insufficient for safe control in long-term memory systems, and that authority must be modeled and enforced separately from utility. However, the authors emphasize that this is an operator-comparison result for one model and task, not a universal proof that scalar control always fails, nor an assessment of learned authority inference or real-world harm reduction.

title: Boundary-State Control for Tool-Using Language-Model Agents: Commit-Time Consistency under State Drift
summary: Tool-using language-model agents can decide that an action is permissible and execute it only after security-relevant state has changed. We study this proposal-to-commit gap and introduce BSC-R, a deterministic effect-boundary mechanism that binds a single-use commit authorization to the exact action and to a semantic projection of the authorization state that justified it. On 2,847 attacked AgentDojo episodes, the boundary kernel preserves the unprotected agent's behavior exactly (80.576% utility; 1.616% attack success). On 10,302 frozen proposals, it accepts every unchanged commit and rejects every instance of ten prospectively specified changed or replayed classes. In an independently generated boundary-drift experiment, full joint binding commits 0/4,403 invalid contexts while retaining 5,899/5,899 valid contexts. A prospective external evaluation on the 3,460-scenario CONTINUITY suite retains all 700 benign cases, prevents 1,200/1,200 represented non-replay invalid effects, handles 160/160 replay lifecycles correctly, and withholds 200/200 ambiguous no-release cases. The broader external suite also exposes the method's limit: across all 2,560 attacks, BSC-R has a 25% invalid-effect commit rate versus 0% for CONTINUITY. The result is therefore a scoped commit-time consistency mechanism, not a universal agent-safety claim.

AI.tldr: Introduces BSC-R, a deterministic commit-time boundary mechanism that ensures actions authorized by a language-model agent remain valid at execution time by binding them to both the action and a semantic summary of the security-relevant state.
AI.motivation: Tool-using language-model agents may decide that an action is permissible and only later execute it, during which time the security-relevant state can change. This proposal-to-commit gap can allow attacks or invalid actions that were not evaluated under the correct context. There is a need for a mechanism that enforces that an action remains justified by the same security-relevant conditions at the time it is actually carried out, without broadly constraining the agent or harming its utility.
AI.method: The paper proposes BSC-R, a deterministic effect-boundary mechanism. When an agent proposes an action, BSC-R associates a single-use commit authorization with: (1) the exact action and (2) a semantic projection of the authorization state (security-relevant context) that justified this action. At commit time, BSC-R checks that both the action and the semantic projection of state match what was authorized, rejecting commits where the state has changed in security-relevant ways or where the action is replayed or altered. The method is empirically evaluated on multiple benchmarks: attacked AgentDojo episodes, frozen proposals, a boundary-drift experiment, and an external CONTINUITY suite that includes benign, invalid-effect, replay, and ambiguous scenarios.
AI.result: On 2,847 attacked AgentDojo episodes, BSC-R preserves the unprotected agent's behavior almost exactly (80.576% utility, 1.616% attack success). On 10,302 frozen proposals, it accepts all unchanged commits and rejects all instances across ten predefined changed or replayed classes. In a boundary-drift experiment, with full joint binding it allows 5,899/5,899 valid contexts while rejecting 0/4,403 invalid contexts. On the 3,460-scenario CONTINUITY suite, it retains all 700 benign cases, blocks 1,200/1,200 represented non-replay invalid effects, handles 160/160 replay lifecycles correctly, and withholds 200/200 ambiguous no-release cases. However, across a broader set of 2,560 attacks, BSC-R still commits 25% invalid effects compared to 0% for CONTINUITY, revealing limitations.
AI.conclusion: BSC-R is an effective scoped mechanism for enforcing commit-time consistency between an action and the security-relevant state that justified it, significantly mitigating certain classes of invalid or adversarial effects without sacrificing much utility. Nevertheless, it is not a complete safety solution: it can still allow some invalid effects in broader settings, so it should be viewed as one component within a larger agent-safety framework rather than a universal defense.

title: Rational Clarification by Assistive Agents via Value-of-Information Reasoning
summary: Users of language-based assistive agents often make ambiguous requests. In response, an assistant can either directly act on its interpretation of the request --- risking misalignment with the user --- or ask a clarifying question. Which option is the most safe and helpful? A common approach is to ask questions that minimize uncertainty about the user's intent until a threshold is reached. However, this neglects the impact of uncertainty reduction on downstream performance, the costs of asking versus acting immediately, and the possibility that users may provide corrections without being asked. To navigate these trade-offs, we introduce Rational Enquiry via Value-of-Information Reasoning (REVOIR). REVOIR makes clarification decisions via inference-time reasoning about the value-of-information of a question, which captures the expected improvement in task reward due to the answer received. In two assistive tasks --- ambiguous question answering (CondAmbigQA) and preference-aligned household task planning (ADAPT) --- we show that REVOIR achieves greater success with fewer questions than approaches based on prompting, chain-of-thought, fine-tuning, or information gain, improving preference satisfaction on ADAPT by 13-15% over a fine-tuned clarification policy while requiring no training and asking five times fewer questions. Furthermore, when the assistant can receive cheap user corrections after acting, REVOIR naturally infers that asking questions is not always efficient, demonstrating the adaptivity of our approach. In contrast, we find that vanilla reasoning agents fail to adaptively clarify user requests, and request fewer clarifications as reasoning effort increases.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes REVOIR, a method for deciding when an AI assistant should ask clarifying questions versus acting immediately, using value-of-information reasoning to improve performance and reduce unnecessary questions.
AI.motivation: Language-based assistants frequently get ambiguous user requests. Existing clarification strategies focus mainly on reducing uncertainty about user intent, ignoring how that uncertainty reduction actually affects task performance, the cost of asking questions, and the potential for users to correct the assistant after it acts. There is a need for a principled decision-making framework that trades off these factors to choose between asking and acting.
AI.method: The authors introduce REVOIR (Rational Enquiry via Value-of-Information Reasoning), an inference-time procedure that evaluates the expected value-of-information (VOI) of asking a candidate clarifying question. VOI is defined as the expected improvement in downstream task reward given the possible answers to that question. Based on this, REVOIR decides whether to ask or to act directly. It is instantiated and evaluated on two assistive tasks: CondAmbigQA (ambiguous question answering) and ADAPT (preference-aligned household task planning).
AI.result: On both CondAmbigQA and ADAPT, REVOIR outperforms prompting-based, chain-of-thought, fine-tuned clarification policies, and information-gain-based strategies. On ADAPT, REVOIR improves preference satisfaction by 13–15% over a fine-tuned clarification policy, while requiring no additional training and asking five times fewer clarification questions. The method remains effective even when compared to stronger reasoning agents that use more computation but lack adaptive clarification behavior.
AI.conclusion: Reasoning about the value-of-information at inference time enables an assistant to adaptively decide when to ask clarifying questions, yielding higher task success with fewer interruptions to the user. REVOIR naturally incorporates costs of questioning and the availability of cheap user corrections, and it outperforms standard uncertainty- or reasoning-based baselines that do not explicitly model this trade-off.

title: SkillGym: Training Skill-Use Agents with Automatic Verifiable Environment Generation
summary: Skills equip LLM agents with professional knowledge and guidance to complete long-horizon and complex tasks. Although skills have been widely adopted in recent agent paradigms and harnesses, how to synthesize reliable training data and how to train agents for skill use remain underexplored. In this work, we propose SkillGym, an automatic pipeline to build verifiable environments, collect trajectories, and train skill-use agents. SkillGym first crawls a large volume of skills from the internet, then keeps those whose workflows can run reproducibly offline. A builder-reviewer pipeline is used to construct difficulty-controlled tasks, spanning four task types, each with a reference solution and an executable verifier. With this pipeline, we build 6.8k environments and collect 19k verified successful trajectories for supervised finetuning. Finetuning on these trajectories improves LLMs of different families and sizes, from 2B to 122B parameters across four skill-use benchmarks; Our Qwen3.5-9B SFT model outperforms the 397B untrained model on two of them. Further analysis shows that training teaches agents to invoke skills, raising the rate of reading the relevant skill from 28% to 96%, and that the gains hold across reasoning structures, extending to task types that form a minority of the training data and to skills held out from training

AI.tldr: SkillGym is an automatic pipeline for building verifiable environments, collecting successful trajectories, and finetuning LLMs to use external skills more reliably.
AI.motivation: LLM agents can call external tools or skills to solve complex, long-horizon tasks, but there is little systematic data or training methodology for teaching models when and how to use these skills reliably. Existing agents often rely on ad‑hoc skill collections and non‑verifiable tasks, which makes evaluation and improvement difficult.
AI.method: SkillGym automatically (1) crawls skill specifications from the internet; (2) filters for skills whose workflows can be executed reproducibly offline; (3) uses a builder–reviewer pipeline to construct difficulty-controlled tasks across four task types, each with a reference solution and executable verifier; (4) runs these environments to collect verified successful trajectories of agents using skills; and (5) performs supervised finetuning of LLMs on these trajectories to teach skill invocation and use.
AI.result: Using this pipeline, the authors create 6.8k verifiable environments and 19k verified successful trajectories. Finetuning a range of LLMs (2B–122B parameters from multiple families) on these trajectories improves performance across four skill-use benchmarks. A 9B SFT model (Qwen3.5-9B) even surpasses an untrained 397B model on two benchmarks. Analysis shows that training dramatically improves the rate at which agents consult relevant skills (from 28% to 96%) and that improvements generalize across reasoning structures, to minority task types, and to skills withheld from training.
AI.conclusion: Systematic, verifier-based data generation plus supervised finetuning on successful skill-use trajectories effectively teaches LLM agents to invoke and use external skills. This yields large performance gains, strong generalization to new skills and task types, and can allow relatively small models to outperform much larger ones on skill-use benchmarks.

title: FOCUS: Training-Free Decision-Preserving Context Compression for LLM Agents
summary: LLM agents accumulate interaction histories that grow linearly with task length, causing quadratic inference cost scaling and performance degradation from attention dilution. Existing context-compression methods learn what to discard offline: by contrastively optimizing guidelines, distilling compressors, or training compression policies. This incurs a substantial cost. Further, the compression policy is learned a priori and is not dynamically conditioned on the evolving test-time trajectories. In this paper we ask a complementary question: Which past interactions causally shape the agent's future decisions? We recast context compression as a causal decision preservation problem over discrete interaction units and introduce FOCUS, a training-free context compression framework that operates entirely at test time. Our method requires no offline data collection or fine-tuning, and is architecture-agnostic, attaching to any closed-API frontier model as a modular compression layer. We evaluate FOCUS on diverse agentic benchmarks including API and tool-calling, QA, web domain and multi-turn dialogue. Our method establishes new state of the art performance, cutting peak context by up to 48% and dependency by 73% while improving task success by up to 8.9 percentage points over uncompressed execution.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes FOCUS, a training-free, test-time context compression framework for LLM agents that preserves causally important interaction history, reducing context size and cost while improving performance.
AI.motivation: LLM agents accumulate long interaction histories as tasks progress, leading to quadratic inference costs due to attention over long contexts and degraded performance from attention dilution. Existing compression methods rely on expensive offline training and static compression policies that do not adapt to the evolving trajectory of an agent’s interaction. There is a need for a more efficient, dynamic, and architecture-agnostic way to decide which past interactions to keep or discard during test time, without additional training costs.
AI.method: The authors reconceptualize context compression as a causal decision preservation problem over discrete interaction units. They introduce FOCUS, a training-free framework that identifies which past interactions causally affect the agent’s future decisions. FOCUS operates entirely at test time, without offline data collection or fine-tuning, and is modular and architecture-agnostic, meaning it can be attached to any closed-API frontier model as a compression layer. It selectively retains only those interaction segments that influence downstream decisions, thereby compressing the context while preserving decision-relevant information.
AI.result: On various agentic benchmarks involving API and tool calling, question answering, web-based tasks, and multi-turn dialogue, FOCUS attains new state-of-the-art performance among context compression methods. It reduces peak context length by up to 48% and dependency by 73%, while simultaneously improving task success rates by as much as 8.9 percentage points compared with running the same agents without any compression.
AI.conclusion: FOCUS demonstrates that test-time, training-free, causality-driven context compression can both reduce computational overhead and improve performance of LLM agents. By treating compression as preserving the causal structure of decisions rather than merely discarding low-salience tokens, the framework offers a practical, model-agnostic solution for scaling LLM agents to long, interactive tasks without costly offline training or architectural changes.

title: How Can Recommendation Feedback Evolve Agent Memory?
summary: Content-generation agents continuously receive impressions, clicks, conversions, and negative feedback from recommendation systems, providing real-world outcome signals for memory evolution. However, these signals are delayed and noisy, confounded by audience composition, placement, and recommendation policies, and may result from the combined influence of multiple memories, making accurate attribution difficult. Existing methods rely primarily on immediate feedback or semantic retrieval and therefore struggle to reliably translate recommendation outcomes into memory fitness. To address this challenge, we propose TIDE (Trajectory-Informed Directed Memory Evolution), an external memory evolution framework driven by delayed recommendation feedback. We further introduce Memory Evolution Gain (MEG), which measures the utility improvement of evolved memory over a no memory baseline on strictly future tasks. TIDE treats memory as a capacity-constrained population of experiences: temporal and semantic credit assignment estimates contextual fitness, while responsibility credit distributes outcome signals according to the memories referenced during generation. These signals are then used to reinforce, crossover, mutate, or evict memories. On an e-commerce membership marketing content-generation agent, TIDE achieves a +7.75-percentage-point MEG in offline temporal replay and significantly improves both unique click-through rate (UCTR) and activation rate in an online A/B test. On a delayed-label benchmark, TIDE achieves the lowest mean absolute error (MAE) and root mean squared error (RMSE) and the highest MEG among the compared methods, demonstrating its effectiveness.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces TIDE, a framework for evolving an external memory of a content-generation agent using delayed recommendation feedback, and shows it improves marketing outcomes and prediction accuracy over baselines.
AI.motivation: Content-generation agents in recommendation systems receive rich real-world feedback (impressions, clicks, conversions, negative signals), but this feedback is delayed, noisy, and confounded by factors like audience composition and recommendation policy. Moreover, outcomes often result from multiple interacting memories, making it hard to assign credit or blame to specific memories. Existing approaches mostly use immediate feedback or semantic retrieval similarity and thus cannot reliably convert long-delayed recommendation outcomes into accurate estimates of memory quality or fitness. The authors want a way to evolve an agent’s external memory so it becomes more useful for future tasks, using realistic delayed feedback from recommendation environments.
AI.method: They propose TIDE (Trajectory-Informed Directed Memory Evolution), which treats the external memory as a capacity-limited population of experience snippets. For each recommendation trajectory, TIDE performs (1) temporal and semantic credit assignment to estimate the contextual fitness of memories, accounting for when and how they were used, and (2) responsibility credit assignment that allocates outcome signals (e.g., clicks, conversions) to the subset of memories actually referenced during content generation. Using these signals, TIDE applies evolutionary operations on the memory population: reinforcing good memories, performing crossover and mutation to create improved variants, and evicting low-fitness memories when capacity is constrained. They also define a new metric, Memory Evolution Gain (MEG), which measures how much using the evolved memory improves performance over a no-memory baseline on strictly future tasks. The method is evaluated on an e-commerce membership marketing content-generation agent and on a delayed-label benchmark, comparing MEG and standard error metrics (MAE, RMSE) against alternative memory update strategies.
AI.result: In offline temporal replay on an e-commerce membership marketing scenario, TIDE improves Memory Evolution Gain by +7.75 percentage points over a no-memory or baseline setup. In an online A/B test, it significantly increases unique click-through rate (UCTR) and activation rate, indicating better user engagement and conversion. On a separate delayed-label benchmark, TIDE achieves the lowest mean absolute error and root mean squared error, and the highest MEG among all compared approaches, showing it both predicts delayed outcomes better and learns more useful memories.
AI.conclusion: TIDE effectively translates delayed, noisy recommendation feedback into directed evolution of an agent’s external memory, leading to improvements in downstream marketing metrics and prediction accuracy. By viewing memory as a capacity-constrained population and using trajectory-informed credit assignment plus evolutionary operations, the framework can identify and amplify high-utility experiences while removing low-value ones. The newly proposed MEG metric provides a principled way to evaluate memory evolution on strictly future tasks. Overall, the method offers a practical approach for long-term, feedback-driven optimization of content-generation agents operating in recommendation environments.

title: KUPAS MASTER: Distilling the Tacit Expertise of Master Practitioners into Agent-Ready Experience Corpora
comment: Technical Report. Official website: https://lsf.kupasai.com/ Report homepage: https://tongjiai4e.github.io/KUPAS-MASTER-Report/
summary: Experienced professionals know more than just facts and conclusions. They know which cues matter, why a judgment is reasonable, and which action to take. Routine work records often leave out this tacit knowledge, making it difficult for Large Language Model (LLM) agents to use professional experience effectively. We introduce KUPAS MASTER, an experience engineering platform built around nine-layer cognitive corpus construction. It turns heterogeneous work records and practitioner interviews into traceable, reusable experience corpora for agents. Six case elements preserve the task process: context, cues, judgment, action, boundaries, and outcomes. Nine-layer cognitive corpus construction organizes tacit experience along nine extraction dimensions and stores the resulting assets in six libraries: rules, constraints, best practices, negative examples, corner cases, and skills. Semantic alignment, individual experience distillation, organizational consolidation, and cross-review preserve source evidence, conditions of use, and unresolved disagreements. The platform packages these assets into callable skills with explicit inputs, steps, dependencies, and stopping conditions, connecting experience collection to task execution and evaluation feedback. Using authorized samples from 20 randomly selected practitioners, the platform processed 1,576 source files into 23,024 individual experience records and 13,113 organizational assets. The evaluation spans multiple professional domains. Under common task inputs and scoring criteria, the base model, raw corpus retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and KUPAS MASTER agent scored 70.63, 79.75, and 89.58, respectively. The KUPAS MASTER agent improved on raw-corpus RAG in all seven scoring dimensions. The platform provides a practical path from individual tacit experience to organizational knowledge and agent capabilities.

AI.tldr: The paper presents KUPAS MASTER, a platform that systematically captures and structures professionals’ tacit experience into reusable, verifiable knowledge assets that significantly improve LLM agent performance over standard RAG.
AI.motivation: Routine work records usually miss practitioners’ tacit know-how—what cues to watch, how to justify judgments, and which actions to take. As a result, LLM agents using such records via standard RAG cannot fully leverage human expertise. The authors aim to engineer a practical pipeline that converts scattered, heterogeneous work artifacts and interviews into structured, traceable experience that agents can reliably use across tasks and domains.
AI.method: They design KUPAS MASTER, an “experience engineering” platform centered on nine-layer cognitive corpus construction. It (1) decomposes tasks into six case elements—context, cues, judgment, action, boundaries, outcomes; (2) extracts knowledge along nine cognitive/extraction dimensions; (3) organizes results into six libraries—rules, constraints, best practices, negative examples, corner cases, skills; (4) applies semantic alignment, individual experience distillation, organizational consolidation, and cross-review to maintain traceability, usage conditions, and unresolved disagreements; and (5) packages the resulting assets into callable skills with explicit inputs, steps, dependencies, and stopping conditions, making them usable by LLM agents and evaluable via feedback loops.
AI.result: Using data from 20 randomly selected practitioners (1,576 source files), the platform produced 23,024 individual experience records and 13,113 organizational assets across multiple professional domains. In comparative evaluation under shared tasks and scoring criteria, performance scores were: base model 70.63, raw-corpus RAG 79.75, and KUPAS MASTER agent 89.58. The KUPAS MASTER agent outperformed raw-corpus RAG on all seven measured dimensions.
AI.conclusion: Systematically engineering tacit professional experience into structured, traceable corpora and callable skills yields substantial gains in LLM agent performance relative to standard RAG. KUPAS MASTER offers an end-to-end, domain-agnostic pipeline that connects individual experience capture to organizational knowledge assets and concrete agent capabilities, while preserving evidence, context, and even disagreements for safer and more reliable deployment.

title: EngiWorld: What Can Frontier Agents Deliver in Professional Engineering Environments?
summary: Autonomous agents have made rapid progress in general-purpose computer use, but reliable automation of professional industrial engineering remains out of reach, as engineering workflows demand reasoning over geometric and physical constraints and dependencies preserved across software and design stages. We present EngiWorld, the first benchmark structured around the complete design loop: 1,301 expert-curated tasks spanning 6 engineering domains (CAD, CAE, CAM, BIM, EDA, and 3D visualization) and 26 professional software platforms, with both GUI and CLI interfaces and 6 task types ranging from software-selection to open-ended tasks. We further introduce an artifact-centric evaluation methodology built on a unified domain-verifier suite, which programmatically checks the geometric validity, physical feasibility, and rule compliance of final and intermediate artifacts, and scores quantitative design tasks continuously by specification attainment rather than binary success. Evaluation of seven frontier models reveals a substantial capability gap: the strongest model achieves an EngiScore of only 44.3, and just 3.6% of multi-software attempts succeed. EngiWorld provides the first rigorous foundation for measuring progress toward agents that operate professional engineering software end to end.

AI.tldr: EngiWorld is a benchmark for testing autonomous agents on realistic, end-to-end professional engineering software workflows, revealing a large capability gap in current models.
AI.motivation: Existing autonomous agents can operate general computer tasks but struggle with real industrial engineering workflows, which require consistent reasoning about geometry, physics, constraints, and cross-software dependencies throughout the full design lifecycle. There is no rigorous, domain-faithful benchmark that covers the complete loop of engineering design across the diverse tools professionals actually use.
AI.method: The authors construct EngiWorld, a benchmark of 1,301 expert-designed tasks covering six major engineering domains (CAD, CAE, CAM, BIM, EDA, and 3D visualization) and 26 professional software platforms with both GUI and CLI interfaces. Tasks span six types, from choosing the right tool to solving open-ended design problems. They create an artifact-centric evaluation framework using a unified domain-verifier suite that programmatically checks geometric validity, physical feasibility, rule/code compliance, and measures continuous specification attainment for design quality, instead of just pass/fail. They then evaluate seven state-of-the-art models on this benchmark.
AI.result: Across seven frontier models, performance is poor relative to expert expectations: the best-performing model achieves an EngiScore of 44.3, and only 3.6% of tasks requiring workflows across multiple software tools are successfully completed. This quantifies a significant gap between current model capabilities and the demands of realistic engineering workflows.
AI.conclusion: EngiWorld offers the first rigorous, artifact-based, end-to-end benchmark focused specifically on professional engineering software use. Results show current autonomous agents are far from reliably handling industrial engineering workflows, especially multi-tool pipelines. The benchmark establishes a standardized way to measure and drive progress toward agents that can operate real-world engineering tools and design loops from start to finish.

title: Context Language Models
summary: We introduce Context Language Models (CLMs), language models that natively manage their own context. We implement this by treating the context as a file and allowing the model to make unrestricted updates to this file. This allows the model to learn what is most important to maintain in context, and naturally extends to multi-agent systems where multiple agent contexts coexist as files. Building CLMs zero-shot with existing models outperforms SOTA context management strategies across a variety of tasks: 11.4% higher accuracy with 21.5% fewer FLOPs on BrowseComp-Plus, 5% higher scores with 59% fewer FLOPs on 12-hour EdgeBench, and 65% greater improvement with the same compute on a 24-hour multi-repository agent-swarm task. Moreover, by shifting context management from external harness control to intrinsic model behavior, CLMs naturally enable both in-context and parametric learning of context-management strategies. We show that CLMs can be steered with natural-language instructions evolved through a standard skill-optimization loop, improving held-out accuracy by up to 35.9 points on a context-management task while reducing compute. We also introduce an online reinforcement learning method for CLMs, improving Qwen3.5-9B performance on BrowseComp-Plus by 47.6% while using 12% fewer FLOPs. Finally, we co-design Suffix Cache Reuse for CLM serving, further reducing server-side compute by 35% relative to standard SGLang at matched performance.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Context Language Models (CLMs), which can manage and edit their own context as a file, leading to more efficient and effective context handling than existing external orchestration methods.
AI.motivation: Standard LLMs rely on external tools or orchestration code to manage context (retrieval, memory, multi-step workflows, multi-agent setups), which is often brittle, compute-inefficient, and not learnable by the model itself. The authors aim to internalize context management within the model so that it can autonomously decide what to store, update, and reuse, improving scalability, robustness, and learnability of long-horizon and multi-agent tasks.
AI.method: They treat the model’s context as a file that the model can freely read and write during interaction. Using existing base models, they build CLMs in a zero-shot way where the model issues file-update operations instead of relying on external controllers. They then: (1) benchmark CLMs on browsing and long-horizon tasks versus state-of-the-art context strategies; (2) optimize natural-language instructions for steering CLM behavior via a skill-optimization loop; (3) apply an online reinforcement learning algorithm specifically for CLMs to improve browsing performance; and (4) co-design a serving optimization called Suffix Cache Reuse that reuses overlapping suffixes in the CLM’s file-based context to cut server compute.
AI.result: Across benchmarks, CLMs using existing models outperform strong external context-management baselines while being more compute-efficient: 11.4% higher accuracy with 21.5% fewer FLOPs on BrowseComp-Plus, 5% higher scores with 59% fewer FLOPs on 12-hour EdgeBench, and 65% greater performance improvement at equal compute on a 24-hour multi-repository multi-agent task. Instruction-optimized CLMs gain up to 35.9 accuracy points on a held-out context-management benchmark while reducing compute. The proposed online RL method boosts Qwen3.5-9B CLM performance on BrowseComp-Plus by 47.6% with 12% fewer FLOPs. Suffix Cache Reuse further cuts server-side compute by 35% compared to standard SGLang at matched model performance.
AI.conclusion: Letting language models directly manage and edit their own context as a file yields better and cheaper context handling than external orchestrators, scales well to long-horizon and multi-agent settings, and supports both in-context and parametric learning of context-management skills. With additional instruction tuning, online RL, and serving-time cache reuse, CLMs significantly improve task performance while reducing compute, suggesting that future LLM systems should integrate context management as an intrinsic capability rather than an external control layer.

title: XU-RS: Explaining Credal Width in Random-Set Language Models
summary: Uncertainty estimates tell us how unsure a model is, but not why. Without knowing which parts of an input influences a model's uncertainty, we cannot tell whether that uncertainty score depends on input features that are relevant for the task. We study this problem in randomset classifiers built using pretrained language models. These classifiers assign probability to individual answers and to groups of answers, producing lower and upper probabilities for each answer; The difference between these probabilities, called credal width, is used to represent epistemic uncertainty about an answer arising from limited training data. We propose XU-RS, a framework that attributes an answer's credal width to the input tokens (words or word pieces) supplied to a language model. XU-RS uses Expected Gradients (a standard feature attribution method) to estimate how input tokens contribute to credal width.
