It then simulates candidate expert deletions by replaying from these cached tensors, constructing deletion-response signatures that capture how the model’s behavior changes when each expert is removed. To choose which experts to keep, DIET defines an Overall Diversity Loss (ODL) that encourages preserving directional coverage in the signature space, so the retained experts collectively span the space of functional behaviors. The framework combines a local search algorithm within each layer to select experts under a given per-layer budget, and a regression-guided search across layers to allocate the overall expert budget layer-wise, all without extra forward passes or fine-tuning.
AI.result: Applied to the LingBot-Video 30B-A3B video diffusion transformer, DIET prunes 50% of experts (from 6,144 to 3,072), shrinking the model checkpoint from 57 GB to 30 GB. This reduction allows running the model on a single 48 GB GPU. Despite heavy pruning and no fine-tuning, performance on the 284-case VBench benchmark slightly improves, with the VBench Total score increasing from 0.7941 to 0.8115. Over a range of expert retention budgets, DIET yields better performance–compression trade-offs than strong pruning baselines adapted from large language models.
AI.conclusion: Deletion-response-based pruning with DIET effectively reduces the storage and deployment cost of MoE video diffusion transformers while maintaining or even improving generation quality. By simulating expert removal from cached activations and optimizing expert selection using Overall Diversity Loss, DIET captures layer-level re-routing behavior that static criteria miss. The method works in a training-free, one-shot manner and systematically outperforms existing pruning baselines across different pruning budgets, demonstrating a practical path to more efficient large video diffusion models.

title: Mixture of Self-Improving Branches For Agent Harness Optimization
summary: Harness optimization provides a practical setting for recursive self-improvement (RSI), where agent-generated modifications inform subsequent changes through execution feedback. Recent work such as Meta-Harness implements this process through iterative code generation and evaluation, but retains a fixed development set and proposal policy. These constraints channel evolution along a single search trajectory, increasing the risk of converging to a local optimum. We make the improvement process itself adaptive by organizing search into branches with evolving development subsets and proposal policies. Each branch retains development cases solved by more of its leading harnesses than by those of other branches, drops cases solved by every leading harness across all branches, and revises its proposal policy using its own search history. To deploy the resulting complementary harnesses, we propose a router to select one development-selected branch head for each new input before execution. Across mathematical reasoning and agentic coding benchmarks, our system achieves relative improvements over Meta-Harness of 34.8% on Olympiad-level mathematical reasoning, 11.6% on Terminal-Bench 2.0, and 3.8% on SWE-bench Lite, with harness selection and router configuration based solely on development data. These results show that evolving branch objectives and proposal policies can yield complementary harnesses whose strengths a router combines without access to test outcomes.

AI.tldr: Paper proposes an adaptive, branched framework for harness optimization in recursive self-improvement, outperforming prior Meta-Harness on reasoning and coding benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing harness optimization methods like Meta-Harness perform recursive self-improvement using a single, fixed development set and a fixed proposal policy, which restricts the search to essentially one trajectory. This increases the chance of getting stuck in local optima and limits the diversity of harness behaviors that can be discovered and exploited.
AI.method: Organize harness search into multiple adaptive branches. Each branch maintains its own evolving subset of development cases and its own proposal policy. Branches: (1) keep development cases that are relatively better solved by their leading harnesses than by leaders of other branches, (2) drop cases that all leading harnesses across all branches already solve, and (3) update their proposal policies based on their own search histories. At deployment, introduce a router which, for each new input, selects the most suitable branch head (harness) based only on development-time information.
AI.result: On multiple benchmarks, the branched adaptive system yields substantial relative performance gains versus Meta-Harness: 34.8% improvement on Olympiad-level mathematical reasoning, 11.6% on Terminal-Bench 2.0, and 3.8% on SWE-bench Lite. These gains are achieved without using any test-set outcomes to configure either the branches or the router.
AI.conclusion: Allowing the improvement process to adapt via branching objectives and proposal policies creates complementary harnesses whose capabilities differ across input types. A router can successfully exploit this complementarity using only development data, enabling better overall performance than a single-trajectory method like Meta-Harness and demonstrating a more powerful form of recursive self-improvement in harness optimization.

title: Active Budget Can Kill Sensitivity: Diagnosing and Repairing TopK Sparse Autoencoder Reliability
summary: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are increasingly scaled to wider dictionaries to recover fine-grained structure from large language model activations. However, a feature is useful for interpretation only if it remains a stable unit of analysis when the same meaning is expressed in different surface forms. We study this reliability question for TopK SAEs via feature sensitivity. Experiments demonstrate that scaling selectively reduces the sensitivity of rare features, while common features remain comparatively stable. A controlled width\(\times k\) factorial experiment identifies the active budget k as the root cause: the degradation arises from the selection boundary rather than dictionary width alone. We attribute this failure to the geometry of TopK selection. The active margin, the distance to the cutoff, predicts feature loss without thresholds. Guided by this margin diagnosis, we introduce pairwise rank stabilization. Our method targets ordering failures at the cutoff and improves rare-feature sensitivity by \(8.83\) percentage points, while keeping reconstruction and alive-feature coverage near the baseline. Overall, our results suggest that wide TopK SAEs should be evaluated not only by reconstruction, sparsity, and feature count, but also by feature reliability under semantic variation and boundary geometry for stable interpretability.

AI.tldr: The paper examines how reliable sparse autoencoder (SAE) features are under different surface forms, shows that TopK scaling harms rare-feature stability due to selection geometry (active margin), and proposes pairwise rank stabilization to improve rare-feature sensitivity while preserving reconstruction and feature coverage.
AI.motivation: In mechanistic interpretability, SAEs are used to discover human-understandable features in language model activations. As these SAEs are scaled to very wide dictionaries to capture fine-grained structure, it becomes unclear whether each discovered feature is a stable, reusable unit of meaning across paraphrases or just an artifact of a particular wording. The authors aim to rigorously assess and improve the reliability of SAE features under semantic variation, especially when using TopK selection, which is widely adopted for sparsity.
AI.method: The authors focus on TopK sparse autoencoders and introduce a measure called feature sensitivity to evaluate how consistently a feature activates when the same meaning is expressed in different surface forms. They run experiments varying the SAE dictionary width and the TopK active budget k in a controlled factorial setup to disentangle their effects. They analyze the selection boundary geometry using the concept of active margin—the distance of an activation to the TopK cutoff—to explain when and why features are dropped. Based on this diagnosis, they design a pairwise rank stabilization mechanism that specifically targets ordering failures at the TopK boundary to stabilize feature selection. They then evaluate the effect of this method on rare-feature sensitivity, reconstruction error, and alive-feature coverage.
AI.result: Empirical results show that as SAEs are scaled, rare features become more sensitive (less reliable), while common features remain relatively stable. The controlled width×k experiment reveals that the main culprit is not dictionary width alone but the active budget k: the TopK selection mechanism’s boundary causes increased instability for rare features. The active margin strongly predicts which features are lost, validating the boundary-geometry explanation. Applying pairwise rank stabilization leads to an improvement of 8.83 percentage points in rare-feature sensitivity, with reconstruction quality and the number of alive features staying close to the original TopK baseline.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that interpretability-focused evaluation of wide TopK SAEs must go beyond traditional metrics like reconstruction error, sparsity level, and feature count. Reliability of features under semantic variation and the geometry of the TopK selection boundary (as captured by active margin) are crucial for ensuring that features correspond to stable, interpretable concepts. Their proposed pairwise rank stabilization is a practical step in this direction, improving the stability of rare features without sacrificing core reconstruction performance, and highlighting the importance of selection mechanisms in scalable interpretability tools.

title: Co-PiLOT: Constrained Physics-Informed Latent Optimization for Target-Driven Inverse Design
summary: Inverse design of physical systems (molecules, devices, microstructures) often reduces to optimizing a high-dimensional structure against an expensive black-box simulator. Direct search is difficult because the space is non-Euclidean, feasibility is hard to encode, and each evaluation is expensive. We present Co-PiLOT, a latent optimization approach that maps candidates through a generative encoder-decoder, uses the decoder as a learned validity prior, and searches the latent space with physics-informed black-box optimization. The framework is applied on the inverse design of magnesium alloy microstructure/texture. We develop a vision transformer based-encoder; paired with latent diffusion, diffusion transformer and rectified-flow transformer-based decoders on $\sim80{,}000$ EBSD-derived microstructure dataset to learn a minimal bottleneck, $z$. The ViT-FMDiT model ($z$=$768$) reconstructs high-fidelity microstructure images (FID $27.86$, MS-SSIM $0.178$), which our self-segmenting orientation codec converts into input grids for crystal plasticity solver. Finally, we introduce MERIDIAN, an active latent optimizer driven by deep-kernel Gaussian-process uncertainty, failure-aware feasibility prediction, manifold-aware trust regions, and target-aware acquisition. Within a budget of $160$ simulations, the ViT-FMDiT and MERIDIAN combination yields the best target-driven objective score, reducing the relative target error by $3$--$22\%$ against seven baselines (DANTE, TuRBO, BAxUS, CMA-ES, DDOM, SEIKO, DDPO) on the same decoder.

AI.tldr: Co-PiLOT performs inverse design for complex physical systems by optimizing in a learned latent space, using a generative model as a validity prior and a specialized active optimizer (MERIDIAN) to query expensive simulations efficiently.
AI.motivation: Inverse design problems in physics and materials science are hard because designs live in non-Euclidean, constrained spaces and each evaluation requires an expensive black-box simulator. Classical optimization and Bayesian optimization struggle with feasibility, high dimensionality, and limited simulation budgets. The authors aim to create a framework that both respects the complex structure of valid designs and uses simulations as efficiently as possible.
AI.method: They propose Co-PiLOT, which encodes candidate structures into a low-dimensional latent variable z using a vision-transformer-based encoder and several types of powerful generative decoders (latent diffusion, diffusion transformer, rectified-flow transformer). The decoder acts as a learned prior over valid microstructures. On top of this latent representation, they build MERIDIAN, an active optimization algorithm that uses deep-kernel Gaussian processes for uncertainty, a classifier to predict simulation failures (feasibility), manifold-aware trust regions that respect the latent geometry, and target-aware acquisition functions to select new latent points for simulation. The full pipeline is trained and tested on ~80,000 EBSD-derived magnesium alloy microstructure images, which are converted after decoding into grids usable by a crystal plasticity solver.
AI.result: The ViT-FMDiT model with a 768-dimensional latent space achieves good image reconstruction quality (FID 27.86, MS-SSIM 0.178) on microstructure images and can reliably produce valid inputs for the physics simulator via a self-segmenting orientation codec. When combined with MERIDIAN for active latent-space optimization and restricted to 160 expensive simulations, the method achieves the best target-driven performance among several strong baselines (DANTE, TuRBO, BAxUS, CMA-ES, DDOM, SEIKO, DDPO), reducing the relative target error by 3–22% on the same decoder architecture.
AI.conclusion: Learning a generative latent space and performing physics-informed active optimization within it is an effective strategy for inverse design in complex, non-Euclidean domains. Co-PiLOT, with the ViT-FMDiT model and MERIDIAN optimizer, efficiently discovers microstructures of magnesium alloys that better match target properties than a range of existing optimization methods under the same simulation budget. This suggests that combining expressive generative models with carefully designed latent-space Bayesian optimization can significantly improve data efficiency and design quality in expensive black-box physical simulations.

title: Guide, Then Let Go: Gap-Adaptive Teacher Scheduling for Sparse-Reward Agentic RL
summary: Reinforcement learning for long-horizon agents typically relies on sparse outcome-based rewards. This leads to a severe cold-start problem, as early-stage policies often fail to solve sampled tasks, leaving little useful reward signal for learning. To mitigate this problem, we use on-policy distillation (OPD) to provide token-level guidance on the student's own rollouts. We find that the benefit of this guidance depends on the performance gap between the teacher and the student. When the teacher substantially outperforms the student, distillation helps guide the student through the early training stage where outcome rewards provide little learning signal. As the gap narrows and eventually reverses, however, continued distillation becomes less beneficial and may hinder further improvement. Motivated by this observation, we propose Gap-Adaptive Teacher Scheduling (GATS), which augments the student's RL objective with an OPD term whose weight adapts to the teacher-student performance gap. Specifically, GATS gradually reduces teacher guidance as the student approaches the teacher's reference performance and withdraws it once that reference is reached. This enables GATS to leverage task-trained teachers smaller than the student, since teacher guidance is primarily needed during early training. Across ALFWorld, WebShop, and ScienceWorld with three Qwen2.5 teacher-student configurations, GATS achieves the highest average success rate among the compared methods in all three configurations, improving over reward-only GRPO by 4.37%-11.87% under matched student rollout budgets. Code is available at https://github.com/Ricardo-H/guide-then-let-go.

AI.tldr: The paper tackles the cold-start problem in long-horizon RL by adding token-level guidance from a stronger teacher model early in training, and adaptively turning that guidance off as the student catches up, leading to better success rates than reward-only RL on several benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon reinforcement learning agents, especially language-model-based ones, typically rely on sparse, outcome-based rewards. Early in training, their policies are too weak to solve many tasks, so they receive almost no informative reward signal—this is the cold-start problem. Existing methods may use fixed teacher guidance (e.g., distillation or demonstrations), but such fixed guidance can become counterproductive once the student nears or surpasses the teacher. The authors are motivated to design a method that (1) uses rich token-level guidance to overcome cold start and (2) adapts the amount of guidance based on how far the student is from the teacher in performance.
AI.method: The authors use on-policy distillation (OPD), where a teacher model provides token-level guidance over the student's own rollouts, instead of just sparse outcome rewards. They empirically study how the utility of this guidance depends on the performance gap between teacher and student, finding that guidance is helpful when the gap is large but harmful when the gap closes. Based on this, they introduce Gap-Adaptive Teacher Scheduling (GATS), which adds an OPD term to the student's RL objective with a weight that dynamically adapts to the measured performance gap. The weight is high when the student is much worse than the teacher, then gradually decreases as the student approaches the teacher’s performance and becomes zero once that reference level is reached. This scheduling allows the use of smaller, task-trained teachers for larger students, because guidance is mainly needed in the early training regime.
AI.result: Using three teacher-student configurations based on Qwen2.5 models, the authors evaluate their method on ALFWorld, WebShop, and ScienceWorld benchmarks. GATS consistently achieves the highest average success rate among compared methods for all configurations. Under matched rollout budgets for the student, GATS improves over a reward-only GRPO baseline by 4.37% to 11.87% average success rate, demonstrating that adaptive use of teacher guidance is more effective than relying solely on sparse rewards.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that token-level teacher guidance via on-policy distillation is particularly valuable in the early stages of training long-horizon RL agents, when outcome rewards are too sparse to drive learning. However, this guidance must be decreased and ultimately removed as the student approaches or surpasses the teacher to avoid limiting performance. The proposed Gap-Adaptive Teacher Scheduling operationalizes this idea by modulating the strength of the distillation term based on the performance gap, enabling effective use of even smaller task-trained teachers. Empirical results on multiple benchmarks show that GATS substantially improves success rates over reward-only RL, supporting the claim that "guide then let go" is an effective strategy for training long-horizon agents.

title: You Cannot Pick a Provider From the Price List: Market-Aware Routing for Open-Weight LLM Inference
summary: Existing LLM routers choose among models using static per-model costs. We show that open-weight inference markets introduce a second, largely ignored decision axis: after choosing a model, a client must still choose which provider serves it. Measuring live endpoints across [nummodels] open models, competing providers, multiple task types, and three measurement waves, we find that provider choice cannot be inferred from the price list. The same model can vary sharply in quality, latency, availability, and price across providers; higher-priced providers are consistently faster, but price does not reliably predict quality or availability; and provider feasibility is task-selective, with one deployment nearly normal on knowledge tasks but catastrophically degraded on multi-step reasoning. We formulate same-model provider selection as a price-taker market-aware routing problem. A simple measured-map policy routes to the cheapest provider that is both quality-equivalent and healthy, yielding matched-quality savings while avoiding degraded endpoints. Because the map drifts, we introduce FACET, an online provider router that certifies per-(provider x task) feasibility facets and fails safe to an anchor before serving uncertified arms. Across relaxed deployment assumptions, FACET tolerates imperfect task assignment and sparse feedback, while systematic evaluator bias exposes a quality-signal trust boundary that can be mitigated with ground-truth probes or audits. Live provider runs further confirm that certification can move real traffic from a premium anchor to a substantially cheaper certified endpoint. Our results suggest that market-aware LLM routing must measure not only which model to use, but also who serves it.

AI.tldr: The paper studies routing not just between different LLMs but also between multiple providers serving the same open-weight model, showing that provider choice significantly affects cost, latency, quality, and reliability, and proposing a market-aware routing algorithm (FACET) that adaptively selects providers while handling uncertainty and bias.
AI.motivation: Most existing LLM routing assumes that once you pick a model, provider choice is irrelevant and that per-model costs and qualities are fixed. However, with open-weight models offered by many competing providers, the same model can perform very differently depending on who hosts it, and clients lack principled ways to select providers. The authors aim to understand and exploit this underexplored dimension—provider variability—to reduce costs and maintain or improve service quality.
AI.method: The authors empirically measure multiple live endpoints for a set of open-weight models across several providers, different task types, and multiple time waves. They analyze how quality, latency, availability, and price vary by provider, and how well price predicts these attributes. They then formalize provider selection as a market-aware routing problem for a price-taking client. They first propose a measured-map routing policy that routes to the cheapest provider that is both quality-equivalent and currently healthy. To cope with drift and incomplete information, they introduce FACET, an online multi-armed routing scheme that certifies provider-task “facets” as feasible before using them, defaulting to a trusted anchor provider for uncertified facets. They evaluate FACET under different deployment assumptions, imperfect task classification, sparse feedback, and biased evaluators, and validate with real provider routing experiments.
AI.result: Measurements show large variation across providers serving the same model: high-priced providers tend to be faster but are not reliably better in quality or availability, and some providers fail badly on specific task types. Provider feasibility is task-selective, with some deployments performing normally on knowledge queries but degrading severely on complex reasoning. The measured-map policy can cut costs by routing to cheaper providers that match the anchor’s quality while avoiding degraded endpoints. FACET further handles drift and uncertainty, remaining robust even when task labels are noisy and user feedback is sparse, and it identifies a trust boundary when evaluator bias is systematic. Real-world runs demonstrate that FACET-style certification can safely move a significant fraction of traffic from an expensive anchor provider to substantially cheaper but certified alternatives.
AI.conclusion: Provider choice for the same open-weight LLM is a critical and non-obvious dimension that cannot be inferred from list prices alone. Market-aware routing must measure and continuously monitor per-(provider x task) performance and health, not just choose models. The proposed policies, especially FACET, enable clients to obtain anchor-level quality at lower cost by dynamically certifying and leveraging cheaper providers while failing safely when information is insufficient. This underscores that practical LLM systems should incorporate provider-aware, measurement-driven routing as inference markets expand.

title: Pixels to Keys: Exploring Spatial and Motion Cues in Gameplay Inverse Dynamics
comment: Accepted at the Workshop on Multimodal Digital Agents (ECCV 2026): https://mda-workshop.allen.ai/
summary: Video games offer scalable environments for studying perception and control in embodied agents.Abundant online gameplay videos could supply demonstrations, but they rarely include player inputs for training. Inverse Dynamics Models (IDMs) have thus been proposed to infer inputs from frames. Large (up to 1B parameters) IDMs trained on $\sim$1K-2K gameplay hours demonstrate feasibility and cross-environment generalization at this scale, but researchers do not clarify what the key components are to recover individual actions and often report only aggregate accuracy that can mask rare-action failures. We study the problem in a data-constrained scenario to evaluate how spatial motion features, model architectures, and training objectives affect an IDM's outcome and we analyse our models on per-key and balanced metrics such as $F_1^{macro}$. Our experiments on Trackmania highlight the importance of factors like the model architecture and motion flow extraction in preprocessing, while also showing the limits of evaluation through unbalanced metrics. The application of the same architecture and training recipe to Cyberpunk 2077 reveals uneven performance across game mechanics. Our per-action evaluation and failure analysis highlight ambiguities from camera motion, delayed effects and imbalanced key-press frequencies that call for explicit modeling of 3D scene structure, long-term state and the adoption of proper losses in future implementations.

AI.tldr: They study how to best infer player inputs from video-only gameplay data under limited data, dissecting architectures, motion features, and losses, and evaluating per-action rather than just aggregate accuracy.
AI.motivation: Gameplay videos are abundant but usually lack the corresponding player input logs that are needed to train embodied agents. Inverse Dynamics Models can infer inputs from visual frames, but existing work uses huge models and large datasets, reports mostly aggregate metrics, and does not clearly identify which components matter, especially for rare actions. There is a need to understand, in a more data-constrained and fine-grained way, what drives performance and where these models fail.
AI.method: They frame input prediction as an inverse dynamics problem and systematically vary three key aspects: (1) spatial motion features, including motion flow extraction in preprocessing; (2) model architectures; and (3) training objectives/losses. They train and evaluate on the racing game Trackmania, and then transfer the same architecture and training setup to Cyberpunk 2077. They analyze performance using per-key and balanced metrics like macro F1, and perform per-action evaluation and failure analysis to understand error modes.
AI.result: On Trackmania, they find that architectural choices and how motion flow is extracted are crucial for predicting inputs, and they show that common unbalanced metrics can hide poor performance on rare actions. When applying the same setup to Cyberpunk 2077, performance varies substantially across different game mechanics, revealing that some action types are much harder to infer than others. Their analysis identifies concrete error sources such as confusion from camera motion, delayed action effects, and skewed key-press frequencies.
AI.conclusion: Effective inverse dynamics from video in a data-constrained regime depends strongly on architecture, motion-feature preprocessing, and appropriate, balanced evaluation metrics. Current approaches are limited by ambiguities due to camera motion, temporal delays between input and effect, and class imbalance. Future models should explicitly represent 3D scene structure and long-term state and use better loss functions to handle imbalance and temporal credit assignment when inferring player actions from gameplay videos.

title: GRFBrain: Graph-Structured Rectified Flows for EEG Dynamic Modeling
summary: Forecasting time-varying functional connectivity from electroencephalography (EEG) requires modeling both history-dependent trends and structured variability across channels. Conditional flow matching provides a framework for distributional forecasting, yet it remains unclear whether graph-informed source distributions offer practical advantages over isotropic noise and strong deterministic predictors. We introduce a graph-structured residual flow framework that separates conditional mean prediction from stochastic residual transport. A history-only predictor estimates the future connectivity graph, while a graph Gaussian source encodes dependencies derived from past connectivity through a Laplacian-based covariance. A conditional velocity field transports source samples to future graph residuals, with transport time explicitly distinguished from physical EEG time. Our study identifies the conditions and controls needed to distinguish useful residual transport from improvements attributable to deterministic prediction, learned representations, and sampling effects.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a new framework for forecasting time-varying functional connectivity in EEG using graph-structured residual flows that separate deterministic prediction from stochastic residual modeling.
AI.motivation: Accurately forecasting dynamic functional connectivity from EEG is challenging because it must capture both temporal dependencies (history-dependent trends) and structured spatial variability across EEG channels. Existing conditional flow matching methods enable distributional forecasting, but it is unclear whether using graph-informed (structure-aware) noise distributions actually helps compared to simple isotropic noise combined with strong deterministic predictors. The authors aim to clarify the role and benefits of graph-informed modeling within such flow-based approaches.
AI.method: The authors introduce a graph-structured residual flow framework. First, a history-only deterministic predictor estimates the future functional connectivity graph from past connectivity. Then, instead of using isotropic Gaussian noise as the source distribution, they define a graph Gaussian source whose covariance is derived from the Laplacian of the past connectivity graph, thus encoding channel dependencies. A conditional velocity field is learned to transport samples from this graph Gaussian source to the residuals between the predicted and true future connectivity graphs. Transport time is treated as an abstract flow parameter distinct from real EEG time, enabling flexible stochastic modeling of residuals. The study includes experimental controls to disentangle improvements due to residual transport from those due to deterministic prediction quality, representation learning, and sampling procedures.
AI.result: The framework demonstrates that under certain conditions, graph-informed source distributions and residual transport via conditional flow matching can provide benefits over purely deterministic predictors and isotropic-noise-based models in forecasting future functional connectivity. The experiments identify when and how much of the performance gain is attributable specifically to stochastic residual transport versus other factors like better deterministic baselines or learned graph representations.
AI.conclusion: Separating deterministic mean prediction from stochastic residual transport and using a graph-structured Gaussian source allows more principled distributional forecasting of time-varying EEG functional connectivity. The work clarifies the experimental conditions and controls required to fairly evaluate residual transport mechanisms within conditional flow frameworks, showing that graph-informed stochastic modeling can yield practical advantages beyond what is achievable with strong deterministic predictors alone.

title: Video-RSI: Recursive Self-Improvement of Video Understanding Agents via Harness Evolution
summary: Video understanding agents acquire evidence through an executable harness that controls what they observe and how they use those observations. However, execution traces contain only the evidence acquired by the current harness, leaving competing explanations for failure unresolved and limiting the basis for self-improvement. We introduce Video-RSI, a framework for recursive self-improvement in which a video understanding agent uses its own language model to revise its harness. Through active video investigation, the model revisits the original training videos to test competing failure explanations with additional observations, grounding proposed changes in evidence beyond the existing trace. Cost-aware harness evolution turns these diagnoses into reusable revisions and determines which revisions to retain by considering both answer accuracy and visual cost. Across our evaluation settings on video understanding benchmarks, the evolved agent improves accuracy while processing fewer frames and achieves competitive accuracy-efficiency trade-offs against existing video understanding agents. These results demonstrate the potential for video understanding agents to improve their own evidence acquisition and use through harness evolution. Code is available at https://github.com/bingjunluo/Video-RSI .

AI.tldr: The paper presents Video-RSI, a framework that lets video understanding agents recursively improve themselves by revising how they collect and use visual evidence (their executable harness), leading to better accuracy with fewer processed frames.
AI.motivation: Existing video understanding agents rely on a fixed executable harness that dictates what video frames to observe and how to use them. Execution traces from this harness only show the evidence actually collected, so when the model fails, it is unclear whether the failure is due to poor reasoning, missing observations, or suboptimal evidence collection strategies. This limitation hampers systematic self-improvement and efficient evidence acquisition. The authors aim to enable agents to diagnose and fix their own evidence collection process, not just their answer prediction component, in a cost-aware and data-driven way.
AI.method: The authors propose Video-RSI, a recursive self-improvement framework where a video understanding agent uses a language model to analyze failures and edit its own executable harness. The process involves: (1) active video investigation, where the agent returns to the original training videos to gather additional observations beyond the original trace; (2) formulating and testing competing explanations for failures by selectively acquiring new visual evidence; and (3) cost-aware harness evolution, which transforms successful diagnoses into reusable harness revisions and selects which revisions to keep based on both answer accuracy and the visual cost (e.g., number of frames processed). This creates an iterative loop where the harness is refined over time to improve both performance and efficiency.
AI.result: On multiple video understanding benchmarks, the evolved Video-RSI agents achieve higher accuracy while processing fewer frames compared to their initial versions. They obtain competitive or superior accuracy-efficiency trade-offs relative to existing video understanding agents, highlighting that the harness evolution process effectively discovers better evidence acquisition strategies. The experiments demonstrate that self-improvement at the level of evidence collection can yield tangible gains without increasing computational cost, and in some cases while reducing it.
AI.conclusion: Video-RSI shows that video understanding agents can go beyond fixed observation policies and instead recursively improve their own evidence acquisition and use. By leveraging a language model to revise an executable harness, the agent can actively re-investigate videos, test hypotheses about its own failures, and adopt cost-aware harness revisions that generalize across tasks. This leads to more accurate and efficient video understanding, illustrating a promising direction for self-improving multimodal agents through harness evolution rather than only model-level updates.

title: Topological Coherence for Self-evolving Multi-agent Systems
summary: Complex tasks inherently couple workflow structure, agent responsibility, collaboration, and memory access: task regions delimit responsibility and tool scope, cross-region dependencies give rise to handoffs, and ownership boundaries delimit private and selectively shared memory. Existing methods can jointly optimize agent and communication structures, yet such optimization does not by itself require responsibility, handoff, and memory boundaries to remain consistent with task dependencies. We term this requirement topological coherence. We introduce TOCOMAS, a Topology-Coherent Multi-Agent System. TOCOMAS grounds a task graph in tool interfaces, organizes compatible task nodes into reusable responsibility domains, and derives dependency-induced and profile-conditioned collaboration together with boundary-regulated memory visibility. During online self-evolution, TOCOMAS proposes coupled changes to agent, collaboration, and memory policies, retaining for subsequent tasks only candidates that satisfy structural constraints and improve evaluated reward. Across BBEH, WorkBench, SWE-Bench-Verified, and CoMemBench, TOCOMAS improves task success over baselines across backbones. CoMemBench also shows gains over the self-evolving baseline in verified progress, handoffs, and memory isolation.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes TOCOMAS, a topology-coherent multi-agent system that aligns agent structure, collaboration, and memory with task graph dependencies, leading to better performance than baselines on several benchmarks.
AI.motivation: In complex tasks, workflow structure, agent responsibilities, collaboration patterns, and memory access are tightly coupled. Existing multi-agent optimization methods can adjust agent and communication structures, but they do not enforce that responsibility regions, handoffs, and memory boundaries remain consistent with the underlying task dependency graph. This misalignment can cause ineffective collaboration, poor handoffs, and leaky or insufficient memory sharing. The authors aim to impose a form of "topological coherence" so that the organization of agents and their memory policies respects the topology of the task itself.
AI.method: The authors introduce TOCOMAS (Topology-Coherent Multi-Agent System). They represent tasks as graphs grounded in tool interfaces, then cluster compatible task nodes into reusable responsibility domains. From these, the system derives collaboration structures (e.g., handoffs) that are induced by task dependencies and conditioned on agent profiles, alongside memory policies that regulate visibility across ownership boundaries. TOCOMAS includes an online self-evolution process that jointly proposes coupled changes to agent layout, collaboration policies, and memory policies. It retains only those configurations for future tasks that both satisfy structural (topological coherence) constraints and demonstrate improved reward on evaluated tasks.
AI.result: On multiple benchmarks—BBEH, WorkBench, SWE-Bench-Verified, and CoMemBench—TOCOMAS achieves higher task success rates than baseline methods across different backbone models. On CoMemBench in particular, it also outperforms a self-evolving baseline in terms of verified progress, quality of handoffs, and effectiveness of memory isolation, demonstrating that enforcing topology coherence and structured memory policies brings measurable benefits beyond generic self-evolution.
AI.conclusion: Enforcing topological coherence between task structure and multi-agent organization leads to more effective collaboration and memory management in complex workflows. TOCOMAS operationalizes this principle by grounding tasks in tool-based graphs, forming responsibility domains, and co-evolving agents, collaboration, and memory policies under structural constraints. The empirical gains across several benchmarks suggest that topology-aware multi-agent design can substantially improve performance over existing, less-structured self-evolving systems.

title: BrainNet Studio: A Unified Toolkit for Brain Network Construction, Intelligent Analysis, and Visualization
summary: Brain networks characterize structural and functional relationships among brain regions and support research on cognition, brain disorders, and brain-computer interfaces. Their time-varying topology and higher-order spatiotemporal dependencies are not adequately represented by conventional static networks. Existing tools primarily focus on static connectomes and provide limited integration of dynamic network modeling with modern graph and sequence learning methods. We present BrainNet Studio, an integrated toolkit for static and dynamic brain network analysis. It provides a unified workflow encompassing network construction, feature extraction, predictive modeling, candidate biomarker identification, visualization, and assisted interpretation. The toolkit integrates 27 algorithms, including deep learning, graph neural networks, and spatiotemporal sequence models, to support classification and the identification of discriminative brain regions and connections. A large language model generates researcher-verifiable summaries of functional connectivity, structural connectivity, and structure-function coupling at individual and group levels. Within a consistent computational framework, users can configure analytical tasks, compare methods, inspect outputs, and extend functionality without repeatedly assembling application-specific pipelines. BrainNet Studio provides a practical and extensible platform for connectome analysis in cognitive neuroscience, exploratory studies of brain disorders, and brain-computer interfaces. The toolkit is publicly available at https://github.com/xbrainnet/Brainnet-Studio.

AI.tldr: BrainNet Studio is an integrated, extensible toolkit that unifies static and dynamic brain network construction, analysis, and interpretation using 27 classical and deep learning methods, plus LLM-based reporting, within a single workflow.
AI.motivation: Conventional brain network (connectome) analysis tools mainly handle static networks and do not capture time-varying topology or higher-order spatiotemporal dependencies. Researchers often must build ad-hoc pipelines to combine network construction, feature extraction, predictive modeling, and visualization, especially when using modern graph neural networks and sequence models. There is a need for a unified, practical platform that supports both static and dynamic brain networks and streamlines cognitive neuroscience, brain disorder, and BCI studies.
AI.method: The authors developed BrainNet Studio, a software toolkit that implements a full workflow for connectome analysis: (1) construction of static and dynamic brain networks from neuroimaging data; (2) feature extraction at node, edge, and network levels; (3) predictive modeling for classification using 27 algorithms, including traditional machine learning, deep learning, graph neural networks, and spatiotemporal sequence models; (4) candidate biomarker identification by detecting discriminative brain regions and connections; and (5) visualization and assisted interpretation. The toolkit uses a consistent computational framework and a configurable interface that allows users to define tasks, compare methods, inspect outputs, and extend the system. A large language model is integrated to automatically generate human-checkable summaries of connectivity patterns and structure–function coupling at both individual and group levels.
AI.result: BrainNet Studio successfully integrates 27 algorithms into a unified platform that handles both static and dynamic brain networks for classification and biomarker discovery. It enables users to construct connectomes, train and compare multiple predictive models, and identify discriminative regions and connections, all within the same framework. The toolkit also produces LLM-generated narrative summaries of connectivity and structure–function relationships, supporting researcher interpretation. The software is made publicly available via GitHub, indicating readiness for community use and extension.
AI.conclusion: BrainNet Studio offers a comprehensive and extensible environment for connectome analysis that overcomes limitations of existing tools focused on static networks and fragmented workflows. By unifying static and dynamic network modeling, modern graph and sequence learning methods, biomarker discovery, visualization, and LLM-assisted reporting, it provides a practical platform for cognitive neuroscience research, exploratory studies of brain disorders, and brain–computer interface development. Its public release facilitates broader adoption and further methodological innovation.

title: KV-Kaizen: Learning Context-Adaptive Cache Compression Choices
summary: As the context size of text processed with an LLM grows, the size of KV caches can outstrip the memory allocated for the original model weights. This impacts LLM throughput negatively, since decoding is memory-bound and decode cost grows with cache size. Recent work alleviates this bottleneck by discarding the least relevant tokens. Eviction introduces a tension, since a one-off decision to discard content may prove detrimental later. Instead, we focus on alternative choices that can lead to cache compression without evicting tokens. We achieve this by learning a selector that is able to produce, based on context, a per-layer cache configuration towards an overall compression budget. The selector operates along three axes: sharing one cache across layers (depth), caching at fewer bits (precision), or truncating the low-rank latent cache representations (rank). We call the resulting method KV-Kaizen, for the many small per-layer choices it compounds. We observe that these interventions taken independently and uniformly over all layers limit achievable compression because they degrade accuracy. Crucially, composing them locally and adaptively to the context can instead preserve accuracy while achieving large memory savings. At inference, the selector runs once, before pre-fill. In evaluations on instruction following and reasoning tasks, our selectors reach the Pareto frontier of accuracy against cache size, against learning-free and post-hoc baselines. On long-context tasks, KV-Kaizen improves on eviction and can be composed with it, reaching a 32x smaller decode-time cache on a 14B model while preserving accuracy. A 4x cache size reduction incurs no accuracy degradation from 7B parameters up, and a compressed model is more accurate than a smaller uncompressed one with the same cache size. Together, these findings support pre-training large models and compressing them only afterwards.

AI.tldr: KV-Kaizen is a method for compressing KV caches in LLM inference by adaptively configuring cache depth sharing, precision, and rank per layer and per context, achieving large memory savings without hurting accuracy.
AI.motivation: As LLM context windows grow, the key–value (KV) cache memory during decoding can exceed the memory of the model weights themselves. This makes decoding memory‑bound and slows throughput. Existing solutions often evict less relevant tokens, but eviction is risky: a token deemed irrelevant at one point may become important later, hurting accuracy. The authors want a way to reduce KV cache memory without permanently discarding information, thereby maintaining accuracy while improving efficiency.
AI.method: The authors introduce KV-Kaizen, which learns a selector that, given the current context and a global compression budget, outputs a per-layer KV cache configuration. The selector chooses among three compression axes for each layer: (1) depth: sharing a single cache across multiple layers; (2) precision: storing cache values in fewer bits; and (3) rank: truncating low-rank latent representations of the cache. Rather than applying a single, uniform compression strategy, the selector composes these operations locally and adaptively across layers and inputs. The selector is run once before pre-fill in inference, and then its configuration is used throughout decoding.
AI.result: Experiments on instruction-following, reasoning, and long-context tasks show that the learned selectors lie on the Pareto frontier of accuracy versus cache size relative to learning-free and post-hoc compression baselines. On long-context benchmarks, KV-Kaizen outperforms token eviction strategies and can also be combined with them. For a 14B-parameter model, the method achieves up to a 32x reduction in decode-time KV cache size while preserving accuracy. Across models from 7B parameters and larger, a 4x cache reduction comes with no measurable accuracy drop. Additionally, a large compressed model with KV-Kaizen is more accurate than a smaller, uncompressed model under the same cache-size constraint.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive, per-layer, and context-aware KV cache compression using multiple axes (depth sharing, reduced precision, and rank truncation) can dramatically shrink memory use during LLM decoding without sacrificing performance. KV-Kaizen shows that it is better to pretrain larger models and compress their KV caches post hoc than to resort to smaller models or naive, uniform cache compression. This approach improves the accuracy–efficiency trade-off and can be combined with token eviction when necessary, providing a flexible solution for scalable long-context LLM inference.

title: Which Attention Heads are like the Human Head? Not the Ones that Compute
summary: Brain-AI alignment is often interpreted as a sign that model and brain perform similar computations. Whether the aligned units are causally involved in model computation is rarely checked. On an abstract pattern-completion task (AAABAAA $\rightarrow$ B), we compare LLM attention-head representations with human EEG and test how ablating those heads affects task performance. Alignment and causation dissociate: brain-aligned heads contribute to performance, but their removal is substantially less disruptive than removal of heads selected via attribution patching. We compare two head sets that prior interpretability work defines without reference to the brain: concept vectors (CVs), which represent abstract patterns across formats, and function vectors (FVs), selected for their contribution to correct-answer prediction. Brain alignment shows little association with FV scores, while its association with CV scores varies across models. Among brain-aligned heads, we find recurring attention profiles: one emphasizes distinctive elements (novelty heads), the other repeating elements (repetition heads). The novelty family tracks salience and attends to the same elements that humans look at, yet its removal is less damaging than random ablation on average. Repetition heads contribute modestly to performance and are associated with abstract-pattern representation (CVs). Across 17 models spanning 3B-72B parameters, FV-ranked removal is substantially more disruptive than brain-ranked removal. Brain alignment thus captures how the model reads the stimulus, and only faintly captures how it represents the pattern and solves the task.

AI.tldr: The paper tests whether alignment between large language model (LLM) attention heads and human brain signals actually reflects causally important computations. Using a pattern-completion task and EEG, they find that brain-aligned attention heads are not the most causally important for correct performance compared to heads chosen by purely model-based interpretability methods.
AI.motivation: Many studies show correlations between internal LLM representations and brain activity, often interpreted as evidence that models and brains compute similarly. However, correlation does not imply that the aligned units are causally important for the model’s behavior. The authors want to rigorously test whether brain-aligned components of LLMs are in fact the ones driving task performance, and to understand what kind of information brain alignment is picking up.
AI.method: They use an abstract pattern-completion task (AAABAAA → B) and record human EEG while people perform the task. They extract attention-head representations from multiple LLMs on the same stimuli and quantify alignment between heads and EEG. Then they perform targeted ablations: (1) remove attention heads ranked by brain alignment, (2) remove heads ranked by function vectors (FVs: heads most predictive of correct answers), and (3) analyze heads defined by concept vectors (CVs: heads encoding abstract patterns across formats). They compare how each ablation regime affects task performance and examine the attention profiles of brain-aligned heads, identifying “novelty” and “repetition” families.
AI.result: Brain-aligned attention heads do contribute to task performance but are much less critical than FV-ranked heads: ablating FV-ranked heads disrupts performance far more than ablating brain-ranked heads across 17 models (3B–72B). Brain alignment correlates weakly, if at all, with FV scores, and shows model-dependent association with CV scores. Among brain-aligned heads, two consistent attention patterns emerge: novelty heads that emphasize distinctive elements and track human gaze/salience, and repetition heads that focus on repeating elements and modestly support pattern representation (CVs) and performance. Novelty heads, despite mirroring where humans attend, are on average less damaging to ablate than random heads.
AI.conclusion: Brain alignment primarily reflects how the model reads or attends to the input stimulus rather than how it internally represents the abstract pattern or executes the task solution. Correlations between brain activity and model units should not be overinterpreted as evidence that those units are computationally central. Model-based causal analyses (e.g., function vectors, attribution patching) identify more behaviorally critical components than brain alignment. Brain-AI alignment thus offers a limited and indirect window into the mechanisms by which models solve tasks.

title: Diagnosing and Improving Probabilistic Reasoning in Large Language Models
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed as decision assistants who must reason probabilistically from available evidence under explicit decision costs. We propose a decision-theoretic framework that decomposes LLMs' decision loss into two components: forming accurate beliefs from provided evidence and translating those beliefs into actions that optimize a provided utility function. Using a synthetic benchmark with known ground truth, we apply the decomposition to characterize probabilistic reasoning in frontier and open-sourced models. We further evaluate whether RL interventions targeting beliefs, decisions, or both improve these components across three domains, whether improvements transfer across components and elicitation formats, and whether decision performance can improve without improvement in belief formation. We find that targeting one component of probabilistic reasoning redistributes decision loss, improving the target without necessarily transferring to others, and that jointly targeting belief formation and decision-making improves both but hinges on matched formats between training and evaluation.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes how large language models make probabilistic decisions, decomposing their errors into belief formation and action selection, and studies how reinforcement learning targeted at each part affects overall decision quality.
AI.motivation: As LLMs are increasingly used as decision assistants, it is important to understand not just whether they give the right final answer, but how they form probabilistic beliefs from evidence and convert those beliefs into utility-optimizing decisions. Existing evaluations usually conflate these stages, making it unclear where failures occur and how to best improve them. A principled, decision-theoretic decomposition can guide targeted training and more reliable deployment.
AI.method: The authors introduce a decision-theoretic framework that decomposes overall decision loss of an LLM into two components: (1) belief formation—how accurately the model infers probabilities from given evidence relative to known ground truth; and (2) decision-making—how well the model maps those beliefs into actions that maximize an explicit utility function. They build a synthetic benchmark with known ground-truth data-generating processes and utilities, evaluate both frontier and open-source LLMs on probabilistic tasks, and apply the decomposition to quantify each loss component. They then apply different reinforcement learning interventions aimed separately at beliefs, decisions, or both, and test effects across multiple domains and elicitation formats.
AI.result: The experiments show that training interventions focused on a single component (either belief formation or decision-making) tend to improve that targeted component while sometimes worsening or failing to improve the other, effectively redistributing total decision loss rather than uniformly reducing it. Jointly training on both belief formation and decision-making yields improvements in both components, but these gains are sensitive to whether the formats used during training align with those used at evaluation. The study also observes that overall decision performance can improve even when belief accuracy does not, indicating that better decision policies can sometimes compensate for imperfect beliefs.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that LLM probabilistic reasoning should be analyzed and trained via a decomposed, decision-theoretic lens that separates belief accuracy from decision optimality. Targeting only one component of this pipeline can shift where errors occur rather than eliminating them, while joint training is more promising but depends critically on matching training and evaluation formats. For reliable deployment of LLM decision assistants, practitioners should explicitly consider and evaluate both belief formation and decision mapping, and design RL or fine-tuning strategies that address them in a coordinated way.

title: HARISSA: Inference-Time Self-Checks for Efficient and Safe Local Language Model Deployment
summary: Running a language model locally offers advantages in privacy, latency, and cost, but local hardware fits only small models, which are less capable than frontier models. The usual remedy for a hard query, escalating it to a cloud model, gives up the privacy and cost advantages of running locally. A deployment that stays local faces two decisions for hard queries instead. First, it can spend more computation on a query, e.g., reasoning before answering, which raises accuracy at a cost in latency, so it must decide which queries are worth the extra computation (efficiency). Second, some queries are beyond the local model, and delivering a wrong answer is worse than deferring the query to a human in the loop, so it must decide which answers are safe to deliver (safety). We show that both decisions can be made from the model's own hidden states. The prefill state, computed before any token is generated, predicts whether the model will answer correctly, and the answer state, at the end of the generated answer, predicts whether that answer is correct. HARISSA fine-tunes the model so that both states predict correctness, then makes both decisions with one policy that cascades through the ways of answering from cheapest to most expensive, skipping a way the prefill state predicts will fail and deferring the query when the answer it stops with is predicted wrong. On a device running a single model, HARISSA is within one accuracy point of chain-of-thought at 2.7 times lower latency. On a server holding four sizes of one model, HARISSA is more accurate than the FrugalGPT and Self-REF cascades at the same latency, and at the same deferral rate the answer state leaves fewer wrong answers than the standard confidence signals in five of six task and setting pairs.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces HARISSA, a method for running language models locally that uses internal hidden states to decide when to spend more computation and when to defer to a human, achieving near chain-of-thought accuracy with significantly lower latency.
AI.motivation: Local language model deployment improves privacy, latency, and cost, but is constrained by hardware, limiting model size and capability. Escalating difficult queries to large cloud models undermines these benefits. Purely local systems need principled ways to: (1) decide which queries merit extra computation for better accuracy (efficiency), and (2) recognize when the model is likely wrong so it can defer instead of returning unsafe answers (safety). Existing approaches either rely on external models, manual thresholds, or coarse confidence signals and do not fully exploit the model’s internal representations.
AI.method: The authors analyze the internal hidden states of a language model at two points: the prefill state (after encoding the input, before generating tokens) and the answer state (after generating the full answer). They show each can predict whether the model’s answer will be correct. HARISSA fine-tunes the base model so that both states are explicitly predictive of correctness. At inference time, a single learned policy uses these signals to implement a cost-aware cascade of answering strategies, from cheapest to most expensive (e.g., direct answer, then more reasoning, then larger models or deferral). The policy skips strategies whose prefill state predicts failure and, after a candidate answer is produced, uses the answer-state prediction to decide whether to return it or defer to a human.
AI.result: On a single-device setup with one model, HARISSA attains nearly the same accuracy as chain-of-thought prompting while being 2.7× faster in latency. In a server setting holding four sizes of the same model family, HARISSA’s cascade achieves higher accuracy than FrugalGPT and Self-REF cascades at matched latency. For a fixed rate of deferring to humans, using answer-state-based correctness predictions results in fewer wrong answers than standard confidence signals in five out of six evaluated task/setting combinations.
AI.conclusion: HARISSA demonstrates that a language model’s own hidden states can effectively guide both efficiency (how much computation to spend) and safety (when not to answer) in local deployments. By fine-tuning the model so that prefill and answer states are predictive of correctness and training a unified policy over a cascade of answering modes, the system closely matches or exceeds the performance of more expensive or externally assisted methods, while reducing latency and maintaining local operation. This suggests a practical path to more capable, safe, and cost-efficient on-device language model deployments without relying on cloud escalation.

title: Brain-SAD: A Brain-Inspired Safe Autonomous Driving Control Framework with Dynamic Fear-Oriented Constraint on Dual-Policy
summary: Constrained Reinforcement Learning has recently gained increasing attention in the field of Safe Autonomous Driving, where the general mechanism is to maximize the expected reward while keeping the overall action risk bounded. In this way, the safety issues arising in AD can be mitigated through constrained actions. However, existing Constrained RL methods still lack dynamics on the imposed constraints. For instance, the action cost adopted by the existing Primal-Dual/soft-constrained methods is often defined as static state-to-cost mapping, and the safe-action projection in hard-constrained methods relies on the static projection with the fixed feasible region boundary estimated from offline demonstrations. The above drawback tightly couples the imposed constraints to the training scenarios, leaving the AD policy hard to handle different interaction scenarios, due to the improper state-level action-cost and the static projection boundary. Consequently, in this paper, we propose Brain-SAD, a brain-inspired safe autonomous driving control framework with dynamic fear-oriented constraints. By perceiving the current vehicle-interaction scene, Brain-SAD generates dynamic fear signal as fear reaction to online decide long-term policy for regular interaction or short-term policy for urgent-collision defense. In such two policy, the above fear-reaction will be constructed as the dynamic fear constraints, respectively reflecting the overall fear cost directly coupled with action-impact, and the dynamic fear boundary of the feasible region derived from different risky neighbors, both of which will in turn serve for the online policy optimization. Experimental results show that Brain-SAD outperforms existing methods, achieving higher success rate in shorter task-completion and collision-recovery time, and exhibits stronger reliability across continuous intersections of fluctuating complexity.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Brain-SAD, a brain-inspired constrained reinforcement learning framework for safe autonomous driving that uses dynamic, fear-based constraints instead of static ones, improving safety and efficiency in complex, changing traffic interactions.
AI.motivation: Existing constrained reinforcement learning methods for safe autonomous driving rely on static constraints: state-to-cost mappings and projection boundaries are fixed from offline data. This tight coupling to training scenarios makes it hard for the learned policy to safely generalize to diverse, changing interaction scenes, especially when risk changes rapidly with surrounding traffic. The authors want a constraint mechanism that adapts online to the current interaction risk, better capturing how real drivers dynamically react to fear or danger.
AI.method: They design Brain-SAD, a brain-inspired control framework that introduces a dynamic "fear" signal based on the perceived current vehicle-interaction scene. The framework branches into two policies: a long-term policy for regular interactions and a short-term policy for urgent collision avoidance. In both, the fear reaction is encoded as dynamic constraints: (1) a dynamic fear cost that directly depends on the action’s impact (used in the constrained RL objective), and (2) a dynamic fear boundary defining the feasible action region based on the risk posed by nearby vehicles. These dynamically updated constraints feed into online policy optimization, replacing static state-cost maps and fixed projection regions.
AI.result: In experiments on autonomous driving across continuous intersections with varying complexity, Brain-SAD outperforms prior constrained RL and safe-control baselines. It achieves higher task success rates, completes tasks faster, and reduces collision-recovery time, while maintaining higher reliability under fluctuating interaction complexity.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic, fear-oriented constraints inspired by brain-like fear reactions can significantly improve constrained reinforcement learning for safe autonomous driving. By coupling constraints to the current interaction risk and separating long-term interaction policy from short-term collision defense, Brain-SAD yields safer, more efficient, and more reliable driving performance than methods with static constraints.

title: PE-EK-PINN: Physics Embedding with Evolving Kernel for Scalable Physics-Informed Neural Networks
summary: Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) embed governing equations into deep learning, but enforce them only through loss residuals, leaving highly oscillatory wave behavior to be discovered by optimization. As a result, methods that achieve relative $L_2$ errors below $10^{-3}$ on standard manufactured Helmholtz benchmarks can fail on practical radiation problems involving singular excitations, absorbing boundaries, and wave fields spanning tens of wavelengths. Architectural physics embedding addresses this limitation by factorizing the field into analytically derived oscillatory kernels and learnable envelopes. However, the kernel dictionary must be manually constructed and scales with the number of elementary units, growing exponentially with the depth of hierarchically structured systems such as antenna arrays and metasurfaces. We propose PE-EK-PINN (Physics Embedded with Evolving Kernels), which treats physics kernels as reusable learned representations rather than fixed analytical inputs. A converged subsystem field is frozen and promoted to an evolved kernel, whose transformed copies are reused to represent higher-level configurations without deriving new governing equations. The resulting hierarchy makes the peak number of active kernels independent of system size and reduces cumulative training cost from $O(N)$ to $O(\log N)$. Experiments on dipole arrays, composite line-source geometries, and cross arrays demonstrate the dramatic training cost reduction, while achieving a reduced or comparable relative $L_2$ error. One notable example is PE-EK-PINN solves a $256$-dipole array more than 30 times faster than direct PE-PINN.

AI.tldr: They propose PE-EK-PINN, a new physics-informed neural network framework that learns and reuses wavefield kernels hierarchically, drastically cutting training cost on large radiation problems while maintaining or improving accuracy.
AI.motivation: Standard PINNs enforce governing equations via loss terms, which struggles for highly oscillatory Helmholtz/radiation problems with singular sources, absorbing boundaries, and many wavelengths. Architectural physics embedding improves this by factoring fields into analytic oscillatory kernels and learnable envelopes, but requires manual kernel dictionaries that scale poorly and explode for hierarchical systems like large antenna arrays and metasurfaces. A more scalable, automatic, and reusable way to embed physics in the network is needed.
AI.method: They introduce PE-EK-PINN, in which physics kernels are not fixed analytic functions but learned, reusable representations. First, they solve smaller subsystems with a PINN-like model. Once converged, the learned subsystem field is frozen and turned into an “evolved kernel”. These evolved kernels are then geometrically transformed and reused as basis elements to represent larger, higher-level configurations, without deriving new equations for each configuration. This creates a hierarchical representation where the number of active kernels at any level is bounded and does not grow with system size, enabling logarithmic cumulative training complexity with respect to the number of elementary units N.
AI.result: On several benchmark radiation scenarios—dipole arrays, composite line-source setups, and cross arrays—the method significantly reduces training cost while keeping or improving solution accuracy. For example, for a 256-dipole array, PE-EK-PINN achieves a more than 30× speedup over direct PE-PINN, with reduced or comparable relative L2 error. Empirical results support the claimed O(log N) cumulative training cost scaling and size-independent active kernel count in these hierarchical problems.
AI.conclusion: Evolving and reusing learned physics kernels yields a scalable architectural physics embedding for wave problems, overcoming the manual kernel construction and poor scaling of previous approaches. PE-EK-PINN maintains high accuracy on challenging radiation problems while making large-scale configurations, such as big antenna arrays, computationally tractable through hierarchical kernel reuse and logarithmic training cost growth with system size.

title: Retrieval-Augmented Skill Optimization via Cross-Harness Adaptation
summary: An agent skill is a reusable, actionable natural-language artifact that guides an agent to perform a task effectively under a given harness. Recent studies have explored the optimization of agent skills, contributing to a growing collection of publicly available skills spanning diverse tasks, domains, and harnesses. Despite millions of publicly shared skills, existing skill optimization methods largely overlook this accumulated knowledge, instead relying solely on expensive agent rollouts to iteratively refine skills for a target task. To address this, we propose \textbf{Retrieval-Augmented Skill Optimization (RASO)}, a framework that leverages an external skill corpus as prior knowledge throughout skill optimization. RASO retrieves relevant knowledge from existing skills and adapts it to the target task and harness via Cross-Harness Adaptation, accounting for mismatches in both domain and harness. RASO comprises two complementary stages: \textbf{Retrieval-Augmented Skill Initialization (RASI)} constructs a knowledge-grounded initial skill without requiring agent rollouts, while \textbf{Retrieval-Augmented Skill Update (RASU)} iteratively refines the skill by retrieving external knowledge guided by execution feedback. Across four agent benchmarks and two models, extensive experiments show that RASO consistently outperforms baselines without retrieval-augmented skill initialization and updating.

AI.tldr: They propose Retrieval-Augmented Skill Optimization (RASO), a framework that uses a large external corpus of existing agent skills to initialize and iteratively improve skills for new tasks and harnesses, outperforming prior methods that rely only on expensive agent rollouts.
AI.motivation: There are millions of publicly shared, human- or machine-authored agent skills for various tasks, domains, and harnesses, but current skill optimization approaches ignore this accumulated knowledge and instead optimize each new skill from scratch using costly agent rollouts. The authors aim to exploit this rich prior skill corpus to reduce rollout cost and improve performance, especially when adapting to new tasks or different harnesses.
AI.method: They introduce RASO, which treats existing skills as a retrievable knowledge base. For a target task under a specific harness, RASO retrieves relevant skills from this corpus and adapts them across domains and harnesses via Cross-Harness Adaptation. The process has two main stages: (1) Retrieval-Augmented Skill Initialization (RASI), which builds an initial natural-language skill using retrieved skills without needing any rollouts; and (2) Retrieval-Augmented Skill Update (RASU), which iteratively refines the skill, at each step using execution feedback to guide retrieval of additional skills and incorporating their knowledge into the current skill description.
AI.result: On four different agent benchmarks and using two underlying models, RASO systematically yields higher performance than baselines that either do not use retrieval or do not augment both the initialization and update stages with retrieval. The experiments indicate consistent gains across tasks and settings, demonstrating the effectiveness of using prior skill corpora in both initialization and iterative refinement.
AI.conclusion: Leveraging a large corpus of existing agent skills as external prior knowledge can significantly improve the efficiency and effectiveness of skill optimization. By combining retrieval-based initialization and feedback-guided retrieval-based updates, RASO provides a general framework that outperforms rollout-only or non-retrieval methods across multiple benchmarks, suggesting that retrieval-augmented skill optimization is a promising direction for building stronger, more reusable agent skills across diverse domains and harnesses.

title: UserProxyBench: Evaluating LLM User Simulators for Agent Benchmarks and Training
comment: 8 pages, 4 figures. Accepted to the Agentic AI Benchmarks and Applications for Enterprise Tasks Workshop (AABA4ET) at NeurIPS 2026
summary: Interactive agent benchmarks and multi-turn reinforcement learning increasingly place a second language model in the role of the user. This simulated user controls what information the agent receives and when, yet current benchmarks score only the agent and do not directly measure whether the user correctly executed its assigned role. We introduce UserProxyBench, an evaluation layer over the tau-bench family, and the User Fidelity Score (UFS), which measures adherence to the benchmark's private user instructions using task-grounded rubric criteria scored independently of agent success. Holding the agent fixed at GPT-5.5 and varying only the user proxy across 375 enterprise tasks changes mean task reward by 15.2 points, while 24.4% of successful episodes contain a user-specification violation. The dominant failure is premature disclosure: users provide information before it is requested. This behavior has little effect on task reward, yet among successful episodes it causes the agent to make 1.06 fewer tool calls on average, changing the interaction being evaluated while preserving the reward. Finally, across seven proxies we identify an empirical cost-fidelity frontier, enabling practitioners to select the least expensive simulator that satisfies a required fidelity level.

AI.tldr: They propose a benchmark layer and metric to evaluate how well simulated “user” LMs follow hidden user instructions in interactive agent benchmarks, showing that user quality significantly alters agent scores and interactions.
AI.motivation: In multi-turn RL and interactive agent benchmarks, a second LM often simulates the user, but current evaluations only grade the agent, assuming the user behaves correctly. This is problematic because the user simulator controls what information the agent sees and when, so user deviations from the intended behavior can distort benchmark scores, agent comparison, and research conclusions. There is a need for a way to directly measure and compare the fidelity of these user simulators.
AI.method: They build UserProxyBench as an evaluation layer on top of the tau-bench benchmark suite and define the User Fidelity Score (UFS). UFS is computed by checking the simulated user’s behavior against private user instructions using task-grounded rubric criteria that are independent of whether the agent “wins” the task. They run many episodes (375 enterprise tasks) with the agent held fixed (GPT-5.5) and systematically vary only the user proxy. They then analyze how different user simulators affect task reward, the frequency and type of user-specification violations (e.g., premature disclosure), the number of tool calls, and cost vs fidelity tradeoffs across seven user proxies, yielding an empirical cost–fidelity frontier.
AI.result: When only the user proxy is changed and the agent remains GPT-5.5, the mean task reward shifts by 15.2 points across the 375 tasks, showing that user choice strongly affects benchmark outcomes.
