Among episodes where the agent succeeds, 24.4% still contain at least one user-specification violation by the simulator. The main failure mode is premature disclosure of information before the agent asks for it. This early disclosure barely affects top-line task reward but reduces the number of tool calls by about 1.06 on average in successful runs, meaning the evaluated interaction pattern is changed without altering final scores. Across seven user simulators, they map out a cost–fidelity frontier that quantifies how much one must pay to reach a given level of user fidelity.
AI.conclusion: User simulators in interactive agent benchmarks cannot be treated as perfect or interchangeable; their fidelity meaningfully changes both benchmark scores and the qualitative interaction traces. The proposed UserProxyBench and User Fidelity Score provide a way to explicitly measure and compare how well simulated users follow their hidden instructions, separating this from agent success. Premature information disclosure is a common, under-penalized failure that alters tool usage patterns without hurting rewards, potentially misleading evaluations. By establishing an empirical cost–fidelity frontier over different user proxies, the work gives practitioners a principled way to pick the cheapest user simulator that still meets a desired fidelity threshold, leading to more trustworthy and reproducible agent evaluations.

title: Probability is Not Enough: Exploring and Counting Divergent Tokens for Reasoning Uncertainty Quantification in LLMs
comment: 25 pages, 16 figures, 8 tables. Under peer review
summary: As the chain-of-thought reasoning capabilities of large language models improve, evaluating and calibrating their reasoning confidence is becoming increasingly important for quantifying the uncertainty of their answers. Current methods for estimating the confidence of large language models are generally based on probabilities of selected key tokens, but the underlying mechanism remains unclear. Our pilot study finds that replacing selected token probabilities with coarse substitutes can also improve calibration, motivating us to further explore effective signals of model confidence. We introduce Divergent Token Confidence (DTC), a framework that estimates confidence by counting tokens at which two models strongly disagree during decoding. DTC identifies these divergent tokens using the Jensen-Shannon divergence between next-token distributions evaluated along the same reasoning trajectory. We find that their count is almost negatively associated with answer accuracy, thereby serving as a simple yet effective signal for uncertainty quantification. DTC supports both white-box and black-box evaluation using auxiliary models, without explicit training and affecting the generation process. Experiments across multiple model families and six mathematical benchmarks demonstrate improved calibration over probability-based and verbalized baselines. Under white-box evaluation, the count-only estimator achieves an average expected calibration error of 13.0%, compared with 32.7%-42.4% for standard full-sequence confidence methods. In black-box settings, it also improves calibration over the original verbalized scores. For example, mean expected calibration error falls from 32.1%-40.2% to 13.7%-16.3% on DeepSeek-V3.2. These findings provide new insights for improving reasoning uncertainty quantification in large language models. The code is released at https://github.com/szu-tera/DTC.git.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Divergent Token Confidence (DTC), a new way to estimate LLM reasoning confidence by counting tokens where two models’ next-token predictions strongly disagree, yielding much better calibration than standard probability-based methods, in both white-box and black-box settings.
AI.motivation: Existing uncertainty estimation for LLM reasoning usually relies on probabilities of selected key tokens or full-sequence likelihoods, but these approaches are poorly understood, often miscalibrated, and may not reflect true reasoning uncertainty. The authors observe that even coarse substitutes for token probabilities can improve calibration, suggesting that current confidence signals are suboptimal and motivating the search for alternative, more robust signals of confidence that better track answer correctness without retraining or altering generation.
AI.method: They introduce Divergent Token Confidence (DTC), which measures model uncertainty by counting the number of positions (tokens) along a chain-of-thought where two models’ next-token distributions strongly disagree. For a fixed reasoning trajectory, they compute Jensen–Shannon divergence between the next-token distributions of a main model and an auxiliary model at each step. Tokens whose JS divergence exceeds a threshold are labeled "divergent"; the total number of such tokens becomes a confidence proxy (fewer divergences imply higher confidence). DTC can be applied in white-box mode (using internal variants or checkpoints of the same model family) or in black-box mode (using external auxiliary models and verbalized scores), without training or modifying decoding.
AI.result: Across multiple LLM families and six math reasoning benchmarks, DTC-based confidence shows a strong negative correlation between the count of divergent tokens and answer accuracy, demonstrating that divergence count is a good uncertainty signal. In white-box evaluation, a simple count-only estimator achieves an average expected calibration error (ECE) of 13.0%, substantially outperforming standard full-sequence likelihood-based confidence methods, which yield ECEs of 32.7%–42.4%. In black-box settings, DTC also improves over models’ own verbalized confidence scores: for DeepSeek-V3.2, mean ECE drops from 32.1%–40.2% to 13.7%–16.3%. These gains hold consistently across evaluated models and benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that disagreement in next-token distributions between models along a shared reasoning trajectory provides a simple, interpretable, and effective signal for quantifying uncertainty in LLM reasoning. Counting divergent tokens, defined via Jensen–Shannon divergence thresholds, yields substantially better calibration than probability- or verbalization-based baselines, in both white- and black-box scenarios, without training or interfering with generation. This suggests that token-level distributional disagreement is a promising direction for improving confidence estimation and reliability of chain-of-thought reasoning in large language models.

title: Character Training for Risk-Averse Agents
summary: Risk aversion in resources could prevent misaligned AI agents from causing catastrophic harm. Misaligned but risk-averse agents would tend to favor safer strategies like making deals with humans over riskier strategies like rebelling. We train agents to be risk averse through character training, finding that persona traits provide a robust mechanism for instilling risk preferences. To do this, we construct a model constitution describing constant absolute risk aversion (CARA) over an agent's resources and instill it through on-policy distillation. Despite never seeing the benchmark's decision format during training, character-trained models are competitive with baselines trained directly on it, and generalise better than them out of distribution on two of our four models. We also modulate different aspects of the constitution, finding that token budget and model choice are the most influential aspect of character training to instill risk aversion. We conclude from these results that character training is a promising and scalable way to instil broad dispositions, which we can use to our advantage in mitigating risk from misaligned AI agents.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how to train AI agents to be risk-averse over their resources using character (persona) training, aiming to reduce the chance that misaligned agents take catastrophic, risky actions.
AI.motivation: Misaligned AI agents might take high-risk, high-reward strategies that could cause catastrophic harm. If such agents could be made risk-averse over their resources, they would prefer safer options—such as cooperating or negotiating with humans—over dangerous actions like rebellion. Developing scalable methods to embed such stable risk preferences in AI systems is therefore a potential safety mechanism for mitigating risks from misalignment.
AI.method: The authors design a model “constitution” encoding a constant absolute risk aversion (CARA) utility function over an agent’s resources. They then use character (persona) training and on-policy distillation to instill this constitution into language model agents: the models are trained to behave as if they have the specified risk-averse personality, rather than being trained directly on explicit decision-format benchmarks. They also systematically vary different aspects of the constitution and training setup—such as the token budget and model choice—to see how these factors affect the strength of induced risk aversion.
AI.result: Agents trained via character training to embody a risk-averse persona perform competitively with baseline agents that are trained directly on the benchmark’s decision format, even though the character-trained agents never see that format during training. Moreover, on two of four evaluated models, the character-trained agents generalize better out-of-distribution than the baselines. In ablation-style analyses, token budget and model choice emerge as the most important levers for successfully inducing risk-averse behavior, while other constitution details matter less.
AI.conclusion: Character (persona) training based on an explicit risk-averse constitution is an effective and scalable way to instill stable risk preferences—specifically, risk aversion over resources—into AI agents. Because such risk-averse dispositions can make misaligned agents more likely to choose safer, cooperative strategies over risky, catastrophic ones, this approach appears promising as a tool for AI risk mitigation and for shaping broad behavioral dispositions in advanced AI systems.

title: NeuronEye: Query-Guided Visual Concept Activation for Vision-Language Reasoning
summary: Current vision-language models (VLMs) encode visual information in dense hidden states where object identity, spatial layout, and local attributes are implicitly entangled rather than explicitly disentangled, limiting their ability to isolate and modulate the specific visual evidence required by a given language query. Inspired by sparse population coding and top-down modulation in biological vision, we introduce NeuronEye, a plug-in framework that constructs a sparse, concept-level neuron vocabulary from intermediate VLM representations and selectively activates query-relevant visual concepts during inference. NeuronEye decomposes vision-token states into an overcomplete sparse basis organized by concept-level clusters, uses the language query to activate relevant clusters and localize the patches where selected concepts are expressed, and injects the focused evidence back into vision tokens. A complementary suppression mechanism attenuates dominant perceptual directions to preserve weaker but relevant cues. All operations run in a single forward pass over a frozen VLM backbone. On Qwen2.5-VL-7B, NeuronEye raises CV-Bench overall accuracy by +3.1 with gains of +9.5 on Distance, and improves BLINK Multi-view by +8.3, with similar trends on LLaVA-1.6-7B. These results suggest that sparse neuron vocabularies can serve not only as post-hoc interpretability tools but also as active interfaces for concept-level visual reasoning.

AI.tldr: NeuronEye is a plug-in framework that builds a sparse, concept-level neuron vocabulary on top of existing vision-language models to focus and modulate query-relevant visual evidence, improving visual reasoning without retraining the backbone.
AI.motivation: Existing vision-language models encode visual information in dense, entangled hidden states where object identity, spatial layout, and attributes are not explicitly separated. This makes it difficult for the model to isolate and modulate the specific visual concepts needed to answer a given language query, limiting both interpretability and fine-grained control of reasoning.
AI.method: NeuronEye constructs an overcomplete sparse basis (a neuron vocabulary) from intermediate vision-token representations of a frozen VLM. It clusters neurons into concept-level groups, then at inference uses the language query to: (1) select relevant concept clusters, (2) localize image patches where these concepts are expressed, and (3) reinject the corresponding focused evidence into the vision tokens. Additionally, it applies a suppression mechanism to attenuate dominant, potentially distracting perceptual directions so that weaker but relevant cues are preserved. All this is done in a single forward pass without modifying or training the backbone VLM.
AI.result: Integrated with Qwen2.5-VL-7B, NeuronEye improves CV-Bench overall accuracy by +3.1 points, including +9.5 on the Distance subset, and boosts BLINK Multi-view performance by +8.3 points. Similar performance gains are observed when applied to LLaVA-1.6-7B, demonstrating the generality of the approach across different VLM backbones.
AI.conclusion: Sparse, concept-level neuron vocabularies can function as active interfaces for modulating visual evidence in VLMs, not just as post-hoc interpretability tools. By enabling query-conditioned activation and suppression of visual concepts in a single-pass, frozen-backbone setting, NeuronEye enhances concept-level visual reasoning and improves performance on challenging vision-language benchmarks.

title: Do LLM Agents Execute the Plans They Declare? From Planning-Mode Declaration to Pattern-Specific Execution
summary: Large language models (LLMs) enable agents to solve long-horizon tasks by generating a plan and then executing it in an environment. However, successful planning requires two distinct capabilities: selecting an appropriate plan for the task and executing it faithfully. Existing planner--executor systems can fail at either stage, while final task success alone cannot distinguish selection from execution failures. We therefore study the Plan Declaration--Execution Gap and introduce Planning-as-Routing, where an LLM declares one of four planning modes: Predefined, Sequential, Hierarchical, or Search, and a deterministic router dispatches the task to the corresponding pattern-specific executor. Across four benchmarks and three LLMs, we find three consistent patterns. First, generic Plan+ReAct often fails to preserve declared planning structure, especially for longer plans: across three benchmarks, only (22)--(45%) of trajectories preserve it, whereas pattern-specific executors enforce the intended structure. Second, planning-mode effectiveness varies across environments and models: Search performs best on ALFWorld, Hierarchical on SWE-bench, and the strongest pattern can vary across models within the same benchmark. Third, the largest gains come from execution: pattern-specific executors improve task success from (0.48) to (0.92) on ALFWorld and from (0.36) to (0.44) on SWE-bench Verified over Plan+ReAct. Current LLMs, however, do not reliably select the strongest mode for each task, although few-shot examples improve selection in some benchmark--model combinations. Overall, reliable agent planning requires both effective mode selection and faithful execution: routing substantially closes the execution gap, while task-specific mode selection remains open.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Planning-as-Routing, where an LLM first chooses a planning mode and a deterministic router sends the task to a matching executor, significantly improving faithful plan execution over generic Plan+ReAct agents.
AI.motivation: Planner–executor LLM agents often fail either in choosing a suitable plan or in executing their declared plan, but final task success cannot tell whether errors come from plan selection or from execution. The authors want to explicitly study and reduce the gap between what an LLM declares as its plan and what is actually executed, and to understand how different planning patterns work across tasks and models.
AI.method: They define the Plan Declaration–Execution Gap and propose Planning-as-Routing: the LLM first declares one of four planning modes—Predefined, Sequential, Hierarchical, or Search—then a deterministic router sends the task to a pattern-specific executor that enforces the corresponding structure. They evaluate this setup against a generic Plan+ReAct baseline on four benchmarks and three LLMs, measuring structural fidelity of execution and task success, and analyzing how different modes perform across environments and models as well as how well LLMs can select the best mode.
AI.result: They find that generic Plan+ReAct frequently violates its own declared plan structure, especially for long plans, with only about 22–45% of trajectories preserving the planning structure, whereas pattern-specific executors always enforce it. They also show that the best planning mode is task- and model-dependent: e.g., Search is best on ALFWorld, Hierarchical on SWE-bench, and the strongest mode can differ across LLMs on the same benchmark. Execution-focused improvements from pattern-specific executors are substantial, boosting success from 0.48 to 0.92 on ALFWorld and from 0.36 to 0.44 on SWE-bench Verified compared to Plan+ReAct. However, LLMs do not yet reliably pick the strongest mode, though few-shot prompting helps in some settings.
AI.conclusion: Separating plan selection from execution and routing tasks to pattern-specific executors largely closes the execution gap in LLM agents, demonstrating that enforcing planning structure yields major gains. Nonetheless, reliably choosing the best planning mode for each task remains unsolved, implying that future work should focus on improving task-aware mode selection in addition to execution mechanisms.

title: Stochastic World Models for Verifying Vision-Based Neural Feedback Systems
summary: Verifying a vision-based neural feedback system requires a model of the observations its controller acts upon. Such a model must capture the variation the sensor produces, while remaining tractable for closed-loop analysis. Generative adversarial networks (GANs) have served as perception surrogates, but they are large, reproduce complex scenes poorly, and are hard to verify. We explore stochastic world models as a richer class of perception surrogates. We train a world model with physically grounded latents, built from operations that standard verifiers bound. It reproduces held-out frames more faithfully than GAN surrogates with up to 130 times as many parameters. To verify these surrogates, we develop a procedure that combines falsification, adaptive refinement, symbolic, and backward analyses. On an emergency braking benchmark with a GAN surrogate, our procedure resolves the entire state space, 38% of which the state-of-the-art verifier left unresolved. On the RGB version of the benchmark, where no verification results have previously been reported, our procedure resolves over 80% of the state space with a world model surrogate.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes and evaluates stochastic world models as verifiable perception surrogates for vision-based neural feedback systems, showing they are more faithful and more amenable to closed-loop verification than GAN-based surrogates.
AI.motivation: Vision-based neural controllers depend on complex sensor observations, making formal verification hard because we need a tractable yet realistic model of the sensor’s output. Existing GAN-based perception surrogates are large, hard to verify, and often fail to reproduce complex scenes well, limiting closed-loop safety analysis. The authors aim to develop a perception surrogate that is both realistic and more amenable to formal verification, enabling stronger safety guarantees for systems such as emergency braking controllers.
AI.method: The authors construct stochastic world models with physically grounded latent variables and architectures composed of operations that standard neural network verifiers can bound. They train these models to reproduce camera frames and use them as perception surrogates. For verification, they devise a hybrid procedure combining falsification (searching for counterexamples), adaptive refinement of the surrogate or state space, and both symbolic and backward reachability analyses to reason about closed-loop behavior under the learned perception model. They compare their world model surrogates to large GAN-based surrogates on benchmarks, including an emergency braking scenario with both abstract and RGB observations.
AI.result: The trained world models reproduce held-out visual frames more faithfully than GAN-based surrogates, despite the GANs having up to 130× more parameters. Applying the proposed verification procedure to an existing emergency braking benchmark with a GAN surrogate, they are able to resolve the entire state space, including the 38% of states that a prior state-of-the-art verifier had left unresolved. On a more challenging RGB version of the benchmark, for which no prior verification results existed, their approach with a world model surrogate successfully resolves over 80% of the state space.
AI.conclusion: Stochastic world models with physically grounded latents offer a more faithful and verifiable alternative to GAN-based perception surrogates for vision-based control systems. By designing the model architecture with verification in mind and using a combined falsification–symbolic–backward analysis procedure, the authors substantially increase the portion of the state space that can be formally analyzed in safety-critical tasks like emergency braking, including more realistic RGB settings.

title: Thinking Before Thinking: Scaling Agentic Inference Through Meta-Reasoning
summary: As agents take on longer and more complex problems, controlling the execution becomes a task in its own right. Each step in the run brings new control choices, like which partial work to build on, whether to start fresh, or when to stop. We introduce agentic meta-reasoning, an inference-time harness that makes these choices an explicit and structured reasoning process. Workers carry out the task-level computation, while a controller consolidates what the run has established, explores next options, assesses what each option is worth under the remaining budget, and dispatches the chosen work with context drawn from persistent memory. Between decisions the controller carries only a compact account of the run rather than replaying its full history. Our baselines span production coding agents and research harnesses, together with a Direct Control Agent using the same workers and compute budget allowance. On ProgramBench, which tests long-horizon agentic capability through program reconstruction, meta-reasoning achieves 71.5% with GPT-5.5 against 58.0% for Codex; with Opus 4.8 it achieves 67.2% against 65.5% for Claude Code. On the other benchmarks, spanning abstract reasoning, multi-domain long-horizon reasoning, and proof generation, it gains between 3.6 and 4.2 points over direct control, averaged across three frontier models. It keeps improving over the tested budget ranges where direct control plateaus, though its overhead can hurt at small budgets. Artifact-graph analysis reveals more reuse of earlier work, higher coverage of correct solutions in most settings, and nonuniform gains in final selection. These results indicate that spending computation on structured control becomes more important as agents scale to longer runs.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an inference-time meta-reasoning controller for long-running AI agents and shows it improves performance and compute efficiency on long-horizon tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing agents tackling long, complex problems must implicitly manage control decisions like which partial solutions to extend, when to restart, and when to stop. Current approaches often use ad hoc or simple control logic, leading to inefficient compute use and plateauing performance as runs get longer. There is a need for a principled, explicit mechanism to control and structure agent execution, especially as tasks and horizons grow.
AI.method: The authors introduce agentic meta-reasoning: an inference-time harness that separates control from task-level work. Multiple worker agents perform the core task computations, while a controller: (1) consolidates the state of the run into a compact representation; (2) enumerates and explores next options (e.g., which partial work to refine or whether to start fresh); (3) evaluates the expected value of each option under a remaining compute/budget constraint; and (4) dispatches the chosen work, providing appropriate context from a persistent memory. The controller operates over a compressed account of the run rather than replaying full histories. They compare this to production coding agents, research harnesses, and a Direct Control Agent using identical workers and compute budgets, measuring performance across several benchmarks.
AI.result: On ProgramBench, a program reconstruction benchmark for long-horizon coding tasks, the meta-reasoning harness with GPT-5.5 achieves 71.5% versus a 58.0% baseline using Codex, and with Opus 4.8 achieves 67.2% versus 65.5% for Claude Code. Across other benchmarks—abstract reasoning, multi-domain long-horizon reasoning, and proof generation—the meta-reasoning controller yields average gains of 3.6–4.2 points over the Direct Control baseline across three state-of-the-art models. It continues to improve as the compute budget increases, unlike direct control which plateaus, though meta-reasoning incurs overhead that can reduce performance at small budgets. Artifact-graph analysis shows more reuse of intermediate work, higher coverage of correct partial solutions, and uneven but positive effects on final solution selection.
AI.conclusion: Explicit, structured meta-reasoning about control decisions at inference time can significantly enhance the effectiveness of long-horizon agents. By investing part of the compute budget into a controller that manages which partial solutions to pursue, how to reuse prior work, and when to stop, agents achieve better performance and scalability than direct, unstructured control. These findings suggest that as tasks grow longer and more complex, sophisticated control policies become a key lever for improving agent capability and compute efficiency.
